text: 10-year-old Kalicia is the firstborn of the Francis triplets. She is always the life of the party, with a quirky sense of humour and is the glue that holds the triplets together. She is very active and loves swimming, dancing, gymnastics, playing piano, painting and is a straight-A student. She is an absolute joy and positive influence with her infectious smile and positive attitude. In May 2022, Kalicia complained of pain in her right leg. The following day while getting into the vehicle to visit the doctor, her femur spontaneously broke. Initially, we thought it was a simple fracture from playing as she presented no symptoms prior to this. However, the tests, scans and biopsies discovered what turned out to be the life-changing diagnosis of osteosarcoma, an aggressive form of bone cancer. She continues to display remarkable positivity during her difficult journey, far greater than any 10year old can display. She has been a brave warrior through her hospital visits, treatment and chemotherapy. Help Kalicia win this fight against Osteosarcoma. Let's do all we can to support her and her family during this difficult time. All donations are appreciated to assist with her medical expenses during this battle. We would also appreciate it if you share and keep her and her family in your prayers as she continues this fight.

Hello! My name is Amy Rossiter Crist. I have a 45-year friendship with Angela Gay Kinkead which began at West Virginia Wesleyan College. To be specific, Angela Gay or "AG" as we called her, was our dorm floor RA. Our lively and rambunctious crew undoubtedly jump-started her leadership education! In early August, Angela Gay was diagnosed with Mantle Cell Lymphoma, a rarer and aggressive blood cancer. A series of quick actions led her to MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston TX, where she filled the very last spot in a 50-person, 2-year clinical trial. Her stellar medical care is essentially free. This Go Fund Me is organized to alleviate associated travel costs. For convenience and cost savings, Angela Gay temporarily lives near her mother and brother in Wichita, making her initial treatments more accessible. (She's stepped away from her professional duties for these first six weeks.) Currently, her weekly travel routine is a 12-hour, 615-mile drive from Wichita to Texas with "Super Brother" Sterling Dean along as sidekick and navigator. Once there, Angela Gay undergoes infusion and oral immunotherapies with follow-up consultations. After a two-night hotel stay near the medical center, the brother-sister duo hit the road back to Kansas. Gas, hotels and meals are out-of-pocket expenses. Each trip costs approximately $ 700. That's: *24 hours * 1230 miles * $700 Cycle 2, commencing this December, will require monthly treatments with flights from her Charleston, WV home to Houston. Cycle 3 begins in December '23 with bi-monthly treatments. One can easily understand the rigor and financial challenge of her treatment plan. Our dear friend reports positivity after the first three treatments! Please consider supporting this ongoing effort as she drives, flies and fights for her health. THANK YOU to you; Angela Gay's "deep and wide" circle... Please share. Blest Be The Tie That Binds Our Hearts in Christian Love

Katie Stembridge is a beloved sister, daughter, and friend. She was recently in a severe car accident that has left her in the ICU in critical condition. She suffered multiple spinal injuries, fractures to her pelvis and legs, burns, and damage to three out of four of the arteries that feed her brain. Katie’s family is with her as doctors at UAB are doing everything they can for her. What she and her loved ones are going through is incomprehensible. Many thanks to the kind people who have reached out offering prayers, love, and support. Our hearts hurt for the Stembridges right now, so this fund was created for those looking for a way to support Katie and her family tangibly at this time. The hope is to ease some additional stress, as they are facing a lengthy stay out of town in addition to medical bills. Any amount is greatly appreciated, along with continued love and prayers for Katie and those closest to her.

The 2022 IMA Push-Up Challenge On Sunday December 4th we’ll be holding our 15th annual Push-Up Challenge. Since its inception In 2008 as an effort to restock the Walpole Food Pantry during the Great Recession The Push-Up Challenge has helped dozens of local families experiencing hardship. This years Challenge takes on a special meaning as we’re doing our push-ups in support of Mr. Jackson. As many of you know Andre fell ill in May of 2022 and hasn’t been able to return to the school. What most don’t know is the severity of his illness. Andre contracted a dangerous infection that did not respond well to antibiotics. Were it not for the fast action of some concerned Impact families and the great care he received at Mass General he wouldn’t be here today. The infection spread through his body resulting in numerous surgeries to remove affected areas. He’s healing now but the results of the procedures will take months to heal and will affect his ability to live without assistance. As you know, Mr. Jackson is as private as he is kind and being the recipient of any help from others is the last place he ever intended to be. We don’t know exactly what the future holds or what the long-term needs will be, we only know for sure that some assistance will make a big difference in the near future. Andre always poured himself into the Push-Up Challenge. He was always overwhelmed by the amount of effort and kindness he saw from our students. The helpfulness the funds provided were immeasurable. Many people have asked me over the last six months what they could do for Andre. Not having an answer or a way to show our appreciation for all he means to us has been frustrating. If you would like to help, please consider: • Joining the Push-Up Challenge: Do 10 minutes or a full day of Push-Ups for someone who can’t. • Sponsor one of our Amazing Students: 1 penny per Push-Up is all it takes. • Contribute to the IMA Push-Up Challenge GoFundMe. • Spread the word, he’s made an Impact on a lot of people the last 20 years. • Write him a note and drop it off at the School. The highlight of his day is hearing how all his friends and students are doing while he’s away. Thank you for your time and support, and thank you for being part of Impact. Patrick Lynch

On 12/10/22, Aerodrome Ice Skating Complex is proud to bring back the 3v3 Phoenix Cup Charity Classic to help raise money for families affected by cancer. This year, we are supporting the Ortiz family, and their son Dylan. Let's meet Dylan Ortiz! Dylan is a 6 year old boy and expert of all things Captain America, Godzilla, and Teen Titans, among many other things. He is the #1 big brother to his 4 year old little brother, Alex, and he has taught him everything he knows. He looks up to both his dad, a sheriff deputy with the Montgomery County Sheriff’s Office, and his mom, who works for the Conroe Parole Office. He knows they love him very much and they are proud of his bravery during the journey he has ahead of him. In September 2022, Dylan was diagnosed with Leukemia and has a long battle to take on. But like Captain America, he is ready for whatever cancer may bring his way. We are so happy to have Dylan be a part of our Phoenix Cup and Houston Ice Hockey family. Thank you for supporting Dylan and his family during this difficult time. The funds raised by our event will go directly to Dylan's family to help support them during the struggles that come with being affected by cancer. Thank you.

The hardest walks lead to the best destination, and for me, that would be home. However, most of you know by now that I’ve lost my ability to walk due to 6 compound back fractures that cannot be operated on at this time. I was already seriously compromised by medical issues that I have openly shared on Facebook with all of you so you could lift me up in prayer, send good karma, positive vibes, gifs or memes that made me laugh. Your love, support and standing in the gap with me and for me have helped get me through these LONG hospital stays. I’ve been working hard in rehab to get better and stronger so I can go home. I am on the road to recovery and God is good and hears my prayers. To go home requires a lot of medical supplies and equipment. I have a lot of the supplies because we had to fit our house for them when Alex suffered his anoxic brain trauma but I’m still in need of several things.There are 26 stairs to get into my house and on the main level. I’ve only been able to do 4 stairs in rehab and it puts a lot of pressure on my spine so my treatment team suggested we sell our house, add to our downstairs so there is an extra bedroom and a kitchenette or get a chair lift and an electric power lift chair recliner to have full access to the main level of our house.Needless to say, we were overwhelmed by those choices as they all came with large financial commitments (which we had no idea how we would meet at this time). The amount of grief and the weight of the decisions either way feels crushing.Then several of you from my army and Prayer Warriors said you would like to help and others probably would too so I should set up a fundraiser. Since the choices in front of me are heavy and harder than I imagined and I have been reminded that I’m not alone, I have set up this fundraiser and I haven’t done it lightly and without a lot of thought, but we do need help and this is a great idea.If you can help in any way, we would greatly appreciate it. If you prefer to go through Venmo, PayPal or CashApp, just let me know and I can send you the information.As always, I love y’all BIG.Healing or Heaven~Paige~

Maggie suffered a spinal stroke on Saturday, October 29, 2022. She is a 21 year old nursing student originally from San Diego, California, going to school at Houston Christian University in Houston, Texas. While in Houston, she also worked as a part time nanny for three families to help pay for school as well as her living expenses. The spinal stroke has left her with paralysis in her legs. She is currently in rehab learning how to walk again but also how to live with her current disability. Full recovery is unknown but she is determined, strong and working very hard at getting stronger every day. She has feeling in her hips and toes at this point and time. I am Maggie's mom, Rebecca. Her dad and I live in Florida. We are here with her in Houston to hopefully help her transition from rehab back to her apartment. In doing so, I am realizing all she will need at home to make her transition possible. The insurance will cover a basic wheelchair. She will need a transfer shower chair, removable shower head, and toilet riser/safety rails just to name a few. I have also been doing research on a better wheelchair that will make getting around easier for a young active person like Maggie. Those types of wheelchairs cost anywhere from $1,000 to $1,800. I have had a lot of people reach out and ask how they can help. A go fund me was also suggested to me early on but I hesitated because I'm not very good at asking for help. But this is not about me! This is for our girl. She is going to need as much help as she can get. From the cost of medical bills she hasn't seen yet, the cost of adding equipment she never imagined she would need, to the loss of her income her jobs provided that she will not be able to continue at this time. If you can help in any way, I know she will greatly appreciate it. This will be linked directly to her and she will receive every dime donated. She's a lot like me and would never ask for help but I know this would make her new life a lot easier! I will also post here any and all progress that is made. I thank you from the bottom of my heart for your prayers for her continued healing and for your generosity to help her concentrate on her recovery.

Hello, my name is Cheryl Thomas, and I am fundraising for Taylor Ross. Taylor Ross is an experienced registered nurse for intensive care, Telemetry, and Neurology Unit patients and a single mother to her 9-year-old son. On May 26, 2021, Taylor fell victim to an Ischemic Stroke at 30 years old. On the evening of May 25th, Taylor completed a twelve-hour shift as an ICU nurse. Once she arrived home, she prepared her son for school, dropped him off at 7:00 am, and immediately returned home. She planned to begin her regular after-work routine of showering, eating breakfast, and taking a nap. Taylor would typically shower immediately after work due to COVID. Taylor remembers feeling nauseated, thinking she may have food poisoning from something that was eaten earlier. The last thing she remembers is preparing to take a shower. Taylor went into the bathroom, collapsed, and fell unconscious. She was unsure how long she had been out. Taylor faintly remembers her phone ringing and her friend on the other line stating that her speech was jumbled. The friend immediately called Taylor’s mother and said she needed to go and check on her because she did not sound well, she was confused, and something was wrong with her speech. Taylor’s mother called her immediately. She could tell something was very bad, then called 911 and rushed to the house to check on her. Taylor’s mother, the ambulance, and the fire trucks arrived simultaneously. They found her on the bathroom floor, and it was apparent she had suffered a stroke. Looking back at the timeframe, Taylor feels the stroke occurred around 9:30 – 10:00 am after her mother left for work. She was home for approximately four hours alone, struggling before help arrived. Taylor was rushed to the nearest hospital, which also happened to be where she worked. Taylor was a patient now, with her ICU co-workers taking care of her. Once Taylor was well enough, she transferred to an inpatient acute rehabilitation center. Her total stay was nine weeks before she was able to return home. Taylor is on the road to recovery, but it has been challenging. She has substantial medical bills exceeding $80,000 and is now in a custody battle for her son since her stroke. Taylor has had custody of her son since birth. At the time of her stroke, he was seven in a half. She is his primary caretaker and provides for all his financial expenses. Initially, she could not talk or walk after her stroke and had lost complete function of the right side of her body. She has regained the ability to speak and can now speak fluently and articulately. She has accomplished walking without assistance after eight months of therapy and has no cognitive impairment. Unfortunately, the stroke has left her with limited use of her right arm and hand. She continues in ongoing physical therapy. Although the road has been difficult, Taylor’s challenge is far from over. She hopes to return to work as an RN Case Manager, Telephonic RN, Utilization Review RN, Triage RN, etc. Taylor would love to have a spinner knob for her steering wheel and a left-foot accelerator. We hope to raise $100,000.00 to assist with medical and legal expenses.

Merci merci merci!! ********************************************** Hallo, mein Name ist Petra und ich sammle Spenden für einen chirurgischen Eingriff, den mein Bruder Harvey dringend benötigt. Ich möchte meinem mutigen Bruder helfen, der nicht mehr alleine weiterkämpfen kann. Der Eingriff wird nicht von seiner Krankenkasse übernommen. Deshalb bin ich sicher, dass wir alle zusammenkommen und alle notwendigen Mittel für seine Genesung aufbringen können. Nach einem Zittern und einer Schwäche in seiner linken Hand wurde bei Harvey im Januar 2018 ein Glioblastoma multiforme Hirntumor im Stadium 4 diagnostiziert. Stellen Sie sich vor, Sie sind ein werdender Vater und hören eine so knochentrockene Diagnose mit einer Überlebensrate von ein paar Monaten. Er war am Boden zerstört, aber entschlossen, es zu überwinden. Er hat alle Widrigkeiten besiegt und in diesen vier Jahren eine invasive Operation zur Entfernung des Gehirntumors, Runden von Chemotherapie und Strahlentherapie hinter sich, die er zweimal hatte (zuletzt im Oktober dieses Jahres). Er hat an experimentellen Behandlungen in ganz Europa teilgenommen und dabei geholfen, die Forschung zu diesem verheerenden Krebs zu unterstützen, damit andere Menschen Hoffnung auf eine Behandlung haben. Er arbeitete auch Vollzeit und begann, seine kleine Familie großzuziehen, und freute sich darauf, 5 Jahre lang krebsfrei zu sein. Covid-Jahre kamen und obwohl er eine extrem anfällige Immunität hatte, trug er viel zu dem Unternehmen bei, für das er arbeitete, und ihre kleine Familie begrüßte im August letzten Jahres ein zweites kleines Mädchen. Er war glücklich und hoffte auf eine schöne Zukunft. Regelmäßige MRT-Scans zeigten keine Anzeichen des Tumors und er erlangte seine ganze Kraft zurück. Auf einem Scan im September 2021 tauchte erneut ein weißer Fleck auf, der zu einem schnellen Wachstum zu einem 7-Zentimeter-Tumor führte, der seine Gesundheit und Mobilität rapide verschlechterte. Zweitens war eine gefährlichere Strahlentherapie erforderlich. Er hat alle vierzehn seiner Termine tapfer überstanden, wissend, dass dies seine geistige Gesundheit und seine körperlichen Fähigkeiten beeinträchtigen wird, in der Hoffnung, den Tumor wieder schrumpfen zu lassen. Aufgrund der Strahlung und der Größe des Tumors bekam er Anfälle und Schwierigkeiten, die linke Körperseite zu bewegen. Er tat weiterhin alles, um seine Mobilität zu erhalten, aber die Auswirkungen wurden zu groß, um damit fertig zu werden. Text in Nederlands -- Deutsch -- English Nederlands In januari 2016 heb ik uitvallen van mijn spraak en ook mijn rechter hand/arm gehad. De huisarts en ook de neuroloog hielden het in eerste instantie op stress (wij waren net met een nieuw project gestart op het werk), maar ik was er zeker van dat stress niet de oorzaak was. Na veel aandringen mocht ik dan voor het eerst in mijn leven in een MRI. De uitslag kreeg ik op 19 februari 2016 te horen – jij hebt MS! Mijn hele wereld stortte op dat moment in. Ik wist nog niets over MS, alleen dat ik ooit in een rolstoel terecht zou komen. Zover is het gelukkig nog niet. Ik kreeg medicatie voorgeschreven om de MS te remmen. Helaas wordt door Neurologen in Nederland niet gesproken over dat er ook een optie is om de MS te stoppen. Dit is op dit moment nog geen optie in Nederland wellicht dat dit in de toekomst nog verandert maar dit zal dan voor mij te laat komen. De eerste medicatie had erg vervelende bijwerkingen zoals haaruitval, jeuk over het hele lichaam en een ongelooflijke vermoeidheid. Ik voelde me net een zombie, geen puf om wat dan ook te doen. Daarna met een andere tweede medicatie die beter doet wat verwacht mag worden en met minder bijwerkingen is het voor mij veel verdraagzamer. Maar helaas wordt mijn MS steeds zichtbaarder. Auto rijden doe ik nog maar beperkt, fietsen achter iemand aan, niet alleen, lang lopen gaat alleen nog met stokken (of andere steun) en werken gaat ook maar halve dagen omdat dan mijn ogen te erg achteruit gaan. Je wordt er onzeker van. Wat kun je nog en hoe lang? Ik heb vroeger actief paard gereden, eerst endurance, daarna, toen dat niet meer ging, dressuur en springen in de bak, toen springen niet meer ging dressuur en uiteindelijk heb ik mijn paard met veel pijn in mijn hart moeten verkopen. Dan probeer je een nieuwe sport te zoeken, maar dat is niet zo makkelijk. Geen snelle sport, want de signalen komen vertraagd in mijn hersenen aan, geen sport met veel lopen of rennen, want ik kan niet op mijn benen vertrouwen. Inmiddels ben ik aan het fitnessen onder begeleiding van een fysio. Lekker veilig, en het helpt met de coördinatie van mijn benen. HSCT is een stamceltransplantatie en kan MS STOPPEN. Hierbij wordt het bestaande immuunsysteem door middel van chemotherapie “vernietigt”. Ondertussen door eigen stamcellen eerst te oogsten en daarna terug te plaatsen wordt het hele immuunsysteem uiteindelijk weer helemaal opnieuw opgebouwd. Het immuunsysteem is dan weer gezond en valt eigen zenuwcellen dan niet meer aan. De behandeling is klinisch bewezen en goedgekeurd, maar wordt in Nederland helaas niet toegepast bij MS patiënten en ook niet vergoed. Voor de therapie moet je nu nog naar het buitenland. Helaas niet om de hoek, de opties zijn Moscow, Mexico, India of Israël. Na veel gelezen te hebben en de politieke situatie in acht nemend is mijn keuze op Mexico gevallen. Hier kun je meer info vinden over Stamceltransplantatie <URL> De behandeling is overal redelijk vergelijkbaar. Het traject duurt 4 weken. In deze 4 weken wordt je opgenomen in de kliniek in Puebla, Mexico, samen met een “caretaker”. Ik hoop dat mijn man mee kan gaan. Het traject begint met een uitgebreid onderzoek om vast te stellen dat je verder geen contra-indicaties hebt. Dan worden de stamcellen “geoogst” en ingevroren. Dan volgt chemotherapie om het immuunsysteem te vernietigen. Daarna worden de eerder geoogste stamcellen weer geïnjecteerd zodat er een nieuw immuunsysteem wordt opgebouwd. Het hele traject duurt 4 weken en heeft in mijn “categorie” van MS (ik heb RRMS) een slagingspercentage van boven de 80% Vind ik het eng? Ja! Wil ik het doen? Jazeker. Ik ben allang blij als de MS op dit niveau gestopt wordt. Er zijn kansen dat mijn beperkingen verminderd worden. Dat zou mooi zijn, maar dat is niet het hoofddoel. Het hoofddoel is het stoppen van de MS en jullie kunnen erbij helpen. De therapie is kostbaar, zo’n 60.000 Euro en die hebben wij helaas niet op de plank liggen. Deutsch Im Januar 2016 hatte ich Sprachausfälle und auch meine rechte Hand/Armkonnte ich nicht immer benutzen. Der Hausarzt und auch der Neurologe dachten zunächst, es sei Stress (wir waren gerade mit einem neuen Projekt auf der Arbeit gestartet), aber ich war mir 100% sicher, dass Stress nicht die Ursache war. Nach langem Drängen durfte ich mich zum ersten Mal in meinem Leben einem MRT unterziehen. Ich habe die Ergebnisse am 19. Februar 2016 erhalten – Sie haben MS! Meine ganze Welt brach in diesem Moment zusammen. Ich wusste noch nichts über MS, nur dass ich eines Tages im Rollstuhl landen würde. So weit ist es zum Glück noch nicht! Mir wurden Medikamente verschrieben, um die MS zu verzögern. Leider sprechen Neurologen in den Niederlanden nicht darüber, dass es auch eine Möglichkeit gibt, die MS zu stoppen. Diese Behandlung ist derzeit in den Niederlanden nicht möglich, vielleicht ändert sich dies in Zukunft, aber für mich wird es zu spät sein. Das erste Medikament hatte sehr unangenehme Nebenwirkungen wie Haarausfall, Juckreiz am ganzen Körper und unglaubliche Müdigkeit. Ich fühlte mich wie ein Zombie, zu nichts in der Stimmung. Das zweite Medikament, das besser tut, was zu erwarten ist, und mit weniger Nebenwirkungen ist für mich viel verträglicher. Aber leider wird meine MS immer sichtbarer. Ich fahre nur noch eingeschränkt Auto, beim Radfahren fahre ich am liebsten hinter jemandem her, nicht alleine, langes Gehen ist nur mit Stöcken (oder anderen Hilfsmitteln) möglich und Arbeiten ist nur halbtags möglich, weil dann meine Augen zu stark verschlechtern. Es macht dich unsicher. Was kann ich noch und wie lange? Früher habe ich aktief geritten, erst Endurance (lange Abstands/Ritte), dann, als das nicht mehr ging, Dressur und Springen in der Halle. Dann war Springen keine Option mehr (wegen der Sicht) und schließlich musste ich mein Pferd verkaufen weil ich nicht wusste an welchen Tagen ich genug Kraft hatte um sie Abends zu versorgen und zu reiten. Dann versucht man, einen Sport zu finden, aber das ist nicht so einfach. Kein schneller Sport, weil die Signale verzögert in meinem Gehirn ankommen, kein Sport mit viel Gehen oder Laufen, weil ich mich nicht auf meine Beine verlassen kann. Ich trainiere jetzt unter Anleitung eines Physiotherapeuten. Sicher in der Sportschule, und es hilft bei der Koordination meiner Beine. HSCT ist eine Stammzelltransplantation und kann MS STOPPEN. Erst werden die eigenen Stammzellen über das Blut entnommen. Mittels einer Chemotherapie wird dann das vorhandene Immunsystem „zerstört”. Danach werden die zuvor gewonnenen eigen Stammzellen wieder eingebracht. Der Körper baut das Immunsystem wird wieder auf, dieses ist dann wieder gesund und greift die eigenen Nervenzellen nicht mehr an. Die Behandlung ist klinisch erprobt und zugelassen, wird aber leider in den Niederlanden bei MS-Patienten nicht angewendet und auch nicht erstattet. Für die Therapie muss man jetzt noch ins Ausland. Leider nicht um die Ecke, die Optionen sind Moskau, Mexiko, Indien oder Israel. Nachdem ich viel gelesen und die politische Situation berücksichtigt hatte, fiel meine Wahl auf Mexiko. Die Behandlung ist überall ziemlich ähnlich. Der Prozess dauert 4 Wochen. Während dieser 4 Wochen werde ich zusammen mit einem „Versorger“ in der Klinik in Puebla, Mexiko aufgenommen. Ich hoffe, mein Mann kann mitkommen. Der Prozess beginnt mit einer ausführlichen Untersuchung, um festzustellen, dass keine Kontraindikationen vorliegen. Dann werden die Stammzellen „geerntet“ und eingefroren. Dann folgt eine Chemotherapie, um das Immunsystem zu zerstören. Danach werden die zuvor geernteten Stammzellen erneut injiziert, damit ein neues Immunsystem aufgebaut wird. Der gesamte Prozess dauert 4 Wochen und hat eine Erfolgsquote von über 80% in meiner „Kategorie“ MS (ich habe RRMS). Finde ich es spannend? Ja! Will ich es trotzdem tun>? Na und ob! Ich würde mich freuen, wenn MS auf diesem Niveau gestoppt wird. Es besteht die Möglichkeit, dass meine Einschränkungen reduziert werden. Das wäre schön, aber das ist nicht das Hauptziel. Das Hauptziel ist es, die MS zu stoppen, und ihr könnt dabei helfen. Die Therapie ist teuer, ca. 60.000 Euro und leider haben wir die nicht im Sparstrumpf. English In January 2016 I lost my ability tos speak correctly and also lost my right hand/arm coordination. The GP and also the neurologist initially thought it was stress (we had just started a new project at work), but I was sure that the problems were not stress related. After much insistence, I was allowed to undergo an MRI for the first time in my life. I got the results on February 19, 2016 – you have MS! My whole world collapsed at that moment. I didn't know anything about MS yet, only that one day I would end up in a wheelchair. Fortunately, it's not that bad yet. I was prescribed medication to inhibit the MS. Unfortunately, neurologists in the Netherlands do not talk about the fact that there is also an option to stop the MS. This is not an option in the Netherlands at the moment, maybe this will be in the future, but then will be too late for me. The first medication had very unpleasant side effects such as hair loss, itching all over the body and unbelievable tiredness. I felt like a zombie, not in the mood to do anything. Then with another medication, which better meets the expectaionand with fewer side effects it is much more tolerable for me. But unfortunately my MS is becoming more and more visible. I only drive a car to a limited extent, cycle after someone, not alone, long walking is only possible with sticks (or other support) and working is only possible for half days because then my sight deteriorates too much. It makes you insecure. What can you still do and for how long? I used to actively ride horses, first endurance, then, when that was no longer possible, dressage and jumping in the arena, then jumping was no longer an option due to my sight, dressage and eventually I had to sell my horse with a lot of pain in my heart. Then you try to find a new sport, but that is not easy. Not a fast sport, because the signals arrive in my brain with a delay, not a sport with a lot of walking or running, because I can't rely on my legs. I am now working out under the guidance of a physiotherapist. Nice and safe, and it helps with the coordination of my legs. HSCT is a stem cell transplant and can STOP MS. The existing immune system is "destroyed" by means of chemotherapy. Meanwhile, by first harvesting your own stem cells and then placing them back, the entire immune system is eventually rebuilt from scratch. The immune system is then healthy again and no longer attacks its own nerve cells. The treatment is clinically proven and approved, but is unfortunately not used in the Netherlands for MS patients nor is it reimbursed You still have to go abroad for the therapy. Unfortunately not around the corner, the options are Moscow, Mexico, India or Israel. After reading a lot and taking into account the political situation, I chose Mexico. Here you can find more information about Stem Cell Transplantation <URL> The treatment is quite similar everywhere. The process takes 4 weeks. During these 4 weeks you will be admitted to the clinic in Puebla, Mexico, together with a “caretaker”. I hope my husband can come with me. The process starts with an extensive examination to determine that you have no further contraindications. Then the stem cells are “harvested” and frozen. Then follows chemotherapy to destroy the immune system. The previously harvested stem cells are then injected again so that a new immune system is built up. The entire process takes 4 weeks and has a success rate of above 80% in my “category” of MS (I have RRMS). Do I find it scary? Yes! Do I want to do it? Yes, of course. I'll be happy if MS is stopped at this level. There are chances that my limitations will be reduced. That would be nice, but that's not the main goal. The main goal is to stop the MS and you can help. The therapy is expensive, about 60,000 Euros and unfortunately we do not have it on the shelf. Nicola

Hi hi, my name is Cheryl and this Go Fund Me is for My daughter Tracy. Tracy is facing a lifesaving operation for a rare cancer. She lives in Fort Davis. The surgery will be in San Antonio. She is in need of funds for travel and expenses not covered by her Medicaid. I will let her explain in her own words... I have a date! FINALLY!! After 7 months!!! Allow me to fill you in on the details, because this is one of the most important dates of my life: 8 months ago, I noticed a mass that was growing where my left breast used to be before I had the radical mastectomy (breast removal) to treat the cancer I was diagnosed with when I was 28 and Liam was 5. Since we now live in West Texas and I am on federally funded health insurance (Texas Medicaid), it was impossible to get an accurate diagnosis from a competent oncologist here. After months of watching and feeling this hard mass grow meanwhile having to be my own health advocate, I managed to get the biopsy material sent off to Mayo Clinic with minimal cooperation from either the medical professionals or my insurance company. Mayo Clinic confirmed that this is a rare form of bone cancer, chondosarcoma. It is rapidly growing in a very serious location - my ribcage - pushing against my lungs and quite possibly on a heart valve causing my blood pressure and heart rate to sky rocket. I was referred to both a lifesaving thoracic surgeon as well as a fantastic oncologist in San Antonio, as the only treatment of this kind of cancer is surgical removal of the tumor with very wide margins. In other words, it doesn’t respond to chemo or radiation, and I will have thoracic (chest) surgery with a minimal of SIX RIBS REMOVED. And subsequent rebuilding of my chest cavity. My surgery date is November 30th, 7:30 AM at University Hospital in San Antonio. I cannot express how relieved I am to get help. Having said all that technical medical stuff, I would like to open up a little more. The last cancer that I battled, I survived, thank God... but I neglected my emotional wellbeing. I was so very happy to have survived and overcome the physical effects of cancer, but I was blind-sighted by the emotional effects that cancer would have. I didn’t open myself up to the love and healing that the people that care about me offered, because “I am(was) strong enough to do it all alone and no one else needed to suffer from my cancer.” I was so private that I demanded to be alone throughout my numerous oncologist visits, taking it all on by myself. Well, little did I know, the opposite happened. Neglecting my emotional wellbeing, and taking it all on alone, caused more pain and suffering for me and my loved ones than I could have ever imagined. And when I did absolutely HAVE to ask for help, I would feel horrible because for whatever reason, I didn’t feel like I truly deserved it. I suffered intense detrimental emotional repercussions, spiraling me into a self consuming addiction that compromised every thing that I survived cancer for, every thing that I lived for. After a tremendous amount of work, I have since recovered from addiction and isolation and I am dedicated to truly living and truly loving. Now, as I write this, I will not underestimate the healing power of love. And the only place where love can live is where vulnerability and openness is found. And I also know that asking for help doesn’t make me weak, or unable to battle this ugly disease. Asking for help allows those who love me (and my family) a chance to be a part of our healing. Asking for help means that I am strong enough to know I cannot do this alone - and that me and my family don’t have to carry this burden alone. There are beautiful and generous people all around us that want to help and in helping us, it gives them the opportunity to be more of the loving people that they already are. So thank YOU for the support, thank YOU for the love, and thank YOU for the prayers, thank YOU for taking the time to read this. I can say now with my whole heart, no matter the outcome, that I have truly loved in my life and I have allowed others to love me. Love heals all, love transcends all, and love is worth it all.

He was so nice and instantly invited me to stay with him through the storm, but first, we had to help his friend protect his new home. When Andres was up on the ladder, I really saw him for the first time. He wasn't just a Miami party guy; he was a kind, caring man who always lends a helping hand. I knew I could build a life with him. Helpfulness is Andres' most fundamental character trait. Just about every weekend, he lends a tool or assistance to a neighbor. When we had kids, I never had to coax him into changing a diaper or taking care of them. He always just shows up, glad to be of service. I didn't know him for the first 40 years of his life, but I believe he has always been this way. When our son (a spitting image of his father) was a toddler, he would often sigh and leave his toys to help me when he noticed I was cleaning. It was so adorable because he was having fun playing, and I didn't ask him to stop, but there was a deep internal motivation inside of him, prompting him to be helpful. It was a part of his essential nature, and I have no doubt he inherited that from Andres. I imagine Andres has been helping others since he learned how to walk. Now, I am reaching out in the hopes that others can help him. Battling cancer is hard enough. Working through treatment is pushing the boundary of what is possible. Worrying about how to pay for it all makes this just too much. It weighs heavily on his mind, and he needs that burden lifted. I understand that everyone is in a financial pinch right now. Inflation is painful and the holidays are expensive. I'm asking for you to please help in any way that you can, even if it's just a few dollars. Even small donations can add up to a big relief. We just need a bridge to get us to the other side. I'm praying that our community will help us build that bridge. The money that we raise will go directly towards our monthly expenses during Andres' treatment and our share of his medical bills. If there is enough, we will put a bit towards grocery delivery. My disability makes grocery shopping an extremely difficult task, so for the last couple of years, Andres has done it. Additionally, if local friends are able to help with shopping, please let me know. This is going to be a hard Christmas for us. There is no way around that fact. Andres will be at his very worst on December 25th. It is hard to see how we will get to the other side of this, although I know we will. Even though this Christmas won't be particularly jolly, we have the hope that we will receive the precious gift of life-saving treatment for Andres. That's something to hold on to. Anything you can do to help make this a bit easier will be deeply appreciated.

FDNY EMT Ashley Diaz is a 5-year veteran for the FDNY, as well as, a mother to her four-year-old son. On September 15th, 2022, she was the victim of a senseless act. With just minutes to live, this woman who had dedicated her life to serve others was at the mercy of the response and service of her peers. Due to the remarkable response of the NYPD and the FDNY EMTs she was being treated within 2 minutes. Even in this critical traumatic moment, Ashley remained conscious and leaned on her training, literally instructing the first responding officers of her needs in order to keep her alive. The most critical treatment being the proper application of a tourniquet. Her only concern was to live another day for her son. The result was a week in a medically induced coma, an amputated right leg, missing teeth, multiple fractures, ongoing surgeries and numerous lacerations and abrasions across her face and body. Ashley was also informed that she can no longer work the field as an EMT. She was looking forward to starting her paramedic training in the near future, helping her to eventually accomplish her dream of being a RN. Today even though she’s still remains hospitalized , Ashley is in good spirits. With the overwhelming support from family and friends she is able to remain positive about the situation. After countless surgeries, she will be a candidate for prosthetics and will be able to watch more Marvel movies with her son which they both enjoy so much. Though grateful to live another day, her previous operations, and future treatments have been costly. Unfortunately, this is the beginning of a long, strenuous journey. She has to undergo more surgeries, months of physical therapy to ambulate on a prosthetic, and adjust her home and lifestyle to handicap accessible. FDNY EMT Diaz has served New York City for the past five years, solely Coney Island, Brooklyn; giving compassionate care to thousands of lives over the years. Outside of work, she is an even better friend, the best mother, loving daughter and sister. It would mean the world if you could donate to help her ease the burden of the financial deficit created by current and future medical expenses, a prosthetic, child care for her son, and retrofitting her home to fit her needs. Thank you for taking the time to read this message. Please cherish your loved ones each and everyday. ASHLEY STRONG!

Hi, my name is Jeremy and my mother, Kirsten, aka Kiki, developed Triple Negative Breast Cancer in 2018. For those who may not know, TNBC (Triple Negative Breast Cancer)is considered a more aggressive type of breast cancer, mainly because fewer targeted medicines treat TNBC. Studies have shown that TNBC is more likely to spread beyond the breast and more likely to recur (come back) after treatment. That being said, when patients have a complete response to therapy beyond five years, they have longer periods of NED (no evidence of disease) which means that the cost of treatment is especially high. Please consider helping my mother with her mounting medical bills and getting her desperately needed treatment.

To Mallory's cherished community, It is with heavy but full hearts that we find ourselves here in support of our beloved Mallory. Her courage and strength shine through in the beautiful letter she has written you all below. Thank you for your generosity, support, and love that keep us all fighting alongside our MalMal. Mallory here. In my mind, I am a young, healthy, happy newlywed who is thriving in her career, planning a family and living the beautiful life I dreamed of as a kid. When I look in the mirror and see someone else, puffy, pale, sunken and sad, I am heartbroken as the nightmare of my reality hangs over me. I knew that I had a 30% recurrence rate within the first three years of being diagnosed with breast cancer, but never did I think that it would happen in this first year, nor that I would be metastatic. I thought I was done and I was healing. I was back to work, exercising, brushing my hair! Using mascara! The terminal diagnosis doesn't stop being shocking. It doesn't stop being terrifying and it continues to enrage me. What makes me the most mad is that I like hard work. I need a challenge, I thrive on intensity but this is not what I wanted to use my energy or my time for. I wanted to run my own successful business, support my husband, be a mom. It wasn't something I actively thought about, but I wanted to live a long, limitless life. And I still do. But everything now is a conscious choice to both extend my time here beyond the scary statistics, and to have that time be filled with my beloved people. Not for a moment since my diagnosis one year ago have Chris and I ever been on our own. Thank you. So, here we go again, asking our community to help us build strength, hope and ease for this (hopefully) very long road. We have the opportunity to come together to care for our dear friends whose story could have unfolded for any of us. On July 4, 2022, Damon and Lori’s lives forever changed. After several weeks of increasingly severe migraines and weakness, Lori drove herself to the ER seeking relief. The news was not good. Devastatingly, the MRI revealed 2 brain tumors, spurring the medical team to immediately airlift Lori to Louisville’s Norton Hospital for further evaluation and treatment. The findings: a Grade IV Glioblastoma (GBM) — an extremely aggressive cancer of the brain. This diagnosis was such a cruel blow, especially given that Lori had already beaten cervical cancer found in 2015. What followed next is hard to fathom, especially for someone so young, healthy and in the prime of her life. The following months have been very physically and emotionally trying. Lori’s first step was a craniotomy to remove as much cancer as possible; with GBM, complete resection (removal) isn’t possible. While the surgery was a success by medical standards, the craniotomy left Lori with left-side weakness, a loss of sensation, and greatly limited mobility. Next, with help from friends, Lori entered Frazier Rehab for intensive in-patient rehabilitation. She and Damon lived in the hospital for weeks. Lori’s tremendous work ethic helped her to weather arduous 8-hour days filled with physical, occupational, and speech therapy — all while still recovering from brain surgery just a week prior. With GBM, the length of rehab stay isn’t dictated solely by the physicians. Rather, the aggressive nature of GBM requires a shift from post-op rehab to the “standard of care,” which cannot begin during in-patient rehab. Once released, Lori went on to complete her initial standard of care treatment, consisting of 15 radiation treatments in Louisville over 3 weeks while taking 42 straight days of Temodar, a chemotherapy drug. At the same time, Lori was doing physical, speech, and occupational therapy twice a week at a neuro-specific rehab facility. Thankfully, recent advancements have added another treatment to the GBM standard of care. Optune, an FDA-approved device, is worn almost 24/7, sending waves to the brain to slow the growth of cancer cells by stopping their division. In extensive clinical trials, the rate of 5-year survivors doubled while wearing Optune. We are so thankful that Optune is an option for Lori. That said, no decision is easy with Glioblastoma. Damon and Lori got a crash course in clinical trials, exhausting all options before committing to the Optune device. Unfortunately, you cannot do clinical trials pre-progression while wearing Optune, so many variables must quickly be weighed to ensure the best and most timely treatment path. Having opted for Optune, its use began as soon as radiation stopped. The device consists of 4 arrays that cover Lori’s head and a battery pack she must carry at all times. Lori’s head must be shaved to use the device, which will be worn for the remainder of her life. Finally, once Lori got through the initial standard of care phase of treatment, she was given a 4-week break from chemo to allow her brain to heal. Thereafter, Phase II began. Over the next year, treatment will consist of 12, 28-day cycles, wherein Lori will take 5 days of chemo doses at least twice the dosage of her original cycle followed by a 23-day break. This regimen is subject to change based on how Lori’s body responds and how the tumor reacts. MRIs will be used to regularly monitor for the progression of the GBM. Throughout all of this, there have been bright spots. The team at Norton Cancer Institute is one of the best. Damon and Lori vetted, researched, and sought other opinions — something suggested by the Norton team. They have confidence in the team’s ability to give Lori the best possible treatment. Lori was able to start Optune a few weeks early, thanks to the team at Norton. And genetic testing revealed that the GBM was a methylated tumor, which is usually a sign that a patient will respond to and better handle the chemo drug Temodar. Last week, Lori completed the first 5 days of Phase II of her new chemotherapy. This increased dosage caused increased fatigue, stomach issues, and loss of appetite. Overwhelm abounds. In addition to navigating a life-changing surgery, completing rehab, enduring neverending treatment, and weathering endless insurance concerns, Lori must also figure out how to navigate a new life that is so much different from the one she had. And the life that Damon and Lori had just a few short months ago, was pretty sweet. After 8 years together, Damon and Lori wed in 2021 and just celebrated their 1-year anniversary on October 10. Following a few years of planning, they are building their dream home in LaRue County. Having broken ground in November 2021, they hope to move in just before Christmas this year. Lori now primarily uses a wheelchair, so medical equipment and modifications will be necessary to fully enjoy their new home. These needs are costly and not covered by insurance. For example, $20,000 is needed to install a platform and stair lift to enable Lori to enter her home and go downstairs to be with their reptiles and amphibians they enjoy so much and have taken to educational events. There’s also the $2,200 monthly out-of-pocket cost for Lori’s Optune treatment plus about $400 each month for chemo and other prescriptions that insurance won't fully cover. Medical supply needs, travel costs for treatment, and more are especially concerning, given that Lori can no longer work. Another unexpected worry was that Damon’s insurance changed mid-treatment, leaving them with much less favorable coverage and even more to figure out. The financial and emotional burden this GBM diagnosis has caused is devastating. Together, we have the opportunity to make this next year a little easier and more comfortable for Damon and Lori. With our support, we can help them move into their new home and enable Lori to enjoy what she's dreamed of and worked for all of these years. Please help us raise $60,000 to cover the cost of the platform, lift, and the next year of their known out-of-pocket medical expenses.

On Friday 10/28 around midnight our sweet Ryan was involved in a devastating motorcycle accident. The accident took place while Ryan was riding alongside a friend. The details of the accident are still unknown, however tragically Ryan’s friend did not make it and passed away on scene. Ryan was rushed to the hospital with multiple life threatening injuries to his body; trauma unimaginable. After many long surgeries, blood transfusions, intubated and sedated in the ICU for several days, Ryan finally woke up. This was just the start of the fight to survive. Ryan had to be sedated and intubated just a few days later, with another procedure and longer stay in ICU. Fear and total helplessness set in on his family. The nightmare phone call that Ryan’s parents, Ashlie and Matt, received in the early hours of the 28th, thousands of miles away at their home in Washington, is one no parent ever wants to receive. While Ryan’s life hung in limbo, Ashlie had to pull herself together and make the flight to Arizona with her mom by her side, as Matt stayed home to tend to their five other children. Once she arrived at the hospital, she has not left Ryan’s side. Ashlie and Michelle, grandma, have spent every day from morning til night, praying and pushing for Ryan to get through. Now, three weeks after the accident, against all odds and by Grace of God, Ryan is alive and in rehabilitation! His trauma surgeons could not believe the day they heard he wiggled his toes. The orthopedic surgeon said, it’s a miracle and they did not know if he would survive let alone be able to move his toes! What a blessing to be able to say Ryan is where he is today. The road will be long and extremely difficult for Ryan. He now has to learn how to do the simple things, we take for granted. Getting himself to a seated position in bed, is painful and very challenging. Ryan is not able to weight bare let alone stand. He will be in a wheelchair until his body can take the pain and push through. Walking is something he is determined to make happen, and we pray and have faith knowing the fight in this boy is strong, and that day will come! While Ryan will be working every day with rehab, it is uncertain how long this process will take and how long it will be before he can get back to the life he knew before. For now it’s all still very questionable with many sad days, days filled with anger,tears, defeat, and loss. Ryan struggles every day wondering why he survived and his friend didn’t. Why did this happen; why was he out on his motorcycle. There are so many questions, with no answers. But God is good and answered our prayers, and kept Ryan here with all his loved ones and friends, allowing him to continue his journey of life. His life may look uncertain and different than he planned, but it is a precious gift and I feel honored to be part of it. If you feel it in your heart to contribute to the family and assist with care and the many expenses they are facing while Ryan continues to fight this battle, it would be beyond a blessing.❤️

En cuestión de unos minutos, la vida puede cambiar para siempre. [scroll down for English] La imagen de encontrar a mi bebita flotando boca abajo en la alberca es una que jamás podré sacar de mi mente. La tomé en mis brazos. Le hice primeros auxilios mientras llamaba al número de emergencia. Ella no despertaba. Cuando la ambulancia llegó, pensé que les estaba entregando sólo un cuerpo. Pensé que ella ya no regresaría. Pero regresó. Los paramédicos maniobraron y lograron llevarla al hospital con pulso, en donde un equipo de excelentes médicos la estabilizaron. Desde entonces, nuestra pequeña ha mostrado mejoras continuas. La inflamación en sus órganos se redujo. Las infecciones cedieron. Sus pulmones poco a poco fueron recobrando fuerza. Con el paso de los días, comenzó a mover sus manos, sus brazos y sus hombros. Luego su cabeza. Luego abrió sus ojos. A los pocos días de ser trasladada a un hospital público, Noa fue desconectada de su ventilador y pudo respirar por sí misma. Desde entonces, nunca volvió atrás y sus pulmones sólo se han ido haciendo más fuertes. Hace unos días, Noa finalmente llegó a casa, en donde la estamos cuidando ahora. Ella todavía no puede hacer cosas básicas como tragar o controlar el movimiento de sus ojos. Sus extremidades permanecen en un estado de tensión la mayor parte del tiempo. Sin embargo y pese a todo pronóstico, ella está aquí. Nunca piensas que algo así te va a pasar a ti. Y nunca te imaginas que serás capaz de atravesarlo. Las ganas de vivir de Noa, su fortaleza y valentía, es lo que nos ha dado fuerzas a nosotros para seguir luchando junto a ella. No dejamos de creer en el milagro de volver a ver su sonrisa. Buscando casos similares al de Noa fue como encontramos al Dr. Paul Harch, especialista en tratamiento de niños con secuelas de ahogamiento mediante medicina hiperbárica. El doctor ha logrado resultados positivos en la rehabilitación de muchos niños, incluyendo mejoría de las funciones motoras, cognitivas, estado de alerta, tono muscular, visión y equilibrio, entre otras áreas. Conseguimos una entrevista con él y aceptó tratar a Noa. El tratamiento implica trasladar a Noa a New Orleans, Louisiana. La duración de nuestra estancia allá puede ir de 5 hasta 8 semanas. Todo ese tiempo, necesitamos pagar por hospedaje, alimentos y medicamentos, independientemente del costo del tratamiento y los gastos del viaje. El Dr. Harch también nos comentó que el paciente promedio visita la sala de emergencias al menos una vez durante su estancia. Por obvias razones, no podemos contratar un seguro de gastos médicos para Noa, por lo que tenemos que contar con suficiente dinero para solventar estas eventuales visitas. A todo esto hay que añadir los gastos de las consultas pediátricas mientras estamos allá, así como los de cualquier terapia de rehabilitación adicional que nos indique el doctor. Debido a que necesitamos poder movernos todos los días a la clínica en una situación controlada, también tendremos que rentar un auto y pagar la gasolina que consumamos. Por eso es que estamos pidiendo su ayuda, ya sea económica o para compartir la historia de Noa. Todo suma en esta situación, no hay cantidad pequeña. En cualquier forma en que puedan apoyarnos, les estamos eternamente agradecidos, de todo corazón. No sabemos por qué Noa regresó después de haberse ido tanto tiempo. Queremos creer que el milagro de su vida tiene un propósito. Queremos creer que es el principio de un milagro más grande. ------------------------------------------ In a matter of a few minutes, life can change forever. The image of finding my baby girl floating face down in the pool is one that I will never be able to get out of my mind. I took her in my arms. I performed CPR while calling the emergency number. She didn't wake up. When the ambulance arrived, I thought I was just handing them a body. I thought that she would no longer return. But she came back. The paramedics maneuvered and managed to take her to the hospital with a pulse, where a team of excellent doctors stabilized her. Since then, our little girl has shown continuous improvements. The inflammation in her organs was reduced. The infections subsided. Little by little her lungs have regained strength. As the days passed, she began to move her hands, her arms and her shoulders. Then her head. Then she opened her eyes. A few days after being transferred to a public hospital, Noa was disconnected from her ventilator and was able to breathe on her own. Since then, she has never looked back and her lungs have only grown stronger. A few days ago, she finally arrived at our house, where we are now taking care of her. She still can't do basic things like swallow or control her eye movement. Her limbs remain in a state of tension most of the time. However, despite all odds, she is here. You never think that something like this will happen to you. And you never imagine that you will be able to go through it. Noa's desire to live, her strength and her courage, is what has given us the strength to continue fighting alongside her. We do not stop believing in the miracle of seeing her smile again. Searching for cases similar to Noa's was how we found Dr. Paul Harch, a specialist in the treatment of children with drowning sequelae using hyperbaric medicine. The doctor has achieved positive results in the rehabilitation of many children, including improvements in motor and cognitive functions, alertness, muscle tone, vision and balance, among other areas. We got an interview with him and he agreed to treat Noa. Treatment involves moving Noa to New Orleans, Louisiana. The duration of our stay there can range from 5 to 8 weeks. All that time, we need to pay for accommodation, food and medicine, aside from the cost of the treatment itself and travel expenses. Dr. Harch also told us that the average patient visits the ER at least once during her stay. For obvious reasons, we cannot buy medical insurance for Noa, so we need to have enough money to pay for these eventual visits. To all this we must add the expenses of pediatric consultations while we are there, as well as those of any additional rehabilitation therapy indicated by the doctor. Because we need to be able to move every day to the clinic in a controlled situation, we will also have to rent a car and pay for the gas we consume. That's why we're asking for her help, whether it's financial or to share Noa's story. It all adds up in this situation, there is no small amount. In any way you can support us, we are forever grateful, with all our hearts. We don't know why Noa came back after being gone so long. We want to believe that her life has a purpose. We want to believe that this is all the beginning of an even bigger miracle.

Last summer, my mom, Erin, found a lump in her breast. Her first doctor assured her that for most cases like hers, the tumors were benign. Hers wasn’t. It was triple negative breast cancer, a notoriously aggressive form of breast cancer. In less than 30 days, she began five months of chemotherapy. Then, shortly after treatment started, she was hospitalized due to complications from chemo, lost all of her hair, and had a double mastectomy. Gratefully, she eventually received the news she was cancer-free. After healing from her double mastectomy, my mom underwent the first of several breast reconstruction surgeries. The first surgery had major complications—lasting 11 hours instead of the typical 6—and the surgeon wasn't sure if the tissue transfer would be viable. Thankfully, it was, but the recovery was (and continues to be) strenuous—emotionally, physically, and financially. My mom has continued to work full-time throughout her cancer journey and treatments to keep her medical benefits and maintain an income. It hasn’t been easy. So, we wanted to create this GoFundMe for her. If you’re wondering why it’s just starting, you can look to my mom’s selflessness (and stubbornness); when brought up at the start of her journey, she assured family and friends that she would be okay. However, after revisiting the idea repeatedly, she acknowledged that her stress would lighten significantly with financial help. I’m grateful she agreed to this, because while she’s “technically” fine (thanks to medical insurance that’s absorbed most of the bills), she has hit her very high out-of-pocket deductible for the past two years. She’s also paying out of pocket for cancer-related treatments, like acupuncture, to relieve ongoing neuropathy from chemo. And she will continue to face expenses over the next five years as they continue to monitor for cancer recurrence. So I know that some extra support would make a real difference. So, if you read through all of this (apologies—I am an English graduate student, though), thank you. And if you feel moved to donate, I can assure you your money will go to a kind, resilient woman who will receive it gratefully. With love, Devon Thomas (one of Erin's four children)

I still hesitate to type these words, but I am starting this Go Fund me for my 39 year old brother in law Brian Geskermann was recently diagnosed with a rare blood cancer, called Multiple Myeloma. Brian is married to my best friend and sister Angela, and together they share two beautiful boys- Henry, 2.5 and Joseph, 5 months. Their lives are just getting started together. If you know Brian, he would never ask for help or complain. He is selfless, kind, genuine, smart, adaptable, resilient, a go-getter, wonderful husband and irreplaceable, remarkable father to my nephews. I realize this is a typical response to a cancer diagnosis- but gosh he and his family do not deserve this. No one does. We have had so many kind hearted people in our lives ask how they can help, so I thought I’d put this out there. Here is Brian’s journey so far, as I know many of you may have questions. Brian’s Story: Over the 2022 summer Brian had been experiencing hoarseness in his voice that eventually exacturbated to difficulty breathing with exertion. A CT scan found a problem in his trachea, and in addition, saw two lesions or masses in his vertebrae in his neck. Bloodwork was also done, and the results of this was the reason he was referred to Oncology and Hematology next. In late August he had a biopsy of his throat- no cancer, but diagnosed “ Subglottic Stenosis” of the trachea. To this day the doctors are still unsure if this is connected to the multiple myeloma. Parallel to this, he met with an Oncologist, and— per the bloodwork & lesions on his vertebrae, was diagnosed with Stage 1 Multiple Myeloma. In a nutshell- this is a mysterious blood cancer and treatment outcomes vary with each individual diagnosed. This cancer starts in the bone marrow and the cancer cells eat away at the bone, causing these lesions. Brian has since had a PET scan which showed several lyctic lesions ( holes in his bones) in his T1 and T3 vertebrae in his neck, spine, and two in his hip. In addition he’s had a bone marrow biopsy which showed about 50% of his bone marrow is affected at this time. On October 5th, 2022 Brian started chemo. He’s on a cycle now of several pills per day and 2 injections every few weeks. After a 4 three week cycles, he will have another PET scan and his stem cell transplant to wipe his system clean to rid of any cancer ( we hope). He's a champ. How Can Your Funds Help? Brian and Angela both work full time, with their boys in full time day care as well. My sister is a 2nd grade teacher in Milwaukee, and the most remarkable teacher at that. Her students are so lucky to have her and she has found a lot of peace and solace at her job with her students during this time. Brian will continue to work full time for as long as he can until the transplant. We anticipate Brian’s stem cell transplant will be in late January 2023. What we know is that after the transplant, he will be quarantined in the hospital for around three weeks. After the procedure, he will need to be isolated from Angela, the boys, and public, for an additional few months as his immune system will have been completely wiped out. This means no work and reduced income, and Angela shouldering the load of the house, my nephews, and making sure Brian is taken care of. The two of them will need a lot of support, especially during this time. With this go fund me, we are hoping to use the money not only for medical bills, but help with a meal service , housekeeping, nannies/babysitters. Each and every dollar donated is SO appreciated, there are no words to describe our gratefulness. We will keep paying it forward as we can. We are so grateful for those joining us as well as those that have been following along in Sydney's fight to BEAT CANCER! Sydney Magness (Lippa) was diagnosed with leiomyosarcoma, a rare cancer in August of 2021. Over the past year she has gone through several rounds of strong chemotherapies and a period of radiation which we were hopeful would all work to shrink the tumors enough to have them surgically removed. Due to the intensity of her treatments, she was unable to work most of last school year. However, after radiation was over in late June, she was feeling better and had a beautiful wedding on July 2nd. She went on an amazing honeymoon to Puta Cana and upon returning home was hospitalized for severe pain. At that time she learned the cancer had spread to her kidney, her lungs and to some areas in her arms and legs. In addition to the oncology care she’s receiving at Hopkins, we knew we now needed something unconventional to help fight this cancer and discovered a book called Starve Your Cancer, by Janet McLellan. The author, a physio scientist, cured her own stage 4 cancer using a metabolic approach which blocked the many pathways cancer can use to grow and spread. We discovered that the endocrinologist who wrote the forward in her book happens to practice in Annapolis, Maryland less than an hour away. He agreed to see Sydney and immediately put her on an intensive protocol of off label medicine and supplements to kill her cancer cells and stop them from being able to spread. She had her first appointment with him at the end of September and by mid-October her scan showed her tumors had already begun to shrink! The costs of these metabolic treatments are expensive and neither the endocrinologist visits nor costs of the medications are covered by her insurance. She was again recently hospitalized due to a staph infection that turned into sepsis-praise God for effective antibiotics. Although Sydney is back to work so far this school year, she is missing many days of work due to appointments, treatments and hospitalizations. To know Sydney is to love her. Her unwaivered faith throughout this journey has shown a glimpse of God's goodness to everyone she has come in contact with. Together with continued prayers and your generous support we will fight to beat this!!! Matthew 7:25

Hi, my name is Hannah and I am fundraising for my friends Steve and Kate Prosch! I have known both these delightful people most my life. They both have such beautiful hearts for others. Those of you who don't know, these last few weeks have been incredibly stressful! But you see, sometimes people with chronic illness have someone they love become ill. It's always scary when someone you love is sick because you don't want your loved one to suffer. But if you suffer from chronic illness and pain you have the added fear of, " what am I going to do! He takes care of me! How will I be able to take care of him?" Well, that's where I'm at! My amazing husband of 34 years has stage 4 metastatic uveal cancer of the liver. It started out as ocular melanoma almost 6 years ago. It is extremely rare. He was treated with radiation and although it was very traumatic and his vision in that eye was lost, we were so relieved to hear the radiation was working and his tumor was shrinking. Every 6 months we traveled to Portland for check ups and here at home he had scans every 6 months to check for metastasizing to his liver! We made it to 5 years and his oncologists were so happy! 5 years was the goal! After 5 years the chances of metastatic uveal cancer went way down! Phew! We made it! Big sigh of relief. Well, here we are 6 years post surgery and we received the news! My amazingly husband who has so faithfully taken care of me through all my chronic health issues and many surgeries has stage 4 metastatic uveal cancer of the liver! What? How can this be! He is my everything! I won't lie, I have never been more scared in my life! But then something amazing happened! I felt the peace of God! I now know that God is going to be with me and give me the strength to take care of my husband and support him through this journey! I will be there for him just like he has always been there for me! And I can honestly say, it is well with my soul!

I’m doing this because I cannot think of anyone who has done more for her friends and family, me included, always putting others before herself. She helped my daughters and I financially to get out of an unsafe living arrangement several years ago without even giving it a second thought, that’s just the kind of person Lisa is. She has been a single mother, in a single income household, for over a decade and is fiercely independent. Like most strong people I know it is difficult for her to ask for help...so I’m asking for her. A few years ago Lisa started dog sitting as a way of making a little extra income and fell in love with it. She quickly began talking about her dream of having her own dog daycare one day and this past March that opportunity finally arrived in the form of an existing daycare business that was for sale. Lisa purchased that business March 30th, 2022 and “Oh The Pawsabilities” was born. She had a vision of being able to provide meaningful employment opportunities for folks with developmental disabilities and was working with local organizations to help with recruiting. Then, on May 2nd Lisa was hospitalized and was diagnosed with ITP, immune thrombocytopenia. This is an autoimmune blood disease that causes her immune system to attack her platelets, the cells that help your blood clot. Very low platelets can lead to severe internal bleeding. Over the next six months there were three more hospital stays, including one where they discovered Lisa had bleeding ulcers.Treatment for ITP requires finding the right medications that work, which can be different for many people. The first two medications she was prescribed showed no improvement, so she now has started weekly treatments hoping for some success. Due to her health issues Lisa was not able to invest herself and her time in “Oh The Pawsabilities” to put all of her plans and dreams into fruition. Because of this, Lisa had to make the difficult decision to close the business, just six months after opening. This loss has devastated her, both emotionally and financially. Because of her illnesses and diagnosis of ITP she has not had steady income since March, and now has no income coming in. Due to the weekly treatments she’s receiving to improve her platelet count, she does not know when she will be able to return to work. Most people ask “what can I do to help” and right now what Lisa needs is financial support until her health improves. Whatever you can give helps and is appreciated more than you know. Let’s show Lisa the love and support she has so graciously shown others until she is back on her feet. Thank you.

Cancer can take many forms, at any point in life. Sometimes it starts at birth, resolves, and comes back in different clothing! What a rollercoaster... Emily has been on such a ride, starting with eye cancer as a baby, which was resolved (phew!), but it liked her so much it came back as Leiomyosarcoma twice. She received surgery to remove a bagel sized tumor a few years ago with great success. 2 years after ago, her scans came back abnormal again(persistent bugger), showing a small nodule on her flank, and multiple lesions on her liver. It’s on like Donkey Kong. We have embarked on a journey of discovery, both of ourselves and the medical world as a whole. Currently she is receiving interstitial laser therapy in her liver to reduce blood flow to the tumors, which has been hugely successful, alongside systemic laser through IV multiple times a week. We are now embarking on the second part of this journey...microwave ablation! This means they will insert a probe into all of the tumors and hit them with microwaves to destroy the cancer cells, the body will then work on taking out the trash! Emily is a prime candidate for this procedure because all of her tumors reside on the outside of the liver, and are easily accessible for the probe. This will mitigate any damage to surrounding cells that are not the cancer. This is a very brief procedure (1-2 hours) and involves live CT imagery, while they place the probe into the exact locations of the lesions. She will spend one night in the hospital and then go in daily to our Mexico clinic for IV support, and then the hard part...waiting! We will do scans again in a few months to see how the tissue has reacted (the team is expecting a complete disappearance of tumors) and are very hopeful for a Cancer free Christmas! This has been an amazing journey, and we are so thankful for being able to go on it together, but it is not without the dedication of our family, friends, and the medical team that has supported us on it. Unfortunately when you are going it alone outside of the normal medical system, it does not come without great cost. Life is priceless, but care rendered is still paid by someone. The first round of treatments to where we are now has been $50k. Each week we are here costs about $13k, the surgery itself will be $16k, then another week of clinic IVs and support, totaling $92k. We are so incredibly hopeful that this will be the end of Emily’s cancer journey (medically speaking), but we are not out of the woods yet. Our spirits are high, and we are thankful for everyone who has joined us on this journey, and who we have met along the way. If you would like to follow along the journey, Emily has a blog she updates as we progress in the healing process; There Is No Stage Five <URL>

As you may know, Kylie was diagnosed with the rare disease CRPS when she was 15. She finally found a treatment that worked, but insurance suddenly stopped covering it. Each treatment cost $2400 now and the cost of travel. Kylie is a kind person known to many as “Sunshine”. She is passionate about improving the lives of others in both her personal life and career aspirations. CRPS is the most painful condition known to the world. Kylie has tried many different treatments in the past with little effect. These treatments allow Kylie to participate in more life activities and experiences and have less days planned around her pain. We have appealed the insurance company, but they have deemed the treatment experimental despite the positive feedback and results from Kylie’s treatment physician’s practice. Kylie used to get treatment every month and depended on them to function. Kylie’s CRPS isn’t curable, but these treatments improve her quality of life. Our goal is to raise $10,000 to pay for 4 treatments and travel over 2023 to help her. Even a single treatment is worth it to Kylie. About CRPS: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome is a rare chronic pain condition thats caused by trauma to a limb or body region or a direct nerve injury. CRPS is a whole body disease involving the central and peripheral nervous systems. Due to the rarity of the disease, getting a diagnosis can be hard and may take multiple doctor visits. Some signs and symptoms of CRPS include, Continuous burning or throbbing pain in a limb or area. Changes in skin color, temperature, sweat rate, hair and nail growth rate in the limb. Sensitivity to touch or temperature Muscle tremors, spasms or loss of muscle tone (atrophy). Loss of function or mobility of the limb. CRPS has been described by some physicians as “physical PTSD”. The body does not recover from the initial injury and has a continued, prolonged, and exaggerated pain response that is the hallmark symptom of CRPS. Any injury from stubbing your toe and fracturing it, to a scratch on the arm could be the initial injury. A positive feedback loop of pain signaling is then set in motion and over time, pain sensitivity increases via a processed called central sensitization. Treatment approaches to CRPS include pain relievers, anti-convulsants, Dorsal Root Ganglion (DRG) implants, peripheral nerve block injections, and intravenous infusions. Kylie has a DRG implant and has tried all of these treatments and only found significant lasting relief with the infusions. Being a whole body disease, CRPS take a heavy tolls on mental, emotional, and social health. CRPS has been nicknamed the “suicide disease” because of the severity of the constant pain. A flare can result in having to cancel plans, call off work, or miss class, and over time can lead to the loss of friends and relationships. Most CRPS patients have some degree of disability which will progress over time with the disease leading to increased reliance on family and friends for assistance. These add to the emotional and physical stressors on the body, which only increase the likelihood for flares and increase pain sensitivity.

Hopefully all of you have gotten by with a little help from your friends. We’re asking, whether you know Yony or not, to lend us your hand and give a lot of help to our friends.
