Hi, my name is Sienna. I'm a little older now than I am in that picture, but it's just one of my favorites with my mom. I have wanted to start a GoFundMe for my mom, but she was always too embarrassed because she didn’t want to accept help from others. It’s finally gotten so bad that she allowed me to do it. I wasn't sure which category to list this under because my moms physical situation is what has 100% contributed to her financial situation. I asked her to write down the very stressful and painful situation she is in right now. This is what she wrote... "Hi, my name is Karyn. This is the most humbling experience I've ever had in my life. Asking for help like this. I have always been the one that wants to help people, and now I'm the one asking for it. I have degenerative disc disease, and it has not only gotten worse over the years but has now caused me to have so many other chronic pains throughout my body. I now have neuropathy in my feet, as well as extreme pain in my tailbone, down my right leg, and in both of my buttocks. This all started many many years ago as arthritis, but over the years has turned into so much worse. The arthritis is in my hands, which I can deal with, but my back, feet, and leg pain are why my quality of life is completely gone. I have a beautiful, amazing, loving daughter...and I can no longer do anything fun with her! It's the most depressing thing in the world. She will be gone before I know it, and she will have no good memories with me...only listening to me cry in pain every day and telling her I'm sorry that we can't go hiking together - workout together - go to movies - go for walks - go to the amusement park...the activities are endless that I can no longer do with her. I can only sit or stand (without excruciating pain) in 30-minute increments if I'm lucky. I then have to lay down and curl into a ball on my side to take the pressure off the nerves in my back. I can no longer work in the field that I love, which is Event Planning/Coordinating. It requires too long of hours, too much travel, and especially too much bending and lifting. I am a shell of my former self (metaphorically speaking) as I can no longer workout, which is slowly affecting me both mentally and physically. In the past, I have seen countless chiropractors, physical therapists, acupuncturists, doctors, and surgeons. This was when the pain wasn't even close to what it has become in the past couple of years. I've done everything from TENS (shock treatment)...to LESI (spinal injections of corticosteroids into the covering of the spinal cord in your lower back). This was more painful than giving birth to my daughter. Yet where I'm at right now, with the unbearable chronic pain, is the absolute most pain I have ever experienced. I have had spinal x-rays, and two MRI's... the first MRI was in 2015, and the most recent was 2017. I have added photos showing how there is no disc left in the lowest part of my spine, and it's bone on bone (part of the bone, along with the entire disc, has deteriorated completely). My last MRI was over 5 years ago, and I can't imagine what it would look like now. I will need to get an updated MRI to even take the next step which is surgery. I have applied for disability, which is a very long process, and they are extremely critical of who they accept or reject. I'm currently waiting to see if I am accepted. I have seen two different surgeons, (back when I had insurance) - and they both said that I definitely need a spinal fusion, and will most likely need more in the future, as my discs are deteriorating. This surgery can run anywhere from $30,000 to $50,000 - and can take up to three months to even be able to heal and start to walk again (depending on the person). This leads to the other reason I need financial help. I have used all of my savings/401k to keep up with my bills...I have borrowed from family (which I am so grateful for), but I am at least three months behind on everything. My car was repossessed in the middle of the night on October 24th. My mom had just passed away at the end of August, and October 25th was her birthday. Not only did I wake up very sad thinking of her; but I also had bill collectors calling me every 15 minutes; when I saw that my car had been towed...that was all I could handle. I had what I'm sure was a panic attack. When I called the bank that my car loan is through (Capital One Finance), they gave me the information for the towing company and told me how much it would cost to get my car. With the 3 months of late payments, late fees, and the towing fee (which alone is $390), it was more money than I could even think of coming up. After 10 days (from the 26th), she said that they will ship the car to Las Vegas for auction (I live in Utah, it is 10 hours round trip). They ended up shipping the car to Vegas on Oct. 1st (which was 3 days earlier than they told me). I think that I just unloaded so much that has been bottled inside me. This is so embarrassing asking for help, but I just know things will get better; they have to. Thank you from the bottom of my heart to anyone who can donate! I promise you that one day I WILL PAY IT FORWARD! Sincerely, Karyn" This is Sienna again. My mom is the most giving and caring person, but she is in a spot right now where she really needs help. Anything you can donate to help would be greatly appreciated!! Love, Sienna

The doctors claimed that since all the tissue was removed, there wouldn't be a chance for cancer to reappear there. They performed reconstruction surgery, and the next year or so was one surgery after another due to infections. In 2021, I had a severe case of Covid that developed into Bilateral Pneumonia. Despite how progressed the Pneumonia was, my symptoms were practically gone in just a few months, as if by miracle. Now, as of Oct 31, 2022, I have been diagnosed with Cancer again, this time much worse. The doctors found cancer in my lymph nodes during an unrelated surgery. These lymph nodes must have been overlooked during my cancer treatment in 2012, because they indicate that cancer has also spread. Hers2 + metastatic breast cancer..This will be my most brutal battle yet, but I don't plan to back down. With Chemotherapy and Radiation treatments around the corner, I will soon be financially in a challenging position. With my one and only son soon graduating from college at UAH, he has had to move back home and take care of me during this time. He is all I have, and despite it being his final year of school, he is giving up his time and risking his schooling to be here helping me. This situation sprung on us so quickly that sometimes we still wonder if it's just a nightmare; However, in the same way, God has helped me through so many other illnesses, and I have faith that he will once again guide me through this situation. The funds raised will be put towards my treatments that are starting soon. Factor in all work related income has9 dissipated. We have no idea how long this process will take or how much the exact cost will be, so we are setting a goal of $7,000 to help us through the initial stages. Thank each for every one of you who have already donated. From the bottom of my heart I can't thank you enough.

Now Aaron and his family need some help and consideration. In the last 18-months he has had one medical fiasco after another. It started with elusive spinal issues. In the midst of diagnosis he had to undergo an emergency appendectomy. The doctors had him on PT extensively and that surgery interrupted the process. The therapy only modestly helped while interrupting income. Then he was encouraged to undergo a series of injections that insurance initially was purported to cover. It was not ultimately covered, and it did not work either. This event set Aaron and his family further back. After that, a work injury and bad luck led to umbilical hernia surgery. More money and more time focus diverted through the Fall of 2021. In March this year, he tripped and snapped his humerus at the ball clean through. This incident required the use of a sling for six weeks. Weeks of struggling through work. Remember, he is a musician. Speaking as someone who once had a hairline fracture of my humerus, it still pains me to this day. I cannot imagine a complete break. Later, possibly because of the fall and possibly because of the simple failure rate of any surgery, Aaron’s hernia re-ruptured, requiring surgery in August. It was much more extensive compared to the first procedure. Indeed, more expensive. A mesh was placed to hold everything as it was meant to be beneath the abdominal muscles. It is excruciating surgery. More time that he could not be with his students. Debts mounting. More difficulty working and teaching as a result. Finally, as some of you probably saw, on October 11th, Aaron's large dog bolted out of the front door. He spotted some prey. Aaron grabbed his collar, and the dog dragged him down a flight of concrete steps. This incident shattered his scapula and eight ribs. Potentially it has damaged the hernia repair from August. What would you do if suddenly your child began having unexplainable symptoms such as tics, fine motor regression, intrusive dark thoughts, OCD, separation anxiety, loss of academic skills, enuresis, and sensory issues? You’d go to the ends of the earth to figure out what happened and help them get back to health. WHAT IF YOUR CHILD’S HEALTH INSURANCE COMPANY REFUSES TO PAY FOR TREATMENT? You’d come here. This is Adam’s story. At age 7, Adam developed debilitating symptoms after a sinus infection. This gifted child, who could read before Kindergarten and played the piano, suddenly could not add 4+2. He started having extreme issues in school with academics and functional skills and ended up with special education services. Adam’s illness progressed so severely that he was finally hospitalized for six weeks. During that time, I spoke with a pediatric specialist who knew Adam had developed an autoimmune illness called PANDAS or PANS. It stands for Pediatric Autiommune Neuropsychiatric Syndrome. It’s the result of infections - usually strep infections, but it can be caused by other infections as well. Basically, your immune system tries fighting the infections but starts attacking healthy cells in your brain, causing inflammation. Brain inflammation is debilitating - children can’t think or function normally. Inflammation in his gut also caused numerous food allergies and other gastrointestinal issues. This specialist recommended treating the source of Adam’s illness - his immune system. Adam received high-dose IVIG when he was eight years old, and after follow-up treatment, I thought he was cured. He lived his best life for six years, becoming an accomplished cellist, an Eagle Scout, and getting accepted to a highly selective college. But this past year, Adam’s world came crumbling down. After another sinus infection in the fall, his health rapidly went downhill. He had breathing problems and what we thought were ulcers. He developed joint pain and brain fog. It finally got so bad that late this spring, he was tested for infections. SURE ENOUGH - Adam had Lyme disease, two viral infections, strep in his tonsils, and mold mycotoxins in his blood. All of these were causing his immune system to stay in overdrive, and his PANDAS/PANS was back! Once again, I contacted his PANDAS specialist. He’s started treatment with antibiotics and antivirals. Mold mitigation specialists found sources of mold in our house, which were poisoning Adam. Over the past two months, Adam has had dozens of doctor’s appointments and blood tests. Some have been covered by insurance, and some have not. He had surgery to remove his tonsils and adenoids, and we had to leave our house for six days while the mold specialists tore out the drywall and made repairs. These challenges have led to thousands of dollars of out-of-pocket costs. Then... there is the cost of the IVIG treatment he needs to reset his immune system. It costs $27,000. Health insurance has refused to pay. We will appeal - but we NEED your help urgently. The primary treatment Adam needs to reset his immune system is an Intravenous Immunoglobulin treatment. It is an infusion of immune proteins prepared from human plasma. After that treatment, his immune system will heal and begin acting normally. With support from other medication and elimination of allergens, Adam will be back to baseline by next May. ADAM NEEDS THIS IVIG NOW! He can’t wait; symptoms only get worse. We must pay upfront for the procedure and appeal the health insurance decision. We still have to pay $12,750 out-of-pocket even if we win the appeal. Please help us raise $10,000 towards Adam’s IVIG treatment. Any amount helps.

After a year of doctors’ appointments and roughly two dozen medications that would not eliminate our mom’s recurrent abdominal pain, she was diagnosed with inoperable pancreatic cancer last month. Overnight, our lives were pushed into the complex world of a life-altering illness. We now talk in terms of the pre- and post-diagnosis days. Tras un año de consultas médicas y más de 20 medicamentos distintos que no le quitaban el dolor abdominal recurrente a nuestra mamá, el mes pasado le diagnosticaron cáncer inoperable de páncreas. De la noche a la mañana, nos vimos inmersos en el complejo mundo de una enfermedad que cambia la vida. Ahora nos referimos a los días en términos del antes y después del diagnóstico. Over the past six weeks, we have learned that pancreatic cancer is understudied and unpredictable, demands tough, quick decisions, and in our mom’s case, causes paralyzing pain. We do not have words to describe the anguish of seeing mom contort and sob when painkillers do not act fast enough. Durante las últimas seis semanas, hemos aprendido que el cáncer de páncreas ha sido poco estudiado, es imprevisible, exige decisiones difíciles y rápidas y, en el caso de nuestra madre, provoca un dolor paralizante. No tenemos palabras para describir la angustia de ver a nuestra mamá contorsionarse y sollozar cuando los analgésicos no actúan con suficiente rapidez. Mom began complaining of abdominal pain that radiated to her back last fall. She sought treatment from multiple specialists who ordered labs and imaging tests. She even underwent a colonoscopy. The diagnoses ranged from osteoporosis to irritable bowel syndrome. Initially, some of the medications they prescribed would numb the pain, but it would eventually come back, and as time went on, it only got worse. El otoño pasado, nuestra mamá empezó a quejarse de un dolor abdominal que se extendía a la espalda. Buscó el tratamiento de varios especialistas que le pidieron pruebas de laboratorio y de imagen. Incluso se sometió a una colonoscopia. Los diagnósticos iban desde osteoporosis hasta síndrome de colon irritable. Al principio, algunos de los medicamentos que le recetaron sí calmaban el dolor, pero este volvía a aparecer y, a medida que pasaba el tiempo, solo empeoraba. When tramadol had no effect on her one October evening, she went to a nearby private hospital where a doctor ordered an ultrasound. A few minutes later, she was told the ultrasound showed a mass in her pancreas and was given an oncology referral. She was admitted to the hospital the following morning due to uncontrollable pain. On a scale of 1 to 10, her pain surpassed 10. Cuando el tramadol no le hizo efecto una tarde de octubre, fue a un hospital privado cercano donde un médico le mandó que se sacara un ultrasonido. Pocos minutos después, le informaron que el ultrasonido dejaba ver una masa en el páncreas y le remitieron a oncología. A la mañana siguiente ingresó en el hospital por un dolor incontrolable. En una escala del 1 al 10, su dolor superaba el 10. While hospitalized, she underwent a CT scan that revealed the size and location of the tumor within the pancreas. It was then that an oncologist told mom the tumor cannot be surgically removed because it is wrapped around a major blood vessel. The pain is the result of the tumor pressing on nerves. Mientras estaba hospitalizada, le hicieron una tomografía que reveló el tamaño y la ubicación del tumor en el páncreas. Fue entonces cuando un oncólogo le explicó a nuestra mamá que no le podían extirpar quirúrgicamente el tumor porque este estaba enrollado alrededor de un vaso sanguíneo importante. El dolor es el resultado de esa presión del tumor sobre los nervios. We sought other opinions. A biopsy eventually revealed mom’s cancer is advanced pancreatic adenocarcinoma. It also confirmed the tumor’s location, meaning mom’s only treatment option is chemotherapy. Buscamos otras opiniones. Una biopsia mostró después que su cáncer es un adenocarcinoma pancreático avanzado. También confirmó la localización del tumor, lo que significa que la única opción de tratamiento para mamá es la quimioterapia. A few days later, another oncologist, whom we can only describe as godsent, calmly addressed all of mom’s doubts over chemotherapy. No other doctor had done so. Adelaide was born with a unilateral left-sided cleft lip and palate, which means that she has a large opening in her upper lip and the roof of her mouth (the palate). During the 20-week ultrasound, Beau and I were excited to see our new little girl for the first time. Our ultrasound technician chatted with us during most of the ultrasound and then became quiet halfway through. We both noticed this ultrasound took longer than our first child's (Sedona's) ultrasound. We didn't think much of it until I walked in for my appointment next week with our OBGyn. She came in with a somber face and said, "we have some news regarding the ultrasound," and explained they were suspicious of a cleft lip and palate. The likelihood of being able to breastfeed was very low, she would need many surgeries over 18 years, and she may have problems with feeding, speech and language development, hearing issues, ear infections, and problems with her teeth. I was stunned. We would need another ultrasound with a perinatologist to confirm. I spent the next month knowing that he would disprove the original ultrasound or that it may just be a cleft lip. The ultrasound confirmed both the cleft lip and cleft palate; the perinatologist told Beau and me that she would likely have the opening from the top of her mouth to the back (from the hard palate and extending to the soft palate). I spent months trying to wrap my head around the diagnosis and went through stages of grief over her future. When she was born, Beau and I fell in love immediately and realized God gave us to her exactly how she was meant to be. We are so blessed and lucky to have such a happy and beautiful baby who is healthy in every other way. Our craniofacial team is located at OHSU in Portland, which means we travel to Portland for all of Adelaide's cleft-related appointments. We are lucky enough to have a pediatric orthodontist on our team. The orthodontist created a device for Adelaide called nasoalveolar molding (NAM), a presurgical therapy that reduces the size of the lip, gum and nose before her first surgery. We drive to Portland every Monday to every other Monday to have her doctor adjust this device. We are looking to raise $20,000 to cover the costs of extra medical fees, travel, accommodations, additional time away from work for her appointments in Portland, and future therapy that Addy will need.

Al Dennis was feeling a little dizzy at home one August morning. When he fell suddenly, his wife Betty rushed him to the hospital. In a hospital waiting room Betty, and soon the entire family awaited news. What was wrong with Al? When could he come home? Anyone who has ever sat in a waiting room knows how excruciating that time is. For the Dennis family, hours became days, days became weeks, and weeks became months. Al was transferred from Marinette county hospital to Madison, then to Oconto. Doctors, nurses, family, and friends tried to hold on to hope as they continued to find the cause and hopefully a cure, as Al continued to fight for his life in and out of consciousness, with breathing tubes, feeding tubes, and monitors everywhere. It’s been over 80 days since that fateful morning, and Al is now considered stable, and just transferred to Luther home in Marinette where he will be able to receive long term physical therapy and support. Al will continue to heal and learn to cope with big life changes such as a feeding tube and limited mobility with the support of his family and community. The Dennis family finally has some answers too. After 3 spinal taps the cause of the encephalitis was finally diagnosed. A simple tick bite carrying the extremely rare Powassan Virus caused this devastating disease. This disease is so rare, in fact, that there was a total of 20 cases reported in the United States in 2020. The people who survive, as Al did, face a long recovery process. (Source: ArboNET, Arboviral Diseases Branch, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) The health insurance will not cover the nursing home care that is required for Al to begin his long journey to recovery, and hopefully home. This is anticipated to cost the Dennis family $11,000 a month out-of-pocket. Once Al meets certain milestones in his recovery, The Dennis family hopes to welcome him home. Due to the severity of the disease, this will be a long process. We anticipate this cost to very quickly become unobtainable for any family to afford and therefore are reaching out for assistance from those who would be willing to help. Al worked as a pipefitter in the local 400. His wife Betty worked as the head cook in the Wausaukee school district, where their 4 children attended school. Whether you can answer the call to help financially, or in other means, the family welcomes your continued prayers, love, and support as they continue down the difficult road to recovery. Hi all. As most of you know, I am Amanda's sister, and many of you know that Amanda recently underwent brain surgery and has been in the ICU. Last Thursday(11/03/22), Amanda had a surgical procedure called a corpus callosotomy. This procedure splits the corpus callosum (the bundle of nerves connecting the brain's two hemispheres) to prevent more seizure activity. Her surgical team was able to meet their goal of at least 50-70% separation. This means she may have to go back at a later date to have a laser surgery to fully complete the procedure. We were initially reassured that this procedure had a 90% success rate in typical cases. Of course, Amanda isn't considered a typical case because of her Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and having a double cortical layer. This procedure could ultimately leave her with split-brain syndrome and/or disconnective brain disorder, meaning that the two halves of the brain are no longer communicating. For example, she could be thirsty and grab a cup but not know how to get the cup to her mouth to take a drink, or she may want to write something and pick up a pencil, but she won't remember that she needs to put the pencil on paper and use her hand to write. So far, Amanda is making good but slow progress; however, she is very weak. She cannot lift her arms even to feed herself. She has pretty severe left-sided weakness in her extremities. She is also unable to control her bladder and bowels. Amanda can talk for just a minute or two before she is completely worn out. She will be working with OT, PT & speech in the upcoming days. We're hoping she will be discharged next week, but that is only if she continues making progress. My goals and reasons for reaching out are to help make Amanda feel comfortable at home and to help our mom cover additional expenses. Once Amanda is discharged, she will need to go to a nursing home for some extensive therapy unless we can bring that therapy into her home, where Amanda is most comfortable. She may need special medical equipment (a wheelchair, an upright walker, a more modern hospital bed, etc.), and as you can imagine, those items are pricy. The walker alone is just over $600. Going with a wheelchair would also mean making a few minor home modifications, like widening doorways. Our mom has taken a month of unpaid leave from work to be with Amanda during her procedure and recovery, and that unpaid leave may need to be extended based on Amanda's needs. Any money raised here will go directly to Mom to cover Amanda's medical expenses, any needed medical equipment, travel costs for post-op medical appointments and the hotel stays for those appointments, and to help replenish the loss of Mom's wages. I would also like to thank everyone who has reached out to us and to those who are keeping Amanda and our family in their prayers. We are incredibly blessed to have so many wonderful friends and family members cheering for our Amanda. Thank you for your time, Ashley

How a simple knee surgery changed our family lives!! On July 19th my mom went to have her knee replacement surgery. This landed her in the hospital with bilateral Pneumonia followed by a long recovery at home and during this become dependent upon an oxygen tank and hose which limited her ability to get around. After some time she FINALLY was healthy enough to get surgery for her knee replacement WHICH was successful , thank God . On Friday August 19th She had extreme difficulty breathing and was rushed to the emergency room . At 1st it was a scare of a possible blood clot in her lung, but all test and blood work confirmed it was not a clot. The Doctors had her take a CT scan and it showed that she had a Mass on her lung. Her pulmonary Dr. sent her for a petscan. As her breathing had worsened so did our thoughts of the possibility of cancer. She concentrated on her knee replacement therapy to keep her mind off any thoughts of the Big C . On august 25th she had surgery to put in a broncial stent and retrieve a biopsy of the mass. The mass was blocking her airway. The procedure provided her with some relief and we patiently waited 3 weeks for the results of the biopsy . During this time she was very limited and pretty much was house bound. September 9th , on my Dads birthday , she recieved the call that it was CANCER ! To make matters worse it is a rare cancer called small spindle cell sarcoma . It is treatable , but it is a very rare type of cancer that usally isn't found in the lungs . Surgery is not an option because she would lose her entire lung . For the weeks that followed we went to many Dr appointments for multiple opinions , but all had the same concerns. she decided on radiation treatment. She has gone through tons of tests while going through chemotherapy. She had to have another procedure for her bronchial Stent to be cleared out. The very next day she under went a procedure for a port to be placed under her skin for her chemotherapy treatment She had to be tattooed for the area where radiation will be done on her right side by her sholder area Her treatment is 5 days a week and for 7 weeks. My Dad has been her trooper as he takes her everyday even at her weakest when she can hardly breath or walk but a couple of steps. They do it. They Never miss a treatment. The tumor is shrinking , but she is still having extreme difficulty breathing . To top things off , her Stills disease she has been struggling with since childhood flared up. she had to be put on 80mg of steroids. She quickly dropped 35lbs and has no appetite to eat. She's drinking substitute drinks for protein and electrolytes. For those who truly know my mom she absolutely hates to drink anything and usuallyoy takes a few sips of water or cola , but with the threat of hospitalization, She is sure drinking them up . Her Stills disease , which is an autoimmune disease, she was diagnosed with at 6 years old has been a constant problem and has started to flare up. It took myself time to take this all in with what stressful struggles my family has gone through since my husband's latter accident. I now couldn't believe my mom has cancer . I had no doubt and know she will fight, but what saddens me and what i dont understand is why she always has had to fight her entire life?? My dad is amazing. Taking her wherever they need to be. We are Heather Arroyo and Phillip Boyd and unfortunately, life has given our sister, Angie Bergquist, a need for us to set up this GoFundMe site. Angie is in need of support right now and probably will be for quite a while. Anyone that knows Angie, knows she can be stubborn and thinks she can do everything on her own. The past six weeks have brought her to a place that we would have never thought or imagined she would be in, and she is needing all of our help.Please read her story and consider helping if at all possible. Donations will go towards medical insurance deductibles, gaps in coverage for some treatments and missed work. Angie and her family need our help so they can focus on her care without distractions. We would also appreciate your sharing of this site in your social media or emailing it to any friends or family that may not use social media. On October 2nd, Angie tested positive for Covid. Our lives have already been severely affected by this terrible illness, so she has been and continues to be very cautious of Covid. Her early symptoms were typical, but she still saw her primary physician and was prescribed the antiviral medicine Paxlovid to help with symptoms. Some symptoms cleared up within a few days, but she continued to feel weak and fatigued. A week after testing positive, she slept 10 -12 hours a day, began losing her appetite, felt fatigued most of her day & had weakness and pain in her legs while standing and walking. On October 12th and again on October 16th, she had negative Covid tests. She was very relieved to be able to return to teaching piano lessons in Bloomington, yet she still felt tired and fatigued throughout her day. Her legs still hurt, and her left leg would feel like it was cramping or had a charley horse at times. About a week later, Angie thought that she needed to slow down because she had been tripping on rugs in the house more often than usual. By October 24th, Angie felt that her fatigue and weakness had gotten worse. She struggled with keeping her workday schedule straight and would catch herself nodding off while teaching students. She was concerned about how quickly she was wearing out after starting her day. Angie was now tripping and falling during her workday as well as while at home. So, after falling at work in between piano lessons, the school nurse called Angie’s husband, Jeff, and told him that she had really been struggling thought her workday and needed to get checked out. Jeff took Angie to Urgent Care and after meeting with a physician had blood work done. The blood work did not show anything definitive, so a follow up appointment was made with her regular doctor as well as with a neurology therapist. Another week goes by, and Angie is no longer comfortable going anywhere that involves having to walk much. She began to self-evaluate herself; could she have MS, did she have a stroke, was she anemic or was she suffering from long Covid? She realized that she could really hurt herself if she didn't do something; so, she swallowed her pride and began using a cane while at work and a sit/stand walker while at home, during times she didn’t feel comfortable moving around on her own. On November 4th, after meeting with her regular doctor, an MRI of her head was scheduled for the following Sunday. We both came to visit Angie the weekend of her MRI. With school having started back up and everyone's schedule filling up with activities, we hadn't all been together since Summer. We have a group text to keep each other up to date with what we and the kids are up to. During the past few weeks, we noticed that some of her texts weren't making sense, or she would have to retype what she had originally meant. We were both taken back by the changes we saw in our sister. She constantly either touched or held her head from headaches that she just couldn't get to go away, her speech was slurred at times, the left side of her face appeared a bit droopy & she had difficulties using her left leg, arm & hand. Jeff and Heather saw Angie have a seizure, it was brief, but very scary, and we all just wanted the MRI to happen so that we could find out what was going on. On November 6th, Angie’s MRI revealed a nectarine sized tumor with substantial swelling in the right forehead area of her brain. She was sent to the Methodist hospital emergency room in St Lous Park. A neurosurgeon reviewed the MRI, determined that Angie should be admitted immediately & had a CT scan taken of her brain. The following day, a neurologist reviewed the results of the MRI and CT scan and determined that samples of the tumor needed to be collected and tested. A follow up CT scan was taken of her whole body and aside from her brain, no further ongoing concerns were seen. Angie slept or was in and out of sleep 18-20 hours a day. When she was awake, she was coherent, but had a faraway stare and replied to questions with simple 1–4-word replies. It was difficult to determine how aware she was of the situation because she was not showing any emotion. Angie was given pain medication and seizure controlling medication through IV up until the day of her biopsy surgery. The day prior to her surgery, another CT scan was taken of her brain, and did not show any change. On November 9th, Angie had neurosurgery on her brain to obtain tissue samples of the tumor for further testing. The biopsy surgery went well with no complications. Following surgery, Angie was moved to an ICU room and continued to be given pain medication, seizure controlling medication & a steroid to help reduce the swelling of her brain tissue through IV's. The steroids seemed to be doing what they were supposed to be doing. Her fatigue decreased, her speech improved, and she seemed to be on as normal of a sleep schedule as possible for being in a busy ICU. Her short-term memory, vision in her left eye & use of her left hand & leg were still of concern to her doctors. On November 11th, the initial pathology results came in. The biopsy showed that Angie has a rare form of brain cancer, a low-grade lymphoma. As of now, they are calling it lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma (Waldenstrom Macroglobulinema). This is a type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma that affects white blood cells. Since this is a very rare cancer, Methodist hospital will be requesting a referral for a Neuro Oncologist at either the U of M or Rochester Mayo. We will have more specific details regarding possible treatment options once further testing is done and we are given the final pathology. At that time, we will schedule time to meet with a Neuro Oncologist. Angie has daily occupational therapy and physical therapy so she can strengthen her muscles, work on her mobility & increase the use of her left hand and foot. She enjoys getting out of her ICU room and being able to move around and get some exercise. On November 14th, Angie had a bone marrow sample collected. The procedure was done in her ICU bed, they took a 1.5-inch bone sample, the size of angel hair pasta noodle then collected a large amount of bone marrow to determine if any cancer is present. On November 15th, Angie had a Xray video taken of her mouth and throat and no issues were found. As a result, she was taken off her soft food diet. Later that afternoon, she got more good news, she was finally able to move out of her ICU room and back into a regular hospital room. In her new room, she is no longer connected to any monitors and gets to wear her own clothes.The following day Angie was given a SPEP (Serum Protein Electrophoresis) test that measures the amounts of antibodies in her blood to see if there are any additional concerns. The test result did not show any further areas of concern. Angie met with her doctor and an oncology doctor, and they told her that she needs another PET scan, to confirm if there is cancer anywhere else in her body before she can go to the U of M for further consultation. Jeff and Angie met with her social worker and were told that she can go home while having further daily occupational therapy and physical therapy with a home health aide. Angie still needs a lot of therapy but has gotten strong enough to be able to have it at home or at an outpatient rehabilitation center, if need be. On November 17th, Jeff and Angie met with the Oncology doctor and were advised that her bone marrow sample did not show any further cancer. We will update this site as we learn more about Angie's condition and her recovery. Jeff has been with Angie every moment the hospital has allowed him to be and their daughter, Bella, has also been with her mom every day to visit. Her mom is her rock, and she has had a very difficult couple of weeks. Now that you have an understanding of what brought you here, we will share how you can help Angie. Angie has a one-of-a-kind personality. Her love of piano, her honest advice, her love of teaching, her love of watching Bella play volleyball, her love of flowers and her family-loving nature – are all qualities we have all seen, grown to love and associate as a part of why we hold her so dear to our hearts. Now, she needs all our love more than ever, as she begins her treatment and recovery. She is one of the most determined people we know, and she will no doubt show her strength throughout this, but she is needing help to lessen the burden of taking on what has placed upon her shoulders. Please consider donating to this GoFundMe site to help offset costs that she is going to experience as she fights until her body is free of cancer. Funds will help with these unforeseen medical expenses ensuring Jeff and Bella are able to be with Angie during the long road ahead. Any amount will help relieve some financial stress and is greatly appreciated. She will not be able to teach her piano students while she receives treatment and recovers. Jeff will continue to be away from his job at AT&T, in Minneapolis, to drive her to her appointments for treatment and therapy as well as providing medication and care until they are able to be assigned an in-home health care aid to assist Angie throughout her day. Thank you for reading this, sharing this site and for all the continued thoughts and prayers.

My name is Avery, and I’m setting up a fundraiser for my mother, who has recently been diagnosed with Rheumatoid Arthritis. Rheumatoid Arthritis is a chronic inflammatory disorder affecting many joints, including those in the hands and feet. Basically, it makes the body's immune system attack its own tissue and joints. In severe cases, it attacks internal organs. Rheumatoid Arthritis is a crippling and devastating lifelong disease and effective treatment of the disease itself, rather than symptom treatment, is extremely expensive. My mom is a do-it-yourself, use-your-hands, down-in-the-dirt, kind of woman. A diagnosis that primarily effects the ability to move is especially devastating for a person like my mother. She's a hard worker and always gets the job done, whatever the task is. She has worked for Walmart for the last 13 years and lives within her means. She does whatever extra she can to support her kids. Her kids have always come first. That's why we, my brother and I, will do whatever it takes to make sure my mother remains healthy and pain-free. When my mother was first diagnosed, my brother and I immediately thought of stem cell treatment. My brother, Max, has been an athlete most of his life and has more recently become a marathon runner and mountain climber. As a result, he has learned a lot about the generative benefits of Stem cell therapy on athletic injuries. The more research we did, the more we discovered that Stem Cell therapy is an extremely effective treatment for Rheumatoid Arthritis, but it is impossibly expensive and difficult to obtain in the United States. Conventional medical intervention in the United States is to prescribe steroids, anti-inflammatory drugs, and immunosuppressants, which only delay the deterioration of the body and also usually cause harm. Stem Cell Therapy is nonconventional in the sense that the approach is meant to "reset" the immune system so that it stops attacking the body, and it's proven to be effective. So we sought out international stem cell therapy treatment centers. The closest, and shockingly, most notably recognized stem cell therapy institute is located right across our border, in Tijuana, Mexico. It's called the Cellular Performance Institute. Ed Clay founded Cellular Performance Institute in search of curing his own mother’s RA. His mother has been in remission from her RA since 2012. Ed Clay and his treatments have been raved about by athletes, including Joe Rogan, all over the world. The cost of treatment for RA at Cellular Performance institute is $27,000. We are also asking for help with an additional $2,000 to cover my mother’s rent and utility bills for the two weeks she will be receiving treatment. We will not be able to book the treatment until the cost is paid in full, which is why we decided to create a fundraiser to get my mother treated as quickly as possible. In the meantime, she will be medically supervised by her doctor's in Arizona, where she lives. Thank you for taking the time to read and share. We are so grateful to have such an amazing community of people who support us as a family. Any amount helps. More information: <URL> <URL>

“One Day at a Time” was my 2022 promise. In January of 2022, I was very busy with wedding date requests, studio appointments and traveling to clients. After having worked behind the chair for more than 20 years, I wanted to transition my career to reflect more of a work/life balance, and so I started to venture into new techniques that could help women with hair insecurities, and although it was fulfilling, I took on more than I could handle. I wasn’t taking it “one day at a time ,” and my body was telling me to slow down. By March of 2022, I felt that my body was telling me that something wasn’t right. It began with some sharp pains in my chest area which I thought might be a result of trying new hair techniques that overly stressed my arms. But I felt it again sometime in April/May, and by July of 2022, during a self-exam, I felt something in my breast, and I knew I needed a mammogram right away. I had an appointment in early August and was only able to schedule a biopsy 20 days later. The idea of waiting that long to find out whether it was cancerous or not was unbearable. So I called almost every day to see if I could get in earlier, and I called different places to see if I could be seen sooner - it was impossible to find an earlier appointment. So after a week of calling and filling out papers for other places to have the procedure done earlier, I thought maybe instead I should be thinking about these 20 days as being the start of my “one day at time.” My one day at a time to enjoy this time I have before my son begins first grade. My one day at a time to enjoy the rest of the summer with my family and make memories. My one day at a time to listen to what my body needs. My one day at a time to be present. The week before my 43rd birthday, I was diagnosed with stage 2 invasive breast cancer. Before I knew it, I had appointment after appointment with doctors and surgeons and the amazing team at Dana Farber – all working together to come up with a plan to make sure I get through this. I had to cancel all the weddings I had booked for 2022-2023 and to let my clients know that I will not be able to work for a while, as I couldn’t promise anything while going through chemotherapy. While I take it one day at a time, I am unable to work due to my weekly chemo infusions followed by surgery and radiation plus more surgeries. Our medical insurance will only cover part of my treatment and I am asking for any financial help you can donate as I fight through this disease with my loving husband and my beautiful son right by my side. I never thought this is how I would have to slow down, but so it is. I’m fighting for my life one day at a time, and we appreciate, with so much gratitude, all the love and the help you can find it in your heart to give.

Fundraiser for Ariana (Squeaky) Fight First, our family is asking you to Pray for our sweet Ariana and all her family members during this extremely difficult battle that has just begun. Ariana (Squeaky) was diagnosed with an extremely rare form of brain tumors (Malignant Mixed Germ Cell with Yolk Sac Tumors). These types of tumors account for less than 5% of all brain tumors in children. Many of you know Ariana and how amazing and loving she is. Her strong will and fighter mentality have just begun to be tested in this battle to overcome this disease. This is a war against her body, time, and brain tumors. Which is a whole hell of a lot, but in true Ariana fashion, she has maintained the “I just have to Suck it up, buttercup” motto built with her Papa (Jon). As surprising and harsh as that may sound, this has always been a family mantra to stay strong, never quit, and endure all challenges, and has always been from a place of love and encouragement. In other words, when something is too hard, and you’re ready to give up or quit, it is ALWAYS “Suck it up, buttercup!”. Stay strong, don’t give up, you got this! Ariana’s current treatment plan is very aggressive. Due to type of aggressive tumors, Ariana’s Chemo treatments require 3 different types of Chemo medications. Ariana received her first round of Chemo treatments November 1, 2022. Her Chemo treatments are 3 hours, long multiple times a week for a cycle of 6mos. The Chemo medications being used are very aggressive, causing a variety of other complications within her body, requiring Ariana to be monitored very closely. Radiation treatment will begin once it is determined if the cancer is solely in her brain or if it has spread throughout her body. Here is what we know so far about each tumor. The 1st tumor This tumor is located on the Occipital (visual) portion of her brain. This tumor’s size and aggressiveness have caused a rapid deterioration in Ariana’s eyesight. Because it is compressing the visual portion of her brain, it also causes severe headaches, nausea, dizziness, loss of balance, etc. Currently, Ariana has lost vision in her left eye and has limited vision in her right eye, and no peripheral vision. There is no way to correct the vision that has already been lost. Now it’s a matter of trying to save her remaining vision. The chemo/radiation treatments that must be used can also harm the healthy brain cells, nerves, and tissues the tumor is connected to. Thus, resulting in additional complications. The 2nd tumor This tumor is located on the pituitary portion of the brain. The pituitary portion of the brain has 2 parts (left & right) & is called the “Bodies Central Command Center”, which controls many of our body’s major functions. This tumor has destroyed the pituitary portion of Ariana’s brain, impacting most of the systems our bodies require to function properly. This requires Ariana to be on multiple medications, therapies, and treatments throughout her life since many of her body's systems will no longer be able to function normally on their own. This causes her to become weak, tired, loss of appetite, constant thirst, joint pain, dizziness, and the list goes on and on. Various medications are being used to try to level out her body's system. One of the complications created is Diabetes Insipidus, or “Water Diabetes,” as commonly called, impacting her body’s ability to regulate the amount of water it stores and releases through her kidneys and bladder. Currently, the focus is to get her body to remain strong during and after her chemo/radiation treatments without causing any further damage to her body or brain and limiting the additional side effects. As you can imagine, this is not only a devastating diagnosis for Ariana and her family to receive but also a financial hardship. Krysta is a single mother to Ariana and her brother Albert (Alex). The Chemo/Radiation, medications, treatments, monitoring, etc., make it impossible for Krysta to work. Krysta must be there for Ariana’s medical needs and still be a mommy to Alex. Hello! My name is Lexus, and I need help raising money for Arlow's double cataract surgery! I got Arlow when he was a little over 8 weeks old, and he quickly became the sweetest and *fluffiest* part of our lives. The first few months of his life were typical - your normal puppy behaviors. When he was around 18 weeks old, I noticed that his puppy behavior was no longer "puppy behavior." His appetite for water never slowed down, nor did his frequent urinating. It was to the point where we were getting up every hour throughout the night for potty and water breaks. I finally decided to send a urine sample to our vet to rule out any serious issues. On October 17th Arlow was diagnosed with juvenile diabetes. It was a massive shock for not only us but our vet too. Our vet had never diagnosed a patient as young as four months old. The next day we began our insulin journey. It was a complete lifestyle change not only for Arlow but for us too. Our days became in sync and strict. We tested his BG (blood glucose) twice a day before every meal to ensure it was safe to inject his insulin. Our vet bills started slowly adding up, as well as all the materials needed to ensure his BG levels were safe. On October 26th, we noticed Arlow squinting more than usual. It was relatively sunny that day, and pollen was flying through the air, so I assumed his eyes were irritated from those factors. The next day he would not open his eyes and had unusual discharge coming from them. When he finally opened his eyes, he could no longer see things around him. We were able to get a referral to an internal medicine specialist and an ophthalmologist for his eyes. Our ophthalmologist and internal medicine specialist are about 2 hours away from our home. Traveling for appointments means frequently taking off work early, which is tough when vet bills are adding up. On November 8th, our ophthalmologist found a late immature cataract in his right eye and a hyper-mature cataract in his left. He also had mid-subclinical lens-induced uveitis in both eyes. Arlow developed cataracts in both eyes only a week after his diabetes diagnosis. The only treatment for cataracts is surgery in which all of the lens is removed except the clear "envelope" around the lens. This procedure, called phacoemulsification, involves the removal of the cataract using ultrasonic energy (the same procedure used in humans) and, if possible, the placement of an artificial lens to restore focus. The estimated cost of pre-operative diagnostics, surgery, hospitalization and treatment is $6,200. If there are any complications after the surgery, the estimate may be exceeded. The estimate does not include additional medications or rechecks beyond the first three visits after surgery. Thank you for reading about Arlow's journey. ANY amount donated is greatly appreciated. Arlow is only 5 months old and still has so much life left to experience. He brings so much joy into the world, and I would love for him to see it for himself. Please get in touch with me if you have any questions, as I would be happy to answer them.

Hey everyone! I know I am long overdue for a health update; truth is, I was still struggling to find answers for over another year since I last posted, and was so afraid of being this vulnerable online. I didn’t want my life being 100 percent revolved around chronic illness because that’s what it felt like every minute of the day for so long. I had felt that I had failed everyone because I was seeing some of the best doctors and still not making much progress in symptoms or finding answers for a long time. Life was extremely rough for many many months, and it still is. I know I have seen some of you in person, and majority of you I have not. There is so much behind my smile that I don’t share out of fear and judgment, but now I feel like I am finally ready to share. After seeing around 30 doctors and what felt like eternity searching for answers, I was finally diagnosed with late stage chronic Lyme disease and mold toxicity this past February. I was bed ridden for practically one year praying every single day that God would take me. I wish I was exaggerating, but there are MANY misconceptions about Lyme disease that are not true. The biggest one being it’s easy to treat with antibiotics and that treatments are covered by Insurance. Lyme disease is SO INCREDIBLY COMPLEX , it can take around 10 years just for a diagnosis. Throughout my last update to now, I’ve still had numerous blood tests, MRIs, countless breakdowns, IVs, traveled to Oregon, Texas, Missouri and Florida to see other doctors. I found the best results in Missouri. I eventually discontinued seeing my doctor in Missouri because it was during the height of the pandemic and it was too hard on my body to keep flying back and forth. Plus the anxieties of the pandemic did not help. The doctor in Missouri had told me my liver, gallbladder, small intestine, large intestine and thyroid were not functioning properly. This was before the Lyme diagnosis, as Lyme attacks the whole body systemically. I have done countless treatment protocols over the past year, and have not been seeing the results I want. My organs are still not functioning properly, it’s been two years like this, and I’m afraid things will continue to go downhill if I don’t take action. I have decided to take a leap of faith, and pursue treatment in Mexico this coming January and will be staying around 6 weeks at an inpatient healing clinic where I will have 24/7 care. The protocol will be an intense 6 days of treatments with one day off weekly for around 6 weeks. This clinic focuses on cleansing the internal organs and healing the body on a cellular level. I know some people that have been to this clinic and have seen miraculous results. Lyme disease treatment is not covered by ANY insurance, nor are majority of the Lyme literate doctors. I’ve been on the best Kaiser Permanente insurance health plan this whole time, but it hasn’t helped me much. I’ve spent around 60k out of pocket on doctors and treatments so far. Going to Mexico I know is going to be expensive, but compared to the US prices of the same treatments, I’ll be saving thousands of dollars. To give a comparison, around one thousand dollars of treatment in Mexico is equivalent to 5-6 thousand dollars If I were to get this same treatment done at home. Treatment in Mexico is around $1,250 a day, but in the long run I know I will be saving money by pursuing treatment there. While it scares the hell out of me to travel to Mexico and get treatment done away from home, I know I am much more afraid of what will happen if I didn’t go through with this. Hi, my name is Brianne, I am starting this go fund me to help my sister-in-law Ashley Russell and her family with her fight against cancer. All proceeds will be used to help with medical expenses, bills, lodging for treatments and follow-up, and help with food or other unexpected expenses that may arise. Please allow me to share her story. Ashley Russell, now 33 years old, became pregnant via IVF in 2021 after waiting 10 long years for her husband, Josh, to be free and clear from his fight against cancer. They were excited and ready to take on this new life as a family of 3 and finally become parents! In November of 2021, while Ashley was 8 months pregnant, she noticed a lump in her breast. She was evaluated, which was thought to be mastitis (an infection of the breast tissue). On December 18, 2021, Ashley went into labor. Upon admission, her breast was now a solid lump. Ashley gave birth to a beautiful, healthy boy early on December 19, 2021. A biopsy of her breast was done while she was in the hospital. On December 21, 2021 she was told it was likely cancer but had to wait for the final result to determine the type and staging. December 28, 2021, 9 days post-partum, Ashley, Josh, and Thaddeus's whole world was struck with the terrible news they feared; Ashley's biopsies came back as Stage 4, Triple Negative, Inflammatory Breast Cancer. This type of cancer is very aggressive and rapidly growing for those who do not know. Now the fight begins; instead of Ashley, Josh, and Thaddeus being able to enjoy all the joys of this new and exciting time as a new family, they now have this news to worry about and fight against. Ashley is being seen and treated by the amazing Doctors at Mayo Clinic, Rochester, MN and a local oncologist at the Monroe Clinic. She had a PET scan before the start of treatment, and it was found that cancer had metastasized to other major organs, the bone, lymph, and other breast. Ashley has gone through 3 different chemotherapies and 1 immunotherapy. She is not a candidate for surgery. Currently, her body is not tolerating the full dose of therapy, and she is missing many days of work due to being ill. On Tuesday, November 8, 2022, Ashley collapsed while walking into their house and became incoherent. Thankfully Josh was there by her side and was able to catch her. She was rushed to the ER via ambulance and was further evaluated. MRI showed a new lesion on her brain; she developed a fever shortly after requiring admission into the hospital. Currently, the local oncologist is collaborating closely with her oncology team at Mayo Clinic to determine the next steps. Ashley and Josh have missed several workdays tending to her needs, care, and treatment. This will be an ongoing strain for them emotionally, mentally, and financially. Ashley and Josh deserve to be able to focus on her health, fighting this cancer, and watch their baby grow without the added strain of how they will manage to pay all these extra expenses while missing several days of work. Thaddeus deserves to spend time with his mommy making her smile during her difficult days. There is nothing more comforting and healing than the love and snuggles of your baby. By donating to Ashley's fight against cancer will allow them a little peace of mind on the financial strain they are enduring and allow them to focus on her health and being with Thaddeus. On behalf of Ashley, Josh, and Thaddeus we want to thank you for your generosity, prayers, positive vibes, and well wishes. Kindly, The Russell Family

Hi, my name is Ash (he/him or they/them), and I am a trans man getting top surgery on Dec 6, 2022. I have known my whole life I was trans, even when I didn't have a name for it. I repressed these feelings for a long time, believing that it wasn't possible for me to transition. I was scared that I wouldn't be accepted by family or friends, and my own self hatred for wanting to transition let me continue this way for a long time. In 2021, I saw a few old friends and acquaintances 'come out' and talk about getting top surgery. While I was happy for them, I couldn't ignore the intense jealousy that crept up inside. I actually tried to ignore it for several months, but one day I couldn't do it anymore. I was sitting in our kitchen while Madde (my spouse) was cooking and I told her that I thought I was trans. She was nothing but supportive and has helped me work through what I needed in those early days and continues to. Since finally accepting that truth, I have slowly come out and have been met with an outpouring of love and support from my friends and family. I am lucky. I'm grateful my son will get to see my true self, and I get to be his dad. However, the things I need to finalize to make it so I can finish up my top surgery and get my legal documentation in place are expensive and a significant burden for our family to bear. I am pushing forward on the surgery date because my mental health suffers every day I haven't been able to get it. The future looks bright - our family is planning on having another child, and I look forward to being healed and doing skin-to-skin with our new baby in a way that is affirming for me as a dad. The money I'm asking for will help with the following things. While I am on his birth certificate, because I am not biologically related, I do not automatically get the same legal parental rights that Madde has as the birth parent in Iowa. This is an issue that disproportionately affects queer and trans people and presents a financial burden that most heteronormative and/or cis couples do not have to face. With ongoing challenges to LGBTQ relationships on both state and federal levels, this process provides me with equal parental rights that could otherwise be challenged. For anyone local - we are also putting together a meal train for the couple weeks after my surgery. If you are interested in helping out that way message me or Madde directly. Thank you for spending the time to read through this. I appreciate any support you can give, including sharing this for others to see. A few days after his 13th birthday, Austin and his family received a shocking diagnosis at a well Doctor's visit. His parents requested additional blood work after an unexplained Cranial Bruit. Austin never felt sick because he never knew how it felt to be well. They found a significantly elevated creatine level, resulting in a trip to the emergency room. Ultimately, after several days of testing and a kidney biopsy, Austin and his family discovered that Austin was in stage 5 Kidney failure due to a genetic kidney disease that he was born with. This type of kidney disease often goes undetected until the child is at end-stage kidney failure. Soon after his diagnosis, Austin underwent surgery to have a port inserted into his chest for his Dialysis treatments. Austin, who loves to play sports (especially soccer) and is a diligent student, found out that he could never again play the sports he loves. He could only attend school with a modified schedule to accommodate his 3-day-a-week dialysis schedule, which was devastating. His parents also needed to change their work schedules to bring him to and from his treatments. What no one knows is waiting for a kidney transplant, even as a minor, can take many years to find the right match. A Kidney Transplant poses many risks and is a lifelong illness, with years of hospital stays and medical bills. The average lifespan of a donated kidney is 10-15 years, so Austin will likely have to have more than one transplant over his life. Any help to support Austin and his family through this trying time is greatly appreciated. This go fund will help with Medical expenses for his treatment and costs to cover all of the missed work days for his parents to be with him through his treatment. If you are interested in becoming a living donor, please get in touch with his parents, Brandon and Audrey Oliver. Thank you for your support.

One summer afternoon my dad was working on his shed when something would happen that would change his life, and not in a good way unfortunately. After the surgery, we watched nurses try to wake him. There was no response. He was yelled at, slapped, and hit. I even tickled his feet, the one thing that always worked at home, and nothing. Healing from a surgery that required a titanium rod and screws to give you a chance at walking again has been difficult. Then the bill showed up. I saw his face drop, and his eyes reddened as he looked at it. I thought I would see tears down his face. Fast-forward to today, after all the dust settled, he finds himself owing close to $100,000. The worst things always happen to the best people and my dad is no exception. Here we are today. Trying to figure out what to do next and talking to everyone we can. I hope you reading this has been touched with my dad’s story. I hope you’re able to extend a hand with even a little to help us during this difficult time. Estarán en nuestros corazones de por vida... y bendecidos para siempre amén ✨ _______________________________________________________ Ibis Catalina de Buenaño es una mujer poderosa y fuerte, y lo ha demostrado éste año y medio de lucha contra una enfermedad muy dolorosa para ella y para nosotros, el 17 de noviembre del 2021 la diagnostican con Cáncer Gástrico fase 4, un tumor en la boca del estómago y metástasis en un ovario. A principios de mayo del 2021 comenzó a tener un cuadro severo de acidez, dolores de estómago, muchos vómitos, y pérdida de peso abrupta, la llevamos a varios especialistas pero ninguno sospechaba nada, ningún examen médico, ninguna endoscopia determinaba que pasaba en su estómago, ya que los resultados reflejaban que todo estaba bien, meses después se logra ver una bacteria alojada en su estómago llamada Helicobacter pylori, gracias a Dios teníamos un diagnóstico e inmediatamente le dieron su tratamiento, había algo que no estaba bien ya que los síntomas eran más fuerte que el tratamiento, su cuerpo no toleraba ningunas pastillas, ni remedios, absolutamente todo lo que ingería era vomitado, llevándonos así a pedir la opinión de muchos especialistas, debido a que los vómitos no paraban, la acidez, ni el dolor, ni siquiera el cambio fuerte de sus hábitos alimenticios dieron resultado. En vista de su cuadro severo de deshidratación y sus varias visitas a emergencias del hospital de Los Ángeles, la someten a otra endoscopia más y ese 17 de noviembre 2021 nos dan la noticia de lo que arrojó la biopsia de ese momento, Cáncer Gástrico en FASE 4, ¿cómo es que de un dolor de estómago y unos meses de vómitos se convierten en un Cáncer fase 4?. Ni los médicos tienen esa respuesta, a partir de allí queda hospitalizada hasta nuevo aviso. Con ese diagnóstico tan duro había que hacerle todos los exámenes para determinar los pasos a seguir y darle lucha a este Cáncer. Este proceso tiene varias fases, y asimilarlo en tan poco tiempo no ha sido nada fácil para todos, y explicarlo para que lo entendiéramos también fue un reto, no hay manera de que sea manejable mentalmente hablando entre la diferencia de idioma y lo complicado que se volvió todo de un día para otro. Los doctores y sus diagnósticos no eran del todo alentadores, ya que este cáncer va muy rápido y crece de manera muy agresiva, sin embargo, harían lo imposible para combatir la enfermedad... Eran tiempos de COVID y nadie podía acompañar a mi mamá en las noches en el hospital, sentirse sola sin alguien de la familia era un golpe duro emocionalmente hablando y comenzó a tener ataques de ansiedad muy fuertes, lo único que podíamos hacer era darle ánimos y tener fe en el equipo médico El Cáncer gástrico es uno de los más agresivos y a mi mamá en pocos días le cubrió todas las paredes del abdomen y el útero, su estómago ya no podía hacer su movimiento natural al procesar alimentos sólidos y debido al tumor alojado en la boca del estómago hacía que fuera imposible expulsar los líquidos que se generaban diariamente, y se fue llenando e inflando como un globo. La primera fase consistía en hacer una cirugía mediante laparoscopia donde por una cánula iban a colocar una malla en el tumor ( llamada Stent) que hiciera espacio para que la comida fuera hacia el estómago y así alimentarse de manera normal, si todo salía bien y el cuerpo reaccionaba bien iban a proceder hacer una cirugía más profunda para extraerle el tumor... era muy lógico así que accedimos como familia al procedimiento, vimos mejoría el primer día, pero pasaban las horas y fueron apareciendo los síntomas de nuevo, y con más fuerza, el procedimiento de la malla lo hicieron 3 veces más, había que intentar las veces que fuera necesario. Sin embargo, los doctores nos dieron la noticia que lamentablemente mi mamá no podría ingerir más alimentos sólidos, y que procederían a darle alimento intravenoso que la iba a mantener hidratada y con los suplementos necesarios. Sin mucho que pensar aprobamos todo proceso que llevara alguna mejoría. Después de 20 días hospitalizada salimos con la ilusión de que todo iba a mejorar, y que poco a poco iba a ir sintiéndose mucho mejor... La segunda fase comienza con la alimentación intravenosa llamada (TPN - Total Parental Nutrition) mi mamá estaría conectada todas las noche mediante su alimento, y renunciar completamente a la alimentación regular, y todo lo que eso mentalmente implica, que no hace falta explicar, fuimos entrenados (mi papá, mi hermana y yo) para conectarla desde casa como si fuésemos enfermeros graduados, había que tener sumo cuidado a la hora de conectarla ya que tenía una vía en la vena que iba a estar por muchos meses y había riesgo de infección así que con mucho cuidado logramos conectarla todas las noches, sin embargo las complicaciones llegan porque al recibir todo ese líquido el estómago se llena más rápido y la única manera de sacar el mismo era a través del vómito o extraerle parte del líquido (peritoneal) con una jeringa en su abdomen inflamado, cada 10 días tendríamos que llevarla al hospital para que le hicieran ese procedimiento donde siempre sacaban aproximadamente 3 litros de líquido y aliviar solo un poco su estómago. Pasaron pocos días y el 25 de diciembre 2021 tuvimos que llevarla de emergencia, porque sus vómitos no paraban y se estaban tornando un poco oscuros, los médicos decidieron comenzar con las secciones de quimioterapia cada 10 días, para ver cómo reaccionaba su cuerpo ante esta nueva fase, rezando por su recuperación el 30 de diciembre la dan de alta, mi mamá sacó todas sus fuerzas y con nuestro apoyo y con la ilusión de volver a casa para Año Nuevo, comenzó el período de combate con su cáncer. La tercera fase comienza con ataques fuertes de ansiedad insoportables para ella, su mente no procesa todos los cambios en su cuerpo y el dolor que esto le generaba, no podía conciliar el sueño, las náuseas eran muy fuertes y los vómitos ya no eran algo oscuros si no completamente oscuros, ese color nos preocupaba mucho y el 4 de enero 2022 volvemos a emergencias, los médicos nos dan la noticia qué hay algo sangrando adentro y qué hay que hacer secciones de radioterapia inmediatamente para parar el sangramiento, le instalan un cateter que va desde el estómago hasta la nariz, pasando por su garganta... una fase muy dura y traumatizante para mi mamá ya que el tubo la lastimaba mucho, era la única manera de extraerle los líquidos y que no vomitara, estuvo en cuidados intensivos por varios días, los ataques de ansiedad fueron cada vez más difíciles más consecutivos, hicimos una petición al equipo médico que estaba al mando si existía la posibilidad de que algún familiar se pudiera quedar con ella en las noches para ayudarla a sobre llevar los episodios de ansiedad, y después de tanto protocolo lo logramos mi papá se quedaba en las noches con ella sin embargo tuvieron que darle medicación fuerte en varias ocasiones, verla sedada era tan difícil de procesar, y la angustia de no ver mejoría nos destrozaba el alma, verla sufrir era muy doloroso para toda la familia, solo nos quedaba rezar y pedirle a Dios un milagro, al verla tan afectada por el tubo nasal, los médicos deciden instalarle un tubo que iba desde el estómago saliendo por el pecho hasta una bolsa sellada, y así poder drenar los líquidos desde casa de manera menos dolorosa, le hicieron la cirugía y todo salió muy bien, cuando los sangrados pararon y los vómitos dejaron de ser tan seguidos, la dieron de alta. En este punto investigamos que otras opciones tenía mi mamá para combatir su enfermedad que fueran menos agresiva, todos sabemos lo que implica una quimioterapia y su efecto principal era náuseas y vómitos, así que decidimos investigar y hablar con una especialista en medicina alternativa, que básicamente era un tratamiento por fases que consistía en ese momento en terapias de Desintoxicación, terapia de oxigeno, infusiones de alta dosis de Vitamina C, jugos naturales, enemas de café, sellado el intestino permeable, tratamiento integrativo con adaptógenos y suplementos, existía un problema muy grande y era que mi mamá no podía ingerir nada porque todo era devuelto mediante el vómito, entre los síntomas tan intensos y la falta de tiempo ya que el cáncer avanzaba muy rápido, decidimos como familia no intentarlo en este momento. La cuarta fase consiste en sesiones de quimioterapia cada 10 días, y alimentación intravenosa, cada semana le sacaban la sangre para monitorear y en base a sus resultados darle la mejor calidad de suplementos, así pasaron varios meses muy estabilizada, y poco a poco las sesiones de quimioterapia estaban dando resultados, los síntomas y los ataques intensos de ansiedad estaban disminuyendo poco a poco, hasta estaba ganando un poco de peso y se sentía con fuerza, estábamos ante un verdadero milagro, todas las noches de hablar con Dios también estaban dando resultado sin duda alguna, aferrada a la vida mi mamá volvió a recuperar su sonrisa y sus ganas de ver crecer a Micaella (su nieta). Llegar Agosto a su cumpleaños muy recuperada era un sueño que estábamos viviendo todos como familia, todos apoyándola y ayudándola a seguir era nuestra tarea diaria. Comenzó Septiembre y de repente volvieron aparecer los síntomas de ansiedad fuertes, de insomnio, calor corporal muy fuerte, y ataque de tos muy seguidos, tenía una coloración rara en la piel donde salía el tubo que tenía instalado del estómago al pecho, le hicieron varios exámenes y placas, determinaron que el tubo estaba infectado, y proceden a cambiarlo, y dejarla hospitalizada por varios días en observación, al llegar a casa aparecen de nuevo los síntomas más y más fuertes, ante las consternación de verla de nuevo en un cuadro crítico vuelven a someterla a exámenes y vuelven a darse cuenta que el tubo volvió a infectarse y esta vez por la tos constante se hizo un nudo dentro del estómago, en vista de todo el cuadro los médicos deciden retirarle el tubo definitivo, quedándose solo con 2 opciones para la expulsión de líquidos, el tubo nasal o la expulsión natural, es decir, el vómito. Mi mamá quedó traumatizada con el tubo nasal así que esa no era una opción para ella cómoda, lo único que quedaba era combatir los síntomas con medicación, y así llegamos a lo que estamos sufriendo hoy en día. Para la fecha actual, los médicos determinaron que la quimioterapia no funciona y se suspendió definitivo, incluso la alimentación intravenosa no es del todo favorable para ella porque ya su cuerpo no está soportando llenarse de líquidos, porque ya no hay manera de sacarle esos líquidos de una manera fácil o cómoda para ella, en vista de lo avanzado y agresivo que ha sido todo su proceso con la enfermedad, mi mamá se opuso a la decisión de suspender la alimentación intravenosa, porque al no tener ningún tipo de nutrición, evidentemente su cuerpo iba a empezar a descomponerse mucho más rápido. A este punto él oncólogo nos ofreció el servicio de "hospicio" y dentro de mucha confusión porque no sabíamos qué es lo que significaba, nos explicó lo que se trataba, fue demasiada información por asimilar, y la realidad es que no estamos aún listos para tomar esa decisión. Sin embargo el cuerpo de mi mamá ha decidido vomitar y toser hasta el cansancio, no puedo explicarles en palabras el dolor que esto le genera a ella diariamente, estamos a la vuelta de pasar al programa de hospicios que amable y dolorosamente el equipo médico del hospital de Los Ángeles nos están ofreciendo, pero en medio de la tristeza por tantas malas noticias, volvimos a mencionar la opción de tratar la medicina integrativa y hablando con mi mamá (siempre tomando en cuenta sus deseos) quiere intentar cualquier cosa mientras ella no sienta más dolor. Y para nosotros como familia, es importante intentarlo todo por ella. Hoy estamos en un país que no es el nuestro pero que le agradecemos cada día por la ayuda por todos los esfuerzos, y por aplicar toda la tecnología que poseen para combatir esta enfermedad tan inclemente, hoy estamos lejos de nuestra familia, combatiendo junto a mi mamá esta dura travesía que nos ha tocado. Por eso cuando digo que Ibis Catalina de Buenaño es una mujer poderosa y fuerte, es porque ha luchado día a día contra su cuerpo, contra el cáncer y contra su propia mente por seguir estando con nosotros. Como familia unida vamos a seguir intentando lo que esté en nuestras posibilidades y en la de ustedes nos puedan ayudar, no hay ayuda pequeña ni grande, ya que no tenemos más recursos monetarios para continuar, y no quisiéramos que este fuera un obstáculo para SALVARLE LA VIDA a mi mamá y luego mirar hacia atrás y decirle que todo lo que pasó no fue en vano y fue la enseñanza más poderosa que nos pudo dar como la cabeza más importante y fuerte en nuestra familia. Los amamos con todo el corazón a todas aquellas personas que puedan colaborar, estarán por siempre en nuestros corazones.

Mi nombre es JORGE FERMIN. Ayudame a ganar la batalla contra el Cáncer. Hola: Mi nombre es JORGE FERMIN. Venezolano de 68 años de edad y he sido diagnosticado con CÁNCER DE PRÓSTATA. El diagnóstico inicial fue ELEVACION DE PSA SOSPECHA DE ADENOCARCINOMA DE PRÓSTATA, por lo que cual se decide realizar una biopsia prostática ecodirigida la cual se realiza sin complicaciones. El resultado de la biopsia realizada fue negativa, sin evidencias de NEOPLASIA. Sin embargo regreso a control con los resultados de un nuevo antígeno prostático el cual trae valores de PSA TOTAL de 23NG/DL, el cual seguía siendo alto. En vista de esto se solicita hacer una Resonancia Multiparamétrica de Próstata. Dicha Resonancia se realiza y los resultados reportan áreas anormales escala PIRADS 5. Se programa otra biopsia prostática pero esta vez Ecodirigida (Cognitiva). El resultado de esta segunda biopsia fue positiva. ADENOCARCINOMA bien diferenciado GLEASON SCORE (3+3). Se me realiza un GAMMAGRAMA OSEO el cual es negativo para enfermedad Metastásica. Dado estos resultados se plantea tratamiento quirúrgico: PROSTATECTOMÍA RADICAL ya que es el momento ideal para realizarla debido a que el Cáncer está encapsulado. Se extraerá la próstata por completo con fines curativos. Todos estos exámenes han sido costeados con algunos recursos propios y de familiares. Pero ya los fondos se han agotado y dado mi situación económica, aunado a un país donde los costos de la salud han aumentado considerablemente, me es difícil cubrir los altos costos que implica dicha cirugía y los gastos post-operatorios el cual supera los $ 7.000,00.
