On September 20, 2022 Dan and Kelly Tasche joyously welcomed their adorable little boy Henry into the world. However, after the doctors spotted some signs of trouble, Henry was rushed to Children’s Hospital in the early morning hours of September 21. The amazing doctors there performed emergency exploratory surgery and discovered Henry’s intestines didn’t fully develop and weren’t attached, a very rare condition called an intestinal atresia. Unfortunately, the two sides of Henry’s intestines are very different sizes, so the only option doctors had was to leave part of Henry’s intestine outside of his body attached to an ostomy bag. This will unfortunately be the case until the smaller side develops enough to give doctors the ability to perform a second surgery to finally attach the two sides and allow Henry to live a normal life at home. Henry has been quite the trooper (as have his amazing parents) but he’s had numerous curveballs thrown his way - most recently a pretty serious intestinal infection and then RSV. Timelines for Henry were a little up in the air until recently. Doctors were finally able to define a timeline for Dan and Kelly, but unfortunately the second surgery won’t be possible until January of next year and with the recovery required after the procedure, it’s very likely that Henry won’t be home until March 2023. Dan and Kelly have been living their lives in multiple places since Henry was born, traveling back and forth between their home and the hospital, and they recently made the difficult decision for Kelly to return to work after six weeks of leave. As you can imagine, expenses add-up quickly. With medical care (multiple surgeries, MRIs, X-rays, and a 5+ month NICU/ICC stay) crossing into two calendar years, out-of-pocket maximums will have to be paid twice, daily travel to and from the hospital, and most taxing, significant amounts of unplanned unpaid time off work to be with and care for Henry during his stay at Children’s and when he gets home. The support that Dan and Kelly have already received has been amazing and so appreciated. All of the thoughts and prayers over the last six weeks have meant so much to them. The organizer of this effort is Julie Fordham, Kelly’s sister, and everything raised through this effort will be given directly to Dan and Kelly to help support them on this long journey.

Hi everyone, my name is Stephanie Konarski, and Dan is my older brother. Dan is a wonderful, caring person I love with all my heart. It's been heartbreaking to see him endure sudden serious medical emergencies, but I'm so grateful he is alive and fighting with all his strength to survive. He is currently recovering from the effects of being in a coma and will also be starting cancer treatments soon. Dan has a beautiful optimism, quiet strength, and courage that can carry him through his coma recovery and cancer treatments. However, the medical bills are beginning to pile up. Dan has been unable to work since his health problems began. His wife, Natasha, has not left his side since the onset of his medical issues. She has been the constant and consistent support he needs. Since she has devoted her time to caring for Dan, she has been unable to work either. Any financial help for Dan and his wife Natasha is greatly appreciated. He has a tough battle ahead of him, and medical bills shouldn't prevent him from getting the care he needs or add any additional stress and anxiety while he is doing everything he can to fight for his life. With your help, Dan can afford his necessary medical treatment. The costs for his medical treatment so far have been astronomical. The hospital bills for the hospital stay and the testing have amounted to more than $35,000. Bills for the surgery and the rehab stay will be coming in shortly. We expect the total cost for the lifesaving medical treatments he has had so far will amount to more than $50,000. And he still needs to go through cancer treatments. Any little assistance you can spare would help Dan and Natasha immensely. Dan's Story On July 14th, Dan had a sudden seizure early in the morning. He had no history of seizures, so this was very alarming. He was rushed to the hospital, where they found bleeding on his brain. By doing an MRI, doctors found that he had two tumors on his brain. Brain surgery was quickly scheduled to remove one of the tumors to prevent an even worse and more deadly seizure and to test for cancer. Four days after the seizure, on July 18th, Dan was taken into brain surgery. The doctor was able to remove one of the tumors successfully. But two days later, Dan fell asleep and wouldn't wake up. On my birthday, July 22, Dan was officially in a coma. The doctors tried different ways to get him out of the coma. My family and I were in agony, waiting to see if he would even survive. They gave him a 50/50 survival rate at one point. Then while he was still lost in this deep sleep, we received the results of the biopsy from the tumor. It was stage 4 melanoma. All of us were shocked and distraught. We didn't know if he would even survive the coma but knowing he had a massive battle against melanoma after he woke up was incredibly heart-wrenching. But Dan is a survivor. Dan is a miracle, as the hospital staff would say. About a month after he was first sent to the hospital, Dan squeezed his wife's hand. He was starting to wake up from the coma. I learned that waking up from a coma is nothing like in the movies or on TV. It's very slow and even just being able to lift a finger is an amazingly encouraging sign. Dan spent almost two months recovering from the coma in the hospital before moving to a rehab center in Greenport to focus more on physical, speech, and occupational therapy. Dan had to relearn how to walk, talk, eat, and do various "simple" tasks I never even thought of daily. Now that Dan is growing stronger physically and gaining back the weight he lost in the coma, the next step is for him to be able to finally go home and then start his cancer treatments. Dan will continue physical therapy to increase his ability to walk and complete everyday tasks while also going through cancer treatments to fight melanoma. Dan has a tough road ahead of him. But his optimism through all of this truly amazes me and helps us all believe he can make it through this. Dan, myself, my parents, my brother Kyle, Dan's wife Natasha, and everyone else who loves Dan greatly appreciate any donation you can spare. He's a fantastic person with a caring heart who deserves this chance to survive. I appreciate your support!

On October 4th 2022 Danny was sent to the Emergency Room by his foot doctor with swelling and purplish color to his right foot/ankle, when the lab work came back it showed he was in septic shock, renal failure, and gangrene in the right foot at which time he was admitted into the hospital in ICU. You can help prolong Darin's life by making a one time investment in his care. Exchanging just one $6 coffee a week could help impact an entire human life. On October 12, 2022, Darin was officially diagnosed with Motor Neuron Disease: ALS or Lou Gehrig's Disease. On average, it costs $125,000-$200,000 out-of-pocket a year to live with this disease and prolong life. Currently, he's lost 80% function of his arms and hands. Walking has also become difficult. However long or short his life will be, we want to provide the best care, allowing him to enjoy every second he has left without pain or worry on how his family will make it through. There are promising studies finding drugs that slow progression, and soon, there could be a cure. We must fight ALS, keep Darin as comfortable as possible, and battle through until a cure is found. Medical bills have already started to come in. We also need to buy a single-level home, to find one that will rent to us under our circumstances, or remodel my father's to accommodate Darin's wheelchair and handicap needs. We will donate extra received, above our expenses and needs, to help benefit others in Central Oregon. If we can, we want to pay it forward as a thank you to our wonderful community, friends, and family for showing us support. ROAD TO DIAGNOSIS, DISEASE, AND NEEDS: Since Darin received the Covid vaccine in February, he began experiencing muscle cramps and twitching throughout his body. He had two laryngospasms that rendered him unable to breathe, setting off a medical diagnosis treasure hunt. He has had countless tests, including blood count tests, antibody tests, blood tests for many similar diseases, autoimmune diseases, genetic tests, vitamin deficiency, metal levels, brain and spine MRI, CT scan, EKG, pulmonary exam, dental exams, sinus exams, and muscle conduction tests. The only blood test that came back abnormal was low vitamin D. (He is "perfectly healthy!") The muscle conduction test showed both upper and lower motor neuron misfiring and muscle death. All the other tests were normal levels or negative. By eliminating every test possible that may have similar symptoms, he has been diagnosed with ALS. This disease is usually fatal within 1-3 years of onset. There is no known cause or cure. Most who live longer are incredibly wealthy and can afford the expenses that go along with trial drugs and experimental treatments. The only FDA-approved medicine, Riluzole, is only given in a 30-day trial and may be an out-of-pocket expense. It has been shown to slow the progression of the disease by only 3 months, but when you have a limited amount of time, you take what you can get. Several other medications show promise but are out of pocket. A new drug approved recently is not going on the market for months and has shown little to no improvement in current symptoms in most. A product called voice banking stores Darin's voice and words. When he can only communicate with his eyes on computer technology, it will talk to others in his voice instead of a robotic voice. This is extremely important to Darin. He may lose the ability to control his body, but he doesn't want to lose his voice in this world. We will have to pay out of pocket for this. Along with that service, we will need a single-level home, a wheelchair-accessible vehicle, lifts, a specialized bed, and equipment so that his family can care for him and all his needs. Kelly will stop working to care for Darin full-time, which is both of their wishes. Darin would like for his family not to have to focus on expenses on top of his long-term care. This disease destroys muscles, killing each one off. He will become incapable of any voluntary movement, including his breathing. Currently, he has lost 80% use of his arms and hands. He has trouble getting up, turning over, and going up the stairs in their condo. He will still have his beautiful mind and senses. He will still feel others' touch even though he won't be able to move. He will have his intelligence and wit despite not being able to talk. He will still move his eyes and communicate with them through unique technology. He will continue to hear and smell. We need to give him the ability to travel comfortably to doctors, go places he has always wanted to go, experience life with his family and have some way to communicate with his 4 kids, who still need him. Please donate. Thank you again for being a part of our ALS fight and family.

I don't want to do this. I don't think anyone ever truly wants to do this. But I believe we have reached a point in my mother's five-year battle with Glioblastoma - a fancy word for the suckiest brain cancer possible - that it is genuinely necessary. My mom never wanted her cancer story broadcasted to the world; she just wanted to live her life as normal as possible for as long as she possibly could. Unfortunately, we have reached a point in this journey where normalcy has to go on the back burner and instead, survival is the priority. My mom was diagnosed with glioblastoma in 2017. Like all crappy awful cancer diagnoses, it was a punch to the gut. 6-12 months life expectancy WITH treatment and surgery. That was what we were told. Here we are five years later; she is the 3% of people diagnosed with glioblastoma to survive over five years, but not without its significant obstacles. Since 2017, my mother has had 4 intense brain surgeries, radiation, multiple types of chemotherapy and she wore a device on her head for a year that required her to shave her head daily. She has participated in 2 clinical trials that involved a device being put into her skull and a cold virus being injected into her brain. She has suffered from all of the chemo side effects, aphasia, and right-side paralysis. I don't know how she's done it this far, but we are so grateful she has. Fast forward to today, after everything she has been through, she is currently recovering at Northwestern Hospital from her 4th Brain surgery after her tumor began growing again. We were told surgery would be risky, but she bravely agreed to do it. Her doctors devised a new treatment plan, and hope was still alive. Her recovery hasn't been easy this round, and she is now in need of some inpatient rehab to help her walk steadily again. No idea how much that will cost but off she goes. While waiting for approval, my father received notice that the insurance will likely deny her treatment plan. Excuse my language, but what a crock of shit. It will then have to be paid for out of pocket,on top of five years worth of treatments and surgeries that have already cost them everything they have worked for. They will continue to appeal the claim if it's denied, but there's no telling where it goes from here, and time is not something we have to waste. They would never ask for help financially. So instead, my sister and I will now because they have both suffered more than we can stand, and Debbie's not done fighting just yet. Any donations are appreciated beyond measure and will go toward assisting with medical bills. Also, no one tell Kev we are doing this yet; he will yell at us :) Lastly, Cancer sucks. My heart goes out to everyone that has to go down this road.

Hello, my name is Valerie Delgado. I am a military spouse, mom of three very active kids under the age of 10, avid reader, and amateur woodworker. I am also suffering from several health conditions, with the most critical for my health and wellness being the loss of my vision due to a degenerative eye condition called keratoconus. I was erroneously diagnose with astigmatism at the age of twelve, but the diagnosis was changed to Keraroconus once my usual eye doctor noticed that my vision was deteriorating at a speed which was nor normal for a child my age. After the formal diagnosis at 14 years old, my doctor attempted to slow down the condition with a number of treatments that were available at the time, including hard contact lens of different kinds, and then the 'piggyback' mode, with soft contacts going on top of the hard contacts to hopefully make my eyes tolerate the hard lenses. Unfortunately, my eyes rejected the lenses each time, causing severe pain whenever they were inserted, and the inability to see or even keep the lens inside my eyes no matter what we attempted. With little else available, at 15 I was told that my only option was to wear glasses and wait until my eyes deteriorated to the point where corneal surgery would be my only option. This was, of course, completely devastating to me as a teenager. I was faced with the fact that I would most like be going blind, and my career in the military (which was something many people in my family— including my Korea war ver grandfather— had done before me) to end before it even began, since I had preemptively taken the test to join the army in preparation for it. I was an avid sports fanatic as well, and played anything I could, including basketball, baseball, and softball. I could no longer do those, as I couldn't tell distances apart and my reaction time was completely gone due to my vision problems. Keratoconus also often left me experiencing color auras, light spots, vertigo, and crippling migraines that would knock me down for days, and later weeks at a time. All my plans for the future were struck down, leaving me drifting with no real idea of where to go and what to do next after I finished high-school. At nineteen years old, I reconnected with my best friend since third grade after we hadn't seen each other for three years, and we fell in love and married after my husband had decided to join the military. While experiencing all of the firsts of a married couple, like getting our own home and having our first child, I was being treated for the condition, but not much advancement had been done for me to be able to fix my worsening eye condition. This came to a head in 2020, when I began to see an uptick in eye fatigue, dizzy spells, migraines, and episodes of blurred eyesight. I could no longer do the things I loved, including writing, drawing, or even watching TV without squinting to get some semblance of on image, which led to more fatigue and headaches. After a PCS to Florida, I was sent to an eye specialist, where they finally told me it would be possible to fix my vision with new surgeries that had now been approved by the government to treat conditions such as mine. The only issues came from insurance suddenly telling us that my eye condition wasn't advancing fast enough for them to cover anything, despite me being treated for 12 years and going from struggling to see to being legally blind. My vision, however, is still worsening, and I can't wait until I go fully blind to do something. I need this surgery, and the sooner I get it the higher are my chances of not having corneal scarring (which can stop the chance of getting the surgery), or even a rupture of my cornea from the pressure as it bulges outward. Everything in my life, from playing with my kids to doing my hobbies, depends on me having my eyesight. I need this surgery to take care of my kids and watch them grow. I absolutely cannot wait, as I can feel it worsening month by month as I struggle more and more to use my eyes for anything. Donations would go towards saving up for the surgery, which would be done in Pensacola by an excellent corneal specialist who has done her best to get my plan to approve my surgery to no avail. Hello. My name is Amber Bridges. Friend and cousin and Pastor's wife of Kyle and Desiree. Many of you know that Desiree has been on a health journey with Pancreatic cancer for over a year. She is amazing and strong and has a wonderful support system with family and church family. I am including the most recent update from her loving husband, Kyle. They are getting ready to encounter multiple flights a month to Houston to participate in a clinical trial. Some travel may be reimbursable, but not for 4-6 months. Here is the update from Kyle: Desiree Update 10/30/2022: It’s been a while since we posted anything online, we have had several asking for an update so here is where we are right now. Desiree has been on the same chemo now for about 8 months-ish. After the last couple of visits (we go to Houston every-other-month) with her team in Texas, they concluded that her current treatment isn’t working like it was before. The decision was made to look into other options (in addition to changing chemo meds) because there were really no great other options on the market that are FDA approved. She has been through two of the three chemo’s currently on the market that are approved for her situation. Awhile back they sent off for genetic markers and to find out the make of this tumor and then the goal is to match a clinical trial with her genetic markers and go from there. They said it usually take 4-6 weeks to get some results, that was about 4-5 months ago. They told us if we heard something then she was a match but if no one contacted us it was likely she wasn’t a match for anything currently available. So, skipping forward to this last week, we had not heard anything so we were told that nothing was currently available. The plan was to switch to another chemo that is “last in line chemo” (least effective) because she has tried 2 of the 3 FDA approved treatments available in her case. She was scheduled to begin this next round of chemo on Monday, October 31. After months of frustration that nothing was happening (tumor shrinking) and things were going in the wrong direction, we got a call that MD Anderson may have found a new option. A call was setup with the clinical trial team at MD Anderson earlier in the week and they went over a few options with us. But, as quick as we had some decent news the possibility fell flat. In order to get into these clinical trials, a new biopsy had to be obtained to make sure the bio-markers from the initial biopsy 18 months ago hadn’t changed or mutated. Desiree’s team said that the tumor is currently unstable to the point that it was not safe to get a new biopsy. So the plan was setup to try the last FDA approved medication that she would qualify for because the clinical trial options were not a possibility. Before the dust was settled over that news, we had a call that the team found a different way to safely biopsy the tumor and that she would NOW likely qualify for clinical trials. So, as you can imagine, emotions have been all over the place recently. Now, skipping forward to today, we are waiting for all appointments to be scheduled. In the next couple of weeks we will begin the process of a clinical trial. With the clinical trial there are multiple appointments and things that have to be completed first to check all the boxes. The next trip down she will get the first dose of medication (infusion treatment) and then over the next few months we will be back and forth to MD Anderson in Houston multiple times for medication or appointments associated with the trial. She will have an infusion every 21 days (approximately) after all the initial appointments are completed. Through all of this Desiree has been one heck of a fighter. She has been in some fairly significant pain and there have been several sleepless nights. I am asking for your prayers over all aspects of this next journey as we are back and forth to Houston several times. Please pray for God’s healing power and that it will shine though and bring Glory to his name during this process. Please pray for each infusion to kill the tumor and all signs of cancer. Please pray for strength, clarity and peace. Please pray for our kids, Joel & Lauren. We cannot thank you enough for all the messages, calls, meals, and more.!! We are thankful for the amazing support system around us and love you all! Thank you for your generosity!!

Unfortunately we have noticed that kyzr is no longer "feeling" when his sugar is going low. Low blood sugars can be extremely dangerous and put kyzr at risk for seizures (especially at over night) . Even with a continous monitor on kyzr its far from perfect technology and is about 20 minutes delayed in showing blood sugars and can vary about 20% from actual blood sugar. When kyzr is asleep and his blood sugar drops he doesnt respond to alarms and we have to physically shake him to wake him up (the dog will be trained to do this, allowing kyzr to do over night visits with friends and be more independent as needed while he is growing up). This is the scariest part of type 1 diabetes, as it is a very real possibility that night time lows end up in seizures or even kyzr never waking up. Diagnosis story: In February of 2022 we noticed what we thought was a growth spurt in Kyzr . He was 6 years old at the time and eating like a grown man on steroids ! We tried upping the amount of protein he was eating but he was still insanely hungry . Kyzr does ninja at a local gymnastics gym, he is pretty talented and extremely dedicated and self motivated. When Kyzr told us that he couldnt do any flips we started to worry a little but thought that maybe he had been training too much and needed a break. I began to suspect that Kyzr might need a diabetes test after reading an article about covid causing diabetes in kids (we all had covid about 6 weeks before). I called his doctor and asked for a diabetes test, she said his sugar was probably dropping (causing the shaky legs, mood swings, and some other symptoms) that we should give him OJ and bring him in the following day. So I went and got some OJ from the store and also bought a scale . I noticed Kyzrs collar bones were more noticable than usual (thought he was thinning out from a growth spurt). When my husband got home from work we went to the store. Kyzr was INSANELY thristy while at the store and also had to pee ... ALOT . While walking through walmart Kyzrs legs began to give out , he said he couldnt feel his ears and his mouth felt funny . That was soon followed by his vision going in and out with huge black spots. We left the store and I began to really worry that this diabetes test couldnt wait until the following day. I had my husband stop at a walgreens and I bought all the stuff to do a blood sugar test at home. When we tested kyzrs blood it would not read on the meter. About this time kyzr looked grey and was slurring his words like a severely drunk person. I rushed Kyzr to the ER and he was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes (noone in either of our families is type 1). We were told kyzr was in diabetic ketoacidosis and was very near a coma. Kyzrs blood sugar was at 777 (a normal blood sugar is around 80 to 120). Kyzr had lost about 10 pounds and his body was in complete starvation mode even though he had been eating nonstop. They started an IV drip of insulin and said they would transport him in an ambulance to Riley childrens hospital once he was stable. Kyzr spent 5 days in the hospital at IU North riley ICU. In the blink of an eye his whole life changed. We are now 8 months into our journey and learning more and more everyday.

Context:﻿ Devin Glim is a former member of the 2018/19 Youth Action Council at the Disability Justice Network of Ontario. He played a key part in advocating for city-funded sidewalk snow removal in Hamilton, Ontario, by writing opinion articles, helping organize delegations at City Hall, one-on-one meetings with Council members, and more. He also was a key organizer around our campaign to Reform the Assistive Devices Program in Ontario, which resulted in a motion being read at Queens Park by the Accessibility Critic. Devin has a disability that limits almost all body movement, and with isolation during the pandemic, his movement capacity has declined. This assistive device/arm would allow Devin to be independent as he lives his life, and it is the opinion of DJNO that devices like this should not be privatized. For this reason, we are supporting him with his quest to fundraise for an assistive device. He has a demo to test out a Jaco Robotic Arm but cannot purchase the product without some support and is now asking for our help in supporting the cost of an expensive but much-needed assistive device. Here is what Devin has to say: Hi everyone! I’m doing an online fundraiser for a Jaco Robotic Arm and would be absolutely thrilled if you would be willing to help me out!! I do not like asking for help for anything, and I acknowledge the contexts and struggles that are being faced by so many today. However, I also realize that the extra abilities the arm would give me would allow me to complete my studies, have an impactful career, and live my life with dignity and more independence than I have ever known. Unfortunately, but not surprisingly (lol...), there is no public funding for this type of device, and private insurance is no help at all, so here we are! I do not take any donation for granted and I will be forever grateful to everyone who helps me make this happen. The arm would make an immediate and incredible impact on my life and those around me, and I cannot wait to use my new abilities to pass it forward and continue the generosity and efforts made to dismantle the obstacles preventing people from accessing the devices and supports that they need. About The Arm: Have you ever been stuck outside mid-January because the electronic-door button is out of reach; hoping that someone walks by that can open the door for you? How about ordering a drink at a café only to find out there are no straws? Want a snack but nobody is around? Itchy nose?? The above scenarios are a daily reality that would disappear with the Jaco Robotic Arm. From the simplest tasks to the most complex maneuvers, the Jaco arm is amazing! It is easily operable with the same controller as my wheelchair and opens a world of possibilities that I never thought possible. Thank you so much for reading this, and if you are able, please consider helping me reach my goal. Devin Glim

My name is Annie, and I am starting this GoFundMe to support my 29 year old boyfriend, best friend, and life partner, Jacin Banks, in his battle with testicular cancer. On October 5th 2022, Jacin visited his general practitioner to get a lump he discovered on his left testicle checked. An ultrasound was ordered immediately, leading to an MRI, confirming a malignant tumor encompassing the entire testicle. Jacin was then referred to a urologist, who established an orchiectomy was necessary, and all cancer and tumor markers be done immediately. Jacin had just moved to Houston in June to start his life with me and only recently started his new job, which included a waiting period for medical benefits, so his orchiectomy had to be postponed until November 7th. The month between his diagnosis and procedure was a gruesome one. Due to the size of the mass, Jacin was in constant pain through his legs, back, and abdomen every day. He could not sit comfortably at work and was up most nights with terrible night sweats and aches. The surgery successfully removed the tumor and testicle; however, the pathology from the orchiectomy was very disappointing. The pathology determined Jacin's tumor to be a mixed germ cell tumor, 60% seminoma 40% embryonal carcinoma. The embryonal carcinoma is a rapidly spreading, more aggressive cancer, meaning chemotherapy would be the next step in his treatment. Jacin has many tests, scans, and oncology appointments ahead, causing him to take many unpaid days off of work and have lots of financial hardship. Jacin and I have big dreams to start a family one day, but due to the high probability of infertility from the treatment, we are seeing a fertility specialist who has determined the course of action is to bank as much sperm as possible as soon as possible. Cryopreservation at this capacity is very costly as insurance does not cover this type of treatment. If you have the privilege of knowing Jacin, you know he is the kindest, most gentle spirit with a smile that lights up every room he enters. Even the minute he woke up from surgery, he had the warmest smile on his face and wouldn't stop thanking the nurses for all they did for him. He is full of optimism and has a way of making every person he comes into contact with feel seen and important in their interaction. Jacin has so much enthusiasm for life and a hunger for knowledge, and I know he is destined for so much greatness. He had just applied for air traffic control school in June and started a new job in a new city so we could begin our life together, only to be hit with the devastating diagnosis of testicular cancer. We are determined to do everything in our power to make his dreams a reality so he can live the fulfilling life he deserves. Jacin has a very long journey ahead to fight this, and we are asking for your help in any capacity to get him the treatment he needs and help us achieve our dreams of having a family of our own one day. We are so grateful for the village that surrounds us and showers us with so much love and support every step of the way.

JESSE'S STORY Jesse was born on September the 4th, 1990. This was three years to the day that we lost our first child, so we always considered Jesse a true blessing with a birthday that we could never forget. If you know Jesse, you probably have a hard time believing that he was an especially shy child when he was very young. He was born in California but raised in his early years in Japan. His first language was both English and Japanese. While we spoke English in the home we lived in the Japanese community so all of his friends were Japanese. He grew to be a gifted singer and sportsman. He played varsity basketball all four years of high school and football as well. While working at McDonald’s during his high school years someone was captivated by his Rich baritone voice as he took their order at the window. The next thing we knew he was on the local TV Morning Show known as the Sacramento’s Golden Voice guy. Also during his high school years he achieved the level in our churches boys program that is equal to the Boy Scouts Eagle Scout. He went to a small Bible school in Texas (SAGU – His Father’s alma mater) on a basketball scholarship. But once he got to college, he quit basketball so that he could receive a scholarship for music, and he traveled with a men’s quartet throughout his college years, all over the south and west. He graduated with a degree in intercultural studies. He also enjoyed photography as well as mountain climbing. . He did some of his study time in college overseas where he made some wonderful friends. After graduating he was able to travel to Iran with his camera and brought back some fabulous pictures. Recently he moved to Salt Lake City where he is now a manager at CarMax. He spends much of his spare time outside mountain climbing and camping and fishing. He loves the outdoors. And until this cancer hit him he has been a very healthy, strong, young man. As he looks to his future, he would love to have some kind of a ranch or a farm where he can work outdoors. His grandpa was a true-blue cowboy. I wonder if that isn’t where he got the idea. He dreams of owning a sailboat in Greece where he can take Summers and take his family and travel the Mediterranean and enjoy time with his family and hopefully a wife someday. He places a high value on family and would love to have his family around him all of his life. He also still has a desire to contribute to humanity as a whole and find something where he can make an impact on the world. He’s given that a lot of thought lately, recently especially. He would like to leave a legacy, not just family, but he would like to affect change or impact culture and Society in a larger way. Of course, he’d love to buy a house and some property and even entertains the hope of getting into real estate. We have included some pictures so you can understand his life’s journey and his zest for life. JESSE'S FINANCIAL NEED Below is an explanation of Jesse’s expenses that we are aware of as of November 2022: • Unpaid medical expenses (2022) - $6,000 (Amount not covered by insurance) • Unpaid medical expenses (2023) - $6,000 (Amount not covered by insurance) • Other Medical/medication expenses - $4,000 (Includes alternative medicines, over the counter medications, Etc.) • Loss of income - $6,000 (Late 2022, Early 2023) • Other expenses - $3,000 (estimated guess only) Total - $25,000 JESSE'S MEDICAL DIAGNOSIS Many of you are wondering, how did Jesse find out that he had cancer? Has this been going on for a long time? What’s the story? Read on: On October 3rd 2022 Jesse was examined for a lymph node issue that had been present for about a year and a half. This included blood Labs X-ray and ultrasound that showed abnormal attributes. On the 10th of October 2022 he had a CT scan of his abdomen that showed multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the abdomen and groin, “concerning of Leukemia or Lymphoma.” On the 17th of October he had a PET CT scan with contrast which showed widespread hyper metabolic, in lymph nodes, skeleton, spleen, and at least two nodules in his lungs. It appeared to be lymphoma. At that time, he was admitted to Huntsman Cancer Institute in Salt Lake City for potential complications with his liver. His liver enzymes were way off the charts. There was some concern that they wouldn’t be able to treat the cancer with his liver operating like it was. On the 18th of October he had a biopsy done. He had an MRI of his brain for possible cause of eye pain that was coinciding with cancer symptoms. And on the 21st of October He was discharged with stable Liver health pending completed pathology report of the biopsy and had an appointment with the hematologist to plan treatment. It was determined that even though his liver is damaged, it is working well enough for them to treat the cancer. There was a consultation initiated with Mayo Clinic for a second opinion. They have confirmed the findings of the Salt Lake cancer Department. On the 24th of October he had a future planning appointment where they discussed the options for him since he is a young man and since cancer treatment could very well leave him sterile. On the 27th of October he had a consultation with the hematologist where they confirmed that he had lymphoma both Nodular Lymphocyte Predominant Hodgkins and Diffused Large B-Cell Non-Hodgkins (per transference caused by undiagnosed NLPHL). Basically, this means that when he beats this cancer, he will have beaten cancer twice, and we hope you will pray to that end.

Hello, my name is Andrea Smoley. I am Ashley's cousin. I wanted to start this GoFundMe along with Doug's family to help him and Ashley(Doug’s wife) while Doug recovers from Guillain Barre Syndrome. On November 3rd, 2022, Doug Watercott’s journey took a devastating turn. Our self-taught, jack-of-all-trades and all-around good guy suddenly faced a rare disorder (only 1 or 2 per million people worldwide). Now facing debilitating symptoms, impending medical bills and lack of income, those that know and love Doug (affectionately known as “Red” to most of central Minnesota) are looking for ways to support his incredible wife and caregiver, Ashley, as they barrel into their new reality. Doug’s journey started with a vacation that was cut short due to a gastrointestinal illness that came on suddenly and stopped them in Sioux City, Iowa October 26th on their way to visit friends in Texas. His symptoms worsened, forcing them to turn around and return to their home in Albany, Minnesota. Once home, Doug improved but started to feel worse again. Now experiencing dizziness and just not feeling like himself, he decided to check in with his hometown clinic a week later. At the clinic, he was given Meclizine, a medicine to treat dizziness, and then sent home. The following day Doug slept most of the day, and when Ashley returned home from work, she found him with a fever, blurred vision, slurred speech and difficulty walking. Ashley took him to the ER in Melrose, where they treated him with IV fluids and Meclizine and then was sent home. Friday morning (November 4th), Doug showed increased difficulty with speech and could not walk without assistance, so they returned to the ER in Melrose. Many tests were administered, and they ruled out a stroke but ultimately decided to transfer him to St. Cloud Hospital, where a lumbar puncture would be performed to help diagnose him. As the day went on, his condition continued to decline, his words became indistinguishable, and he grew very weak. On November 5th, the doctors gave a preliminary diagnosis of Miller-Fisher Guillain Barre Syndrome brought on by his earlier gastrointestinal illness. Doug’s symptoms worsened; he became unresponsive, was in pain and had difficulty breathing. Ashley has been advocating for Doug wholeheartedly every step of the way. Through exhaustion and tears, Ashley continued to assert that Doug needed more care. Finally, late that evening, he was admitted to the ICU and intubated, which was a tough decision. As hard as that was, it has given her and Doug’s family comfort, knowing that he will receive one-on-one care and won’t struggle to breathe. The number one priority is for Doug to be able to rest and begin the healing process. The prognosis for Doug’s recovery is optimistic, but he will face many physical challenges. Doctors anticipate his recovery will take the better part of a year. The road ahead is long and filled with many unknowns for Doug and Ashley. Doug is a go-getter from sunup to sundown, and we all want to see him back on his feet as soon as possible! While Doug will remain in the hospital for an unknown length of time, he is where he needs to be, and we want his number one cheerleader to be able to be with him and continue advocating for his recovery. Doug will be unable to continue working as a mechanic for the foreseeable future, leaving their finances in limbo and adding duress to Ashley, his primary caregiver. We want Doug’s recovery to be the primary focus going forward! Those that know Doug and Ashley know they are inseparable; they come as a unit. They are both hard-working, fun-loving, and love socializing with their community. Friends and family congregate in their yard for BBQs and fires: all are welcome! Doug has even been known to flag down the patrolling sheriff in Albany for a fish fry. Doug and Ashley do so much for others. This GoFundMe is a chance for all of us to support them while Doug recovers and gets back on his feet. Doug is a strong and determined man who will get through this! Thank you for supporting Doug and Ashley during this difficult time.

A Public-School Administrator, our mom, assaulted and strangled by a student, needs our help!! Four years ago today, our mother was the Dean of Students at a Massachusetts public school. Four years ago today, our mother was assaulted and strangled by a student. Four years ago today, our mom’s life flashed before her eyes and the world as she knew it changed forever. Four years ago today, our mom (Liane Bachant Jalette) left the house excited for another day at school. On this day, she was casually dressed in jeans and a long sleeve pink Ivory Ella shirt to support her school’s dress down day supporting women and breast cancer. Four years ago today, our mom went to work doing what she loved, working with children and preparing them for the future. She has always had a passion for helping others and wanting to make a difference. Our mom comes from a family of educators (and now I join the line as an educator); teaching is a big part of who we are. She has been changing the world one student at a time for 25 years. Now is the time for us to unite together and give back to her. Our mom’s entire professional career has been as a teacher, coach and administrator in both public and private schools throughout Massachusetts and Rhode Island. On October 26, 2018 Liane Bachant Jalette of North Smithfield, RI, our mother, had her lifelong dream come to a screeching halt. She was viciously assaulted and strangled by a student. Mom was diagnosed with a traumatic brain injury, post-concussion syndrome, PTSD, thoracic disc herniations, permanent nerve damage, and more. She suffers daily from headaches, numbness, pins and needles, dizziness and major balance issues (she has fallen twice in the past six months, one time breaking her foot), and she is in a tremendous amount of pain. If you look at her from the outside, she looks like your average middle-aged woman, but she is suffering physically and mentally. Over the last four years, our mom has endured countless doctor’s appointments: psycho-therapy, CT scans, physical therapy, cortisone injections, facet injections, ablations, speech therapy, vestibular therapy, MRI’s, X-Rays, and so much more. Doctors have recommended some specific treatment options; however, workers compensation doesn’t cover those treatments. Your donations will help her be able to pay for those treatments and for unpaid bills. Workers’ compensation is only paying mom 45% of her salary. Her case has been tied up in court for FOUR years, and it is taking a toll on her and our family. We are asking for your help. Mom needs a lifeline right now to help lessen the burden. She has never once complained about the pain she is in. We know she’s in pain, we see it on her face and how pale she gets from the pain as the day goes on, but you will never hear her complain about it; that’s not in her nature. She continues to care for us and provide all that she can for us. This is not something, as a family, we ever imagined having to endure. My sister and I never imagined writing about our mom and the desperate needs of our family. This burden is unfathomable in so many ways, and it is for the long term. The medical treatments are necessary for the lifelong and life-altering injuries our mom has sustained, and the bills are piling up. The doctors have all agreed that our mom, age 53, is totally and permanently disabled. This devastating news has been beyond difficult for our mom to wrap her head around. She loves education. She loves working with kids, and in the blink of an eye, that was stripped away from her through no fault of her own. Our mom has always put us first. When we are sick, mom takes care of us; when we need a ride, mom drives us; when we have extracurricular activities, mom is cheering us on; when we need a shoulder to lean on, mom is there. If you know me, you know my mom is my best friend, and she has never failed to teach or support my family and me. She has taught us that strength is not always about muscles. She has always believed in us and encouraged us to be ourselves. Mom is our hero and has shown us that women can be anything they want to be in life. Mom was always there to pick us up when we fell, and now it’s our turn to pick her up. Please consider donating to our cause. Educators across the country are enduring and expected to do so much more than ever before. Awareness for the countless assaults educators across our nation are facing, like our mom, is happening at an alarming rate. It must stop. Maybe raising awareness of what happened to our mom will help others to speak out and get the support they need. At the very least, please share this story, my family’s story, my mom’s story. No donation is too small; anything will be a tremendous help to our family. Thank you in advance for taking the time to read about our amazing mom and your willingness to help. We will be forever grateful, and we will absolutely give back once she is on her feet again.

This week our sweet Ellie was diagnosed with leukemia. — Over the last few weeks, Ellie just didn’t seem herself. The bubbly and playful two year old we knew was no longer interested in some of her favorite toys or snacks. She saw a variety of doctors to determine what could be causing her discomfort, but her symptoms were pointing in so many different directions that identifying a source was becoming difficult. After about three weeks with no progress towards feeling better, it became more concerning. On Tuesday, November 1, Ellie was taken to a local urgent care as we thought her symptoms may be pointing to a UTI, which can be common in children her age who might be potty training. But after taking one look at Ellie, the urgent care doctor said that she needed to be taken to a local emergency room immediately to check her blood counts. Ellie’s numbers were all either too high or too low, immediately indicating some form of malignancy; and after more blood draws and tests, it was confirmed that Ellie has Leukemia. No child deserves to bare the burden of a cancer diagnosis, and no parent should have to watch their child suffer through this. Fortunately, Ellie is in great hands. Her care team was able to identify, diagnose and begin treatment to help Ellie feel stronger in the first 24 hours of being seen. They are confident that an intensive round of inpatient chemotherapy over the next 30 days will lead her to a “cured” status. She will then continue chemotherapy monthly for two years to be fully in remission and ensure the cancer never comes back. There is a long road ahead for Ellie, her parents, and her 15-month-old sister, Rosie. But with the support of family, friends, and her amazing care team, we KNOW she will get through this! The next 30 days will present many challenges for Ellie and her family - logistically, financially, mentally, and more. We are creating this fundraiser to help ease the burden and cover the cost of meals, transportation, medical bills, and anything else needed to help Ellie fight this terrible disease. We are all so proud of how brave Ellie has been and how strong her parents are. Please consider helping Louie, Emily, Ellie, and Rosie through this. Even just sharing this page will help make a huge impact. Thank you! Ellie’s Family

3 days ago on October 26th, Emily was feeling down and not like herself. We all felt that maybe she could have the flu from the symptoms she was experiencing. She went to an urgent care and was sent home 3 hours later after all tests for flu, covid, etc., were negative. Around 5pm she received a phone call from the Doctor who saw her at the urgent care and was told something was so wrong with her blood work that the machine thought it was broken. She was then directed to go to the hospital immediately and so she did. Once arriving to the hospital, Emily was still very confused with what was going on. She had vitals and more blood work done while waiting for a room. After waiting for a few hours in the hospital lobby, Emily was called back to a room in the ed. In the room Emily was laughing and smiling FaceTiming her mom while waiting for a doctor. A doctor comes in and discusses her symptoms and reasons for coming. After some more talking and tests, a doctor finally comes in with some answers. In Emily’s words, “ The doctor came in and asked me how I was doing and again asked what my symptoms are and have been. He stopped talking and just paused and looked at me for a few seconds and I started to get really anxious because of the look on his face. He then broke the silence and asked me if I had any family close by that could come to the hospital. I told him no family, only my boyfriend who was already on the way. He then sat his hand on my leg and said something to me that I never expected to ever hear. He told me my white blood cell count was 156,000 and that a normal white blood cell count is 4,000-11,000. He then paused for a few seconds and spit it out, Leukemia. I instantly felt a panic come over my body and started to cry, freak out and feel so hopeless. I called my family and told them to come right away and they did.” It is now day 3 in the hospital and to learn more about Emily’s Leukemia, she has had a bone marrow biopsy, a lumbar puncture, and tons of blood work and tests as well as a pic line inserted. The chemo will cause Emily to lose her hair and this is something she is very upset about. Yesterday (10-28-22) was her first day of chemo and today she did her chemo through her pic line IV. It is now October 29th and Emily is feeling better, but still not there yet. Her white blood cell count has decreased by 40,000. We are on the right track, keep Emily on your mind and in your prayers. We will keep everyone updated.

We have contributed to many of these, but never in a million years thought we would be organizing a Go Fund Me... especially not for one of our children. Our daughter, Erica Peterson, was having some symptoms that she thought resulted from having covid earlier this year. A close extended family member, who was her age, unexpectedly passed away from a cardiac event in March and Erica could not stop thinking about him. She started wondering if she should get checked “just to make sure” her symptoms were not anything to worry about and that she was ok. Because she has had a heart murmur for a long time and had an echo done in her late 20’s which was fine then, the cardiologist at Froedtert ordered a follow-up echo. The results of the echo showed that she has hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). It is a genetic disease of the heart that is passed down from generations. She was born with it and it manifests in your 30’s. It is an abnormal thickening of the septum between the two lower chambers of the heart which has caused an obstruction in her left ventricle. It can cause dizziness, light headedness, passing out or sudden cardiac events. She cannot do any aerobic exercise, shoveling or running and is restricted to very low activity. She can walk for exercise and can climb stairs (if taken very slowly). She has to monitor her BP daily and watch her heart rate as it cannot go over a certain number. The next set of tests were an extensive stress test followed by a 30 day halter monitor. After that she had to have an angiogram to make sure her veins, ventricles, etc. were all healthy. Based on the results of these tests, the only “fix” is to have open heart surgery. Her surgery is scheduled for November 21, 2022. She will be in ICU for 24-48 hours following surgery and then 2-4 days in a regular room. Recovery is 6-10 weeks and she will not be able to drive until her chest is completely healed. She can ride in the car to doctor appointments, but only in the back seat where there are no air bags. She will have to be on medication the rest of her life to keep the disease at the stage it currently is at and to hopefully not have it progress. She will also have to have yearly tests to monitor her heart. We are all very scared, but have faith in God and know that she will pull through this. We are also extremely thankful for her guardian angel because she would not have gotten checked if it was not for him. Her doctor said that it could have been catastrophic if she had gotten pregnant without having this condition fixed. As parents it is tough to watch your child go through something like this and feel totally helpless. You cannot take it away; there is nothing you can do to make it better. Erica is very proud and we knew that she would push back on a Go Fund Me so we waited until we had her trapped in the car on a weekend trip. We told her we cannot take this away; we cannot make it better BUT we can help with the financial stress they are under. Not only are they extremely worried, but they are also worried about the financial strain this surgery will be on them. The payment plans she currently has with her doctors already are crazy. Her out of pocket has not been met and is $7,000. She will be off work 6-10 weeks and will only receive a small portion of her salary (out of which her insurance premiums will be deducted). Erik is working, but when he takes off to be with her, it will be without pay. She knew she would not win the argument and agreed to let us set this up. If you are at all able to help them, please contribute. Every little bit will help and they would be extremely grateful. Helping to ease the financial stress will help in so many ways. Thank you in advance and hugs & love to all of you. Carol & Dan

Hi, Welcome to Erick's medical journey! Erick had an incredible, adventurous, healthy summer! He returned to school in late September with a new nurse. On Sunday, October 23rd, the neurology team put in discharge orders. However, Erick had other plans. Instead of discharging, a "Rapid" was called, and Erick was transferred to the ICU for respiratory distress due to suspected aspiration pneumonia. A viral pannel and culture were done to determine the reason for the rapid respiratory decline. It was positive for RSV. Erick held strong for 48 hours but then took a turn for the worse. He was then intubated. He went into Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome, and his lungs almost completely collapsed on both sides. He was also showing signs of septicemia. Odds were staking against him in real time! He managed to fight through the worst of it, and we began the slow process of weaning him off the vent. It took two weeks, and we extubated (removed the breathing tube) on Saturday evening, November 12, 2022. He was first placed on Nasal BiPAP and then needed the "scuba" mask for better support. Just over 24 hours after being extubated, he was once again intubated due to his left lung recollapsing. Now we are on day 30 of hospitalization for what we thought would be a max of 3 days. Due to Erick's critical condition and distance from Winona, I, mom, have been unable to work. I took all of my available PTO to cover the first two weeks of this hospitalization. There is no specific discharge date yet, and Erick's 6th birthday is Thursday, November 24th. I am hopeful that friends and family will support us through this unexpected battle and help us celebrate Erick's birthday. An incredible community of people worldwide has followed Erick's journey and sent us love and support. We are forever grateful for all that we have received. Thank your continued thoughts, prayers and love.

As we are all aware, Timmy is one of the most enjoyable people you will ever meet! He is lovable, funny, and easy to be around. This is the guy we all know and love! Tim’s Story In August, Tim experienced two “migraine headaches.” The intensity, pressure, and pain were so severe he made an appointment with his primary care physician. He was given medication to try. In September, the headaches continued - eleven of them in three weeks. He returned to his physician and was given another prescription. At that time, he asked if he could have a scan to rule out any additional concerns but was told to try the new medication first. By the end of September/early October, Sam began noticing some forgetfulness, minor speech issues, and occasional trouble with Tim’s balance. Tim spent the first weekend of the month with his dear friend Danny, who also noticed his difficulties. On Monday, October 10th, Sam along with Tim's mom, Marcia, took him to the Emergency Room. He was given a few scans as well as an MRI, where the team discovered a brain tumor. Tim stayed in the hospital for a few days to decrease the swelling in his brain, and surgery was scheduled for the following week. Tim underwent successful surgery on October 18th to remove as much of the tumor as possible without additional damage to the healthy tissue. After recovering in the ICU for a few days, he was able to return home on Saturday, the 22nd. Before being discharged from the hospital, Tim and Sam met with members of the medical team who confirmed that the tumor was cancerous and further treatment - including another surgery - would be necessary. On Halloween, Tim and Sam attended the post-operative appointment. The team felt confident they could remove additional portions of the tumor, increasing the effectiveness of additional treatments. They were clear that the diagnosis is incurable but that there are also success stories of patients who have surpassed expectations. We know that Tim will fight to become another success story! Things move unpredictably and quickly in the medical world. As such, Tim’s second surgery was completed on November 3rd. This will likely be followed by radiation and chemotherapy treatments to keep the tumor from growing. With his megawatt smile and endless dance moves, nine-year-old V won the hearts of students and staff at his Sioux City, Iowa, elementary school. He is the epitome of Mr. Personality with a bit of mischievousness, a kid who brightens the room without saying a word – or breaking out in dance. He was even featured as part of the school’s 5 Days of Joy campaign in December 2021. V’s personality isn’t his only superpower. He is also smart, the kind of child that is destined to go places. V didn’t speak any English when he entered first grade. By the 2021-2022 school year, he was fluent in English. Without knowing his background, you would never guess that V wasn’t born in the United States. Over the last three years, he worked hard at school. In turn, his teachers and staff at his school were extremely dedicated to him. It takes a special child to stand out in a school with many high achievers. V is that student. In mid-April 2022, V suddenly stopped attending school. No one knew where he went or when he would return. Despite efforts to locate him, there were no concrete answers on when his friends and teachers would see him again. Months passed, and his school community worried they may never see him. One day in August 2022, his school received a concerning message out of the blue from someone who said that V had been intentionally abandoned thousands of miles away from Sioux City. V was safe but was desperate to return to his home and school. V was left on the side of a road, and a good Samaritan, who had been orphaned himself, found V and gave him a place to stay. Most importantly, he vowed to help V return to the place he loves – his home and school in Sioux City, a world away. Amazingly, V and the gentleman that took him in saved up enough money to purchase a cheap phone so they could make contact with V’s school. Over the last couple of months, a group of people who care about V – including a favorite educator of his - have been trying to figure out a way for V to return home. Countless messages, photos, and video chats have allowed the school to keep in contact with V. Many of the video chats end with a simple, yet heartbreaking question from V: “When are you coming to get me?” Running into constant obstacles because of technology, paperwork, laws, and more hurdles, it has felt hopeless at times and difficult to stay positive about how to get V home. Last week, V was hospitalized with malaria. Because of poor living conditions, V was also extremely malnourished. The dangerous living conditions that V is currently in make it imperative that he returns to Sioux City as soon as possible. In the last few days, another group of local angels stepped in to help. Because of their collaboration, V now has the paperwork he needs to return home. There is also a family ready to provide him with the love and support he needs. The only thing standing in the way of V’s journey home is the funds necessary to cover the cost of travel expenses and the cost of medical care once he returns. Months without proper nutrition and the trauma of his ordeal have taken their toll on nine-year-old V. His once vibrant smile is a little dimmer because of his experience. There are many children that need help in Sioux City and across the world. We ask for your generosity to save one of these kids – a boy that goes to sleep at night, not dreaming about the latest video game or a new toy, but praying about returning to his fourth-grade classroom and his home in Iowa. Please Note: Any money raised beyond the initial fundraising goal will go directly to V’s ongoing care and needs once he returns home as well as a savings account for him to use for college.

We all know and love Steven Carabuena as that witty kid that can make seemingly anything funny. Or as the kid who works extra hard at his job to prove his worth. Or that brother/son/ cousin that’s always there to help out whenever you need him. Or the uncle that’s so weirdly afraid to hold his niece/nephew. On November 11, 2022, Steve was diagnosed with a rare cancer called Primary Central Nervous System (CNS) Lymphoma. Steve’s case is especially rare because he’s only 31 years old and has no comorbidities. He was diagnosed 2 weeks after he developed 6th nerve palsy and the MRI showed a mass in the pituitary area. His first symptoms were cross-eye/ lazy eye and headaches. After symptoms worsened (light and sound sensitivity and extreme nausea), he was admitted and more masses were found in the adrenal glands. The biopsy confirmed everyone’s fears of cancer. Primary CNS lymphoma is a cancer that has no staging and considered very fast growing. Because of the aggressive nature of the cancer, Steve has already undergone the first of 5 rounds of chemotherapy at Augusta University Hospital. He is being treated by an excellent oncology team led by Dr. Ayushi Chauhan. The prognosis is uncertain because of the rarity of the disease but the team is optimistic and hopes that after 4 months of treatment, Steve will be able to lead a normal life and put this behind him. In the meantime, Steve is unable to continue working at Augusta airport as an airside operations agent. Steven has to undergo physical therapy to help keep his strength up in between chemotherapy treatments. Family from both in-state and out of state are generously making plans to come and stay to help Steven with his daily living needs and help cover his financial needs while he is out of work. Some of Steven’s biggest struggles right now are dealing with the loss of appetite, nausea and depression. This GoFundMe is being created at the urging of Steven’s many friends and family that want to support him during this trying time. Funds will go towards Steven’s medical fees, rent and food. This page will also be used to keep friends and family updated with his treatments and his condition. Most importantly, we ask everyone to pray for his recovery! Thank you for your generosity and your prayers! Private donations may also be made through Venmo @steven-carabuena

We are writing this as part of the Montana Rebels Basketball Family. If you have a child in Bozeman, MT, who has been involved in any competitive basketball in the last ten years, you have likely had the opportunity to have Justin Reynolds train your athlete. You may have also been fortunate enough to have him coach your team, but if not, you or your child have likely heard of his generosity. He has been known to take entire teams to movies, to dinner, get professional team pictures, buy basketball shoes for someone who needs them, or take a whole team to an NBA game at his own expense, but always for the benefit of the kids. Right now, it’s our turn to help him. Justin and his fiancé, Brittani Currier, have been going through a very long and challenging journey to expand their family. They have spent the last four years navigating the emotional and expensive journey of infertility. Through multiple medical interventions, the couple was able to conceive, and in April 2022, they were ecstatic to find out they would finally become parents! The due date was January 2023, so they began planning as new parents do. The pregnancy was challenging and required many additional doctor visits and medications. It was progressing as it should until September 28, 2022, when it was determined Brittani had developed preeclampsia. This is a medical condition that causes dangerous levels of high blood pressure. It required immediate hospitalization and additional precautions to protect mom and baby. Unfortunately, the condition worsened, and Brittani had to be life flighted from Bozeman to Billings, MT, where they have more advanced equipment to treat this diagnosis and very premature infants. An emergency C-section was performed in the early morning of October 1, 2022, and the beautiful Nyla Ann Michelle Reynolds was born. She was just 26 weeks and 2 pounds but came out fighting. She was considered healthy for her gestational age but still developing in many ways. This required Brittani to stay with Nyla in the NICU in Billings and Justin to complete a daily commute from Bozeman to Billings while juggling coaching and working. Unfortunately, after a few days, the doctors discovered Nyla had a PDA, also known as patent ductus arteriosus (PAY-tent DUK-tus are-teer-ee-OH-sus), which is a common heart murmur in a premature infant. The Billings doctors attempted to treat Nyla’s heart murmur with the medications and equipment available to them. Still, they ultimately decided it would be better to transport the family to Denver Children’s Hospital to repair the heart defect. On October 19th, Brittani and Nyla were flown to the new hospital, and Justin joined shortly after. During the transfer, Nyla caught a severe staph infection. Although many life-saving procedures were attempted over the next few days, they could not save her from the invasive infection in her tiny body. She fought as long as she could, but on October 22, 2022, she departed this world and gained her angel wings. Their heartbreak has been followed by a flood of bills from 20+ days in three hospitals; two specialized NICU stays for Nyla, life flights, and many other things not covered by insurance. Not only are we asking for prayers, but we’re also asking for donations to help this couple navigate the next steps of their journey. Any monetary donations will go towards astronomical medical expenses, transportation costs, end-of-life expenses, etc. Thank you for your consideration and generosity.

On October 25, Randy Burtz updated his friends and family on his month in Russia, undergoing a risky treatment for Multiple Sclerosis, posting on Facebook: "Well, I’m finally back home after a month in Moscow treating Multiple Sclerosis. I’ve been pretty quiet about my health struggles, but I finally felt like sharing a little bit. About 4 years ago I started experiencing symptoms (loss of balance, memory problems, muscle spasms, etc.) and MRI’s confirmed autoimmune demyelination (a telltale sign of MS). After years of dealing with relatively worthless doctors and deteriorating health, I had gotten to the point where I was resigned to the fact that I was going to have retire from a job I love so much at Western (the university and my colleagues have been incredibly supportive). They call MS a snowflake disease (not because it only affects liberals), because it impacts everyone who has it in different ways. Like a recent article said, “Put 20 of us in a room and you will have 20 different lists of symptoms.” Multiple Sclerosis means “many scars” where the autoimmune demyelination leaves scars (called lesions) on the brain where permanent damage occurs. While there’s a wide range for “normal”, 10-15 lesions is average. At the last count I have 30 lesions. Many people show physical symptoms (difficulty walking or writing) others show cognitive decline such as memory, decision-making, and speech (such as mixing words up and difficulty finding words). I fall into the latter category, so Erin and I often hear “he looks fine!” or “you seem to be doing great!”, because I don’t have the more visible version of this disease. Dealing with comments like that and is one of the reasons I’ve remained silent. Other than knowing how much this has impacted Erin and the boys, it has been the one of the most frustrating things about all of this. With very few treatment options available, I decided to seek a rather risky treatment that includes a high-dose chemotherapy (it’s called hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation and is the same treatment that Selma Blair received for her MS) that attempts to reset your immune system to keep it from attacking your brain. Why Russia!? The same treatment is actually offered at the Seattle Cancer Care Alliance, and in Denver, Chicago, etc. Many countries around the world offer it for free to their citizens to treat MS. Unfortunately, insurance will not cover the treatment and the cost is a minimum of $240,000 in the US. We’ll still spend decades paying it off, but the same protocol was 1⁄4 the cost in Moscow, and it’s one of two places that offer it to international patients. The Russian Dr. Fedorenko has been performing the treatment for 13 years. He and the staff are as kind and caring as you’d hope to find. Still, a month in a Russian hospital was pretty surreal! We really won’t know if the treatment has worked for a year or so, but it is the first time in a long time I have felt any hope for the future." If you know Randy, you can imagine how difficult it was to get him to agree to let us create this GoFundMe. But, if you know Randy, we're sure that you agree it's inconceivable to imagine a world in which everyone who loves him, Erin, Carson, and Hudson would allow them to spend the next decade paying off medical bills alone. Let's add to the hope for the future that Dr. Fedorenko and his team have given the Burtz family by helping to defray some of those medical costs.

I’m Ollie. I’m 8-years-old and I have a rare brain condition called Lissencephaly. Basically, my brain is almost totally smooth. The doctors said I’d be unable to learn anything. I’m super smart, love traveling and studying the world, jazz/blues music, painting, writing poetry, the Avengers and I want to graduate from school and own my own floral design shop someday. I also have seizures every day. I have sensory processing disorder, cortical visual impairment, a similar physical situation to cerebral palsy and have had so many surgeries and medical procedures I can’t list them all here. And with so many medical and social challenges, I deal with a lot of anxiety and sadness. I’m sure some of you can relate to that part. It’s hard to make friends when you can’t talk on your own, you’re in a wheelchair and you look and act differently than everyone else. I don’t get invited to things other kids do and I feel trapped in my own body since my mom is the only one who can help me communicate so far. A service dog would help me in many ways. My seizures are triggered by many things, often by feelings. Having a built-in best friend who doesn’t care that I can’t talk out loud yet or if I do something weird would give me confidence to enter a room full of “normal” kids and help me stay calm. Staying calm keeps seizures away, which keeps me safe and on less medication. It would keep my sensory overload down and prevent panic attacks from building. It also gives me what I want most—a friend who gets me and loves me just as I am. I know this is a lot of money to spend on a dog. But this dog is coming with over a year of training to help my personal challenges and will be legally able to come with me most places as a medical assistant. And since I’m not-so-secretly Iron Man, I’m thinking that Jarvis is the perfect name for my new sidekick. What do you think? Thank you for anything you can do to help my mom and dad with this expense. You all are officially on #TeamOllieandJarvis already. If you’re curious about where I’m getting my dog, check out this Puppy Prep series they did with Buzzfeed!

This is a call for support for my funny, smart, caring, hardworking, and tough-as-hell friend Selila. You know those times in your life when things fall apart and you need your community to come through for you? Selila is going through one of those emergency times now. During the pandemic, her teaching job got downsized. She is disabled, and has been dealing with the kinds of long-term medical conditions that could dishearten anyone, but now she’s lost her income and medical insurance. There is zero family support system in her life, only lots of friends who love her but weren't aware of how bad things had gotten. That's who she is; she does her best to keep her problems to herself and handle the situation on her own. More than anything, Selila wants to work, to take care of herself. I have never seen anyone try so hard to find another job, especially someone with her kind of strong resume and excellent job history. She'd gladly work as a waitress, work in a factory, anything, but she can't physically do those things. Due to severe neuropathy from chemo, she needs leg braces and two canes or a walker to get around, which drastically constrains her mobility. Every week she sends out dozens of job applications to anything available, but nobody is hiring her. She can work just fine from home -- but when other candidates have applied with equivalent qualifications and the ability to walk, somehow they are always "a better fit." She's hustled up a variety of freelance tutoring and writing work, but it barely makes her enough to eat. She can't afford to see a doctor, and she's about to be evicted from her home. Her dog and cat mean everything to her, but you cannot bring animals to a homeless shelter. What do you do when you've got nowhere to go? This messed-up world can leave you out in the cold if you are disabled but there it is: a good person got hit with a lot of bad luck, and fell through the cracks. If we can chip in enough for her to live on while she finds a way through this and on to a new chapter of her life, she'll do it. She's just trying to survive. About Selila: I've known Selila for over twenty years now, and seen her through good times and bad. She tends to be shy at first, but as soon as you get to know her you learn how fun and awesome she is, and her friends love her dearly. Selila lives in a small basement place in Washington, D.C. with her dog and cat, and she's made that space a cozy home for the past two decades. Getting by in the city on an art teacher's salary has been tight, but she's been devoted to that job and to her students, and she's made it work. She has always managed to take care of herself and her beloved animals, to keep forging ahead and going strong no matter what obstacles she's faced down. And over the last few years alone, she's had serious obstacles thrown her way, with half a dozen operations for cancer and increasingly difficult physical challenges. But I've seen her pull herself together shortly after those massive debilitating operations and get right back to work, again and again, because her work ethic is phenomenal and she is dedicated to her students. She never wants pity, never wants to ask for help. I’m here asking for her, because she needs us. As tough as she is, as strong as she’s always been, this is something she can’t go through alone. How we can help: Selila needs a break, she needs to rest and heal, she needs enough of a financial safety net to give her a chance to find a way forward. She’s going to leave DC and come stay with us for a little while, just to have some breathing space where she can regroup, recalibrate, figure out what comes next, without the constant threat of homelessness hanging over her head. We've got a good guest room, but it's only a temporary housing solution. So what I'm asking for is a crowdfund to help Selila cover moving expenses, as she packs up her whole adult life. She needs to get a storage unit, so she won't have to lose absolutely everything. She needs to pay her utility bills to keep the lights on through November. She will need money to put down for rent once she finds someplace else to live. And it would be good if she were able to cover a few living expenses like food and medicine for her and her animals. With all the painful challenges she's facing, having the security of some cash in the bank can make all the difference to help life seem possible again. I know times are rough for most everyone right now, but if we all chip in together, we can keep her afloat until she's able to rally and do it on her own. We have to take care of each other. For anything you can do to help, thank you.
