Hi everyone! My name is Ali Williamson, and I’ve set up this page for my dear friends. Meet the Trammell family: Kent + Alisha, Smith, Fisher, and Virginia! Their middle son, Fisher, has been diagnosed with Severe Aplastic Anemia [SAA]. Aplastic Anemia is a deficiency of all types of blood cells caused by failure of bone marrow development. It is a rare condition, less than 20,000 per year. With SAA, Fisher is very susceptible to infection, and every day, "no big deal" things like the common cold are extremely dangerous. They make weekly, almost daily, trips to the clinic. Recently, there have been more trips to the ER for fevers. Fisher is experiencing pain, ulcers, and sores from treatment and side effects of SAA. But, as some of us know, "Sunshine Fisher" continues to keep a positive attitude. So, where is Fisher in treatment/what are his treatment options? A. Bone marrow transplant (BMT) from a full sibling match. Unfortunately, after testing, neither sibling is a match. B. An unrelated fully matched donor. Fisher has one match, but unfortunately, that person is unavailble to donate at this time. So if you haven’t yet, please consider joining BeThe Match . C. Immunosuppressant Therapy (IST). Fisher has received this treatment, and we hope this treatment begins working SOON! But until it does, we wait and pray. D. Haplo Transplant. A half matched donor, meaning Kent or Alisha giving a bone marrow transplant. The biggest encouragement we have is that even though they are at plan C in Fisher's treatment, God doesn’t have a plan A, B or C. He only has The Plan. And even though that doesn’t make it easier, we know God loves Fisher and He has a plan to prosper him and not to harm him, a plan to give him hope and a future. And we believe in that plan above all others. The Trammell Family values your prayers, and I invite you to pray for Fisher as often as you think to. I started this page in honor of Fisher and the Trammells to ask for financial support as they continue to battle through. While there are certainly other tangible ways to serve our friends, at this point, it would benefit them the most. Donations will be used for medical bills, medication costs, child care, medical equipment, and unexpected expenses that have continued to arise. Thank you so much for your generosity! #PrayforFisher

My name is Dan Albert, and I am trying to raise money for my niece, Melody Albert, who has been battling a rare form of muscular cancer called Synovial Sarcoma. This cancer is typically found in children and young adults, with only about 250 cases diagnosed each year. Melody is a vibrant, intelligent and loving 30 year old who has dedicated all of her free time to helping animals through a local rescue. This spring she started feeling discomfort and weakness in her left shoulder and arm. After multiple blood tests, MRIs, and X-Rays, she was quickly diagnosed with synovial sarcoma and referred to Dana Farber Cancer Institute in Boston. They are the best of the few who treat this rare cancer and treatment there was determined to be her best chance at survival. Fortunately, chemotherapy could be started at home. By June she was in-patient at St. Francis for her first of two aggressive, week long treatments. To further shrink her tumor, her doctors insisted that she stay in Boston for 5 weeks of radiation treatment alongside two weeks of chemo. She was determined, however, to make it home on the weekends to see her beloved dogs, boyfriend, and family regardless of how sick she was. Since her first consultation at Dana Farber, her doctors were very clear that every effort would be made to save her her life, but there would be significant physical sacrifices in order for that to happen. It was determined they would have to remove her arm, shoulder, clavicle, two ribs, and her thyroid in order to eradicate the tumor. In October, her doctors and surgical team from both Dana Farber and Brigham Womens Hospital successfully preformed the 8 hour surgery. From start to finish, she received the best care possible. Her post op MRI determined that she was officially cancer free. It should be noted that Melody has taken every step of this terrifying journey with dignity, strength and courage. She remains incredibly upbeat and positive, while dealing with a roller coaster of emotions that go with mentally healing after this type of trauma. She is in intense physical pain and coping with the unimaginable repercussions of phantom limb syndrome. We are incredibly grateful she is here with us. We are doing our best to offer all the emotional and financial support we possibly can, but a lifetime wouldn’t be enough to pay off the medical bills that have accumulated and notices from debt collection agencies have already started coming in. She has been out of work since starting chemotherapy and the combined loss of income, costs for chemo, radiation, surgery and travel make this situation that much more devastating. I have set up a go fund me in her name in hopes that she can pay off those debts and focus on what really matters; living a long and happy life.

FOR THE LOVE OF CHRISTY... This is the story of our sister Christy Dennis Gilday’s battle with cancer and why we need your help. Christy was diagnosed with Stage 4 metastatic triple-negative breast cancer and has exhausted her treatment options in our home state of Tennessee. She is currently undergoing experimental treatment in Houston, Texas, at MD Anderson Cancer Center, and we are fundraising to help with her housing and travel expenses. When Christy had her mammogram done, they found a small lump in her right breast. At the time, the radiologist did not think it was anything to be concerned about, so nothing was done about it. Soon, Christy could feel the lump by touch and realized she needed to do something about it. When she got in to see the doctor, the lump had become large enough that she could see it on the surface of the skin, and the skin had even started to change color. She was diagnosed with Stage III triple-negative breast cancer. It’s very fast-growing, very aggressive and very hard to treat. Christy started chemo, and here came the hair loss, the nausea, the skin problems, the nail problems, the fatigue, the chills, the intestinal problems, the pains, the insomnia, and all the other issues that come with this treatment. The next step was the mastectomy, followed by radiation. Now it was time just to wait to see how it went while she healed. Then came the first new nodule at the incision site. Then the next and the next and the next. The oncologist did not think it was the cancer but maybe from the radiation. The radiologist did not think it was from the radiation but maybe from the cancer. No one was sure what it was. At this point, it was time to head to a bigger hospital for more help. Once Christy got there, they ruled out more radiation, and the treatment plan became chemo and immunotherapy. Then in stepped the insurance company. They said a big N-O to the immunotherapy. Too new. Not proven yet. Too expensive. NOT APPROVED. DENIED. So a new plan was made to start the rounds of a new chemo med and see how she responded to it. At first, things seemed to be going well. Christy’s newly regrown little curls were gone. The infusions were harder and more debilitating. The side effects were worse. As awful as it was, the hope was that it was really getting in there and killing off the cancer cells. After a few rounds of the new chemo med, the nodules were not getting better. Christy’s chest started to swell, sores came up, and they started to ooze and weep. It became inflamed, and Christy began to have more and more pain. She started having a harder time breathing. Christy was not responding to this new treatment. The oncologist was able to get Christy into a clinical trial. It involved another chemo med, but along with it, she was finally going to get the immunotherapy drug that her insurance company had denied. We hoped and prayed and waited. By this time, the wounds on Christy’s chest were excruciating. It felt like acid had been poured on her skin. The pain and swelling went all the way up to her shoulder, around to her back, below her rib cage. The nodules had seemed to coalesce into one large mass on her chest. It was harder and harder for her to breathe. Christy was in so much pain that she could not get out of bed some days. The first round of the new chemo and immunotherapy was the hardest, most debilitating treatment she had had so far. After the second round, Christy’s husband, Mark, stepped in. Christy’s hair was starting to grow back in. Right away, he felt that this new treatment was not working or else Christy’s hair would have already fallen out. The mass on her chest was getting bigger. The pain was getting worse. Christy thought she was starting to develop more nodules closer to her other breast. Something else needed to be done. Christy was able to get an appointment at MD Anderson Cancer Center at the University of Texas. We had high hopes that they would tell us they knew just the thing that was going to fix her right up. We were not that lucky. The only option that Christy has at this point is experimental treatments, so now Christy is starting a Phase I trial of a new treatment where the immunotherapy drugs are injected directly into the tumor. Christy has to stay in Texas during her treatments, which means housing costs, food costs, transportation costs, etc., for the entire time that she is there. This is where we have to ask you all for help and support. Our family will give Christy and her family all the assistance and support that we can, but it may not be enough. We are asking for donations to help cover the expenses of Christy’s time being treated at MD Anderson. You cannot imagine how she has fought this. If there is anything that they can do for her at MD Anderson, she needs to stay there as long as possible. These donations will go straight to Christy's family to help cover the cost of housing, traveling back and forth to Texas, food, and everything needed while she is being treated there. We really hope that you can find it in your heart to help support this wonderful woman and her family. We desperately need them to be able to keep fighting. Anything helps and is so very much appreciated. We pray every day for miracles to happen for Christy and hope that you can be one of those miracles.

On July 10th, 2022, just 6 days before her biggest concert ever, and 2 days after the release of her first album, our niece and daughter, singer/songwriter Emily Clark suffered from debilitating pain in her jaw and face. After going to the emergency room and being sent home with ibuprofen, the pain would not recede and her primary doctor sent her for an emergency MRI and to see a neurologist. She was diagnosed with a brain aneurysm and an extreme case of Trigeminal Neuralgia on July 14th. Trigeminal Neuralgia is sometimes described as the most excruciating pain known in medicine today and causes intense, stabbing, electric shock-like pain which is caused by irritation of the trigeminal nerve, a nerve that sends branches to the forehead, cheek, and lower jaw. Most people who develop Trigeminal Neuralgia have it firing in two of these nerve branches during an episode, and Emily has all seven firing at once. An action as routine and minor as brushing your teeth, eating, or even the wind can trigger an attack and immobilize the person who suffers from it. Needless to say, a singing career is a long shot for someone experiencing these unpredictable episodes. The neurologists prescribed anti-convulsive medications to her and she was able to perform that weekend, but since then, in spite of increasing the dosage, her attacks have worsened and side effects from the medication have become more severe. Her doctors in Montana referred her to a neurosurgeon at the University of Washington who performed a barrage of tests and due to the severity of her case suggested she have brain surgery to treat the compression of the nerve. Her surgery is scheduled for Dec 2nd, 2022. It will be six weeks to two months before she is able to work at her job or lift more than 10-15 lbs, not to mention continue to develop her musical career, travel to perform, promote her album and follow her dreams. She has worked so hard on her singing career over the last 10 years; working her way up from low-paying gigs, singing backup with other musicians, networking, hustling, promoting, songwriting, practicing with her band, paying her band instead of herself, hosting concerts, and contributing her funds and time to her musical community. She finished recording the main tracks of her album on March 15, 2020, just 5 days before the pandemic shut everything down and put further production on hold. In spite of that, this summer it seemed like all of that was just starting to pay off. Aside from any uncovered costs associated with the surgery, hospital stay, and paying for a place to stay near the hospital in Seattle for 12-days of outpatient observation, Emily is facing two months with no income or way to pay her monthly expenses as she recovers. While we are still unsure of her medical costs and what is covered by her insurance, we estimate she will need at least $7500 to cover rent, food, travel, lodging, and other miscellaneous expenses in order to make it through this without falling too far behind on what she has worked so hard to build for herself. Thank you so much for reading this far and considering a donation to help a wonderful human being overcome hardship! Kate O'Brien (Auntie) & Amanda Wray (Mom)

Anaplastic Ependymoma, Type A, grade III In December 2016 Mason came home from school sick with flu like symptoms. By Christmas Mason was throwing up every day. After numerous doctor visits, he was diagnosed with anxiety. However, our gut told us it was something much worse! Mason didn’t eat, was losing weight, and started to go numb on the right side of his face . He was terrified to leave his bed because he would throw up. We finally demanded a CT scan and on January 10, 2017 our worst nightmare came true. The doctor said, “your son has a large brain tumor and it looks like cancer.” I’ll never forget those words; in that moment, we thought we were going to lose our son. Next thing you know, we’re in an ambulance being rushed to USCF where our lives changed forever. Mason was given medication and steroids to help ease his pain as we prepared for surgery. The next day he went thru an MRI which confirmed a large tumor near his brain stem which would require a miracle to remove. The chief surgeon Dr. Gupta of UCSF completed emergency surgery on January 13, 2017. It was the longest day of our lives. We had to watch our scared 10 year old little boy go into the surgery room where he underwent a 14 hour brain surgery. We prayed ALL DAY for a miracle. When we got the results that night it was the best outcome we could ever hoped for! The entire tumor was removed with minimal nerve damage! The surgeon predicted he should make almost a full recovery and be about the same ol’ Mason. We shared the news with family & friends in waiting room as we cried & celebrated. The biopsy confirmed that Masons diagnosis was Ependymoma Type A, an extremely rare and aggressive malignant brain tumor. During recovery from surgery Mason battled extreme pain and suffering like we had never seen. The medications made him extremely violent, hallucinate and he rarely slept; this continued for weeks. Mason had to stay at UCSF for almost 2 months while he went through daily rehab to relearn to talk, walk, eat, and much more. In mid February Mason began radiation treatment 5 days a week for 6 weeks. He made a comeback to the baseball field that June & after only 3 games he was back on the mound. Things seemed to be going well, his MRIs every 3 months showed no recurring tumors untill April 2nd, 2018. We were devastated to hear that the tumor had recurred. The MRI revealed that the tumor was in an even worse spot & would be too risky of a surgery. Dr. Gupta recommended Gamma Knife surgery, a very potent radiation beam to basically burn the tumor in hopes of killing it. In mid May of 2018, Mason got the surgery done & we were able to bring him home that day without any side effects, amazingly. UCSF would continue to monitor the second tumor every 3 months . In May 2019, we were shocked when his MRI revealed growth in the second tumor that previously received gamma knife surgery. Mason went home upset. We were once again devastated. Masons medical team requested to re-scan in 8 weeks to ensure the tumor was in fact growing, and not just changing form. Unfortunately, on July 29th 2019 a MRI detected that the tumor had almost doubled in size! Mason was scheduled for surgery 7 days later. On August 6th, 2019 Mason underwent a second brain surgery to remove the tumor. After 8 hours of surgery, his surgeon was able to remove the entire tumor once again! Mason’s recovery went very well and he was discharged from the hospital 5 days after surgery!! In November 2019 Mason started complaining of back pain. His scans didn’t detect anything concerning and they continued to watch his spine until a scan in July 2020 detected what we knew was there (since Mason began experiencing excruciating pain by then), 2 tumors in his lower spine. They also detected 2 new spots in his brain. Mason had surgery in September to remove the two tumors in his spine. During surgery they found a malignant substance running all throughout his spine that they were unable to get with surgery. It was recommended that he receive full brain and spine proton radiation. We had to relocate down south for 3 months for this treatment. Mason lost his hair, was extremely sick, throwing up several times a day, and lost significant weight. For treatment his head was locked to a table for 45 minutes while feeling extremely ill...sometimes even having to take a break to throw up. Treatment ended in December 2020 and we returned home. Mason remained sick for months and in April 2021 his symptoms increased to the point of being hospitalized. It was detected that the radiation caused severe necrosis (swelling) in his brain. Mason is currently battling extreme effects from radiation necrosis and has two remaining tumors in his brain that are being closely watched (one inside his brainstem). His symptoms include numbness on his entire left side, paralysis on his right side of his face, difficulty swallowing, lost vision in his right eye, severe nerve pain, and inability to walk, he can’t sit up on his own, and has slurred speech. Mason is in pain everyday. We try to manage it with medications, but sometimes we can’t. In addition, all the medications have side effects, especially the steroids that have caused him to swell up and gain almost 50 lbs. Recently (February 2022), Mason developed a severe infection in his right kidney (it is suspected to be from chronic steroid use) that required emergency surgery. He stayed in the hospital for almost a week and will required an additional surgery 6 weeks later to remove the stent that was placed to help drain the infection. I’m May 2022, despite Mason’s ongoing pain, he was determined to participate in an inpatient intensive rehabilitation program where he stayed in the hospital for 5 weeks to work on his mobility. This program helped to jumpstart his goal of walking, but it has proved to be a slow process and we continue daily rehabilitation services in an outpatient setting now. Mason has so many ongoing struggles that he faces with such dignity. He currently remains in a wheel chair, has lost hearing in his right ear, has issues with vision in his right eye, nerve pain throughout his body, bi-weekly infusions at the hospital, daily physical and occupational rehab, kidney issues, a new diagnosis of osteonecrosis in his shoulders, and ongoing pain throughout his body. Mason also still has a tumor INSIDE of his brainstem that has been stable for almost 2 years now. He receives quarterly MRI of his brain and spine. Despite all of this, Mason still remains positive and has many passions that he is motivated to pursue in life!! He has been drastically improving after taking some very expensive supplements so we are fundraising to cover these costs and to keep his body healing. Thank you!!

This is a Go Fund Me, for our dear uncle Faisal Moid, a young father of three, battling Central Nervous System Large B-Cell (Brain) Lymphoma. He was not only an amazing husband but a great father, brother, uncle, son, and great friend to all those around him. In early 2022, Faisal started to show some symptoms like nausea, vomiting and seizures which indicated there was something wrong. He was rushed to the hospital where they diagnosed him with Encephalitis or brain inflammation. He was kept at the hospital and then transferred to a rehabilitation center to assist him further. However, things started to get out of hand and further tests were needed. After a discussion with the panel of doctors, he was moved to another hospital. They completed a brain biopsy, from which it was confirmed that he has CNS Large B- Cell (Brain) Lymphoma. During this entire process, he was placed on the ventilator as he wasn’t breathing well on his own and suffered from pneumonia many times. Eventually required placement of Tracheostomy, which is a tube in the tracheae and a stomach tube called percutaneous gastrostomy for him to stay on the ventilator for an extended period. This also provided him with nutrition via a stomach tube as he is unable to swallow food on his own. The medical team discussed the future of his health and life with his family. It was suggested to start systemic chemotherapy consisting of three drugs including high-dose methotrexate following a specific protocol for the treatment of his Central Nervous system large b-cell lymphoma. So far, he has received 4 cycles of chemotherapy with breaks in between. There were days when he wouldn’t open his eyes at all CNS Large B-Cell Lymphoma is a very rare condition, it carries a grim prognosis if left untreated. The past 8 months have been especially challenging for Faisal and his family, as they have been dealing with Faisal’s Cancer treatment and the big change in their life. His kids are very young and extremely close to their father. His family is utterly devastated and depressed, however, they haven’t given up hope. Faisal has no idea of where he is, and who he is. He is showing signs that he wants to fight cancer and be there for his family. Faisal’s panel of doctors has suggested a treatment plan, which has shown improvement in other patients with the same diagnosis. Unfortunately, this treatment will take time and his body's reaction to the treatment will confirm what the next steps would be. His treatment is not fully covered by health insurance as he was self-employed. He is still in the hospital at the University of Pennsylvania, today is day #68, and he has started to show some signs of improvement with the chemotherapy. He will be ready for the transition from the Hospital to the Rehabilitation center. He would continue to require admission back to the hospital from time to time to receive his cycles of chemo. For the foreseeable period, which can range from 6 months to a year. The insurance plan only covers a certain portion of his medical and rehabilitation and once Faisal is in a condition to be moved back to his home, the medical and rehab wouldn’t be covered by the insurance plan anymore. He has a long road to recovery, and once he can go home, rehab and medical team visits are necessary. Faisal’s Financial Situation Faisal, being a self-employed contractor, has not been able to work ever since his first admission to the hospital in early 2022. His wife has been trying her best to do a full-time job to maintain their finances. When she should be looking after her husband, she has been working 40 hours a week to make ends meet. His two older kids have been working 10 hours per week to assist their mother. They don’t have any government assistance. Due to their financial challenges, they need all the help they can get for now and for his future treatments. Our Goal for This Fundraiser: The goal of this fundraiser is to: 1. Be able to pay his remaining hospital bills after discharge 2. Be able to pay for treatments and medications that the insurance plan doesn’t cover. 3. Be able to get rehabilitation assistance at his home once he is moved back. This treatment plan is the only hope for the survival and recovery of Faisal. Your donation will give Faisal and his family the support they need. We appreciate any assistance that you can offer.

In March of 2021, Jeff was diagnosed with Stage 4 Colon Cancer with Peritoneal Carcinomatosis. Over one and a half years have passed since his initial diagnosis and their need for prayers and financial support are critical. Following his diagnosis Jeff had to leave his union construction job and recently Christina had to take unpaid leave from work to support and care for him. This Go Fund Me Account will provide financial support to Jeff and Christina to pay medical expenses and monthly bills. Jeffrey’s Story: The family planned a vacation to Cocoa Beach, Florida in the spring of 2021. Prior to vacation Jeff was having a slight pain in his abdomen and attempted to see a doctor; due to unforeseen wait times; however, Jeff was not able to get an appointment with a doctor. Shortly into their vacation the pain in Jeff’s abdomen became unbearable and they went to an Emergency Room in Florida. Tests revealed fluid in his abdomen and doctors advised that he follow-up with his primary care physician following their trip. Two days later the pain worsened, and Jeff’s abdomen was significantly swollen. They spent half a day at Cape Canaveral Hospital undergoing various tests, results indicating that that Jeff had some sort of cancer in his abdomen and the fluid buildup in his abdomen was a symptom. The doctor advised Jeff to follow-up with a doctor immediately. This news was shocking. Despite pain and symptoms neither Jeff nor Christina expected this news and certainly not while on family vacation with Kaila. After traveling home, Jeff immediately went to a primary doctor who set up a multitude of tests and referrals to oncologists and gastrointestinal specialists. They met with a specialist in colon cancer at the Mayo Clinic, which proved to be overwhelming as the doctor would not perform surgical procedures and did not offer alternative care options. Wanting a second opinion they met with an oncologist at Regions Hospital Cancer Care Clinic, which provided a path forward and more positive outlook. Jeff’s care team at Region’s prescribed FolFox Chemotherapy as an initial treatment. Jeff began chemo soon as possible and results were good, his cancer started to shrink, and he started to feel better. Following several rounds of chemo, Christina began to research Minnesota surgeons able to perform a debulking surgery with the goal of removing as much cancer as possible from his body. Christina located a surgical team at the University of MN that on October 5, 2021, performed a nearly 6-hour surgery to remove the cancer. Initial surgical results were promising, as Jeff healed quickly and started to feel better. However, a few months later symptoms returned. A scan concluded that the cancer was back. Since his surgery Jeff has experienced daily ups and downs. He as struggled with extreme pain, nausea, and bowl obstructions which resulted in over 15 visits to the emergency room between January and August of 2022. Limiting and changing his diet were no longer sufficient as Jeff’s weight continued to dramatically decrease. Doctors placed a tube in his stomach to allow fluids to drain and in his intestine to provide nutrition. In September 2022 Jeff has been dealing with an obstruction due to Superior Mesenteric Artery Syndrome (SMA) which caused his upper intestine to distend. Currently, doctors are trying to get tube feeding to work, but it is unclear at this point if they will be successful. If not, Jeff will have to move to Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPM), which is IV-provided nutrition. Jeff’s journey and this season of life has not been easy of Jeff, Christina, or Kaila. There have been setbacks and successes and through it all Jeff, Christina, and their families have remained hopeful and positive. Please consider making a financial donation as one method of support for their family. Sincerely, Andrea Steiskal (Christina’s sister)

Following the impact with the truck my father was thrown from his motorcycle approximately 50ft directly into small trees and bushes. He laid there until an unknown angel came to his rescue and dialed 911. From what I’ve been told, when emergency crews arrived, he was not breathing and was clinging to life. The immediate life-saving measures taken by the Southbridge Police Department, Fire Department and EMS personnel were nothing short of remarkable. EMS personnel did their best to stabilize my father before they rushed him to UMass Memorial Medical Center. His injuries include a broken femur, broken pelvis, broken nose, and broken vertebrae in his back and neck. He also suffered 6 broken ribs that punctured his right lung. During his emergency surgery, the medical professionals had to utilize several blood transfusions due to the amount of internal bleeding from the injuries. Thankfully, he has already had several successful surgeries and is responding extremely well to treatment thus far. I learned everything I know from my old man and he once said in sum and substance, if you work hard and continue to remain dedicated to your craft with enough passion, you will reach your goals and nothing will stop you from being successful. Unfortunately, my father needs all of you right now. He will not be able to work for the foreseeable future; he will need extensive care, medical treatments, and therapy to continue his road to recovery. His injuries are life changing, and we still do not know the extent of how these injuries will impact his day-to-day life. I want to take this time to recognize all of you that have taken the time to send your kind words and positive thoughts to our family. Your prayers and continued support are remarkable. My dad will need all the love and financial support he can get during this challenging time. My family is forever grateful! I love you all!

Hello! My name is Betsy Dodge and I am starting this fundraiser to help support my beautiful sister Amy Edwards! This past year has been extremely difficult for her and her family!! Here is her story! In November of 2021, Amy was diagnosed with breast cancer at the age of 42. Because of a strong family history of breast cancer she made the decision to go with a bilateral mastectomy. In January she underwent her mastectomy, along with the first stage of reconstruction. Following her 2 month recovery she developed lymphedema in her right arm, hand, fingers, breast, and torso which required physical therapy for months. In August she had her 2nd stage of reconstruction with the insert of breast implants. Exactly one month after this surgery, Amy developed a serious staph infection in one of her breast implants. Within hours of the infection starting it quickly turned to sepsis and Amy’s life was almost ended. She was rushed to Fairview Southdale for emergency surgery to remove the infected implant. She needed oxygen as her lungs filled up with fluid as did her whole body. Devastatingly, because of the severe sepsis and the toll it took on her body her kidneys shut down and she was now in acute renal failure. She was again in surgery to have a dialysis port inserted into her jugular. With her creatinine numbers being 10x the normal amount she started dialysis immediately. She continued on dialysis for the 15 days she was hospitalized. Half way thru her hospitalization she also acquired a secondary infection called C. Diff due to the strong antibiotics she was getting intravenously. Following her release the drs feared her other breast implant was becoming infected as well so she again went under the knife to have it removed. She was then started on outpatient dialysis at 5am every other day and had to travel an hour to get there. She received outpatient dialysis for weeks until her kidney numbers were safe enough to taper off. Because of the severe damage to her kidneys, Amy will alway be in stage 2 renal failure but the symptoms can be managed at this time without the need for dialysis. Two weeks ago he dialysis tunnel catheter was removed and she can now concentrate on regaining strength and her health. She battles side effects from her damaged kidneys but is thankful to be off of dialysis. Amy has started anti cancer drugs and hormone therapy to reduce her chances of a reoccurrence. Her next surgery for further reconstruction will be in mid December. The financial, emotional, and physical toll this year has taken has been catastrophic for Amy and her family. Amy and Brent have 4 beautiful children and they have all been through so much. If we can lessen the financial burden of her extensive medical bills I know that they would be so grateful!! Thank you so much!!

Hi, my name is Teresa, and I’m setting up a fundraiser to assist with medical and out-of-pocket expenses for the most dynamic and loving person I’ve ever known. Kelcey Wiginton, a 46-year-old female, originally from Dallas, Texas, has always had the desire to be a caregiver. As a child, she would routinely rescue animals and aspired to become a veterinarian; however, going through college, she found her passion and graduated as a doctor to help people. She went on to treat patients in poverty-stricken areas of Africa. She then took care of patients in Puerto Rico, then in the Middle East, and currently serves in Clearwater, Florida. She donates a huge portion of her time to help students in doctorate programs have the right training and resources to graduate as successful physicians and focuses the majority of her efforts on the best ways to optimize patient results. Early this past summer, Kelcey was blindsided by discovering that she had stage 4 ovarian cancer that had metastasized up into her abdomen. Facing a grim prognosis from traditional US medical hospitals and physicians, she began visiting and treating at different medical and holistic centers that offered her a better potential outcome. However, nothing worked. She was dying. The entire summer, she was unable to leave her bed except to go for treatments, spent July 4th in the hospital, couldn't eat solid food for months, and dropped down to only 85lbs. Always willing to give the shirt off her back to help others, she has been unable to work or volunteer since May, spent all of her savings and maxing out credit cards, trying to find a way to beat the cancer and live. In September 2022, she was rushed by ambulance to a local hospital, with her electrolytes and nutritional levels plummeting. Her tumor was too large, her intestines were unable to function, and she was told there was nothing that could be done to save her. They told her that she was terminal, refused to give her IV nutrition (which was critically necessary at this point), told her to sign a Living Will document, offered only palliative care, and introduced her to the hospital chaplain. Kelcey’s life of serving others was coming to an end. Fortunately for Kelcey, her family refused to give up. They researched and found a facility in Mexico that could offer her life-saving emergency care as well as effective cancer treatments not utilized in the US. In a matter of only 18 hours, they located the facility, packed clothes, bought airplane tickets, drove 1 1⁄2 hours to the airport, flew to San Diego, California, crossed the border, arrived at the hospital and was quickly taken into the ER. It was a huge leap of faith, and it is a miracle that she even made it there. Within the first 24 hours of care, Kelcey was already showing signs of responding. Her electrolyte and nutritional levels were on the rise. She was stabilizing and realizing that she’s got a chance. A few days later, the surgeon went in to try to remove the tumor. Within 30 minutes, the surgeon came out of the room to report to the family that there was nothing he could do because the tumor had wrapped itself around the intestines and organs and had formed a “frozen abdomen”. He said that if he tried to remove it, she would die on his table. The family decided not to attempt it but to begin the oncological and immunological treatments. Within days, Kelcey was transferred to another hospital location and began receiving treatments to fight the cancer directly. She has also been receiving constant IV nutrition until which time her intestines are free of the tumor obstructions and she can begin eating on her own. The good news to report is that her tumor has shrunk from 18cm down to 10cm, and her organs are beginning to function better. The intense pain she has dealt with for nearly five months is reducing, abdominal swelling is reducing, and there is hope! She remains in the Mexico hospital, receiving consistent IV nutrition and other as-needed medications. They do frequent bloodwork to assess any alterations in her health from the cancer treatments and respond immediately. She has had to have two blood transfusions for low hemoglobin and has needed other additional treatment modifications. 2 weeks into her hospital care, she acquired a bacterial infection on top of everything else, which required high doses of antibiotics. Between multiple tubes in and out of her body, numerous diagnostic imaging scans, ongoing treatments, requirements of remaining hospitalized for the time being, and the overall discouragement of the situation, Kelcey has been learning the challenges of being a "care receiver" rather than a "care giver" and is trying to keep her spirits up. Many people have been praying for Kelcey and sending her love and sweet messages. She still requires the IV nutrition until she can eat solid food. She will need additional cancer treatments, more diagnostic scans, surgery for tumor removal, and post-surgical treatments to ensure the cancer is fully gone. This is projected to take another 8-10 weeks and the ongoing costs of treatment is overwhelming. The debt incurred so far surpassed $100,000 and is projected to be approximately $100,000-150,000 more. As one who has always taken care of other people, she would never consider asking others to help pay for her care. However, her life depends on it and, as her friend, I am asking for her. Please consider helping Kelcey in her greatest time of need. Any amount, large or small will be greatly appreciated. God bless.

Hey friends and virtual friends! I have literally ran out of options for getting my son the help he deserves. If you have followed our story for any length of time, you’ll know that we have tried EVERYTHING we know to try. There is so much unknown in Drew’s diagnoses. We have known since birth that he has a rare condition called Cerebellar Hypoplasia. This is a neurological condition where the cerebellum is off-centered or too small and as a result he has bad eye sight and very bad balance issues. He isn’t your sports player. We started at a neurologist and behavior specialist at a very early age and tried medicine after medicine after medicine. We also narrowed down ADHD, ODD, SPD, etc. Studies also started showing that behavioral issues were related to his cerebellum issue. After years of no success, I felt the Lord tug at my heart to take him off all medication for that timeframe. So, I did, and we coasted through the next few years. He started going to a behavioral type school and it comes with its challenges (as in, picking up behaviors from others that once didn’t exist), but what do you do when he was pretty much kicked out the public school system and you don’t have the option to homeschool? So, we lived day by day and somehow managed. In May 2021, Drew had an episode at school where he was threatening to hurt his sister when he got home, etc. As a result, we were forced to take him to the local ER for a psych eval. After 5 or so days, no one would accept him (due to no available beds), so we were sent home. That entire thing was literally a joke and where I learned about the many flaws of our healthcare system. Y’all, it’s bad. After that, I got him in with a psychiatrist and literally had to wait almost 7 months (ugh). Back down the medicine route we went, but when I say we were desperate, that was an understatement. The next month we had a baby and it went downhill from there with Drew’s behavior. Some of the things we have experienced I’m almost too embarrassed to say, but it’s our life. Let’s just say that he has been getting rough with the baby, the dogs, his sister, and now more and more at school. It’s hard to explain as it’s not all aggression, a lot of it is impulsive and I know that’s hard to understand unless you truly know my boy. Having the baby really did a number on him as far as adjustment, but we worked extremely hard from the get go to ensure that Drew got the attention he needed...and in fact, the baby doesn’t get enough attention because of Drew. But, here we are. As a result of all this behavior, I chose on my own to try to get him in a mental hospital. In July, he was admitted for 6 days and again we got absolutely nowhere. All I gained out of that was a $1300 hospital bill along with Drew spiraling out of control. In the past few weeks, we’ve seen a huge spike in his bad behavior at school. Just to help you understand I’ll list a few... making verbal threats of killing (kid is scared of everything, but it’s not taken lightly, especially in a school setting), he backtalks (not like your typical teenager), cusses like a sailor, throws rocks and items at the school staff, and the worst one...making himself throw up and then he throws and spits it at others. Sooooo embarassing. Anyways, fast forward to this past Monday and the threats and such started again and off to the local ER we went again. I knew the drill and in all reality knew it would be pointless, but if you know how messed up the healthcare system is, then you know it’s all about checking off boxes. So, we went through with it, not to mention I had no choice because he was placed under a 1013. Several places were considering him until they realized we had insurance (like, are we kidding!) ...24 hours later he was accepted at a place 5 hours away AND within 12 hours I was called to say they were not a good fit for him. Are. We. Kidding??? So, off we go to pick him up tomorrow. And no, they won’t transport him home I created this go fund me because Drew has had door after door closed with excellent opportunities in front of him, but because we have insurance and little things like that, he becomes ineligible. REALLY?! I’ve tried for social security, disability, you name it! DENIED! We’ve been told there is a waiver that kids like Drew could benefit from and usually get approval (based on all the above), BUT it’s a very long process and likely gets denied multiple times before getting approval. Heard it takes almost 2 years to gain approval and the paperwork is insane. It’s literally 3inches worth of paperwork to fill out along with contacting every Dr he has been to in his entire life for statements and records. My psychiatrist has mentioned a local lawyer that specializes in this Katie Beckett waiver submission, but it’s roughly $1200. I’ve never asked for a penny in my entire life because I feel like this is my burden to carry (and because it’s a pride thing), but y’all, we are desperate. The amount of bills we have for Drew are ridiculous so we don’t have the $1200 just laying around ...Many of you ask me over and over what you can do for me and I always decline any help. It’s still even hard for me to do this, but again, we are beyond desperate. If we can get approved for Katie Beckett, then he gets put at the top of every list and can get some ABA therapy underway MUCH faster. Everyone (drs) is saying that no matter his true diagnoses, that no doubt he would benefit from this therapy. ________________________________ If you feel led to help, it would help us find the sweet boy we know we have deep down in there. It would help give our boy a chance at a life worth living. It would help us get him the doctors he needs, the help he deserves and the life we know he should be able to grab ahold of. At the very least, your donation will help us get one step closer to achieving all this and more. If you can’t give or don’t feel led, we understand. In place of a donation we only ask for your prayers as we navigate these next few months with Drew. I long for the day I can update on Drew that, “this time it worked!” But unfortunately that’s not the update I get to give quite yet. XOXO- Tessa

We are Dave and Donna Fenty, raising funds for our daughter Danielle. She has just turned 18 and is now eligible to receive a groundbreaking set of treatments called TMS or transcranial magnetic stimulation. This new treatment is non-invasive and uses magnets to stimulate areas of the brain that are either too pronounced or not being stimulated enough. Danielle suffers from ADHD, OCD, anxiety disorder and Autism Spectrum Disorder. Hi, my name is Joe and I am hoping to garner donations to help my dog Beau's recovery while also donating every penny of surplus to non-profit animal blood banks. Beau is a yellow labrador who has brought happiness to the many faces he has come across. He will be turning 4 years old this coming 11/27. My sister entered a horrific scene on Monday (11/7/2022) at around 8:30 am. Beau was found in my room vomiting immeasurable amounts of blood. I had already left for my responsibilities that day and could not drop what I was doing. With my sister and dad monitoring Beau and keeping me updated throughout the day to see if any improvement could be made, Beau had become increasingly limp and unresponsive. As each hour went by to see if his symptoms improved, Beau remained unlike his energetic and attentive self. He was unable to take more than a few steps at a time. As the day went on, I finally arrived home at 7 pm and was not greeted by the loud barking and excitement I usually would have received from him. Instead, I had to find where in the house Beau was. I entered the living room and saw him stand on all fours but with his head down and unable to make eye contact with me. At this point, the seriousness of this morning had grown alarmingly. Beau had laid down to rest on his side for an hour after I started monitoring him when suddenly his eyes opened wide and rolled back. His legs began to perform running-like motions while still lying on his side, followed by his body stiffening up as he began urinating. I am no professional, but I believe I had just experienced my dog having a seizure before my eyes. At his moment, I called my sister, and I scrambled to get Beau in the car for emergency help. At 9 pm the only available help we could find was Healing Hearts Emergency Animal Hospital in Laguna Hills, CA. Beau had to be carried in and after a brief explanation of his clinical presentations that day to the vet tech, Dr.Berschauer and team went straight to work. 3 long hours were spent in the waiting room as they worked to stabilize Beau's condition. A staff member had guided us to an exam room by midnight and we met Dr. Berschauer and began investigating any possible explanation for Beau's condition. Beau had been cleared of any likely tumors, ulcers, and rat poison ingestion. Other possible reasons can include ingesting NSAIDs but my household's testimonials have ruled out even that. Thorough screening could not give us any leads to the source of the cause. At midnight, it had been discussed that a possible blood transfusion would be put into play. Beau's hematocrit levels at admission was 13%. Normal for dogs is 35%. After discussing Beau's treatment plan and leaving Beau in Healing Hearts' hands, I received a chilling call an hour later from the hospital saying they were moving forward with an emergency blood transfusion. Shortly after his first blood transfusion, Beau's hematocrit levels rose to 26%. Just as things were looking great, Beau began a terrifying episode of bloody diarrhea all over the hospital floor. The doctor estimated at least a 2-liter loss or more. His hematocrit levels were down to 16%. The photographic documentation of the scene had led everyone to believe that the outcome would not look good. As we entered the early 7 o clock morning of Tuesday, 11/8, I received another phone call from the doctor, being notified that Beau's prognosis was not the brightest as the night and early hours of the morning went on. Beau had come close to depleting the hospital's blood and platelet transfusion supply. I could not hold myself as I had to return to my responsibilities for the day, knowing I could not be by his side. Other possible treatment plans were discussed, as the supplies were primarily allocated to Beau. If Beau could not stabilize by the end of the day, things would get ugly. As I went about my day, I received another phone call at 11 am. Beau had continued having bloody diarrhea and was hitting the last bag of blood transfusion supplies. Everyone at the hospital was now restless as I was. I spent my lunch break trying to collect my emotions while also being unable to control them. I prayed and prayed for his second chance. I prayed not to receive another phone call from the doctor until I visited Beau that night. Nighttime came around that Tuesday and I rushed to see Beau. As I entered the room, I found my boy with catheters hooked up to his paws but looking tremendously brighter since I had left him the night before. My prayers were answered and heard. Things were finally looking great. One of the biggest blessings and miracles in all my life. I had been informed that Beau had stabilized as Tuesday continued. I was told to remain cautiously optimistic about his condition. Many test screenings and vital checks were performed. We were finally all able to see the light at the end of the tunnel. Some workers had worked a 24-hour shift to remain by Beau's side and ensure his vitals had stabilized. Tuesday ended with a bit of progress. Wednesday comes around, and Beau is looking closer to normal now. Plans are already being arranged to bring him home very soon. The stool seems watery and, at times, solid at this point. Fortunately no presence of blood. The team's hard work and harsh clinical decision-making finally prevailed and improved Beau's condition. Many of the staff members are in shock at the comeback Beau has made at this point. The intensive gastrointestinal bleed that Beau had endured was costly. We still have no known culprit to the issue. Staff members were inches away from using their certified pets to donate blood to keep Beau alive. As of now, Beau is back to his expressive and happiness-spreading self. So with that, I politely ask for any help you can offer. Any donations or sharing of this story is just as helpful to me. The amount I have aimed for will entirely go toward his medical costs. Any money received after his medical expenses will be donated to non-profit animal blood banks to support other pets needing emergency blood transfusions. With Beau's story, I hope to raise awareness about how critical it is to research the purpose of non-profit animal blood banks and how they can potentially save your or a loved one's pet one day. Please, any donation or sharing of this story is much appreciated. Thank you for taking the time to read Beau's second chance at life. He will continue meeting random faces and placing a smile on them. Whether you can help or not, please do me a favor and show your fur child some love. Their time with us is temporary as ours is with theirs. Every second spent with them counts. Thank you, and God bless.

We have all heard the phrase “Its not a sprint, it’s a marathon.” I’ve always thought I was able to apply that logic to many challenges but like most of you I never have seen it played out in its truest form until I’ve watched someone I love battle cancer. When that diagnosis hits your family you quickly learn to dread, hate and respect the marathon. In April of 2021 our beautiful Aunt Melanie started her marathon when she was diagnosed with Glioblastoma. We were told, very strictly, not to google it...but I think every single one of us sprinted to our computers to see exactly what kind of beast we were up against. Glioblastoma. Wtf. Glioblastoma: an aggressive form of cancer, incredibly difficult to treat and a cure so far away. While the rest of us stopped breathing, questioned the accuracy of the diagnosis and asked the universe why this was happening...Melanie put on her battle gear. She told us all how much she loved us – then she got to work on the first leg of her race. Her first brain surgery was in May 2021 and accompanied by those she loves most – Mel cranked her favorite tunes in the car and danced and sang all the way to the hospital. Not then, and not a single time since, has she let this disease get the best of her. Her heart is still in charge, even if her brain isn’t cooperating – and she has protected us all along the way. Mel began radiation and chemotherapy with her fiancé, mother, daughter and siblings by her side every step of the way...and Mel kept smiling for them. She smiled for all of us. She smiled so much it was hard to see her as a sick person. In July of 2021 Melanie went in for a second surgery due to an infection within her skull caused by the first surgery. Not that any of her surgeries were expected, but this one threw everyone for a loop. It seemed like such an unnecessary (avoidable?) step back. As with every marathon you will encounter hurdles so like the champion she is she carried on. Surgeries and treatments in the COVID era often meant she faced hospital stays alone with only her phone to communicate. She texted and called from her hospital bed – spewing love and positivity to all of us. Asking us about OUR lives and insisting she was ok. We stayed away so we didn’t get her sick, but we took solace in knowing that our beautiful bombshell was going to be ok. Following 6 months of chemotherapy, March 2022, her tumor returned. They scheduled yet another brain surgery to remove as much as they could. Mel texted from her hospital bed again, sending lots of love and happiness. Everything was still going to be ok. Just a minor set back, they’ll take out everything they can – and she’ll be back home with her family where she belongs. She’s done it before, she can absolutely do it again. June 2022 her doctors did a post-op image to see what April’s surgery accomplished. Which, unfortunately, wasn’t good news. Melanie’s tumor was progressing. Her texts came in stronger than ever – all the love and positive vibes – but there was no more fooling those outside of her home. This beast is growing, but so was the fight in Mel. In July Melanie and her team of supporters packed themselves up and headed to the Dana Farber Institute in Boston to be evaluated for clinical trial options. She had yet another surgery that removed about 98% of the tumor and then hit it hard with a clinical trial 2 weeks later. 98% of the tumor? That’s practically 100% surely the clinical trial could zap out that 2%, right?? Just a few days ago Melanie returned to the Dana Farber institute to see about that 2%. The tumor progressed, clinical trial therapy was not working, and therefore no longer an option. Our hearts are struggling to understand Mel’s brain and what this all means now. What we do know is that Melanie’s marathon continues, and she will be starting immunotherapy treatment from the Syracuse location in coordination with the Roswell Cancer Center. Melanie has unconditional support from her family, community and friends all over the country but these surgeries, trials and everything in between (as too many of you know that have fought or helped someone fight this beast that is cancer)...its expensive. Very expensive. We would love to wave a magic wand over Mel’s beautiful brain and heal her from the inside out, but there is no wand, if there was her family would have found it by now. But we can help in this leg of her race and run next to her. A monetary donation isn’t a cure, but Mel’s brain has some healing to do and as the fight continues so do the costs associated with the marathon.. Please sponsor our beautiful badass in the fight of her life. I promise she would be the first to jump in line to help you <3 To learn more about Glioblastoma please click the link below: <URL>

Calling all “Prayer Warriors” and “Giving Hearts” to come together for our dear friend Dorian Boliaux. We’ve known Dorian for over 33 years since we first began our careers as Flight Attendants for United Airlines. She is an extraordinary person of faith, family, love and true friendship, and God sure knew what He was doing when he brought us together many years ago. Unfortunately, Dorian’s world was turned upside down in September when she was diagnosed with Multiple Myeloma, a blood cancer of the plasma cell. Plasma cells in your bone marrow produce antibodies (proteins) to help make up the immune system. She was also diagnosed with AL Amyloidosis, a rare disease found in the bone marrow, causing proteins called amyloids to build up in the organs and tissues throughout the body, potentially causing organ failure. These are related to the immune system that produces antibodies to fight infections. It is a rare combination of diseases that only affects about 3-4 people out of 1 million. Dorian has a long road ahead of her while undergoing treatment. Her doctors have told her that she will be unable to work for the next year and a half due to her extensive chemotherapy treatments and exposure as a Flight Attendant. If you know Dorian, you know she is one of the hardest-working people you’ll ever meet. As a sole provider, losing her only source of income while adding costly medical bills to her monthly expenses will cause her extreme financial hardship. Dorian was shocked by this devastating diagnosis. She has always been very healthy and was utterly unaware of the illness in her body. She attributed some recent minor health issues to jet lag and being on her feet too much while flying around the world. By the AMAZING GRACE OF GOD, HE surrounded Dorian with angels on earth who recognized something wasn’t right with her. With their help and consultation, a sequence of miraculous events began, and God Himself guided her path directly to the brilliant doctors at The Mayo Clinic in Jacksonville, Florida. “All things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are called according to His purpose.” Romans 8:28. Diagnosing this combined disease is extremely difficult and often delayed, typically taking several months and several different doctors to diagnose. God was watching out for Dorian, and she was diagnosed in a few days! She is now receiving the best possible medical treatments while under the care of world-renowned doctors who happen to specialize in MM/Amyloidosis at one of the few clinics in the world that treat this combination of diseases. Wow, what a miracle, God is so good! She is currently receiving aggressive Chemotherapy and monoclonal antibodies. Once complete, she may need to follow up with additional bone marrow/stem cell treatments to cleanse her bone marrow and eradicate all cancer. While her case is very complicated, her doctors feel this was caught early, and after seeing some initial results from the chemo, they are feeling very optimistic. Another miracle! Despite this life-changing diagnosis, Dorian’s faith is stronger than ever, and she truly feels the power of God and the Holy Spirit surrounding her, guiding her every step. Her love and belief in Jesus cannot and will not be shaken. She knows she is never alone...He is with her always...His unconditional love will carry her through. She is very optimistic and faces her illness with incredible courage, strength, honesty and amazing grace. It is no coincidence that only days before her diagnosis, Dorian was on a layover in South Africa and while on a safari, she was fearlessly walking with the Lions. “A Lion, mighty among beasts, who is fearless and retreats before nothing” Proverbs 30:30. The Lion is an emblem of Christ, and just as Dorian walked with the Lions, Christ walks with her... and we all walk together. Dorian is a Chicago native who remained in the Lake Zurich area close to extended family and friends while raising her two beautiful children, Jack and Danyel. Three years ago, United opened a flight attendant base in Orlando, Florida and Dorian relocated to the warmer climate to accommodate her healthy and active lifestyle. After making many new friends and becoming very involved with her church, Dorian decided to make the Florida lifestyle permanent. She recently closed on a home for herself in Daytona Beach. Dorian is fiercely loyal in her faith and lives her life with a humble and giving heart. She is self-sufficient and very proud, not one to ask for help. Therefore, we will ask for her. On her behalf, we call on all “Prayer Warriors” to lift Dorian in prayer daily for complete healing, specifically, praying for God’s miracle to cleanse her bone marrow and restore her organs (heart, kidneys, liver) to perfect health. We are calling on all “Giving Hearts” to donate any amount you can to help relieve the challenging financial burden this is causing her. Through the generosity of friends, family and perhaps a shared cause, we hope to take this heavy burden of stress away from Dorian so she can focus entirely on healing her body and soul. She has been extremely touched and humbled by the outpouring of love, prayers and positive vibes that have been coming her way since her diagnosis. Please keep them coming! She feels so blessed to be in the hands of her incredible doctors and in the hands of God Himself. With her amazing medical team, our continued prayers, and her strong faith, we know she will be healed! From the bottom of our hearts, we thank you very much for your prayers and any contribution you can make to help our beautiful friend in need. Please feel free to share, and God Bless. With our love and gratitude, “Team Dor.”

A message from Geddy's older brother Owen Geddy’s Medical Journey Recently, my 5-year-old brother Geddy was struck by a complicated health tragedy. A problem we first thought could be handled by a nebulizer treatment soon turned into nights at the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU). On October 20th, after the urgent care x-ray showed his right lung had completely collapsed and his chest cavity was full of fluid, Geddy was taken to Children’s Minnesota Hospital ER. After several hours and a CT scan at Children’s, he was transferred to the PICU at Gillette Children’s Hospital via ambulance due to a lack of PICU beds available at Children’s. Since arriving at Gillette, Geddy has been admitted two separate times into the PICU, has had a total of 3 chest tubes inserted, and is now in his fourth week in the hospital as of November 10th. Within a few days, my brother went from a happy 5-year-old child to developing severe necrotizing pneumonia and empyema which caused severe pneumothorax and has a pulmonary abscess. Currently, his lung continues to leak air into his chest cavity and his medical team is trying to allow his lung time to heal in hopes that the leak will seal. Unfortunately, the longer the leak continues, Geddy’s medical team thinks it may confirm he may have a bronchopleural fistula. If this is indeed what is causing the air leak, further intervention will be required and potential surgery. It’s too early at this time, but Geddy’s medical team has indicated that the worst-case scenario could be removal of a lobe or entire lung. Even with the best-case scenario, Geddy is looking at a long road to recovery as at least 50-60% of his lung could have long term damage. Geddy’s Story Geddy is 5 years old and has grown up with a loving mother (Sue), father (Bob), and brothers (Owen and Asher). He is currently a Kindergarten student and loves playing outside in his free time. Geddy has just begun his first sport, soccer, and has wanted to run track, play basketball, and play baseball, all of which will be on hold for a while. He enjoys activities such as fishing, sports, arts and crafts, and going to the park. Geddy has already stated his dream occupation includes becoming an engineer, a shrimp farmer, regular farmer, and an astronaut. Geddy is loved by all family, friends, and educators. I, with the support of my brothers in Sigma Alpha Epsilon at North Dakota State University, have decided to set up this GoFundMe for a couple reasons. The first reason is that no parent should have to worry about the financial hardship of a situation when their child’s life is at stake. The second reason is to show support. Geddy has received letters from fellow classmates, neighbors, educators, and family, all of which puts a smile on his face. With this GoFundMe, I hope to show him the support coming from all of you. The final reason is because I have found that it is okay to ask for help, and in hard times such as this is when you need outside help. Please feel free to help support my family in any way you see fit. We are thankful for every one of you and appreciate your generosity and kindness during these difficult times. Thank you.

Her only cure is a bone marrow transplant. There are less than 1,000 cases of Griscelli's in the US and not a very well-known disease. Friends, family, and lovers of good causes. Here goes nothing. I write to you humbly asking for help. We have an opportunity that could be incredibly life-changing for our family, but we can’t do it without you. Brady has been approved for a therapeutic neurological program that is not yet FDA-approved, so therefore not covered by insurance, meaning it’s cash pay. The amount due for this opportunity is $55k, which doesn’t include travel, lodging or food. Your eyes probably popped out of your head just now, as did mine when I first heard that figure. After speaking with the program’s developer personally and understanding how long & how much it has taken to get this program into practical use, the dollar figure seems appropriate. Still, it is so much money! So here I am begging you for some of yours. For those of you who don't know about our Brady, let me give you a quick backstory on how we got where we are today. Brady’s birth was a difficult c-section; his head was lodged under my liver, and he was in the frank breech position. His first Apgar score was only 4, which means he wasn’t getting as much oxygen as he could have. His development was slow as a baby, but by age one he was doing everything but walking & talking, and he was the happiest little man. Brady started having seizures just before 14 months of age, and things quickly took a turn for the worse. He wouldn’t breathe during seizures, and in the very beginning he ended up on a ventilator for a week before he tried to breathe again. We repeatedly thought we were going to lose him. He was just a tiny baby, but the doctors threw so many meds at him desperately trying to get seizures to stop and prevent more bouts of apnea. Seizure meds didn't help him, and Brady’s little body didn’t metabolize them like it should, so he was a tiny zombie most of the time. One year, 3 PICU stays, and about 10 floor room stays later, we learned about cannabis to treat seizures and decided to pack up and move to Colorado from Kansas City. We weaned Brady off all the seizure meds. It was the best decision we’ve ever made, and we truly believe that if we had stayed the course in KC, he would have died. Still, the beginning of life in Colorado was rough because when we got here, Brady started seizing constantly. The doctors chalked it up to the altitude and sent us on our way. About two months later Brady spiked a fever, and we ultimately learned he had a bleeding ulcer. That had been the cause of the constant seizing since the move, but the damage was already done. All those seizures caused serious brain damage. He lost all development and couldn’t even hold his head up anymore. He was exclusively tube-fed. He had no smile, no expression, and we tried pharmaceuticals again with no luck. We finally found the strain of cannabis that helped to prevent his seizures, and we set off on our new journey to get Brady moving again. Around this time I was diagnosed with breast cancer, so now we had to deal with the issues surrounding chemo & the surgeries I needed on top of our new Brady. Life took a significant detour, but we powered through. Fast forward seven years, and Brady has head control, good trunk control, and communicates well with his Talker using his eyes, but he doesn’t sit unassisted, talk, crawl, walk, use his arms, etc. Development has been incredibly slow, and thanks to all those seizures, Brady now has the diagnosis of cerebral palsy. After I learned about NeuroCytonix I immediately reached out asking for information. I had meetings with the administrator & the team’s pediatric neurologist, who made a case for Brady to the developer. I met with the developer, Dr. Trujillo, and he approved Brady for his program. It’s in Monterrey, Mexico, which is a super-hub for technology & medical innovation. It’s a 28-day program with no days off from treatment. Based on an FDA double-blind placebo study they recently completed, their success rate is 90%. They will be applying for Mexican FDA approval, followed by US FDA approval. It will take years for this to happen. As any parent of a special needs child knows, time is not always a luxury our kids have, so we can’t just wait & hope for FDA approval. The NeuroCytonix study was of 50 children in Mexico with CP. Half got the treatment and half got the placebo. The half that got the treatment have done so well that they are currently working to raise funds for the other half that didn’t get treatment. This isn’t to say the 25 kids that got the treatment are magically neurotypical, but abilities improved in 90% of those children. If we can get Brady even close to where he was before seizures began, we will be in incredible shape and will work his little tail off to keep the momentum going. The brain is an amazing thing with amazing capabilities, and I am a stubborn, hard-working mama who will stop at nothing to get her child everything he needs to thrive. But we don’t have $50k. We’ve thought about taking out a loan but adding more debt doesn’t make sense for us after all the money we’re spending on other therapies & treatments for Brady that insurance doesn’t cover. I’ve not been a big fan of crowdfunding in the past, but now I get it: when the opportunity of a lifetime approaches, you do what you can to make it a reality. I am also working on some side hustles to raise money, as I really have no idea how well this will be received. You might think I’m being selfish, or greedy asking for your help, but what parent wouldn’t do everything they can to improve their child's quality of life? Let me share just a bit about the brilliant mind behind all of this: Dr Trujillo’s mission is to “Cure the Incurable''. He got his Doctor of Science degree in Neurosciences and Molecular Virology at Harvard University. He was the first doctoral student at Harvard University to combine the studies of neuroscience and virology and the first Mexican in the history of Harvard to obtain a Doctor of Science degree in Medical Sciences. Dr. Trujillo founded the Pan-American Society of NeuroVirology. He has held several faculty positions at Harvard, the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke at the NIH, and the University of Maryland. Dr Trujillo is the co-inventor of a patented medical device for the treatment of Human Papillomavirus (HPV) and the prevention of cervical cancer. He has received numerous awards, professional titles, and honorary doctoral degrees from the NIH, Harvard University, and the Pan-American Society of Neurology. He is a member of the American Academy of Neurology, the Biophysical Society, and the American Association for the Advancement of Science. There is so much more I could list about Dr Trujillo, but as far as I’m concerned the most impressive thing about this man is how relatable he is and how passionately he wants to “cure the incurable”. The fact that he is achieving this in our lifetime is such a blessing, and one way or another we will get Brady to his clinic. NeuroCytonix isn't only helping kids with Cerebral Palsy. They are treating all sorts of brain injuries. One woman I spoke with took her daughter there in September and told me there were a few professional rugby players & one member of the Seattle Seahawks there getting treatment. She said she watched them change before her eyes. Concussion, TBI, Alzheimer's, Autism, Epilepsy, you name it, and they can probably help. They have only done the FDA study specifically for children with CP, so that's all they can say they've successfully treated, but it will eventually be so much more. Their machine repairs neurons and the damaged neuronal pathways caused by the various injuries the patient has sustained. This request is a very humbling one for me; I don’t share a lot publicly about our life, but it seems now is my time to ask for help. If you can donate or share this with people who may be able to help, we will be forever indebted. This is such a lofty request and I have hesitated to share it for weeks, but I am putting my pride aside and asking for the only thing Brady needs that I can’t provide by myself. Levi will turn four years old on December 29, 2022. He was born with a rare genetic mutation of the ACTA2 gene that was not diagnosed until he was two years old. This mutation causes a disease known as Multisystemic Smooth Muscle Dysfunction Syndrome (MSMDS). There are only 50 people in the world that have this mutation. This disease is rough and causes problems in different ways for different patients. It affects all the smooth muscles in your body; those are all the muscles we do not control. It caused him to retain a large Patent Ductus Arteriosus in his heart that we have yet to figure out if or when a heart surgeon can close it. The MSMDS caused Levi to develop multiple systemic health issues. Levi has a large bladder that has led to urinary tract issues. Levi manages Gastro Intestinal tract issues with his esophagus and periodic vomiting. Doctors say Levi has already suffered small strokes and is at severe risk for strokes in the future, especially when under anesthesia. Another major concern is his extreme pulmonary hypertension. Pulmonary hypertension is a chronic lung disease that made him oxygen dependent at age 2. While we play Oxygen Cord Olympics now, you can imagine the massive change our family experienced putting an oxygen cord on a two-year-old. Levi has frequent appointments 90 minutes away from home in Minneapolis to see his six specialists for his many medical diagnoses. Since learning about Levi's diagnosis, we have searched for other families dealing with MSMDS and doctors specializing in its treatment. We discovered a new Facebook group for MSMDS patients and family members a few weeks ago. We reached out to the person who started the ACTA2 Alliance and who is in contact with doctors spearheading research into the condition and possible treatment. These doctors are based in Boston, and in May they will help host a MSMDS conference that will benefit our family. While there, we hope to have the doctors leading the most up-to-date research evaluate Levi in person. For two days at the conference, he would get to play and interact with kids who are just like him (or mostly like him), and his sisters could meet other siblings who know what it's like to have a sibling with a rare chronic illness. We will learn about the latest research and new ways that we can help Levi while interacting and learning from other parents who know what it is like to have a kid with the same obstacles as Levi. We are asking for donations to help cover the cost of travel for this upcoming conference. Any donations would help fund airline expenses because driving 19 hours with Levi would be extremely hard on him and his sisters. Donations would also cover hotel expenses, food while we are there and a rental car. They would also help cover expenses for oxygen or medicine while there. We also have not yet figured out if these doctors will take our insurance or if it will be something our insurance will cover for the doctors to see him. This amount we have put as our goal estimates what we think will cover our travel and miscellaneous travel-related expenses. We put this Go Fund Me campaign together because people have been asking how to help Levi and this is currently the best way. Any donations that are given are greatly appreciated. Thank you all in advance for whatever you can help with!
