On October 29th our world was flipped upside down. Kaelin has been sick on and off for the past few months. She was able to make it to her daughter's wedding and celebrate her 49th Birthday while battling a pretty intense case of pneumonia. Unfortunately, one week later her body decided it had enough. This caused her to go to the Hibbing ER. While she was there they performed a CT scan and discovered a mass that was the size of a tangerine on the upper right quadrant of her right lung. Due to the discovery and size of the mass, she was transferred by ambulance to St. Mary's hospital in Duluth, MN. After performing a biopsy on the mass, the results concluded that it was Stage III Small Cell Carcinoma. This type of cancer is fast-moving and aggressive. Due to the location of the mass, it was deemed inoperable. Kaelin's only chance of fighting it is through Chemotherapy and Radiation. We are hoping that she will be a candidate for further treatments in the future, but at this time she is not. The day she was informed she had Stage III lung cancer they started her on a compound chemo treatment. Kaelin had 3 days of Chemo and her body did not handle it well. At this stage and with the aggressiveness, they have moved so quickly with treatments to shrink the size of the tumor and just a hold of helping her survive with this. She has had no time to process the gravity of the situation or what the next 12 weeks of chemo look like or the financial toll it will have. After her first round of chemo, she remained in high spirits, even though her body was rejecting everything being pumped into it. Fortunately, she was able to become stable enough to return home where the real challenges started. She was hospitalized from October 29th- November 7th. Returning home for Kaelin was extremely difficult. Within days she lost her hair, experienced severe muscle atrophy, and all of the accompanying side effects of her disease and the chemotherapy. She has had really good moments where her optimistic and positive attitude has continued and it's incredible to see her relentless self being so positive. But the reality of the situation is that it has been very rough for her and unfortunately it became too much for her to handle. On Monday, November 14th Kaelin was experiencing severe pain and an inability to get a full breath in. She was transported by ambulance again to the Hibbing ER. They discovered that her lungs were infiltrated by what looked like an infection or possible bleeding. They intubated her and transferred her by ambulance again to the ICU at St. Mary's in Duluth. At the ICU they performed another biopsy and discovered that Kaelin was having a reaction to one of the chemo medications. This is extremely rare. Further scans showed the infiltration clouding her lungs was causing her to not be able to breathe on her own. She has been placed on life support but, we are hopeful that the steroids and antibiotics can kick this and clear her lungs. After having two rough nights in the ICU, Today, November 16th we have been granted a small win. Kaelin is responsive and her stats are remaining stable. She is requiring less oxygen with the opportunity to start weaning her off of the ventilator and give her the chance to breathe on her own. After another scan, the result showed that the chemo is working hard and effectively shrinking her tumor. As well as, the steroids are trying hard to clear up the infiltration in her lungs. These may be small wins but they are huge in getting Kaelin off life support and back home. This type of cancer is known to spread quickly to the brain and other parts of the body. Thankfully, Kaelin is in the clear of it spreading for now, but she has a PET scan coming up at the end of the month to determine if this still remains accurate. Earlier this year, in May, Lindsay went to the Emergency Room due to experiencing what we now know was a type of seizure. Unfortunately, the ER doctor misdiagnosed her and told her she just needed rest. Her symptoms worsened over time with headaches, fatigue, and declining cognitive ability. On July 31, she experienced severe headaches, nausea, and a more intense seizure. After consulting Lindsay’s aunt (an ER doctor), the decision was made to get Lindsay to the ER ASAP and ensure they did the necessary brain scans. Her husband, Ken, rushed her to the emergency room, taking their 7-month-old son, Jaden, with them. Despite going to the same ER with the same symptoms, the team was shocked that no scans were done during the visit in May. After being scanned, Ken and Lindsay were given the devastating news that her brain had a large tumor in her left temporal lobe, significant swelling in the area, and a shift of her brain’s midline. Lindsay was immediately hospitalized and given IV medication to decrease brain swelling. On the morning of August 2nd, she underwent brain surgery to remove the tumor. Initial pathology revealed a probable glioblastoma, a cancer of the brain tissue. However, there were other findings that were not consistent with a glioblastoma. Therefore, additional testing was performed by UCSF Health. After completing the test, UCSF Health consulted with the National Institutes of Health for further extensive evaluation. Finally, in mid-September (more than a month later), it was confirmed that Lindsay’s brain cancer was categorized as pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma. This rare cancer accounts for less than 1% of all brain cancers, with very little research and information about how it affects the individual. Although little is known about this type of brain cancer, we remain hopeful and pray for her recovery. Lindsay underwent an arduous recovery process, including multiple medications plus physical, occupational, and speech rehabilitation therapy. She relearned how to walk unsupported and speak more clearly, and gained enough energy to spend a little time with her baby Jaden every day. After much planning by her care team, Lindsay began radiation and chemotherapy treatment on October 5th. This, unfortunately, causes more side effects of profound fatigue, pain, and sleeplessness. With a long road ahead, she continues to meet with her care team and undergo additional tests and evaluations. She has been bravely staying the course, but each day is an emotional and physical struggle dealing with the treatment process and the unknown. Lindsay and her family appreciate any donation that can help lift the burden of financial stress from the inability to work and medical bills, allowing them to focus on her treatment and recovery. Thank you so much for your love and support.

However, shortly after the injury I began experiencing extreme wrist pain. This pain soon traveled up my arm and affected the entire upper right side of my body. I was diagnosed with a rare condition known as thoracic outlet syndrome. This condition causes compression of nerves between the clavicle and rib. This results in excruciating pain in the entire upper body. Treatment and diagnosis is further complicated by a lifetime of repetitive stress from drawing, scoliosis, and myofascial pain which causes muscle spasms. Within months, I lost my art business, my ability to work, and my insurance coverage. I have lived every minute of every day for the past five years in constant pain. I am not ready to give up the chance of recovery. This winter, I’m flying to Boston to have diagnostic and treatment procedures done by one of the only Thoracic Outlet Specialists in the country. The downside, obviously, and the reason I’m writing this request (which feels embarrassing and weird) is the huge financial cost so that I can get better. I guess you could say I have hope now, and I’m putting myself out there even though it’s uncomfortable because it’s my only path forward. I am reliant on my partner to drive, cook, clean, and solely provide for our family. I've fully lost the ability to work, even at a low impact job. I've lost the ability to draw, as I'm not able to hold a pen without extreme pain. As many people in the USA have experienced, living with a severe medical condition can quickly bankrupt a family. As a result of me being unable to work and paying for medical care, we are struggling to afford basic necessities. *MENTAL HEALTH TRIGGER WARNING* I am in need of mental health treatment as soon as possible and what I’m going to share with you is a very deep and personal story. My name is Ash Nave and I suffer from severe depression and extreme suicidal ideation. This is what I'm raising money for. I am raising money to help pay for a treatment program that is known to alleviate severe symptoms of depression. TMS is a non-invasive, non-medication treatment that is used when other depression treatments haven’t been effective. The program itself is an FDA-approved method that sends magnetic pulses into the brain to help stimulate brain activity. Between 80-90% of people with depression experience significant improvements from TMS treatment and about 60% of patients report complete remission for their depression. This is why I need your help. I recently lost my job and cannot afford this treatment alone. TMS is an intensive 8-week program with five treatments per week. With financial aid, the program costs $6,000. Without financial aid, the program costs $8,100. Thankfully, I’ve been approved for financial assistance and start treatment the first week of December. This is why I’m choosing TMS. I’ve been in and out of talk therapy for over a decade, I’ve been hospitalized for multiple suicide attempts, and I’ve been on numerous anti-depressants, mood stabilizers, and ADHD medication. None of these treatment methods are working and my depression is getting worse. This month I had my most recent suicide attempt. This is the first attempt I’ve had in over 3 years. You see, depression can come in waves. There are moments when I see clarity above the fog, times when I am genuinely happy, but these moments no longer outweigh the bad. I am so used to feeling alone that isolation is my normal. I am so used to feeling worthless that worthlessness is my normal. I am so used to being unable to love others or accept love from others that resistance is my normal. There is so much pain that hides behind a smile and oftentimes people never see past that smile. And I’ve been hiding behind mine for a very long time. This is my story. When I was a little kid, my mom struggled with addiction and left me, so I was cared for by other family members until she got the help she needed. And when that day came, when I finally started living in her care again, I experienced many years of child abuse and neglect. At the age of 7, I was molested by my neighbor and when I told my mom she did nothing. Didn’t call the police. Didn’t find counseling or take me to the hospital. Instead she kept it a secret from family and friends so that she wouldn’t lose custody of me again. At the age of 8, I experienced violent child abuse for the first time. My mom and her friends were intoxicated one night and one of her male friends thought it would be funny to put me in a dryer and turn it on. I can still remember kicking and screaming in the dark. I can still remember how scared I was. That was the first time I had a panic attack, that was the first time I thought I was dying, and I was only 8 years old. When I was 11 or 12, my step dad broke my nose. I must have said something out of line because he chased me up the stairs and smashed my face against the carpet until my nose was broken. I remember laying there, crying in my own blood until he screamed at me to clean it up. Again, my mom didn’t take me to the hospital or call the police. This is around the time when I stopped caring about school. This is around the time when people made fun of me for having a big nose. This is around the time when I realized that if I hate myself more than anyone else, no one can hurt me. Suicidal ideation was my closest friend as a teenager because it was the only thing that helped me silently deal with the abuse at home and bullying at school. I've been fighting to keep myself afloat for a very long time, and I'm so tired. I'm 28 and I think about ending my life more than I've actually been able to live it. But each day, I strive to be the best version of myself, despite everything I've been through. And people that know me well know I am trying my best. This is me giving my all to stay afloat. Losing my job out of nowhere and getting assaulted on public transportation last week has triggered such a trauma response that TMS is my only hope right now. I’m seeing this time of unemployment as a window of opportunity to seek out a much needed, more intense mental health treatment method. I have never advocated for my own life more than I am right now. And to whoever is still reading this, thank you for listening to my story. If you or a loved one is experiencing suicidal thoughts, please reach out to someone for help. You can call 9-8-8 anytime you are in crisis. You deserve a chance at life just as much as I do. Mike spent six days in intensive care and was transferred to Spaulding Rehabilitation Hospital in Boston. Mike's prognosis is that he may never walk again, but there is a chance, and Mike is fighting as hard as he can to get there. Mike is a father of two children, Liam and Michaela, and enjoyed a very active lifestyle with them before his accident. He loves playing soccer, lacrosse, skateboarding, snowboarding, hiking and mountain biking and was sharing his passion for athletics with his kids. Mike is incredibly caring and generous, learning from an early age as an Eagle Scout that giving back to his community was an essential part of his life. We sincerely thank you for any donations or sharing of this page on social media. All this to say that with this success came many concussions – estimated that he endured at least 40 in his lifetime. While we are so proud of our dad for what he achieved, we can’t deny that it has negatively impacted his memory and the quality of his life. As a result of his worsening condition, he is increasingly dependent on others to maintain daily tasks and upkeep. Unfortunately, we have reached the point where we must find an assisted living home to ensure he can receive quality care and the best quality of life. The four of us are all young professionals striving to get on our own feet, let alone support our dad and his need for care. We have been extremely fortunate to have our dad’s closest friends support his life for the past nine years; however, it has come time to expand our fundraising efforts for what will likely be one last time to help him transition to assisted living. The neurological symptoms have never been treated whenever I first found out about my heart condition 2 years ago. However, whenever I went, they told me that it's rare for girls my age to have my condition and they are unsure of how to treat it since usually people ages 60-70 have what I have. Hi all. I'm Diana Chao, founder & executive director of Letters to Strangers (L2S), the largest global youth-for-youth mental health nonprofit. I founded L2S when I was 14 years old, and though many know it today as a global organization active in over 20 countries, the road to get here would've been impossible without the incredible drive and support of people I've met along the way. One such person is Reuben. Reuben Reeves is our West Africa ambassador and the founder and president of our Liberia Chapter. Reuben and I have worked together for over 3 years now, starting back when he was still a teenager. Mental health can be a harsh and alienating topic, especially among non-Western communities where traditional values may be particularly stigmatizing - I knew this firsthand as someone from a rural village in the poorest province of China. Though Reuben faced the same struggles in his home country of Liberia, he was still determined to do his best to lead our efforts on the ground and make mental health personal, one letter at a time. Over the last three years, Reuben has quite honestly blown my mind. He led efforts on multiple collaborations with universities, created a 24/7 Mental Health Resource Center in downtown Monrovia, and spearheaded the first, toll-free, 24/7 pan-African mental health hotline. In his very first year at this, he was able to work with the Office of the Liberian First Lady. All while balancing school and familial duties, and with the limited funds we could provide as a small, student-run nonprofit. Back in 2017, I was named one of Nile Rodgers' We Are Family Foundation's Global Teen Leaders. As one of the only nominations I ever made, Reuben unsurprisingly and well-deservedly also eventually won the award in 2020, chosen as one of just ~30 around the world. A few days ago, Reuben was robbed by armed individuals who followed him into his home. He lives alone and was brutally assaulted, leaving him with internal bleeding that will keep him at the hospital for at least another week or two with no clear signs of improvement. All of his belongings were stolen, including his prized laptop and phone, the very technology that allowed us to connect halfway around the world in the first place. In fact, I had gifted him that laptop a few years ago to aid him in his work, and it was in trying to protect all of that that he ended up unable to escape the situation. More than anything, Reuben is fiercely loyal, deeply committed, and proudly ambitious. He dreams of a better world and created other organizations like Rehab Africa to do whatever he can despite not having much himself. His team on the ground, plus those of us far away, want to help him recover the costs of his lost items and rest in the hospital without worrying about medical bills. To be honest, I'd happily pay for all of this myself if I could. Unfortunately, I myself lost my father a month ago after two brief but immensely nightmarish months of watching him rapidly deteriorate under multiple end-stage diseases, and our family cars also completely broke down. Covering all of these costs has taken all of my savings, and we're still waiting for more medical bills to come, so I am no longer able to pay this out of pocket. I grew up under the poverty line and know how precious every dollar is - that's why I didn't bother or want to ask for help with my own situation. But this is my friend, and after everything that has happened, I cannot bear to lose anyone else. So, for my birthday this year, I ask you to consider donating to our efforts to help rebuild Reuben's life and cover his medical costs. To be honest, $3000 is not a lot when you think about medical costs from an American healthcare perspective - my own father's journey set me back tens of thousands of dollars. As someone who's only been working full-time for a year (not on L2S, which I do as a volunteer) after graduation last year, that was basically all I had. But that's exactly why I'm fundraising for this - $3000 is not such an out-there cost that it seems impossible, yet it can make such a huge, life-changing difference. Any amount we raise over this, I'll discuss with Reuben on how best to use it. I'm thinking that he should invest in a security system to protect himself in the future, but we'll keep you updated. Due to the the sheer number of steps involved in transferring funds from the U.S. to Liberia, instead of having each donation go through all those processes each time, we'll aggregate the donations to me first personally, and then I will send all the funds to Reuben or an approved family member of his directly. I am more than happy to provide receipts of this. I remember back in 2020, when I was named a L'Oreal Paris Women of Worth, there was a period of time when the public could vote for one out of the ten honorees to receive additional funding. Without me asking or even implying it, Reuben put the voting link as his bio link across all his social media for the month, constantly campaigning for me and posting almost every day reminding people to vote. I don't think he knows I noticed, but I quietly cried, wondering how I had gotten so lucky to meet people who believed in me like this, and who I wanted to do everything I could to support, too. Watching my father deform in front of my eyes seared into me just how unpredictable and cruel life can be, and in this world, how incredible, how miraculous it is to find people who are willing to fight with you for a cause that means so much. I haven't even yet met Reuben in person. I don't want to take these friendships for granted. Help me help my friend - but only if you have the money to spare. I thank you: deeply, humbly, from the bottom of my heart. PHOTOS OF PEOPLE REUBEN IMPACTED THROUGH L2S LIBERIA:

2022 has been one of the most brutal years in our family’s history. My sister Irina Borodowsky's breast cancer diagnosis (Stage III) came only a month after the news of her daughter’s father’s death from COVID-19. My niece was burdened with navigating both the grief of her dad’s sudden passing and the terrifying threat of cancer taking her mother away in the same year. Our family is spread out across the US, Canada, and Cuba, but despite the distance, we all put our energy into supporting them in whatever way we could. Cooking meals, driving her to treatments, running errands, cleaning their home, taking care of her daughter, and offering consistent moral support.I had a lot of faith, because Irina is a tough cookie and truly one of the most hardworking people I know. A single mother to a teenage daughter, she runs her own business with so much dedication that she rarely takes time off. Even while her body was becoming increasingly frail during aggressive chemotherapy, she continued to show up at work to keep her small company afloat. Ironically, her company is a lab dedicated to analyzing individuals' unique genetic maps to assess their predisposition to illnesses, and using that knowledge to help prevent them from falling ill. One of the most challenging chapters in her breast cancer journey was coming to terms with the cumulative effects of the chemotherapy treatments. It had given her neuropathy, which meant she would not be physically capable of returning to work as quickly as she had hoped after her final major surgery. In the meantime, the bills for all her medical care continue accumulating. Our mother always told us that there is nothing in this world as important as your health. And I’ve always told my daughter that everything in life has a solution, except death. So, I told my sister not to worry about the medical bills, and focus all her energy on getting through the aggressive chemo treatments that were prescribed as her only option for survival.“It is not how much we give, but how much love we put into giving.”Family, friends, and kind souls, we humbly ask that you show empathy and solidarity with my dear sister and everything she has been through to make it this far in her cancer journey. All donated funds will go directly and exclusively to Irina to help relieve the substantial medical debts and expenses associated with her cancer treatment and related needs. Please consider giving any amount you can spare. It may be a cliché, but every little bit really does help. Regardless of your donation capacity, you can make a valuable impact by sharing the link to her fundraiser with your friends, family, and extended networks on social media. I’m sure you can imagine how hard it is to have your message noticed among all the noise online, and we only have a limited time before our fundraiser reaches its deadline. We thank you from the bottom of our hearts for your support today and pray that God will bless you tenfold for your kindness! The world needs more of it now than ever before.

As some of you may already know, my dad, Pat Barnes, had a fall on September 22, 2022 which resulted in a severe spinal cord injury. Shortly after the fall, he underwent emergency surgery at the UVM Medical Center to make more room inside his vertebrae for the swelling to go down. Thankfully, the surgery was successful, but for a few weeks my dad was unable to breathe on his own. He was given a tracheotomy and relied upon a respirator to stay alive. During this time he had no way to communicate with us except by nodding and mouthing words, all the while dealing with intense pain, discomfort, and the shock of his new reality. It was an extremely frustrating, heartbreaking, and terrifying period in this waking nightmare, but thankfully, it was short-lived. My dad has fully regained the ability to breathe on his own and can now speak and eat freely, but he is currently a quadriplegic completely devoid of independence. There is an incredibly long journey ahead for my dad (and for my mom) while he tackles physical therapy to try and regain as much movement as he can. We are told there is no way to know how much he will get back, but the first six months are the most important. Whatever the outcome, it is highly likely he will never have the level of mobility he had prior to the fall. With this, my parents will need a number of things to live a semi-normal life. Some of these include alterations to make their home wheelchair accessible (wider doors, an upgraded tub and toilet, etc.), modifications to their vehicle (or possibly a new accessible vehicle), smart tools for performing everyday tasks (since my dad is limited to the power of his voice), specialized rehabilitation equipment, and more. Plus... hospital bills... As much as we don't want to, my family and I are asking for support with these expenses as it's likely my mom will be retiring early to help my dad with his daily needs. We are in the beginning stages of selling a second car and a camper and are evaluating other ways to save or acquire grants, but it won't cover everything. So far in this journey, we are extremely thankful for all the prayers, well wishes, delicious meals, and help with tasks around the house. These gestures have helped make us more comfortable, taken worries off our plates, and given us extra time to deal with things and be by my dad's side. We have now reached a point where reality is sinking in and finances are the next big burden. If you are able to help in any way, even if it's just a few bucks or sharing this GoFundMe with others who might be able to contribute, it would be truly appreciated. I love my dad so much. My brother and his two grandsons love him too. And no one in the world loves him more than my mom, Susie Barnes, who has thoughtlessly devoted nearly every second of her life to him since the fall happened. This money is just as much about making her life easier as it is his, and I thank you from the bottom of my heart for being there for us in this super challenging time. - Heather Barnes

As a community, we are considered a village that stands for justice and demands wrongs be righted. Our sister (Seattle, WA resident) has been severely wronged and is calling on us for help. We are a community that supports one another to fulfill human rights and ensure that our families are safe from incidents like these. Please open your hearts to our sister in need and help in any way you know. Below is her story through the vital support of a fellow concerned friend. We urge you to be a part of relieving a person in affliction as our Prophet Muhammad (SAW) said: “If anyone relieves a Muslim believer from one of the hardships of this worldly life, Allah will relieve him of one of the hardships of the Day of Resurrection” - Muslim We are writing this letter on behalf of a Somali-American mother Farhiyo Jama in dire need of us to stand up for her now. Our sister is a recent victim of domestic violence, a traumatized mother-to-be with only a few days left to deliver, and a sole struggling provider of 7 young children under 18. We are writing to advocate for her and her children with a call to bring awareness to her struggle because they mirror so many other women's struggles. We also want to address the impending danger silence has on these kinds of cases in specific communities. Lastly, through our efforts, we hope to gain your support and assistance in coming to the aid of one who has been oppressed. On July 13th, 2022, our Somali sister and her now ex-husband, who shares four young children and an unborn child, had an argument. The confrontation resulted in him attacking her with a glass bottle. He hammered the bottle into her face multiple times, causing her to faint from the impact, leaving irreversible damage to her left eye, and she is now completely blind in her left eye. After committing the act right before all of her children, he escaped from the scene and sought shelter inside other homes with community members. Some community members granted him refuge for approximately three months while police searched for him. No one spoke up or provided information to the police about his whereabouts. Some believed the crime did not warrant drastic measures such as holding the offender accountable for his actions through the court. The mother's life, the state of her unborn child and the irreparable trauma it has brought to her children were not enough for anyone to call the police and report him. In the end, after living with the terror of his sudden return to their lives, he was thankfully placed into police custody but was quickly released on bond. Our sister attempted to plead with the community for help when he was missing. She called for everyone to stand up for her. However, astonishingly throughout the days following the attack, she was overewhelmed by the support and help she recieved from the somali community here in Washington State. However, she also found that some people sided with her ex-husband. Demands were made for her to forgive him because he was the father of her children. They implored her to practice patience in the face of the trial and seek reward from God. However, as a people with religion and morals, we can all agree that even Allah teaches us to practice justice. This man's actions are inexcusable. The cultural concept that a man's mistakes need to be overlooked and that a good woman is forgiving will lead many mothers and daughters to place their lives in jeopardy. The scale needs to be balanced, not in favor of one gender over the other. Women should be treated with kindness, respect and dignity. After July 13th, our sister's life changed for the worst, and her children's lives will never be the same. After sharing her story and raising awareness, we hope to prevent such situations from occurring again. Our other concern is raising enough funds to cover her immediate and extreme expenses. Your generous donations will help her pay for shelter and treatment to address the whole family's trauma and other financial burdens. It will also allow her to pay off her outstanding medical expenses and pay for follow-up treatments for her affected left eye. She is heavily pregnant and due on November 30th, 2022. Her newborn child's expenses will also be covered through your donations.

Hi Everyone! I would like to first introduce myself, Tiara Green, from Chicago, IL, and I am 25 years old. I am writing this plea on behalf of my mother, Shantwania Green, also known as "Twania". My mom is 55 years old, has been married to my Dad, Tim, for over 35 years and is a mother of 3 (Timmy, Tre & myself). My mom has been a Registered Nurse for 30 years, fighting the front line extensively for many years. Being a first responder, my mom worked the front lines during Covid-19 and all other crises that affected the healthcare system. She did it proudly while still fighting her own ailments, including chronic asthma and exposure and contracting Covid-19 multiple times. After recovery, my mom was so focused and determined to return to work and help the patients she affectionately loved and pledged to help with all she had. Twania is known for her affectionate smile, loving spirit and loud but warm laugh. She makes people laugh in whatever room she enters. She is definitely a joy to all that she meets. Unfortunately, on the night of October 24, 2021, my mom and I worked the day shift at the hospital and came home as usual. My mom began complaining about not feeling well and having trouble breathing. We tried to manage her breathing at home by giving her a breathing treatment, but it became too severe and required a hospital visit. My mom became so panicky because of the inability to breathe and informed us to call the ambulance. My Dad called the ambulance, but due to the ambulance taking a long time to arrive, my mom shouted for me to get her to the hospital “now”. My mom was afraid that something terrible was about to happen, that she wanted me to get her to the hospital even if I had to drive myself, which I was forced to oblige. My mom shouted out these fearful words that I still hear often when she mentioned, " it felt like she was about to die". Those words were--and still are--very painful to hear, but I knew at that point she was serious, and I had to get her out of there. While my Dad ran back inside to grab his shoes, my mom told me to drive because she couldn't breathe, and it was getting worse. The weather that night was very dreary; rain was pouring, and there was very low visibility, but we got her to the car, and I began to proceed to the hospital. While driving, my mom became lethargic and eventually lost consciousness. I tried to revive her while all the time still attempting to get her to the hospital. We were stopped at a stop light, which turned green, and we continued to proceed to the hospital. Out of nowhere, a car suddenly appeared and hit our vehicle, which caused a significant car crash. Our car was totaled, and I had to pull my unconscious mom out of the vehicle and place her on the ground to continue CPR until the ambulance arrived. By the grace of God, I was able to get my mom revived before the ambulance arrived, but she went out again. They continued working on her on this cold, rainy, dreary roadway. Before it was all over, my mom had made it to the hospital, and within the first 24 hours, my mom had gone into cardiac arrest “4 times.” My mom was in a coma for almost a month. Following that, she eventually opened her eyes, which was the best day ever. She has been fighting and pushing to get back ever since! During this last year, my mom has had many trials and tribulations during her recovery. She is still fighting so hard to come back to herself. She has been to multiple facilities and is doing extensive therapy, but the recovery is happening slowly, and healthcare expenses are piling up very rapidly. Truthfully, it’s taking a toll on our family. While we continue to assist in her recovery, we are drowning in medical bills and other expenses. Still, we are determined to get her the extensive therapy she needs to get her back to her vibrant self and get back to working in the nursing field. Twania absolutely loves nursing and helping others while giving that pleasant demeanor and smile! My mom is currently recovering from an anoxic brain injury. Her doctors are very optimistic she will recover fully, but it will take some time. This time has been challenging, but we are pushing through with the assistance of family and close friends. We are desperately asking for any assistance you can provide for our family to help bring this first responder back to her natural radiant self. She desperately wants to continue supporting the fantastic patients she absolutely adores. We are a family of faith and know she has a testimony to share. Trust me, we all cannot wait for that day to arrive. As an RN nurse in the healthcare field for 30 years, Twania has been fighting to come back, and her family is asking for your help during this time. We really appreciate every one of you as we continue fighting with Twania to recover fully. Thanks so much, and always remember to #Fightliketwania On Behalf of Shantwania (Twania) Green RN

“I think I found a lump. It feels spiky around the edges.” That’s how my wife, Julie, woke me up on August 18, 2022. She already had a routine mammogram scheduled for September 14th, so we tried not to worry about it. You can imagine how well that worked out. The mammogram verified that there was something—some mass—in her right breast, so they scheduled a diagnostic mammogram and ultrasound the following week. I sat beside Julie while the technician dialed in the image: a misshapen blotch darker than the surrounding, healthy tissue. The radiologist pointed to a rhythmic flicker of bright color in the center of the blotch. “That’s blood flowing through the mass,” he said. “That’s a very strong indication that it’s cancer. Let’s schedule you for a biopsy.” He said it out loud, without hesitation. Julie didn’t say a word; she just looked at me as if this wasn’t real. Julie reached out to friends who have been through cancer for advice. Her friend Kim told her this was the worst part, waiting and not knowing what would come next. Kim assured Julie that the team was working for her even if she had not heard from them. Kim was spot-on. We’ve been married for ten years, after surviving the deaths of our previous partners. During that time, I’ve learned how to calm Julie’s lifelong fear of needles: a cold cloth on the back of her neck so she doesn’t throw up, a warm hand in hers after that. She told me of the time her daughter Amanda was sitting in her lap getting a routine vaccine, and she began to sink into the chair almost fainting. Amanda, then five years old, said, “It’s okay, Mom does this all the time.” October 6 was the biopsy. The nurse gave her Ativan an hour before the procedure to calm her. She told me, “Scott, if I start talking Southern, just tell me to settle down. You know that happens when I’m stressed.” Julie said she felt like she was surrounded by four angels: two doctors, a radiology nurse at the ultrasound station and a nurse standing behind her head holding her hand, talking and rubbing her hair for support. She didn’t feel any pain, but the sound of inserting the three clips, like a staple gun, was a bit surprising. The clips help locate the exact area for further treatment and show up on a mammogram or other imaging test. The biopsy determined Julie has invasive ductal carcinoma in her right breast. Hearing that for the first time... saying it ten, twenty times or more... it never sounds less unreal or less frightening. October 25 was her first meeting with the oncological surgeon. Everything is coming into place. After an hour of conversation, questions, and diagrams, it was clear her path was set. Julie is the perfect candidate for a procedure called oncoplastic reconstruction. Two surgeons work together to combine breast cancer tumor removal (a lumpectomy) and plastic surgery techniques (reconstructive surgery) at the same time for breast conservation. This allows more normal tissue around the cancer to be removed. November 3, 2022, we met the plastic surgeon who will perform the reconstruction. He also agreed oncoplastic reconstruction was the best solution for Julie. Because she is a size DD, he can preserve her breast to a size C. No mastectomy is needed. He also acknowledged what I’m going through as her husband: his wife also had breast cancer. November 22, 2022 is a full day at OHSU with blood draws, inserting a reflector into the breast, and injecting nuclear medicine into the nipple that will flow to the lymph nodes to detect any further cancer cells, and another ultrasound. The next day the cancer will be removed. The pathology report should take two weeks. At this point, we’ll know what the duration of radiation will be. There is no indication that chemo will be needed, and we hope this stays true. Julie has agreed to be in a research study through OHSU called CAMPERR. It’s a two-year study based on patients with different types and stages of cancer to support the development of a blood test. The hope is to detect cancer at early stages when treatment can be more effective. There is no monetary value for her, but it gives her the satisfaction that she can somehow leave this situation with the knowledge she is helping someone in the future. Complicating matters, it’s a four-hour, 195-mile round trip from our home in Rockaway Beach to the Oregon Health Sciences University (OHSU) Knight Cancer Center. Julie, who loves researching, started looking into grants and funding for cancer patients. She found a few, and submitted applications for them, but the shortfall would be devastating. Julie’s insurance pays 80% of the cost of hospitalization. An AARP survey found the average cancer treatment in the U.S. costs $150,000. That leaves at least $30,000 unpaid, and that’s if things are typical. And we’re definitely in the 68% of Americans estimated to be unable to afford a $400 medical emergency. After exhausting those options, she turned to me in tears. “I think I’m going to need a GoFundMe,” she said. “I hate having to ask for money, but I don’t know what else to do.” Your donations will go to pay for expenses our insurance does not cover. Furthermore, our 1930 home needs critical repairs to help Julie while she is recuperating. Our goal will cover known costs and leave a small cushion for the unexpected—recalling that cancer itself was unexpected four months ago. Thank you for everything you do. And please know that this Thanksgiving–the day after Julie’s surgery–you are who we’ll give thanks to.

Three years ago, at the age of 41, Phoebe Search received a diagnosis of Stage 4 breast cancer. Years of mainstream, alternative and experimental treatments with varying success followed her initial diagnosis. Throughout her treatment, her spirit never wavered. However, on October 7, Phoebe left this world and crossed over the rainbow to join her firstborn son, Rafa. She left behind her husband, Juan, her 11-year-old twins, Luca and Xavier, and many individuals who loved her and whose lives were better for having known her. She also left behind her small childhood nuclear family: her younger brother, Jim, and her beloved mother, Sherrie Lee. Sherrie Lee has struggled with age-onset dementia for several years. However, within the last year, her condition deteriorated until it was no longer possible to leave her at home unsupervised for any length of time. Phoebe was Sherrie's guardian until the time of her death. With Sherrie confined to a home, Jim is working through legal channels to transfer Sherrie's fixed monthly income, guardianship, and medical power of attorney into his name and take over the responsibility of managing his mother's care. While sifting through bills, it was determined that substantial outstanding expenses weren't covered over the past few months. Given the tragic and sudden circumstances surrounding this transfer of guardianship, Jim hasn't been able to prepare financially for the expense. It will be several months before the legal proceedings conclude, and he has access to Sherrie's monthly income, which won't cover most of the outstanding medical or legal expenses. Please consider helping defray the costs related to Jim's transfer of his mother's legal, financial, and medical care. On a personal note, this family is incredibly special to me. Phoebe and I taught together the year I was pregnant with my daughter. Her mother retired from teaching that year, moved from Binghamton to NYC, and moved in with Phoebe in Brooklyn to be closer to her children. I recall a visit to our classroom where Sherrie pointed to my growing belly and stated, as though it were a foregone conclusion, "When you go back to work after your maternity leave, I am taking care of your baby." And so it was. Sherrie cared for my tiny children for about five years. She, Phoebe, Jim, Juan, Luca and Xavier are all imprinted on my heart. Please consider helping them weather yet another financial hardship related to the tragic passing of my dear friend.

Help the Ball Family with Medical Expenses, organized by Stephanie and Marianne. Sean (15, turning 16 on Nov. 7th) and Joshua (14) were victims of a hit-and-run on October 31st around 10 pm. The boys were struck while walking to meet their mom after trick or treating. We are raising funds to help the Ball family with the medical bills, as both boys suffered significant trauma and injuries. Since they were young, their laughter has been contagious and fills the room with joy. Sean and Joshua have been active in football and basketball. They are the eldest sons of Joey Alanis Ball and Rob Ball, big brothers to Westin (9). The boys should be focused on everyday teenage life, making friends, playing sports, and working towards their driver's licenses. The fateful events on Halloween put normal day-to-day life to a halt. The following is a personal account of the events on Halloween as told by Joey Ball (Sean and Joshua's mom): "Around 10pm on Halloween, Sean and Joshua were walking from a neighborhood that they had been trick or treating in, to a nearby park where I was waiting to pick them up. As they were nearing the entrance of the park they were both struck by a vehicle. Sean was hit first and landed in the ditch. Then Joshua was hit and landed in the street. I was nearly 50 feet away when this happened. I didn’t see it, but I heard it. I quickly drove forward to the entrance of the park to see that my boys both had been struck by a hit and run. These images will haunt me forever. There was an Angel of a human that helped console me and manage the boys until the paramedics and police arrived. We were all taken to Grady hospital. Both boys were placed in the same trauma room in the ER. That was bittersweet. I was thankful to have them both close, but it was also unbearable to watch not 1, but 2 of my boys being treated simultaneously. I am so thankful that Rob and Lisa were there to help divide the attention to help comfort the boys. Joshua had significant road rash, bumps and bruises and overall aches and pains. Miraculously there were no broken bones. He was discharged yesterday morning and seems to be on the mend with the exception of some wounds that will take time to heal. Sean took more of the brunt of the injuries. He has a concussion that is expected from the impact. He had a severe laceration to the nose that required surgery along with a large laceration to his left elbow that tore into his tricep which required surgery as well. He is still in recovery and dealing with quite a bit of pain. He will remain in the hospital until it is more manageable. Thank you to all who have been praying for our family. We have been shown so much love and support it truly amazes me."

In October 2020, Jeremy, only in his 40’s, was diagnosed with Early Onset Parkinson’s Disease. Jeremy is a freelance Director of Photography, which means most of his work day includes holding up a big camera on his shoulders for a long time and keeping it steady. As the disease progresses, one can imagine Jeremy's challenges not only in his work but in his everyday life activities. Here’s the back story: In 2018, due to a congenital chest deformity, Jeremy’s sternum was collapsing into his heart and lungs. He had a massive chest reconstruction to his sternum and rib cage so he could breathe properly and to stop his chest from deforming his heart. But his recovery was excessively slow, due to what they now have discovered to be Parkinson’s. It wasn’t until October 2020 that Jeremy would be officially diagnosed with Early Onset Parkinson’s Disease. In February of 2021, Jeremy slipped on ice-covered stairs and broke several vertebrae in his back. Following months of therapy, Jeremy has continued to improve but still struggles to work long days on set. His determination and physical therapies keep him moving forward. As many of you may know, Lynn has faced her own health challenges. Lynn had one of her kidneys removed in her early 20’s due to a renal vein deformity. Fun fact, Jeremy and Lynn actually spent their honeymoon at the Mayo Clinic when they gave her the diagnosis. Despite Lynn’s continued various health struggles over the last years (including fibromyalgia), she had just begun being able to work for a food delivery service while also homeschooling their awesome and genuinely kind son, Griffin. This July, she was diagnosed with severe endometriosis, and Lynn had a full hysterectomy. While the doctor removed much of the endometriosis, some had to be left behind to avoid further damage to Lynn’s only remaining kidney. Lynn had to return to the hospital with a severe infection due to surgery complications. This has left her unable to work once again. Jeremy, Lynn, and Griffin need your help: Over the years, medical bills have continued to pile up, and now they have found themselves with very little income coming in. They have utilized all resources available to them and are now at a point of critical need. There is an upcoming clinical trial that will be an expense and alternative therapies that have proven effective but are NOT COVERED BY INSURANCE. As we all know, Parkinson’s disease is not an easy road. Jeremy loves to work. He wants to work, but some jobs are getting more challenging. May we all give of what we have been given. Your generosity can relieve a tremendous financial burden on this family. Please pray for Jeremy, Lynn, and Griffin, and may we be the hands and feet of Christ. Thank you for loving on this family. May God be glorified.

Please consider supporting 11-year-old Aaron and his family as he undergoes a bone marrow transplant with the goal of beating ALD. In 2016 the McMillan family received a diagnosis that no one ever wants to hear. In Deana’s own words, “When your child is diagnosed with a life-threatening disease, there are a lot of unknowns. You feel lost, you cry a lot, and you don’t know what the future holds. There are lots of questions.” The feelings of defeat, terror, and hopelessness quickly shifted to ones of determination to learn as much as possible, to connect to specialists, and to figure out how to walk this new path together for the health and life of their little boy. How It Started Aaron was just five years old when he was diagnosed with Adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD). His diagnosis was discovered after he went into an adrenal crisis following his 5-year immunizations. At the time of diagnosis, Aaron was just one of two boys in the state of Kansas who had been diagnosed with ALD. In other words, this is rare. Very rare. He was also diagnosed with Adrenal Insufficiency (AI). These diagnoses can be life-ending. The protocol for care involves MRIs every six months for preventative catching of early signs. It involves steroid dosing to help with the adrenal insufficiency. It involves many doctors, medical jargon, unexpected trips to the hospital, and trips out of state to meet with specialists. Up until recently, Aaron’s treatments have been successful in helping him remain healthy and active. Today Today, Aaron is a vibrant 11-year-old boy in 5th grade who has a love for many things such as reading, brain puzzles, animals, science and Legos. He wears a big smile with an infectious laugh. He’s referred to as a superhero. The Learning Curve According to ALD Connect: Adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD) is an X-linked disease that is caused by an underlying genetic mutation in the ABCD1 gene, which affects the body’s ability to create the protein that helps the process of breaking down very long–chain fatty acids (VLCFAs). The saturated VLCFAs build up in the brain, nervous system, and adrenal gland and eventually destroy the myelin sheath that surrounds the nerves. ALD affects approximately 1 in 17,000 people worldwide. <URL> After the McMillans learned more about Aaron’s diagnosis, they were given some hope by starting Aaron on a special low-fat diet and Lorenzo’s Oil, a combination known for assisting with normalizing the accumulation of the very long-chain fatty acids to help slow down the progression of ALD. Recently, however, the McMillan family was told the disease has now progressed into the cerebral form, despite all their efforts. Next Steps: Please Consider Helping Aaron and his family are now facing many unknowns as Aaron undergoes a bone marrow transplant in Minneapolis, MN. This procedure will hopefully stop the progression of the disease in his brain. It is a long road of many months ahead. The family will be living in two locations for most of this period of time. Deana will stay in MN with Aaron where they will live for the next 4-5 months while Aaron receives the transplant and recovers. Travis will initially travel with them but is only able to stay for a few short weeks before returning to Wichita to work. We ask that you please consider supporting Aaron and his family, as the financial strain is very real. The medical expenses are mostly covered through insurance, but the loss of a working income, the costs of living in two places, the costs of traveling back and forth for the family to see each other, and so many unknowns will all add up quickly. Your support will allow the McMillans to cover unexpected costs and focus on what is most important right now–helping Aaron get better. Side note of who we are: Organizers of this GoFundMe are two of Deana’s friends - one lifelong friend from childhood and one friend who has shared knowledge and experience and helped guide their path of being ALD parents.

Hi Friends, Over the past five years, I have been very vocal about my son Dominick’s health. During my 26-week ultrasound appointment, rhabdomyomas (tumors) were found on his heart. After dozens of tests and scans, it was confirmed that Dominick had a genetic condition called Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC). Doctors and specialists told us to prepare for the worst. Since hearing those words, something inside me changed forever. Its now my sole job to advocate for Dominick and give him the best life possible. TSC is a rare genetic condition that causes tumors/tubers to grow in many different organs systems. Growth most often occurs in the brain, skin, heart, eyes, kidneys, and lungs. Dominick is affected in his skin, heart, kidneys and brain. Dominick has too many tubers in his brain to count on an MRI, and brain involvement puts him at a high risk for TSC-related seizures. This brain involvement has also contributed to an autism diagnosis, sensory needs, and behavioral challenges. As many of you know, Dominick suffered from a terrible, long seizure a month ago that caused him to be put on a ventilator. This was a seizure we never saw coming, resulting in urgent transport to Pittsburgh Children’s Hospital, days of anti-seizure medication with terrible side effects, and a scare to all who love him. We are beyond grateful that Dominick came out of this ordeal without any known lasting effects. Some are not as fortunate. This leaves us with one main goal: to be one step ahead of future seizures by foreseeing and treating them before they get out of hand. How is that possible? With a seizure dog. We are currently in the process of obtaining a seizure dog for Dominick through Dulebohn Service Dogs. This process will take approximately 12-15 months. The cost is $17,500 plus expenses for a weeklong training session in Wapakoneta, Ohio. This fundraiser is to help find Dominick his perfect match! Every dollar donated will be applied to Dominick’s seizure dog account to cover the costs of the vetting and matching process, the advanced training specific to Dominick and his needs, and the weeklong class attendance before receiving his dog. How will a Service Dog help Dominick? *Seizure response dogs are trained to alert a family member or caregiver of a seizure up to 15 minutes BEFORE a seizure begins (and sometimes even 24-48 hours before!). This will allow us to begin treatment immediately. *Dogs are trained to lie next to their owners during a seizure to help the owners from injuring themselves, and others will stand next to their owners to break their fall and prevent injury. *Seizure response dogs can be trained to press alarm buttons or other pre-programmed devices that call for help. *They are often trained in mobility assistance, such as helping their owners get up and walk to a safe place before or after a seizure. *The service dog will also be trained in behavior disruption – interfering in and distracting Dominick during periods of difficult behavior. *Most importantly, this will give us peace of mind that Dominick will be monitored day and especially at night while he sleeps. The fear of a nighttime seizure has prevented a sound night’s sleep since his birth. Thank you for your consideration in helping us with this endeavor.

Tämä voi tulla nyt monelle ihan puskista, mutta mulla todettiin pahanlaatuinen (gradus 2) aivokasvain loppuvuodesta 2020. Ihan alusta alkaen meille painotettiin, että kyseessä on parantumaton syöpä, ja hoidoista huolimatta kasvain tulee aina ennemmin tai myöhemmin kasvamaan takaisin. Koska taudinkuva on niin arvaamaton, mitään tarkkaa elinajanennustetta ei kukaan uskaltanut meille antaa, mutta haitari oli parista vuodesta max 25 vuoteen, riippuen miten kasvain reagoi hoitoihin. Kasvain leikattiin pikaisella aikataululla ja saatiin poistettua melkein kokonaan. Liitännäishoitoina sain vielä 6 viikon sädehoitojakson, joka loppui ruhtinaalliset 3 päivää ennen tyttäreni Adan syntymää, jonka jälkeen aloitin vielä 6 kuukauden sytostaattihoidot helmikuussa 2021. Loppujen lopuksi kroppa toipui kaikista koettelemuksista yllättävän nopeasti ja pääsin palaamaan töihin jo huhtikuussa, vaikka sytostaattikuurit olivatkin tuossa kohtaa vielä päällä. Meidän “normaalia” ja rauhallista arkea kesti suunnilleen vuoden verran, kunnes tämän vuoden syyskuussa aloin saamaan jälleen epileptisiä kohtauksia. Viimeisin magneetti lokakuussa varmisti, että kasvain on ehtinyt 6 kk aikana kasvaa huomattavasti ja oli jo n. golfpallon kokoinen. Valitettavasti hankalan sijaintinsa vuoksi kasvainta ei voi tällä kertaa leikata, lisäksi kasvain on jo poikkeuksellisen lyhyessä ajassa ehtinyt muuntautua pahanlaatuisimmaksi luokan 4 aivosyöväksi, glioblastoomaksi. Useamman lääkärin suosituksesta seuraavat askeleet tästä ovat lisää sädehoitoa ja sytostaatteja. Koska kyseessä on ns. loppuvaiheen syöpä, julkisella puolella tarjotaan vain palliatiivista, eli oireita lievittävää hoitoa, eikä kasvainta lähdetä enää sädettämään yhtä aggressiivisesti kuin aikaisemmin. Tämän lisäksi ensimmäinen hoitokerta on vasta 3 viikon päästä, joka on tautini ärhäkkyyden vuoksi yksityisen puolen syöpälääkärini mielestä liian myöhäinen aloitusajankohta. Yksityinen syöpäsairaala Docrates on sitä mieltä, että nimenomaan aggressiivisella hoidolla voidaan mahdollisesti pidentää jäljellä olevaa elinaikaani, jonka vuoksi haluaisin luonnollisesti jatkaa hoitoja yksityisellä puolella. Glioblastooman elinajan ennuste on synkkä, vain 14-16 kk hoitojen kanssa, jonka vuoksi koen, että nyt täytyy kääntää kaikki kivet ja yrittää taistella tätä tautia vastaan parhailla mahdollisilla hoidoilla mitä Suomesta vaan löytyy. Tässä kohtaa pyydänkin nöyrimmin apua teiltä. Sädehoitoni on arvioitu maksavan 25 000 euroa ja minkä tahansa suuruinen lahjoitus helpottaisi taloudellista taakkaamme. Kiitos paljon avusta!

The family managed to get him medical care throughout the Middle East with some temporary palliative care with some success. Since they moved to the US, he has been the sole provider for his family. At a young age, Saber learned to take care of his mother and younger brother. Life was good Alhamdulillah, he was working full-time to provide for his family while attending Richland college and pursuing a career in Business Administration. In the past few months, Saber's health condition started to deteriorate as a result of a problem with his kidneys. Last July, he visited the Nephrology Associates of Dallas for consultation and treatment. He was evaluated at the center, and the doctors told him that both of his kidneys are functioning below 5%. This is NOT common in young people, and the symptoms that he is exhibiting are usually seen in patients that are over 50 years old. They gave him medication and said to monitor his progress in a month. In mid-October, he returned for a follow-up visit, which included a comprehensive medical exam, blood test and imaging which confirmed the final stage of chronic kidney disease (stage 5 CKD). The doctors told him he will need a kidney transplant as the ultima cure for his medical condition to sustain life. The doctors told him he will need a kidney transplant as the ultima cure for his medical condition to sustain life. In the meantime, he should be ready for dialysis. This was devastating news for the 20-year-old Saber and his family. On October 26th, Saber was admitted to Medical City Dallas hospital for Peritoneal Dialysis (PD), where they inserted a tube in his abdomen with a dialysis solution that absorbs waste and excess fluids. The procedure was successful and he has been to the hospital several times for follow-up and doing his hemodialysis daily. This has been an exhaustive procedure both financial and psychological. The transition to dialysis remains an important milestone for Saber, as this is the ultimate cure for his condition. A smooth transition from chronic kidney failure to PD initiation with prior preparation and planning is associated with better short-and long-term results. It also allows the patient to be both physically and psychologically readied for the potential rigors of renal replacement therapy. Transitions in care while undergoing dialysis are critical to patients’ success at home, and to reduce hospitalizations and long-term care facility use, both of which present a risk of PD technique failure. A kidney transplant involves surgically placing a healthy kidney from a donor into the patient’s body. After a transplant, he will need one-month hospitalization at ICU; and to take medications for the rest of his life to keep his body from rejecting the new organ. The chances of having a kidney transplant in the US are very slim. Of the more than 500,000 patients on chronic dialysis in the US, less than one-fifth are active on the kidney transplant waiting list. The family has found a donor in Iraq and Saber will travel overseas with his mother to get his kidney transplant surgery once the funding is secured. My name is Aubrey, and I've created this GoFundMe to help my dad, Craig, pay for the next phase in his cancer treatment. In April 2020 my dad was diagnosed with State 4A cancer, specifically a version of squamous cell carcinoma that had taken over the bone in his upper jaw, and part of the sinus and nasal cavity on the left side of his face. In May, he underwent an 11-hour long surgery that involved removing the large tumor, taking out bone from his jaw, the entire roof of his mouth, and detaching and re-attaching his nose. He lost all of his upper teeth, and did an auto-donation of both bone from his left leg, as well as skin. They also removed lymph nodes from the left side of his neck. He had several custom plates and rods put in, as well. The procedure was absolutely brutal and involved an oncological surgeon and two plastic surgeons. Post-op my dad then underwent thirty rounds of radiation, as well as various forms of physical and oncological therapy, as well as speech therapy. I went into caretaking more almost full-time that summer, driving him to and from all of his various doctor appointments M-F and helping him with whatever he needed at home. Then, about two and a half weeks out from his 12 month PET scan, as my dad was finally meeting with the oral surgeon to start dental reconstruction, they found another tumor. The short version is that the cancer was back, and now considered to be reoccurring. Because of this, my dad would no longer be able to get dental implants, because that area in his body will have to be monitored for the rest of his life. My dad had a second surgery in mid July, but since the tumor was in a more difficult spot to reach this time, he's gone through another thirty rounds of radiation, as well as chemotherapy, and has now started immunotherapy. The next phase of his treatment involves the hyperbaric oxygen chamber, which he will do alongside the immunotherapy. For those who don't know, this is meant to help speed up the healing process, which has been slowed down from the radiation and chemo. He will go through thirty rounds in the chamber, M-F for six weeks, while also going through immunotherapy for the next six months. Once that's over, he will undergo another surgery to fix some things with his lip, a wound under his nose, and a hole in the roof of his mouth, at which point he will undergo ten more sessions in the chamber. Once that's over, he will finally be able to get a custom bridge - aka teeth - and be able to eat solid foods again. The reason for this GoFundMe is because Medicaid - the only insurance my dad has because he can't work - doesn't cover the hyperbaric oxygen chamber. It's $625 per session, totaling $25,000. His partner, Jennifer, has had to work multiple jobs to support them both throughout this entire process, and has obviously been under an extreme amount of stress and grief. While all of us in the family will ban together to help out as much as we can, I don't know anybody who has a spare $25k laying around. This process has been incredibly difficult on me, my dad, and his partner especially, as well as the rest of our family. Watching the extreme physical changes my dad has undergone has been really, really hard. This is the first time in his life he's had to deal with any major health problems, and it's incredibly scary. Thank you so, so much to anybody and everybody who chooses to donate to this cause. I will be taking him to and from all of his appointments again, and am inexplicably grateful for any help we can get. I know that cancer is something that affects so many people - too many people. My hope is that he will finally be able to get past all of this and live out the life he desires. Thank you.

4 weeks ago, Emily was admitted to the hospital while experiencing severe symptoms such as muscle fatigue, inability to swallow, speak and blurred vision. After several tests, CT scans, CAT scans, MRIs, X Rays and a spinal tap-they ruled out a stroke and Miller Fisher Syndrome and started treating her for Myasthenia Gravis. They immediately started her treatment. She received 5 IgG treatments for 3 hours a day and five plasma transfers, where nurses had to watch over her each time until complete. We expected a full recovery in a few days. However, her health declined significantly and quickly. After one week in the hospital and four plasma transfers later, she began to experience respiratory failure and was transferred into the ICU and placed on life support. Within 48 hours of being placed in the ICU and a few more tests later, It was determined she had colonic necrosis, and her colon was dying. She was immediately taken into emergency surgery, had 12 inches of her colon removed, a Colostomy procedure, and a tracheotomy and four days ago, they discovered she had a blood clot in her leg and her lung. To sum it up, her body has been through the wringer in a short amount of time. Fast forward to this week, and we finally got the answers we had been waiting for. A diagnosis. A firm diagnosis and treatment plan. Emily is experiencing a very rare, complicated and deadly disease that has left her with almost complete paralysis, except for her fingers and toes. Her lungs are still in a state of paralysis, so she is on a ventilator, other loud machines, lots of tubes and IVs that keep her motor going. But she is fighting every day for her recovery and fighting hard. During these last four weeks, Emily has endured pain many have never felt. She has experienced the kind of fear that no one should ever have to experience. The kind of sadness that only happens a couple/few times in your entire life. And she has also fought tooth and nail to stay alive. She has taken steps in the right direction with her recovery, and we couldn’t be any more proud of her. With that being said, she will remain in the ICU on a ventilator for another couple/few weeks until she can breathe on her own a little better (also, happy news: she was able to stay off of it for 10 hours the other day and today she was taken outside for the first time in 4 weeks and felt the sunshine on her face) She will then be transferred to an inpatient rehabilitation facility where she will undergo physical therapy, occupational therapy and speech therapy that will allow her body to get back to walking, talking and eating again. We are hopeful and optimistic for a full recovery, but this journey will take months of intensive treatment, rehabilitation and a lot of love, support and prayers. As hard as this is on Emily and her family, we have accepted that this is not an overnight fix, and we all have a very long journey ahead, but mostly Emily and her little family, Jarett and William. She will miss the holidays with family, her son's second birthday and other special dates that are very important to her. But we are thankful she is alive and kicking this thing's ass, and that’s all that matters to us. She has amazing nurses doing everything they can to keep her comfortable and positive, even washing and braiding her hair. ☺️ We are so fortunate that she still has the ability to write and communicate to us what's on her mind, her feelings about all of this and of course, even in her condition, she still finds a way to be a businesswoman and make sure her clients and shop are taken care of. If you know Em, you are a lucky person. She has spent the better part of her life (17 years) doing what she loves best. She owns and operates a Barbershop in Sacramento called “The Rev”, which is her other baby. She dreamed of having a place of her own that was all-inclusive, judgment-free, and provided nothing but peace, friendship, love and happiness. And In 2018, she did just that. She wants her clients and Rev team to know how lucky she is to have you all. The Rev wouldn’t be what it is without you all. She has a beautiful one-year-old son that is the light of her life. She is one of, if not the funniest, people I know and finds a way to cheer almost anyone up. She loves to sing, paint and create and is the best friend anyone could have. This has truly been the hardest thing for her to endure, mentally and physically, as well as for her family. Thank you for loving my Sister, thank you for checking in and thank you for the continued support. The outpouring of support and love from our community has made this reality a little easier to go through. Right now, Emily needs all the love and support, and If you find it in your heart to help, we just ask that you continue sharing her story, posting your sweet words, even a text to her (someone will read to her) If you want to send us your favorite photos together, we can hang them up for her or even writing her a letter of encouragement to read would mean so much! ♥️ It’s the little things. Please do not feel obligated to give, but a little goes a long way, especially with the amount of time she will be in the hospital and rehabilitation center. ♥️ Thank you so very much from Em's Family.

This appeal is made on the behalf of Rajesh Rajagopalan. Rajesh is a refugee who suffered a brutal attack while being held by the Australian government on the island of Nauru. After multiple surgeries, Rajesh had been left partially paralysed, and is slowly recovering from his serious injuries with the help of friends and medical staff. But he needs ongoing financial, physical and emotional support. Please take a moment to read Rajesh’s story below and if you can, make a donation to help aid his recovery. Rajesh’s story (Picture) Rajeshkumar “Rajesh” Rajagopalan is a 36 year old Tamil refugee from Sri Lanka. In his home country he was detained multiple times by the Sri Lankan army and was interrogated, assaulted and abused without ever being charged. Fearing for his life, Rajesh left Sri Lanka by boat, arriving in India and then setting out for Australia as an asylum-seeker in 2014. Due to the Australian government’s offshore processing policy, Rajesh was transferred to Nauru. Despite being recognised as a refugee in 2015, he was kept on Nauru for 7 years, from 2015 to 2021, at first in refugee camps and later in community detention, but with limited freedom. Violence against refugees on Nauru is a common occurrence. In February 2021, while riding his bike, Rajesh was deliberately run down by a car and bashed. The car then reversed over him in what has been treated as an attempted muder. The attackers stole his bike before leaving him for dead. The car used in the attack on Rajesh. (picture) After the attack, Rajesh was in a coma in Nauru for four days. His injuries were too many and too severe to be treated at the small hospital and it was thought he would not survive. However, following demonstrations and protests by his friends and fellow detainees, he was transferred to an Australian hospital under the Medevac process. Rajesh on life support. After 8 months of intensive treatment in hospital with some signs of recovery, he has been released into the community. But the injuries he received have totally changed his life. He cannot walk without physical support and is partially paralysed on one side. He still requires regular medical interventions, including physiotherapy and counselling to cope with the trauma caused by the attack. He is struggling to come to terms with the loss of his health and his future prospects. Injuries to Rajesh’s left arm. (picture) Rajesh receives some government support to cover a part of his medical expenses and accommodation, but it is nowhere near enough to pay for food, transport, clothing and other living expenses. He is only surviving due to the generosity of friends and supporters. He is still uncertain about his long-term recovery and quality of life, as well as his prospects in Australia. Rajesh is a genuine refugee, recognised by the UNHCR. In coming to Australia, he sought a life free from persecution, where he could work, contribute to society and help to support his ageing parents and other family members back in Sri Lanka. Instead, the Australian Government forced him to live on Nauru, despite the fact that detainees were often victims of crimes there. The attack on Rajesh was deliberate and unprovoked, and was a direct result of the Australian Government policy that sent him there. We are aiming to raise $10,000 to help Rajesh continue his recovery. Funds raised will help to pay for prosthetic aids, trauma counselling, ongoing medical treatment and to cover the gap in his living expenses. We hope you can contribute even a small amount to give Rajesh hope for a brighter future after so much suffering. (picture) For more information regarding Rajesh and his story, or to discuss any other ways to support him during these difficult times, please contact Sujan Selvan (0421 832 255) of Tamil Resource Centre or Geraldine Moore (0408 512 522) of Bayside Refugee Advocacy and Support Association. Earlier this week, my mom called me with horrific news: my brother had been in a serious accident while biking to work in Japan. The sudden news of his departure has shattered the lives of his family. Anything you can do to ease their burden as they try to pick up the pieces would be greatly appreciated.

Josh (father of 2) was returning home early Sunday morning when he looked up into his review mirror and saw headlights barreling towards him. Josh is on I-205 headed north to I-84 so that he can return home to Troutdale. The SUV he sees in the review mirror is going more than 120 mph. His Mini Cooper is hit from behind, and Josh is sent into the divider. Josh and his car are rolled six times to end up sitting nose up car impaled by rebar in a construction zone. Josh has no idea how long he was unconscious. When he comes to, he sees police lights in the distance. Josh screams for help, but due to the distance and a collapsed lung, he goes unheard. Badly injured, bleeding and covered in gasoline, Josh somehow pulls himself out of the vehicle and walks towards the flashing lights of the cop car. The Police Officer on the scene is investigating the SUV that hit Josh and doesn't know another vehicle was involved. The SUV has no plates, and the driver is missing. Josh is briefly questioned before the Police Officer realizes that Josh is severely injured and is asked to sit down. At this point, Josh collapses, and the police officer calls an ambulance. Josh is rushed to the hospital and survives the night. Multiple injuries are cataloged, including a Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI), a collapsed lung, a partially severed ear, facial fractures, spinal fractures, Chemical burns, broken ribs, and many other issues. He spent three days in the hospital and has been released. He requires substantial help to do tasks we all take for granted daily. Expenses that would typically be taken care of by the SUV's driver and their insurance can't be as they fled the scene, and there has been no update from Portland Police on the investigation or even if one is taking place. We will update you below as information becomes available. Please share this and donate if you can. It's currently unclear when or if Josh will be able to return to work. Josh has always been a hard worker and is too proud to ask for help. So on behalf of his family and friends, Please share and donate. Shawn Higgins mother to Josh’s 2 kids and his accountant will be in charge of all funds donated here. UPDATES: Orginal Post Date 10/27/2022
