Hi, I'm Alicia and I am fundraising to help with the medical bills that my current condition warrants. I have health insurance which has covered a lot of the medical bills this year but it seems that my condition will require more funding and on-going care until this is resolved. In March of 2022, I began noticing that I was short of breath after walking a flight of stairs. This was concerning as I have been active and fit my whole life. I went to my doctor and had a CT scan done, and when I got the results, I was shocked. The radiologist found that my lungs are full of tumors. Some are small (1 cm), and others are quite large (9 cm.) The medical professionals immediately thought I had cancer that had traveled to my lungs and must be pretty advanced. This initial diagnosis came as a blow to my entire reality, as you might imagine. From that moment, everything changed. I was run through many tests, including CT scans, blood tests and biopsies. The lung biopsy led to a complication related to the drugs they used to numb me, and I lost 30% of the vision in my right eye. In the end, they found no cancer (so thankful) but did find that I have an extremely rare condition called Benign Metastisizing Leiomyoma. There are fewer than 170 cases of this type of tumor, so there is no pre-documented course of action to rid me of them. All the doctors know is that estrogen feeds the tumors (as does stress.) In August, I began an experimental treatment using a strong pharmaceutical to suppress estrogen. After 3.5 months on this drug, I had another CT, and the tumors are still growing. In early January, I had been feeling worse and was admitted to the hospital two weeks ago for hypoxia. One night, I woke up at home unable to intake oxygen or breathe and was immediately admitted to the hospital where I needed to be continuously monitored. Currently, my doctors are still evaluating my condition and it has been a challenging journey given the rarity of this illness. When I finally am able to go home, I will need to be continuously monitored and will need a nurse and hospital equipment to feel comfortable. Although my health insurance is covering some of the expenses, it is still a financial burden and I have already spent my savings on this condition. I am grateful for any support during this time, as it will help alleviate the financial burden and allow me to focus on my health. Thank you for your support during this time. I am confident that with the right care and support, I will be able to overcome this challenge and move forward with renewed energy and optimism.

Last October, I was diagnosed with Acute Lymphocytic Leukemia (ALL). I was in some of the best shape of my life at the time, training to run my first marathon ever. After being diagnosed, at first, all I could think about was how my diagnosis would change my life forever and handicap me from doing all that I wanted to accomplish in life, chief among them—running a marathon. A few days went by, and I decided I decided f*** that. Cancer’s not going to stop me, and I’m going to come back and run that marathon. In fact, I want to be the fastest to complete a marathon after getting a bone marrow transplant. As I received six rounds of intermittent chemo and a bone marrow/stem cell transplant over this past year, I used the goal to run that marathon to push myself every day to fight the cancer by getting myself back into shape. In April, I could barely stand up for longer than a minute without needing to sit back down after being in the hospital for a month and losing 25 pounds from my transplant the month before. In August, I couldn't run more than a mile because my body was still all messed up. It seemed like I would never reach the light at the end of the tunnel—my goal of completing a marathon in October, which would be one year from my diagnosis and seven months from my transplant. But I continued to push through, working out constantly, sometimes two or three times a day, because I knew my body would continue to respond. September came, and suddenly, I felt like I could push myself to longer and longer runs. The scariest part of cancer to most people is that you have no idea how it will react. No idea whether the treatments will work or not, which depending on your attitude, can destroy your sense of hope. Well, in my view, the cancer’s already decided how hard it's going to fight. What matters is how hard you fight. There are plenty of ways to fight cancer through your own choices (exercising, sleep, diet, stress relief, relationships, and environment). Once you realize you have the power to beat cancer through your decisions, it becomes way less scary to battle. Today, seven months after my transplant, I finished that marathon. I became the fastest to complete a marathon after a bone marrow transplant (to my knowledge from google since I'm the only one insane enough to try lol.) Finishing that race was the sweetest vengeance I could give to cancer. This accomplishment is also a huge show of thanks to those that helped me get to where I am—my parents, family, friends, doctors, nurses and my German donor. Without all of you, I would not have been able to do this. I hope that this can be an inspiration to help other people get through similar battles when they cannot see the light at the end of the tunnel. The end is always there. Even if you can’t see it, you just need to keep pushing forward. The light might be just around the bend. On another note, my sister is currently battling Acute Myeloid Leukemia for the 4th time in 4 years and just had her second stem cell transplant this past September. She had a very tough go of it from the transplant with numerous harsh side effects. Please pray for her and the continued success of her treatments. She fought cancer before me and is a big reason why I ran and was able to stay confident throughout this process. It truly takes a village of people to beat cancer, and I was the beneficiary of so many different people's hard work and care. My sister and I have been the recipients of multiple treatments developed by the Leukemia & Lymphoma Society (LLS). I would like to pay it forward to the next person and raise money for LLS. We have come so far in battling this disease, but we still have much more to accomplish. The Leukemia & Lymphoma Society® (LLS) is a global leader in the fight against cancer. The LLS mission: Cure leukemia, lymphoma, Hodgkin's disease and myeloma, and improve the quality of life of patients and their families. LLS funds lifesaving blood cancer research around the world, provides free information and support services, and is the voice for all blood cancer patients seeking access to quality, affordable, coordinated care. On October 29th while at a men's retreat in the Catskills Paul developed severe abdominal pain and nausea. A nurse practitioner was called who administered acupuncture and advised bed rest and clear fluids. Over the day and night his conditioned worsened and on Sunday October 30th, despite his wife's pleas to go to a hospital in NY, Paul drove 5 hours home to be closer to family. Paul's wife noticed he had become jaundiced and immediately brought him to the ER at Central Vermont Medical Center in Berlin where a CT scan revealed he had diverticulitis and a small bowel obstruction. It was then that Paul began vomiting blood. An NG tube was placed, morphine and Zofran administered and he was admitted. During the night Paul developed peritonitis (a deadly infection) and was prepped for a 7am partial colectomy that took 7 hours. Two surgeons removed a 5-6 inch section of his colon and he was sent to surgical recovery. Over the next 3 days not only did his condition worsen but his roommate tested positive for COVID-19. Paul was moved to the COVID section for observation and quarantine. As Paul's pain and nausea continued he was medicated with Toradol, Dilaudid, Oxycodone and Fentanyl despite his family questioning whether this was safe and effective or just causing a tolerance to narcotics. On Sunday November 6th, Paul was continuing to be in severe pain and nausea as well as becoming dehydrated and suffering from lack of sleep and beginning to break down mentally. His wife spoke with his attending physician and questioned whether or not a CT scan should be done to rule out any new underlying causes in lieu of adding more narcotics. The physician refused the CT scan, stating it would be too much radiation and stated he never over medicated his patients to the point of addiction, even proudly claiming he had 90 year olds on Fentanyl. Paul's wife pointed out that through their combined experience working in Treatment Court, the Re-entry House Program and Recovery Coaching he was not able to be sure of that his patients were not drug seeking from outside sources and that the largest demographic of untreated people with addiction were the elderly. On Monday November 7th a new attending physician saw the amount of pain Paul was in and immediately ordered a CT scan. The results showed an abnormality. When his surgeon looked at the results he ordered a contrast CT scan to see if Paul had developed a leak in his bowels. The contrast was introduced and since Paul was not eliminating this caused excruciating pain, causing Paul to scream for hours-so much that he could be heard from the elevators. The results came back: he had developed a leak over the weekend in his bowels. He was becoming septic and needed another emergency surgery. A surgery that could have happened sooner. Paul was in surgery for two hours to repair the leak and clear out the leakage. An iliostomy was performed and a temporary colostomy bag put into place. In the recovery room Paul's wife spoke with the anesthesiologist who confirmed that Paul had developed a tolerance to the narcotics and would need assistance weaning off of them. He was transported to ICU for observation as his temperature had gotten so high he was melting the EKG electrodes placed on his body. On Tuesday November 8th it was discovered that his Creatinine levels were high suggesting acute kidney damage from the Toradol. Paul had to withdraw from his Clinical Mental Health Counseling Residency program at Capella University and give up his hotel room and plane ticket to Chicago coming up later this month. He will be out of work for an undetermined amount of time and in recovery. He will be needing several post op follow up appointments as well as another operation to remove the colostomy bag and close up his stoma. His wife has had to take a leave of absence from her job to be his caretaker and advocate. Both have applied for short term disability but will also need extra help paying for: *Medical bills *Legal assistance *Home Health Aide *Doggy Daycare for Prudence and Poobah during the first few weeks of home recovery *Adaptive or Assistive equipment for showering, walking etc *Nutritional Counseling

I am here to ask for your help and support for me and my 2 amazing children in this hard time. Please check your breast on a regular basis. As my experience shows, it can happen to anyone. Peace! They try not to touch or stimulate her too much so if anything needs to be done, it’s only done twice a day. Dear friends and family, I’m writing this on behalf of my wife, Liz. Please help me save her. Though it was hard not to see friends or family or go out to dinner, we buckled down, sprayed everything with isopropyl alcohol, wore masks even outside, snuggled up, loved NFL Sundays, and kept Covid free for two years. Life was good. Unfortunately, as the pandemic dragged on and waned into “less malignant” Omicron, I caught Covid in early June 2022. Liz got sick a few days later. While I recovered in a week, Liz still hasn’t. Her Covid developed into a devastating case of Long Covid. Covid has left Liz unable to sit or stand, unable to work, unable to watch shows or pass the time even for a few hours. She has been bed-bound since July. She has chronic anxiety, dyspepsia, nausea, vision problems, pressure headaches, chills, adrenaline rushes, light and sound sensitivity, and a rapid heart rate and blood pressure issues exacerbated by dysautonomic and CNS dysfunction, POTS, PEM, and MCAS. She still has a fever, sore throat, constant malaise, and labored breathing. Physical activity leaves her tired and short of breath. Even sitting up and standing make her feel extremely sick. It is hard for her to eat food, sleep and manage the pain. I now take care of her 24 hours a day. She needs help getting food, drinking water, and taking medications. Several times a day, I carry her to the bathroom since she needs help getting there even though it's 15 feet away. She’s lost 20 pounds and, at this moment, is on nearly 30 different medications, supplements, and vitamins. When she’s able, we hug each other, cry and laugh when we can. However, the illness is taking our lives away. We have used up our savings and will continue to need more medical treatments for the unforeseen future. It is taking a toll on our finances and, ultimately, our future. While Liz has made some encouraging incremental improvements over the last three months, she’s nowhere near well enough to manage on her own. Reaching full recovery could take years. The next few months, especially, will be an expensive endeavor, physically, medically, and emotionally, as we look for effective treatments. Long Covid is a new illness in the medical field. There is no comprehensive treatment―much less any cure―for people who are suffering from Long Covid. And the worse your symptoms are, the more expensive the treatments. My wife has already seen countless doctors and Covid specialists and been to the emergency room. She has taken a mind-boggling amount of supplements, vitamins, and prescription medications to roughly $10,000―out-of-pocket with insurance. Medical bills and credit card balances are ballooning with no signs of slowing down as we have to explore new treatments and better medical options. She is looking at the following treatments: IVIG (15K) Apheresis (20K) Dysautonomia Center (5000) Dr. Leo Galland first visit (1500) and follow-ups (500/visit) Dr. Jordan Vaughn (200/visit) IncellDX cytokines and immune sub panel testing and consultation (850) Stellate Ganglion Block (3500) Northwestern Long Covid treatment center (200/visit) Supplements, vitamins, medicines (2000) Liz’s short-term disability is now running out and I’ve had to reduce my hours at work to give her the care she needs. With our income sources dissipating rapidly, we desperately seek help to get us out of this Long Covid tunnel and into the light. Anything you can do to help would go a long way to getting us there! A CT scan showed he had acquired aspirated pneumonia, so they quickly moved him to the ICU floor and put him on oxygen, where he remained for the next several days. On October 4th, he was moved off the rehab floor to a different floor to address his needs. They were not able to move him to Madison due to beds not being available. His medical team put a stint in to drain the fluid through his stomach. The procedure went well, and the doctors were pleased with the outcome. The rest went very, very quickly. The bike flipped and Billy took the majority of the impact to his left side and then, we believe, as the bike was flipping, he took another impact to his right side. Our free spirit son was not wearing a helmet. It is not required in the state of Florida. Our son is still as handsome as ever and you would never even know he was so sick by looking at him. However, Billy experienced 13 severe brain bleeds and multiple Diffuse Axonal Injuries on both sides of his brain with some being in the sleep center of his brain. Diffuse axonal injuries are the shearing (tearing) of the brain's long connecting nerve fibers (axons) that happens when the brain is injured as it shifts and rotates inside the bony skull. For some, recovering from a diffuse axonal brain injury is possible—but there are no guarantees with such injuries. The severity of the brain lesions, which areas of the brain they are in, your treatment, and many other factors can affect whether or not you make a full recovery. Billy is a kindhearted, full of life, gentle giant. The love he has for his family and friends is unconditional. He has a precious 4 year old son who absolutely adores and needs his daddy and the love of his life, Samantha who has the kindest, most loving soul. She has not left his side! His work on this earth is not over yet We are all holding on to the “possible”side of things. We are begging God to grant us a miracle. We have been very humbled by the love we have been shown this far by so many of our family, friends and even people we may not know personally. It is very hard for us to admit that it will be impossible for us to be able to support our son by ourselves financially during this journey but it is something that we have had to realize very quickly. In January 2018, I lost my grandfather Thomas Long at the age of 77 to pancreatic cancer. A veteran of the U.S. Marine Corps and a well-known small business owner in Cortland, NY, he was a fixture in his community and the anchor of my extended family. In September 2022, my roommate Thomas McClelland lost his uncle Mitchell Quint at age 53 after a hard-fought battle with pancreatic cancer. As we sat in our room reminiscing over the good times we had with these role models, Tommy and I came to a simple conclusion: Pancreatic cancer was unfair and something had to change. Unlike other cancers that can be caught early on and treated effectively, pancreatic cancer is often discovered late in its disease process. The lack of early warning signs and screening tests has led pancreatic cancer to become one of the leading causes of cancer-related deaths. The five-year survival rate of this disease is just 11%. As I sat in my ceramics class the next day, I couldn't stop thinking about how eerily similar our families' experiences with pancreatic cancer were. For both of us, the disease progressed much faster than we could make sense of it in our heads. It felt like one moment everything was fine, and the next, we had lost someone we had looked up to for years. As I trimmed a cereal bowl that day in class, an idea struck me: what if I could in some way focus my newfound hobby to make money and raise awareness for pancreatic cancer research? Here, the Pottery for Pancreatic Cancer Marathon was born. On October 28th at 4:00 I will begin my 24-hour marathon of throwing, trimming, and glazing ceramic pieces in the Notre Dame ceramic studio. I plan to finish as many high-quality mugs, bowls, and vases as possible during this event, and ask that you donate to this page for a chance to win some of my work. Every dollar donated will go directly to the Lustgarten Foundation for Pancreatic Cancer Research. Please keep in mind that I am not a professional potter, just a college student who has taken up a love for ceramics. For additional information on this event feel free to follow along on Instagram @MattLongPotteryCo For more information on the Lustgarten Foundation for Pancreatic Cancer Research, feel free to visit Lustgarten Foundation Home Page ** As per GoFundMe terms of service no raffles, sweepstakes, giveaways, or promotions are offered in exchange for any donations made to this campaign**

Just a few short weeks ago, my sister Emilie received the news no body wants to hear. She has been diagnosed with breast cancer. Her breast cancer is HER2 positive. The HER2 cancer contains a protein that promotes rapid growth of cancer cells. Emilie will have a PET scan completed this Thursday to see if her cancer has spread elsewhere in her body; however, her doctors remain hopeful that it hasn’t. In these past two weeks, Emilie has undergone numerous biopsies and tests and these won’t be ending soon. She has seen oncologists, radiologists, surgeons, genetic specialists, dietitians, and fertility specialists to name a few. She has had to make many big, life changing, personal decisions with little notice. Emilie will have her port placed Friday and begin Chemotherapy within the next two weeks. She will continue chemo through February. Throughout her treatment with chemo, she will have continued lab work and PET scans to ensure her tumors are shrinking. Once she is finished with chemo, she will have a double mastectomy with lymph node removal. Once the surgery is complete, she will have more chemotherapy and possibly radiation. This current treatment plan is somewhat tentative, depending on her PET scan results. Emilie currently resides in Florida and is a Behavior Interventionist at an elementary school where she works with special needs kids. Throughout this entire process, Emilie will have to miss work not only for her appointments and chemo, but also on her bad days when she isn’t feeling well. She will quickly run out of paid time off. Her medical bills are already piling up and several aspects of what she has to go through are not covered by her insurance. Emilie does not like to ask for help, but with everything happening so suddenly, we feel this is the best way to help her as she doesn’t need any further financial stress added on to what she is already going through. Emilie has a long journey ahead of her. This has completely come out of nowhere and is totally overwhelming, as it would be for anyone. During her treatment, she will be limited on visitors to immediate family only as she will have a weakened immune system. We would appreciate all of the prayers, encouragement, and positive vibes for Emilie. If you’d like to reach out to Emilie or send her something personally, please reach out to my parents, myself, Kaylie, or Natalie and we will get you in contact with her. She is tough and we know she will beat this. Keep fighting Em! We love you!

Hello everyone! My sister Audrey gave birth to a beautiful baby girl on Tuesday, November 15th 2022. Hattie Blair. They are still currently at CMH. Thankfully, good news has been coming their way. Hattie’s bladder, stomach, brain, and heart are all functioning normally. The biggest issue, however, is that Hattie has what they call a fistula, meaning that the opening for her rectum is in the wrong spot; she has a muscular sphincter that doesn’t line up with the rectal opening. The surgeon has a plan, but with Hattie being only a little over 5lbs, she is too small for surgery and has to wait until she’s 3 months old.Until then, Audrey and Caleb are still waiting on tests for other organ function. They will also have to learn the process that the doctors are using to help Hattie pass her stool until the surgery can be completed. This isn’t the birth story that the Choates were hoping for, but they are thankful for this beautiful little girl that God has created and they trust in Him to put good doctors in their path and to get their little girl home as quickly as possible. Thank you so much for you love, prayers, and support for this family.

Our father, Bill Cunningham, was living a very normal life in Olathe, Kansas. He was doing all the things he loved like running, lifting weights, yoga, and enjoying time with our mom. Late August came around and his “normal” changed forever. What began as muscle spasms in his legs escalated to tingling and numbness and then to falling unexpectedly. His primary care provider prescribed medication, but it was ineffective. On August 30, 2022 while walking into the ER he fell. They began to run CT scans, MRI’s, blood work and later a spinal tap. Our father did not realize at that moment that the short walk into the ER would be the last time he would ever walk or even feel his legs. An MRI showed that he had cervical stenosis in several discs and an infection in his spinal fluid. While still in the hospital, he started to lose feeling in his feet and lower legs. Each day the paralysis progressed up his body and doctors couldn’t agree on a medical intervention. It was heartbreaking watching our dad lose the ability to use his legs and we all felt helpless sitting and waiting for answers. Many of his symptoms weren’t making sense or aligning with initial diagnoses, so they began sending off blood and spinal fluid samples to labs in Utah and the Mayo Clinic. After a week the paralysis was starting to spread up to his hands. The neurosurgeon finally agreed to do surgery for cervical stenosis. He also recommended spinal cord rehab in Lincoln, NE at Madonna. With two of us (myself and Janel) living in the Lincoln area, we agreed this would be the place to be as our mom would have a place to stay. Our father arrived at Madonna on September 15, 2022, via ambulance transport (this $5000 service was not covered by insurance). We all were so excited for him to have the opportunity to be evaluated and begin therapy. He got settled in and was ready to do the work. Unfortunately, our dad was dealt another setback. The second night's stay at Madonna did not go as planned and he was taken to the Bryan East ER with trouble breathing, pain in his neck and extremely low blood pressure. He had suddenly lost what feeling he had left in his arms and hands. The ER doctor found a large hematoma on his neck where he had previously had surgery. By that afternoon he was transported to Bryan West for another surgery to remove the hematoma. He spent about a week in the ICU before coming back to Madonna. After being at Madonna for only a couple of days, he was back in the ER for a blood clot in his leg. He had an IVC filter placed. It took yet another week for insurance to approve him to go back to Madonna from the hospital. During these weeks of waiting in the hospital, dad lost valuable therapy time. We are happy to report he has been back at Madonna for the last several weeks and has begun therapy. It’s hard to swallow these words, but our father now lives as a person with quadriplegia. We are hopeful that he will regain some movement with intensive therapy, time, hard work, and most of all patience. Those of you who know our father know how active of a man he has always been. Losing the ability to use his arms and legs has been devastating. We don’t know how he does it but Dad has remained positive and hopeful! For now, our father is authorized through Medicare until the end of October. His Doctors have recommended that he transition to another skilled nursing facility to continue rehab. Some of you may not know this, but our dad was in the Air Force for nearly 8 years. Thankfully, we will be able to utilize Veteran benefits and he can be transferred to a VA Spinal Cord Injury clinic either in Minneapolis, MN or St. Louis, MO. We hope to find out in the next week where he is going. Our mother will have a place to stay while he is there, but for us girls this will be more difficult. As a family we are experiencing how quickly life can change in a blink of an eye. We don’t know what the future holds, but we know that there have been out-of-pocket costs not covered by insurance and there will be many other expenses along the way during his rehabilitation journey. Our mom is also facing hardships, as she been traveling back and forth to different hospitals, traveling out of state, eating on the go, and has little time or energy to give to the various tasks of daily living. We are fortunate that Lindsey is home in Kansas keeping an eye on the house while our mom is out of town and providing support when she is home. We also have to begin planning for dad to come home, which will also require multiple expenses. We will need to have transportation that will accommodate a wheelchair and make many modifications to their home so dad can have access to all the things he needs. Many people have reached out or asked how they could help so we have decided to start this Go Fund Me to help support our parents. We are so very grateful for any support you may be able to provide for our family. “Alone we are strong... together we are stronger.” We also ask if you would consider saying a prayer for Bill’s strength and recovery or adding him to your prayer list as he continues rehab and prepares to move to a new city. Thank you!! Megan, Janel and Lindsey

With the closing of RMCH L&D and prenatal services, patients in the greater Gallup area who are not IHS eligible currently have to travel to Grants or ABQ for prenatal care. Over the course of a normal pregnancy, this can mean 10-20 visits, creating untenable transportation costs, time away from work, childcare needs and more. Many patients are making the 2-4 hours commute, but others are going without care entirely. Given this need, Gallup Community Health is making key changes to our services. We will begin offering prenatal care, provided by our family physicians with our OB/GYN team consulting for high risk cases. We are working closely with Cibola Hospital in Grants, as well as partners in Albuquerque to make deliveries as seamless as possible without local L&D services available. Thanks to these partners, we have the equipment needed, but insurance costs are very high to add prenatal services. As Gallup's nonprofit, community-led clinic, we are looking to the Gallup community and our supporters near and far to help fund the $20,000 increase in insurance costs. This is a one-time need, as we fully expect clinic revenues to cover this expense long term, but your help with this start up need helps bring a much-needed service back to Gallup. Val Wangler, MD Executive Director Gallup Community Health

On April 12, 2022 our sweet father, Spiro Pavlidis, suffered a traumatic fall at home. He fell down in our living room, and hit his head on the floor. Our mom and brother rushed to help him, but they figured out immediately that he was very badly hurt. He suffered life-threatening injuries, including massive brain bleeding and swelling that required brain surgery. He was rushed to the hospital where he spent 3 months undergoing several operations, including a brain flap craniectomy to reduce the swelling in his brain. The surgery required removing a portion of his skull. We remained optimistic despite the horrible circumstances and had no idea this would impact him so severely. Our dad’s recovery has been very complicated. For a long time, he would not wake up. He kept getting infections and doctors were pessimistic about his prognosis. We never gave up hope. One of us was at his bedside every day, even though COVID precautions meant that only one of us could be there at a time. After almost three months in the neurological intensive care unit, our father underwent a second significant surgery, a cranioplasty, to replace the piece of his skull that was removed. It was after this second surgery that he woke up fully and began his road to recovery. Full recovery from a brain injury such as the one our father suffered is possible, but he requires intense therapy to be able to regain lost function. Our father worked tirelessly to provide for us all of his life. He is an immigrant who came to the United States with nothing. He put himself through college and then owned a restaurant, working grueling hours. Even though he was so busy, he made time to spend with us and, later, delighted in spending time with his grandchildren. Prior to this accident, he always enjoyed perfect health and loved helping his family. We eventually convinced him to finally retire, so that he could spend more time with us and begin to enjoy life a little more. He has three amazing grandchildren, one son, two daughters, and a devoted wife of 45 years, and many other relatives and friends. He was planning a big trip to Greece to see extended family, but it had to be cancelled when he was injured. After he was discharged from the hospital, we had no other option than to transfer him to an acute neurological rehabilitation facility. We searched throughout Florida, but the only brain injury rehabilitation centers that accept his insurance would only keep him for 3 weeks---far too little time for the intense therapy he needs. He couldn’t walk, talk, eat, or move his arms upon his discharge from the hospital. He is currently at the only rehabilitation facility that allows him to stay until he is fully rehabilitated, however, this facility does not accept his insurance, so the only option is self-pay. The self-pay amount is astronomical per day. Our father started at this rehabilitation facility on July 15, 2022, and he is still there. He is making progress and has begun speaking, along with taking part in physical therapy and learning how to walk and eat again. He has come a very long way since he was first admitted, but he still needs more time to fully regain his lost function. We have researched ways of paying for this therapy without insurance, but it seems like there are no options. We are currently paying for his rehabilitation out of pocket. The cost is overwhelming and reaching out to Brain Injury programs has not yielded any results. We are sadly in need of financial help to fund our father’s recovery. We wouldn’t be asking if we hadn’t already run out of our family resources. We are heartbroken and running out of options. We are grateful for any help, regardless of the amount. All of our lives are forever changed by this horrible accident, but we hope that through therapy, our dad can regain his independence and health, so that he can enjoy the rest of his life.

This happened to my dad Thursday October 27, 2022. I'll leave it in his words: "I was attacked yesterday morning while walking my dogs in Carrol-Oaks Neighborhood. I picked them up to avoid any trouble and the Pit-mix charged. I was knocked down and my dogs were ripped from hands. The Pit mix knocked me down a total of 4 times. He wanted my dogs. The little Black dog Char had her abdomen ripped open and her intestines were hanging out. Delilah my little tan dog had her leg almost torn off. She has puncture wounds all over her body. Neither dog is out of the woods yet. My Vet bill for 4 hours of surgery per dog is about $5,000. And Char is still at the Emergency Hospital. I am fortunate that Brodie Animal Hospital reduce my bill considerably. Restores my faith in Veterinary Care. I haven’t gotten my Hospital bill yet. We all know what that visit will cost. Here is the Kicker, it was the Pit- Mix 2nd time to attack. Once wasn’t enough. The owner probably can’t afford to fix his fence. He can afford to feed the dog. Have 3 cars in his driveway. The Pit would have outright killed Delilah. The Pit was enjoying his time assaulting us. The Woman Angel, who saw Char running with her leash still attached. Char in shock and adrenaline flowing ran 1/2 mile toward home with her intestine hanging out. That wonderful woman stopped her and she was calling for help. I finally caught up, limping from the attack. My Angel brought out towels and put my shaking self into her car with both of my bloody dogs. She drove us to Brodie Animal Hospital. They immediately came out and started saving my dogs. Brodie Animal Hospital are wonderful compassionate people. The Drs, Assistants, and virtually everyone there showed their professionalism and passion for helping. Chelsea, I will forever be Grateful for your concern and help in reducing my stress and shock. The exposed bladder can't store urine or function normally, resulting in urine leakage (incontinence). Problems caused by bladder exstrophy vary in severity. Thankfully, bladder extrophy is treatable with surgery. During Matthew’s time in the NICU at Christ Hospital Danny and Kate spoke to pediatric urologists, along with many nurses well educated on this type of condition, who advised surgery is the best option for Matthew. They have been connected to the Children’s Hospital in Milwaukee and their urology/bladder extrophy team. Surgery is scheduled for November 15th. Danny and Kate will be making multiple trips back and forth from Oak Forest, IL to Milwaukee due to having a 2 year old son at home to care for as well making it impossible for both parents to be with Matthew full time as he recovers in the PICU. The Messini family has been through a lot in these past few years. Rachael has undergone 7 surgeries for endometriosis, 4 of which were over the past 3 years. Unfortunately, just as she was finally getting her life back, she began to have challenging and painful neurological symptoms. After many tests and brain and spine MRIs, they discovered that she had something called Chiari 1 Malformation. This means that her brain is herniating out of the opening at the bottom of her skull into her spinal canal - causing numbness on the right side of her face, numbness and weakness in her arms and hands, vision problems, internal tremors, memory loss, sudden hearing loss that comes and goes, migraine aura, dizziness, and pain at the base of her skull... She is scheduled to have surgery on November 28th where her neurosurgeon will decompress the brain stem, remove part of her skull and C1 vertebrae, cut open her dura (the sack that the brain and spinal cord sit in), add a dura patch, and create more space for her brain tissue. This is the only treatment for type 1 Chiari Malformations. This surgery aims to relieve symptoms, relieve the pressure on her nerves, and prevent further nerve damage and the formation of a syrinx (a fluid-filled pocket, or cyst, in the spinal cord) by restoring the CSF flow. As we all know, having surgery takes a major toll - not just physically, but emotionally and financially. With this being the 5th surgery in a matter of 3 years, the financial burden is heavy and at the moment, unpredictable. In addition to the mountain of surgical costs from these past 3 years, Rachael will need to begin physical therapy again as well to regain mobility in her neck after the brain surgery. Any amount given would help lift the weight of this load and be such a blessing to the Messini family. Thank you so much. Love, time, faith, and hope. How do you measure all of them? However you measure them; if you’re reading this right now, I bet you’ve wished to have more of each one of them at some point in your life. "There's only one thing more precious than our time and that's who we spend it on." - Leo Christopher Justine and Jason never felt these emotions stronger than when Edison left the world before he was able to bring even more love and joy to his family. They were extended all of these gifts by a device called a Cuddle Cot. The Cuddle Cot is a cooling blanket that preserves the infant's body so that parents and families can spend more time with the child and gives them time to grieve. It works by circulating cold water to a small flexible hard pad placed under the baby. The cold pad reduces the infant’s core body temperature through direct contact. The system allows the baby to stay cool near the parents. This device allowed Jason and Justine to spend 48 hours with Edison that would not have been possible without this amazing technology provided by URMC Labor and Delivery Unit. Access to a Cuddle Cot is limited at hospitals at this time, leaving some families without this option. The Arpag family is asking for donations to purchase an additional Cuddle Cot for the Labor and Delivery Unit at URMC. Their hope is at least one more family will have the gifts of love, time, faith, and hope. Through your gracious donation, we will be fortunate to purchase a Cuddle Cot in the memory of Edison Walter Arpag for future families and infants. Their gratitude for any and all donations, no matter how small, could help them reach their goal. Their hearts will be full, with any donation you may be able to contribute.

Anyone who parks in the Norfolk Street parking garage at Rutgers School of Dental Medicine knows this familiar face—but few know his name or his story. “My grandkids don’t believe me when I tell them that Grandpa works at a dental school. ‘Then why don’t you have any teeth?’ asks my youngest.” Richard has worked at the parking garage for years. He works hard to keep students safe when they are heading home after a long day at school. ‘I’ve seen it all working the night shift, but they don’t bother me anymore, I just worry for the students sometimes. I make sure to do my job and keep the place locked up at night. I love working here and seeing so many people.” Richard estimates he sees about 500 drivers come into his garage every day. “My favorite thing about working here is the food truck. I love that little place around the corner. I like sandwiches, but I can’t chew them. I have to swallow a lot of stuff whole. I’m always scared to eat in my booth—if I choked, no one would find me until it’s too late. The dentist says I don’t have any bone and need two screws put in. It sounds nice but I’ll never be able to afford it. Between trying to support myself and my family, I struggle to make ends meet.” When Richard’s brother passed away in October 2022, Richard took on new responsibilities to keep his extended family afloat. “If I had nice teeth and a nice smile, boy, I don’t know what I would do,” he says. “I’d be able to smile, and maybe people wouldn’t be so scared of me. I could eat a little better, too. That would help with my diabetes. I want to be around to see my grandkids grow up. I tell them I’m not going nowhere, but I don’t always believe it with all of the stuff I have going on with my health and my mouth.” Your donations will go to help Richard fund his dental care and continue being a valuable part of the Rutgers community. Thank you for your contributions.

While adjusting to life with no stomach has been a struggle, it is one I have managed. After a couple days of steroid treatment, the swelling in my brain was reducing and I started waking up. After a week or so, the tumor was able to be removed. After testing, they found the tumor was a glioblastoma and it was unrelated to the pancreatic cancer. We also found out that the testing for a genetic trait for successful treatment did not prove positive. I have now been given a not so positive prognosis of less than a year, even with radiation and chemo. After battling this long already against having had pancreatic cancer, I have started treatment for the brain cancer, regardless of the terminal prognosis. That brings me to the reason for this fundraiser. I have always had a bucket list goal to get to New York City and see the Christmas Tree at Rockefeller Center. Costs involved are the flight there, the hotel stay, food, etc. And due to the popularity of NYC at that time of year, costs are a bit higher. Please consider helping me achieve this bucket list goal with a financial contribution. Any amount would be greatly appreciated. Even if you’re not able to help financially, sharing this with friends would also be very appreciated. Thank you, Rick

On September 23, 2022, Jay had suffered a stroke at home. Thankfully, his wife, Khendy was at home at the time and was able to call for medical help within those critical moments. From the signs that he was showing, she knew he was having a stroke and along with their children , they pleaded for him to stay awake until the ambulance arrived. In the emergency room, the doctors were very straightforward and advised Khendy that they were not sure if Jay would make it, considering the size of the bleed that occurred. The brain shift was very significant and only time would tell what his deficit would be. For the next week, Jay was admitted into the ICU and put under sedation in critical condition. He would undergo numerous tests quite frequently such as CT Scans, ECHOs and X-rays to give doctors an understanding of what was happening internally & most importantly neurologically. MRI’s would later be done when Jay was more stable. That week was very crucial in determining what steps would be taken next because the doctors had to wait until the swelling and bleeding subsided. When Jay finally opened his eyes a few days later of being admitted, there was a small glimpse of hope that started to overcome the worry and sadness upon everyone. During that week, it was also recommended for him to have surgery for a tracheostomy to help with breathing effectively and a PEG tube to help with food digestion to make sure he was still receiving the vital nutrients needed for recovery. Fast forward to a month since his stroke, Jay has made such amazing progress in such a short amount of time. His doctors are impressed with his progress and anticipate for him to improve even more. Everyday, you can find Khendy at his bedside making sure that he completes his daily occupational, physical and speech therapy. He continues to follow commands, recognizes people and answer questions using his eyebrows and hand gestures. With his therapist’s assistance, Jay also sits upright a couple times a day and is now starting to stand & sit on the edge of the bed to help strengthen his body. Some days, you can even find him bobbing his head at times to his favorite local music when played and showing Shaka. While therapy continues to help strengthen all his muscles each day, his right side which is also his dominant side, is the side that was greatly affected. Because of his young age of 44, the goal is for him to get transferred to REHAB Hospital of the Pacific located in Oahu, where he will undergo extensive therapy in hopes of getting him back to where he was before the stroke. However, before going to Oahu it has been recommended that he continues therapy at Hale Makua Kahului to strengthen his endurance. On October 26, Jay was discharged from MMMC and transported to Hale Makua. With that being said, medical expenses for hospital stays, tests, and most importantly therapy continue to add up for Khendy and their family as the days go by. She continues to be by Jay’s bedside and unfortunately, has not been able to return to work just yet. The stress of a financial burden should never cross her mind being that this happened so unexpectedly. Jay was an active Kali (Filipino Martial Arts) Professor, a long time employee of 20+ years for Alamo Rent a Car, and a caring, funny and outgoing guy before this. The road to recovery will not be an easy one, but Jay proves everyday that he is willing to fight and get stronger so he can finally come home. Any donation, big or small is greatly appreciated. We thank you so much from the bottom of our hearts for the outpouring of love, prayers and strength for Jay.

On behalf of Robin & Sandra Brinkley, I'm managing the fundraising effort for Robin, my father-in-law, to enable him to undergo new cancer treatment in his fight against stage four squamous cell carcinoma. ROBIN'S ORIGINAL DIAGNOSIS In July of 2020, near his home in Lyons, Georgia, Robin had a small lesion removed on the surface of his cheek. Within a few months a concerning lump formed near the wound, prompting doctors to order a biopsy. In October of that year it was determined that Robin had squamous cell carcinoma, a kind of skin cancer that can form inside the body or in the lower layers of the skin. On October 27, 2020, Robin had his first of two surgeries and it proved to be substantial. Surgeons removed all lymph nodes in the right side of his neck, as well as numerous facial nerves, each wrapped in cancerous tumors, resulting in partial paralysis and permanent deformation on the right side of Robin's face. On November 3, the same day that Robin's eldest daughter Amanda was undergoing surgery for breast cancer, Robin had his second surgery, this one designed to improve the use of his right eyelid. EARLY TREATMENT After surgery, as is standard, Robin began a daily treatment of radiation, over six weeks, targeted at his cheek and surrounding areas. After radiation ended in February of 2021, an early-summer CT-scan showed cancer spreading to Robin's upper chest muscles and neck. Robin's doctors recommended a type of radiation not offered locally: proton raditiation, coupled with chemotherapy, at Emory University Hospital in Atlanta. This required an eight-week initial stay in Atlanta, followed by regular trips every three weeks for the remainder of the year; each drive to Atlanta was a six-hour roundtrip. The treatments were intense and debilitating, as the focused radiation on Robin's neck forced him to re-learn how to swallow food. In December of 2021 the treatment concluded and the following February's CT-scan showed the aggressive neck tumor was still growing. In fact, the news was the worst yet: squamous cell carcinoma was detected in additional organs of Robin's body, resulting in a "stage four" diagnosis. Determined to fight, Robin elected to continue regular trips to Atlanta for the next six months for a new schedule of intravenous immunotherapy treatment. While this treatment was effective in eliminating some of the additional tumors most recently found, and even stifling the aggressive neck tumor, the immunotherarpy ran its course and lost effectiveness in August of this year. Robin's doctors tried unsuccessfully to get him into a new clinical trial and subsequently prescribed an intense intravenous antibody treatment, which Robin began last month in September. This particular anitbody treatment has minimal life extension projections, and while its effectiveness is officially yet to be determined, it is clear to the naked eye that the neck tumor continues its growth. ALTERNATIVE TREATMENT Now, October 2022, exactly two years from his first diagnosis, Robin's Primary Care Physician recommended something new: alternative treatment outside the United States. Because of his doctor's recommendation, and having exhausted all other options, Robin reached out to the CHIPSA Hospital, in Mexico, and soon discovered that he was a candidate for Gerson Immunotherapy Treatment. Well-regarded and one of the oldest Alternative Cancer Treatment centers in North America, the hospital has seen many of its squamous cell carcinoma patients extend their lives by years, and even cured. After two years of pursuing all of the treatments that traditional biomedicine has to offer -- surgery, radiation, proton radiation, chemotherapy, immunotherapy and monoclonal antibodies -- and at every stage lead by faith, hope and love in a healing and merciful God, Robin and Sandra are heading to Mexico on October 23 for the three-week treatment. Aside from the medical bills from the last two-years for the various insurance-supported treatments (which, due to the frequent trips to Atlanta, has cost Robin and Sandra about $20,000 annually, out of pocket), the CHIPSA Hospital, naturally, must be paid for outside of the framework of health insurance. A single three-week program of intensive in-patient treatments, inclusive of airfare, lodging and meals, is $50,000. For some patients, one treatment program proves effective; for others, two or three additional treatments, over the course of several years, could be expected. On behalf of Robin and Sandra, I invite you to consider donating to their treatment expenses. Any amount is appreciated, and all of the GoFundMe proceeds will go directly and exclusively to Robin's fight with cancer. Join the fight and support the Brinkley family.

Hi, my name is Mari Kay, and I am raising funds for my brother in law, Rodney Camps. In April of 2022, Rodney suffered a mild heart attack while spending a normal morning in the woods doing what he loved most, making wood. Not knowing what it was, he made an appointment to follow-up with his local doctor and was passed to cardiology. It was determined at that time, he had some blockage and would require a stent, but during the stent procedure, it was determined that he would need a double bypass due to this blockage. On July 5th, Rodney went in for a routine double bypass procedure as a follow-up to this mild heart attack and stent procedure. The surgery went great, in fact, he was done an hour earlier than expected and went into recovery, or so we thought. As they tried to wake him, his lungs were having issues oxygenating. Basically, this means he was not able to pull the needed amount of oxygen from his lungs to his blood to allow his organs to function properly. At this point, he was left paralyzed and, in a coma, as they tried to understand his issue. Over the next few weeks, the medical staff would treat him and slowly begin to wake him up, only to have to put him back under as there was no change. At the point of exhausted resources in Marquette ICU, he was med flighted down to University of Michigan hospital on July 19th and placed in the Surgical ICU. At the hospital here, he was left in the paralytic state, as they tried to find the issue in his lungs. They did discover a very rare bacteria that was present in his lungs that was the causing this issue. This bacteria, Serratia Marcenscens, is a very strong infection that causes issues in the respiratory and urinary track that causes a lining inside that does not allow any fluid or gas to pass through. This bacterial can also mimic pneumonia, and although we treated this, it would return as soon as the treatment would stop. Once we did have the cause, a very strong treatment was started that started to cure the issue. Although we started making progress one night in particular, Rodney coded and had to be resuscitated. This caused the doctors to actual implant a pacemaker and start dialysis on him to help his body recover from the many days of paralysis and drugs in his system. In the time at the UofM hospital, Rodney went through many rounds of antibiotics, a tracheostomy, CT scans, and X-rays, as well as being on ventilation for almost 6 weeks On August 27th, he was transferred out of the ICU to another hospital in Ann Arbor to continue his therapy and dialysis as well as recovery. He spent the next 30 days achieving many milestones in his recovery as he fought so hard to get back to healthy for his family and friends. On September 28th, he was transferred to Stonehill rehabilitation facility in Dubuque Iowa to continue his therapy and recovery from this horrific event. At this point, he no longer has any dialysis or tracheostomy, he moves around this facility in a wheelchair with the affectionate nickname “Speedy”. He is currently transitioning from a wheelchair to a walker as he starts to gain his leg strength back. Although he has only been at this facility for a little over 2 weeks at this time, he has made amazing strides in his recovery. He will continue to recover at this facility until he is able to walk on his own and get back to taking care of himself. Through this incredible journey, many ups and downs, we want to thank everyone for their thoughts and prayers as well as the help of people around us. We will continue to fight and move forward until once again; he is home in the woods!!

Laura Core’s “core” has always been easy to see. Smart. Funny. Generous. A fierce competitor. And Laura is responsible – as she was last January when she took a ride-share service home after a night out with her husband Mark and two friends. They were hit by a drunk driver just a few blocks from their home. Laura’s injuries in the crash were devastating. First responders who arrived on the scene did not think she would survive the night. She suffered fractures to her C6 and C7 vertebrae, leaving her with a significant spinal cord injury and incomplete quadriplegia. Laura also sustained several broken ribs, a broken elbow and suffered a traumatic brain injury. She needed 25 stitches in her head. But Laura is nothing if not a fighter. She was initially in a coma and had no feeling in the lower half of her body. She spent two weeks in the OHSU ICU, then four weeks at a rehab facility before she was sent home to continue her recovery. Her family had to retrofit her home to accommodate her limitations. Her husband Mark – also injured in the wreck – had to quit his job to be her full-time caregiver. Laura’s road to recovery is hard-fought and never-ending. She works with a physical therapist five days a week. Laura also undergoes regular vision therapy, gets Botox injections to alleviate muscle spasms, and has frequent acupuncture and massage treatments. She has made remarkable progress over the past ten months. Her medical team is astonished at what she has accomplished, considering the severity of her injuries. However, Laura still has significant physical limitations and endures constant nerve pain. That's why she and her medical team are exploring alternative therapies that may improve her mobility and lessen her constant and excruciating nerve pain. One promising option is cutting-edge stem cell therapy, which is currently only used in trials in the United States but is widely used in other countries to treat spinal cord injuries. Unfortunately, most alternative medical treatments available to Laura, both within and outside the United States, are not covered by her insurance. Laura needs our support as she continues working on her recovery. She needs assistance with the costs of ongoing physical and emotional therapy. She also needs various medical equipment, including mobility aids and adaptive exercise equipment, which are not covered by insurance. One day, Laura hopes to be able to use an adaptive car to get to work on her own and become more self-sufficient. An amazing friend, daughter, wife and mother, Laura has always been the first to step up to help. She volunteered in her Duniway and Sellwood PTAs and classrooms, put in endless hours of charitable work and coaching, and raised funds for CASA for Children, all while juggling a full-time job, two kids and even running Hood to Coast several times. Those of us fortunate enough to know Laura cannot say enough about her grit, determination, and courage. But she and her wonderful family need your help. We are asking because they would never ask for themselves. Please help Laura regain her shining “Core.”

Karen King is battling Multiple Myeloma, which is cancer that forms in a type of white blood cell called a plasma cell. In multiple myeloma, cancerous plasma cells accumulate in the bone marrow and crowd out healthy blood cells. Myeloma cells inhibit your body's ability to fight infections and also affect your bones, leading to bone pain, thinning bones and broken bones. All of which Karen has faced, and this is her 2nd round of fighting this disease! While there have been life-changing physical effects due to having Myeloma and going through treatment, the financial effects have also been vast and life-altering. Below is a little glimpse into who Karen is, the fight that she's been waging, and a look at how this has effected her financially. Please give generously and know that 100% of the money you donate will go directly to Karen to help her meet her financial and treatment needs. About Karen: First, she's the mom of 7 biological kids (but loves to gather the extras!). She loves to cook and feed others, she's a certified health coach that has studied nutrition for almost 30 yrs. She's also an ordained minister who has a passion for seeing people whole: spirit, soul and body. She has a vision to have a ministry that helps others get healed and free in every area of their lives. She hopes to one day have land to start a healing ranch to bring this vision to pass! Financial Impact: "After the initial diagnosis and then remission, I continued to have upper back pain which didn’t resolve. This caused me to not be able to stand for long periods of time without taking meds or to sit for long periods of time. Sitting was actually more difficult and exacerbated this pain. I knew that I would not be able to tolerate a desk job or sit in an office for long periods of time. I was able to help with in the kitchen for short periods but would eventually needs meds to help." "My son bought a second house for me to move into and rent from him recently, which helped reduce my rent payment. Since the recent test result and treatments, several of my kids are covering that payment and my daughter has moved in to help me physically as well as contribute to finances." "Using alternative therapies like IV's helped me recover more quickly, but they are not covered by insurance so I am now in debt over $15,000. I haven’t been able to resume these therapies like I need because of the high costs of these therapies as well as the higher cost of living that is happening now. " Her Cancer Story: (In her own words) After feeling like I tore a rotator cuff playing volleyball with my kids in July 2019, I went to see an orthopedic doctor. After trying several remedies, it was apparent that something else was going on, so the doctor ordered a CT scan. After a few weeks, I had my follow up appointment. The doctor was visibly upset, as he just received the report right before my appointment. When he carried over a box of tissues to where I was sitting, I knew something was wrong. “You’re not going to tell me it’s cancer, are you doctor?” “I wouldn’t kid about a thing like that,” he said. After reviewing the report with me, I assured him that I was ok, and that my purpose in life had not been completed yet. I was shaken but not despondent. I walked to my car and called my sister. She encouraged me and asked if I would like her to contact the rest of the family, which I did. From there I called my kids, and we met that evening to discuss this news. As it turns out, my dad has a close friend who lives near him in Georgia who is an oncologist specialist. Dad contacted him on my behalf and the doctor offered to call me to talk about the diagnosis. Dr. Radhakrishna Vemuri, M.D is his name, and providentially not only was his specialty oncology, he himself had a diagnosis of cancer in the brain. Not only did this give him a perspective unique to most oncology doctors, but he felt it one of his missions to inspire hope in cancer patients. He even wrote a book called “Hope For Cancer Patients at All Stages of Illness.” As one can imagine, the conversation we had that evening impacted me greatly. I got off that call encouraged and hopeful, which made my talk with my kids so much easier as well as helping me to communicate that message with them. I would be alright, I told them. The weeks that followed were interesting, to say the least. I informed my place of employment, who made me go on immediate FEMLA, or short-term disability. (For several weeks prior, I repeatedly asked to work from home to accommodate the severe pain I was in physically. I couldn’t even carry a lunch bag, as the pain in one shoulder started to radiate across my chest into my other shoulder. In hindsight, it’s obvious why- it wasn’t a tear, but my bones were breaking due to the multiple myeloma. My requests were met with a resistance and an obvious callousness to my pain. In fact, my boss suggested I put protein bars in my desk if I couldn’t carry a lunch bag.) Within days of leaving work, I woke up and was unable to walk. I literally had to crawl to the bathroom, which because of the broken clavicles, made the pain almost unbearable. I was awaiting my initial appointment with an oncologist, so this was unexpected and scary. Eventually I met with Dr. Scott Cross who would become my oncologist. He was recommended to me and I came to find him to be highly respected by others in his field. He laid out my treatment plan which consisted of radiation followed up with a “cocktail” of chemotherapy medications. He talked me about my diagnosis and let me know we would have to do a full MRI before moving forward with treatment. The MRI would be used to document the extent of the cancer and the bones that were broken due to the cancer. He also prescribed me pain meds which helped me function and move a little easier. Unfortunately, getting the MRI done proved to be challenging. Because of the broken bones and compression fractures in my spine, I was unable to tolerate laying on my back for even a moment, much less an hour for the MRI to be done in the lumbar, thoracic and cervical regions of my back, even with heavy duty pain meds. The alternative was to admit me to the hospital and be sedated for the MRI. It took several days to get this done, but it was successful. I also met Dr. Paul Mitchell who was the neurosurgeon that would treat me. It was obvious that I needed a kyphoplasty, which is a process of injecting a cement like substance in between the vertebrae where the cancer had eroded areas of the spine. The kyphoplasty was scheduled quickly and within a short time I was up and walking around with more stability and less pain. While I was in the hospital, I started the process for radiation which consisted of mapping the body, and I received a treatment before I was discharged. Once I was discharged from the hospital, I went through a couple weeks of radiation treatments and then moved into the chemotherapy treatments. Little by little the pain decreased, and my numbers came into normal range. I was able to support my body by getting nutritional IV’s and using healthy supplements. I was also receiving microcurrent treatments from a practitioner that helped me greatly by treating me at a greatly reduced cost. All of these made such a huge difference in my ability to tolerate conventional oncology treatments. By summer of 2020, I was able to function normally. Starting November of 2021, I experienced some things that caused me some very difficult emotional months. By the spring of 2022, the lambda light chain numbers, which are an indicator of multiple myeloma started to climb and I started having back pain which necessitated the use of pain meds again to function. In September, I went in for another MRI to check the back pain and it was discovered that I had a fracture in my spine in the thoracic region. I was told by the oncologist to get to the ER immediately. They wanted me admitted to the hospital for another MRI and this was the quickest way to facilitate that. They were also concerned about spinal cord impingement and possibility of needing emergency surgery. I was able to get the MRI and they found a lesion at T10 which caused the fracture. Drs. Cross and Mitchell decided that radiation would be the best solution to shrink the lesion/tumor and kill the cancer in that area. They saw that there were some bone shards that could possibly damage the spinal cord if anything more invasive was attempted. I was again mapped for radiation before I was discharged and then scheduled for radiation treatments for the next couple weeks. I also started a new round of chemotherapy treatments to bring those lambda light chain numbers down. As of now, the numbers are dropping and getting closer into range. A follow up MRI will be scheduled in the next few months to check the status of the fracture in the spine. Since I have been able to somewhat reduce the pain meds and the multiple myeloma numbers are dropping, I believe the spine is healing. Since I have had a total of 4 medications for chemotherapy, I am slotted to be eligible for a newer therapy called CAR-T. This therapy shows promise for longer-term remission for multiple myeloma patients. I will stay on this current treatment for several months and then another medication will be used for maintenance. Dr. Cross has advised me that as I am on the maintenance meds, the CAR-T therapy will continue to be refined and improved which will benefit me in the long run.
