While in the US, I had the privilege of meeting Stephanie and Rohan. They have become my friends. This family is going through something devastating, and many people have reached out asking how they can help. With my friend’s permission, I want to share their story and ask for support for this wonderful family. Five years ago, Stephanie ventured to the USA on a Cultural Exchange Program to continue her calling to educate. The experience was going so well. But, nearing the end of the program, the unexpected happened. On October 2021, Stephanie and Rohan were blessed with a beautiful baby boy named Joel. They were so excited to become parents for the first time. Joel was doing very well! After checking most things off the list for discharge, Joel had to complete a car seat test. Unfortunately, he failed the test three times due to low oxygen saturation. As a result, he was transferred to the NICU for further evaluation. Upon getting to the NICU, they realized that he could not maintain his oxygen saturation. As such, he had to be placed on oxygen support. As the weeks went by, he required more oxygen support. Thankfully, he was able to get the care he needed. Eventually, this situation would resolve...or so we thought. Joel’s health declined until he was eventually placed on life support. His condition was so bad that he had to be transferred to a Specialist Children’s Hospital. Upon arrival, the medical team began investigating the cause of his low oxygen saturation. After several weeks of life support and extensive testing, it was revealed that he had bilateral diaphragm weakness, so his lungs could not expand fully. Now that the reason for his breathing issues has been established. The family hoped and prayed for a miracle. The medical team informed the family that there was an underlying cause for Joel’s diaphragm weakness, so they continued the testing process to ascertain the cause. This process was long and daunting. After more months of testing, no solution was forthcoming. As a result, they were given the option of providing Joel with a safer long-term ventilation mode while they continued their research. After much prayers and deliberation, he underwent surgery for a tracheostomy and a gastrostomy. This meant Joel would continue his life with a breathing tube supported by a portable ventilator and a feeding tube. Just when they thought the troubles were over, four (4) months into his NICU stay, Joel developed seizures. The seizures were so bad that even multiple medications at high doses could not control them. The episodes eventually caused changes to the background of his brain, which contributed to severe developmental delays and other complications. Hence, Joel required therapy to aid in his recovery. This new development led to additional testing and a more extended stay in the hospital. Joel spent the first six (6) months of his life in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit. He has been home since April 2022 and has had at least seven (7) other hospitalizations. The health struggles appear to be never-ending, as he’s seemingly getting weaker by the day. Nevertheless, we continue to pray and hope for the miracle. This journey has taken a toll on the family emotionally, physically, and financially. The most devasting part of the situation is that this happened when Stephanie’s teaching contract in the US expired, which means her plans to rejoin her husband with their son in Jamaica had to be placed on hold. Due to the severity of Joel’s medical condition, he cannot travel, and at least one parent must be home (in the US) with him at all times. This means both parents must take turns traveling back and forth on a tourism visa to avoid the issues that may arise from overstaying in the country. Now that Stephanie is no longer in the teaching program and must be home full-time to care for Joel, the family has to depend solely on Rohan’s salary in Jamaica which cannot meet the complete financial demands in the US. The emotional burden is more than any family should have to bear. Not to mention the financial stress of monthly bills and legal fees as the family seeks legal help in finding a more feasible way of maintaining stability in the US as they care for their sweet baby boy. At the same time, he continues to receive treatment and hopefully, a formal diagnosis. Please help support the Kong’s family and bring them a ray of hope and comfort during this challenging time. We are all just absolutely devastated! Please send prayers for his healing and that Joel gets his miracle.

Many know that Jeremy and Mera’s oldest daughter, Florence, has epilepsy. For the most part, medication has kept seizure activity to a minimum. Unfortunately, in March of this year, her seizures began to break through her medication. All medical care happens in Portland, so there are more significant wait times between appointments. In the meantime, her seizure activity has continued to escalate, including days when Florence experiences 40 plus grand mal seizures. The physical, mental, and emotional toll on her little body are heartbreaking. A year ago, Florence started kindergarten at Madrone Trail and was flourishing. As of today, she is unable to go to school. Florence just celebrated her 7th birthday, but a recent psychological evaluation shows that her cognitive levels have declined to those of a three or four-year-old. She has been subject to test after test, which has determined that she has a malformation in her brain and that the seizure activity is coming from three locations. One of these is operable; the other two are not. The location of the operable one affects Florence’s impulse control, which means that she cannot regulate herself and, as the doctor put it, causes her to be in an “unhinged state.” This plays out with constant activity as well as unregulated behavior, and when coupled with the constant threat of seizures, it creates a need for 24/7 supervision. She is currently on heavy seizure and ADHD meds; however, she still seizes daily (some days are better than others) and seems to become more unhinged the longer this progresses. Just before all this began, Jeremy and Mera started their self-employment journey. They began building a recording studio with high hopes of being done mid-summer. Neither could have foreseen this medical journey they would have to take with Florence. DIY construction deadlines have been pushed back multiple times and recordings delayed due to the numerous OHSU trips and the pure exhaustion they feel as they care for Florence and the boys. Jeremy and Mera both exist with a sleep deficit, as all the activity in Florence’s body causes her to be up most nights until 1:00 AM. However, the boys, ages 2 and 4, are up by six every morning. They are in the middle of a special need situation as they try to keep their heads above water. None of the above paints a clear picture of the heaviness of the circumstances and watching their daughter, our granddaughter, wither before their eyes. Florence rarely smiles or laughs, no longer likes cuddles (I miss this the most) and is a shell of who she was. On November 14th, Florence will have the first of two procedures on her brain. In order to determine the exact location and size of the seizure activity, the first procedure will be a stereo EEG where they will drill 8-15 tiny holes in her skull and insert an electrode into each one. This will require at least a week's stay and possibly longer, depending on the readings they get and how she responds. It will be followed by a week of monitored home recovery. The skull holes will take about six weeks to heal. The second surgery will remove the malformation in her brain and must occur within three to four months of that stereo EEG. It will require another week or more up in Portland with a much longer recovery and aftercare period. Many have asked us how to help them as they go through this. First and foremost, please pray. Below is a list of specific things that can be prayed over in the coming weeks and months. On a practical level, this fundraiser aims to lighten the financial burden, helping Jeremy and Mera be one hundred percent available to care for Florence before and after surgeries, including the many trips to and from Portland, loss of income, and provision for home care/respite. We want to allow them to team up in the daily care, relieve one another, and get much-needed rest. From experience, Florence always needs to be watched, and one person/parent cannot do it alone, especially with two other children to care for. Things to pray over: For Florence - Both procedures – no complications, and they would accomplish what they need to with little side effects, specifically with the second surgery and possible long-term effects in areas of her memory and emotions Wisdom for the whole medical team assigned to her Protection from harm with the constant seizure activity For Jeremy and Mera - God would give them the physical, emotional, and mental strength to care for Florence. Provision to function from a place of rest and not exhaustion. Caspian and Atticus - Comfort and peace when the rest of the family is up in Portland. They have never been gone from their parents this long. Thank you so much for taking the time to read this lengthy description. We know the power of prayer to heal, restore, and bring peace amid our fears and the unknown parts of Florence's story. We appreciate the outpouring of prayer and love for the family from so many of you. We could not get through this without it.

Dear Fit Fam, We are calling on the love and support of our amazing community to help one of our most beloved member families battle lymphoma. Our member community has come to know and love the Overstreet Clan. Their family, headed by Brian and Kristin Overstreet, have been members of our community since 2010, when we opened the doors of our first location, CrossFit Liberation. Brian and Kristin have been with us since the beginning, and their children, Katie, Samantha, and Molly, have grown up with our community from their early teen years into adulthood. Their oldest daughter Katie, her husband Victor, and even his older brother Emerson were members until a few years ago when work opportunities and Katie and Victor’s dream of starting their own little family relocated them to Manassas. The Overstreet's are like family to Ruben, me, and so many others within our community. They have been embedded in the Alexandria/Kingstowne/Springfield community for over 50+ years. They are genuinely some of the best humans we know; always there to help a friend or loved one when they are in need. And now, it Is our turn to show them that same love and support. We were devastated when we learned a few weeks ago that Katie was diagnosed with Stage 3 Hodgkins Lymphoma at about 34 weeks pregnant and only 30 years of age. As Katie was nearing the end of her pregnancy, with about six weeks until her due date, she came down with a bad case of COVID. While at work as a teacher in Manassas she started having trouble breathing and went to the hospital to get checked out and to make sure that she and the baby were okay. They kept her overnight to run some tests and later discovered that Katie had Hodgkins Lymphoma. In a matter of 24 hours, their families’ lives were turned upside down. They were suddenly being forced to make tough decisions they never thought they would have to make, including expediting their second child's birth so that Katie could begin treatment immediately. On September 30th, they were blessed with a beautiful, healthy baby boy named Luca, who arrived five weeks early. Katie was given a few days home to enjoy their wonderful new blessing but then had to begin to prepare herself for an incredible fight. Last Friday, a little over a week after Luca was born, Katie started her first round of chemo treatments. No new mother or young family should ever have to face this ordeal. While she should be at home resting, snuggling and loving her two little ones, and allowing her body to heal and recover from the trauma of giving birth, she is instead having to put all of her energy into fighting this horrific disease. Their beautiful little family of four and the rest of the Overstreet clan have a long road ahead of them, steeped with many challenges. We know they will face many financial ordeals with mounting and unknown medical bills. Katie and Victor are teachers in Manassas, and Victor is also a US Army National Guard member. As Katie undergoes treatment, she will be forced to go on disability, which will further strain their financial security as disability only pays a fraction of an individual’s total salary. And we all know that teachers are already horribly underpaid for their essential work. We can accomplish amazing things as a community when we come together to achieve a goal. Over the year﻿s, we have raised thousands of dollars for countless causes and organizations. And now we can do so for one of our own member families in need. We hope we can help ease some of the burden, worry, and stress they may soon be facing, so they can focus on what truly matters: getting Katie healthy. Therefore, we are calling on our community to help us raise funds through this Go Fund Me to help ease some of the daunting living/medical costs that Katie and Victor will face. We are asking all our member families from CrossFit Kingstowne and CrossFit Liberation to consider donating. Small or Large, every little bit will help. In addition to the GoFundMe page, we will host a fundraising event at CrossFit Kingstowne on Saturday, 12 November. We will host the Rogue 1000/750# Challenge and add another fun element of a 1-mile run. Anyone who wants to participate can sign up for a heat time to do the lifts, which include the Bench Press, Deadlift, and Squat and then a mile run to follow. We will not be charging an entrance or registration fee, but instead, we ask you to consider making some form of a donation to the GOFUNDME instead of a registration fee. If you do not want to participate in the physical portion of the event, you are still welcome to come out and cheer on the individuals who will be participating and consider making a donation. We will have food and beverages available as we bring the community together to support this amazing family. This event is open to anyone who wants to participate, even non-members. We have also made Overstreet Strong T-Shirts (pictured below) as another means of raising money. The shirts are Violet Purple for Hodgkins Lymphoma Awareness. We will be posting a pre-order form where you can sign up to purchase and secure a shirt. The t-shirts will be $30, with proceeds donated to the GoFundMe page. We will release more details about the 1000/750# + 1 Mile Run Challenge Event on 12 November, along with a sign-up for heats and the pre-order form for the t-shirts, on our SugarWOD page. We truly hope this amazing community can come together to show this incredible family how much they mean to us as Katie, her husband, their two little ones, and the rest of the Overstreet/Souza clan begin the fight of their lives. We truly appreciate any level of donation you can make, small, large, anonymous or not; all of it is appreciated. In addition, we will be holding a raffle leading up to and during the event on the 12th. Please let us know if any in our community want to donate a service or item for the event. Much love to you all, and thank you for helping this wonderful family. Carrie and Ruben

My name is Theresa - and most likely I will have other people managing this site from here on out, but I wanted to be able to tell you my story in my own words. Up until a few months ago, I had been very healthy. I worked out regularly and really watched what I ate. I was especially sometimes given a hard time for the way I guard my sleep habits. I lifted weights, went to yoga weekly, and I practiced meditation, EFT Tapping and prayer regularly. Everything was going well in my life! I started getting headaches in August of 2022 and they became increasingly worse. I was been given a clean bill of health this February, so at first I wasn't too concerned. I was diagnosed with COVID-19 on Septemeber 18th and then was in the ER every week after that for the headaches, bleeding around my optic nerves, ear infections and general fatigue. I was given a COVID infusion treatment called Redemesvir, that I had an allergic reaction to. All of my CT scans were clear at these visits. On October 13th I went to the ER again and this time I was admitted to the hospital after a blood draw revealed that all of my blood counts were low - my hemoglobin, white and red cells. After being subjected to many tests, including MRI, ultrasounds, spinal tap and bone marrow biopsy - I was diagnosed on October 21st with Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS), which is a pre-leukemia in my bone marrow. Basically, my bone marrow has stopped making healthy blood for me and I will need aggressive treatment right away. The treatment includes an initial 30 days in hospital, where I will receive aggressive chemo for 10-12 days to get me into remission. During that time, we will seek a bone marrow donor and I will need to eventually go to Denver to receive a transplant. After the transplant, I will also need to be in isolation for 30 days. My oncologist feels that because of my age and health, I am a good candidate to receive this treatment and be successful. By the way, this is the same cancer that Robin Roberts of "Good Morning America" had. She is 10 years post-bone marrow transplant and is doing well. I am hopeful for the same outcome!! So how can you help? • Prayers - I BELIEVE in the power of prayer!! Good vibes, good energy! • Donate Blood - My blood type is B Positive and I always thought that was so great! It doesn't matter what type YOU are because so many people need blood and I have already received 5 blood transfusions. • Consider being a donor for bone marrow on Be The Match. The testing is easy, and they just swab your cheek to get you into an international registry! You could save a life - maybe even mine. • Write letters or send cards to me. Words of encouragement mean SO MUCH!!! • Donate to my GoFundMe campaign. While I do have medical insurance covered, I unfortunately do not have any disability insurance offered through one of my jobs, and I am also an entrepreneur and was getting ready to open a new business before all of this took place. • BE POSITIVE! I need positive energy/words/encouragement. If you cannot be positive or helpful, please refrain from contacting me or commenting anything negative to me. • Consider making a purchase from my Amazon wishlist (link to be provided later), for items I may need for comfort while I am hospitalized. • LIVE LIFE! Take chances, travel, love, laugh and be happy as much as possible. I have been incredibly blessed the past few years that my hard work has allowed me to build a beautiful life and experience so many things I had always wanted to do!

My niece April and her husband, Jeremy, have two daughters, Jerricka and Madalyn. Both girls were born with “Micro deletion,” A rare genetic condition caused by a tiny missing part of one of the body's 46 chromosomes. As a result of this condition, seizures are incessant; hospital stays are continual. Unfortunately, this "Dis-Ease" has and will continue to destroy their childhood, hinder their potential, and likely shorten their time in this life. But that's not even half of it. A few months ago, Madalyn suddenly started having insomnia, personality changes, and even hearing voices in her head; she called these voices her "fake friends"; They would tell her things like "your parents are going to die." or "your parents are dead" Can you imagine a child having to constantly hear such things, with no way to escape it, and no way for her parents to protect her from it? Recently a trigger of cluster seizures sent her to a Children’s Hospital in St Louis, Mo. By the time they arrived, she was in a comatose state. Days later, she suddenly wakes up, asking to sit up and get some water. They tell their parents she scored high for Catatonia. Because she is no longer critical, she is moved to the Neurological floor. They don’t have a room there, so they are trying to find a placement in a Psychiatric facility but so far, they won’t take her because of the seizure disorder. Mom and dad won’t leave her! They need help financially to survive. They live four-plus hours from the hospital. This family rents a little house in Republic, Mo., which is over 100 years old. I keep feeling that since they can’t come up with anything solid, maybe it’s the house, a house that old could have chemicals, lead, and other things they wouldn’t use for homes built in the last couple of decades. This family needs help; they need a break! Please help ❤️ April's story can be read in more detail below. We were blessed with two beautiful girls. Jerricka 14 and Madalyn 12. My pregnancy with both girls were healthy with no signs of complications. Upon Delivery with Jerricka the doctors noticed her heart rate was dropping so I went back for an emergency C-section. Jerricka entered the world a healthy beautiful baby. Around 5 months old was when we noticed something was wrong. We had taken her to the hospital and the news came back that she was experiencing seizures. We set up appointments with a neurologist and medication was prescribed. 2 years later and Jerrickas sister Madalyn was born. Healthy no signs of complications during My pregnancy and no signs of complications during labor. At 5 months old Madalyn started showing signs of seizures. Several failed attempts of getting anyone to believe what she was experiencing was seizure activity. In fact at one point they called it sleep apnea. The neurologist that we had for Jerricka refused to add Madalyn as a new patient said he wasn’t taking new patients. I ended up switching neurologists and found one that would accept both girls. The Neurologist wanted to do genetic testing to see if we could find answers as to why they had a seizure disorder. The answers revealed that both girls have what they call a Micro Deletion in Chromosomes # 16. Seizures are just something that comes with that mutation. Several years later and still struggling with epilepsy with both girls. January 24th of 2022 Madalyn tested positive for Covid. 3 days into Covid she started experiencing hallucinations. Madalyn swore she saw a pregnant woman and her son coming in a random door of our house. She swore she saw a group of kids running out our front door. She swore every time we would go somewhere we would have people in the trunk of our car. A week after the hallucinations started she began to experience horrifying nightmares where she truly thought she found her mom dead. I heard her crying out and tried waking her sister up to tell her that mom was dead. I ran into the bedroom to comfort Madalyn and tell her it was just a really bad dream. She had a nightmare where she thought our house was on fire and her sister didn’t make it out. I reached out to Madalyns Neurologist in desperate need of help for her daughter. She was placed on a medication for a mood stabilizer hoping that it would work. Neurologist ordered that we be admitted into the hospital for further testing. April 18th was the start of a 5 day admission. They did a 3 day video EEG, MRI of the brain, encephalitis panel and a lumbar puncture. Every single test came back clean and clear. As some will say, that's great news. It truly is. Although, it left Jeremy, and I with no answers. A referral was placed for a psychiatrist for Madalyn. Little to no help in that direction and I feel like they just keep running into brick walls. Medication after medication. The hallucinations are still going full force and have been getting worse. Madalyn says she has a thousand “fake friends” that only she can see and hear. These fake friends have now reached a point where she will not shower on her own as she claims they are watching her. She will not use the bathroom by herself as she also thinks they are watching her. Her fake friends have told her to “grab a knife and slice her throat”. I had taken Madalyn to the hospital to receive some help for her. She ended up having to come home because there weren't any beds available. Her fake friends have told her she isn’t worth living anymore. Her fake friends make Madalyn believe that they stick needles all over body. She will lay there stiff as a board and won’t move because she truly believes that it’s really happening. When her parents try to prove to her that it isn’t real and show her that there aren't any needles she screams at the top of her lungs as if she really feels the pain. My husband and I have moved their bed into the girls room for further protection and to keep a close eye on Madalyn. November 3 at 5:15 AM I Woke to the sound of Madalyn seizing. Rescue med was given and it didn’t pull her out of it so I had to call for help. When arriving at the hospital and several seizures later they finally were able to get them under control. They were discharged from the hospital and walked out side for Jeremy to get there to pick them up. Madalyn was complaining she had a headache and I thought it was due to all the seizure activity and meds that were given. Madalyn stood up, looked at her mom and fell out in the grass area where they were sitting and fell into another seizure. I yelled for help and the security guards called for help. Madalyn was rushed back in to a room in the ER. Madalyn began having cluster seizures. The nurse was saying that she was experiencing apnea due to all the medication she was given. Madalyn was transferred to another hospital. When she arrived she was still actively seizing. The Dr told me they feel something more serious is happening and she needed to get airlifted to the children’s hospital in STL. By the time she got there she was unresponsive but able to breath on her own. Days later she suddenly wakes up. With all the tests running, nothing comes up! No answers. In and out of consciousness for days. Suddenly, she wakes up asking to sit up and drink some water. They told us she scored high for Catatonia?? Because she is no longer critical, she is moved to the Neurological floor. It’s not supposed to happen this way. The toughest of the tough is counted on to survive the unsurvivable, like he always has. Richard St. Hilaire, from birth, it has always seemed, showed no fear, ever, end of story. Always the guy to run toward danger rather than away from it. Even when he started dropping weight over the winter of 2018 and received the heart-breaking news in March of 2019. Pancreatic cancer. The one cancer that causes grown men to look away to hide their tears, knowing the death sentence it carries with it. Richard ran right at it with the fearless conviction that all who’ve known him have counted on. If you live or have lived anywhere near the town of Kingston, New Hampshire, you know or have heard of Richard. Even if you didn’t know him, you may be alive because of him, you may have bore witness to the fireman with the impossibly wide chest beating down a fire, or quite simply, you may have been able to drive home during a Nor’easter because of his efforts. You probably haven’t heard many stories of Richard graciously accepting accolades for all he’s done over the years. That is just not how he’s wired. He does his job, whether it be firefighter, emergency responder or town Road Agent because it’s part of his DNA. The town of Kingston has honored Richard in the past year or so with dedications and awards for his service, fully aware that they are about to lose the face of their town, the man that has given so much and asked so little in return. He joined the Kingston Fire Department in 1978, but those in the know will tell you that he actually became involved in 1972 when he was still in Junior High. From that time forward, he was always a part of the local emergency teams. He went on to become a trained fireman for NASA, racing out onto the tarmac at Pease Air Force Base to support emergency landings. He was part of the safety crew that flew nuclear weapons out of Pease, as well. In 1986, Richard was voted in as the town’s Road Agent and has kept that position even while the cancer spread through his system with a vengeance. And still the caring for others continued. He has taken care of the town’s needs, no matter the size or scope. Richard’s mantra has forever been to do whatever it takes to get the job done. He has faced cancer the same way, with a relentless fervor, smiling through the pain, spending time with his three grandchildren, Kaylee, Kylie, and Logan. Living his life to the fullest even while it was being stolen mercilessly from him. Even during this battle with pancreatic cancer, Richard has found a way to give. He has participated in numerous clinical trials that will help future cancer patients. His longevity through this process is something of legend at Massachusetts General Hospital. For those of us that know and love him, rock star status is nothing new, but when it comes from hardened doctors and nurses, those that deal with death on a daily basis, it is truly impressive. It has taken extraordinary efforts from those who love and support him to convince him that there are hundreds, if not thousands of individuals that want to help him in any way they can. That is why you are reading this page right this very minute. Richard needs help. But in typical Richard fashion, he’ll be the last to ask for it and the help is not even for him, but for those loved ones he will leaving behind. His family will be left to pick up the pieces, face the enormous debt that four years of fighting cancer leaves behind. They will also have to face house repairs and countless other costs without the backbone of their lives with them. A fairy tale ending would have our boy recovering completely from the deadly disease that has ravaged his body and going on to live a long and wonderful life with his wife Vivian by his side and his daughter Kristen, her husband Dan and their family a toy-cluttered lawn away. We are in dire need of such fairy tales, as they are what helps us cope with funerals. Please do what you can to continue his legacy of caring when he no longer walks among us.

Recently, one of our dear friend—Yoshi—was assaulted by a stranger while making an UberEats delivery. This violent attack was unprovoked and senseless. Yoshi explained to the woman that she had no right to block the parking spot and asked her politely to move so he could park his car; he also mentioned that he would only take 5 minutes, but she would argue that they needed this parking spot for her son. Parked a few cars ahead was a U-Haul truck and the man in it (who happens to be the woman’s husband) cursed at Yoshi, immediately telling him to “get the f*ck out of here,” and other curses as Yoshi was speaking with the woman. The woman eventually moved, but that only enraged the man, causing him to approach Yoshi’s passenger window as he continued yelling and cursing at him until his wife pulled him away from Yoshi's car window. After parking and getting out of his car, he saw a young man standing nearby. Yoshi asked the young man if he was with the man and woman, which he indicated he was. Yoshi then told the young man that it wasn’t cool to yell and curse at him as he didn’t do anything wrong, but then the young man disclosed that the man was his dad and asked Yoshi if he had a problem with this situation. With intense in-patient rehabilitation, he has started to regain movement in his leg, and just yesterday was able to squeeze his hand for the first time since the event. Toby is 37 years old and has two sons, Jack and Wyatt who are 3 1⁄2 and 11⁄2 respectively. Maggie, our daughter, is Toby’s wife and Jack’s and Wyatt’s mother. Toby and Maggie have a good marriage and love each other and their boys. Hola me llamo Yoibeth, estoy recaudando fondos para el tratamiento de Theo, hijo de mi amiga Jill Burgos, y que fue diagnosticado con un tumor cerebral, el pasado 19 de julio de 2022. Fue operador el 25 de julio de 2022, para extirpar un tumor, de un tamaño considerable. Tuvo una resección parcial. Al recibir la patología del mismo, les confirman a sus padres, que el tumor es maligno (cáncer) y el mismo se había esparcido a su medula. (Metástasis). Estamos viviendo un día a la vez, por que así es, hoy nos alegramos por que la hemoglobina subió, mañana nos alegramos por que subió de peso, la otra semana nos alegraremos por que ya esta comiendo más, dentro de varios semanas nos alegraremos por que volvió a correr bien, y mas adelante por que ya forma oraciones en su habla. Por lo que el pronostico de Theo, es: FELICIDAD TOTAL HOY. ¿COMO EMPEZÓ? Esta historia comenzó por que Theo, no estaba caminando bien. Nos preocupamos y decidimos ir a urgencias, para descartar cualquier tema en el oido que lo hacia perder su equilibrio, o algún tema serio neurológico. La Doctora del cuarto de urgencias, ordena hacer un CAT y en el mismo, pues evidentemente había una gran masa de casi 10 cm en la parte posterior-arriba-izquierda. Se programó una operación de urgencia, ya que el tumor estaba haciendo mucha presión. La intención de esta cirugía era sacar todo lo que se podía, y así fue, se sacó aproximadamente un 60%. Lo además estaba muy comprometido con la masa cerebral. Luego de la operación de casi 10 horas, la recuperación fue cada día mejor. En nuestra cita con el oncólogo, recomendó iniciar quimioterapias lo más pronto posible, por lo que iniciamos 4 semanas posteriores a la operación. Este tipo de tumor necesita un tratamiento bastante agresivo y no podíamos optar por Radioterapia por que no es beneficioso para niños menores a 3 años. ( Su sistema nervioso aun no está formado completamente) El primer bloque de quimioterapias, se la administraron hospitalizado. 4 a 5 días hospitalizados Luego descanso de 21 días. y cada 7 días iba por una dosis de quimioterapia ambulatoria. Gracias a Dios, estos 3 ciclos intensos pasaron muy rápido y su cuerpo respondió muy bien. Con responder muy bien, me refiero a que no hubo nada fuera de lo esperado. Como en todo tratamiento quimioterapeutico, hay vomito, pérdida de cabello, dolor de cabeza, hay llagas en la boca, debilidad para caminar, cambios de humor, falta de apetito, recuento bajo de plaquetas, glóbulos rojos, glóbulos blancos, transfusiones de sangre, de plaquetas y a lo ultimo FIEBRE, el terror de los inmunosuprimidos. El próximo paso es ver los resultados de la resonancia magnética: Cerebral y de Columna, para ver la respuesta al tratamiento. Según los resultados, tiene la posibilidad de volver al salón de operaciones para extirpar más tumor y luego de esto, seguimos con quimioterapia de mantenimiento. Muchas personas preguntan, y tu como lo ves? Lo vemos super fuerte, jugando, viendo TV, utilizando su moto, su scooter como puede, ya que la quimioterapia o el propio tumor, le ha limitado el caminar. (camina, pero muy inestable) y lo más importante de todo, SIEMPRE, SIEMPRE, con una SUPER SONRISA, una sonrisa de niño Feliz. Evidentemente, nadie está preparado para una situación así o similar, ni física, ni emocional, ni económicamente. Y para algunas personas es difícil pedir apoyos de cualquier tipo, sin embargo, si esta dentro de tus posibilidades apoya esta causa, para que Theo pueda tener un tratamiento oportuno y constante que lo pueda llevar a la remisión. Muchas gracias por leer hasta aquí y que Dios te bendiga enormemente. Agradecemos tener a Theo en tus oraciones.

Our friend Tracy was recently diagnosed with cancer after suffering from a fractured vertebrae back in June. The MRI for the back injury revealed not only the fracture but the discovery of what turned out to be multiple myeloma. Her treatment involves IV and oral chemotherapy drugs, bone strengthening injections to assist with healing the compression fracture and to keep her bones strong during treatment. She also received a 2 week series of radiation treatments to help shrink the growth that was discovered in the process of finding out she had cancer. The doctors say that her body is responding well to treatment! She is on track to prepare for a Stem Cell transplant. This is a two part process, starting with the collection of her good stem cells, and then at a later date, the transplant. After stem cells are collected, she will be hit with a strong dose of Chemotherapy, wiping out all of her stem cells (where the myeloma cells are generated). She will then go in for the transfusion of her good stem cells back into her body. For people with multiple myeloma this is be a total re-set of the immune system, and involve, at minimum, a two week stay in the hospital. Once she is released from the hospital, the first 100 days after the transplant are very important to her recovery, involving frequent monitoring and careful living to avoid infection of any sort. Recovery can take anywhere from 6 months to a year. The ultimate goal of this procedure is to prolong her life in a remission stage. Meeting with the doctors felt like a time to reflect in what has been a whirlwind of testing, scans, biopsies, diagnoses and jumping right into a treatment plan. Although Multiple Myeloma is a rare blood cancer, treatments have come a long way to bring a high quality of life for these patients. Tracy has had time to reflect on her meNu business - what it has grown to become, and all that she would like it to be in the future. As her close friend, I can say I’ve witnessed her dedication, passion and creative spirit in action, and am frequently truly amazed. I hope that this diagnosis and treatment will not bring her business to a halt, for the future looks bright and has much potential for creative projects to come. Although she is unable to work at this time, and the paperwork involved with disability is still in process (and will only cover a small portion of her cost of living), if we all pitch in, the meNu business and all of the necessary equipment costs can be covered until Tracy is in full remission. If you know Tracy, you know she is one of the most dedicated, hardworking, creative and driven human beings out there, and has tirelessly given all of herself to cultivating her design business, meNu and her passion project PEN15® Pencil Club over the past decade. She is now being called to put all of that vibrant, colorful life force back into repairing her cells and resting. She needs our help! If you are able, please consider giving a monetary donation to help Tracy take care of her fundamental bills and payments that don’t stop. Thank you so much for being apart of Tracy's life and supporting her on her healing journey!

I lost my loving husband and father to my beautiful children to brain cancer on July 27th, 2020 at the age of 27. How my world was turned upside down within 3 months, never imagined I could feel so much pain and suffering. I tried to get my life back on track after grieving and trying to be strong for my babies, I thought YES! We are finally getting some normalcy back and trying to live a better life. Here comes September 15 2021, I was feeling pain on the right side of my abdomen, while pushing my childrens stroller. I ignored it for a day or so, but on the 17th I couldn't tolerate the pain anymore and went to the emergency room. Within a few hours I was in emergency surgery to have my inflamed appendix removed, the surgeon noticed alot of abnormalities and took a biopsy during the removal. I was then told the biopsy was sent to the lab and the doctor will schedule a follow up once the results are in. Follow up came on September 24th 2021, and I was officially diagnosed with High Grade Metastatic Appendiceal Adenocarcinoma a extremely rare cancer with an estimated incidence of 0.15-0.9 per 100,000 people. The average age of onset is between 50 and 55 years, me being 25 at the time of diagnosis being a little extra rare. On November 1 ,2021 I started my first round of chemotherapy sessions (folfoxiri) around the 6th treatment, I developed a blockage due to the cancer, that has prevented me from eatting solid foods. That prompted the doctors to insert a gastrostomy tube (g-tube) to help drain food and fluid from my stomach. After 12 excruciating sessions and going down from my normal weight of 100 pounds to a scary 61 pounds, fast forward to present day, chemotherapy has stop responding to my cancer and I am at a stage where I need to find a different solution so being written off by conventional healthcare, I have discovered holistic cancer treatment options. I refuse to give up. I have been through hell and back in my life and thats ok, but my children have already lost one parent to cancer and I will not let this cancer take me from them. While I still have breath in my lungs, I am going to fight until this cancer goes into remission. My last stitch effort is the wonderful facility in Scottsdale, Arizona called Envita Medical Center who specializes in my type of cancer, and they have treatments that may save my life. I am scheduled to start on October 27th,2022. The issue is cost, this facility doesn't take insurance and all treatments are out of pocket. My treatments will cost around $100,000 give or take, depending on how many treatments are needed (estimated to be more then 12). The money will help me fund the lab test cost, the treatment cost, and the funds to make the six hour move from California to Arizona until my treatments are complete. I am strong in my faith and I am a strong women and I refuse to give up, I will not give up, I am unstoppable.

Once he was born, I heard my name less and ‘Aren’t you Richard’s mom?’ more, which made me proud. Twenty-five years later, I am still Richard’s mom, an educator, and now Sheila, who is learning more about depression as a mental illness hidden behind my son’s amazing yet pain-filled smile. Depression has no face. My son attempted to end his life twice these past two weeks. As a parent, I have always tried to make home the safest space for my children; however, the safest place for my son Richard is also the most expensive—inpatient hospital care. I am reaching out for financial support because while I accept that he is hospitalized and safe, thoughts about the cost of the two ambulance rides, emergency room visits and ultimately being committed weigh heavily on my mind along with the guilt of those thoughts. Our high-deductible health insurance plan will not cover the costs, especially since the deductible has not been met for the year. Richard doesn’t qualify for other financial support because we carry him on our insurance—the catch 22 of our lives. My worries about hospital finances do come with experience. Last year Richard was hospitalized for four days, and the billing for that was just under twenty-four thousand dollars. We didn’t have to pay it all, but we currently make payments. If Richard can leave the hospital after the 72 hour hold, he will have spent seven days in the hospital. Your contribution will help pay down the medical bills that will arrive, most likely right after Thanksgiving and help us focus on other financial responsibilities due to loss of work, such as rent, car, and school tuition payments. This past year also brought hope and many proud moments. Richard worked and led as an assistant manager, regained his health by maintaining a healthy eating and workout regimen (I wish I had his abs), began living independently, and began taking coding classes at the UofMN. We understand better that depression is not something one ‘snaps out of’ or ‘a phase’ one grows out of—it is ever-present. To quote Maya Angelou, “when you know better, do better.” That’s our plan as well. At the local level, joining NAMI National Alliance on Mental Illness will help us better support Richard, ourselves, and others. As Richard’s mom and educator, I am still proud and want him to reach his potential as well as be an advocate for others who struggle with mental illness. Thank you in advance as we support Richard’s road to recovery. Richard's mom

“It takes a village to raise a child.” Sometimes it takes a world village with just a few dollars ($5, $10, $25) to spare. Gary Nguyen (Daddy), Keri Nguyen (Mommy), and Ty Nguyen (Sonny) could use your financial help as they adapt to Gary's diagnosis of severe Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension, a disabling condition brought on by his nearly three-year battle with post-covid issues. He cannot do even light household duties without being at risk of passing out. Oh, and he has an 18-month-old toddler running around in a 24-month-old’s body! The Short Story – How COVID in March of 2020 changed their lives Gary got COVID at the beginning; March 2020. For months, he couldn’t work. Brushing his teeth rocketed his pulse rate to over 140 and exhausted him to bed rest. This stretched for six months when he would at least try to work half a day, but his employer could not accommodate him. X-rays, CTs, Specialists, no one had answers. “Sounds like long haulers, Gary, sorry.” as they shrugged their shoulders... He’d have some decent days and then waves of horrible days. Bedridden. His wife was on hospital watch as his oxygen levels would bounce between “barely okay” and “GET TO THE ER!” This continued throughout 2021. The Coronacoaster, they called it. Excellent, a fun name for a horrible ride! For those that know Gary, he did his best to smile and make the best of a terrible situation. While unable to hold a traditional job, he found a remote contract position to help take care of his family in 2021 and into half of 2022. That's when it became too much. The brain fog, extreme exhaustion, involuntary naps, and illness after illness finally hijacked his life. By the way, Ty was born on May 6, 2021. The highlight of the year. No rest for the weary but many smiles and laughs to go around. The Bad of 2022 The first week of January – Keri had her birthday. Ty went to daycare for the first time. Four days later, he brought home Omicron – the newest in COVID. While Ty handled it just fine and looked amazingly cute, Gary was bedridden again. Every couple of weeks, a new bug from Ty would send Gary back to bed. Before long, it was impossible to hold any job when calling out every other week. This employer was incredibly accommodating, but Gary finally stepped away because he knew he was hurting the team. And by stepping away, he could focus on finding medical treatment and building an incredible care team. The Good of 2022 The fantastic care team now consists of his primary care doctor, a cardiologist, a pulmonary specialist, a speech therapist (cognitive), a physiotherapist, amazing nurses, and a mental health therapist (This is stressful!). A caring, concerned [expensive] medical team that would not accept shoulder shrugging was able to track down the illnesses and provide us labels for what Gary has been going through: Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension - Pulmonary hypertension is a type of high blood pressure that affects the arteries in the lungs and the right side of the heart. Patients with pulmonary hypertension cannot perform any physical activity without symptoms. Dyspnea and/or fatigue may be present at rest, and discomfort is increased by any physical activity. Post-Exertional Malaise (Post-Exertional Symptom Exacerbation) – A disabling and often delayed exhaustion disproportionate to the effort made. It is sometimes described as a “crash”. The activity that can trigger this worsening of symptoms can be something that was easily tolerated before, such as a shower, a walk, working at a desk, etc. Long-COVID Autonomic Dysfunction - Long-COVID, also known as Post-Acute COVID Syndrome, is the development of chronic and potentially debilitating symptoms, including fatigue, cognitive impairment, weakness, headache and dizziness, among many others. For Gary and Keri, accepting and adapting to the new diagnoses and situation has been exceptionally challenging for the past two months. Fortunately, Ty has been blissfully unaware and the happiest baby on the block. Well, that about sums it up; sorry it ran a little long for a short version! And that’s why Gary, Keri, and Ty could use your help right now. The best way to help would be with a monetary donation (use of funds breakdown below). Every $5 or $10 helps immensely. If you’re unable to help that way, sharing their story and fundraising page with your personal and/or professional networks would be amazing too. And most importantly, keep them in your thoughts and prayers. Thanks for taking the time to read their story. Hi my name is Kelly and Joe is my brother. I have started this account in hopes to raise funds for Joe's medical expenses. This all started Monday Sept 26, Joe was helping our brother Don with a project he was working on, while throwing out debris at the county landfill Joe accidentally stepped on a nail that went threw the bottom of his shoe into his foot. He went home that day and cared for his injury best he could and got a tetna shot the following day, by Friday he was in such excruciating pain and his foot had become very swollen. I took him to the ER on Saturday they treated him with IV fluids, antibiotics and pain meds. They wrote him a prescription for oral antibiotics and advised him if it did not start feeling better with 72 hours to come back in. He felt a lil better when We left the ER, Unfortunately that didn't last long, within 36 hours we were back in the ER . By this time his foot was extremely swollen and the pain worse than before. They took an xray and found a abscess had formed and it was most likely infected. The 1st procedure was to go in and remove/drain abscess . While in surgery the surgeon became concerned in what he saw .well, actually it was what he didn't see that was the problem, it was the limited amount of bleeding while doing the procedure, they then ordered a MRI of his leg and that is where they discovered Joe's Fermoral Artery had a 99 % blockage. They then scheduled him to have a stint put in (a procedure that normally would take an hour ) Joe was in the operating room for over 3 hours. The Doctor explained To us the magnitude of the blockage and that a stint would not have corrected the problem, the Doctor was able to unblock and open up Joes artery to get bloodflow to reach just down below his knee. The Doctor was doing what he could to preserve as much of Joe's leg as possible, the Dr then placed him on TPA in hopes to reduce the amount of blockage ( a clot busting medicine that had risks that could lead to Joe bleeding out ) The Doctor did another angioplasty procedure now trying to clear his lower half of his leg and to gain more bloodflow to Joe's injured foot and the Doctors efforts were succesful, Bloodflow and antibiotics were now getting to his foot , By this time Joe's injured foot had been deprived of adequate bloodflow and antibiotics for now 11 days. While recovering from his 2nd angioplasty procedure in the ICU his hemoglobin dropped suddenly, In efforts to find where he was bleeding they did an endoscopy and discovered he had a bleeding stomach ulcer. Thankfully they were able to get that under control. After a few days in the ICU and a couple of debridements on his foot later, we remained hopeful and positive that he would fully recover. The Dr's gave it a few days to see how his injury would respond due to the length and lack of adequate bloodflow to his injured foot. The Doctors had to make the decision that would be best for Joe's recovery. They had to amputate his right great (Big) toe . After the amputation a wound vac was put in place and a skin graph procedure was done While all of this was going on Joe was served an eviction notice and was evicted from his home. (Between hospital visit we were cleaning out his house). When they discharged Joe from the hospital after 31 days they prescribed him with antibiotic infusions to fight the infection within his bone. These infusions that would need to be administered threw a pic line every 6 hours for the next 36 days. He also will need labs drawn weekly to be sure that the antibiotics are working. 9 other medications that are also needing to be filled along with follow up Doctor appointments. Joe does not have any health insurance. The Dr has projected that he will not be able to bear weight on his foot until January. Without being able to work, we have filed all the paperwork in hopes of obtaining some government assistance but we will not know if he's granted eligibility for atleast another 90 -120 days. My husband and I have opened our home for Joe to stay with us while he is recovering. We are staying positive and I am trying to do my best to do all we can for a healthy recovery for Joe Any amount of donation, thoughts of inspiration would be greatly appreciated. IF you know Joe, you know he has never met a stranger. We plan on staying focused on the positive. Learning to live as an amputee will have its obstacles and challenges.All Money donated will go to directly to help with medical expenses. We Thank all of you who will keep Joe in your thoughts and prayers ❤.

We are the Van Wyk Family: Judson, Lena, and our daughters, Lily (age 1.5) and Junia (expected early 2023). After a routine ultrasound in early October, we received the hard news that little Junia has a condition called Spina Bifida. The Short Version: Spina Bifida requires surgical closure of the exposed spinal tissue. Remarkably, it is now possible to perform this repair in utero through fetal surgery—halting progressive damage to the spinal cord earlier and potentially leading to greater mobility and decreased need for repeated surgical interventions in infancy/early childhood. At the advice of our medical team at Duke, we are pursuing this surgery at Minnesota Children's Hospital in Minneapolis in mid-November. We will be required to remain there for about a month and are seeking help for the many costs associated with this surgery and the medical care needed after Junia is born. What is Spina Bifida? According to the Spina Bifida Resource Network: "Spina Bifida is one of the most common, permanently disabling birth defects in America. It occurs when the neural tube, which forms the spinal cord and vertebral column, does not close completely during the first several weeks after conception. Each year about 1,500 pregnancies are affected by Spina Bifida in the US. "Living with Spina Bifida is different for every person. The spectrum of disability ranges from mild to severe. People with spina bifida often need many surgeries over their lifetime and have lifelong disabilities, including paralysis in the lower parts of the body, mobility challenges, and loss of bladder and bowel control. "Most children with spina bifida can and do live long productive lives, thanks to advanced medical techniques and support systems." (Learn more at <URL> Our Journey We know God has been preparing us for this for a very long time, as we actually met while living in a community in Durham, NC for folks with and without intellectual, developmental, and physical disabilities. There, we found lifelong friends worthy of love and respect and saw how much those experiencing disability have to give our community. We know that this diagnosis is only one part of Junia's story, and that she is a beloved child of God who will bring great joy and giftedness into our family and world. Per the advice of our medical team at Duke University, we are pursuing fetal surgery for Junia at Midwest Fetal Care Center at Minnesota Children's Hospital in Minneapolis. As mentioned above, performing the repair of the spinal defect in utero halts progressive damage to the spinal cord earlier than the traditional postnatal repair (performed 24-48 hours after birth). This remarkable surgery has the potential to significantly decrease Junia's need for brain and spinal surgeries in early childhood, improve the likelihood of walking and other motor functions, and positively impact cognitive development. We have done a great deal of prayer and research about this surgery, sought advice from the best doctors, theologians, and ethicists we could find, and feel confident that this is the best decision for our daughter. The surgery is tentatively scheduled for November 15, and will require us to remain in Minneapolis for about a month. Lord willing, we will then be able to return home and deliver Junia at Duke. At that point, the prognosis is uncertain, but a NICU stay and further surgery are likely. We particularly ask for prayer that Lena will not go into preterm labor and can carry Junia until at least 35 weeks. Our Need As one would expect, this journey will be expensive. We are planning for costs from the surgery and hospital stay itself, travel to Minneapolis, a possible extended stay at Duke, and the (likely) very involved medical journey to come with our little girl. I never wanted to be this guy, but here I am. I recently found out that I have a cancerous tumor on my tongue. My lymph nodes will also be removed on my left side of my neck. They will then do a flap surgery, removing a portion of skin from inside of my wrist and blood vessel and use this for reconstruction. Then they will take a skin graft from my leg to cover this and I’ll need a wrist brace while healing. After my tumor is removed, I will have a 7-10 day hospital stay. I will have an NG tube (feeding tube) during this time. After this they will do a swallow study and make sure I get enough nutrients in before they remove the tube. If I don’t I will have to go home with it. I will need to have speech therapy but should regain most of my function but it will take several weeks (1-2 months). If radiation is needed, that will make the recovery longer. This is all a guesstimate for now. From the little bit of research I’ve done, this surgery can be upwards of 9-10 hours, and it can take months if not a year or more to regain my speech as I know it today. If I can’t speak, I can’t work. Of course my bills are going to be insane, but right now the main concern is making sure I can stay on top of monthly bills and my rent. I have filed a disability claim, but it is still pending and I have no idea how long it will take to receive payments. Even if you cannot donate, thank you for reading this far ❤️ and if you can donate, please know how much I appreciate your help!

Hello! Welcome to the mission to bring Cindy home! My name is Jenny & I'm writing on behalf of my mom. In early September, my mom had surgery to repair a hiatal hernia (for those in healthcare, she had a Nissan Fundoplication). Things went as expected post-operatively; she's the dream patient and follows orders to the letter of the law. She had a smooth recovery and received surgical clearance to live her life (including travel). My parents flew out to the UK the second week of October and began touring around the English countryside. My dad's mother was British and he has many childhood memories in the UK - this is a brilliant excuse to want to explore the countryside. A week into their adventure, my mom developed excruciating pain and a rock-hard abdomen. She was rushed to their nearest hospital where she perforated in the ED on October 17. We now know her surgical wrap from early September was too tight, cut off circulation, her tissue developed ischemia and necrotized, and she perforated her stomach. She almost died before getting to the OR; it's pretty heartbreaking to hear her tell her story. She was praying to die because she was in so much pain. She required a big chunk of her stomach (all the dead tissue) to be surgically removed. Her post-operatively experience in the UK has been long and complicated. She, unfortunately, has a leak somewhere and is battling intra-abdominal sepsis. We suspect she's developed abscesses or fistulas but has not had a proper CT scan (the contrast on the last CT scan infiltrated and the images were suboptimal). They did see a lot of smuts including fluid around her spleen which is not good. A new drain was placed in interventional radiology but the drainage output has been minimal, raising concerns it's not working and she now needs further procedures/interventions. Her cultures are positive and making matters more complicated, she has become resistant to the antibiotics. This is a dangerous and potentially life-threatening situation. My parents are optimists and eternally see the good in people (God bless them) so they would not approve of me speaking poorly of the NSH (the British healthcare system). I flew out and was there for nearly 3 weeks. What I will say is this: I was utterly horrified. The medical care felt like 1972. Paternalism rules the roost. Cleanliness is not next to godliness. Medical care is reactive at best and even then, that might give them more credit than deserved. Her surgeon has been particularly challenging and has blocked the transfer multiple times. I genuinely believe if we do not privately medivac her home immediately, she could die there. My father is an emergency/trauma nurse practitioner. He spent nearly 20 years in the Air Force serving and has practiced in acute care for 45 years. My mother is basically a saint. She has dedicated her life to serving others. She was raised as a missionary kid and as an adult has always been active in the SDA church and is passionate about volunteering in the community; in recent years she worked to rehabilitate homeless individuals in their community (Mount Vernon, WA). Our family as a whole has dedicated most of our lives to serving others. It's in our blood. We are caregivers. It's very unusual for us to need help and even harder for us to ask for help. But now we need it. My parents always travel with travel insurance. I can hear my dad's voice in my mind when I share his life motto: in life, you adapt, improve, and move on. Planning for plan B is second nature for us. Unfortunately, plan B let us down this time - we have been told this is a pre-existing condition. Not only has her healthcare been self-pay in the UK, but we now need to fund her return. Your donation to the mission will help pay for the medical team, medical supplies, and the private jet to bring her home utilizing the company International SOS. The cost of this service is more than you can imagine and is not the amount we hope to raise. My family is personally moving heaven and hell to pay for it ourselves, but we need help to bridge the gap. I can truly say your donation and kindness will help save the life of the most amazing person I know. My mother has a heart of pure gold. She sees the good in all things and has and will spend her life "paying it forward." Thank you for reading her story and supporting the mission. My family cannot thank you enough.

We are two of Warrior Wade’s awesome Aunts and creating this Go Fund Me in hopes to supplement and offset the financial stresses placed on the family of our younger sister & brother in law, Allison & Matt Warren. They will be supporting their youngest son Wade through his Cranio journey that will require additional unpaid FMLA leave for Allison, extensive travel, medical, & equipment expenses. Please consider donating if you are able and continue to lift them with your prayers and positive thoughts. Wade’s Story - On October 3rd Wade had his routine 2 month appointment. The pediatrician noticed an abnormal head shape and referred Wade on to a pediatric plastic surgeon and neurosurgeon. On October 14th Wade received a head CT which confirmed his diagnosis of metopic craniosynostosis with triagoncephaly. Metopic craniosynostosis is premature fusion of the metopic suture. The metopic suture runs from the anterior fontanelle (front soft spot) to the tip of the nose. If the fused portion of the skull is not corrected, Wade could develop increased intracranial pressure, optic nerve pressure, blindness, and developmental delays. Wade will be having the endoscopic craniectomy surgery on November 10th in El Paso, Texas with Dr. David Jimenez. Dr. Jimenez invented the endoscopic craniectomy surgery in the 1990s and has done more cases than any other neurosurgeon world wide. For this reason, people travel all over the world to have him operate on their children. Wade and his family will be in Texas for approximately 10 days for pre-operative appointments, helmet fittings, surgery, the hospital stay, and post-operative appointments. Wade will be required to wear a helmet for up to a year after surgery to help restructure his skull and protect his head from injury. Because of the rapid head growth during the span of a child’s first year of life, Wade will likely need 3-4 helmets. Each helmet costs $2,500. Wade and his family will also be required to return to El Paso for additional post-operative appointments and helmet fittings.

She is not ready to retire fully yet, instead pushing on to finish her archival work in St. Louis on her own participation in the 21 movements listed on her website. Since Laura has been so important to the causes of women’s rights and human rights and has given so selflessly to all of us, it is time to give back, by helping her in this time of need. We, her friends and colleagues would like to make sure she doesn’t have to worry about her medical costs. Photo: Francine Case, Laura, and Bob Case at Dance The Vote 2022, produced by Joan Lipkin on the steps of the Missouri History Museum. Photo credit: Francine Case Please donate as much as you can to help Laura through this crisis! We would love $20,000 by her birthday next week and hope to reach $40,000 by Thanksgiving. P.S. As you probably know, Laura’s accomplishments over a career spanning more than half a century are epic, including... Co-founder of her college chapter of the Committee for a Sane Nuclear Policy (SANE) in 1960 — and she continued her antinuclear work with Women Strike for Peace (their Wiki page), inspired by their December 11, 1962 breastfeeding demonstration and testimony at the House Un-American Activities Committee (read more here). She has worked with the Women's International League for Peace and Freedom (WILPF; website link) since 1962, and she’s still working on these issues through WILPF, CODEPINK Women for Peace (website link), and the American Association of University Women (AAUW; website link). Most recently she celebrated her birthday for 8 hours sailing on the Golden Rule down the Mississippi, from Portage de Sioux to Kimmswick, through fabulous locks and past St. Louis. This very sailing ship sailed into harm's way in 1958 in a Quaker demonstration in waters where nuclear bomb tests were being held around the Marshall Islands (read more here). Right now they need crew members. Please sign up! Picket captain in CORE and American Committee on Africa in NYC. 1961 Head Start teacher in Puerto Rico (she's fluent in Spanish!) and NYC. 1961-2 Archivist activist in the Free Speech Movement UC Berkeley. 1964 Early and international archivist of the Women's Liberation Movement (WLM). 1968 Founded women’s liberation movement newsletter SPAZM, the only national women's liberation newsletter between April and December 1969 (read more in the Vice.com article, The Legendary Women's Rights Activist Who Mailed Obama A Coat Hanger, here). Co-founded the first women's liberation newspaper, It ain't me Babe. 1970 Author, editor, and publisher of essays, bibliographies, books (The Women's Songbook [1971], Films by and/or about Women Internationally [1972], and Female Artists Past and Present [1973]), and microfilms of the records of the WLM, 1968- 75:Women and Law, Women's Health/Mental Health, and Herstory (serial publications). These microfilms have been purchased by 450 libraries in 14 countries, and now they have been digitized. They are distributed by the fabulous National Women's History Alliance in Santa Rosa, CA ( <URL> Campaign leader for a jazz and blues radio station that showcased women in the San Francisco Bay Area. 1976-8 Campaign coordinator for repealing date and marital rape legal privileges in 45 states, DC, and 20 other countries. Participant in and collector and curator of 21 social movements between 1961-2022. Supporter and producer for artists and their events... theatrical, historical, musical, etc. ***** Laura has been a teacher, educator, and organizer in many different capacities, from teaching in Head Start in Puerto Rico (she is fluent in Spanish) and Headstart in New York, and kindergarten in Berkeley, CA, to educating the American people, as an activist and a speaker, about abused women and children, women’s rights to reproductive freedom, and women’s liberation. In the late 60s, Laura founded the first historical archive of what was to become the women’s liberation movement – the Women’s History Research Center, in Berkeley, California. Laura’s amazing archives are now in various academic and other libraries across the country (see the whole list of libraries here). Those are the original documents of 21 social movements over 50 years. In 1968, Laura called for the revival of International Women’s Day, which is now celebrated across the world, and named National Women's History Month in 1969 and provided resources for that nascent movement. She was an early member in the mid-70s of the Coalition of Labor Union Women CLUW, and still is.. and is a card-carrying union member, and advocate for the rights of all workers in all ways, including the right to be free of sexual harassment in the workplace. Through her early organization starting in 1978, the National Clearinghouse on Marital and Date Rape (NCMDR) Laura successfully worked alongside lawyers, victims/survivors, and politicians, as an advocate and a resource, in the successful state-by-state campaign to make marriage and date rape illegal. To this day, many people don’t know that marital and date rape were not crimes in a staggering number of states until well into the 1980s, and Laura X challenged that reality to benefit women and victims everywhere. Laura published her bibliographical memoirs in the 90s, Accomplishing the Impossible: an Advocate’s Notes from the Successful Campaign to Make Marital and Date Rape a Crime in all 50 U.S. States and other Countries. In June of 1993 North Carolina was the last state to make marital rape a crime in some part of the statutes. In 2001 Mary Institute gave Laura their Distinguished Alumna award; for this service and in 2009 the University of Missouri at St. Louis UMSL gave her their Trailblazer award. Along with her existing unfinished archives, which are being worked on in a wondrous church space the Laura's Social Movement Archives rents with other nonprofits in St. Louis, Laura dedicates her free moments, seven days a week, to promoting historical events and figures, museums, foundations and charities, voting awareness, writers and artists, important films, and progressive politics. She is also active as an advisory board member on the Emma Goldman Public History Papers Project the 4th and final 853-page volume that chronicles the life and work of Emma Goldman (donate here). I am Beth, and I am fundraising for my daughter, Savannah! On August 26th, Savannah was a hardworking, healthy, self-motivated, beautiful, 21-year-old thoughtful, loving daughter, girlfriend, educated social media manager, and mother of two (beautiful cats). Within 17 days, she began stuttering, then was unable to speak or work or even be alone due to sudden onset seizures. On the 17th day, she had 62 unexplained seizures (over 3,700 seconds of time spent unable to control her body’s movement)...and had no idea what was happening. On that 17th day (October 14th), we watched her seize 62 times, averaging a loss of consciousness between 15-90 seconds...we counted each one...and realized something else had to be done! We received confirmation that afternoon that the referral we had to Stanford was denied. We knew the ER here couldn’t help us (see long story below); we knew these seizures and her symptoms were getting worse; we knew this had progressed rapidly from stuttering to not being able to speak, to having seizures, to who knows what else was next. On Saturday, the 15th, we knew what we had to do...we packed up and headed to the Stanford ER. They were outside of our Network of providers, but it didn’t matter. I couldn’t watch her have another seizure without having a plan to try and help her. We were seen by the best doctors and specialists in the US and they did not disappoint. They admitted her, hooked her up to another EEG with full video monitoring and watched her closely overnight. By 1:30 pm the next day, we had a diagnosis. Functional Neurological Disorder – FND or sometimes referred to as Conversion Disorder. What is FND? I didn’t know either, and most doctors are still in the dark about it. The easy answer is that her hardware is fine, but her software has a glitch. Someone with FND can function normally; they just can’t at that moment. Their brain cannot send and receive signals properly, and there is a disconnection in the function of the lobes and emotional processing. Memory, concentration, cognition, and the processing of sensations also can be affected. FND causes real symptoms that significantly interfere with how you function and cope with daily life. If you have FND, your unplanned movements and symptoms occur without you consciously starting them and are inconsistent and distinct from symptoms that are intentionally produced. FND can involve any part of your body. Symptoms may appear suddenly, increase with attention to them, and decrease when you are distracted. All funds donated will be used for medical bills (not covered by insurance / out-of-network expenses), noncovered medical equipment, travel expenses to and from Stanford, and general bills as she cannot work. Where is she now? Savannah is still a self-motivated, beautiful, 21-year-old loving daughter, girlfriend, and mother of two (beautiful cats) who has FND and is fighting every day to get her old life back. She gets up every day and continues to have an amazingly positive attitude. Although we don’t know what the future holds, we are tapping all resources possible to give her the best possible chance of returning to a normal life. The head of neurology at Stanford gave her the FND clinic referral we were hoping for; we will be getting her into Cognitive Therapy and have a plethora of other tests that need to occur as we continue to rule out other secondary issues. We don’t know how long she will be out of work or how much her medical bills will end up costing, but we know that we will do what it takes to get her the care she deserves. Back Story – Prior to the seizures starting This is a journey no one expected, wanted, or ever thought possible. Savannah woke up like it was any other day, proceeded to get ready for work, taking care of her two cats (Ziggy & Greyson), and then it began. Her words didn’t come out of her mouth like normal. She had never stuttered a day in her life until now. We went to the Emergency Room (ER) that evening, where we spent 7 hours. By this point, she had brain fog, stuttering, headache, eye pressure and inability to focus. Her diagnosis was anxiety and stuttering, and she was told to follow up with her primary care doctor. Three days later, she couldn’t speak at all...just like that, no words would come out. At this point, we were starting to get worried as we started to see eye fluttering, unusual neck movements and hand tremors, but we were reluctant to go back to the ER, so we waited. A few days later, we were back in the ER after she had gone in for a pulmonary test that ended with the Emergency Room rapid response team being called to help her. This time, the ER performed a functional MRI of her brain, an EKG and echocardiogram of her heart, and an EEG to watch her brain movement. They kept her for two nights and ultimately discharged her, indicating everything seemed normal and we should probably try going to Stanford if she continued to have these symptoms. No reason for her stuttering, inability to speak, hand tremors, brain fog, uncontrolled eye-rolling, sensitivity to light, headaches, etc. On the evening of her discharge, a new and worsening symptom started – unexplained seizures! Nothing can ever prepare you for watching your daughter have a seizure...even one is too many. Our lives changed entirely between that first seizure on October 6th and October 14th. These seizures worsened in duration and frequency, and she could not work, drive, or be independent. When she wasn’t having a seizure, the headaches and brain fog prevented her from doing everyday things. I have had to work more from home, her stepdad took a leave from his job, and we all had to learn how to protect her from harm when these seizures happened. If you have continued this long, we appreciate it. If you cannot donate, please keep her/us in your thoughts and prayers.
