SPD makes it very difficult for Willow to feel comfortable and calm in her body. Willow has been to various therapies in her life, and while they have been helpful in some areas, none have reduced her hair pulling. As parents, we have worked hard to learn and grow in skills that help Willow with other difficulties, but we have found it causes her more stress when we attempt to help her manage her Trichotillomania. About a year ago, we were in a crowd of people at a flea market (one of her least favorite places), and she calmly asked someone standing nearby if she could pet her dog. The lady was quick to say yes, and before I knew it, Willow was lying in the Standard Poodles' thick fur, as relaxed as we have ever seen her in a crowd. She stayed that way for about 10 minutes. The owner kept encouraging her to relax as we enjoyed the flea market (close by, of course), but we finally told WIllow it was time to let them enjoy the flea market. Willow had a completely different demeanor after that experience. Later in the day, we saw them again, and the owner told Willow she could pet the dog again. I started chatting with the owner, who shared that Truly was a retired Service Dog. She could tell by Truly and Willow's connection that something was special about Willow. We shared a bit of her story, and the owner shared that she believed a Service Dog could be a huge help to WIllow. John and I walked away, both thinking the same thing... This encounter was NOT a coincidence. And so began our dreaming and researching to find a way to make this happen for Willow. We started working with a local non-profit that trains Service Dogs and gives them to families at no charge. We thought this would work out, but they changed their minds near the end of the application process. We were incredibly disheartened by this news but later learned that they couldn’t do what we needed -- we needed to work with an organization specializing in psychiatric service dogs. Meet Aspen. Aspen is a 13-week-old puppy bred with the intention of becoming a psychiatric service dog. She is a Sheepdog Poodle mix. When talking with a psychiatric service dog organization we discovered last week and sharing our story, we became even more confident that this would be the best move. However, there are no local psychiatric service dog non-profits. The total cost of attaining a service dog through this organization (the dog, the training, the long-term support, etc.) is $17,000 (the average cost of training alone is $20,000+). I explained this would be something we would have to save for or fundraise. The owner ended up giving us a generous discount. We believe Aspen can help lessen the pressure on Willow and our entire family as Aspen will provide the Trichotillomania support she needs. In doing so, Willow will gain independence and confidence, reducing her anxiety and increasing her peace. We have been praying for peace and pigtails for five years. As her parents, her peace is so important to us, but we know how desperately she wants to trade bald spots for pigtails, so we want that for her too. If you're still reading, thank you. If you plan to give, no matter the amount, thank you. There are no words to express the love and support Willow and our entire family have received from our community. From prayer to great parenting tips, all the fluffy stuffed animals sent her way, and everything in between, you have been there for us, and we are so grateful.

We never wanted to make this campaign - in fact, we never thought we would ever need to - but we’re in a situation where we can’t see a way out and so now we are turning to our friends, family, and kind strangers for help. Our son is Athan Palazzo. Athan means eternal life. He is certainly full of it! Energetic. Kind. Sweet. He’s everything you’d want in a young boy. Unfortunately, when he was two years old he received a diagnosis that shaped our lives: Autism & Autoimmune Dysfunction. Athan has a severe case of it which already means an impediment for his future - challenges we were ready to face head-on - but we could not have imagined what came next. Athan has an autoimmune dysfunction. It’s a bit technical but in short, it causes what we have come to call ‘flares.’ Even a common illness like a cold or flu can cause a ‘flare,’ meaning his immune system goes haywire. Endless crying. Erratic pacing. Obsessive-compulsive routines. Our son disappears before our very eyes. In an instant, that loving, friendly boy is replaced with the frustration and pain of his condition ravaging his body. It is heartbreaking. We have been battling this for the last five years, but even after all the doctor appointments and tests it feels as if we are no closer to finding a working system that Athan can thrive in. Then, by god’s grace, we came across a group of doctors in Austin who agreed to take on the case. Inspired by the research of world-renowned neurologist Dr. Robert Melillo, the Austin Center for Developing Minds is having breakthrough success stories using cutting-edge technology where other typical methods have failed. They examined him physically and mentally, plus they did comprehensive lab testing. We couldn't believe it! And the result? They said they could help him. Finally, someone listened to us and had faith in us. Now Athan has a real shot of living with his condition in a way that it doesn’t stop him from being, well, him. However, as you can imagine, all those medicines and treatments and frequent meets-up come with a cost. This is America after all. And unfortunately, we were not ready for the fees, especially for a full-time career. We’ve even done a full breakdown of the costs for you to see and let us tell you, it adds up fast. He turns 7 soon but is still in diapers and unable to talk, unable to communicate basic needs or discomfort, but if we can afford these cutting-edge therapies, then overcoming these obstacles becomes a real possibility, That’s why we are reaching out to ask for help in covering Athan’s medical fees. We realize that we are asking for a lot but we’re not asking anyone to ruin themselves financially. We’re just asking that you pledge something towards our cause. Just something. Anything. A couple of dollars really will go far in helping us reach our goal. And if you can share Athan’s story with other people, we have a bigger chance of finally getting him the help he needs. It will prove that someone out there really cares about Athan and believes in him. So thank you for reading. God bless.

Michelle needs our help! For a number of years Michelle has suffered from immense abdominal and pelvic pain. After years of doctor visits, test, and trial and error she finally received a diagnosis – endometriosis! This disease is a painful disorder in which tissue similar to the tissue that normally lines the inside of your uterus — the endometrium — grows outside your uterus. It can grow anywhere in your body and affect multiple organs. Michelle's is mostly in her pelvic and abdominal region and ranges from a daily dull ache to excruciating, crippling pain that is all-consuming and debilitating. In addition, she has recently been diagnosed with adenomyosis, the sister of endometriosis, in which these same tissues grow in the muscle wall of the uterus. Unfortunately, the average diagnosis of endo takes patients 7 years and Michelle's case has been no different. She's lost count of how many doctors she's seen since she moved to the Jersey City area and their treatment options have ranged from multiple types of birth control to "have some wine” to an IUD to vaginally inserted Valium. In the fall of 2021 Michelle saw yet another doctor who finally diagnosed with her with endometriosis and offered a surgical option- what's called “the gold standard” of treatment - a laparoscopy with excision of the endo tissue. The day after Thanksgiving in 2021 Michelle had her first surgery, where several inches of inflammation/scar tissue were removed, as well as fibroids (Fibrosis was discovered during surgery.) Dishearteningly, the biopsy came back as “no evidence of disease” - how could that be? Her symptoms were very real and very painful and the surgeon found significant inflammation and scar tissue that had to be caused by something! The surgeon concluded that her current treatment – birth control/IUD – was suppressing the disease to microscopic levels, making it impossible to remove the root cause of her pain. Michelle's insurance did not cover the surgery (other than the hospital facility fees) because the procedure was "not proven to work". Further appeals failed and Michelle paid thousands of dollars for a procedure that ultimately proved unsuccessful. After her recovery from surgery, Michelle felt relief for the first time in a long time – she was thrilled! Unfortunately, her relief was short-lived. Within two months, the pain returned with a vengeance. For several months, she returned to her surgeon for experimental radio wave treatments that cost $800 a session – but the treatments proved useless. Because this was experimental, insurance also denied these costs and Michelle again paid out of pocket. Frustrated, Michelle ended her journey with this particular doctor and began a new search to find answers and treatment that could improve her quality of life. There are a surprisingly very few surgeons in the U.S. who specialize in endometriosis, recognizing it as a whole-body disease and who are capable of performing the excision surgery needed for a cure. Enter Dr. Ken Sinervo of The Center for Endometriosis Care in Atlanta, Georgia! At the advice of a friend whose life was saved by Dr. Sinervo, Michelle went for an in-person consult in August 2022. Dr. Sinervo immediately recognized both the endometriosis and the adenomyosis and recommended a major, detailed surgical plan. This plan includes a month of “pre-surgery preparation” that, through medication, will encourage the endometrium tissue to grow exponentially so that during surgery it can be easily seen, identified and removed completely. Over the last few months, Michelle's quality of life has suffered tremendously. Her condition continues to deteriorate – she has more bad days than good and the bad days are much worse than they have ever been. She has had to take time off from work due to illness and is more often than not, forced to stay at home near her heating pad and bed due to medication she is taking to manage the pain. But thanks to Dr. Sinervo, for the first time in a long time, Michelle has HOPE! Hope for a life free from pain and endless medications. Hope that she can return to the active life she had before! Michelle has surgery scheduled at the CEC in Atlanta on November 28, 2022...a year and two days from her first surgery. During this time she will live in the Atlanta area for about 3 weeks to follow up with Dr. Sinervo himself. Similar to the surgery in 2021, insurance has once again denied coverage for this surgery. (*for more information on why please see the end of this plea*). In fact, if the CEC files the claim with her insurance, her copayment would be approximately $41,000. Instead, Michelle is going to self-pay the CEC and her current estimate is $9,000 to $21,000 for the surgeon’s costs. She is incredibly grateful that insurance WILL cover most of the hospital fees and expects additional costs from the anesthesiologist. The funds we are asking for will cover the cost of the Center for Endometriosis Care’s fee. Your donations will also help with the living costs for the time she needs to spend in Georgia. Michelle has already spent thousands on her medical care herself and this time is reaching out to the community for help. Anyone who knows Michelle knows that she is unimaginably generous and regularly goes above and beyond for the people and animals near and dear to her. Now is our chance to give Michelle back her quality of life. (there’s lots more dogs who need saving and Michelle is their hero!) Rest assured that Michelle as the beneficiary, has direct access to your donations, they will be deposited directly into her bank account. Thank you so much for your support! Every penny counts and is so appreciated. *Why doesn't insurance cover this procedure? Please see information below from endofound.org A 1992 Medicare Part B ruling grouped removal of endometriosis via fulguration, ablation, coagulation, and excision as one and the same thing. All insurers base how they reimburse on Medicare tables. There is literally no code in these tables for excision surgery because of the above. Excision is the only specialty not recognized by the American Medical Association (AMA). There are no boards or standard certifications. The American Congress of Ob-Gyn's (ACOG) also does not recognize excision as a specialty, and does not recognize excision as the gold standard of surgical therapy for endometriosis – even though there are hundreds of clinical, peer-reviewed journals that say otherwise. Medical schools don't teach excision or identification of endometriosis – because doctors literally cannot make a living doing it unless they are at a major university. “Standard of care” protects doctors. This healthcare term basically means that if the type of treatment you are giving patients is similar to what your peers give, you are protected from negligence charges. Even when, as in the case of endometriosis, hormonal treatments including the pill, have been shown to be palliative for many women at best, and further damaging at worst.

Anyone who knows Megan and Ricky knows that either one of them would drop absolutely anything to help someone else. Whether in the classroom, in their community, for their family or friends, or doing whatever they can to help animals and their humans, they are some of the most selfless people you’ll ever meet. And now it’s our turn to help them in a time of need. After a long journey of infertility struggles, Megan and Ricky finally got their precious baby Beckam in their arms this year, and that little smily baby has brought a light to the lives of everyone around him. Suddenly though, right after Beckam turned 5 months old, their world turned upside down when they began noticing seizure-like symptoms happening rather frequently. After a confirmation of seizures at a local hospital, Beckam was transferred to a larger facility for further testing. EEGs confirmed seizures on the left side of his brain, and after a whirlwind of tests, discussions, more seizures, medicines, and a traumatizing 48 hours for this little family, doctors arrived at a diagnosis of infantile spasms, a form of childhood epilepsy in infants. The lead neurologist currently on Beckam’s care team is optimistic, and will begin a regimen of anti-seizure meds to help calm (and hopefully STOP) these seizures so that Beckam can get back to as much of a normal life as possible. We are hoping with Megan Ricky for a best case scenario where the right cocktail of medicines works quickly, and that Beckam outgrows these seizures and does not have to suffer from the risk of them in the long term, though he remains at high risk for the seizures to continue. At a minimum right now, Beckam needs to remain in the hospital for at least the upcoming week while doctors monitor his reactions to the medications they’ll be using to slow/stop the seizures. This, along with the overall cost of having a child in the hospital, is why we are reaching out for your help... Fortunately Megan had the motherly instinct to not return to her teaching job this school year. Unfortunately, that meant that she has lost her insurance and had to switch she and Beckam’s coverage over to Ricky’s insurance. They had already met their deductible for the year on Megan’s insurance, meaning the deductible clock has reset with Ricky’s insurance company. Bad timing on top of a bad situation. In addition to the current and likely ongoing medical costs of managing this condition for Beckam, we want to make sure that Megan and Ricky are fully supported as they adjust to this new normal, loss of work, and travel/food costs getting to and from the hospital and future specialists/appointments. This little family means the world to so many of us and we want to lift at least one burden for them. We know the world is a tough place right now, but if you can spare a little to help them out, no one deserves it more. Thank you. *This fundraiser is created and managed by friends Ligia and Leah on behalf of Megan and Ricky.*

Hi, Grace was diagnosed with ovarian cancer, specifically Mullerian cancer (mixed cancer - carcinoma and sarcoma), in March 2022. But her journey didn’t start there. On December 26th, Grace got COVID. Then in January, she was hospitalized with pulmonary embolisms (blood clots in her lungs). In February, she had a heart attack. When the doctors did imaging, they discovered a mass in her peritoneal cavity. In March, Grace had excessive bleeding from the blood thinners and was hospitalized. At that time, they found she had two bleeding ulcers. Grace had an endoscopy, and both ulcers were clipped. After the endoscopy was done and she was resting back in her room, Grace started to experience numbness on her left side. A brain CT Scan and MRI showed she had a stroke. It was at this time Grace was officially diagnosed with ovarian cancer. Grace started chemotherapy on March 14 at The Cancer Center in Fall River. And in April, she transferred to Dana Farber Cancer Institute in Boston. Grace has numerous chemotherapy treatments and different combinations of chemotherapy drugs, but her cancer is what they call platinum resistant. She was offered to be part of a clinical trial, but after all the testing, her type of cancer didn’t qualify for the trial. Through all of this, Grace has had numerous blood transfusions, paracentesis, thoracentesis, CT Scans, and echocardiograms She recently started a new chemotherapy, Doxil, in September. She has had two treatments, and the Doxil is also not working. Grace has retired from her job, and her wife Jen is currently working 80 hours a week to make ends meet. While Jen is eligible for paid FMLA from one position, paid FMLA is not available at her 2nd job. To those who know Grace know she is an amazing wife, sister, sister-in-law, aunt, cousin, and friend. Her smile is infectious. Grace has a heart of gold and would do anything to help out any one of us in our time of need. So I'm asking at this vulnerable time in her life that we rally behind her as she continues on. Now, it's time that we send back some of that love and support to Grace and to her wife, Jen, who is by her side every step of the way. Anything you can donate will be genuinely appreciated. Anything we can do to help and surround Grace with love is what is most important. Please spread the word. Thank you from the bottom of our hearts. #FriendsDontLetFriendsFightAlone #DonateSharePray

From the top of his head to bottom of his feet. See I know what God can do!!! Am single parent, rised three sons 32, 19, 18 and they have never been too jail. 2 in college. I battle with Lupus everyday and I am cancer survivor!!! The doctors gave me up told my mother I had 24hrs to live. But GOD!!! My GOD!! He’s amazing. I said that to say this!! I know God had MJ. His dad and I continued to pray waiting on the Neurology Specialist to come in to tell us what had happened to MJ. A few minutes later the doctors walked in asking are you MJ parents. Yes!! This area is where a bundle of nerves running from the base of his brain down through the open space in the vertebrae (Also known as the spiral canal). His spiral core is swallowed pressing against his canal. Which caused him to be paralyzed for days. But as the spiral core goes down MJ will start to get some of his feelings back and his moving. MJ is now in paralysis state meaning a loss in the ability to control his muscles movements but it often includes the loss of other functions as well. The doctors said it no way of knowing how much of his control movements that he will regain. It could take weeks, months, or years. It’s not promising that all his mobility will come back. But I do know God is working. Everyday I see change. He’s working very hard in therapy. This young man MJ my son. Always been my humble child. Never gave me any trouble. He’s smart, funny, respectable and loves the game of football. MJ started playing football at the age of four. MJ has always been a hard worker on and off the field. In September 2021, our friend Erika started suffering from severe abdominal pain. Her belly began growing fast, and she was unexplainably gaining weight. The next few months were filled with doctors’ visits, tests and procedures, which revealed that she has a large mass the size of 4 bricks in her abdominal cavity. In December, Erika had a major surgery, where they removed part of her sigmoid colon, appendix and fearing ovarian cancer, performed a full hysterectomy. Unfortunately, later pathology reports revealed a different origin - a rather rare type of colon cancer called mucinous adenocarcinoma. Unlike typical colon cancer you may have heard about, this type is different and the cancerous polyp cannot be easily removed by cutting it out with part of the affected colon. Erika’s rare type of cancer consists of microscopic cells that form in mucin, the main component of the mucus in her abdomen. She was diagnosed with stage 4 (highest stage), which means her cancer cells have metastasized and spread to other parts of body. Statistical studies unfortunately show a pessimistic 5-year survival rate of only 14% after diagnosis (rate of patients still alive after 5 years, from date of initial diagnosis). Because Erika is young and strong, we were hoping she would respond to conventional treatment. She started with four rounds of chemotherapy that made her very sick. Unfortunately it has proven to be ineffective for her type of cancer, and she had another big surgery (H.I.P.E.C.) in April, difficult to perform and extremely risky. They removed 10 metastasis and applied chemotherapy drugs inside her abdomen, hoping this will eliminate the remaining cancerous cells. Erika recovered remarkably well from the surgery over this summer, felt great given circumstances and spent time with family and many of us... we were optimistic she was cancer-free. Regrettably, the CT scan in August revealed 5 new metastases. Erika continues to fight, focusing on slowing down the spread of cancer. She is currently trying a different type of conventional chemotherapy, while also taking various alternative supplements, adopted organic vegetarian diet, and goes on daily walks. Quality of life is very important to her, so she continues spending time with family and friends, takes an occasional trip and started checking items off her bucket list. Erika’s advice to us? “Don’t wait to live your life. Live it today because you never know what tomorrow may bring. Keep up with your annual check-ups and screenings, including the one for colorectal cancer at the age of 45.” (Current recommendation in the US) Finally, let’s talk about money. While Erika has a decent health insurance, which covered most of her medical expenses so far, she has been unable to work since December 2021 and is currently on long-term disability. Her husband Juraj is the family’s only provider, keeping up with mortgage and car payments and other recurring bills. Erika’s parents and aunt, who live in her native Slovakia, take turns visiting and helping to care for her. How can YOU help? This campaign aims to fund Erika’s medical and associated expenses NOT covered by health insurance. She currently spends over $2,000 a month on alternative therapies and additional supplements such as fenbendazole, tudca, coffee enemas, and detoxing supplements, reflexology, lymphatic massage, reiki healing... By raising $25,000, we can lift this financial burden off her shoulders for the next 12 months, so she can solely focus on healing, and living her life to the fullest. All donations (minus the 3% Gofundme fee) will go straight to Erika’s bank account. Erika and her husband would like to thank everyone in advance, from the bottom of their heart, for their continuous support and prayers. Are you ready to donate now?

What is Austin Pets Alive? Hi! Want to join me in making a difference? My team and I are raising money to benefit Austin Pets Alive! Austin Pets Alive was first established in 1997 as a no-kill plan for all animals. Later on, in 2008, it became a rescue organization that assists animals in need by providing food, shelter, and medical support. This organization emphasizes decreasing the rate of euthanasia each year and is successfully doing so. In the previous 20 years, they have provided more than 20,000 surgeries for animals in need and are continuously growing. Why is it important? On average, 920,000 shelter animals are put down every year in the United States, Shelters around the world country put down an estimated 320,000 dogs and 600,000 cats each year. Between 4000 and 10,000 animals are euthanized daily. 9 out of 10 euthanized animals are adoptable and have no problems with them. 5 states are responsible for 51.5 percent of all animals euthanized. Texas is the second highest animal euthanized with 96.7. Texas euthanized a total of 15.5 percent of the total euthanized in the United States. The methods some shelters euthanized animals are carbon monoxide or carbon monoxide gas chambers. This method is sad because these animals are scared in the gas chambers, before passing away. What is the process like to adopt? If you are thinking of adopting a pet it is an extremely easy process with Austin Pets Alive. A personal friend previously adopted a cat from Austin Pets Alive and this was the process she went through. “The process of adopting my cat Sadie was very easy. On the website, there is a catalog of animals of all types, sizes, sexes, and ages. Within this process, you are able to see pictures and videos of animals you are interested in and a brief description. You are also able to contact the fosters and shelters at any time. After contacting the shelter we adopted our cat Sadie over the phone within 10 minutes. Next, we went through a series of documents we were able to sign on the computer. A week later we were able to simply go and pick her up from her foster family.” How can you help? If you are an animal lover like us, help out this fantastic non-profit organization that adopts and fosters pets in the market by contributing to saving lives. There are many ways to help rescue these poor animals, but it all starts with your donations today! Your donations would go towards operations and medical support these animals need to survive. Thank you in advance for contributing to this cause which would mean the world to us. More information about Austin Pets Alive!: To promote and provide the resources, education, and programs needed to eliminate the killing of companion animals. Austin Pets Alive P.O. Box 736245 Dallas, TX 75373-6245 Austin Pets Alive Website

Hi, my name is Laura, my boyfriend is Cory, and our goofy dog Winston is a year-and-a-half 65lb golden doodle. It all started when last Friday we woke up to a little pool of blood on the floor and blood splatter on our door and wall. We checked his mouth, nose, penis, and butt and couldn’t find where the blood was coming from. We took him to the ER from 10:30pm to 2:30am, and four hours later after evaluating him, they said he seemed fine and sent us home. Today, Tuesday November 1st, around 10am Winston was laying down when all of a sudden he started bleeding from his penis all over the floor which was terrifying. We rushed him to the vet, where they performed an ultrasound to look for bladder stones. The results showed no bladder stones, and while they’re going to test his urine to rule out a UTI, they said because his pee looks normal and he’s not straining when he pees, it’s highly unlikely it’s a UTI. We went home feeling a little reassured about the situation but still worried. A few hours later, around 2pm, Winston began gushing blood again from his penis, this time way more and all over our bed. We sped to the vet again, and they advised we try a cone, thinking it could be irritated from him licking himself. This time they took an X-RAY and confirmed again, there were no bladder stones. They mentioned low platelets could be a possibility and this time sent us home with a cone, hoping that without him being able to lick himself the bleeding would subside. Tonight around 8pm, Winston began gushing blood again. This time it wasn’t from him licking himself, as his cone was on preventing him from doing so. He was sitting down when it started for the third time today. With the other vet office being closed, we had to take him to the ER where we currently are awaiting results from blood tests and further testing. We were told we may have to see a specialist to perform a special procedure depending on what they find. Even though this was the third time it’s happening today, it never gets any less terrifying and traumatizing seeing your dog bleeding profusely from their body. Cory and I got Winston when he was a puppy when we lived in Seattle and fell in love with him. We had him when COVID was still at its peak, so we spent a lot of time home with him bonding with our puppy and became a little happy family. The fear of not knowing what’s happening or what will happen scares us and I have not been able to stop crying all day, just praying that our puppy would be ok. Anyone that knows us personally knows that he is our baby and we would do anything to save him. Unfortunately, we did not have pet insurance before any of this happened (currently working on getting that, however we won’t be able to use it for the costs from the last few days). Although I was hoping to announce under happier circumstances, I am pregnant and unfortunately have had to miss some work due to intense morning sickness throughout my pregnancy. Cory and I are excited to welcome our little one next year, however Winston is our “first born”, and truly like a child to us, and we will do everything to make sure he’s ok. Anything would help us tremendously to relieve the financial burden the last few days has had, and unforeseen future medical emergencies/costs that may come from this. We thank you from the bottom of our hearts for taking the time to read this far, and considering donating to help Winston. ~ Cory, Laura, and Winston ❤️

After losing my cat of 9 years in January to cancer, I decided I was ready to open my heart up again to another kitty. We took him to the vet to run tests and the doctor told us he had FIP which is short for Feline infectious peritonitis. FIP is a viral disease in cats that if left untreated is 100% fatal. There is treatment but unfortunately it is not FDA approved here in the US and veterinarians are unable to administer the medication. Luckily the treatment is available for purchase overseas but it is very expensive. Thor will need to receive 84 injections and blood work every 30 days to make sure the treatment is working. Once done with the treatment he goes into an 84 day observation period and needs to get blood work every 30 days to make sure he does not relapse. The treatment luckily has been working and Thor has shown major improvement. The vet visits have been expensive and have put a huge strain on us financially. We couldn’t even think about not trying to help save his life so we’ve done what we could and have been using our credit cards to pay for the bills and treatment. As many of our friends and family know we rescued a St. Bernard named Willow after she was attacked by another dog in her home. What we know about the situation was that the 3 dogs were in a bedroom while the owner was at work and got into a fight at some point during the day. When the owner got home he found Willow covered in blood and bleeding from her neck. The owner didn’t think Willow was going to survive the injury and didn’t take her to the vet that night (Thursday, October 20th) and considered shooting her to put her out of her misery but couldn’t. Willow did survive and the next day we heard about her and Willow was surrendered to us on Friday, October 21st . Willow was 7 months old, 56 pounds, flea infested and highly allergic to them so she had hair loss, she has flat feet from being in a crate and had been attacked by a housemate. She had a laceration in her trachea, multiple bites in her neck and because she hadn’t received treatment all night she had severe swelling and bruising very close to her airway. She had lost a lot of blood and her red blood cell counts were extremely low but the vet felt like she would recover. Willow was given a lot of medicine and was able to come home. We were told at the time to watch for any swelling in her body and if that happened she needed emergency surgery on her trachea. She did well all weekend and was eating great so things were looking up until Monday afternoon when her face started to swell up. Her vet sent us to medvet where she was admitted to their ICU. In the 6 hours we were there her jowels swelled up to at least 4x their normal size. The best of the best in the vet world didn’t know what was wrong with her and she was already fighting an uphill battle being at least 40-50 pounds underweight. She was too sick to undergo any type of exploratory surgery to try to remove any infection from her neck (which was still very swollen from the attack) or her jowels which just kept getting bigger. The vet feared that her airway would close up and they couldn’t do surgery because she was too anemic and there wouldn’t be time for a blood transfusion. She had made it so far and all we kept hearing was her prognosis was “highly guarded”. The vet would drain the fluid off of her and it would come right back. He said he had never seen a case like Willow and didn’t know what to do. He finally sent her home and said there was no reason to keep her there since he couldn’t do surgery if she did decline and that she was best with her family. Well, Willow did great! She came home and went from 56 pounds to 77.6 pounds, she learned to use the dog door, never chewed anything up, played nicely with the other two dogs, loves everyone with her whole heart and follows her Momma everywhere. This girl spent a good majority of her life in a cage according to the Dr’s and has flat feet and a bit of a hunched back but you would never know it. She is extremely well mannered and has never once begged for people food, counter surfed or jumped on anyone. She’s perfect. All of that sounds amazing right? It is except right to this point we had spent $5032 between her vet and medvet. We thought it was over and despite being asked multiple times if we were going to do a gofundme we said no. Today is November 15th and Willow Grace is hospitalized again. Poor Willow was not vaccinated after her initial puppy shots at 6 weeks which meant she didn’t have the full series of shots to protect her from parvo. Willow was diagnosed very quickly which is good, however once again the odds are stacked against her. While she did put on weight and is 77 pounds she should be around 100 pounds based on the weight of her parents (maybe even 120). Her immunity is down because of everything she’s been through and she’s been on 2 antibiotics since 10/21. Her vet planned to start her vaccines on Friday, Nov 11th and had decided that since we didn’t know her history she would start her as if she had none. 20 min. before her appt. for shots Willow started vomiting uncontrollably so versus do shots the vet tested her for parvo. We knew she had been exposed too so that helped. She tested positive but the vet wasn’t extremely concerned. She assured us that there is a very good drug that will stop her vomiting when given by shot and then orally after that and then with her current antibiotic regimen to fight any secondary infections and meds as needed for any diarrhea she wasn’t concerned that Willow would have any complications. The shot worked immediately and Willow ate normally on Friday, Saturday and Sunday. So that $159 vet bill was nothing in comparison to ending up at medvet again. We counted our blessings a little too fast because on Sunday night right before bed Willow vomited which isn’t supposed to happen with Cerenia so we didn’t worry too much at that time. Monday morning she didn’t want to eat and Willow LOVES her food. She did take her medicine with a little bit of peanut butter and it stayed down so at lunch I made her some chicken and rice and thought surely she would eat it but after just a couple of bites she walked away from it and within 10 minutes she vomited. Not good. I called the vet and they scheduled her for Tuesday morning. Throughout the day on Monday she couldn’t even hold down water and she had taken the medicine and it stayed down so I was growing very concerned. Tuesday morning Willow and I got up early and she took her medicine at 4:30 a.m. with some help from Dad we just put it down her throat hoping it wouldn’t come back up and it didn’t. She drank water about 45 min. later and that came right back up. Once we got the vet that’s when I became very concerned. The vet advised me that she’s had one dog in 5 years vomit on Cerenia and he had a blockage. She asked if Willow could’ve ingested anything...toy, sock, stick anything. Probably not, she literally does no wrong. She plays with toys but she doesn’t chew them up. So with all of that said and I know it’s long but I feel like the entire story is necessary...Willow Grace is hospitalized again. This time she isn’t at medvet she’s at her vet Bethel Community Pet Hospital and ya’ll if you live in Clermont County and need a vet they are AMAZING, Dr. Donohue loves Willow so much and really tries to keep her costs down but still provide Willow with the best care. She did not want to hospitalize her. She struggled with the decision knowing that it meant Willow had to go in a cage and be isolated (due to parvo). She tried to think of every way possible not to keep her but also knew that the puppy that exposed Willow passed away. The puppy that exposed Willow had a lot of complications and none of us know for sure if it was only the parvo or some issues at the other vets office with the IV but at the end of the day the Cerenia didn’t stop his vomiting either. It should have and that’s a cause for serious concern for Willow. With that said the hospitalization for Willow is approximately $459 for tonight with another $200 added on for fluids tomorrow and then if she has to stay again as you can imagine that cost will continue to soar. It is what’s right for her. To put this in perspective Medvet is $1300-$1850 a night and we don’t want her to end up there by any means. We did not want to do a gofundme but we’re becoming tapped out. I don’t think Willow is in pain as her pain is constantly controlled with pain meds as needed. I don’t think we’re putting her through more than she can endure or being selfish by keeping her alive, I promise we are not to that point but if we were ever in a position we will put her first. She has a ton of life in her and was just happily running around the yard with her pack (Cali and Dozer). Please share her story even if you can’t donate. Please share the importance of vaccinations. Our other 2 dogs are fine. The puppy that passed away had 2 of the 3 parvo vaccines and was scheduled for his 3rd and contracted the virus – likely at a vet visit. Hello, my name is Conor, and recently my best friend and family member Clementine, who is only 5 years old, has been diagnosed with a terminal illness called chronic kidney disease. The search for answers and diagnosis has broken my heart and my bank account. Please read. The Timeline: Feb 18th Regular Vet - $316.43: Clementine is seen by her regular vet because she's been vomiting frequently for a couple of weeks, not just regular hairballs or scarf and barfs, but liquid. An examination and blood work is done. She is prescribed a short-term antiemetic+antibiotic. The vet emails me about the blood work and says: "Normal blood cell counts, blood chemistry panel and urinalysis. No signs of metabolic or systemic disease."* This turns out to be untrue, which was explained to me by the Doctor I see on 10/20 (8 months later!!!)*. However, she recovers well with the antiemetic, and the excess vomiting ceases. So at this point, I still suspect nothing serious. (*Side note, I want to make it clear, I'm not accusing any veterinarians of malicious intent or wilful misconduct, the problem is within the system of categories, conduct and protocols on the subject of kidney disease. The current protocols has put veterinarians just doing their job and following guidelines in the unfortunate position of ignoring blatant kidney disease (extremely common killer of cats!) and sending patients on an expensive wild goose chase that can make things worse.) Fast forward to June, I started noticing Clementine being very picky with her food, refusing to eat it all or refusing certain types outright. For her 5 years with me, she's been pretty exclusively a wet-food cat, I thought maybe she was just getting tired of eating the same old stuff, so I tried some dry food (which she's almost never been given), and she ate it up. I figure it's just a phase, and keep trying new foods, with the dry food as a backup. By 7/2 this had escalated to outright refusal of all food and water. After a full 24 hours of not eating or urinating and a night's rest with no change - I rushed her to Urgent care. 7/3: Urgent Care Animal Hospital - $681 - Diagnosed with some inflammation in the bladder, possible mild struvite crystals, given pain medication and mirtazapine. Told to keep her medicated so she'll eat only wet food and drink water to normalize her. Veterinarians suggest she might be peeing elsewhere or getting food elsewhere that I'm not aware of; I adamantly refuse the possibility of this but got the impression they thought they knew better. Reacts well to medicine but returns to refusing food after five days or so of being off. It should be noted that blood work was done yet again here, and in combination with her symptoms, pointed to kidney disease, and yet again, an entirely different set of veterinarians made no suggestion of kidney disease to me. At this point, I don't even have "kidney disease" on my radar. I'm trusting the vets, I'm not a doctor. 7/13: Regular Vet Followup- Xrays are done - $375: Finds nothing wrong. I explain that she regresses once the mirtazapine wears off after 4 or 5 days, vets again (different ones!) suggest she might be peeing or finding food elsewhere, am told to place more water bowls around the house and keep trying new foods. I'm concerned and deep inside I feel that they are getting it wrong, but can only follow their advice for now... 10/5: Texas Full GI Panel - $180 - It's now been several months, and Clem is still only acting normal if she's been given the Mirtazipene recently. Suggested to get full Texas GI panel. Panel "shows nothing wrong" and they have no further suggestions for me but to keep "following up". 10/15: After another week or so, I contacted them again, they suggested to bring her in to feel around her abdomen... I thought about it overnight and emailed them back, saying I do not think their facility can properly investigate her issues, and asked for a referral to "wherever the celebrities and richies go". Because whatever this is, it's not professional or serious care. I'm fed up and a little snarky; Thankfully, they did respond with a list of specialists. At this point, I have been doing a ton of research on my own, and something I'd pointed out to the Vets and got no response about was that the medicine seems to work a lot longer than it's advertised for. Luckily after looking into this enough on Google, I was able to get a hit on a search that explained a dying kidney will prolong the effects of medicine. And wow, a lot of these symptoms look familiar! Weird mix of emotions as I think I've figured it out myself but am now even more scared. Thankfully I found an internal medicine vet who was able to get her in quickly. 10/20 Specialist Vet - $1384: I have a long consultation with the Doctor here. He explains it is indeed chronic kidney disease, right in between stage 2 and 3. And also that the system between vets and laboratories is setup and categorized in such a way that conceals obvious cases of kidney disease from the customers. So if you do not demand a real specialist, you can be doomed to a wild goose chase, that can even result in decisions that make the disease significantly worse. He says he and many others have been asking for it to be changed because they could save more patients and get them on a corrective course much sooner. Empathizes with and listens to me a lot which I'm glad to finally experience, but the bad news that has carved out my heart every day since; it's a terminal condition. The truth is there's no way of telling how long she has left. It could be a year, it could be several years, it could be months. He thinks at least 2 years, and that some have even survived for up to 8! I'm bewildered and still in denial in the Dr office, I tell him "this cat has had almost an exclusively wet food diet for her 5 years with me, always access to fresh water, no toxic plants around, teeth brushed, I've audited my home for any toxins obsessively this last few months as well, how can this be possible?" He says while it's uncommon for a cat this young to develop this disease, regardless of conditions, it does happen as some cats are just predisposed to it, and it could also be related to the FIV she had as a kitten (although this was pretty much discarded as she has not tested positive again since being a kitten). Still, having FIV as a kitten could have damaged her kidneys. We talk about the meal plan, supplements, etc and that the next step is to get her to a specialist dentist who is qualified to work on cats with kidney disease. While every vet has said her dental health looks unremarkable (neither perfect or bad), and she has never shown an outward display of dental pain, there could be an infection a normal vet can't see. If such a problem exists, it will massively accelerate kidney failure. Told to expect a $1,000 cost minimum, and easily $2,000 or more if such a problem is found. And this brings us to today. Between July and now, I have very literally emptied my savings account and then some. Not just from the appointments, but hundreds of dollars of food that was eventually thrown out, very expensive supplements, a new water fountain, you get the picture. Over $3,000. Currently, I cannot even go forward with the dental examination plan laid out in the previous paragraph. In our hyper-consumerist decadent society, people are often skeptical of personal fundraisers. His little heart will swell back to normal with time and fluids. Antibiotics are battling the infection and anti inflammatories have brought his temperature down to normal. We were so so happy to hear that he started eating again once his fever subsided! Last night when we picked him up his appetite was shockingly non-existent and we thought he might have just given up. He has decidedly perked up in the past 24 hours and we are very hopeful! This boy is so so sweet despite being treated so horribly. He is just a big bucket of love. All of the staff at the vets office are already attached to him and they commented on how sweet he was despite feeling so awful. Hes not out of the woods yet but he is trying and has made good progress in the past 24 hours. We have total faith one day he will be a nice healthy weight and will be able to run and play on the farm just like our girl Molly does. The two of them are getting along fabulously and shared a bed last night <3 If you feel moved to do so, please help us help this sweet boy get all better. We definitely had no plans on getting a second dog when we woke up yesterday morning, let alone one that would need so much medical care, but what can you do? Hi, my name is Rachel Harrell, and I am writing this on behalf of my family, asking for any support to help ease the recent burden placed on them. On the afternoon of October 16th, my mother rushed our Boston Terrier Gus an hour and a half drive away to a specialty vet Greenville for a perforated small intestine. He was taken into surgery that evening. Stomach bile had leaked into Gus’s abdominal cavity, and while there was no object found that could have done it, the hole was the size of a pinky. He needed surgery immediately to remove the section of the intestine and clean his abdomen. Of course, my mother did it without question. Anyone who has had a pet, whether during childhood or adulthood, knows the solace these family members provide. They are there for us through thick and thin. Stand beside us without judgement. Remind us to live presently and savour every moment we get to live as if it may be our last. All was fine after the first surgery. Despite the 50/50 chance and his low blood pressure, Gus pulled through and was recovering smoothly in the days following. My mother and sister drove the hour and a half see him on Tuesday and FaceTimed me so I could say hello to him while he scowled at the camera lens with his one eye—a glare we call his Eleven stare (shoutout to Stranger Things). It was hard to see him like that, all bandaged up, sporting two pink wraps around his paws and a bind around his Tootsie Roll frame. But at least he was okay, or so we thought. While the vets were doing their morning check-ins on October 20th, they found that Gus was not doing well and that the surgery site was leaking, the contents of his small intestine were leaking into his abdomen again. The only option was another surgery. He is currently in surgery again to repair the leakage. Although it has hardly been a week, the bill has soared. While the cost did not keep her from choosing to help Gus, this debt is an overwhelming burden that has been placed on my mother because she is maxing out credit cards to pay the vet bill. There hasn't been a moment in my life when my mother wasn't working around the clock, 9 to 5, nearly seven days every week, to be able to provide for my sister and I. We are hoping to raise enough so we can get her the surgery right away. Saving will take some time. The surgery is called a tie-back. This involves tying the collapsed cartilage to the side of the larynx to prevent it from creating an obstruction to breathing. My husband and I would also like to let those who share and or donate, that if her total due is less than what is raised, the remaining balance will be donated to another at the clinic who may need help with their fur baby. Hey ya'll, my name is Hannah, & I don't know how to do this, so bear with me here. I'm fundraising to save Shamrock, my friend Haylee's horse. Shamrock, or Sham as most of us call him, is a 5-year-old Quarter Horse and the sweetest horse you will ever meet. Haylee has raised him since he was weaned. She has poured every ounce of her heart and soul into training him & making him the fantastic horse he is today. In return, Sham has brought her solace & joy through some of the darkest times of her life, many of those being in the last year. She has faced so much adversity, it's a wonder she's still standing, & Sham has been there every step of the way. Then, a couple of months ago, Sham started to drop on his topline, & it seemed overnight he lost all of the muscle on his back end. Haylee tried everything she knew to bring it back, but nothing worked. He started to stumble at random when he walked. She had a gut feeling about what was wrong with Sham but couldn't get an equine vet out to see him until last month. This is what he looks like now: They drew some blood to run the tests Haylee asked for to get confirmation of her suspicions, but deep down, we all thought, "it can't be". Wishful thinking, I suppose. Fast forward to yesterday, November 7th, Haylee & I are limping down the road in her truck, pulling 2 of her clients' horses in the trailer, & she finally gets the return call from the vet about Sham's test results. She was correct; Sham has EPM. EPM (or Equine Protozoal Myeloencephalitis) is, in short, a neurological disease. More than 50% of all horses in the U.S. may have been exposed to the organism that causes EPM. This organism is a parasite called Sarcocystis neurona. The disease is not transmitted from horse to horse but is actually spread from multiple animals through the Opossum, or more specifically, their feces, which can contaminate hay & grass, etc. Once ingested, the sporocysts migrate from the intestinal tract into the bloodstream & cross the blood/brain barrier. There they begin to attack the horse's central nervous system. Onset may be slow or sudden. If left undiagnosed & untreated, EPM can cause devastating and lasting neurological damage. Symptoms range from abnormal sweating to seizures & paralysis of the muscles of the eyes, face or mouth. Thankfully, EPM is treatable. The sooner treatment begins, the better the horse's chances are for recovery. 60-70% of EPM cases aggressively treated show significant or complete reversal of symptoms. ( Source: <URL> ) After having had several conversations over the last 36 hours with people with horses with EPM, it sounds as if the younger the horse, the better the results. So why am I telling you all this, and what am I asking for? Treatment for Sham will be expensive. For two rounds of treatment & all of the supplements needed in addition & maintenance medications for about six months after initial treatment, it will cost roughly $2500.00. Haylee is self-employed, running a boarding facility for 15 horses in addition to her own, & the price of hay & feed has skyrocketed this year. She teaches riding, roping & barrel racing lessons to support herself. Let me put it this way; Haylee is the hardest-working woman I have ever come across in my entire life. She gives and gives and gives of herself until there's nothing left. She has done more for me in the past year than I can explain, and she probably doesn't even know it. That's just who Haylee is. Bottom line, she cannot afford his treatment. Because she cannot afford treatment, Haylee has two choices here, but if you asked her, she would say she doesn't have a choice. She could let him live his life & get progressively worse until he one day passes away. Or, she could put him down out of mercy, and for Haylee, that's a no-brainer. But because of who she is, what she does for all of us at the barn, the life she has led and the insurmountable troubles she has faced, I cannot sit back and watch her lose him. Haylee's unending courage, perseverance and flat-out FIGHT is rare in this current day and age. Sham is the one thing that has been hers from the start, the one thing that brings her peace and solace. Sham makes all of it worth it, and I cannot let her lose him. So I'm asking you to please help. Please show my friend that there is kindness in this world and that what she has with Sham matters. Any blessing you can give will be beyond appreciated. If I could pay it all, I would; Sham is worth it. Please help us save Sham.

Meet Mr. Mittens. If you have not followed his story since July, 2022 let me provide a quick overview of his situation. Mr. Mittens was taken off the streets of Hamilton, Ontario where he had lived for the first 9 years of his life. His rescuer is a very caring and experienced animal rescuer who brought him back to St. Catharines. She didn't realize, though, that Mr. Mittens was coming with some very serious medical issues - issues that remained hidden while he was living on the streets but became quickly evident once he was given an indoor foster home. Issues that were far greater than her capacity to fix. Mr. Mittens' medical GoFundMe can be seen here: <URL> So, even though it was hoped that Mr. Mittens could be suitably vetted and quickly put up for adoption it became abundantly clear, after numerous vetting appointments and testing, that he was FIV+ and suffers from chronic incontinence with no guaranteed or easy fix. Both of these medical issues left him, on the one hand, not suitable to be adopted out as a barn cat because of the FIV+ status, and on the other hand, not suitable to be adopted out as an indoor-only cat required by the FIV+ status because of the incontinence. Many efforts were made by both Mr. Mittens' rescuer and Pets Niagara to find him a suitable home somewhere - anywhere! All interested candidates, one-by-one, turned Mr. Mittens down feeling unable to cope with his two major medical issues. Pets Niagara has a sanctuary for pets just like Mr. Mittens. I have 10 years experience dealing with FIV+ cats and know what it takes to keep them healthy. I have even more experience dealing with incontinence in pets and know, also, what it takes to keep the environment clean. On both counts, it's a lot of work. But, we have offered to take Mr. Mittens on as one of our life-long sanctuary residents. In order to do so, we need to build Mr. Mittens his own special little home, here. Unfortunately, Mr. Mittens only alternative would be a very sad end for this sociable, lively and precious little soul. He loves everyone he meets! Purchasing an existing structure and renovating it to suit our needs would be the most cost effective option for Pets Niagara. However, we would still need to find the manpower needed to go to the site, disassemble the structure and transport it back to St. Catharines. We continue to pursue this solution. In the meantime, though, time is of the essence and Mr. Mittens' time in his new foster home is limited. So, we need to also go forward with the plan of building him a little home, now. Our building by-laws permit residents in this City to build outside structures of 100 square feet or less without the need of a building permit or code inspections. UPDATE: Today, November 30, 2022, is the one year anniversary of the groundbreaking for our new shelter facility. Wow how time flies. The Warwick Valley Humane Society is a Not-for-Profit 501c3 NO KILL shelter serving the New York Towns of Warwick, Chester and Tuxedo, with emergency assistant services to adjacent towns. Our organization has managed the animal shelter since it was built in 1968. After 54 years, we were in desperate need of an updated facility. Construction of our new shelter during the COVID pandemic has been challenging but we are nearing completion. Rising costs and delays have fully exhausted the $1.7m in funds and grants we have raised. Unexpected issues, common with every project, have eaten the cushion we had for such expenses. We are desperate to raise the final $350,000 to get us to building completion. We have been and continue incurring rental costs of $4300/month for 2 sites: 1 for the cats, rabbits, ferrets and 1 for the dogs. Our staff has been traveling between the 2 sites multiple times a day for the past year. Our move in was scheduled for December but we are now unable to move into the new facility until sometime after the New Year which will extend our rental costs. Final payment for the construction will be due upon completion, and we have exhausted our donations, loans and grants. We are in dire need of your help to continue our contractual obligations in order to complete this building process! The new building offers our homeless pets a safe, spacious, and healthy environment with mandated ventilation, isolation rooms and an inviting atmosphere to encourage adoptions. We have added 9 new kennels, 7 free roaming cat rooms and are now able to keep our small pets in the same building (previously housed in outlying buildings). Additionally, we have 14 rooms available for adoption at $20,000 which will feature a plaque honoring the adopter. As we approach what by all accounts may be a snowy winter, we are truly desperate for your help so we can continue to meet our building expenses and give all our animals a warm comfortable environment for years to come. ANGELS AMONG US ... Please grab a tissue... Early last week, someone in the community posted that they were moving this week and offered to give away some furniture that needed to be picked up. One of our neighbors knew someone in need, so she went there to help move any furniture they could use. But, what she encountered were two 14-year-old pugs in pretty bad shape, pugs who were possibly going to be left behind—she didn’t know. They were dirty and lying in urine. Toenails were so long they curled under and some punctured and grew into the toe pads. The little girl (pictured right) couldn't use her back legs and her feet dragged backwards behind her when she struggled to move around. The little boy (pictured left) has a large growth on his underside (now determined a skin tag), some small growths on his face, what appears to be an ulceration in his eye, and he is about 12-13 pounds overweight. Kimberly D. is our neighbor whose heart poured into this situation, and she knew she had to get them out of there. She reached out to me because of our rescue efforts and she has fostered for us before. Kimberly spoke with the dogs' owner and visited a number of times during week begging to let her help. The dogs were miserable and didn't deserve to be in such awful conditions. Their mama was so torn over the situation... she felt horrible and she loves her dogs very much, but had become overwhelmed. Before we judge the dogs' owner, please understand she has gone through some very challenging times and life fell apart. The dogs didn't get the care they needed the last couple years but she loves them dearly. With the compassion extended by Kimberly, the woman agreed to let Kimberly help, and even keep the dogs, or euthanize if needed -- but she wanted the opinion of a veterinarian before she would agree to euthanasia. Kimberly picked up the dogs Thursday and their owner cried with sorrow and with appreciation. She didn't understand why Kimberly was pushing so hard to help ... but we know why ... it's because God sent her. The dogs needed her, and their mama needed her. AJ and Ellie both got baths on Thursday, so they smelled fresh and clean, and they likely felt a sense of confusion, yet comfort in the plush soft and clean beds where they rested at Kimberly's home. During the night hours, AJ presented a significant cough, seeming problematic so Kimberly rushed him to the vet. Emergency exam and diagnostics were $905. It was determined his cough is likely a collapsed trachea, for which not much can be done. A full blood panel was done and all his values look pretty darn good, especially for an overweight 14-year-old dog. Ellie had been scheduled for a vet appointment Friday. Upon exam and some initial testing, it was determined she could (should) be euthanized, or $2000-3000 could be spent on testing and diagnostics, but nothing really could be done to help her at her very senior age. Kimberly took the dogs to the park yesterday and they were so excited to be there ... but then Ellie tried to run and she just couldn't. She was frustrated and mad... so Kimberly swept her up and got her home to rest in comfort. The vet, who agreed euthanasia would be best for Ellie, required owner permission to put Ellie to sleep; so with a phone call, the owner agreed to come. She was able to be with Ellie as Ellie was sent to peaceful slumber, as Kimberly stood near with her heart breaking. Their mama was so heartbroken but was able to come to peace with letting Ellie go. I never even met the dogs, and my heart is breaking... my tears are falling. Kimberly has been crying all day :( Before Ellie crossed the Rainbow Bridge, she had a most pampered and loving day at Kimberly's home, knowing she was loved and that someone cared for this sweet baby's life. For AJ, he's staying at Kimberly's house for now. Kimberly is actually one of our fosters and had to get some weight off of a foster dog this past summer (she ended up adopting 10-year-old Gigi). So, she's a pro at home-cooking and calorie counting for dogs now! Kimberly plans on doing some healthy, low-fat cooking for AJ so he can lose some weight and feel the best he can. In the meantime, we would like to know if anyone would like to give AJ an amazing home for whatever time he has left. He's very loving and just needs some special attention ... he's now lost his mama, and he's lost his life-long fur-gal, Ellie. Please let me know if you have a soft spot for senior dogs and would like to take him under wing. Also, I would like to generate a little community fundraiser to help with reimbursing Kimberly for the $2065 she spent helping these two dogs, which includes a visit for AJ on 10/31 to test his eyes, get him vaccinated, and get him some further testing. The doctor said surprisingly, this guy is in pretty good shape and will have some happy times ahead. If you would like to contribute towards Ellie & AJ's vet bills, it would be so appreciated. You may contribute via venmo ( @sherry-petta-1 ) or here on gofundme. I’m including images of the three invoices – Kimberly has already paid them, but we’re hoping with a community effort, this doesn’t all lie on her shoulders. Very often, rescue is happy ... bubbly dogs who get to start out a new and amazing life. Also very often, we encounter situations like this where you simply need to help, even if the dog doesn’t have a lot of time left ... they deserve to have it be the best it can be. ❤ My HUGE thank-you goes out to Kimberly who went above and beyond for these beautiful senior babies, and to all of you who so often lend a helping hand to the rescue with unexpected vet bills. Thank you all. ❤

Since we became our own rescue in March 2020, it has been one of the most rewarding experiences for everyone involved with the Feline Café Foundation. In over two years, we have saved more than a hundred felines and found them their forever homes. But being a cat rescue is not all sunshine and rainbows. For every success story, there are challenges. This work is hard. It can be draining, overwhelming, and heartbreaking, and we have to continuously face the fact that: We cannot save everyone. For instance, we were recently contacted about taking on a young feline in need of urgent medical care. She had suffered complications from pregnancy, resulting in mummified kittens in her uterus, and her surgery was estimated to be $3000+. We had to turn her away as we simply do not have the funds to support her. This was the third feline we were contacted about in the past month who needed immediate medical intervention to survive. We were able to help the first two, but we cannot continue paying for these high-cost surgeries. Meanwhile, our waitlist keeps growing for our intake applications. So many felines need our help, but without the resources available, we continuously have to close our intakes and pray that another rescue can save them. We currently have several cats with special needs in our care, including Bilbo, Loki, and Kobe who are FIV+, and Cleo and Leo, who have FIC. These felines are a strain on our finances and will be harder to adopt. This is a heartbreaking truth, as cats with medical issues are statistically more challenging to find homes for due to the worry of medical costs, which make potential adopters wary. But they deserve a chance just like all our other felines, and we couldn’t just give up on them. Even our cats without special needs can have unexpected medical issues. Foster kitty Potato and Lounge favourite Merlot experienced unforeseen complications with their sterilization surgery, resulting in higher medical bills. Our community has always been there for us through thick and thin. We will never be able to put into words our love and gratitude for you all. You and the folks of this wonderful city answered our plea for help in June 2021 when we did not know what the future held for FCF. We understand that times are tough, but we cannot hide the fact that right now, we need help. While we run many fundraisers year-round, such as our Sponsorship and Monthly Donor programs, they simply do not provide sufficient resources to cover these high-cost expenses. Right now, our vet bills are reaching upwards of $15,000. We are creating this GoFundMe with the hopes of raising the money needed to cover these costs, so we can reopen our intakes and save more felines in our community. Every single donation, regardless of size, brings us closer to this goal. If you are able to make a donation or share this fundraiser with friends and family, we would be incredibly grateful. The support of our community carries us through these difficult times, and we would not be able to do this work without you. For more information, visit <URL> With an immeasurable amount of love and gratitude, Feline Café Foundation Note: We are a registered Not-For-Profit Foundation and can issue donation receipts. Arlo is a 6 year old dachshund. Over the past 3 weeks he has become very painful and is beginning to lose use of his back legs. It started with a little tenderness and guarding of his back and is now progressed to a stiff and rigged posture, dragging of his back feet/unstable stepping and sharp pain with any movement. We have been working with our vet doing daily laser therapy, strict rest and a cocktail of pain relievers, muscle relaxer and CBD. He has been restricted to his crate or stroller if not being held or pottying. Despite these efforts he is still not progressing and is in fact seeming to slowly loose more feeling in his toes. At this point we have exhausted our current resources as well as our Veterinarians. It is suspected that Arlo has IVDD which is not an uncommon disease in dachshunds. It is a debilitating disc condition that can turn into an emergency at the drop of a hat. He is scheduled next week at Blue Pearl in Louisville for their next available appointment to determine what we pretty much already know. He is most likely going to require back surgery to stop the progression and get him moving forward again. What we are being told is he will have an initial consultation with an orthopedic surgeon then immediately scheduled for his CT scan and surgery same day. If any of you have had dogs go through this procedure you are aware it’s very expensive! The quotes vary but we have been given a ball park figure which does not include his hospitalization, medications and general office visits. CT scan and surgery alone could be upwards of $8,000. He will be required to stay hospitalized at blue pearl for about 5 days and will be on a slew of medications as well as therapies and aftercare to ensure he heals to his full potential. We will also be getting a hotel room near the hospital for the duration of his stay (bc we can’t bring ourselves to leave him hours from home). We are going to make it happen one way or another for his sake but any help is greatly appreciated. With my partner being our only source of income at the moment until our baby is born in a couple months, anything will help! Hi, my name is Scott Garrison and I am fundraising for my puppy Atlas. Atlas is a four month old black Labrador mix and was diagnosed with parvovirus on Thursday. Parvovirus is a disease that rapidly attacks the gastrointestinal track of a dog and is very fatal in puppies. Most puppies die within the first 24-72 hours of the disease and without treatment, the fatality rate exceeds 90 percent. With hospital treatment, however, the survival rate is around 90 percent. The first day he was diagnosed, I decided to do outpatient care as his case wasn’t terrible and I was advised it was a valid option for him. He had only been showing symptoms for about a day so we had caught it early on. I took a few days off from work as I was told his case was going to get worse over the next couple days as the disease progressed and he needed to be monitored and cared for. Atlas was very stubborn when it came to taking his medicine and would hold it or gag till he almost vomited so I was only able to successfully get him to take a couple of his medications. I was also told to entice him to eat in any way possible but he just refused anything I tried to give him, treats included. The next morning he was starting to show that he was doing worse and so I decided I was going to bring him back and admit him to the hospital for inpatient care since I couldn’t get him to eat or take medicine. I was called later that night and informed that he wasn’t doing well and would most likely pass before I could make it to the hospital. His blood glucose levels had dropped to an unreadable level and he had become unresponsive. As a result, I rushed there and sat with him and was preparing for the worst. He did, however, try moving around and lifted his head upon seeing me. I was advised that euthanizing him wouldn’t be the wrong choice but neither would holding out till the morning. I decided to wait till the morning to say I at least gave it everything I could and they started putting him on an almost purely sugar solution in hopes of raising his sugar levels. Atlas did stabilize and his sugar levels reached a normal level yesterday. They started weening him off of the sugar solution and his levels stayed up. He even got up and moved around a few times throughout the day, wagging his tail and being a bit more active. With the highs also came some lows and so it’s been an up and down but he is fighting very hard for his life. Today the initial deposit ran out and so he was stopped his treatment. I was told that because of all the help he was being given currently, he wouldn’t be able to survive at home most likely and so I was again faced with the decision of euthanizing or putting another deposit down for 48 more hours. The bills have been piling up because it is such intensive care. I have exhausted my personal funds, opened up new lines of credit such as a CareCredit card, and borrowed money from family to pay for this. I don’t like asking for money, but in this case I don’t have much of a choice. Any donations are greatly appreciated or even just sharing would help immensely. Thank you all very much. Atlas is one of the best dogs I have ever met. He is so loving and playful and has such an amazing temperament that he deserves to have a chance at life. He has become my best friend so quickly and I can’t imagine not having him with me. Even these past couple days have been such an adjustment and I find myself just calling to him or doing things out of habit. As long as Atlas isn’t giving up, neither am I.

As many pet parents, we fear the possible day our beloved pet has a life-threatening illness. During hurricane Ian, I was faced with the worst situation unfolding right before my eyes. While for 4 days, we could not leave the house, I watched my best furry friend slowly become lethargic, unable to drink water, eat food, pee or poop. I originally thought it was stress from the storm, but later learned it was a colonic torsion causing him so much pain that he could not keep down food or water. This life-threatening condition is very rare and is usually only seen in large dogs. My dog Atticus has been by my side for almost 6.5 years and has been the root to my tree of sanity and happiest. He is truly an angel on this earth! And anyone who has met him loves him so much because he is the bestest boy. After the hurricane passed us, I found an emergency clinic nearby, but they had an 8-hour wait for animals that did not show life or death symptoms. His condition was internal, but all the same life-threatening and the clock was ticking. I took him immediately to another ER 30 minutes away and they started doing a bunch of tests. They said he looked healthy but dehydrated. So they sent him home after some fluids with antinausea pills. They said if he throws up even one more time, you have to bring him back because it is more serious than expected. Well, within 8 hours he threw up yellow foam and I rushed him back. Within the hour they brought me a quote for $6300 to do emergency surgery on him to correct the colon twist that is keeping a softball size of fetal matter and gas trapped in his colon. Supposedly very rare, but if left untreated can cause the tissue to die off and start decaying, causing sepsis. A very painful horrific death for a dog who has given me everything. I maxed out every credit card and borrowed money from my grandmother to save his life. Not even 7 years old and I'm about to lose him. What hurts more is that they knew what his condition was on the first set of X-rays and they knew how dire his situation was. After I paid $1600 for his first visit to the ER, I felt like they didn't want to deal with a difficult surgery and that is why they sent him home and didn't tell me. Well, little do they know, I would do anything for this incredible dog who has been the most incredible family member to me. If anyone can help with his medical bill costs, we would appreciate any amount so so much. Even $5 towards his now sensitive stomach food. Or if the best support offered is to share this post. I would thank you to the ends of the earth. I wish everyone could meet Atticus and see what a special dog he is, We used to visit nursing homes prior to covid because everyone loves how gentle and loving he is. Thank you so much from my small furry family here to yours.
