Little Luna, a five month old, was born outside as part of a large unmanaged colony. She and her siblings were rescued and the colony was TNRd. Luna adjusted well to indoor life and went from a scared feral kitten, to a shy, but friendly and affectionate girl. She remained best buddies with her brother and both were placed in a foster to adopt home. Not long after arriving to their new home, Luna was diagnosed with wet FIP. FIP is a viral disease caused by certain strains of the Feline coronavirus. Most strains of feline coronavirus are found in the GI tract. They do not cause major illness and most cats’ immune systems will naturally produce antibodies against the virus. In 10% of infected cats, however, mutations of the virus result in white blood cells being infected with the virus, which then spread to the entire body. The body mounts an intense inflammatory reaction to the infected cells. This interaction between the immune system and the virus is responsible for the development of FIP. Once a cat develops clinical FIP, the disease is progressive and most often fatal, if not treated (Cornell Feline Health Center). Luna’s symptoms began with a lack of weight gain, conjunctivitis, and increased lethargy, which progressed into a fever, a thick, yellow fluid filling her abdomen, head tremors, and a weakness in her hind legs. Treatment for FIP consists of injections of an antiviral drug known as GS. GS has been incredibly successfully in treating FIP, but unfortunately, it has not yet been approved by the FDA. Until that happens, the drug must be purchased on the black market at a high price. Treatment is daily for 84 days, followed by an 84 day observation period to ensure no reoccurrence of symptoms. Bloodwork is recommended every 4 weeks during this 168 day period in order to assess progress. Needless to say, this will all add up. Right now, Luna’s injections cost about $10 per day, so meds alone will cost $840. The cost of bloodwork 6 times during the course of treatment will also be costly. We are hopeful that Luna will respond positively to treatment and there will not be a need to extend the injections beyond the initial 84 day period. While the total treatment costs are great, $10 a day is manageable in order to provide this life saving treatment to Luna, but we need your help. Luna had a difficult start to her life, and she did not come this far on her journey for us to give up on her. We are determined to cure her of this horrible disease and reunite her with her brother and adoptive mom. Please consider a donation to help save Luna’s life. A donation of just $10 will sponsor one of her daily injections. To learn more about FIP, please visit <URL> or <URL>

Hello! My name is Liz, I’ve always had a passion for rescuing animals and have rescued numerous animals over the years. This October I rescued Betty. It had been just over a month since I lost my Barley (I had rescued him 14 years prior) and I was heart broken. Betty quite literally found me at a park. She was in rough shape, covered in burs and mud. It turns out, she needed me as much as I needed her. Easily enough I was able to get Betty cleaned up, get her onto a healthy diet and transitioned into living the life of a pampered house dog. But, the day I got her, I had concerns for her left hip. I knew something was wrong, I had no idea how bad it truly was. I was able to get Betty into the vet for a check up and X-rays. Immediately upon viewing the images, we knew it was serious. It was so bad, my vet didn’t feel comfortable making any recommendations and referred me to an orthopedic surgeon. It turns out Betty suffered a significant trauma (likely being hit by a car or a bad fall while running stray) at least a year before she found me. This trauma resulted in a physeal fracture of her proximal femur and non-union of the hip. No medical treatment or intervention ever happened and the injury worsened, resulting in further destruction of the bone fragments and the joint. Betty will need a Femoral Head Ostectomy (FHO) surgery. This surgery will take out all the broken pieces and allow Betty to live without pain. This surgery is estimated to cost $3500-$4000. She will also need physical therapy to help her learn how to use her body correctly after the surgery. I’ve never asked for financial help for any of my rescues over the years, but it was suggested to me that we all should ask for help sometimes. This has been a year of vet bills already for my furry family, so this big expense will certainly make things challenging. Regardless of any help offered, Betty will her surgery and any further medical care she needs. Thank you to everyone willing to help Betty.

We first met Blu when he was eight weeks old and instantly fell for his big eyes, sweet soul, and oversized paws he had yet to grow into. That might have been around the time you met him, too. Maybe you first saw his face smiling out the truck window on his daily drives around the Snoqualmie Valley or followed his adventures on Instagram (@bluinthepnw) For others, you might just be tuning into Blu's story and asking - What happened to Blu? How can a dog recover from kidney failure? Standing 3 feet tall and 80 pounds at best - Blu lives to tell the story. Blu is a lover and a fighter when he needs to be. Our 2-year-old Border Collie Chow mix started feeling ill in October of 2022 after a weekend trip to the Oregon Coast. We learned Blu was exposed to a bacteria attacking his kidneys - A rare but lethal zootopic disease called Leptospirosis (Weills Disease). While the origin of exposure is unknown, we suspect Blu came in contact with contaminated soil, water, or species while traveling. According to the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife, an outbreak was first recorded on October 28th, 2022, affecting Sea Lions in California and Oregon. Blu was first brought into his primary vet on October 5th, admitted with concerns of low appetite, energy, and 'depression-like' symptoms. He was quickly cleared to go home with antinausea and pain medication noting no remarkable findings. After slow improvement - we decided to keep pushing for answers. Blu continued to lose 6 pounds before our follow-up appointment on October 29th for bloodwork. We proactively started antibiotics, appetite stimulants, and anti-nausea medicine while we waited for the test results. On October 31st, we received results indicating Blu was in kidney failure. Our vet transferred us to Seattle, where Blu was placed in the ICU. The following test results ruled out chronic conditions such as cancer, which brought us closer to our positive Leptospirosis diagnosis. After Blu tested positive, he was isolated in a quarantined unit. At 10PM his first night in quarantine, I received a call that Blu's IV bag had punctured and was administering unsterile fluids, and they noticed fluid was building around his kidney and lungs. I followed their recommendations to switch antibiotics to prevent sepsis, but Blu's condition worsened as the days went by. After we surpassed the initial $5,000 deposit, I asked "are we doing everything we can?" The technician said "No, but we aren't equipped for alternative treatment if he isn't responding to traditional therapies." Here came the Google searches. "Homeopathic foods for azotemia an kidney failure" "Can dogs have kidney transplants" "What is dialysis" Due to the positive bacterial infection, Blu became a candidate for dialysis to treat his acute kidney injury and allow time for his organs to heal. I made several phone calls before I found one doctor in Washington State that was certified to perform dialysis on dogs. But... We needed board approval, payment upfront, and the doctor to return home from his vacation. Blu was transferred to Blue Pearl on November 3rd where he received a feeding tube, and two dialysis sessions. On November 8th, we decided to continue supportive care at home on an outpaitent basis. Supportive care has consisted of water and low-protein smoothies administered through his feeding tube every 4-6 hours and medicine every 12. We began daily vet visits to check his blood levels every morning, staying roughly 3 hours for results to tell if we needed to drop him off for another dialysis day. Blu has improved and is eating on his own. On November 14th, Blu's kidney function began normalizing, and his dialysis catheter was removed. Unfortunately, Blu does not have pet insurance, so he depends on us for 100% of his treatment. While we are grateful to have made the payments thus far, this has caused a significant financial burden on CJ and I. Blu has an estimated 4 weeks of outpatient treatment remaining, where his feeding tube has yet to be removed, and he will continue on medication. Once his kidneys fully heal, Blu will require a prescribed renal diet indefinitely. As of November 17th, Cj and I have spent over $28,000 to receive the treatment necessary to save Blu's life. We anticipate an additional $5,000 to complete his outpatient treatment and around $400/m for his prescribed renal diet. We hope to raise $20,000 to cover outstanding balances and provide Blu with the necessary support he deserves to live a long, healthy life. No amount is too small, and no share goes unnoticed. Thank you for helping spread awareness about leptospirosis and your efforts to support Blu's recovery from acute kidney failure. Thank you to the veterinary specialists who worked day and night to diagnose and save Blu's life. What is Blu's prognosis? Statistically, 60% of dogs and cats with acute renal failure disease either die or are humanely euthanized because of failure to respond to supportive care. Dialysis is usually reserved for those patients in whom medical treatment has failed, and the chance of death without dialysis is almost 100%. In those patients, 50% may recover with dialysis, depending on the underlying cause of kidney failure. While we won't know Blu's complete prognosis until his body fully heals, our veterinary team expects Blu to have an 80% likelihood of fully recovering without premature chronic kidney disease. We will share updates on Blu's condition as he continues to recover. What is Hemodialysis? Hemodialysis involves putting a large IV catheter in a vein and using the catheter to remove a quantity of blood, which is then sent through a machine that cleans the blood. Hemodialysis is effective, but only a handful of veterinary hospitals are equipped to do hemodialys is. Both peritoneal dialysis and hemodialysis are very expensive treatment options. What is Weills Disease? Leptospirosis (Weills Disease) occurs worldwide, but is most common in temperate or tropical climates. There is always a risk of infection for people who have contact with infected animals or soil and water where the bacteria are present. How rare is Leptospirosis? According to the Washington State Department of Health, between zero to five cases of leptospirosis infections are reported each year. Most infections are due to recreational water exposure in Washington or during travel. What are the signs of leptospirosis in dogs? The clinical signs of leptospirosis vary; some animals may show no symptoms. Common clinical signs in dogs include fever, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, refusal to eat, severe weakness and depression, stiffness, severe muscle pain leading to anorexia, and kidney and liver dysfunction. If untreated, Weil's disease can cause kidney, liver, or heart failure. How much does hemodialysis cost? Please note this is not a comprehensive list of all costs associated with Blu's recovery. Could this have been prevented? Yes, in some instances, leptospirosis can be prevented. Blu is up-to-date on his required and recommended immunizations. According to the Center for Disease Control , a vaccine exists but does not provide 100% protection. This is because there are many strains (types) of leptospires (the bacteria that causes Leptospirosis), and the vaccine does not provide immunity against all strains. Your primary vet may suggest additional vaccinations based on your location, lifestyle, and other risk factors. Some veterinarians may warn that the vaccine can have adverse reactions and be linked to premature kidney disease. Currently, the Leptospirosis vaccine is not a legally required immunization in Washington State. Leptospirosis is not a required or core vaccine in many US states. Please consult your primary veterinarian while considering adding the Leptospirosis vaccine as part of your annual shots.

Hi. We are Kristie & Joe, Labowki's Mama and Papa. We received some unexpected and devasting news about our lovable meatball, Labowski. He has Laryngeal Paralysis. Laryngeal paralysis is when the arytenoid cartilage on one or both sides of the larynx cannot open and close properly. With laryngeal paralysis, the cartilage cannot be fully closed and open over the tracheal opening. This part of the throat prevents food and liquid from entering the trachea and airways, leading to significant breathing problems. At this moment, Labowski is having difficulty breathing. We are scared it will get to the point it will get too bad and he'll suffocate if we don’t get him the surgery he needs. The surgery is called Tie Back surgery, which is very delicate and very expensive. But we must do it because he has many more years to live. Can you imagine how heartbreaking it would be to watch your dog suffocate to death in your presence when you know he could have been saved? Some have said, “Put him down; it’s not worth it” I say to them, “Have you no soul”? NO! Labowksi has so much love to give, joy and happiness to expel, and so much life left in him; it’s just not fair that he’s dealt these cards. And if any of you are animal lovers or have pets that are your family, you would do the same thing. Labowki is on about six different medicines daily to deal with this condition. Most of the time, he lays around and sleeps, which is good because he’s not allowed to do anything that would trigger heavy breathing, panting, or getting excited. He’s not allowed to go for walks, play, bark, jump, or have any fun. What kind of life is that for a dog? Labowski’s has had some rough patches in his life. When he was a puppy, someone threw him out of a car window (he hates cars even to this day). He had Lyme disease when I adopted him. He’s eaten a TIN of Altoids, tin and all. He’s eaten two pkgs of Orbit gum (never affected him); he ate a rubber cleaning glove at doggie daycare (found it in the yard 2 days later). And he was diagnosed with Cushing’s two years ago. This dog has been through hell and back but still comes out strong and happy. Please help us help Labowski breathe! Please help us get this life-saving surgery for him soon. We don’t want to wait any longer than we must because we know he’s having difficulty breathing, and I can see the worry and anxiety in his eyes with each breath he tries to take. I know he’s pleading me for help, breaking me. I'm even working two jobs, but I can’t save the money fast enough for this surgery. Please help if you can. We will be documenting his journey pre-surgery, through surgery, and post-surgery. After he’s healed and we are out of danger, we’d like to keep raising money in Labowski’s name to donate to another pet family going through the same thing. This will raise awareness about LP and give raised funds to other families so they can get their fur babes the surgery needed. This surgery is so expensive that no parent should have to watch their dog suffer just to take a breath.

It has always been my passion to work with wildlife. Since graduating in 2017 from the University of Vermont with a Bachelor of Science in Wildlife & Fisheries Biology, I have had the opportunity to live and work in 8 states as a wildlife technician on different projects. I learned early on in my career that I wanted to work with lesser-known species of conservation concern. It was with great excitement that I started graduate school at Antioch University New England in 2020, pursuing a Master of Science in Environmental Studies with a Conservation Biology concentration. While pursuing my degree, I began my thesis study on a bird in my home state of Massachusetts, the Brown Thrasher! While not as well studied as other birds in the region, the Brown Thrasher is just as important! My study aims to determine if the Brown Thrasher has a preferred habitat in Massachusetts. I have had great success researching this bird the past two summers! Once completed, my thesis will be published through Antioch University New England and sent to Massachusetts Fish & Wildlife to help implement conservation and management practices for the Brown Thrasher. The summer of 2023 will be my final field season studying the Brown Thrasher before I begin my data analysis. The data collection takes place in shrubland adjacent to different habitats (farmland, pine barren forests, and deciduous forests) and the shrubby edges of farmland. During early spring, I conduct point counts from sunrise to 9 am and record all birds I see and hear. While the emphasis is on the Brown Thrasher, it is important to document all birds detected in these areas for further analysis. Later in the summer, I return to each field site to collect vegetation data for habitat analysis; this consists of but is not limited to measuring vegetation height, identifying plant species, and measuring downed woody debris. I have applied to a few small grants, but funding has been limited! This summer, my field sites are in Western Massachusetts. I am looking for funding for housing ($700), partial tuition payment for thesis credits during the summer ($1,300), and gas reimbursement ($500). Any additional funding would go towards the remaining tuition costs for my final year in grad school! Please see below for more information regarding the Brown Thrasher. Thank you so much! Alec Woolf In the Northeastern United States, birds residing in shrubland and early-successional habitats are a guild that is declining due to habitat loss in the region (King and Schlossberg 2014). Since 1950, New England has lost 66 percent of its shrubland habitat (King and Schlossberg 2014). Currently, powerline corridors provide roughly 10 percent of shrubland habitat for species in Massachusetts (King et al. 2014). One shrubland avian species that is declining in the northeast is the Brown Thrasher (Toxostoma rufum). The Brown Thrasher can be found from the Northeastern United States to just east of the Rocky Mountains and parts of Texas. In the Northeast, the Brown Thrasher’s decline tends to vary from state to state. Based on breeding bird surveys, the Brown Thrasher has declined from 25-45 %. It is considered a species of conservation concern in several states, such as New Hampshire, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, Vermont, and New Jersey. In Massachusetts specifically, the Brown Thrasher has declined by 32 %. The Brown Thrasher has mainly disappeared from the Southeastern and Western parts of Massachusetts (Mass Audubon 2022). In the Northeast, the Brown Thrasher is found in shrubby fields with young trees, powerline areas, and pine barrens (Cavitt, J. F. and C. A. Haa 2020; NH Fish & Game, n.d). Due to its cryptic nature, the Brown Thrasher's migration patterns are not well known, especially its fall migration. Thrashers are known to arrive in Massachusetts in mid to late April. Based on spring 2017-2022 findings, birders have detected Brown Thrashers along the coast, on farmland, within pine barren conservation areas, and near hardwood forests (E-Bird 2022). Her red blood cell count is struggling to stabilize, but we’re hoping the treatment will continue to work with the slight improvement they’ve seen. To anyone who knows Mike, Sagan is almost constantly by his side. Since the first time she jumped into his car out of the blue they’ve been out on the roads, on the trails, or out hanging around town living life. This unexpected emergency has been overwhelming, and both Mike and Sagan could use a helping hand. We’re still unsure what the cause of her illness is, but we know that she will need immune suppressant drugs to support her body once the blood transfusions are complete. Hello, my name is Katie and I'm asking for your help to fund cancer care for my two dogs, Charlie and Copper. In the span of five days, I learned that my two dogs, my very best friends, both have cancer. My heart is breaking for them. I have done everything for them that I can, and I will continue to do so. Charlie and Copper were rescues in 2011. They are brothers from the same litter and are truly my best friends. They have been by my side for a marriage, a divorce, a move across the country with no money and no plan, living in a friend's spare bedroom, finding a job, finding an apartment, buying a home, and finding myself and love again. They have gotten me through the hardest times of my life and been there for the best times. They are my protectors, my space heaters, my snugglers, and definitely my dishwashers! Copper After their annual checkup in April, I noticed Copper was starting to show less interest in eating. I figured it was because the vet recommended I change their food, and I started putting chicken broth and eggs on his food to make it more palatable. He would eat it, but very slowly. And he drank a TON of water. Then he started to lose weight. A lot of weight. When I took him to the vet in August, he had lost about 50% of his body weight. They ran test after test. Everything came back normal. I was concerned and confused. I began cooking him meals of chicken, sweet potatoes and rice and added coconut oil and duck fat for calories. He gobbled these home-cooked meals up and started to put weight back on! He went from 32 pounds to 40 pounds. Then he stopped showing interest in those meals, so I got him wet food, which he loved... for a few days. He stopped eating again. One afternoon I came home, and he didn't come to the door to greet me. He was lying on the floor behind the couch and looked at me with big, sad eyes. When I picked him up to go outside, he could barely walk. I brought him back in, put him on his bed, and set some wet food in front of him. I was home early from work because Charlie had an appointment to go to the vet that afternoon for a tumor on his lip, so I made sure Copper was comfortable and loaded Charlie into the car. Charlie In July, I noticed a small lump on Charlie's lip. It didn’t look too concerning, so I kept an eye on it. The bump got a little bigger but shrank and stayed that size for a while. In the middle of September, the lump started to grow super rapidly and soon it was large enough that it would bleed every time he ate. I made an appointment for him to see the vet. The appointment was the same day Copper didn’t want to get up to walk. It was a Friday afternoon, October 14th. The vet examined Charlie and was unsure what the growth on his lip was, but agreed it needed to be removed. Charlie was scheduled for surgery the following Monday, and once the growth was removed it would be sent out for testing. Copper I rushed home, with a stop at McDonald's to get cheeseburgers (no onions!) for both dogs as a treat. Copper and Charlie both ate their cheeseburgers, so I felt much better. Copper was still really weak, and I lay on the floor with him for a while, but I was feeling much better about him. By Sunday, though, Copper still didn't want to eat much, didn't want to go outside, and was really lethargic, so I called the vet and made an appointment for him the following day, the same day Charlie was having his surgery. Monday, October 17th, came and I dropped Charlie off for his surgery, which went well. They removed the mass, took chest x-rays, and sent the mass to be tested. I picked Charlie up, took him home, got him situated and then switched pups to take Copper to his appointment. The doctor was excited that he had gained 5 pounds since his last appointment! But I reminded him that he had actually been up 8 pounds before. Since all the previous tests were normal, we decided to do x-rays on Copper's chest and abdomen. The x-rays showed that Copper has two tumors; one above his heart that presses against his esophagus and one in his abdomen that presses against his stomach and intestines. Either one of these tumors would affect his ability to eat, so the fact that he has two explains his rapid weight loss. Due to his age and the size of the tumors, further testing would not help prolong his life. Since the tumors are large, they are likely cancerous. Surgery is not an option, so he is being treated with anti-nausea medication and steroids to maybe shrink the tumors and increase his appetite. This treatment, combined with feeding chicken baby food, peanut butter and wet food, has allowed him to eat and be comfortable for the time being. Charlie On Friday, October 21st, I received a phone call from Charlie's surgeon. The test results from the mass removed from Charlie's lip were positive for amelanotic melanoma. I was told that this is an aggressive form of cancer in dogs, but the x-rays of his chest were clear so it doesn't appear to have spread. She also said they were pretty sure they removed all of the cancer because the edges of the tumor that was tested were clear. I was informed that there is a vaccine for this type of cancer, but it is most often administered monthly. Charlie has been referred to an oncologist so we can discuss further treatment if any is necessary. His surgeon suggested chest x-rays every few months to keep an eye on him, which will be discussed with the oncologist when we have that appointment. As of now, we are waiting to hear from the oncologist to make his appointment. Moving Forward As you can imagine, these trips to the vet have stretched my finances more than I can afford. Surgery, medications, checkups, follow-ups, and special food for Copper have all taken a toll. Baby food is expensive! I am only asking for help to recoup what has already been spent. If more is raised, it will all go toward treatment for Charlie and medication and food to keep Copper comfortable for as long as I can. Would you consider helping me keep my best friends in my life for as long as possible? I don’t know how much longer I have with either or both of them, but I’m asking for your help to stretch that time to as long as possible. Copper, Charlie and I thank you for your consideration and help.

Cosette is fighting tooth and claw to be an FIP survivor, but she desperately needs help to get the only treatment available. Rachel and I adopted Cozi in August of this year, and she has brought so much joy and energy into our household. Unfortunately, in early October, Cozi became increasingly lethargic and developed distention in her abdomen. Testing of the free fluid in her abdomen by her vet concluded that she has a condition called FIP, or feline infectious peritonitis. FIP is caused by a mutation of a coronavirus, which cats come in contact with very regularly. Unfortunately in rare cases like hers, mutations can rapidly become fatal without intervention. FIP is presumed to be a death sentence, as current drugs known to treat it are not yet FDA approved and cannot be recommended or prescribed by veterinarians. However, these drugs are available through some FIP foundations. Though costly, this treatment is known to CURE the disease, not just manage symptoms, allowing kittens to lead full and happy lives. Treatment is 84 days of injections of a drug known as GS-441524. Though not a guaranteed cure, statistics and studies show promising results (about 89% of cats in total remission). Without the drug, Cozi’s veterinarian estimates she will only have a few weeks to a month left with us. We are so desperate and devastated that at just 4 months old, we could lose baby Coz. Please help in anyway you can, and if treatment ends up not working out for our girl, all funds will go towards her vet bills, and the remaining distributed to FIP causes. We have to act fast and be proactive in order to fight this and keep her from deteriorating more than she already has. FIP is aggressive, progresses quickly, and takes so much from cats and their owners.

Hey y’all. I never thought we’d have to do this. But here we are. At the end of September, we had to make the difficult decision to put Trouble down. We were at a point where we couldn’t fix everything that was wrong with him. It devastated our family. Huey hadn’t been a solo cat and I could tell he wasn’t doing well. Fast forward to last week, he was vomiting every day and I realized he hadn’t used the litter all day or eating. Made a vet appointment. The vet agreed it was most likely stress. Took X-rays to be sure there was no blockage. We got some meds, some bland food and told of things don’t improve in a day to come back. That was Saturday the 29th. On Sunday they called to check. At this point he had eaten some of the food but hadn’t gone to the bathroom. The vet said give it a little more time. On Monday still nothing. First thing in the morning I made an appointment for 10:30. This time they’d do blood work. However at this point, he hadn’t gone to the bathroom in three days. They brought him in the back to do an ultrasound. Nothing alarming. Then they did the blood work. His creatinine levels were so high, it was maxing out the machine at over 24. Normal amount is 2. His electrolytes, and potassium were also off the charts. They wanted to hospitalize him immediately. I was quoted between 2700-4k. Not ideal but we would figure it out. I got a care credit loan of 4k. Again, this was Monday. On Tuesday (the 5th anniversary of me adopting him!) we went to visit him. He hadn't eaten at all. But his numbers were decreasing a tiny bit. He hadn’t been producing urine so they had a catheter inserted. He looked weak, hooked up to tubes, but he looked better than he did over the weekend. After trying a couple different foods, we got him to eat! And it was the best feeling. He was purring like crazy. Leaning into pets, and trying his hardest to flop. Yesterday morning (Wednesday) they called with a fantastic update. He was eating (not a lot, but some). His electrolytes were normal! His creatinine level went from 24 to 12!! Granted normal is 2 but this was phenomenal news. They wanted to keep him a couple more days and my new bill quote was $4700. Which was a blow to my stomach. But he was getting better. So it didn’t matter. This morning they called with a new update. Creatinine levels are now at a SIX!!! He was grazing his food. Producing urine on his own. But they don’t want him to relapse. So for sure another day, maybe two. This is where reality hits. I firmly believed on Monday that I was never going to see my baby again. When they revealed his blood work, I was in full blown shock. I don’t even remember driving home. The bill is going to be well over $5,000. I called and increased my CareCredit limit to cover things. But this is a huge financial hit. I don’t ever in a million years expect or want this bill to be fully paid by donations. But some help would mean so much. More than words can convey. Huey is my world. And I mean that from the bottom of my heart. He is the most wonderful cat. Everyone at the vet is in love with him. He’s 20lbs of purrs and snuggles. For five years he’s been the biggest comfort. I’ve gotten through so much because of him. There’s no other creature I could ever spend this much money on. And if this raises even $50 I’ll be eternally grateful.

Thank you for caring enough to be here reading this right now. I’d like to kindly ask for a few more minutes of your time so I can share a little bit more about Daisey Mae, our 11 year journey, and the current situation we have landed as we hope for a fighting chance- together. On December 9th, 2011 my Dad was killed in front of me after being struck by a car while crossing the street. The weeks that followed were a blur of shock, denial, despair, complete heartbreak and emptiness - until one day I found a tiny glimmer of hope. I stumbled on a Facebook post of golden retriever puppies needing homes by Christmas. I already had one furchild, Koby, but after seeing those faces I couldn’t stop thinking about them. I decided I would just go look (famous last words), despite everyone telling me I ‘didn’t need another dog’. I picked one up, then another, then another. Sure they were adorable, but they weren’t ...mine. I thought- maybe it wasn’t meant to be after all. Until right at that moment...I noticed a tiny sleepy one. Her chubby belly up pointed to the sky, paws going all directions, all tucked away in a corner. As soon as I picked her up she opened her tired eyes and looked at me with complete and utter disbelief, like she couldn’t believe I had inconvenienced her like this. She quickly crossed her tiny puppy paws, one on top of another, and stared off into the distance. The. SASS. I immediately burst into laughter. The first time since December 9th that I felt anything other than broken, empty pain. I knew immediately, ‘This is her.’ Since then, Daisey Mae became my ray of sunshine in what felt most days like suffocating darkness. The comedic relief and gentle spirit I so desperately needed to survive my 20’s as I moved to a brand new city alone. She became Koby’s best friend and we became an inseparable unit of 3. She was by my side while I navigated the heaviness of grief, PTSD, severe depression and crippling anxiety. She constantly distracted me with her ability to literally give no shits about anything, ever, in the most pure and mindlessly magical way. Never phased by the years of small apartments, or the countless moves we made around Nashville until I could give them what they always deserved: Their very own yard. Freedom to run. And finally-home that was ours. A lot of people consider their dogs to be family, but for me, they are quite literally all I have. It’s been them and I against the world, in our own little corner of the world, every single day, night, weekend, and holiday for over a decade. It’s always been us, and only us. My dogs have single-handily saved me in every sense of the word. And now it’s time for me to save her. I want to give Daisey Mae the best possible chance I can. While making the least selfish decisions - because I know that no time will ever be enough. But she deserves as much time as I can fight for her to have. As much time as I can give her to still be the giant happy goof ball that she is. So now, as we navigate Daisey’s newly diagnosed Thyroid Carcinoma and begin to learn her prognosis, options and treatments: This fund is for her. We thank you from the bottom of our hearts for any support you can give. Even the tiniest bit can and will help. I hope to have positive updates sooner than later.

She's worked incredibly hard and leads an independent life as a Pediatric Occupational Therapy Assistant. On Monday, Oct 17th, Dimitri was rushed to Summit emergency in shock, and declining quickly. After running diagnostics, it was found that he had a perforation of the GI tract near the duodenum. By this point gastric juices and air had spilled into his abdomen, and he was in sepsis. The gastric juices wreak havoc on the rest of the internal organs, and it's an uphill battle to try and save them from SIRS (Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome) that comes along with his diagnosis. He was given less than a 50% chance of survival and we had to put $11,000 down as a deposit to get started. Understanding that Dimitri was - 1. Previously a very healthy dog before this situation 2. A working service dog that has already had over $20,000 invested in his training, mobility gear, and care. 3. A lifeline for Courtney - We did everything we could to help get him through this. Summit's amazingly dedicated staff went above and beyond to save him. And he required everything they had. Dimitri survived 4 hours of intense surgery. But no forien object was found that caused the perforation, leading to concerns of potential cancer, so biopsies were sent out. Having gotten Dimitri from an ethical breeder with longevity in her lines, Lydia was confident that cancer wasn't the case, and we were thrilled to get confirmation on Friday 10/22 that it was not cancer. Dimitri spent 6 days in Summit's Critical Care unit battling the damage the gastric juices caused to his abdomen and fighting sepsis. He had 3 IV's (one central line in his neck), an NG tube (in his nose), and a catheter. On day 3 from surgery, Dimitri began swelling, something that should be dissipating, but was getting worse by the hour. The Vet's were completely baffled by this development and were concerned as they had no direction on how to get him turned around. They changed all of his meds on the possibility that it might be an allergy to one of the many medications he was taking. Thankfully that did the trick, and the swelling began to dissipate. He was discharged on Saturday, 10/22. He still has a long way to go in his recovery, but he is stable enough to come home. At the time of Dimitri's discharge, his vet bill was $15,468. That is an absolute mountain for a young person, but particularly a young person with a disability to take on. Because Dimitri is such an integral part of Courtney's life and wellness, we knew we had to give him every opportunity to be ok. We are beyond grateful for the love, support, and encouragement to start this gofundme to help Courtney with the monumental task of paying off Dimitri's massive medical bill. Thank you for taking the time to read, share, and donate!

My name is Britt and the little angel Lilac, who many of you know on Instagram as @lilacksnothing, is my fur baby. I feel completely helpless right now. Lilac is fighting for her life. My fur baby has been in emergency care since October 10th and in the veterinary emergency hospital’s intensive care unit’s critical care since October 11th. She truly is fighting for her life right now, and on a crazy rollercoaster from pneumonia which is life-threatening to English bulldogs. She developed pneumonia after coming into contact with a bat at my condo building on my terrace, and was recommended for an emergency rabies booster which made her vomit. The pneumonia could’ve started from bacteria the bat carried or it could be from the rabies vaccine which made her vomit. Aspiration pneumonia (from vomiting) can change change to bacterial. She had just given birth to 3 beautiful baby bulldog puppies via C-section, which of course suppressed her immune system. The bat and rabies vaccine added unnecessary stress to her system. It’s ironic and so tragic this happened at my apartment home, as I was being so very careful to entirely keep her protected and away from risks of infections and other dogs, for the safety of her puppies. Following that bat contact, she would not eat anything at all, her temperature started climbing like crazy, and she wouldn’t even open her eyes for me. When I brought her to her normal vet, I was told to go immediately to an emergency room. At that time, my baby was not in stable condition, she required carrying from one place to another. I felt the moving in an attempt to get answers was taxing on her body and I felt hopeless because there was no one medical to take her and keep her comfortable in the meanwhile, like an ambulance could. When she checked into one emergency hospital 3 Mondays ago, there was no mention of lung failure, but she was given nutrition via NG tube and she seemed hardly any better. Even so I was told I would have to keep her in that cage in the emergency room for an additional 24 hours. I yearned to bring her home. I thought to myself there must be a better place for my baby where I could see her get better sooner. I asked for her to be transferred to the regional specialist emergency hospital. When I asked when she would get there, I was utterly astounded when they told me I would have to get her there myself that there was no such thing as an ambulance that transports pets! Unhooking her from all nutrition in order to get her to the next place seemed not great but the only solution. When she arrived the new hospital I assumed they would hook her up right away. After five hours I learned that they had kept her off support entirely during the transfer and in fact she was waiting lifelessly in the back for triaging irregardless of prior emergency efforts. Finally I was called for a financial update and I pleaded to ask a doctor what they had been giving her in the meantime, and I was told she was given nothing because “it’s not possible to provide veterinary emergency care before financial is settled and paperwork is signed”. If only she’d had a place to stay comfortably like an ambulance until they were ready to process her. During her hospital stay, at first Lilac showed very gradual improvement. On admittance they explained that this was a very critical case with lung failure and put her in an oxygen cage at 40% oxygen supplementation. I screamed when I heard this news as it sounded like a death sentence. They said it was essential with comorbidities & emerging pneumonia. Above all, it killed me and I’m sure her too that I was only permitted to visit for only a few minutes in only one scheduled appointment per day. Lilac and I have such an incredible bond, as many of my friends and their fur babies do, she senses when I’m stressed when I’m happy and sad, she travels the world with me, and she sleeps every night in my arms in bed. I asked if she could come home, and the critical doctor said she would likely suffocate en route due to lack of oxygen. If only there was an ambulance service for ill doggies to transport them safely to home or a preferred environment. Two Fridays ago, I brought in a spiritual leader from the community and Lilac’s favourite peanut butter cake. Despite some residual snot-like fluid from her nose, she seemed 90% better to me. I could see it in her eyes that she wanted to come home. She even poked her head and neck way out of the oxygen cage, to show me she was doing better. However, the docs pleaded with me to understand she was NOT better and her pneumonia had in fact progressed and gotten worse according to X-rays. Again I was told safe transport would be an obstacle, and she might die en route and it would be against medical advice to do so, so I kept her there in the hospital with critical care. I thought it was the best option. I just wished so badly and prayed so hard for her to come home. If there had been a doggie ambulatory service at that time, I would have at least transported her safely (on oxygen) from the regional hospital to a local hospital with open format allowing 24/7 interaction with your baby. It broke my heart, and the heart of so many of Lilac’s friends and followers, that in the middle of the night that Saturday the 15th her blood oxygen saturation levels fell to dangerously low levels and she was amped up to more and more oxygen support on a HFOT (high flow oxygen therapy machine). The following 4 Days she was at 100% oxygen support “life support” and taking the tubes out of her nose can cause immediate respiratory arrest followed by cardiac arrest and death. The doctors highly recommended I “give her a peaceful rest” (i.e., permit euthanasia). They were certain there was no coming back from this. How I wished then especially, that the diagnosis was clear and prognosis too, that I could safely get her to a place of comfort. I frantically called around to human ambulatory services, asking if they’d transport Lilac (to which I heard “we don’t do that), then called the SPCA, etc etc. only to learn there’s no such thing as a doggie ambulance. This shouldn’t be. Our fur babies are our family members, and they deserve the proper transport support and care as humans. Risky movements shouldn’t be left to loving pet parents in a time of extreme stress. Just as if a human was in critical shape, medical advice would be to “wait for the ambulance to arrive”, why aren’t our canine friends given the same respect? Since they said she had no change, I at least wanted her home on hospice care. But that wasn’t an option. So I fight tirelessly for my love Lilac! In the following weeks, Lilac worked her way down from 100% to 60% oxygen support, at 40L per minute (that’s 15 coke cans full of oxygen pushed into her nasal cavities per minute). That's a huge amount of support! I begged the doctors on her critical care team to challenge her lungs by reducing the % oxygen support and seeing how she could oxygenate. SpO2 is the metric for oxygenation in our blood (just like in humans). Room air (what we breathe) is 22% oxygen, so that’s why oxygen support of 100% or 60% oxygen is completely incompatible with life and obviously unsustainable. Thanks to the goodness of G-d and expertise of her doctors, with some resistance, and constant changing and balancing of medications administered intravenously, Lilac adjusted to less and less oxygen. From 60% over the course of 1 full week she made it down to 50% at 35L per min, then back up to 55% at 35L/min, then 40% at 30L/min, 40% at 25L/min, 40% at 20L/min, 40% at 17L/min, then back up to 40% at 20L/ min. Fyi, Lilac’s SpO2 did only 89-94 (dangerous!) at first even at 100%(!) but gradually as her lungs healed she did 97 & above at less support. Finally she maintained 99 SpO2 at 35% oxygen support and only 7L last Monday. And X-rays showed she was resolving her pneumonia. Finally she can come home(!!) I thought. WRONG. That’s when the docs and surgeon recommended surgery. A risky surgery, highly invasive surgery, on the airway. Due to weeks on the next thing to a ventilator, they told me her soft palate had elongated and thickened even more than a typical bulldog’s, and I was told that her recovery from pneumonia was hitting a wall—that full recovery and removal from oxygen support would be impossible without surgery. They referenced the SpO2 dropping dangerously to 70s when reduced from 7L/min to 5L/min (that’s what an old man with oxygen tank breathes, 5L/min), and that breathing room air would never be possible for her, i.e., she’d never be able to leave the hospital. They told me the surgery, if it worked, would improve Lilac’s quality of life. I agreed to the surgery as a last ditch effort to get Lilac better. In addition to the shortening of the palate inside her throat, they widened her nostrils, and they performed a tracheotomy. Right now, she’s got a hole in her neck directly allowing outside air in through her trachea. It’s scary looking, but they tell me it’s temporary. My prayer and hope is that Lilac continues getting better and better. Now she’s back in an oxygen cage instead of HFOT, they’re trying still to wean her off (cage) oxygen and remove some medications and reduce some sedation. To keep her comfortable while fighting internally for her life, she was on some pretty heavy sedatives and gnarly antibiotics. For safety measures and nutrition, she has been (even still) fed by NG (nasal-gastro) tube. Today she was able to sit up and stand for a bit, and I was even able to feed her a little bit of baby food very slowly. I count my blessings for these mini-victories. Even so, I’ve accumulated a medical bill far exceeding anything I predicted and now nearing $100,000. Lilac’s Instagram @lilacksnothing has been flooded with outpouring of monetary and emotional support from Lilac’s furry friends and their parents. Several sadly shared with me that their fur babies had died en route to the hospital, others that inclement weather or needs of other family members / children prevented ease of transport. My hope is with this Go Fund Me, I can deliver my sweet Lilac home without her dying of oxygen suffocation on the way, and my greater hope is that I can start an organization with pet wellbeing at its core that helps pet parents in times of need—to get from place A to B safely. From the house to the hospital. From the road the pet was hit by a car, to critical care. I heard a story like this, from another pet parent while in the hospital waiting for Lilac, and his Molly girl was taken from the road she was found (hit by a car) to SPCA by a private vehicle and she could’ve died en route and ultimately SPCA was not the right place for her; time was lost transferring twice unprofessionally. SPCA was used wisely as a means of identification (to contact the owner), but a volunteer-run ambulatory service could carry a microchip reader to cut out unnecessary transfers and preserve critical time needed. With the love and support of caring people like yourself, this ambulatory service for dogs could solely be operated on donations and on a non-profit basis. I’ve identified a huge need, and I am committed to doing something about it. First steps are onboarding licensed veterinary professionals to consult on what tools and equipment are needed, then to outfit vehicles for the purpose, using vet techs and volunteers to operate the EMS vehicles. Every life counts, and time and proper transport can make the difference. Thank You for your love, hope, and support of Lilac and other sickly doggies who can be helped!

Since there was no microchip, identification or name tag except a 2021 rabies vaccination tag, we had to do our best to help him ourselves. When we arrived at the emergency hospital, they took him in and gave us 3 options. 1. We pay in full to keep him there and receive care treatment while we legally take him in - costing nearly $3,000. 2. We pay for antibiotics, pain medication and IV fluid patch for hydration and take him home with us for the night until we could get him to the vet in the morning - costing nearly $400. We decided to go with option 3. Ariana and I took him back to her house after he was given antibiotics, IV fluid and pain medication. From 11pm-8am, we stayed up with the baby all night. We catered to him, gave him water, a bed to sleep in, towels for comfort and lots and lots of love. We took him in to the vet at 8am as soon as they opened. The vet was great and able to take us back as soon as we arrived. From the rabies tag, there was a single ID number to locate the owner. The owner of the dog arrived about 20 minutes later. With all of this being said- surgery is very expensive and we would love some help to go towards his care and recovery. This is no ordinary search for funding. While that is much needed, it’s the story I am about to share is more important. It's a story of friendship, passion, dedication and healing; it's also a story of suffering, deceit, struggle and wounds that will take a very long time to heal. As far back as I can remember, horses have been a part of my life. I did and gave everything possible to be a part of that elite world. The funny thing was it was never about the status; it is a love for a sport so unique that few can ever say they have mastered it. I started teaching riding lessons when I was 14 years old, not realizing the importance of what I was actually doing. I wasn't able to see that I wasn't just some instructor... I was a mentor, giving others that part of me that was so vital to my soul. Over the years, I learned more, took on more responsibilities, and had the great fortune of seeing the fruit of my labor. I recognized how horses saved me, and I was unknowingly saving others through my work. The friendships forged in those barns run deeper than blood and are eternal, and the bonds created with the animals cannot be matched. A little over two years ago, my best friend and I decided that we were tired of working for someone else, someone who didn't share our values, who cared more about the money than what our riding school meant to its students. Someone who couldn't see that what we had was no ordinary business; it was a sanctuary. A place for people to escape reality on the back of a horse, leave their troubles and worries behind them and be truly at peace for a few moments. In March 2020, the world changed. The Covid pandemic left a hole in the existence of humanity, isolating people from their loved ones and locking them in boxes to be afraid to risk getting sick. But we had an escape. We had a place that almost sheilded us from the rest of the world, a place where kids could still go, be outside without masks, away from their electronics and confined spaces. It was then my best friend and I took the plunge. We found a little stable tucked away by the name of Serenity Ranch; the name inspired us to name our business as it encompassed exactly what we had been looking for: peace. With a lot of work, sleepless nights, and stress, we finally secured a lease on what we believed to be a little piece of paradise we never knew existed. I was 38 years old, he was 45, and it was a dream come true for us. We gave our all those first few months, and we did it with pride; we opened doors for people who didn't even know this world existed, and it was glorious! My best friend was finally able to give his daughter her own horse, something that was unfathomable just months before. I was still mourning the loss of my last equine partner, with little hope of ever finding his equal. When one fine day, a big beautiful horse showed up at my gate. It wasn't his looks that drew me to him, it was his eyes. Eyes I had seen before. Eyes that had looked into mine through the best and the worst times. It seemed like this horse was sent to me because the one who had those eyes before him knew a storm was coming, and I would need the kind of love and support that only a horse can give. The storm came in unexpectedly in the form of our landlords Valerio and Mary; at first encounter they presented themselves as sweet elderly couple who wanted nothing but the best for us. I’ll never forget Valerio saying to us “it’s almost like you were sent to us by God as an answer to our prayers.” To this day I’m not sure what exactly he was praying for... victims to torture, slaves, puppets to manipulate and mock. It didn’t take long for our “God sent paradise” to become the darkest circle of hell imaginable. (Dante’s inferno claims there are 9 circles, I assure you there are 10). We tried to keep the peace by going above and beyond, we treated these people and their horses like royalty catering to their every whim. Again we were fooled, the kind gestures my friend and I did in became obligations, those obligations became law, and with every passing day the freedom and “Serenity” we had fought so hard for was ripped out from under us. Valerio made fun of us behind our backs, spread lies, and would tell anyone who would listen that our failure was imminent and that “he gave us six months before we went under”. We tried to brush it all off, but reality was it was eating away at us. As the first year ended, we thought there was no possible way things could get worse. Man, were we wrong. Not only were we robbed of our peace but our privacy as well. To make matters worse the construction company Lennar bought the adjacent 44 acres and began to build a slew of cookie cutter homes literally 7 feet away from our arena. In an effort to find the silver lining I used the construction as an exercise in desensitizing our horses; but that too took its toll. As I’m sure most people don’t know I am On the autism spectrum and the sounds of the machinery triggered the most intense panic attacks I have ever experienced. No one including myself understood what was happening to me and why I was deteriorating so quickly. Things with my best friend began to change as well. Like two caged animals being starved and tortured by our captors, we began to turn on each other. Each fight became worse than the last, and with each one, our anger and cruelty towards each other grew stronger. We had been through rough times before, but nothing like this. But that was not the worst part; the truly devastating part was that while we were busy trying to slash each other's throats, a silent enemy made its way into our midst one that consumed us both mentally and physically. I first noticed it one day as I looked at this man who was once my hero, a robust and fearless force whose presence was enough to make the world stop and pay its respect. My real life version of Hercules, an undefeatable warrior whose name alone instilled fear in the very core of any man. Without warning, from one day to the next, he was gone... a shell of what he once was; meek, subservient.. his vision and passion for life were gone. The raging fire that ignited him had smoldered. I too was an unstoppable force once, brave, determined and ambitious. It felt as if that was another life and a person i no longer knew. I had become consumed by my own demons, and the mental health issues that I once viewed as super powers, became my kryptonite and consumed entire being. Depression and anxiety drove me to the point of not wanting to live... "Where did we go?" I'd ask myself every day. Where did my hero go? Where did my strength go? And the answer was right in front of our faces. We had become slaves to the people we thought were our saviors. For two long years, we gave up our lives, our identities and our freedom because we wanted to keep the oasis alive for others to be able to escape. We fought through the economic recession, which only added to our stress. And to top the sundae off with a cherry, the knowledge that soon enough our lease would end and if we didn't figure something out, all that work, stress and suffering would have been for nothing because we had no where left to go. it became clear that Valerio took pleasure in taunting us, knowing full well that he and he alone held our future in his hands. That he could make us or break us on a whim... he demanded a $12,000 deposit for the renewal and attempted to impose a 77% increase on our rent. We went back and forth using every legal resource available till he finally yielded to something manageable, but by then the damage was irreparable. My friend was ready to throw in the towel and shut it down. This brought on a whole new set of anxieties and fears that consumed what little was left of me. What were we to do? The night we decided that there was no other choice but to renew for another year was one of the most devastating nights I've ever lived. I cried and cried till there were no more tears; I lay in bed feeling as if my heart had been torn from my chest and that my soul would never be the same. I don't know what or how my friend felt that night, and I don't think I could bear knowing. All I had was infinite sadness... and the little oasis we struggled to keep alive for the people who depended on us. The next day, I received a call from a friend asking me if we had signed and renewed... I tried my hardest to hold back tears as I told her we didn't have a choice and would have to do so. Then it happened, the veil of darkness was lifted, and a ray of hope began to shine through..; she offered to lease us her property! It wasn’t just any property, it was my home, the property that made me the person, rider and trainer I am today. The same place where this one of a kind friendship was forged. The property owner had her own reservations and winds as she too had been burned two years prior by the cruelty and spite of her previous tenant. She too had to heal from the damage he had caused both to her property and as a person. You may wonder what exactly you are donating to... the restoration of hope. To the proof that even the darkest nights end. You are donating to strenthening two people who have been bulldozed by circumstance. An opportunity to find our strength and dreams again, and most of all, reclaim our freedom. As the days draw closer to our being able to leave this place and start our lives over again, please know that your donation is going to the noblest of causes... Love. Love of a sport, Love of an animal, Love of the person who stuck by in the darkest hour. True friendship is the kind that you'll find once in a lifetime if you're lucky. Any little bit helps, and I hope, in return, our story can be of help to someone else, a reminder that the darkness doesn't last forever and keeping faith and being persistent is the only way out of it. Thanks for taking the time to read this, and those who can and want to help us financially will not go unnoticed and we will be forever grateful for the contribution towards our dream. UPDATE: It’s been a little over a month since we left and restarted our lives in a more peaceful environment. Little by little we are finding the strength to do all the things we originally dreamed of. We have acquired some new animals to give the barn life beyond just horses and create an environment that is unique. We have an abundance of projects on the horizon including the equine therapy program I have always wanted. The future is looking brighter than ever and our spirits and ambitions are almost fully restored. Our goal remains the same as there is much to be done mainly the goal of building the necessary obstacles to become of the first eventing barn in Miami. We plan to take our horses and riders to their first event in April 2023. Please keep us in your thoughts and keep sharing our story. Any and all donations are greatly appreciated and we have put them to good use, good deeds and keeping our hope alive. Another huge thanks to all our supporters and any future ones as well.

He died at 11:13 that night after we put down nearly $7600 for hospitalization for 4 days. Our hopes were so high that they could get him to pull through and turn around. Only after knowing Shadow for two days, we were heartbroken for this poor guy who suffered from the neglect of his own owners. Because Shadow died shortly after we left, the whole $7600 was not spent. But we are still stuck with the $1300 bill. The owners have showed no intentions of helping pay us back. Hi, I'm Lexie, On Thursday afternoon while I was on my lunch run, I was seriously hurt. I went off on a normal sprint chasing a car and all of a sudden my hind legs gave out from under me. I was rushed to the animal hospital by dad Martin due to the paralysis of my hind legs. I was told I would likely need emergency surgery due to a suspected herniated disc causing compression on my spinal cord. I was in excruciating pain and lost complete use of my hind legs and needed an MRI immediately. The hospital quoted the surgery to cost between $12,000-$15,000. I spent 2 nights in the hospital under neurological observation. I was diagnosed with ANNPE (non-compressive nucleus pulposus extrusion with secondary spinal cord contusion and inflammation), which basically means that my disc had a slight tear in it and the material inside shot up into my spinal cord and paralyzed me from the waist down. Hello, We are the Parrott family- Kyle, Briana, Elijah, Daisy, Duke and Fergus. Our intention for this gofundme is to assist us in paying our sweet pup’s medical bill. Normally we would not ask for help, in fact, we really never do. But, this time we are in absolute need of it given our current circumstances. Our son was born in March, hospital bills are enormous even after insurance. After returning from maternity leave I was laid off due to the mortgage crisis (Briana is a processor). Finding work in the mortgage industry for a seasoned processor is non-existent. In addition, unemployment has not been forthcoming with the payments I am owed. In short, it has been manageable up until Duke’s emergency. These donations would go to his medical bill which is roughly $8,500. The Story: Thursday night October 20th, after dinner we took the dogs out for their normal potty break. Per the usual they ran to their normal spots in the yard. Upon coming in we noticed Duke acting very strange. He was pacing, whining, laying on the couch on his side, wouldn’t respond to treats or peanut butter, trying to vomit and wouldn’t respond to going back outside. Duke would either sit on our feet or seclude himself on and off. Initially we thought he was scared senseless while outside by an animal. We live next to a farm and there is a good amount of wildlife. Everyone went about the evening as usual- getting ready for bed while also keeping an eye on Duke. His odd behavior continued after a half hour or so. We did some research online and Briana was concerned it was bloat. Duke is a very large dog so it was difficult to determine if he had gained some weight or was bloated. After watching Duke curl up and put himself in a corner we called the nearest emergency veterinary. They advised we come in just in case as bloat is a very serious life-threatening condition. Kyle drove Duke to the emergency vet where techs immediately took him back to evaluate. X-Rays confirmed his stomach was twisted 180 degrees, his intestines were twisted and pulled up from his pelvic region and into his diaphragm, organs enlarged and on top of it in shock. He needed to be stabilized as quickly as possible. He was evaluated by four different doctors to confirm the diagnosis. Duke needed emergency surgery to save his life. We were told it’s very possible Duke could die during surgery if his body doesn’t react positively to the medicines to stabilize him. In addition, if his organs were too damaged or already necrotic, he would need to be euthanized. There would be no way to save him from either. We agreed to move ahead with the surgery to save him. Duke is a young dog, 5 years old, sweet and full of life. It would be cruel to have said no to this surgery and disrespectful to this amazing boy. He is our furbaby. Thankfully we had the best outcome possible, there was no necrotic tissue and they would be able to move his organs back where they belong. The stomach was stapled so this would never happen again. His spleen was removed as it was too enlarged at this point. Currently we are home with him resting and recovering. We couldn’t be more thankful for the team at BluePearl Emergency Pet Hospital. In another week we have a follow up for his progress. If you got this far, thank you for reading. Please consider donating to help our family in this tough time. Respectfully, Kyle, Briana, Elijah, Duke, Daisy and Fergus.

My name is Sheila Bunker and I live on a hobby farm in Southwest Michigan with my husband and daughter. We have many pets here who were in need of a home or help, Eddie is one of those. Eddie is a force to be reckoned with. He is a 6 month old mixed breed goat. Eddie came here 3 months ago, after being found lying on the ground paralyzed on his front legs. He was in a pen with lots of other baby goats and they beat him up, badly. Eddie’s owner was injured herself from a fall and was having spinal surgery that week, she asked if I could take Eddie in, without hesitation I jumped in the car to go get him. Our vet examined Eddie and X-rays revealed a broken right shoulder, suspected brachial and radial nerve damage, two hematomas to his ribs and a puncture to his head. Within a few days he was able to stand on his left front leg, move his head and neck and sort of hop around. He was always hungry and curious about this new home and the people and pets here. He lived in a stall in our barn with two gentle hens, and they had a small outdoor yard to enjoy. Soon Eddie became very weak and pale. His tiny body was overloaded with worms and parasites. Aggressive treatment began to support him and kill the worms and parasites. This regime was repeated a few times as the worms and parasites were very stubborn. Through all of this Eddie needed constant care. I would help him stand every 3 hours as he could not get up on his own. Goats are grazing animals, designed to be up and on the move. Being stuck down can cause bloating and death. I would set my alarms and get up in the middle of the night to go out to the barn and stand him, make sure he voided and stooled, offer food and water. Throughout this, I began cold laser therapy to his broken right shoulder and paralyzed right front leg in hopes of it healing better and being able to function again for Eddie. Eddie enjoyed these treatments, he was growing, gaining weight, bounding with energy and hilarious games. I taught him how to give me a “high 5” by head butting my outreached hand. Things were good. Then, tragedy hit. Between the pasture fence and his outdoor pen, horse nettle (nightshade) grew. I did not see it, but Eddie did and he ate some berries and leaves. Nightshade is highly toxic and goats do not live past 24 hours. Eddie grew weak fast, he was screaming and crying out in pain. He could not eat or drink. I sobbed and carried him to the house. Eddie’s vet recommended supportive care, pain medications, electrolytes, Kaopectate and euthanasia. I only left Eddie’s side to care for our other animals, cook dinner, or run quick errands. He had several days and nights where I thought he would die. I would hold him in my arms and tell him how strong and brave he was. I built a chair with a sling to get him to his feet. I could feed him and get him up with this chair. Then a miracle began, he started having feeling and movement to his hind legs. He is not able to walk or stand on them but they are reacting to stimulus and he is moving them. Our vet has referred us to a specialist who will begin treatment on Eddie on December 1, 2022. Eddie will have acupuncture, chiropractic, magnet therapy, etc. The cost for three treatments is $600. After that I do not know what the next step will be, if Eddie will need more treatments or what we will do. But this is a vital time and I need help financially to cover these costs as well as buying supplies for him. His spunky outlook and personality are what make him so incredibly special. He never gives up, and neither do I. Please help me to help Eddie. Any donation is greatly appreciated. Please share this gofundme with all your friends and family. I will be starting a Facebook page for him, as well as TikTok. Above all else, thank you for caring.

Hi, I am asking for help to raise money for my 1 and 1/2 year old cat Elisia. She needs a full mouth teeth extraction.. meaning she will be completely toothless. The surgery is expensive but I have no other option so please, anything helps. She stopped eating regularly about a month ago and when she did manage to eat, it was visibly uncomfortable. She was brought to the vet earlier today and diagnosed with Stomatitis, a very painful, often debilitating, chronic condition caused by an immune response to bacteria in her mouth. This means that she is having allergic reactions to her own teeth — more specifically, the plaque on her teeth. Because plaque lives on the tooth, and it is truly impossible to keep a cat's mouth free of plaque, the teeth usually have to be extracted to solve the problem. Antibiotics, steroids, or pain medication can be perscribed but it's only a measure of control and does not fully cure her pain or ensure that she doesn't get worse. The easiest way to understand is to think of the her teeth as enemies — the gums are attacking the plaque and the tooth. At this point I should mention that tame cats don't need teeth. Teeth are necessary only if the cat has to survive by catching and eating mice. Since we feed catfood to our tame cats, this is not a problem. I know this is a radical procedure and that it sounds horrible but after hours of research I believe it's the best and only option for her to be completely pain free and ensure she doesn't have further dental complications. I have read many accounts of complete recovery in over 80% of cats with this disease. I appreciate any help I can get. If you know any experienced dental vets as well I am open to hearing multiple opinions and better understanding her disease. I know she is in pain and I just want to be able to help her as fast as I can. Thank you.
