Emerald Monbulk wildlife Shelter Emerald Monbulk Wildlife shelter in the Dandenong Ranges is run by the incredibly dedicated Carol Seeger. Carol has been caring for injured and orphaned wildlife for over 30 years. On any given day, it’s not unusual to have several hundreds of animals on the property (aka mouths to feed and care for). Sadly, there is very little support in running a wildlife shelter. Carol takes in orphaned, displaced and injured native animals daily and gets no funding. Everything is paid for out of her (and her long-suffering husband Mark’s) pocket. Our volunteers assist with bringing in supplies; however the costs associated with running a shelter at this scale are incredibly substantial. Carol being the generous person she is, rarely asks for help. What costs are associated with running the Shelter? Formula for our young macropods and marsupials is vital to their well-being and development - a 20kg bag costs over $500. We make up multiple litres of formula daily and go through these bags every few weeks. On top of this we need a constant supply (many kgs) of fruit and vegetables for our birds and possums, meat and insects for our omnivorous and carnivorous birds, and general staples such as seed and pellets. In addition to this, we have the behind-the-scenes costs of running such a set-up - including; water and electricity bills, medications and vet expenses, infrastructure and building materials for adequate housing/enclosures, as well as travel and petrol costs associated with rescues and wildlife transport. What kind of animals does the shelter care for? We care for everything from Eastern grey kangaroos, swamp wallabies and bare-nosed wombats to blue tongue lizards, parrots and even the occasional sugar glider and echidna. A shelter success story.. In early July 2022 one of our rescuers was called out to an adult brushtail possum who had been hit by a car and left on the road. After being assessed by a vet, she came to us with soft tissue swelling around her spine, a pelvic fracture and a concussion. Her prognosis was not great. We moved her into a comfortable aviary and administered pain relief and fluids. She instantly became a favourite amongst volunteers for her sweet personality and love of kale (and mealworms). Often possums get a bad rap due to their displacement in urban environments - they seek shelter in roofs and gardens as much of their natural habitat has been disturbed. You will find though, that possums are full of charm, personality and cheekiness. In late July, our beautiful brushtail was picking up. She was much brighter and gained her balance and movement back. We also noticed that she had gained quite a bit of weight! Just as we were contemplating putting her on Jenny Craig, we noticed our lovely lady actually had a newborn joey in her pouch. The excitement of watching such an incredible recovery, as well as now seeing a healthy baby, was such a miracle. The great news didn’t stop there, however - a few weeks later, we discovered that our miracle baby was in fact, twins! The occurrence of twins in brushtail possums is incredibly rare - so the fact that our, now affectionately named ‘Mama Poss’ survived being hit by a car and carried on two have two bubs is truly incredible. Being in care has allowed her the safety and substantial nutrients needed to care for two young. A task that would be incredibly difficult for her in the wild where food is often scarce. Part of our improved infrastructure and care plan for Mama Poss has included the build of a large soft-release aviary where she can continue to raise her babies until they are old enough to care for themselves. As possums occupy territories, this set-up was done at a release site nearby. This requires considerable planning and logistics both from the build perspective and in terms of care and food supply. What does a day look like at the Shelter? Our morning crew of volunteers arrive around 8:30am. They will start by prepping formula and making up bottles for the orphaned joeys in care. On any given day, there could be 20-30+ joeys (kangaroos, wombats and possums) and a further 10-15+ adolescents, all requiring multiple milk feeds. These numbers spike during spring when young are born and tragically separated from their mums (either through road accidents, cat and dog attacks or natural disasters). Once the morning feeds are complete, healthy babies are taken outside to stretch their legs, enjoy some sun and learn that the outside world isn't so scary. Meanwhile, our volunteers start cleaning out and disinfecting all of the baby enclosures as well as washing and drying the many pouches we go through daily. Our washing machine runs approximately 10 hours out of the day with the hundreds of towels, pouches, blankets and beds that we wash per week). We prep fruit and vegetables for our adult animals awaiting release and our resident birds. We go through kilos of fresh produce each shift. Meat meals are made up for our meat eating birds. This includes kookaburras, magpies, tawny frogmouths, butcher birds and the occasional water bird. A large number of these birds come into care after being displaced as young or as adults who have been hit by cars while catching insects at dusk. Sadly, car headlights attract flying insects, creating a dangerous feeding ground for our nocturnal birds. Once all food is prepped, it is onto cleaning all outside enclosures and flight aviaries. This includes a thorough clean of all floors, feeding and water stations. Aviaries are then re-stocked with fresh foliage, fruits, vegetables and seeds. This ensures enrichment for the birds. Our juvenile kangaroos and wombats also get fed their bottles and supplementary food while they are transitioning to living in the wild. Ongoing foliage collection is a mammoth task and vital to our animals' health and wellbeing. Our dedicated volunteers collect fresh native foliage and flowers daily to ensure our birds and possums are supplied with as much of their natural diet as possible. We also rely heavily on a few kind neighbours who provide freshly cut grass every few days. Our morning crew usually finish up around 1pm before our afternoon volunteers arrive. Our afternoon team will commence the second round of feeds in the early afternoon. This often includes another 20-30 bottles. Once all babies are fed, they are brought back inside for the evening, where they are nice and warm. In addition, we often have a number of baby birds that require constant feeding throughout the day - and they definitely let you know! Our afternoon crew also attend to all of our juvenile and adult ringtail and brushtail possums. As per our other enclosures, this includes a thorough clean, fresh foliage, water, fruit and vegetables. We get dozens of calls to take in baby possums as small as 50g who require milk every 3 hours. The above happens daily - rain, hail or shine. We have a full roster of volunteers who help out 7 days a week as it is a 24/7 job. Carol is always on call - whether it is overnight feeding, pouch checks or rescues, she truly never gets a break. Carol has dedicated her life to helping our incredible native animals and always does so with a smile, incredible warmth, and empathy. We rely on your generosity to help Carol and her volunteers continue to care for our beautiful wildlife. Every dollar helps us make change in these animals' lives and also allows us to continue to educate the public about how special our Australian wildlife is. How will your donations be used? Building new enclosures and aviaries Maintenance and improving current enclosures for animals Setting up safe release sites for the animals raised in our care Bags of milk formula, pellets, seed and vital supplements Bottles, teats and bedding Cleaning supplies (including mops, disinfectants, detergents, cloths etc) Necessary appliances and their maintenance (bottle cleaners, washing machine, dryer etc) Setting up carers with supplies to alleviate the stress on the shelter Petrol to help with rescues Water and electricity bills Vet expenses and medications We appreciate your ongoing support and thank you for being part of this journey with us. Emerald Monbulk Wildlife Shelter Volunteers xx

On October 2, I found a dog tied to a front porch in Charlotte. He was wedged between a gasoline can and some trash, and wouldn't even raise his head as I approached him. After some investigating, I found out this sweet boy had lived outside tied to a tree with a tarp for his entire life. He was estimated to be about 8 years old and had never been to the vet. His owner simply called him "Boy". With the help of his next door neighbor, I was able to convince Boy's owner to let me take him to the vet - as long as I promised to return him. I immediately took him to Veterinary Emergency Group in South Park and my sister, a true angel, offered to cover the costs of his initial visit. Once at VEG, this sweet, but incredibly terrified, boy was found to have severe infections covering his body and ears, and I watched as fleas crawled out of his scabs. He wreaked of yeast, blood, and puss. Despite this, I have never met a more grateful and affectionate dog. He used my body as a scratching post and stared into my eyes unsure if he was in trouble or if we were there to help. The VEG team treated him for fleas and ticks and sent him home with a week of daily antibiotic. When I reluctantly brought Boy back to his owner, I explained to him the importance of making sure that he got his daily dose of meds. The owner then informed me that he was going out of town for a week and planned to leave a bowl of food out back for Boy where he kept him chained up to a tree. At that point, I asked if he would let me "medical foster" Boy for the week while he was out of town. Amazingly, he agreed! When I went to go pick up Boy, my angel sister once again stepped in and wanted to get him up to date on his vaccines. We scheduled an appointment at Spay and Neuter Clinic of the Carolinas. Boy received all of his vaccines, but unfortunately, the vet found he was heartworm positive, covered in severe skin infections, and had an incredibly thick and painful ear infection. For those who don't know, heartworms, while not contagious to other dogs, are fatal to dogs when left untreated. It is also very costly to treat. Boy was on borrowed time without medical intervention. I formulated a plan to ask the owner if he would agree to let me adopt Boy. By the grace of God, the owner agreed when I shared with him Boy's diagnosis, prognosis, and related costs for treatment (roughly $3000). At this point, I renamed Boy to Chance to reflect his second Chance at life! Chance is doing so well being an inside dog and learning how to be a dog from my own two pups. However, he is still battling a severe skin infection, ear infection, and heartworms. Chance's bills have already climbed to over $1000 in the past three weeks. He still needs to undergo heartworm treatment, be neutered, and continue being monitored through skin scrapes for additional underlying infection. Medicines, procedures, and treatment are quickly racking up - but Chance is more than worth it. Chance's road to recovery will be a long one and I anticipate he will be in my foster care through the next 6 months. Once Chance is in full health, he will be available for adoption through me...but good luck to anyone who decides to apply for him because he will only be going to the absolute best home! In the meantime, please consider donating to Chance's care! Any unused funds will be donated to Carolina Animal Network (501c3). We are so grateful for the support, positive thoughts, and prayers sent our way already :)

Okay, so I know you've been getting hit up at least 40 times a day to save Democracy, the whales, Redwood Forest and every other good cause out there. We were unaware that Kaia had some medical issues other than what appeared to be a leaky eye which we thought was just an allergy. Bonnie had to fork out $4,500 in the first two weeks of owning her. This, on top of the $200 we put in for Kaia’s allergy shots, prescription shampoo, anti-biotic eye ointment for an eye infection, and flea and tick control medication before we passed her on to Bonnie. Turns out, Kaia had dental problems. Her mouth was badly infected from a broken tooth and must have been incredibly painful. Kaia would cry any time you touched her face at all. I thought she was crying and confused from so many changes in her little life. When I inquired about the tooth, I was told that the family had known that Kaia had a broken tooth since last November (almost a year). That one tooth and the infection that developed because of ignoring it created problems for the teeth around it. When Bonnie got Kaia, she discovered that the broken tooth had formed an abscess that tunneled so deeply it came out on her face and left a hole. The vet was so concerned the infection would go into her bloodstream and be fatal that he performed emergency mouth surgery the next day. The result was five teeth out, twelve stitches inside her mouth, and two outside on her face. The happy ending is that Kaia is on the mend with an owner taking excellent care of her. That is a good thing. I’m reaching out to see if anyone might be willing to pitch in to help defray some of the costs to Bonnie, a single working woman. The initial financial burden of $4500 was onerous. Most people would have either returned Kaia or had her euthanized. But not Bonnie. Bonnie and Kaia want to thank everyone for their kind words of encouragement and donations of support. Any small donation to help out is genuinely appreciated; no amount is too small. They feel blessed to have found each other, but a few dollars are an added help! Thank you all for your consideration and help.

Hi, my name is Kylie and I work with a dog and cat rescue in Southern California. We get a lot of strays, abandoned, neglected, and high risk animals from all over and then foster them to give them a better chance at finding a forever home. In April, we took in a stray cat with her litter of six kittens, as well as three orphaned kittens, all of whom were just a few days old. We helped raise these babies into healthy young cats and set them up with adoptions with loving families, but two of those kittens stole my heart: Stella and her sister Ara. These two were the prettiest kittens I had ever seen, and we bonded immediately! While Ara was always the smallest of any litter of cats I’ve ever raised, she is mighty and she has no problem reminding you. Stella was also a little spicy, but she definitely has more chill than her sister. She loves to sit in her cat tree in the window and soak up the warmth from the sun. But Stella has been sick. We first noticed that she was having small seizures, so we took her to the vet and they found that she had a fever that was maybe causing them. We treated her for the fever, but she would still have little episodes. We took her back and started treating her for epilepsy with phenobarbital. This was working for a while, but her health started declining. She was very lethargic, wouldn’t eat unless coaxed or fed with a syringe, and started losing muscle rapidly. Pretty soon she would lose her mobility completely and wasn’t interested in water or food at all. We took her to a different clinic to get a second opinion, and after some fluids and testing, we discovered that it was FIP (feline infectious peritonitis). This is a very deadly disease for cats, but there are ways to help treat it. But the cost is enormous. We are trying our best to give our little Stella a fighting chance. Right now, I’m typing this while sitting in front of the oxygen chamber she is in. She is getting an oxygen treatment as well as IV fluids. She had started to crash this morning and these are the emergency measures we had to take. We have gone through our savings with her, and we are at the end of our rope. Please help us help her. Our organization has done so much to help other dogs and cats, but we are coming up short for Stella.

Hello everyone, We are here for our cousin Tony. If anyone knows us, our family is everything. Tony has been going through one of the hardest times in his life. He had to say goodbye to his dog and best friend, Rufus. Sweet Rufus’s sudden and unexpected passing has left us all heartbroken and after doing everything he could to save him. On the night of October 29 and Sunday, October 30, Rufus was not looking like himself. He was moving really slow and didn’t have any energy to walk. Tony took him to the emergency room. The ER ran tests. His blood work and tests came out normal. They only discovered red lesions on his chest. The ER ultimately sent him home with a treatment for a skin infection but they couldn’t find a reason for the lesions. As each day of the week went by Rufus became more lethargic, weak, low energy, no appetite, disoriented, no control of his bladder, and labored breathing. This concerned Tony even more. On Thursday, Nov 3rd, they went to see his primary vet. The only diagnosis the vet confirmed was a UTI and even more red lesions on his chest and abdomen. With his symptoms and the lesions the vet believed it could be cancer. They recommended Tony to take him to the U of I Vet Med Hospital right away. On Friday, Nov 4th, Rufus was admitted to the hospital. This was his third time seeing doctors in less than a week. This ER doctor’s initial diagnosis was cancer. Over night he declined even more. Saturday morning he had a seizure and started showing neurological symptoms consistent with a brain tumor or brain disease. He was transferred to the ICU and the neurological department. On Sunday, he had a neuro consult and the doctors said his symptoms were very consistent with a brain tumor, infectious disease and/or cancer. Tony was able to see him. However this would be the last time Tony would see him up and standing. On Monday morning he was schedule for an MRI to confirm the findings. After the MRI the doctors confirmed with Tony, Rufus had a very aggressive from of cancer known as hemangiosarcoma (tumors in the blood vessels). The cancer had spread to his brain, spine, muscle tissue and skin. He had less than a week to live. After much thinking and discussions with his doctor, Tony wanted to take his pain away. On Monday, November 7, 2022, Rufus went to go chase all the tennis balls he wanted. Rufus was a fighter. He didn’t want to leave his dad side. If you knew Rufus and Tony, then you knew how close they were and how much Rufus meant to Tony. Rufus was his best friend and Tony was his best friend. Tony would always say how much Rufus was everything to him. The love Tony had for him was unmatched. Tony couldn’t leave a room or Rufus’s side without Rufus instantly looking for Tony. The bond they shared was truly amazing to see. This past week was very emotionally draining for Tony. Not only did the emotions of losing your best friend hurt his heart, but it also piled up a hefty medical bill for all the test Rufus had to endure. We are starting this fundraiser to help Tony out with these financial strains during such a difficult time.

I took him to the vet and this is what we found: Image: Screenshot from <URL> Frankie has FIP, a rare feline virus caused by a genetic mutation. Image: Frankie just days before diagnosis. You can tell how sad he is. He normally loves pets and kitty massages but he didn’t want to be touched. He must have been in so much pain FIP was attacking Frankie from the inside out, attacking his organs and his brain. This used to be a death sentence to cats and kittens but as of about 6 months ago, a lifesaving treatment was found. Frankie is getting that treatment. Image: Frankie on Day 21 with his favorite toy Tiny Ted. He carries this little bear around the house in his mouth all the time. He has to have a daily injection for around 3 months, and then go through 3 more months of observation to ensure the virus doesn’t relapse. The trouble is the medicine he needs to be injected with is very expensive and hard to get. To save Frankie’s life and give him a long happy life, I am asking for donations to help with medicine costs. We are already one third of the way through his treatment and he has improved so much. The medicine works and I have my sweet affectionate confident boy back but we are not out of the woods yet. We have almost two whole months of treatment to go before he can be considered in the clear. Until then his life is still at risk from this horrible disease. Image: Frankie Day 4 of treatment. You can tell he is still feeling bad but he wanted to be with Oscar. They love each other and since Frankie started getting better Oscar has started making cakes with his paws all the time! They are best friends. I have tried to start a side business making candles to help cover his medicine costs, as well as pick up extra shifts at work but that is no longer an option so now I have to turn to you. Image: Frankie on Day 13 of Treatment. Will you help save Frankie?

Hi, everyone; thank you for stopping by to learn more about this sweet group of kitties in need. Luckily, a neighbor stepped up to adopt two, and I was able to rescue the remaining seven. I quickly learned the cats had been living in deplorable conditions inside of the home before being left behind and eventually forced outside, where two would be killed by coyotes within a week. I've been told there were up to ten or so more that were unaccounted for by the time I was alerted to the cats - they could have also perished, moved on to neighboring yards (I searched and spoke to many neighbors), or been taken by the previous owner. No doubt these people will repeat this cycle, but all I can do is focus on the cats I was able to find and rescue and do my best to do right by them. They had no outside skills and are not feral or outdoor cats, it is heartbreaking to think about what they have already endured, having been completely defenseless. This also happens to be next door to a home I rescued twelve cats from just two years ago after the homeowner (and feeder of his TNR location) passed away, and the family dumped the cats outside as they were preparing to sell the property. So I was horrified to learn this crew faced a similar fate, especially when their owner had my contact information and could have reached out for help. As a rescuer with other fosters and rescue/TNR responsibilities, I could not take the newly rescued babies in, but a friend is allowing them to stay with her for a bit while we secure rescue placement and homes for them. Overall, this little family is super friendly, with a couple of kitties slightly shy. Unfortunately, every cat was sick when they came off the ground, and none had been fixed. They are now fully vetted - wellness checks, combo tests, vaccinations, flea meds, and deworming. In addition, six of the cats have been spayed or neutered. Thankfully, they've all recuperated well over these last weeks. With lots of TLC, they are free of the URIs, massive ear infections, and gastrointestinal issues that afflicted them. Now it's time for Sunrise, Tommy, Millie, Toffee, Sunshine, Sugar, and Violet to settle into permanent homes and find the forever love and care they deserved all along. ❤️ I am reaching out in hopes of finding support with the following: • Vet bills and other monetary needs • Fosters and adopters • Supplies (food, litter, toys) To date, the vet bills alone total: $2,207.54 (This does not include vaccinations, flea meds, dewormer, or food/supplies.) Upcoming medical bills (TBD): • (1) Spay for Toffee • Follow-up vet visit for Sunrise + 2nd bloodwork to rule out possible thyroid issues I am sharing my Amazon wish list, which includes food and supplies for this crew and other rescue and TNR needs. Anything would be greatly appreciated to help offset the funds already spent to get these guys well. CLICK HERE for WISH LIST I know there is so much need in the rescue world, so I thank you for taking the time to read this plea. We would be so grateful if you could help by donating or sharing! ❤️ Medical receipts. Our first night safe. I'm not a cat owner. I am a cat mother. Flipper is my 26 month old Ragdoll Cat I have raised since he was 10 weeks old. I fell in love with a Mechanicsburg condo 2 years ago... the location? Safe. Price point? Reasonable. Then came the dreaded words from my landlords mouth, "No Pets. No Exceptions". Working an honest program, I was at a crossroads whether to continue my house hunt and pass on the ideal place... or do my best to keep Flipper under wraps. (Getting rid of him was not an option. I'd be homeless before that would ever happen!) Despite going against my gut and what I knew to be wrong, I proceeded forward and moved my cat and I into my condo May 2021. No issues, never a bother; a couple scares here and there when a Chewy package with gigantic paw prints on the box would get delivered for all the world to see a time or two. Aside from that, no one was none the wiser... ...until today. Ten minutes after walking into the office this morning, my phone received a text, and I knew immediately when I saw her, my landlord's, name displayed across my phone. My stomach dropped as I read exactly what I already knew was coming. "The electrician was in your place and said he saw a cat. This is unacceptable, and you know we do not permit animals. This needs addressed immediatley". I calmly got up from my desk, went to the resroom, and lost it. Once I calmed down a bit and caught my breath, I called my mom. I told her what the text said and that I was going to tell the landlord I was babysitting the cat for her. As I said it out loud I knew it wasn't right and albeit a small fib, it was a lie I was being given the chance to come clean about. So I did. I hung up with my mom and called the landlord. I explained everything, expressed my remorse, and begged and pleaded with her. She was admittdley torn, and told me she needed time to pray on it. I received the text message 5 minutes ago. She's allowing both of us to stay, contingent upon a full month's rent for a security deposit. By the end of the year. I quickly agreed because I was so freaking thankful to know we were staying in our home. After hanging up I thanked my Higher Power, splashed water on my face...and then reality hit. Hard. I support myself 100% and work for a non-profit; there's no extra funds after my bills are paid. My mom expressed her gratitude and relief as well, but made it clear she would help me if she could...but cant. So, here I am. Humbling myself and asking for help. I need to come up with 725$ by the end of 2022, right around the corner! I already work 2 jobs and coach cheer so do not have anytime to pick up another gig, or I would! Please, help me keep my house a home...with Flipper.

My name is Eddie, and I need your help. Today. I am employed by, and live with, Tiffany and Tommy. My sole job is to keep rats and mice out of our home. Sad to say, I failed. About three months ago two rats, nicknamed Bonnie and Clyde, somehow entered our home and set up their abode in our stove. Bonnie and Clyde are no ordinary rats; they are super intelligent, clever, cunning & evil. In the course of their stay here they have damaged our couch, countless items of clothing, the stove, dishwasher, a brand-new high-end backpacking gear, ruined piles and piles of food, and disrupted our sleep with their brazen, callous, noisy eating habits. They were actually taunting us by advertising where they were, knowing we could not catch them. I say “we could not catch them,” but it was actually my full-time job to do so. Tiffany and Tommy lent a hand by deploying every rat trap known to man, to no avail. It was a true head-scratcher: How is it possible for two rats to escape capture within the confined space of a home? Well, two days ago the tide finally turned. With every food item out of reach, they resorted to foraging in the hall closet, where the aforementioned backpack (with some protein bars) was stored. Did I mention there is one door in/out of the closet, and that this is a very confined space? When I awoke, I picked up the scent immediately, (yes, I smelled a rat) but also detected their physical presence. So I tiptoed in, which is hard for a dachshund to do, identified the first enemy, and attacked. It was a brutal affair. Bonnie employed moves I had never seen before. And she is (was) strong. A worthy adversary. But I did prevail. But out of the corner of my eye I detected the end of a rat tail sticking out behind a box. With Tiffany’s help moving the box, round 2 began. Clyde was even more formidable. He knows every move in the book: He attacked, he feigned, and he counter-attacked. He appears to have been trained by the Ukrainian army. He was relentless. But species superiority kicked in, and I finally was able to put him down. Unfortunately for me, I did not read the fine print of my employment contract. I am responsible for all damages caused by rodents on my watch. Yikes! I was originally going to do a Go Fund Me to hire an attorney to fight this in court, but the contract appears to be iron-clad, and I really did let my bosses down, so I have decided to do a Go Fund Me to help me reimburse my employer for her substantial damages. I am pretty sure the talk around the house of “animal shelter” is just a ploy to motivate me to pay restitution, but just in case, I would seriously appreciate anything you can do to put this matter to rest. I don't have any money, I don't even have pockets. Unfortunately, this rat destruction is not covered by insurance, so we're in a bit of a pickle. Best regards, Eddie aka Rat Hunter/Couch Potato

Furever Sunny's Journey: Sunny was a Senior horse I had bought for showing as a teenager. I actually took all my car money I had been saving and on my 16th birthday, I bought Sunny instead of a horse! My parents were NOT happy, but I couldn't have been more full of joy! After a few years of trying to show him, I realized he had too many health issues. I knew no one else would give him the love and special care he needed, so I retired him from showing and had a big puppy dog of a horse. He would seriously follow me around in the yard like a huge dog! Sadly we lost Sunny in January of 2022, he would have been 27 in April. I was heartbroken, losing my baby I cared for for 16 wonderful years. April was also the month the sanctuary moved to a new farm, previously at a farm called The White House. I was now in need of a new name, the new farm looking NOTHING like the Presidential White House. I couldn't think of a better way of honoring my late Sunny than renaming the animal sanctuary after him. "Furever Sunny" was reborn... Our Current Residents: Chevy This mini was being kept in a shed, locked away because he was too fat to win his shows. I took him in hoping that he and Sunny would nurture each other, as Sunny had just lost his best friend goat of 12 years! Chevy and Sunny were inseparable! Chevy is the sweetest one on the whole farm! He is now best friends with Ford! Ford This spunky 4 year old was surrendered by a family friend in Napoleon. He was bought as a foal, and not had much handling. It took almost an hour just to catch him, as he was so scared of humans, he wouldn't let you come anywhere near him! He thankfully was given a clean bill of health from the vet besides his much needed manicure! He had not had his hooves trimmed for over a year. His hooves are finally growing in normally, and his manners are coming along nicely too! He went from not letting humans touch him, to not wanting anything but to touch humans WITH HIS CHOMPERS ...we are working on the nibbling manners... Leo This handsome goat was surrendered from a Fostoria family who had purchased them as bottle babies. He is one big puppy dog who likes to follow you around in the yard! Storm This cutie pie was born in the summer of 2022 to an "accidental breeding" whoopsies! The poor baby and his brother did not latch and had to be bottle-fed. The goat breeder in La Rue grew very attached and wanted to see him go to a good home. Sadly, Leo had just lost his best friend Spike, so it was almost like fate! More tears.. are you ready? Days before I went to pick up the baby goat, his mom Storm passed away. When I asked the La Rue woman what the baby goat's name was, she said let's name him Storm, after his mama! Chub and Bub These two inseparable piggies were dropped off at a local horse barn, the owner never returning. Their owner apparently raised them from piglets in the Levis Commons apartments until they got too big! These potbelly pigs and very sweet as a result of their upbringing; they love a good pet and will do anything for a treat! Bub on the left is actually the bigger one, not letting Chub on the right live up to Chub's name! Pig Pig This sweetheart is actually the ONLY girl we have outside at the farm. (There's lots of ladies IN the farmhouse!) Pig Pig the Kune Kune pig was surrendered from a Weston family. She was digging too many holes in the yard! The father was NOT happy about the holes, the pig had to go or else! She was free roaming their farm after their daughter had raised her from a piglet in--- wait for it-- an apartment building! Since Pig Pig was free to roam the farm, she was also getting attached from animals and has some battle scares to show for it, you can see one here on her poor ear! She has made a full recovery and is adjusting to her safe environment. She is still afraid of any other animals, but LOVES humans. She literally begs for belly rubs and back scratches and has been known to just plop over at your feet asking for them! Cindy This sassy lady was brought to the horse barn I was babysitting back in 2006! She is 17 now and only has 2 teeth left. She has to be on a rather expensive liquid diet with a rather unorthodox feeding contraption. Ella Found as a kitten dropped off at the sanctuary's barn. She is Cindy's protégée with so much sass! And was given the much deserved princess name after Cindy. Cindy-ella... Cinder-ella... Get it?! Mica (left) and Ella (right) were found months apart, wandering into the barn. But they were the same age making for an inseparable kitten bond. Sadly, we lost Mica unexpectedly a couple years later. But at the same time 3 kittens were surrendered with their young mother. Ella didn't develop quite the same bond as she did with Mica. She sure does give those kittens a run for their money though! They chased each other around the house play for weeks! Seriously, weeks! I couldn't sleep! I was wide awake smiling though, knowing that Ella's broken heart was being mended with each pitter patter of their paws at 3am! Nakoma She was taken from a hoarding situation in Alabama. There were three litters of puppies?! Thankfully all went to a good home. Nakoma came to mine! She loves helping around on the farm giving kisses to the horses and pigs. She also thinks its her sole mission in life keeping the cats away from Princess Cindy's expensive wet food. After all, if Nakoma can't have any, why should the other cats?? Roosters If you have ever raised chickens or know anyone who has, you know that there are always TOO many roosters in the coup. Did you know that as long as there are no lady birds, the men get along and don't fight-within reason! So many roosters find their way to our sanctuary. Many coming from families in Toledo, where you can have hens, but cannot have roosters in the city limits. Now I said they don't fight within reason, I have found that integrated new roosters into the bachelor coup here, has worked best when they are younger, about 3 months or right when they start crowing. The new men haven't developed as many aggressive habits at this age and they tend to integrate a whole lot smoother! There's been so many surrendered roosters, to the sanctuary I am not sure if even I could keep their names straight anymore?!? One thing is for sure! HONEY RULES THE ROOST!!! (pictured on he left) He is their leader and they all must do what he says! He will also let any human know that he is the BOSS. Hello all! My name is Gabrielle, but most importantly, my beautiful cat's name is Boogie, and she needs some help right now. Exactly one week ago, her life turned upside down. With no prior signs, she woke up on Saturday unable to breathe through her nose, having to resort to using her mouth to gasp for air. We promptly rushed her to VEG Brooklyn's emergency room, where they attempted to treat her. Unfortunately, they could not alleviate her symptoms. Two days passed, and we watched as our girl got weaker and more tired, as she couldn't eat or sleep. We took her to VERG for a consultation, hopeful that it could be something like a polyp, which in most cases, would be easily removable and provide instant relief. After a few hours of pacing back and forth in the waiting room, they handed her back to us and booked her for procedures to look inside, which involved anesthetizing her in two days. We were told not to attempt to force-feed her anymore and to stop giving her any medications. By her appointment on Thursday, she had not eaten, drank, or slept for four days. She relied primarily on her mouth to get air, making wheezing sounds and needing to keep her head extended outwards at all times for more airflow. Boogie couldn't put her head down for more than 30 seconds to even rest. We had to watch as she became more lethargic hour by hour. We still tried to stay positive, even as we had to watch our baby suffer. We dropped Boogie off on Thursday morning to her appointment and waited by our phones all day. It felt like someone had a finger on the clock hands and kept pushing them back. When the doctor finally called me late in the day, I heard her sigh as she began to relay the news. I didn't even need to listen to the words, and everything around me started to intensify until my surroundings just went numb. They couldn't remove the mass, and the CT scan results implicated a 2.2cm mass impeding the left nasal cavity, extending to the nasopharynx. The hopefulness of it being a polyp was almost entirely eliminated. What was once at the bottom of the possibility list moved up to the very first, most probable option. Cancer. It is now Saturday, and what we thought would be a quick visit to the doctor and home by night turned into a two-day ICU stay, with recommendations from the doctors to keep her for longer as we all await the biopsy results. So far, the hospital bills have totaled nearly $9,000 and are climbing. We expect the sum amount to at least double as she is instructed to stay in the ICU until they can figure out the treatment, depending on the biopsy results. Our current possibilities seem to be carcinoma, lymphoma, or, still, crossing fingers, a benign polyp. So far, Boogie has tubes in her nose that bypass the mass, allowing her SOME relief in breathing normally. They also put in a feeding tube and are giving her steroids daily in hopes of bringing down the inflammation to the point where she can be comfortable on her own. But financially, time is not on our side. The biopsy results can take up to a week, and each night stay at the hospital is around $1,500. As we wait for any news, we are trying to help afford any type of treatment possibilities for our Boogie. Boogie just turned 5 last month. She is the most full-of-life, playful, friendly, curious, and sometimes destructive cat ever. She isn't giving up, and we aren't either. Please help Boogie get her second chance at life. It is not her time, and we are ready to fight to prove it. Any contribution helps go towards Boogie's climbing medical bills and the treatment option recommended in the next few days. Whether or not you are able to donate, please kiss your pets for us, and give them all the love you have.

Hi everyone meet moose! Moose is a 5 month old Pitt mix that my boyfriend and I rescued from a pretty bad situation. Moose spent his first 4 months with his mom and sister living outside with no shelter other than a dog house. The only human interaction he ever really had was when they got fed which didn’t happen anywhere close to as often as it should. Moose was the healthiest and biggest pup of the litter but after 4 months his health deteriorated quickly. He quickly became very sick and malnourished. My boyfriend and I finally decided to take moose when we witnessed moose have an attack where he was gasping for air, turning purple and nearly collapsing. After bringing moose to the emergency medical center on bridge st and paying $380 to be told we had to put him down or pay $5,000-$7,000 to treat him and going to Cornell to spend another $600 who diagnosed him with pneumonia and said he had a very low rate of survival. After a week and a half of antibiotics he continued to have his attacks. About a week and a half later We brought moose to another vet to have him put to sleep as these attacks were absolutely horrific and since we did not understand why they were happening or how to stop them we didn’t think it was fair to make moose go through this any longer. however while standing in the parking lot of the vet I looked into moose’s eyes and instantly had one of the most intense feelings in my gut that I have ever felt telling me that I had to fight for this dog and that I shouldn’t give up on him quite yet. I then turned to the vet and asked him how much he would charge me to do some X-rays. He told me the price and then he and his vet tech spent the next 4.5 hours doing whatever they could to try to figure out what moose’s issue was. Finally at 11:30pm we had a probable diagnosis. I was beyond thrilled to finally get some answers for moose. Moose has an elongated soft palate which blocks his airways whenever he gets overly excited. This is what causes his “attacks” when he has an attack which typically last anywhere from 15-20 minutes his muscles contract and his airway gets almost totally cut off, moose’s blood oxygen level drops to a fatal level and just when moose is about to loose consciousness his muscles relax which reopens his airways and he miraculously comes out of the attack. Our vet when telling us Miguel had FIP told us he had probably 2 weeks to live if left untreated and that currently in the United States there is no FDA approved treatment for FIP. This was heartbreaking news to hear, everything felt like it was happening so fast and it was so overwhelming and sad. After a long night and a lot of research later we found options for experimental treatment that is used outside of the US that has a great success rate but is still experimental here in the US and can not offer guarantees. This experimental treatment also is very hard to find and a lot of vets don’t even want to talk to us (in portland) about FIP... Luckily though we have found a community and a few vets who are willing to support us our on journey of saving Miguel’s life from a disease that should be curable in the United States. Gordo, my neighbors' dog, was hit by a car on Monday. The poor boy has extensive injuries: he almost bit through his tongue, he has road rash all over his front right leg, his lungs are bruised, and infection has set in. Worst of all, however, is his back right hip, which is completely dislocated. The vet had no idea how poor Gordo was able to walk at all when he arrived at the clinic!﻿ Right now, the main concerns are pain management, quashing the infection, and letting his lungs heal up. Gordo is currently being medically boarded with the vet to ensure that all those things happen. The doctor says the poor boy must be in excruciating pain, pain so bad that she's putting a fentanyl patch on him first thing. He's in rough shape. Once his body is a bit more stable, it will be time to address his hip. Unfortunately, Gordo is a very big boy - at one hundred pounds, he came by his name honestly - and it's not easy to reduce a dislocated hip in a large dog. In fact, the vet says, they usually don't even try if a dog weighs more than sixty pounds. Thus, she says, the best option is a femoral head ostectomy (FHO). It's a surgery in which they basically go in and chop off the ball portion of the ball-and-socket joint. The socket then stays empty. Because dogs don't have all their weight on their hips like humans, their muscles alone will keep the leg in place, and after recovery, the dog ends up with mostly normal and painless range of motion. Gordo is the absolute goodest of boys. He was the first neighbor to welcome us when we moved into our new house, and he even helped the movers get our stuff through the front door! He deserves many more pain-free years. He also has a little girl at home who's worried sick about him. Carl and I are lucky enough to be in a position to help, in that we speak English and have a lot more animal health knowledge than your average person. However, we won't be able to pay for Gordo's medical needs alone. Though the final amount is yet to be determined, we are probably looking at over $2000 for everything. I told Gordo's little girl, though, that he was going to be okay, so I need to come up with the money somehow! I appreciate every little bit you can give.

Hi guys, my name is Rachel and I'm fundraising for my puppy Ryder's medical bills. I bought Ryder from a breeder in San Diego on Sunday (10/23). He was a tiny little guy, weighing about 1.6 pounds. He is a toy poodle and when I picked him out on Tuesday 10/18, he was super energetic and ran right up to me and just plopped in my lap. He was playing with me and had energy like puppies normally do. However, on Sunday 10/23, when I brought him home, he was showing signs of lethargy right away and threw up once, but I didn't think anything of it. I just assumed it was normal for a puppy to be stressed after going home / to a new place for the first time. He ate dinner and was playing around a little bit, but he would fall asleep at my feet mid-playing with a toy. When Monday morning (10/24) rolled around, I offered him breakfast but he wouldn't eat a single thing. I offered him at least 10 different types of food, including chicken, rice, 3 types of wet puppy food, his normal dry food, treats, honey, peanut butter, etc.) and then he starting throwing up beginning early afternoon. He would drink water and then throw up immediately after, and he was throwing up randomly. He threw up about 15-20 times. At night time, he began throwing up foam and I got super worried and knew something was wrong, so I took him to the ER Monday night around 12:30 AM (10/25). They ran a Parvo test but it was negative thankfully, so they gave him some Zofran and told me he is probably stressed out from the move & he will eat tomorrow. Tuesday morning (10/25) rolled around and Ryder still wouldn't eat anything and he was sleeping nonstop. I would pick him up and put him on the floor to try and get him to eat or drink water and he would fall asleep on the spot. He would drink water and fall asleep at his water bowl. He would go pee on his pee pee pad and fall asleep on top of his pee. He had 0 energy and had some diarrhea. At this point, Tuesday afternoon, I knew something was really wrong. It was now 7 PM (a little over 48 hours after picking him up from the breeder) and he still wouldn't eat a single bite of food or even move at all. I got even more types of food and tried everything, but still nothing. So I took him back to the ER around 8 PM on Tuesday night (10/25) and they rushed him into critical care and admitted him into the ICU. He was extremely hypoglycemic (low blood sugar) from not eating for 2 days. They ran another Parvo test because they said that sometimes it takes a little to show up. Negative again. They also started him on an IV w/ fluids, dextrose and a few medications. Wednesday morning, they were able to run a fecal test. He still wouldn't eat a single bite of food and was sleeping nonstop, so they decided to keep him another night until they could get the fecal results back. Thursday morning (10/27) they got the fecal results back and it was positive for a parasite called Giardia. They said that Ryder was eating a little and feeling better, and that I could come pick him up. I picked him up around 11 AM. He came home and was still exhibiting the same symptoms (extreme lethargy and wasn’t eating at all). I force fed him wet puppy food mixed with water through a syringe every few hours because he is prone to hypoglycemia and it happens super quickly with puppies of his size / breed, and it had already happened the day before. I woke up three times throughout the night to feed him as well. Despite my offering him at least 15 different types of food, he still had no interest in even looking at anything. He was still sleeping nonstop and could barely walk. He was in pain and would keep turning around while he was sleeping to try and get comfortable and make the pain go away. In the morning on Friday 10/28, Ryder was still in the exact same condition and I was so worried about the little guy. I called the hospital and they said I should bring him back in, so I did around noon. He was examined and found to be hypoglycemic again. He was then admitted to the hospital to stay another night for treatment and IV fluids / medications. On Saturday 10/29, I woke up extremely optimistic again. I have remained positive throughout this situation, I have to stay strong for him. I went to visit Ryder around 3 PM and the doctor told me that his ultrasound showed that he had Pancreatitis in addition to the Giardia. Pancreatitis is swelling of the Pancreas and it is unheard of in puppies, it’s extremely rare. Dogs can get Pancreatitis at a way older age from things like a high fatty diet. Ryder has been eating puppy food, nothing high in fat or anything else that would lead to Pancreatitis. The doctors have no idea what caused this, but said it could possibly be from the Giardia or another unknown cause (like a congenital defect of some underlying condition). They told me that if Ryder doesn’t eat in the next 24 hours, we would have to try and place a feeding tube through his nose into his stomach (an NG tube). If they can’t get the tube in him because he is so tiny, that we would have to consider the possibility of putting him down. This whole situation has been hell. I am saying prayers for my baby at this point and hoping that he starts eating today and is able to fight this. I made a GoFundMe page at this time because Ryder’s medical bills keep climbing, and have now totaled over $12,000 that I have to pay out of pocket. I honestly did not expect this at all, nor would anyone expect this to happen 24 hours after buying a puppy from a reputable breeder. I honestly can’t afford these bills right now and am asking for help to pay for his hospitalizations & treatment. I appreciate any amount of support and truly thank you all for considering helping us out in our time of need. Prayers for Ryder <3 Will keep you all updated about his condition within the next few days.

Hey everyone, I’m trying to raise funds for this sweet, young girl, Harla. Harla became very I’ll very fast on Saturday, November 12th and was seen by her primary veterinarian. Since Saturday Harla has received a diagnosis of IMHA - When your dog has IMHA, it means his immune system destroys its own red blood cells. Your dog’s body still produces red blood cells in the bone marrow to replace the destroyed cells, but once they are released into circulation, the immune system mistakenly recognizes them as something foreign, like a virus or infection, and destroys them. This condition is also referred to as autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA). Since her diagnosis on Saturday Harla has needed 2 separate blood transfusions, hospitalization & special care. As of 7pm today, November 16th Harla is being admitted to another Emergency Veterinary hospital for a 3rd blood transfusion. During the course of today, we have received the same medical option from 3 board certified internal medicine specialists and 1 board certified critical care specialist- Harla’s body is trying very hard to bring her red cells back up and with the right care and a little bit more time she should be able to pull through! As of today, Harla’s owner Dave has paid out of pocket for all of her medical care. These funds are solely to ensure Harla can continue to receive the care she needs, as she is expected to need at least one more transfusion and will be receiving a special medication (IVIG) via infusion tomorrow which alone will cost $2,700. Harla is the absolute sweetest dog I have ever worked with and has a lot of fight left to give! Please consider helping Dave offset some of these extensive medical bills and get Harla back on her feet. Donations of any size are greatly appreciated by myself, Dave & Harla!

Hi everyone! A big update on Rue!He was misdiagnosed with Cataracts. His symptoms started with loss of vision. We took him to the ER, they referred us to an eye specialist and they diagnosed him with cataracts. Then soon after that he started developing other issues, such has his inability to move his back legs properly. He’s constantly falling over and has a really hard time getting around and using the potty. I took him back to the vet, they referred us to a neurologist, where he was then diagnosed with FIP. There are different forms of FIP, wet and dry form and then there’s ocular/neuro form, which is what Rue has. FIP is a viral disease that is caused by feline coronavirus. Its estimated that 80-90% of cats get coronavirus, but only 5-10% of cats get infected with FIP, and it is usually cats under 2 years old. Rue is only 5 months old. When I first got him, he could see and run and jump perfectly fine, this disease has slowly been making him deteriorate and it’s absolutely breaking my heart. Now that some time has gone by, there IS medication for it now, but because it’s so new, it’s not yet FDA approved. Which means I cannot get it through the vet. There are other ways to get this medication, and I’ve met some amazing people who are helping with that. Meet Benjamin: Benjamin is a beautiful Golden Retriever 15 months old. Recently, as shown in the video, Benjamin's walk has changed dramatically for the worse. Benjamin must rest after walking for a brief period and if tries to run injures his legs. When eating he lies down to eat. Benjamins Journey: The Veterinarian in Cullman Alabama originally thought it was his hips. Having Hip Dysplasia. Based on the X Rays of his pelvis and legs. In an effort to get Benjamin's help, I turned to the University of Auburn Orthopedic Clinic. After they received a referral from the Vet in Cullman. UA admissions contacted me and stated they do not do Hip replacements at the University. However, they gave me a reference to Veterinary Care and Specialty Group in Chatanooga Tennessee. Benjamin's evaluation was done on Friday, Nov. 4th, 2022 by Dr Peck at the Veterinary Care and Specialty Group. During the evaluation he verified via X-Ray hip dysplasia is evident but not the cause. It's Benjamin's knees. Benjamin's condition is hereditary. If this condition goes untreated Benjamin will eventually be unable to walk. Arthritis and pain will be commonplace for him. The mild Hip Dysplasia now evident will become more prominent due to his knee condition. Dr. Peck's prognosis to correct this condition is called a TPLO ( Tibial Plateau Leveling Osteotomy). Benjamin will need 2 surgeries to correct this condition. Each of the surgeries is estimated to cost between $4,800.00- $5,200. per leg. After each surgery, Benjamin will spend the night in the Hospital and have an 8-week recovery period with a follow-up at 2 weeks and X-rays at 8 weeks to view and validate his progress. Benjamin had his 1st surgery on Thursday, November 10th, and is doing well. I am committed to doing whatever it takes for Benjamin so he may have a normal life. Hi all, for the last couple of weeks Big Mac has been in extreme pain & limping uncontrollably. We made an appointment for the vet to get him checked out. For a small young dog who just turned 1 it was torture to see him in such pain. He was having trouble putting any pressure on his back right leg & we knew something was wrong. During the time, waiting for our appointment we have kept Big Mac as comfortable as possible, decreased his activity level & overall just monitored the situation to avoid further discomfort. This past week during our visit biggie ended up getting multiple x rays to see internally what was causing this unbearable pain. It saddened us to find out that multiple doctors had to figure out what they saw on the x ray. They ended up consulting with an orthopedic surgeon & biggie was diagnosed with Legg Calves Perthes. This is a disease in which the hip bones begin to deteriorate. (This disease is a condition that occurs when blood supply to the ball part (femoral head) of the hip joint is temporarily interrupted and the bone begins to die). How does this happen to such a young dog you ask? Well after our research & discussion with the vets they don’t have an answer, all we know is this is an underlying issue that has been brewing over the last few months which caused the pain to get worse & worse. Also causing his muscle mass in his right leg to shrink to barely nothing. Big Mac just turned 1 October 16, 2022 & finding out this news a little over a week after his birthday destroyed us. We have finally come to the conclusion that he will get getting hip surgery to help sculpt the deteriorating bone, move tendons & help re build the muscle overtime. Yay this is great & we are thrilled BUT... after looking at the x rays the doctors shared that they also see this disease growing on his left hip bone as well. Unfortunately we can’t see into the future & don’t know how bad that side will get, if he will need surgery etc. For now we can only focus on the extreme side, the right hip. As a dog lover, rescuer & trainer I put dogs before myself. My dogs are my life, family & my heart. My family & I would be more than grateful with any & all donations towards Big Mac’s Surgery & Recovery. We are so blessed with such an amazing & strong little Pomeranian who came into our lives unexpectedly. From a Rescue boy who found his forever home to now being in need of a big surgery we would be grateful for all of you animals lovers to help us in a time of need. We thank you for your never ending support for the B squad & our family. When we say we love dogs we really mean we LOVE dogs. Thank you all!!! Nicole, Big Mac, the Frascati family & B Squad!

These orange tabby cuties you are seeing are Ollie and Bob. Ollie was rescued from a good samaritan's backyard. He looks chill in the picture but has been diagnosed with cerebellar hyperplasia, a developmental condition that causes the cerebellum (part of the brain that controls fine motor skills) fails to develop properly. Luckily, the condition is not painful or contagious. His rescuer noticed his legs were very shaky and he had trouble walking - she was able to bring him indoors and contacted Hyde Park Cats for help. We facilitated neurological testing to identify the source of his instability. There is no treatment, but he is still able to live a happy and healthy life in a loving home and is adoption ready! The cat to the left side is Bob, a friendly 2-year-old orange tabby who was recently rescued. He was found by Hyde Park Cats with his tail damaged near the base. To aid in his quality of life, Bob had to undergo emergency surgery to have his tail amputated. Bob thus got his name from his “Bobtail” and will soon be ready for adoption for a warm home. We've helped hundreds of cats like Ollie and Bob with food, medical, and foster care. 2022 has been an unprecedented year of abandoned cats and an explosion of kittens - many found to be sick and injured. Many of our furry clients need extensive medical care, which has depleted our financial reserves and supplies. Chicago area rescues and shelters have been completely full, although this has been a national issue post-pandemic. Hyde Park Cats have committed what we can to support the community and help these poor little friends. We haven't turned any person or cat away that needed help. We need your help to continue our rescue efforts! It costs roughly $125 to get a cat ready for adoption, which includes spay-neuter, microchip, SNAP testing, and vaccines. This does not cover any additional expenses incurred if the cat needs additional medical intervention. We are a 100% volunteer-powered, non-profit rescue - so every donation we get goes towards caring for our cats. Thank you so much for your time and support. Hyde Park Cats counts on every donation, regardless of size, to continue our mission of helping cats and kittens in and beyond our community. More about Hyde Park Cats: Hyde Park Cats is a 501 (c) (3) non-profit organization operated completely by volunteers working to improve the lives of feral, stray, and needy cats and kittens in and around Chicago's Hyde Park neighborhood. We have had over 1000 adoptions since our founding in 2008 and have a robust network of loving foster homes and about 200 adoptions annually. We take in abandoned friendly cats from the street and rehome them. All the cats we admit are spayed or neutered before adoption, as we contribute to the long-term reduction of cat homelessness. When space permits, we welcome cats from open-access shelters as part of our long-term aim of reducing the number of friendly, healthy, and adoptable cats who are euthanized in shelters. We also aim to educate the general public about these issues.

WE REACHED OUR GOAL!! Please help us raise the money for Chester's Laryngeal Tie back surgery Chester spent most of his life living in a kennel and hunting during the bird season. His owner decided to surrender Chester to Central California Labrador Retriever Rescue this past summer. We knew when we took Chester in that he had laryngeal paralysis. LarPar causes the flaps on the larynx to become paralyzed and not function properly, affecting the ability to breathe normally. In some cases, the paralysis is slight and can be managed. When the paralysis advances it can become a dire situation for the dog, with the worst outcome being suffocation. When Chester first came to us, we needed to be mindful of the heat and limit his exercise to the cooler part of the day with shortened play sessions, but he could still enjoy all his favorite activities. Over the last month, Chester has developed episodes of limited ability to breathe...a terrifying thing. These episodes last a few minutes and then his breathing will return to a much less labored inhale and exhale. Chester was taken in to have his larynx scoped, Xrays of lungs and abdomen and blood work done to start the process for surgery. Tie-back surgery will allow continued airflow in and out of the lungs. This surgery is the only option for Chester. He just started to enjoy life outside of a kennel and experience the fun and freedom every dog deserves. Chester is a healthy (aside from LarPar), happy, energetic boy. Please help give Chester the ability to breathe and enjoy his favorite things again. Hi, My name is Allie May. I am an undergrad BFA student at CSULB due to graduate in Spring 2023. I am making this post today on behalf of my cat, Jenny. She is a Turkish Van and Applehead Siamese Mix. I adopted her back in June 2021. At the time, I was going through some pretty significant life changes. I was going through an emotional breakup and had to move to Long Beach to attend college on campus. At this time, I felt very alone and craved the unconditional love that could come from having a pet. Little did I know, Jenny would be the most loving cat I have ever met. I saw her post on a Facebook Community Group for foster cats. I found her black-and-white pattern so beautiful and her polydactylism so unique. Nothing could have prepared me for the amount of genuine unprovoked affection that she has to give. It might be the siamese in her, but she is very talkative and has such a sweet, docile, passive personality. She loves to give kisses and sleeps right by my side every night. She will even go as far as to use her paw to dig up the blanket and crawl under it to get closer. She even has "zoomies" where she sprints around the apartment as fast as possible. I am in the process of trying to get her a big cat wheel again, so she can continue to enjoy running. Before Jenny, I had a lot of pet rats. For those of you who do not know about rats, they have a really short lifespan, approximately 2-4 years. Although they are incredible pets with immense intelligence and personality, it is challenging to cope with how little time you have with them. Even people who do not like rodents can recognize that when one has a pet and loves it like family, it is a huge loss when they are not of your life anymore. With that said, I was so excited to finally get a cat because they potentially have lifespans from 12-18+ years. Even when I adopted her at age four, I had started envisioning Jenny in my future. I am only 24, and I could see her being there for graduation and the transition into my adult career. Perhaps this is wishful thinking, but I could also visualize Jenny being there for my first child. So when I noticed a mass was growing on the left side of her neck, I knew that I would have to start coping with the fact that Jenny would not be there. In fact, I might have even less time than I would in comparison to a rat's lifespan. I adopted her approximately one year, four months and twenty-one days ago. Jenny was diagnosed with an aggressive form of FIV (Feline Immunodeficiency Virus) and Lymphoma. As explained to me, 75% of cats respond positively to chemotherapy and go into "remission." This will depend on the levels of her white blood cell count. The other 25% of cats can become resistant to chemotherapy and will be treated with steroids to be kept comfortable. If Jenny becomes resistant to the treatment, she has perhaps 1-2 months to live. If she responds positively to the treatment, she has hopefully 6-9 months. Financially, I was given three options. The most aggressive chemo treatment (which I cannot afford), the intermediate chemotherapy option that is more affordable, and the cheapest option are only steroids to keep her comfortable until her passing. The intermediate Chemotherapy costs would be $516 every 3-6 weeks, not including the blood tests needed to study how she reacts to the treatments. Every blood test will be $100. I also do not have a driver's license, so I pay the Lyft fees every time she has an appointment. I have a part-time job teaching children art remotely and another part-time job on campus. I receive a monthly housing allowance through the Veterans Affairs Disability Compensation because of my father's status as a disabled Veteran. However, with all the living costs, I still struggle to pay rent and buy groceries. I chose to try and take on the Intermediate Chemotherapy treatment because although I am fighting for so little time, I figure it is better than nothing. Any amount of money given towards Jenny's treatment is potentially time added to her life. I would greatly appreciate any amount just to have more time with her. Thank you for your time, Allie

After several years of dreaming, planning, and preparations, our sweet 6-month-old Avila arrived at our farm in Central Oregon. Avila is a special girl--a foundation Appaloosa, a breed developed by the Nez Perce that was nearly eradicated by the US Government during the westward expansion. These magical horses are known for their bravery, intelligence, and soundness of mind, and Avila embodies all of these wonderful qualities. Unfortunately, Avila arrived with a slight lameness that progressed rapidly into her almost complete inability to walk. We rushed her to the emergency vet and, after several hours during which she received multiple x-rays and other diagnostics, she was diagnosed with a rare joint infection. We were told that Avial required aggressive treatment, probably surgery, and possibly months of follow-up treatments. The vets were cautiously optimistic. We were warned that she might never fully recover due to bone loss in her rear right fetlock (ankle). Needless to say, were devastated. Since we did not have the funds to support Avila's medical needs, we made the heartbreaking decision to send her back to the farm, Vision Quest Appaloosas, in Spokane Washington, where her previous owner can provide the specialized care Avila requires and deserves. We are hoping that as a result, she will fully recover and be able to come back home to us. At this time, Avila is receiving good care, which includes intravenous antibiotics, a special diet, and restricted movement. Blood tests show that the infection is abating somewhat, which is great news! Avila will remain on this course for thirty days after which her health will be reevaluated to see if she will still require surgery at Washington State University. With every passing day, Avila's medical costs continue to grow and we could not in good conscience sit by and do nothing. So, we--Jen, John, and I--have decided to start this fundraiser to help Avila's team give her the absolute best care! Kata is a Sweet, 12-year-old dog with chronic renal disease and needs all the help she can get! Four years ago, Kata was found wandering the streets of Puerto Rico, where a group of volunteers, known as Dachshund Rescue, brought her to Florida (USA), dropping her off with me as her foster mom. From the moment I met her, I knew she’d had a rough life: her front tooth had all fallen out, and her stride was permanently weak on the right side. We connected immediately, only growing closer over the following days. It was in the kindness in her eyes, her toothless smile and the way she nuzzled up to me that I knew we could make a family together, so I adopted her! Ever since, Kata has been every bit as happy and healthy as I hoped she would be, and even though no one knows her age for sure, the vet estimates that she is twelve years old, which is around the age that some of the more complex health problems tend to kick in. Sadly, that is exactly what happened in the past two months. Shaking uncontrollably, throwing up bile, constant diarrhea and refusing food, Kata exhibited symptoms unlike any I had ever seen from her before, and I knew she was in pain. The diagnosis was as frightening as it was life-threatening: chronic renal disease, which in simple terms, means her kidneys are unable to function at optimal levels and will continue to decline. Left untreated, this disease can cause multiple heart attacks, multi-organ failure, and ultimately death within only a few weeks. For four days, Kata remained in the hospital with an aggressive treatment and high doses of intravenous fluids to “flush out” her kidneys and remove the accumulated toxins from her bloodstream. Once discharged, Kata struggled quite a bit to recover, and I thought I would lose her at any moment. It took over three weeks – and a lot of meds four times a day – for her to return to her usual, happy self. Here is the problem: between her hospitalization, home treatment, and medications, the bills have been overwhelming during this time, and I have run up a tremendous credit card debt to save Kata’s life. Her four-day hospital stay came out to $6,500, while her lifetime medications and kidney check-ups will cost around $250 monthly for the rest of her life. This is why Kata and I desperately need your help! If you have ever loved a fur baby, then you know no price is too high in situations like this, so I did the only thing I could do: step up for Kata. Fortunately, this saved her life, but as we move forward, my financial stability remains woefully outside my reach, considering these mounting bills as a single dog mom of three rescues -especially after losing my corporate job due to COVID. As dogs cannot survive without their kidneys and chronic renal disease is not curable and cannot be reversed, I’ve decided to humbly turn to you for help to ensure the best quality of life I can offer to Kata until her last breath, while being able to pay back my credit cards before the interest rate starts to pile up. So, from our family to yours, thank you for getting this far in reading about what has happened to us and for any help you can provide to keep Kata’s kidneys functioning as long and as optimally as possible. Please know that no donation is too small, and whatever you can contribute will be greatly appreciated! Even if you are unable to contribute financially, it will be a blessing if you can share this campaign with your friends and family. Thank you from the bottom of our hearts (and kidneys!)

Unfortunately, once a cat has a urinary blockage, it is likely to happen again, which is exactly what occurred last night, December 27th. Remy's only options were to either have PU surgery to give him a better quality of life or to do the catheter again with no guarantees he will not block again in the future. The bill for his first blockage was $3,500 and the surgery that is needed is estimated between $6,300 to $6,735. We are not in a position where we're able to afford such expensive treatment or future medical bills, not to mention the prescription food and medications he will need after. We greatly appreciate any help we can get or even just well wishes and prayers for Remy. We love him so much and, above all, are so grateful we brought him in when we did.

Concrete and dirt, that’s all Katsu knew. Katsu spent every day, all day living in a backyard in extreme desert conditions. His bed was 2 holes he dug in the dirt himself on the side of the house with no shelter covering his makeshift bed. He had a pungent odor, over grown dewclaws almost growing into his skin, and feces running down his bottom and paws. Katsu got to go home with everything he owned, which was only a container of dog food no collar or leash. He was so excited when the gate opened it was like he knew he was taking his freedom ride! We knew he needed to see a vet right away given the condition he was in; bulldogs NEED humans to intervene and assist with their self-care. It is crucial that all their pockets and folds are cleaned and on a daily basis. These squishy face guys come with a list of health problems, so to neglect his care for almost 2 years has been detrimental to his health. According to his records the last time he saw a vet was at 5 months old (Katsu will be celebrating his 2nd birthday this month). Katsu got his freedom ride but this ride turned into a series of vet visits. First Vet Visit: Katsu had multiple infections and extreme diarrhea; he was prescribed several medications. Its amazing with all thats going on with him this boy is just so happy to be out and about. Second Vet Visit: Whilst bathing him one day we noticed green discharge from his tail pocket, the more I cleaned around it the stronger the smell got. Katsu was in pain anytime we touched his rear; he absolutely did not like it and would bite, it takes 2 of us to clean his back end. We took him to the vet again and Katsu got an extension of antibiotics to try and clear the infection. Third Vet Visit: We then made an appointment and saw a specialist to determine the severity of his tail and if Katsu’s tail needed to be amputated. We were advised that Katsu indeed a tail amputation due to the deep infection and improper growth his screw tail. Fourth Vet Visit: Katsu underwent surgery for his tail amputation and neuter. Whilst he was under we made sure that he also got all of his vaccines and heart worm test. You guessed it! His heartworm test came back POSITIVE!!! Katsu will soon have to undergo heartworm treatment. Fifth Vet Visit: Fast forward.. 2 days after his surgery we took another trip to the vet as he got an infection in his tail amputation incision which of coursed he went home with another medication and due for a follow up visit in a week. We have volunteered with rescues in the past and helped other dogs but have never been in this position with this much unanticipated expense. It has already exhausted our limited funds, and we also have 4 children to care for. Gas prices are insanely high and we are constantly filling up the tank. Katsu has a fantastic vet but each trip is an hour drive each way. We are trying to heal him from the inside out; this meant Katsu also needs to be on high quality food which is also a big addition on top of his medical expenses. We want to continue to help Katsu to give him that second chance he deserves, but our battle is not close to being over yet and his bill keeps increasing. We have already hit $1767.08 just in current medical bills. Katsu still needs to get better before he can undergo heartworm treatment; I’ve been told this procedure will take time and can be quite costly. I can’t even begin to fathom what those numbers will look like. Katsu is a typical bulldog – oh so stubborn. He of course had no training, doggy or house manners, so on top of his health we have been diligently working on all the basics. He has cleaned up nicely, you wouldn’t be able to tell from looking at him that he’s had a rough past and his body is desperately trying to fight infections. Katsu keeps his head high and walks around with a smile on his face curious to what he will discover next. He yearns to make up for lost affection, gets excited to go on walks and meet new people. Katsu has only started to begin exploring his new world; he wants this second change and surely deserves it. Anything helps to go towards his medical bills; your donation is greatly appreciated. Thank you for taking the time to read Katsu’s story and supporting him on his way to recovery! I will continue to update his story... *10/24/22: another vet trip - After the infection in the tail amputation area, the sutures started to loosen as the infection began to heal. Katsu went under again to tighten the sutures. They did a great job and cleaned him up again. Looks like in the near future, we will also be needing a dental in addition to heartworm treatment. **** 10/27/2022 today we celebrated Katsu's birthday. We're unsure if he ever had his birthday celebrated, but we made sure to let him know his birthday is special. Cheers to new beginnings! ***10/17/22 Today was the day for suture removal! Unfortunately, Katsu was not ready and need to wait at least another week and another round of antibiotics. ***11/07/22 The sutures were finally removed today!!! Still have to wait a week until he can have a MUCH NEEDED BATH. **11/20/22 The healing is going great, and he's growing back some hair. We waited a little longer to have a bath "just in case."
