Hi, my name is Jake, and I'm fundraising for my dog Jax so that he can receive his second ACL surgery. I adopted my dog Jax on October 23rd, 2020 from Secondhand Hounds in the middle of the pandemic. Jax is a husky german shepherd mix full of energy and personality who helped keep me active and sane during isolation. Little did I know Jax would lead me to discover my passion for dog training, eventually carving out a new career path together. Jax and I settled into a fun routine of going to the dog park every morning and a long walk in the evening with training sessions in between. We went on trips to Grand Marais, hiking the trails up gunflint in the dead of winter. I became accustomed to bringing him everywhere with me, even quick trips to the grocery store. Being active with him became the parts of my day I looked forward to the most, and I know he felt the same way. In all that time, Jax never had a reason to go to the vet except for routine vaccinations. Thats why it came as a complete and utter shock when in May of 2022 Jax tore his ACL (or CCL as it's known in dogs) on his back left leg while running at the dog park. He was unable to put weight on it. He had to limp and hop his way through life in constant pain and depression for two months before receiving TPLO surgery (Tibial Plateau Leveling Osteotomy) in July. Thankfully during his second week of recovery, Jax started putting weight back on his leg, started to seem more like his happy self, and was even enjoying some slow and steady walks around the block. Unfortunately, after having his stitches removed, he developed an infection and regressed to not putting any weight on it. This was devastating for Jax and I. Developing this type of infection after CCL surgery is uncommon and watching Jax experience such intense pain and discomfort again was truly awful. The infection required an additional six weeks of recovery on expensive antibiotics. After 14 weeks of healing and recovering from this setback, it has been discovered that the infection has returned and the metal plate in his leg must be removed. On top of that, Jax has now torn the ACL on his right side because of all the extra weight and overcompensation he has had to place on it. Jax is only 5 years old and has a lot of life left in him, but I am not even close to paying off the first surgery and sadly no pet insurance will consider him now as the CCL tear is considered a pre-existing condition. These procedures are incredibly expensive, and after weeks of research and professional opinions, there are no good alternatives. So Jax and I are asking for your help; every little bit makes a difference and gets him closer to the road of recovery. He and I are hopeful that this could be the beginning of a new chapter for us, and we're both so grateful for any support you can offer us. If contributing to this GoFundMe isn't an option for any reason, please keep Jax in your thoughts and prayers AND consider sharing my dog training website with anyone who might need a trainer! I'd love to support others in creating a relationship with their dog that is as loving and joyful as mine with Jax! Thank you again for reading and supporting us in any way that is comfortable to you! We are so grateful.

If you can donate, it’s genuinely so appreciated. But if you’re unable to, we completely understand ❤️ Long story, cut “short”: I took in 2 severely malnourished ferrets from a girl, during late May of this year. The male (Sailor) survived, but the female (who he was bonded with), ended up dying in my arms, the exact same night I received them. As the weeks continued, Sailor was closely monitored by my vet and I. He initially only weighed 308 grams (you could literally feel every single bone of his skull), he had gallbladder sludge, his liver values were awful, and he was infested with earmites. As weeks went by (with many syringe feedings and meds later), Sailor improved drastically. His weight skyrocketed up to 980 grams, his gallbladder sludge cleared up perfectly, the earmites were completely gone. The only thing that wasn’t *picture perfect*, were his liver values. While monitoring his liver over several months, I went ahead and bonded Sailor with 2 females, that are almost the exact same age as him. These girls were also “rescues”, but they were nowhere near in as bad of a situation as Sailor was, and in my head, the main goal was to always make sure that Sailor was the happiest he could ever be, from the day I took him in. Between caring for Sailor throughout these past months, and vetting the females prior to them bonding, I’ve paid quite a large amount of money, within a very short period of time. Last week, both girls were diagnosed with Adrenal Disease and needed the Deslorelin implant (which they of course immediately received). Then two days later, Sailors routine bloodwork came back, and his liver values were (surprisingly) significantly worse, after trending downwards throughout this past year. Currently, the plan for Sailor is to do a sedated CT scan (where he’s put under full anesthesia, has an IV, and his entire abdomen is scanned for abnormalities). That procedure was quoted at $800, and is scheduled to happen on November 18th. Based on the answers we receive from that, he will then be scheduled to have a surgical biopsy done on his liver, which will require him to be sedated and (most likely) have an IV during that procedure as well. I love this noodle with everything in me, and I would literally move mountains, just to make sure he never feels unloved in his lifetime, ever again. His vet bills are extremely pricey though, and I’d be lying if I said that I haven’t been building pretty decent debt. Anything is helpful, truly. If you are able to donate, thank you times a million. If you aren’t, just “well wishes” still mean the absolute world to us!

All donations will go immediately to reimbursing the out-of-pocket costs of Hope’s vet and surgery bills. We’re hoping that those who knew and loved Jen will pitch in what they can in her memory. By the way, Hope is looking for her forever home or even a foster home. (Current photo of Hope attached. She likes to sit on top of the warm refrigerator!) Please inquire if you would like to meet her. You will never meet a more grateful and loving cat. She has taught us that so many things are possible with hope. While working in Rhodes this year I was visited every night by this gorgeous stray baby girl, only a few months old. I always fed her and gave her cuddles and blankets. In May, she became pregnant and visited me more frequently, sometimes sleeping inside my apartment where she felt safe. She is the most loving and cuddly cat I have ever met. Very early one morning in July, I was woken up by her outside my door crying uncontrollably. She had been hit by a car, was covered in blood and couldn't walk. She needed medical attention immediately, so I took her to Rhodes town to the nearest Vet Surgery where they, unfortunately, had to remove her whole uterus with her growing kittens as well as operating on her leg - adding a big metal pole to enable her to walk eventually. Costing over 600€. I kept her in a cage in my apartment for 10 days until she was stronger. Everything looked brighter until she grew a big ball of fluid on her hip due to infection, and she started taking antibiotics. As my work contract ended in August and I flew home, I made arrangements for her to be taken care of until I could book her flights to move country. In September, I took flights back to Rhodes to sort her injections and pet passport before flying with her to Italy and making her happy at home here. Flights & Passport costing around 500€. The ball of fluid was still causing problems, so we took her to have this checked. After an X-Ray we discovered that the metal pole inserted in the leg in Rhodes was far too big for her little body and needed to be removed/replaced. The vet believed Jimmy's leg was strong enough to remove the pole, so this was done on Monday in her 3rd operation. Costing 250€. On Wednesday we woke up to find her trembling and crying. She wouldn't eat or drink and could not move much at all. We immediately took her to the vet who X-rayed to find the leg was completely snapped in half as she was not strong enough to be left without a metal pole. Costing 180€. The vet is not able to perform the following operation, and we are now awaiting an appointment with a specialist to be able to save our poor baby girl's leg. We have been informed this will be a very costly operation at 800€ and would appreciate ANY help you can offer our beautiful and loving Jimmy to receive the help she needs.

Hi all <3 This campaign is to help with Jody’s emergency heart failure treatment costs. Jody is the spunkiest, cutest, spryest, sweetest little gremlin-chihuahua mix who - if we hadn't received her diagnosis two weeks ago - nobody would ever guess was sick. She’s middle-aged (her life expectancy is 12-16 years, and she’s 8) but still has a little pup's energy, enthusiasm, and appetite. Two months ago I noticed something was wrong with Jody. We visited the vet and the xrays, bloodwork, and urinalysis showed that she was perfectly healthy. They thought she might be experiencing allergies in response to our new city and possibly changing hormones typical of middle-aged female chihuahuas. We carried on and she seemed to be doing well, and I thought whatever the flare up was had passed. But then two weeks ago, we had come back home from a morning walk and I noticed that Jody was panting even after settling in. We had been relaxed for 30 minutes so it was alarming, and her respiratory rate seemed to only be increasing. I remembered then that she also wasn’t too interested in her breakfast that morning which is s u p e r unlike her. After a quick phone consult we were referred to an emergency vet who instructed us to come in asap. They said what I described indicated she needed oxygen right away and her heart was probably in trouble. They kept her overnight to get her stable and come up with a treatment plan (the longest, most unpleasant night I’ve experienced in a long time), and determined it was what they thought: Congestive Heart Failure. The incredibly good news is that it looks like we caught it quite early and her prognosis is positive. She hasn’t ever and still doesn’t have a cough, her energy is 110% as always, and her appetite is back to extra hearty. She’s responding totally ideally to her new medications and - again thankfully since we were able to intervene early - everything indicates she still has at least a few more good years ahead of her. I went to TX for the weekend and came back to find his leg had swollen so much his old scar burst open and got infected. If you know me, you know I am an animal lover. Most of the time, I prefer to be around animals over humans. I pulled over and waited there for about an hour, went around and knocked on a few doors, and got a lot of honks and middle fingers for blocking the road. I got him loaded up in my car and rushed him home. He was bleeding badly from his feet, abdomen, and nose, so I cleaned him up as best as I could. I left him in the car and I comforted him until we could find an emergency vet. I was sure he wasn’t going to make it, but then I remembered it was my birthday. I looked back at him, and with the eye contact he gave me I knew that I had to save him. I truly believe that this opportunity to save his life was thrown at me, especially on a day when I turned 26 years old. So, I ran inside and grabbed some towels, water, and crackers, and I started to get hopeful. He became more coherent and lifted his head up and drink an entire bowl of water. He licked all over my hands and I sat there rubbing him and talking to him. After getting a call back from the vet, I rushed him in and it was immediately assessed that he had head trauma and a broken femur in his back right leg. I was advised to leave him there with the vet. After a few hours, they called me and let me know that they’d found his owners. I begged them to please keep me updated, and after a long 28 hours, they gave me an update. His official diagnosis is a severely shattered femur which will require extensive surgery to put plates and rods in, as well as severe nerve damage in his front right leg, in addition to some head trauma and cuts and scrapes all over his body. As of now, we are unsure if he will be able to walk on his own again. The official vet bill costs are TBD, but I do know that it is going to be extremely expensive based on his injures. I will know more tomorrow on actual costs, but I would love to get a head start on gathering donations for this sweet baby. The road to recovery is going to be very bumpy, but I know that he will pull through. Having 3 dogs myself, while working a very extensive job and having a wife who is out of town in the fire academy, I will definitely be on the lookout for a reliable foster for him. The recovery will not be easy, especially since it is unknown if he will gain feeling back in his front legs. My name is Carole. Two years ago we adopted an angry, unhappy, and very sassy Maine Coon from our local Humane Society. His previous family adopted him as a kitten and then returned him a year later. He was a beautiful monster, angry at the world, abandoned, and lonely. We renamed him “Kaiju” which is a Japanese word that means “strange beast” (loosely) and was coined to describe the terrible monsters of film and print. You may know them better as Godzilla, Gamera, Mothra, and King Ghidorah. This seemed to fit him extremely well. Over time he gained more names. The Flüf, Kaiju the Magnificent, Angel, Cutiewah, and Devilbaby (just to name a few). These names came as he settled more and more into our lives and became part of our family permanently. A year ago we lost our beloved cat Crosby and Kaiju helped us through the loss. Imagine our horror when, less than a year later, Kaiju began showing signs of illness. A quick visit to the vet at the beginning of September yielded a tentative diagnosis of pyelonephritis (acute kidney infection). He seemed to improve for a week before crashing again, this time with elevated kidney values and a markedly enlarged right kidney. He needed more care than our local vet was able to provide. This prompted the first of many trips to Purdue University in West Lafayette to the excellent small animal hospital there. Purdue is an hour and a half from our home and we made this trip in the hopes of finding out what was wrong with our beautiful boy. After a week, Purdue had narrowed it down to one of four diagnoses - atypical ascending pyelonephritis, renal lymphoma, another type of unspecified kidney cancer, or non-effusive feline infectious peritonitis (FIP). During his stay he experienced an internal bleed from a fine needle aspirate taken while trying to figure him out. That was the day we learned about blood transfusions in cats. Moving forward through more hospital stays and more diagnostic tests. We finally ruled out lymphoma as a cause, pyelonephritis seemed highly unlikely as they were unable to recover anything in culture, and the other kidney cancers did not fit. We finally were given a tentative diagnosis of FIP. FIP, left untreated, is 100% fatal. Treatment for FIP is extremely expensive and involves medication for 84 days minimum. We were able to get him started on the medication and saw a pretty great improvement. It’s working! Unfortunately, fate has intervened again. He has developed an infection in his feeding tube site. Not a big deal except the FIP is depressing his immune system and the infection is much worse than it would be otherwise. We are currently on our way back to Purdue to try and save him with IV antibiotics and, once again, round the clock veterinary care. They are excellent and we can only hold onto our faith in their abilities and care. We have lost so many pets these past few years to untreatable and unavoidable illnesses. We can’t bear to lose Kaiju, too. He is far too young to be facing these kinds of hardships at only 3 1/2 years old. I am reaching the end of my personal resources. This awful journey has been extremely expensive and I can’t bear the thought of getting this close to him making it through alive and just running out of money and credit. I can’t even express the amount of gratitude Earl and I would feel towards anyone who can help us. I hate asking more than anything but I love him more than my pride. I am already in this for close to $20k, and that number will only continue to rise. He’s not ready to go and we’re determined to save him unless there’s just no other choice. We will let him go if we need to but as long as he can make it through, we’re going to give him everything we can. We love him so much. We’ve had to let go of so many before him and losing him, too, would be just too much for our hearts to bear.

When I think I have cried all I can about this, it hits me again like a sucker punch. At sixty-three, suffering a broken heart in addition to my other heart issues is not something I should be going through due to the inexplicable acts of these two incredibly thoughtless individuals that are certainly old enough to know better. Those of you that know the Cavalier King Charles Spaniel as a breed know how gentle, calm, sweet and docile they are. You also know how trusting they are of people, the kind of dog who has never met a stranger. I know without a single doubt how confused and terrified my tiny little sweetheart must have been. These thoughts and the heartwrenching loss of such a special and beloved companion have kept me in a cycle of grief I am not sure will ever resolve. On Sept 15th, 2022, between 6-7 pm, while outside, my husband and I, at approximately 6:30, heard multiple gunshots, voices yelling back and forth, and a very loud vehicle revving and moving fast. I assumed it was someone on a four-wheeler chasing down a deer and trying to shoot it. Since we do not hunt and are unaware of when hunting seasons are, we did not give it much thought at the time. Sadly what I learned was that what had been up until then a relaxing evening was soon to turn into several days of sheer panic. I had taken my little house dog, a 12 lb Cavalier King Charles Spaniel named Princess, outside with me at 6 pm that evening. By 7 pm, I realized she was missing when she did not come to me when I called her to go back inside. Princess was my baby, my buddy, and my constant companion. She had nursed me through a slipped disc and emergency spinal surgery this year, never leaving her spot snuggled under my arm with her sweet little head on my shoulder. She was my nurse and my emotional support pup in every way. I love all animals, yet there are those pets that you mesh with more than others. The ones that become a part of your soul. Princess and I had that kind of connection. So as you can imagine, the panicked search for her began immediately. We were up late into the night, calling, searching, and checking every nook and cranny on the farm. I started to believe that someone must have snatched her, but how? At our place, it would be hard to do that, it was still daylight, and we were only outside for an hour. At midnight I tried to lie down and convince myself that come the morning light, I would find her. Up calling for her on the hour all night, my hopes were starting to dwindle. All daylight hours Friday and into the night again, no Princess. Where could she possibly be? She was never very far from me and always came like a lightning bolt when called. Saturday morning, we rushed off to a nearby outdoor swap meet to see if she had possibly been stolen and if someone might be there trying to sell her. Again no luck. Returning home about noon, I see a flock of vultures circling near the rear corner of our property. With a sinking feeling, I walk that direction to see what they were being drawn to. There lying on the ground, I find my precious pup. Now I am putting two and two together and realizing the chasing and gunfire I had heard in the woods Thursday evening was not anyone hunting a deer. I had heard more than one person's voice, at least one of them on a vehicle with a loud muffler moving fast and shooting. The sad truth is they had used it to chase down my sweet, gentle soul of a pup and use her for target practice, and I heard it while it was happening. Upon necropsy, it was confirmed that my pup had been shot with two different kinds of guns, one large caliber and one small caliber 3-4 times and left on the ground to rot like trash and be eaten by vultures. Where my dog was found who was likely responsible was not hard to deduct. So I filed a report with my sheriff's department, and a detective was assigned to my case. The detective, also an animal lover who expressed his love for his own dog, understood my grief. He interviewed the suspects separately; one lied, and the other confessed. Upon the second interview, the one who had denied it then admitted to killing my pup, but only after he learned his buddy in bloodsport had already revealed to the detective they both were involved. So here is where it stands. Both are 18, and so are legal adults. They are being charged with misdemeanor animal cruelty as per statute as it currently stands. The problem is it will amount to nothing more than a slap on the wrist for what they did and is easily expunged (erased). The detective relayed to me that the prosecutor advised that the best thing to do would be for me to file a civil case against them. I have found a lawyer who will take the case, and he tells me it's a very cut-and-dry win but very unlikely to collect any damages due to their ages and employment. Still very important to do in hopes that doing so will serve as a deterrent to future such acts, as well as essential to me for the chance to tell them what a terrible thing they did in person. I'm sure anything I say causing them any remorse is highly unlikely, but at least I will get to voice my grief to the judge or jury. That, at least, should offer me some element of closure. Princess was wearing a collar with an ID tag on it that had her name and my address, and phone number on it. The ID tag had mysteriously vanished from her collar when I found her remains. While I can not prove they took it for a souvenir, the type of people that would do what they did leaves a troubling question in my mind. I am fundraising to help with the costs of legal assistance so I can do all I can to make it clear to these cruel young men that they should pick better life choices than indiscriminately and brutally killing someone's beloved pet for no good reason. I also plan on pursuing better animal cruelty laws than are currently in force in my state. I have included all supporting documentation surrounding this event while leaving out the offenders' names until they have been officially convicted. I've also redacted the detective's name for now. The identifying details of all those involved will be revealed in future updates. Thank you for your time reading this. Help if you can, please share if you can't. I know that if you love a pet, that you have a special bond with, as I had with Princess, you understand. That alone means a lot. #animalcruelty #holdthemaccountable #betterlaws #gettheirheadsexamined #zerotolerance #noexcuse #saynotoanimalcruelty

Hi, my name is Stephen and I am fundraising for my pup Kirby. Monday started like any other day; I took Kirby out to go to the bathroom in the morning, fed him, told him I loved him, and I went to work. When I returned from work, Kirby was lying down, panting and whining. He wouldn't eat or drink anything, and he wouldn't stand up. He also had diarrhea. I promptly called the emergency vet and brought him in. After several exams, lab work, an X-ray, CT scan, and an ultrasound, the doctors found a tear in his rectum that also had significant tunneling; feces had infiltrated the tear and had infected his bloodstream. He also had a large amount of impacted stool further up in his colon. On top of all this, he also had a bit of pneumonia. Kirby needed to have emergency surgery to open up his abdomen to close the tear, clean out the area, and remove the impacted feces. After the surgery, he was put into a kennel with supplemental oxygen and was being given continuous fluids, antibiotics, and pain medications. He also had a wound drain and a urinary catheter put in. At this point he was very weak and the doctor was worried that he might not make it through the night. Update for 10/26: Kirby has been moved to a larger kennel and no longer needs supplemental oxygen. He had a feeding tube placed overnight and is now getting nutrition. He is still on continuous fluids and antibiotics. The good news is that it looks like he has gained some energy back; however, he still is not able to stand on his own. He is also being given an appetite stimulant to help him get back on solid food. Kirby still has a long road to recovery in order for him to come back home. His body has been through a lot these past few days and he is still considered critical at this point, and he will need to spend several more days in the hospital. He is a strong pup and the best boy so I know he is also working his hardest to come home. Update 10/27 Kirby has gained a little bit of strength back and even took a short walk around the clinic this morning. His red blood cell count and protein levels have dipped a bit so his tube feeding is being increased and he is also getting an infusion of plasma tonight. Update 10/28 Kirby continues to gain strength back and even went and walked outside today, although he still needs a little bit of help standing up. He is still not too interested in eating solid food quite yet so the feeding tube is still in place. The plan right now is to continue rest, fluids, and antibiotics and get him more interested in eating solid food.

My boyfriend and I took a brisk November walk in the park last weekend. When we sat down on a bench to feed the ducks in the pond, two very small juvenile cats appeared out of the woods behind us. They seemed a bit shy, but very curious about the corn and peas we had tossed around. We started feeding them, and looked for any signs of ownership such as collars or spay tattoos, but couldn’t see any. They were social enough to take food from our hands, but skittish enough they didn’t want to be touched. A woman jogging by told us that she walks this park almost daily, and these kittens have been living in the thicket for months. That’s when I knew we had to help them. They were so small, probably only 6-8 months old. They had been getting by off duck food, but with a briar patch as their only shelter, they were completely exposed to the coming winter. And then things got urgent. We discovered cat #3, who had a fishing hook caught in his lip. He led us to the fourth and final cat, who was a great deal skinnier than the other littermates. I called everyone I could think of- Animal Control, local shelters, the humane society, etc. No one would help us trap them, and everywhere we could take them was at capacity. Our only option was to catch and foster them ourselves, or hope they wouldn’t freeze. Over the course of the next 3 days, we spent countless hours trying and trying again to trap these cats and get them the food, shelter, and medical care they urgently needed. Neither of us knew anything about rescuing kittens, but miraculously we were able to get all four of them home. The kitty with the fish hook went immediately to the pet urgent care for surgery and is good as new. The rest went to the vet and got treated for worms and parasites. None of them had microchips. It was a scary couple of first days, but they are all on the road to complete health. They are still a bit timid, but are showing great signs for being socialized. With their condition, I don’t trust a shelter not to euthanize them or dump them back outside since they’re technically strays, back in the snow. We love these fur babies so much, but we have already dug ourselves into a money pit. The cost of suddenly taking in 4 sick or injured animals was definitely unexpected and nothing we’ve done before. The urgent vet bills as well as food/other basic necessities have already cost over $1k. Once they’re healthy enough, we will also need to get them spayed/neutered and vaccinated. We’re estimating this will cost an additional $1k. I know there are a lot of problems in the world- bigger, human problems. But these little kitties deserve a chance. Someone most likely abandoned this litter in the woods months ago, and I don’t want to abandon them too. Anything helps, and everything will go straight to the cats to help them thrive until we can find them loving homes.

Ms. Lillian Sprout was diagnosed with Addison's Disease in the summer of 2020. Addison's disease in dogs (hypoadrenocorticism) occurs when your dog's adrenal glands aren't producing adequate corticosteroid hormones. These dogs can live long, happy lives if diagnosed and treated appropriately. However, with Lily that is not the case as she has a very unique and complicated case. Though she is treated by the best vets, she often experiences episodes of crisis where she exhibits gastrointestinal complications such as vomiting, not eating, and having trouble using the bathroom. She is prescribed high levels of Fludrocortisone and Prednisone daily. She was FINALLY on the mend and having the time of her life, displaying characteristics of Lily before her initial crisis (playful, sassy, and affectionate). Recently, she had begun to exhibit signs and symptoms that we have not seen since her original diagnosis in 2020. She was not at all the dog I knew. Lily became lethargic (needing to be carried everywhere and often collapsing at her destination), vomiting regularly, having trouble using the bathroom, not eating, not drinking, not being able to regulate her internal temperature, and bleeding (both in vomit and out her bottom), and visibly in excruciating pain. She became a shell of a dog but still made it her mission to wag her tail when you showed any concern. With these symptoms, we JUMPED into action and brought her to the emergency veterinary center (two to be exact). The first conducted blood tests and provided her with fluids, and a steroid medication. Leaving us with a referral to another emergency vet because they could not give the acute and serious care that Lily needed. We booked an appointment to see an internal medicine and critical care doctor, however, the earliest appointment is more than a month away. THIS IS A LIFE-OR-DEATH SITUATION! So we brought her to another emergency vet who was more capable of implementing treatments and meeting her needs. She has now been placed in the ICU and will be needing an intensive ultrasound, endoscopy, an NG/NE tube, x-rays, around-the-clock care, etc. Lily is 4 years old, she is too young to be given up until all interventions are utilized or she shows that she can no longer tolerate the interventions and we must accept our losses. Let me start off by saying that if you know me, you know that I hate asking for help, especially financial help. But it has come time that I will need some assistance unfortunately to pay for Lilly Bean’s expenses. Here’s a timeline of unfortunate events: I adopted Lilly Bean, formerly named Oakley, in October of 2021. She was 8 weeks old and was found after hurricane Ida with her sister. An amazing foster, Sally, took them in and bottle fed them until they were ready for adoption. In November, she was diagnosed with wet FIP. It is a virus, a cornonavirus specifically for cats, that most cats have but only a few will mutate. It has historically been deadly to cats, they will only live on average a few weeks after the fluid accumulates in their abdomen. Through some amazing friends and vets, I was introduced to the FIP Warriors Facebook page where the admins helped me to acquire some life-saving meds. I treated her with a shot that burns under the skin every day for 84 days. We both hated it but somehow made it through. She was back to normal and doing much better until April where she spiked a very high fever and had three seizures while in hospital. We began treatment again. In July, I was at a horseshow in Colorado and broke my ankle “hiking” on a mountainside. Surgery was July 15...a plate and 9 screws. I was out of work for 6 weeks. We finished Lilly’s 2nd round of treatments on July 14, the night before surgery. All was well and she was back to being a playful, loving kitten until last Sunday. She showed neurological signs. I brought her in to the clinic and we ran some tests, she has now relapsed for a 3rd time but this time it’s much worse. She has dry FIP, rendering her ataxic and blind. She had another seizure on Wednesday in hospital but it was controlled. She can now see again thanks to beginning the meds proactively. Here we go with a 3rd round of shots. This time she has to have 3 shots per day. She is so tired and so sore. Her poor little body wants to give up but she’s ready to fight! This round of the meds are covered (thanks to some amazing FIP Warrior admins) and we are not giving up on her yet! However, during all of this time, she has racked up quite a bill at my vets office with all of the tests, supportive meds and hospital stays. Any little bit will help. Please help me save my baby’s life. She promises only to growl and hiss a little bit But if you ask for sugars she will give you a lick on the nose.

A Message from Austins Human Parents: Hi! This is Austin. He was born on March 9th, 2022. and came home on May 9th. He is an amazing boy! He likes to keep the floors clean, lol. He puts everything on his bed, toys, socks, shoes, towels... anything he can find on the floor goes on his bed. At around thirteen weeks old, he stopped playing, stopped putting up his toys, and wasn't eating much. We thought he had a bug and would bounce back the next day. Oh boy, were we wrong! The next day he stopped eating and started to walk into the walls. He would walk and put his head in the corner. We knew he needed to go straight to the vet! I called his vet and told them what he was doing. His vet (Mountain View in Keyser WV [phone redacted]) asked how fast we could get him there. The vet suspected that it was a liver shunt. She gave him some medications and special food to eat and asked us to bring him back in two days for testing. The next morning, he still didn't look good and was wobbly. We knew he could not wait another day to go back to the vet. So, the very next day, I called the vet and told them he was on his way back. They only asked how far away he was. They took him in back as soon as he got there and started testing. They confirmed he did in fact have a liver shunt and started him on an IV to flush his system. He began to have brain trimmers, and the vet did not think he would live through the night. We all wanted to give him the best fighting chance, but we did not want to see him suffer. So, the vet took him home and kept his IV going. To everyone's surprise, he started to bounce back! Today he is seven months old, and he weighs 8 lbs. He has to have two medications twice a day before he eats, and he has to eat prescription dog food. He is not allowed to eat any protein. It makes the toxins in his body spike to deadly levels. He could live like this, but it will cut his life very short, and he is very lucky to have made it this far. He has his good days and his bad days. There is a surgery that he can get to close the shunt, and he would have a normal life. He would be able to eat regular dog food and even have a treat! On October 27th, he goes to Bush Advanced Veterinary Imaging [phone redacted] 165 Fort Evans Rd. Leesburg VA 20176) to have a CT done to show where the shunt is. The cost is $1,395-$1,495. Then he will go to Dr. Ganjei at Veterinary Surgical Center [phone redacted] 140 Park Street SE Vienna VA 22180) for the surgery. This surgery will cost anywhere from $8,000. -$10,000. Sadly, we do not have the funds to cover his surgery, and we are asking for donations to cover his surgery. We would love for him to have the best and longest life possible. We appreciate any and all help to cover his surgery.

Mikey was found laying in the road after his rescuers heard the screech of a stopping car. He was taken to our animal shelter, Blount County Animal Center, wrapped in a towel, scared, and crying out. Our doctor examined him and immediately provided critical care with pain medications and oxygen. Nothing was outwardly wrong, except for his distress. After x-rays were taken, the problem was clear: the impact of the car had caused a rupture in his diaphragm. The diaphragm is the muscle that separates the chest from the abdominal cavity. His liver and intestines were now pushing through it, into his chest: a diaphragmatic hernia. This is an internal wound that if not treated quickly, can cause severe respiratory distress and other life threatening consequences. In a matter of weeks, his intestines and liver will press on his lungs and heart as they move into his chest cavity, making it impossible for him to breathe or for his small heart to beat. It can be resolved surgically but but is high risk and we cannot perform it at the shelter. A local clinic is able to preform the surgery, and has quoted the cost at $1200.00 USD. This is more money than our shelter has available. We are asking that anyone with an extra few dollars to please donate to attempt to save young Mikey. He is affectionate, plucky, and an innocent wee soul, and deserves a chance at a long life. If you can’t donate, please share his story. The more people who see his campaign, the more likely it is that those people can donate to help! Thank you and purrs from little Mikey!

I adopted Loki from a rescue in August when he was about 4 months old. He’s the most loving, friendliest, goofiest, and adorable little guy and he loves everyone he meets. He bounces around, adores squeaky toys and is a seemingly happy and healthy 6 month old puppy. Happiness and joy follow him everywhere he goes. Unfortunately on November 8th, the happiness turned into heartbreak. During Loki’s first puppy vet visit his primary vet noticed he had a heart murmur and recommended that Loki see a cardiologist to clear him to go under anesthesia to be neutered. Instead of getting the okay to be neutered Loki was diagnosed with severe valvular pulmonic stenosis. His heart is enlarged and working 5 times harder than it should be to get blood to his lungs. Loki’s only hope at having a good quality of life and prolonging his chance of survival is to undergo a procedure called a balloon valvuloplasty. The procedure is not invasive and isn’t a painful one. He would board the night of the surgery and be able to come home the next day. Hopefully from that day onward he will get the happiness and life he deserves. The only other thing to address his cardiac problems is not a treatment. He can take a medication to slow his heart rate to give his heart some rest for awhile. He is now taking this medication but he will worsen over time and his life expectancy is short. Both his cardiologist and his primary vet said he might be able to live to 2-3 years old but it would not be unexpected if it was much shorter. He’s at moderate to high risk for worsening cardiac disease now. As anyone could imagine, surgical procedures for pets can be astronomical. The procedure Loki needs costs $5829. In addition to the cost of the surgery, he must see his primary vet for a pre-op physical and lab work. 2 weeks after the surgery he needs to see his primary vet again for a follow-up and to get his stitches removed. 3-4 months post surgery he will need another echocardiogram. The cost of the echo alone is $780. Unfortunately the pet insurance he has determined the heart murmur to be pre-existing and they will not cover anything cardiac-related. I want more than anything in the world for Loki to have a good quality of life and this procedure is his only chance. Every cent will go towards the cost of Loki’s surgery. I will be forever grateful to all those who can help give Loki a chance to live a full life that will be filled with love and an endless supply of squeaky toys.

In order for him to live a close to normal life and be able to walk, jump and run again (pain free), he is going to need femoral head and neck ostectomy (FHO) on boths leg. According to our Vet specialist, the surgery cost can range from $5,000 to $10,000. Unfortunately, both legs are affected and none of it will be covered by pet insurance. If left untreated, the bones will collapse due to degenerative changes, leading to severe pain, broken bones, and immobility. At only 9 months old, we want him to have the best life possible. Even with the ability to walk and run again, we are going to have to treat him as a disabled cat the rest of his life buying cat ramps and stairs so he doesn't actively jump on and off the furniture. We will also have to treat him as if he has arthritis with occasional pain meds and supplements. If you love your pets and can empathize with Louie, anything helps. We want to be able to schedule his surgery before he is 1 year old so he can live a normal life again. ~ Donations will help cover the surgery, rehab, medications, regular check ups to follow and potentially a wheelchair for his back legs. We can’t thank you enough for supporting us and Louie ❤️ If you have any questions, concerns text or FB message julia or jess.

On Thursday morning, Tammy, a volunteer with HARTT ( <URL> in Phoenix, came across a post on social media about an injured lab mix who appeared to have been hit by a car. He was lying on the pavement, paralyzed and crawling. The woman who posted about the dog said that she went over, picked him up and placed him on the side of the road, out of the way of oncoming traffic. We are thankful that someone did the right thing and moved him over so he wouldn't be hit again, but unfortunately, he was then just left on the side of the road to suffer alone. When a pet is severely injured, EVERY minute is critical and can literally make a life-or-death difference. Immediately after seeing this post online, Tammy rushed out to find the dog before it was too late - clearly he needed medical care ASAP. When she arrived, she was horrified to see him lying in the rocks, not moving; she thought he was dead. As she approached though, he lifted his little head to look in her direction. Despite being in grave condition, he was such a sweet boy and allowed her to scoop him up. He was so small, barely over 30 pounds! We think he's a Lab/Basset or Lab/Corgi mix. Here's a short video of Louie: Every dog we rescue is special and deserves a name. This sweet boy was given the name "Louie". Tammy loaded Louie into her car and rushed him to the 1st Pet Veterinary Center - North Valley. Initial findings were that he was in shock and his back end was paralyzed. After further diagnostics, it was discovered Louie actually has some feeling but suffered from severe, traumatic fractures to his pelvis. Specifically, this includes sacroiliac luxation with cranial displacement of the left hemipelvis with a fragment that appears to be separated from the rest of the left hemipelvis. He also has a fracture through his left ischium with cranial displacement of the body of the ischium relative to the table. In addition, there is an oblique fracture to the right ilium. (Included is a dog anatomy image showing where all this is located.) He also has issues with bladder tone, which required a urinary catheter be inserted to help him urinate. Overall prognosis is guarded. Louie touched so many hearts on social media. He has the most darling face and looks like a lab, but he has short little legs like a basset hound or corgi. As long as this sweet boy shows a will to survive, we are going to do all we can to give him that fighting chance! We had an angel offer to cover $2,000 towards his vet bill. This was such a blessing at a time when we couldn't wait, allowing us to rush him to the hospital immediately! Unfortunately though, after the latest diagnostics, Louie's bill has significantly increased to now $3,800 just for the hospital stay and initial stabilization. Louie will now require an extensive surgery by a board-certified orthopedic surgeon - we are told the surgery will cost a minimum of $8,000 to $10,000. We need to get Louie on a surgery schedule right away so that he has the chance to live a normal life. HE'S ONLY ONE YEAR OLD! If there are any funds raised beyond what is ultimately needed for his care, those funds will be put towards future dogs that HARTT rescues who need major medical care. Without the support and generosity of people just like you, we would not be able to help animals with this level of trauma - euthanasia would be our only option. Please help us to help Louie - we are so grateful for your compassion! AND, if you might be interested in adopting Louie once he's recovered, please email us at [email redacted]. To learn more about HARTT and our lifesaving field rescues, visit <URL>

Hello, my name is Jaimee and I'm trying to raise money for a dog we now call Lucky. Lucky came to us on 10/15/2022. Not of his own free will, though. I had helped an older gentleman catch his dog near my home a few days prior. I noticed instantly that the loose dog and the dog he was walking were malnourished and terrified. I grabbed her and offered to help him get her back home. Once arriving at his home and seeing how reactive she was the entire walk; if he even so much looked in her direction, I felt a sense of hopelessness. I left in tears that day as I didn't know what else I could do for the dog I had helped catch and the others still at the man's home. Fast forward to the 15th, and my husband calls me from outside to tell me there is a man here wanting to talk to me. I go out, and there is the same man I had helped days prior. He asked me if I would be interested in one of his shepherds. He didn't really have a reason for why he wanted to get rid of him. He just kept saying he needed more attention, and he knew and saw days prior that I had children and dogs of my own. I was relieved as I thought it would be the female german shepherd I had seen days prior. It was not. I came to his home and was greeted by many malnourished dogs. Puppies and adults, all skinny and skittish. He brought out Lucky, which was prior called Sammy. The man's wife joined him outside and told me only one thing was wrong with him. She said she accidentally cut off the sheath of his penis, trying to cut his umbilical cord. The dog was now 2yrs old. Maybe 3 or 4 years old. She said she couldn't recall. I took him not knowing the severity of his genital mutilation and unknown how he was behavior-wise. He was scared. He wouldn't come out from under their chairs on the porch or the woman's wheelchair. They pulled and yanked and got him off the porch. He crawled, belly touching the ground, over to the fence. He would not even look in my direction. The owners talked and talked and seemed like they thought all was well and had nice-looking dogs who were AKC registered etc. The man grabbed this dog by the hair on his hip bones and carried his back end to my car as I had him by the leash. Once I left, my heart shattered, and I cried. Upon getting home, I got him out of my car and into the grass. He lay down and wouldn't get up. He whined and stayed crawling if he did move. His tail was completely tucked under him, and his ears were back. Once I could look at his genitals, my heart dropped even more. He had no covering whatsoever on his penis. Being a Saturday, I contacted our personal vet's after-hours number. She called back, was very concerned, and asked me to text her pictures. She then said we could slowly stretch the remaining skin to create a new sheath, or the only other option was a specialized surgery to transition him to female. He has an apt set up for Monday, 10/17/2022, at our vet for a general check-over and to address the situation of his genitals. This boy is very malnourished. I do not believe he was being fed. I can count every rib, vertebra and his hip bone protruding out so bad. We have been providing him with small meals more often, and he devours them within moments. Thanks to a family member, we got him wormed and treated for fleas with a Capstar as a temporary fix until the vet sees him. We also bathed him in dawn and could not even get half of the fleas off of him. We are hoping to raise enough money to cover the initial vet bills, shots, food etc. Once we have an itemized bill for the remaining care, we will update the amounts needed and provide proof. We do have 3 dogs of our own & 8 children between my husband and I. So any help towards Lucky would be so very appreciated. God Bless!

Hi, my name is Bec, and I foster a LOT of orphaned kittens. It makes me so happy to see helpless infant kittens grow up strong and find forever homes. Recently, a little kitten named Mango was found at a food market in terrible condition. My friend and I, working with Jelly's Place Animal Shelter, took her in, bottle-fed her, cleaned her up and treated her for worms and fleas. She was just one week old! When she was old enough to start eating solid foods, I noticed something wasn't quite right with her butt (odd thing to say - I know); she could not poop properly. She became so constipated that she was in pain every time she tried to poop. And it never improved. Over the next month, I spoke to many vets and did my own research on her symptoms, and we eventually figured out what was wrong. She needs a new butt. Seriously. Mango has what is called 'atresia ani', a congenital (born with it) condition, where part of her colon is the size of a mouse colon - not a cat colon. It means all her poop gets stuck inside her, and it's incredibly painful and difficult to pass. Her only chance for living is to undergo anoplasty or bowel reconstructive surgery. Furthermore, it needs to happen as soon as possible, as waste is building up inside of her. I'm covering the costs out of pocket so that the surgery can happen this Monday (October 31st) - and while I have no regret in choosing this for Mango, I'm worried there may be further costs involved in follow-up surgeries (this often happens with her condition). If you are willing to donate anything, Mango and I would be eternally grateful. Mango came into my life unexpectedly, and while I had originally taken her in as a foster kitten, it turns out she had already found her forever home with me <3 I love you Mango.

Hi, I am Leslie and I am fundraising for Parker (formerly Mr. Kitty) of Leimert Park. Mr. Kitty looked hungry, and although we assumed he was one of the many neighborhood ferals, we dropped the dogs off at home and came back with a can of food, thinking we could leave it there to ease his suffering. Surprisingly, Mr. Kitty came up to us. He ate the entire can of food, purred and let us pet him. He was skin and bones, infested with fleas, and dragging his rear leg. We got him in a cat carrier and rushed him to VCA West LA. VCA West LA ascertained that Mr. Kitty is not microchipped. He also tested negative for FIV and Leukemia. Blood work was done and emergency flea medication and fluids were administered. Mr. Kitty showed signs of chronic anemia, but this, we were informed, is likely a result of the severe flea infestation. Mr. Kitty is also missing a lot of teeth - probably from starvation, and his rear leg appeared broken. After getting a treatment estimate of $3,800, we opted to bring him home (versus hospitalizing him) and take him to our regular vet for a more affordable x-ray option. This reduced the cost of Mr. Kitty's first vet visit to $752.02. On October 22, 2022, Mr. Kitty went to Culver City Animal Hospital. He was given additional fluids, his leg was examined, and an x-ray was taken. His femur is fractured at the hip joint, but this, it appears, happened some time ago. We were informed that Mr. Kitty needs to get his weight up before it can be determined if the leg injury can be repaired or will require amputation. This visit was $427. On November 1st, Mr. Kitty had to take another trip to Culver City Animal Hospital because his cheek was swelling. We thought perhaps it was an eye issue but it turned out the problem was an infected tooth. There was no charge for this appointment but we scheduled an extraction for November 4th. Mr. Kitty had two teeth removed on November 4th. The cost should have been well over $1000 but Culver City Animal Hospital only charged us $800. The next step is getting Mr. Kitty’s weight up and getting him cleaned up from all the dirt, flea dirt, and grime caked on him. He has a strong appetite and Friskies “lil soups” have been keeping him well-nourished while his mouth heals from the recent extractions. We anticipate having Mr. Kitty here with us through his necessary weight gain, whatever leg surgery he needs and his recovery. After that, we will need to find him a home. So far, he seems tolerant of our dogs and cats, mostly through the door, but he is still quite frail. We will be able to better evaluate how he would do in a multi-pet home once he is recovered and his fighting spirit has returned. In the meantime, it is already clear that he will make a great companion for someone. He is such a friendly guy. He must have been really loved at some point. We try to imagine his life, what happened to his people, how he ended up injured and on the street. We cannot imagine what horrors he has been through the last few months. We appreciate anything you can offer to help cover his medical bills. He also needs a better name. We welcome suggestions! 12/15/22 update: unfortunately it turns out Parker (formerly Mr. Kitty) is in the end stages of life, which makes rejoining him unlikely. We are going to keep him here in hospice. Thanks to everyone who has donated.

Hello, my name is Christina Cassone and I am fundraising to help support veterinary costs for our cat Miles. About 2 weeks ago my husband and I brought Miles to the vet due to rapid weight loss that occurred over 2-3 months. Our healthy (chonky) 13 lb boy now weighs just under 8lbs. Our minds wandered, as we all do when our fur babies are sick...hopefully its something easily treated and our boy would be ok. However, blood test and x-ray revealed an extremely enlarged kidney on his right side, so large that it is compressing his stomach leaving him unable to eat more than a few bites of food at a time, as well as the possibility of cancer. But, without doing an invasive and high risk biopsy of the kidney we can't know for sure. The good news is his blood panel is generally normal except for slight anemia. We chose to do a steroid shot for now and consider our options over the next couple of days. This was our day on 10/4, and we contemplated the best choice for Mr. Miles. FAST FORWARD; Today 10/17, we go for a second veterinary visit at our primary vet for a second opinion (we were unable to get an appointment with him initially, which is why we used our different vet). In a short time he looks over Miles bony body, feels the mass that is his enlarged kidney, reveiws the previous x-ray and bloodwork...and without hesitation states "we could just take it out, because whether it's cancer or not, a kidney that large has no business being in there." He says Miles is young, everything else looks pretty good, and he moves on to explain we can then safely get a biopsy/histology from the removed kidney without putting Miles through a painful, risky biopsy on a kidney that really should come out no matter what the result is. With removal, his stomach compression will be relieved and his tummy will have more room for food. His other kidney is functioning well enough that there is a high chance he can live a long healthy life with just one kidney. The other good news is that if it IS cancer and has not spread, we have already removed it. Nephrectomy in cats is performed for things such as cancer, hydronephrosis, nephromegaly, and kidney failure. The procedure takes about 1-2 hrs with a short recovery time involving pain medications and antibiotics. There are always many ifs, ands, and buts that come with surgery and pets. All we know is we love Miles, and have chosen to move forward with the nephrectomy (kidney removal) then go from there. Miles is only 4.5 years old. He was adopted from Animal Friends in Youngwood, PA when he was about 4-6 months old and has been my buddy ever since. He currently still has a good quality of life; he is eating multiple small meals per day due to his tummy compression, he is drinking, playing, pottying, making happy paws biscuits, and relaxing in his favorite basket. There are no exclusive signs of pain, and he is generally a happy boy. These signs are our reasoning for choosing this surgery. Any small donation or sharing our fundraiser will help us reach our goal to cover the surgical cost and any additional medication costs. We also would like to be transparent and have included a picture of our vet estimate. We have high hopes this surgery will give him many more years and we will continue to post updates moving forward. Miles has a few *miles* on his road to surgery and recovery and we beleive he can go the distance. #Milesandmilestogo

The great news is that the tumor(actually a chemodectoma) is slow growing and has not metastasized. We have elected to go forward with a surgery that will remove her pericardium from around her heart. Her surgeon is extremely optimistic and his confidence gives us great hope. She recently had mouth surgery and now these episodes. This combined with some unfortunate life events this year has placed us in this difficult position. We are humbly asking for help to see Mollie through this procedure. Yesterday, Ben and I got some difficult news: Mookie has cancer. We took him to the vet to get a couple of bumps on his stomach checked out because they were red and inflamed. He has had these bumps all summer, and they would alternate between being small and hardly noticeable, to flaring up and getting bigger. We thought they were bug bites, cysts, or some kind of rash. Turns out, they are Mast Cell Tumors. Essentially, mast cells are white blood cells that can degranulate when exposed to allergens and form tumors. This is especially common in both Boxers and Bull Terriers - two of the breeds Mookie is mixed with. The prognosis is good if they can remove both tumors with good margins and no other tumors form. We have him scheduled for surgery on December 1st. The estimated cost will be $1000, dependent on how difficult it is to remove his specific bumps. We are asking for support in covering the costs of this operation. Mookie is the best dog in the world (perhaps I’m biased, but I suspect several of you would agree ) and we want to do everything we can to keep him healthy, but we were not prepared for the cost of this surgery. Any funds raised will go towards the cost of his surgery, medication, and post-surgery follow-up appointments. Mookie has already been through so much: being abandoned on the streets of Detroit, then spending 16 days in a rescue where he had to recover from a terrible case of fleas and of course, a month long treatment for heartworm. We love him with all our hearts, and any support will be greatly appreciated. #MookieStrong

At first, I figured it was because the new apartment is older with lots of little closets and nooks and they’d found their respective chill spots. In actuality, the cats were hiding due to noise in the environment (which has since been remedied). During that time, Mr. Nun was not eating as much (which was hard to tell with the two cats). I first took him to the urgent vet, and they said it may be that he’s been trying to pee too much from the stress and has ended up with cystitis. They couldn’t get enough urine for the test for other issues with the urine itself. They gave him fluids subcutaneously. He was initially treated with an appetite stimulant, opioid, gabapentin, and prescription food. He seemed to be a bit better and then took a turn, becoming weak and jaundiced. I then brought Mr. Nun to the vet, and he was diagnosed with hepatic lipidosis as well as pancreatitis and cholecystitis. Basically, during the days that he was unable to bring himself to eat (hard to tell at first with two cats), his body began breaking down his fat which overloaded the liver. He has since been fed orally with a syringe every four hours, continuing with the Mirataz and with gabapentin. It may be weeks before he is better, so I am trying my best to plan for this and pool resources to arrange for veterinary care. Mr. Nun and I thank you so much for your time, consideration and prayers, and generosity.

About 5 weeks ago Munch was found in the backyard of our college apartment abandoned by the rest of the litter. My roommate and I felt so horrible knowing he was obviously the weakest link and insisted on helping him out. We wanted to clean him up and at the least bring him to a safe shelter. However, at this point, no shelters were taking any more animals. Therefore we decided the best approach was to bring him to the vet to get checked out. At the first visit, he was too tiny to receive any shots or flea medicine but was able to be treated for an eye infection. As the infection subsided and our emotional attachment grew, it was clear something about his eyes was wrong. It seemed as if he always wanted to squint or was wincing. About 3 weeks after the initial appointment he doubled in weight and was able to start the shots process. However, under examination, the vet noticed that Munch was born with a congenital defect called Eyelid Agenesis. During development, Munch never completely grew eyelids which is causing his eyes to fold in. His eyelashes and fur are constantly rubbing against his eyes which is incredibly painful for him and is beginning to scar his cornea. If left untreated Munch will slowly and painfully go blind. Due to how rare this condition is, there are only a number of veterinary ophthalmologists who are able to perform this surgery. The cost of surgery and consultations will be well over $3,000 which is super hard for a busy college student to put out of pocket. It seems as if the only feasible option is to give him up for adoption. However, the thought of him being potentially euthanized because of the expenses required to fix him up breaks my heart. All I'm asking is for you guys to donate whatever is within your means. To be able to give this kitten the surgery he needs is all I can hope for. This precious face is the face I want to see smiling again. It belongs to my dog Kaia who suffered a severe and underserving spinal cord injury. She is only three years old. To all dog owners, who do we know to be the first to greet us when we come home after a long day? Our furry friends. They wag their adorable tails out of an expression of love and devotion and run toward us like it's the first time they've seen us in months. What if that unique moment we share with our dogs is suddenly ripped away? In Kaia's case, she's lost all sensation in the lower region of her spine – her lumbar and sacrum, to be specific. The nerves were crushed, inhibiting any feeling of her right leg, tail, and control over her bladder/bowel movements. As much as I don’t want to believe in the following, I don't know if she will be able to walk or run like she used to. I don’t know if she will be able to wag that little tail again. I am not a medical professional, but I'm grateful to be surrounded by ones who helped me understand Kaia’s situation. While there are still some holes in the comprehensive report, the fact is that Kaia had a meager chance of recovering from the herniated disc if she didn’t get surgery. The disc responsible for holding her bones together was already 80% deteriorating. Another devastating fact is that even with surgery, the chance of her ever fully recovering was 10 to 30 percent, according to her neurologist. The thing about having pets is they can't use words to communicate. They can’t tell you, “Mom, Dad, I’m in pain.” They can’t point to where on their body they need help. You can only make the best guess based on what you see. From one doctor visit to the next, you’re hit with - in this case - a harsh reality. You must decide the outcome of your baby's life based solely on faith and facts. With signs pointing in all directions, I had to go through with the only one with a fighting chance: surgery. If it meant I could see her run like the speeding bullet she is, witness her infectious energy again, and smile every time she leaves her mark of love in this world, I had to take that chance. Our poor dogs look at us with those big, majestic eyes as their one and only savior. I must take it upon myself to put her back together again like she's done for me, hoping to do so with extra helping hands. It's more than a donation. It's an opportunity to pull together all the positive energy that can save her spirit. I ask that if you put in any amount you wish to contribute, you do it with the sole purpose of increasing her chances of being able to function normally again. The exchange becomes more significant than all of us. It's to bring life back into my helpless Kaia, who did not ask for any of this. Her spirit has brightened almost anyone who has come across her tiny paw path, and the least I can do is ask for help from communities who believe in the power of giving. Communities who believe this exchange symbolizes a token of serving a child of God. Trust me when I say that even the smallest amount strengthens Kaia’s journey. The funds would help towards the costs of her surgery performed by Dr. O’Neill at Metropolitan Animal Specialty Hospital, the reoccurring visits with Dr. Ramirez at LA Veterinary Center, and the thorough recovery process, including physical therapy. Most importantly, the funds would go towards Kaia's freedom to be the dog she is. If you are curious about how and why this was brought upon her, I encourage you to ask me any questions and continue learning more, especially if you're a pet owner. I want to leave you with one last thing. The name Kaia means earth, life and the sea. Like Mother Earth, she’s gentle, pure and beautiful. Her full-of-life energy is unbelievable, something you'd know the instant you meet her. And like the sea, her silent strength is what amazes me the most. She taught me to be resilient, patient, and love wholeheartedly without any expectations. She lifts me high, and now it's my turn to be the wind beneath her broken wing. Thank you for your time reading her story, offering your gifts, and spreading the word. They are enough to keep the momentum going. Warmest and heartfelt thanks, Kaia and Kanika

Hello, everyone! My name is Nadia, you may know me as Rosie or Roux, and I’m a self-employed artist from São Paulo, Brazil. I’m a lover of animals, and a happy pet mom to three kitties and a dog. One of them is Mozart, a large black cat who is full of personality and makes everyone fall in love with him in seconds. Mozart was abandoned at a friend’s door when he was just an itty bitty kitty, and brought to my home as a temporary foster. We very much failed fostering on the first night, when I was already sure he was going to stay with us forever. He has since grown into the most affectionate, lovable dork; he is talkative and loves to sing, he enjoys doing parkour at 3AM with his sister Misty, and he loves to cuddle up with his doggy sister Maya for naps. The house has been so quiet without him. Last week Mozart got sick and had to be admitted to a vet clinic. We thought it would be a simple thing, but unfortunately it did not turn out that way. I’ll give the full extent of his diagnosis below, but the most important thing right now is that he’s stable, his surgery went well, and he should be coming home soon. This whole thing was a rollercoaster and we’re so relieved it’s soon to be over, but now we’re also staring at the aftermath of his rapidly increasing vet bills. We unquestionably followed all medical recommendations to ensure Mozart had the best fighting chance he could, but things quickly got to the point where I realized I would need financial help somehow. The full diagnosis details: On October 9th, I first noticed Mozart was acting strange. He had been very vocal and very needy throughout that day, seeking attention constantly, but those are things I’m used to when it comes to him. However, after a long cuddling session, I noticed he left a pool of urine on my desk. That was definitely out of character as Mozart is a very polite boy who has never once peed out of his litter box. From that point, it took me paying a little bit of attention to see he was trying to use the litter box repeatedly without success, and also dripping pee constantly across the house. I had no means to take him anywhere that night, so I rushed him to the vet the next morning. What initially seemed to be a simple urethral blockage, which could possibly be resolved on the next day, suddenly became a much bigger and scarier prognostic. It has been found that Mozart has several stones along both of his ureters, as well as in his bladder. The vet clinic called me in to talk, and explained to me that this condition was, quoting their very words, “incompatible with life”, and the double ureter surgery to get the stones out was incredibly complex, very risky (due to how thin cats’ ureters are), and had a high complication and mortality rates. There was also a modern technique that would give him a double bypass, a procedure with a much better success rate - but it could amount to over 16k in costs. His only hope would be to start medication as soon as possible and hope that any of these stones could be passed naturally. Needless to say, I don’t even know how I managed to walk out of the clinic that night. It all sounded like a sure sentence and I was already trying to make peace with the fact that there was a high chance that I could lose my boy. My wife had to be really strong for the both of us because I was just a complete crying mess. The following morning, however, my wife and I sprung immediately into problem-solving mode and started focusing our efforts into finding him the medication he needed, as well as getting in touch with several pet hospitals and urinary tract specialists. Over the course of the next few days I must have called over 10 places multiple times, sent his exams to at least four different vets, and had several restless nights. We were able to get started on his medical treatment as soon as possible, but that wouldn’t make things any less scary. It was important to keep him under observation at all times, because at any point, any of the stones could block the passage from his kidneys to the bladder and cause a kidney crisis - which would require immediate action. We kept a close eye on him, taking new exams from time to time to evaluate how his condition was evolving. We’ve had several scares along the week, he was almost rushed to emergency surgery once, but eventually we reached a point where he was stable for a few days - although the process has evidently been stressing him out. Last Friday, I finally got in direct touch with a specialist that then started working directly with the clinic to find the best path to move forward. We were to wait a few more days to establish if the treatment was having any effect and make a decision based on that. On Oct 17th, I finally had some good news. His blood work came back and it indicated that the stones are only partly blocking the ureters and not causing any stress to his kidneys. The only thing actively keeping him from being able to pee without the help of a catheter was the stones in his bladder, which unfortunately would require surgery to be removed. This procedure, however, would be much less complicated than a double ureter surgery, so this was a big relief to us. As of Oct 18th, I finally got the call saying that the procedure had been done, everything went well, and he was now recovering from the anesthesia. It’s no doubt that we are sparing no efforts to keep Mozart as well-taken care of as possible. The clinic has been keeping me well-informed of his condition, and we have been visiting him daily - as hard as it is to go back home without him every night. We know all of this is for his own good and we would go to the moon and back if that could help him improve. At the same time, I can’t deny that the financial factor has been at the back of my mind for most of this week. The costs of keeping a pet fully admitted to a clinic for several days climbs very quickly, and both exams, surgery and medication costs will only make that climb much more steep. Initially I had hoped to organize an art sale to raise funds, but right now I need to focus my energy on making sure he fully recovers once he’s home. When a friend suggested the GoFundMe idea to relieve some of that impact on our finances, I couldn’t help but agree and go with it. If you’ve read it this far, thank you for your time. Any amount helps, and if you can’t contribute, sharing it goes a long way as well. All of the funds will go to pay off Mozart’s medication, admittance, surgery and post-op care. Friends and Family, Well, it seems like most of us are destined to reach out for help from time to time, even for our pets. Sadly, this is our time. We were faced with an emergency with our Callie cat this week, and she is currently in the Pet Hospital up in Bellingham receiving care; we hope to bring her home tonight or tomorrow morning. Callie has no prior health issues, and we take great care of her with regular checkups and vaccinations are current. She’s still young at 7 years old. She became ill last Wednesday after being lethargic for 18 hours, not taking any food (which she always has access to dry food and begs for her wet food often) or using her potty box. She ate a little of her dinner Wednesday night and nothing since, but she was drinking some water. I took her to her regular Vet on Thursday and found a 104+ fever of unknown origin; they gave her an antibiotic shot and fluids and sent us home to monitor. We continued to monitor her food/water intake, which was very minimal water and checked her potty box every time she was up. She slept a lot and continued to be lethargic and grumbling every time we tried to get her to take food and water. We set up a camera to monitor when she came to her food and water with no results, and by Saturday night, we felt the situation was worse. If we had to wait until Monday to see her vet again, we would be looking at a Critical Situation. All Vet hospitals in Western Washington are hard to get into and run at capacity, which is why we ended up in Bellingham, an hour away. She was given more fluids, lab work, an anti-nausea medication, pain medication, and an appetite stimulant. We had the option to admit her for ultrasound and further care, and we chose to try and see if the care they gave her would get things moving in the right direction, so we were allowed to bring her home. After 24 hours, no food or water intake happened with a minimal urine output; it was time to get her back to the ER for admission for Ultrasound and further treatment, which included IV fluids, NG tube for nutrition, sedation for ultrasound and tissue samples. We had some excellent news today concerning her eating. She’s been offered baby food twice with good results and is now interested in eating. The ultrasound shows Pancreatitis and general inflammation of the liver, spleen & intestines, which can be expected from not eating. So far, it’s non-cancerous; we’ll have a better idea of what the future holds when the tissue results are in. Hopefully, it will just be a diet monitoring plan. Keeping my fingers crossed and praying a lot. Our costs by the time we are through getting her stable and home are looking to be about $5000. This situation has been gut-wrenchingly stressful, and we don’t want to give up on our girl. We’ve had to pay upfront through CareCredit, which is just about maxed out. We are asking for help to cover some of these unexpected costs. Any donation, no matter how great or small, would be greatly appreciated! Thank you so much for your consideration, Ronna & Stuart Blomgren

Here is the story of Naomi: A few months ago, this little kitty started to come around. It was very hesitant to come near me at first. It would sleep on top of our trash cans or within our flower bed, but it ran away whenever I opened the garage or came home. Each morning, I open the garage and work out. A few weeks later, I officially named her Naomi. I also noticed a small scratch of some sort on her neck. I didn't think much of it. As I kept going on throughout my daily routines, I noticed the "scratch" was getting bigger. I thought it was a tick at first, but I couldn't get underneath her fur to get a good picture. Shortly after, the scratch became a knot under her skin that kept getting bigger until it ruptured. At this point, she had an open wound the size of about a nickel on her neck that was oozing and bleeding. I attempted to call five different animal nonprofits and talked to 3 different vets, and none of them could assist me at a low cost with the situation I was facing. While I don't fully have the resources or capacity to take something like this on, I couldn't let the cat walk around suffering, knowing that I could potentially save her life. So, I scheduled an appointment with my vet Wednesday, November 2nd. Naomi had to be sedated, and the wound on her neck was either from a botfly or some sort of larva that got infected. She had a 103-degree fever, so we are waiting to complete vaccinations till 11/14. She also had fleas and needed medicine to get rid of them. She stayed five nights at the vet for them to monitor her and keep her safe while the wound healed. Good news: She is negative for feline leukemia! This cat has so much affection to give; she is the toughest, most beautiful little thing. Any donation towards her recovery helps, and I am so thankful for any amount you choose to give. Also, if you know of anyone that would be a warm and loving home for Naomi, please let us know, as I cannot keep her long-term. Love, Kenz
