Hi, my name is Karen and I'm fundraising for my sweet wee girl Oona. A little about her and a good amount of info as I want you to understand her situation ... We rescued her from a kill pen in March 2022. Nobody wanted her and it was her last day there before being shipped to Mexico to be slaughtered. (We rescued 3 other horses from there in 2020) Our then 28 year old mare needed a horse closer to her age that she could be besties with. I saw Oona (we gave her that name) online and knew she was our girl. I fell in love with her scared little face and the emotion in her eyes. Her bio was 22 year old grey mare, 14hh, lead line children's horse. I thought she would be a great addition to our little herd and we could give another horse a second lease on life. I went and bailed her out. She had to be caught as she was scared, couldn't blame her for that. She was very underweight and had stringhalt in her back right leg. Stringhalt makes her kick forward when walking instead of taking a regular step. This girl was severely underweight at 650 lbs and her ribs and hip bones were so sad to look at. She was starved by her previous owners. Oona arrived on March 18th, 2022. The day after Patty's 29th birthday. She wanted to be a part of the herd from the moment she saw them. There was a little sparkle in her eyes that she didn't have when I first saw her. It took a month for her to be fully accepted by the others when I could let her in the pasture. At first she and Patty didn't get along but eventually, they would stand and walk together, rest and enjoy shade under Patty's favorite tree side by side. Oona was afraid of people, halter/lead ropes and would turn her back to me. I immediately started her on imported rose hip powder for her stringhalt. We slowly introduced her to feed and worked on trust. It took 3 months for her to realize she wasn't going to be ridden anymore and that a halter and lead rope could be a good thing. Now she volunteers to put it on because she knows it doesn’t mean something bad will happen. I used to kiss Patty on the forehead after she would eat and to say goodnight. Oona watched and learned. When Patty passed away in July, Oona started putting her head down to be kissed. That was the sweetest gesture I could have ever gotten from this little lamb. She knew I was hurting. Oona would go to Patty's tree every day and stand there. She missed her "sister" very much. Jump forward almost 8 months from the time she arrived and she is now 830 lbs! Her stringhalt has calmed down and she loves getting groomed. Oona is no longer afraid of us. I haven't had to catch her since June. As I was working with her to gain her trust, it was obvious that she was both mentally and physically abused. I took my time with her as patience is key. I'm so glad that she opened her mind and heart to me. Maybe the other horses told her I was a good human caretaker and to trust me like they did. Even though she sometimes will seem to have flashbacks, she will look at me, think hard and then come over for a little pet. Oona started to follow me around a bit in the barn and loves my company when she just wants to take a quiet siesta. Did I mention she loves her peppermint wafer treats? She knows I keep them in my right pocket and tilts her head to give me a clue that she would like one...or two for being a very good girl. She loves her herd family and just being a horse. A couple of days ago, Oona didn't want to eat her feed. She had a little that night but left a lot. I thought maybe she ate hay before coming into the barn as we started to introduce a hay ring for them all to eat from. She was fine the next two days. Then on Thursday 11/3, she was off. Laying down in the paddock which is something she would never do especially during the day. I saw her get up and then lay down again a few times. I gave her 2 oz of Formula 1 papaya juice thinking she was in pre-colic and that would soothe her tummy and intestines. I called our equine vet as I didn't want to take a chance. Heart, breathing, lungs and belly/intestine sounds all good. Took blood to run tests back at the medical center. She put a tube up her nose and some blood came out so charcoal/oil was sent up the tube and it would help to grab anything bad (like toxins) and assist in passing it through her system. Benamine was given for discomfort and I was told no food or hay at all but access to water was a must. No problem. I kept an eye on her until I couldn't stay awake any longer. This morning, she was down again. She wasn’t rolling and she was going to the bathroom, but she couldn’t get comfortable. I called the vet and was told to bring her in. Blood work done again and it was all good. Temperature okay. Heart, breathing, lungs etc all okay. Sonogram on both sides of belly and under. Her small intestines were working slower than normal. She was mildly sedated and let’s just say the long gloved hand and arm took over. Her first bit of poop that came out looked okay. The second didn’t. It had hay strands that were not pulverized and she did have an impaction. They were going to keep her there for 48 hours, give her IV and watch. In the morning they were going to do a scope. I paid a deposit of $1000 and when I pick her up, I have to pay the full bill. At that point, it was between $2500 - $3000. On my way home, the vet called me and said something just wasn’t sitting right as she was still showing signs of pain after meds. So he pulled a sample of her stomach/intestine fluids for a test. Normal while blood count for a horse is between 5000-12000. Her count was 111,000!!! She has a major infection in her intestine. So now we have options. Do aggressive meds every 6 hours and when she starts looking better, switch to oral for a couple of weeks. Or just do the oral and hope it is enough. We decided to go aggressive because I don’t want my dear girl to be in pain. Now she will be there at least 5 days as they wait for more tests to come back from the lab. It could be more but the minimum vet bill is now $7000. (read update as it went up). Why am I asking for help? First off, I’m embarrassed to ask for assistance. But this just happened at the wrong time with other vet bills, hay and feed prices rising and personal things, I'm just a wreck. My wee girl should be living the easy life, learning new things and experiencing the love she never had before coming here. She deserves the best care. I think she understood yesterday and today that I was doing what I could to give her help. She was so good letting the doctors and vet techs handle her. She’s come a long way showed that she could trust humans. Today, 11/6, I was just advised that her bill will be closer to $10k (On 11/11, it is approximately $14k with a release date of Sunday 11/13 only if I can pay her bill in full). She has a raised ulcer in her stomach and will be ther until Thursday or Friday. Any donations will be going to her emergency vet bill and care. I’ll be posting the rundown bill tomorrow when they email it to me. The pictures with the black backgrounds I took a little over a week ago to show friends and fellow rescuers how much she has changed. I also posted from the day I first saw her at the kill pen. Oona has gone through so much and she is just starting to enjoy her life. Thank you to all that donate. I will be forever grateful. All my love, Karen (Not a crazy Karen, I promise!) October 23, 2022 --- What a difference! Love, trust and patience! Such a little angel face and doe eyes!

On Monday night, October 24th, our 10-month-old puppy, Sherman, threw up his dinner. We didn't think much of it at first, but he kept throwing up, over and over, into the following morning. We tried giving him water, but that kept coming up, too. Worried, we took Sherman to the vet, who gave him some intervenous hydrating fluids and anti-nausea medication. We thought this would solve the problem. However, as the day progressed, Sherman had no appetite for food. He was still interested in drinking water but kept throwing up after every sip. He was getting increasingly sluggish and uncomfortable, and we were getting scared. Upon returning to the vet, it was recommended that we take him to an emergency clinic so a team of doctors could triage the situation and identify the cause of these symptoms. Since the anti-nausea medication wasn't working and Sherman wasn't interested in eating, they recommended that we check him in to stay the night, where he could be monitored in case the situation worsened. We agreed. They were also concerned that there could be a blockage somewhere in his digestive tract. They attached a catheter to medicate him intravenously and took X-rays and blood samples for lab work. At around 4 a.m. the following morning, we received a call from the doctors, recommending we approve their request to run a NasoGastric tube through Sherman's nose to his stomach. That way, they would be able to feed and hydrate Sherman effectively (since he hadn't eaten in 3 days) and use the line to clear the fluid buildup in his stomach to reduce his nausea. We approved the request, and Sherman quickly started to improve. However, the X-rays and lab work still didn't clarify the cause of the problem. Additional X-rays and ultrasounds were given, and more tests were run. We visited Sherman daily, bringing him food (hoping he would eat) and giving him lots of love and warm pets. On Friday morning, the doctor identified a high level of vitamin C in his blood. It was approaching toxic levels. She believed this could be the cause of Sherman's situation. Once given medicine to help reduce the Vitamin C levels, Sherman's appetite began to return. He still had to be fed most of his food through his NasoGastric tube, but he was starting to snack little by little on the food the technicians were setting out for him. I came to visit the following day, and his tail was wagging again (which it hadn't done in the past week). He ate two treats right out of my hand! We were overjoyed! Still, Sherman needed two more nights at the doctor's before his natural appetite was back, his nausea resolved, and everyone felt comfortable and safe enough to send him home (with medication, of course). We're still not sure what the cause of this episode was. The doctors think it could either be Addison's disease or that his own body could have caused the surplus due to the recent growth spurt he is currently having. We are awaiting test results, which we hope will provide answers and clarify how we best care for our sweet pup from now on. In the meantime, Sherman has been recovering quickly back at home. He has forgotten some potty training rules (he'll remember them soon), but he is taking his medicine like a champ, eating his meals, drinking water, and gaining energy back. Sherman is feeling much better. And he's slowly warming up to playing fetch in the yard again. We're ecstatic to have him back home, healthy, comfortable, and cozy after such an ordeal. We can only imagine how scary and confusing it was for him. We were scared, too. In two weeks, we'll have his next doctor's appointment to review the test results and plan for the future. We have pet insurance, which I recommend, especially after an ordeal like this. However, we're already extremely close to hitting our maximum number of claims since Sherman also needed his vaccinations, neutering, microchipping, and other routine puppy vet visits this year. This specific "adventure" has cost us close to $12,000 out-of-pocket all on its own. This bill is hard to pay off, and while we don't expect anything, we wanted to create a GoFundMe to see what might be possible with the help and support of others. It's always awkward to do something like this. We don't expect to receive the total amount we've asked for. Questo dolcissimo cucciolo si chiama Paco ed è un orsacchiotto di 4 mesi. Quando ne aveva solo 2 ha subito un infortunio ed è rimasto completamente paralizzato per 5 giorni. Nessuno sa precisamente cosa sia successo. Forse la mamma gli é caduta addosso, saltando nel recinto dove lui si trovava con i suoi fratellini e sorelline. L'unica cosa che si sa per certo é che é nato perfettamente sano e nel giro di una notte appena, sono iniziati i suoi guai. Io l'ho adottato un mese dopo perche la famiglia che lo aveva acquistato, non lo desiderava piu, nonostante Paco mostrasse segni di guarigione sorprendentemente veloci. Nel giro di un mese, infatti, era riuscito a recuperare la mobilitá delle zampe anteriorie, parzialmente anche quella della zampa posteriore sinistra e della codina. La destra, tuttavia, rimaneva rigida ed immobile. I veterinari che lo avevano visitato fino a quel momento avevano comunque assicurato ai suoi allevatori, che Paco sarebbe completamente guarito con la fisioterapia. Quando sono venuta a conoscenza della sua storia, Paco aveva 3 mesi e cercava una famiglia che gli volesse tanto bene e che avesse la pazienza e la voglia di fargli fare i suoi esercizi di fisioterapia. Alla prima visita veterinaria, una settimana dopo averlo adottato, mi sono resa conto che i suoi problemi erano ben piu gravi di quanto avessero inizialmente ipotizzato. Questi dottori, infatti, ritenevano che i danni alla gamba fossero stati sottovalutati dai precedenti medici e consigliavano una serie di accertamenti ed esami per scongiurare l'amputazione della zampina. Alcuni di questi sono stati eseguiti immediatamente, seppur costosi. Ma altri piu approfonditi, purtroppo, prevedevano dei costi che io non sono in grado di sostenere. Ad oggi Paco necessita urgentemente di una risonanza magnetica e di una elletromiografia per capire una volta per tutte cosa gli sia successo e definire un percorso terapeutico. Questo cucciolo ha sviluppato una fibrosi del muscolo del quadricipite, che essendo una fibra meno elastica del muscolo normale, non gli consente di piegare la gamba. In aggiunta, essendo infiammato, gli provoca dolore nei movimenti e frequenti ferite selle zampine, a causo del trascinamento dell'arto infortunato. La situazione di Paco é complessa e necessita di essere valutata da un ortopedico/a che sia esperto dell'ambito e possibilmente di questa patologia. In seguito a questi accertamenti, ci sarebbe la possibilitá di sottoporre Paco ad un operazione chirurgica con lo scopo di rimuovere la fibrosi che gli provoca dolore, e avere dei supporti impiantati nell'articolazione, nella speranza che questi gli consentano di piegare il ginocchio e tornare a muovere la zampa. Saró infinitamente grata a chiunque voglia donarmi un aiuto piccolo o grande che sia ma ad ogni caso prezioso. Io non demordo e davanti all'invito di alcuni veterinari di "addormentarlo" rispondo con la determinazione di trovare una soluzione. Paco è un piccolo guerriero e merita di ricevere le cure per guarire un male che se fosse stato diagnosticato subito, si sarebbe potuto evitare. Ho dovuto impostare un importo ipotetico perche ogni visita veterinaria costa dai 200 ai 300€ e ogni intervento dai 1500 ai 2000€. Se dovessi essere cosi fortunata da ricevere piu di quanto serva a Paco, mi premurerò di donare la somma rimanente a qualche altro cucciolo sfortunato su questa piattaforma e tenere i donatori/donatrici informati su come vengono utilizzati questi fondi. Per vedere Paco e i suoi progressi seguitelo su Instagram su Paco_thepiratedog. Grazie a tutti di cuore

On October 26th, our beloved 4-month-old puppy Piper was attacked by another dog. Our apartments were holding an event where residents could go to a food truck parked in front of the main office. This is where a neighbor of ours was standing with their dog. Both dogs were on leashes and near their owners when the neighbor asked if they could meet. I agreed because Piper, a 4-month-old puppy, has never had any issues with the many dogs she has met. My mistake was in my assumption that when a person offers to introduce their dog to your puppy, it is okay to meet other dogs and puppies. The dogs were sniffing and in play position, with Piper even rolling on her side two times to show submission. When my order was called, I proceeded to the side of the food cart to pick up the order. This is when I thought the dogs' interaction was over. I did not notice that the neighbor had followed with his dog and was within my immediate vicinity. I turned to put my order in my jacket pocket and heard Piper screaming - this is when I saw that the neighbor's dog had her jaw locked around Piper’s snout and neck. A bystander had to open the attacking dog's mouth to free Piper. Her snout and neck were seen to be bleeding, and she was clearly in immense pain. With another bystander's help, I took Piper up to our apartment, and that’s when it was noted the wound on her neck was significant and she was going to need immediate medical attention. Piper was rushed to the emergency vet and stayed there overnight to get her wounds treated. The other dog's owner was called about covering the estimated costs, of which he could only provide $250. In our contact with the attacking dog's owner, he revealed he does not have rental insurance coverage - even though our apartments require it. The incident would have been covered under his personal liability coverage, but we cannot claim the incident under our own rental insurance policy, being that he is liable for the damages. On 10/30/22, we noticed that part of the wound was open and seemed to have died back. The vet that performed the surgery in the early hours of 10/27 said that a portion of the skin being reattached did not bleed a lot during the procedure, and she worried it may have lost its connection to the blood supply and could die back. What we saw looked like that had happened. After sending an image to our vet and making a call to the emergency vet where the surgery was performed, we were informed that we should return to the emergency vet for a 2nd procedure. In the second procedure, they were able to remove the dead tissue and suture the wound with a drainage tube. Piper's wounds required a follow-up visit to remove the drainage tube on 11/2/22, and suture removal scheduled for 11/12/22. The total cost for Piper's injuries and follow-up visits exceeds $3,000. We have reported the incident to our apartment as well as Clackamas County Dog Services, and the dog has had no previous incidents. Due to Oregon's "One Bite Rule," no fine or removal of the tenant/dog will be enforced by Clackamas County Dog Services or our apartment. It is explicitly stated in our lease, Oregon law, and by both insurance agencies that the attacking dog's owner is liable for all damages. But he has not been able to provide us with the funds and does not have insurance coverage. He is generally non responsive in our attempts to contact him. The only means we have of pursuing the money is through small claims court, which will also cost us. In the meantime, we have to make monthly payments on the cost of her procedure, and in addition to our other expenses, we are in an extremely tight financial situation. We are not the ones to ask for help in these situations. Still, we are reaching out to our friends and family and those who can help to assist us with the financial burden that has fallen onto us due to another's negligence and inability to take accountability for their actions.

We got confirmation last week that he has a large carcinoma in his right lung. We’re lucky because CT scans confirmed that it’s isolated to this one tumor, but the oncologist has made it clear that chemo treatments will likely not work on such a large mass and surgery is likely the best option. This means that a lobe of his lung will need to be removed and we will be shortly meeting with a surgeon to discuss what this means in detail, and outline all the options. If this is the best route, he’ll be having surgery performed on the lung within the week. To further complicate the situation, he was simultaneously diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathy, essentially heart disease, so anesthesia is a high-risk event which is obviously necessary for surgery. As anyone can attest, Rufus is a one-of-a-kind sort of dog. In fact, he is the most un-dog-like dog you’ll come across, as he could easily be mistaken as a person—albeit a Muppet looking one. Typically, this is not a request we would advertise, or even request at all, but where Rufus is seeing specialist after specialist, facing surgery, x-rays, CT scans, and mounting prescriptions—not to mention whatever post-surgery assistance he may need (of which we won’t know until we consult with the surgeon), all within a two-to-three-week period, we felt that the best path would be to reach out to friends, colleagues, and fellow animal/Muppet lovers to help take pressure off of so much accumulated within such a short timeline. The oncologist and nurses are all shocked that Rufus, who’s tumor is pushing against his lung into his heart, is as healthy looking as he is. He still has incredible energy, friendly demeanor, and honestly provides no indication that he’s as sick as he actually is. We are holding on to this information closely as we believe this means that his strength and perseverance will get him through his surgery and recovery and he can and will in fact beat lung cancer. We humbly ask for support during this time, as such an incredible spirit deserves the best opportunity possible to beat this disease.

Hi! My name is Sara and I definitely never thought I would have to make a GoFundMe but it would mean the world to me if you read all of this. Two days ago we rushed our 7 month old kitten, Bubblegum, to the vet because she had such a drastic personality change and had stopped eating. After a $1200 vet bill, the vet concluded that she has the disease Feline Infectious Peritonitis (FIP). This disease is 100% fatal and will kill her if we don’t get treatment. I had never heard of this disease before but it affects kittens the most because of their lowered immune system. There is only ONE cure and it is not FDA approved in the US because the parent company doesn’t want to release it for veterinary use since they use it for human treatments. The cure is available in other countries though and it WORKS. Our vet could not legally prescribe it to us because of this but thankfully mentioned a Facebook group called FIP Warriors 5.0 that helps people find this treatment. I very frantically joined this group while waiting in the vet lobby and was almost immediately contacted by a moderator who connected me with somebody in our area that could help us. I am truly so amazed by this group of volunteers and the incredible work they do to help very worried pet parents like me. In the span of 24 hours I went from feeling hopeless while I broke down sobbing in the lobby of my vet’s office, to feeling overwhelmingly hopeful as I watched our little Bubblegum get her first injection treatment. It’s not an easy treatment. Bubblegum will require 84 days of a nightly injection and then after that will have another 84 days where we will observe her and cross our fingers and pray that she doesn’t relapse. If she makes it, she’ll be officially cured of this awful disease. It is expensive since it is not FDA approved. One vial costs about $50 and will last us a few days, but her dosage will increase as she grows and puts on some healthy weight. Bubblegum is only 7 months old and we adopted her only 2 months ago. It’s unfair and cruel that this is happening to her, and to us as well because we already love her so much. We don’t feel it’s her time to go at all and we are so willing to give her a chance. She is already such a little fighter. Even if we don’t get any financial help, Dan and I are willing to do what we have to do to pay for this. I don’t think we could live with ourselves if we didn’t at least try the treatments. We live in a very high cost of living area with very high rent though, so we humbly ask for any help that we can get. That said, we aren’t delusional. If her situation deteriorates then we will know what we have to do, but for right now we owe her that chance of survival. All donations for this GoFundMe will go towards buying her treatments and supplies, as well as paying for any related vet visits. This very handsome puppy, Bruno, was surrendered to RPC because he has a luxating patella. At just 11 months old, he has been in extreme pain, affecting his behavior in his prior home. Luxating patella is a painful condition in which the kneecap slips out of position. The groove the kneecap glides in is too shallow, causing frequent dislocation. The condition is very painful and affected dogs will cry out in pain or show changes in their behavior and temperaments due to the pain they are in. And if left untreated, the chronic dislocation will lead to arthritis in the knee, loss of motion and persistent pain. Luckily, surgery can cure Bruno and allow him to lead a normal and pain-free life. Like other orthopedic surgeries, it is a pricey procedure, but very necessary to eliminate the pain Bruno is enduring. The estimate for Bruno's surgery is close to $3,000 and once again we are asking for help so we can get this surgery done as quickly as possible. Please consider donating any amount to Bruno's surgery. Every dollar helps! Despite the pain he is in, Bruno is a very friendly, goofy and energetic Lab puppy. Bruno will be available for adoption after his surgery and necessary healing take place.

Hi my name is Alissa and I’m the proud cat mom of the two cuties Poe and Riley above. I was fortunate and blessed to adopt them from the Feline Rescue Association last October. They are sisters and the sweetest girls, they are inseparable and are each other's Ying to their Yang. As you can see in the photos below Poe has all the sass in speaking her mind and loves to comment on my decorations. Riley is a calm and brings all the zen vibes. They spend the day cuddling each other and each one sleeps on both sides of me at night by my head (of course Riley needs to be under the covers ). They really are truly my children! Last Wednesday was my 30th birthday and my best friend who recently moved two hours away sent flowers to my job from the company Baltimore's Florist. Unfortunately it was not the bouquet she ordered and they didn’t inform her of the change, she is aware Lillie’s are toxic to cats. I was so excited that day I didn’t realize there were two Lillie’s in the bouquet and they weren’t bloomed yet (I ALWAYS CHECK ). On Friday morning I woke up to my worst nightmare. They were throwing up and I didn’t see which one or if both, and there was a half eaten Lilly on the floor. I went into panic mode of course. My neighbor called poison control line for me as I had to run out to meet my boss for a conference meeting and her and my mom managed to get them into the crates and to the emergency vet asap (it truly takes a village and I’m so grateful for mine!) As all of this is happening, my friend contacted the flower shop and spoke with the executive director who informed her this should not have happened and any changes needed to be approved by the person who purchased them. She attempted to contact the direct flower store to find out what kind of lily it was and they REFUSED and said they could not disclose that information! (In an animal emergency that it’s imperative information!!! This isn’t HIPPA of the flowers!) The executive director was unsuccessful in follow up conversations with them and is now looking into things herself for the sequence of unacceptable events. My mom resides in Bowie and took them to cats and dogs. After being told it would be $6,600 on top of the $1.200 they had already charged I was devastated. I could only think the worst was to come already knowing how toxic it is, the thought of loosing them or having to surrender because of these numbers made me fall to the ground. Only to then find out they had not started any treatment even though they had been there for 6.5 hours knowing how time sensitive treatment is and already have gotten permission to start treatment. My mom and I rushed them to Emergency Animal Hospital of Ellicott City and I am so thankful we did as they took exceptional care of them and the charges were not as high! I felt confident that they were in good hands with them and they would do everything they could. They finally came back home to me last night and just had their 24 hour visit follow up and all labs are normal! I am beyond thankful that they are home and healthy (and now I’m an official paranoid helicopter mom even more than before) I never thought I would be in a place to need to create a go fund me but this has been a serious strain on my finances and my mom who also helped me. I (as I always jokingly but in truth say) live independently on a social work salary . There was no way I wasn’t going to figure something out for them and not have them treated due to this but I never imagined we’d be here. I know emergency vets are expensive but MAN, was I truly shocked-this was one of my worst fears and I just again never imagined something like this to happen. I know I felt immense guilt for not noticing it (too much excitement from the birthday I guess UGH) and my friend felt such guilt for what happened. But accidents unfortunately do happen. Poe, Riley and I would appreciate any help that anyone could give to us. They truly are my world and have given more to me than I could ever give to them. They have given me feelings of purpose, joy and have been there to lift me up in hard times and they will never know how much they bring to me!

At first, our goal was to transition the dairy farm to a cow sanctuary and sustainable vegetable farm in 5 to 10 years. Unfortunately, due to the struggling Japanese dairy industry, Potekoro's caretaker must sell the farm by the end of 2022. We now have less than a few months to find a new home for Potekoro. If we fail, Potekoro will likely be sold to a slaughterhouse. The last thing we want is to give up on Potekoro’s life. Luckily, we met our collaborator for this project, Ms.Tani. She runs the Moo Mow Garden in Fukushima, a sanctuary for 11 cows that survived the devastating Tohoku earthquake of 2011. Because of local government regulations, Moo Mow Garden cannot accept additional cows, so we need a new place for the Potekoro & Friends Sanctuary. As of November 2022, we are negotiating with local governments and landowners for a new site. Potentially it will be between 2 and 20 hectares in size (that's roughly 5 to 50 acres). The sooner we raise funds, the sooner we can sign a contract for the land and start setting up the sanctuary. Initial funds are required, but once we establish the necessities for the sanctuary, the cows can live freely with minimal operating costs. The cows can survive by consuming the natural vegetation in abandoned farmlands which will also benefit environmental conservation. Thanks to the fertile cow droppings, vegetables and fruits will continue to grow and will be easily harvested using natural farming methods. Since we are planning to have large enough land for multiple cows to live, we can likely rescue another cow from the same dairy farm. It just depends on how much we can raise. Cows instinctively like to live in groups with their herd mates. If possible, we would like to help them to live in a new land together. With your support, we plan to rescue not just one but two cows. Down the road, we hope to be able to scale the project up and save additional cows. There is a chance that this project could be changed or delayed due to unforeseen circumstances, but we are determined to use all funds collected to help these cows and build a sustainable farm sanctuary. Hello! A few people suggested I set up one of these so Marvin can get the proper care he needs. The backstory: Marvin is a neighborhood cat that does not have a mean bone in his body. I saved up money to get him neutered and ear-tipped in hopes the other cats would leave him alone, but he still gets beat up pretty much daily. Marvin feels safest on our front porch, but he still explores the neighborhood and loves catching mice. On Sunday, Oct. 30 Marvin was attempting to cross the street to come to our house when a large pickup truck struck him. He flew over ten feet and then slid across the road. We were sure he died immediately, but he was still alive on the pavement. We moved him to the grass under a tree where we told him we loved him and pet him in hopes to keep him comfortable until he passed. An hour later, he was still breathing and trying to get up. We moved him to our porch to keep him from trying to get up and cross the street again. By the end of the day, Marv was still breathing and moving into different sleeping positions. I decided to take him into our house to keep him safer and away from predators. He slept all night and all day Monday. He would not open his eyes, eat, drink or move from his laundry basket. This morning (Tuesday) I woke up and Marvin had jumped out of his basket and moved to a corner of the living room. He even ate a bit of soft food! The problem is, we do not know if Marvin has internal injuries because of the truck vs. cat impact. His jaw seems to be broken or busted up as he hard a hard time opening his mouth and his nose is very stuffed up from the injuries making it hard for him to breathe. I am asking for donations so I can at least take Marvin to the vet for a checkup and x-rays. We do not have enough extra money to care for this neighborhood cat. We will also be putting some toward his care but not as much as he will need. This sweet boy means so much to me. My hope is to get him better and keep him safe so he can live much longer.

He is seeing the oncology team at Upstate Veterinary Specialists. On top of the Palladia, Prusten has received IV chemo there, and a treatment called Zolendronate that helps strengthen his bones. Prusten is also getting Palliative radiation treatment that we take him to Canada for. He is going again November 3rd. Osteosarcoma is an EXTREMELY painful cancer, and the radiation is absolutely the number 1 thing that has helped his pain level. We actually didn't realize how much he was hurting until he had radiation. It 100% gave us our baby back. It is over 1000 per treatment. Prusten also sees a holistic Vet at least monthly who does acupuncture and chiropractic care for him. I can't even tell you how much I HATE to ask for help with this. It's really becoming a strain to handle this expense, and I am not willing to give him anything less than the best possible care. All funds will go straight to his vet bills, and if there happens to be any leftover we will donate it to another canine cancer friend in need. Any bit is so appreciated. Thank you all so much for sharing my love for Prusten Foo.

Hi, My name is Jill LaRoche. I have been a hairstylist for 30 years and Animal Rescuer my entire life. I have ALWAYS had a passion for helping animals of all kinds, big and small. Dogs have always been my greatest love. My husband Keith and I have traveled most of the world, and it would always bother me to see animals that lived on the street, hurt or hungry. This year we decided to move to the beautiful town of San Felipe, Mexico. Here it will become my new life of helping dogs & cats in need. It's a small quiet town with an average of only 20,000 permanent residents and about 10,000 from the US, Canada & Europe in the winter months. There are more and more ex-pats becoming permanent residents, as will we. With that, I'm hoping that more money and help will come to spay & neuter these animals. Many of them roaming the streets are pretty happy even though, as an American, it isn't easy to see them out on their own. Mexicans often think of dogs as the protector and cats as the varmin getter. Often they have names, and they are loved, yet they run from house to house during the day and return to the yard at night. Then, there are the forgotten ones. The ones that get shooed away or abused for being a neusance. They can be injured from getting hit by a car or severely malnourished, mostly from tick fever. My goal is to help the sick and injured, feed the malnourished and get spayed or neutered. If there is a chance of getting rehomed, I will do my best to find a loving home. The local shelter is overwhelmed with dogs, cats & mommas having babies in a safe place. Otherwise, if they came from a pretty safe environment, I would bring them back to where they were. Remember, they may often have a home but need help from the community to spay or neuter these animals. My chihuahua Carlito is from Cancun, and since moving to San Felipe, we have rescued Yoda, which has made our life complete.

There is no easy or charming way to begin a story about asking for help to treat your dog’s cancer. But here’s my best shot. My name is Carli, I live in Bloomington, Indiana, and I want to tell you about my best friend—my 4-year-old Great Pyrenees rescue, Raffi. I met Raffi when he was just 4 months old. He already weighed 53 lbs, had just been rescued from a livestock auction, and he was struggling to find his forever home. He had already been adopted once by another family and returned after just one night (we suspect due to slobber-related concerns). At that time, I was planning to move across the country for work and feeling very nervous about doing so totally alone. When I met Raffi, something just felt right. We brought him home with us the night we met him. To be honest, Raffi isn’t what I had envisioned when I first started looking for a 4-legged friend. He can be stubborn, slobbers everywhere, he has 5 extra toes on his back legs, and he never—I mean never stops shedding. And I’ve never met anyone with such a good heart. (Or more toes). Raffi is kind and gentle with everyone he meets—kids, cats, dogs, strangers & friends. He comes running and gladly hops into the back hatch of my Subaru every time I open it, and has slept happily through many a 12-hour trek between Philly and Indiana. He greets me with a big grin every time I walk through the door. Just by being himself, for the past 4 years Raffi has been my closest pal. When Raffi started limping in July of 2022, we never could have expected what was about to happen. As the vet showed us the X-ray of the tumor on his leg, explaining that he had an aggressive bone cancer called osteosarcoma, we were devastated and confused. Only the week before we had celebrated his 4th birthday--this didn't seem possible. The vet explained that Raffi would almost certainly need amputation of his front right leg, and that about 50% of dogs with Raffi’s condition will live as long as a year from their diagnosis, with roughly another 25% living as long as 2 years . We were crushed, but not at all ready to give up on him. We have been working with a specialty clinic in Indianapolis, and his doctors have helped us build a treatment plan to keep him living a comfy, happy life as his silly self for as long as possible. As they predicted, in late September the tumor progressed too much for us to manage the pain, and Raffi became a tri-pawd. Not to be corny, but to watch him recover, adapt, and return to his same old goofy, cuddly, bouncy self (now with a normal number of toes) has been nothing short of inspiring. But the fight didn’t end with the surgery. Osteosarcoma is known for aggressive metastasis, and Raffi’s disease seems to be progressing in a rare way. He has developed skin tumors—a highly uncommon form for this cancer to take—in spite of starting chemotherapy. Because his cancer, as his oncologist put it, “is not behaving,” it’s time for us to look at other options to keep fighting for him. This brings us to GoFundMe. Our doctor has recommended a targeted cancer treatment. This is a program that involves testing genetic material from Raffi’s tumor to look for specific mutations for which more targeted medical regimens can be effective. Because the generalized treatment hasn’t prevented the metastasis, and because the progression of his disease is unusual, this is a way of looking for something that can be aimed at Raffi’s exact disease course. We were so relieved to learn that there are still options for him, but this path isn’t without obstacles. As you might imagine, taking a targeted approach comes with a hefty up-front cost. The testing alone costs $2,600. After the testing, assuming they are able to identify something targetable, there is a $2,000 fee for the medical treatment. The good news is that after those expenses, Raffi has access to those medications for the rest of his life. Of course, there are still diagnostic tests and vet exam fees, which aren’t cheap either. One small mercy has been that I had pet insurance for Raffi—which covered the surgery and several of our initial expenses. Some of our close family and friends have generously chipped in to help cover exam fees too, and it’s kept us afloat this far. But cancer is almost as expensive as it is painful, and we exhausted our insurance coverage a bit over a month ago. As many of you know, I am currently a PhD student at Indiana University, which means I’m not exactly rolling in cash. I don’t believe I could have made it into this program without the opportunities I was able to pursue by moving to Philadelphia. I don’t think I could have made that move to Philadelphia without Raffi. My life wouldn’t be what it is today without him. I want to be transparent; this treatment is far from a guarantee, and it is not a cure. We don’t know what will happen next, and Raffi’s cancer will likely never go into full remission. What we do know is that Raffi’s doctor has seen dogs live as long as 3 years past their diagnosis with this treatment (which, from what I’ve learned, is a huge success for such an aggressive cancer). We also know that without treatment, most dogs with Raffi’s diagnosis will live another 6 months from the time of their diagnosis. Or less. What this treatment can give is a shot at more for him. It’s a shot at more days playing in the snow, to splash around in the creek, play with his cousins, and bark at, well, probably nothing. And, it’s more time for us—for me. It's a shot at more days to come home to his smiley face and stinky breath. More nights falling asleep beside the 85-lb bear who means more to me than anything. A shot at more laughter and love, and the safety of having him with me. More time together. Right now, Raffi seems to be feeling great. He is running, jumping, snuggling, playing, rolling in the grass, smiling, barking, slobbering, and loving us as well as he always has. And I need your help to keep fighting for him.

Reaper is an 11 month old Belgian malinois that was rescued by Mackenzie Vorhees. He spent the first 8 months in a small wire cage outdoors. His breeder was going to shoot him because he “didn’t have the temperament for military or police work.” From the day Kenzie picked him up, she knew the real reason the breeder was going to put him down wasn’t because of his temperament, it was because he had a leg injury that the breeder didn’t want to pay to take care of. It started with a slight limp, nothing too concerning, the vet said it was most likely just sore because he wasn’t used to being able to walk and run around after living in such a small space his entire life. The issue continued to get worse, to the point he wouldn’t put any pressure on the leg at all, so he was seen by a different vet who took X-rays and found nothing. They diagnosed him with panosteitis (severe growing pains), and prescribed him pain medication. A couple more weeks went by and there was no improvement, it actually got worse. He slept all day, he stopped eating, he cried in pain to lay down or if he moved around too much. So he was seen by a third vet who also said it was probably just growing pains. Another month went by, he dropped 7lbs and was extremely malnourished, but was being force fed more than an adequate amount of calories per day. So he was seen by a fourth vet, who took an additional set of X-rays, still found nothing but finally decided he was no longer faced with growing pains, but something more serious. While waiting to hear back from OSU (who ended up viewing his X-rays from the vet and also finding nothing), his family worked on putting weight on him. Spoon feeding him wet food, administering nutrical paste several times per day, and hand feeding him as much dry food as he would eat. Reaper was then finally taken to the Bone, Joint, and Spine clinic in Columbus, where they took a much better x-ray and found nothing but bad news. Reaper needs his hip removed. There was a potential option of a total hip replacement, but the likelihood of any surgeon taking his case with the overwhelming amount of scar tissue, is slim to none. The cause of this issue was one of three things: 1. A fracture that was never properly healed. This is best case scenario, but not likely because there is no evidence of a previous fracture in the rads. The hip removal would resolve this issue with no further treatment. However, that leaves his weight loss unexplained and we will have to do further testing to get a diagnosis for that. 2. An infection caused by bacteria that traveled through the bloodstream and settled in the hip joint, destroying the nearby tissue. This would explain his weight loss and he would need treated for the infection after the hip removal. This would be confirmed by pathology after the surgery. 3. Osteosarcoma, worst case scenario. Very rare in dogs of this age, but would explain the weight loss and the fast deterioration of the tissue. This cannot be confirmed until the hip is removed and sent to pathology. Treatment after the hip removal would not be an option, he would love a very short life, but get to live out his remaining few months without the pain he’s been living with for months. Despite the fact that Reaper has lived in a constant state of pain, and spent the first few months of his life feeling unloved in a kennel, he is the happiest and sweetest dog there is. We want to see Reaper live the longest, happiest, pain-free life he can live with his new family that loves him to pieces and would do anything to give him even just a few months without pain. This surgery will be $4500 and we are asking for help to raise money to make this surgery possible for him. Even if you are unable to donate, a like, a share, and a prayer is more than enough. Thank you for your support!

If you could describe the perfect dog, it would be our Reesie Belle. We rescued her as a puppy from a beagle rescue in 2019. She is the most loving dog and has never meant a stranger. To know her is truly to love her. We call her our baby, because she is exactly that. Every night since we brought her home, she has slept right up against me. She loves to "spoon" and be cuddled. She was so full of life until Tuesday, November 15th, when she suffered a traumatic spinal injury after jumping off the bed. Suddenly she couldn't stand up, walk or move her back legs at all. We took her to the vet, where they told us she has IVVD and FCE. She is now paralyzed. IVDD, or Intervertebral Disc Disease, is a spinal disorder that follows from the herniating of an intervertebral disc inside an afflicted dog. A gelatinous substance that is surrounded by a thick outer layer can be found between the bones and spine in dogs. This substance constitutes the intervertebral disc, and it serves as a shock absorber for the spine. When the intervertebral disc herniates, it can result in concussion or compression of the spinal cord, causing lasting and debilitating damage. A fibrocartilaginous embolism, or FCE, occurs when a piece of the intervertebral disc (the cushion between the bones of your spine) breaks off and enters the blood supply to the spinal cord. We thank you in advance for any contributions to her care and if you can't contribute we thank you for any shares of her fundraiser. Much love, Colleen, Addison, Riley, Flora, Pizza, Dreamer, Sheba, Luke and Stash <3

Hello! My name is Nicole and we adopted Lupita in January 2021. Lupita is a two year old border collie/ cattle dog and we live in Bemidji, MN with my boyfriend and her fur sibling Jovie. She was saved from a shelter in Texas and transported up to Minnesota where we adopted her. She had a rough start in life being in an overcrowded Texas Shelter. Her life before she found her way to the shelter was full of abuse. When we adopted her it took months before she felt fully comfortable and not so shut down. She has had a history of undiagnosed lameness and has been on vetprofen over the past year and it didn’t seem to bother her until a few months ago. I brought her in and she had blood drawn where it all came back normal. We put her on a bed rest for a few weeks and it wasn’t improving. She was just in on November 9th for X-rays where we got her official diagnosis. She has severe hip dysplasia in both hips and the left side is so bad that it is just hanging. I have an estimate from the vet for roughly $3000 that would help fix the left side since her left hip is just hanging. Her right hip will also be around $3,000. A femoral head ostectomy (FHO) will be needed on both hips. Update on 12/11/2022: We will also have to have surgery done on her right hip as well in about 6 months. Her left hip will be a 2-3 month recovery alone and then possibly 3-4 months after that will be her right hip. She didn’t go through all the struggles in life before us adopting her on January 24th, 2021 with the history of abuse, and almost being at risk of being euthanized in Texas with her sister before being saved by Northern Lakes Rescue in Pequot Lakes, MN to have to suffer. We will do everything we can to help her and to have her continue living her best life with us. We love her so much and want nothing but the best. Update: 12/13/3022: Lupita has surgery today on her left hip. I was able to pick her up the next day! She is doing amazing and already walking on her back left by doing a head ostectomy (FHO). We will keep you all updated! Truly, this was not the outcome that we were hoping for as she is only two and a half. She is living her best life with us now and this surgery is important to help her keep living her best life. Thank you all so much for sharing her story! Every share helps! We just want to help her feel better again and I appreciate you for reading her story. Please reach out with questions. Any funds left over will be donated to save Rescue Dogs from death row!

Hi, I’m Terri, and I am fundraising for my three-month-old puppy Rocky. His mom had been dumped off at our worksite in June, soon after having puppies. She was in deplorable shape. I couldn’t help but take her home with me. She is so sweet and beautiful. I took her to the vet, who confirmed that she had recently given birth and was heartworm positive. We scheduled her first heartworm injection for August 20. About a week before that date, I noticed her mammary glands seemed a little swollen, and when I’d let her outside to use the bathroom, she would go underneath the stairs, dig a hole, and lie down in it. That’s when I realized I had brought home a pregnant doggy. Sure enough, on August 20, the day she was supposed to get her first heartworm injection, she gave birth to four bouncing bundles of fur. I loaded them all up and took them to the vet since she already had an appointment so they could get checked out. Sure enough, there was a problem with one of them. He had a cleft palate. Dr. Hubbard said I had two choices. One was to euthanize him. The other was to tube feed him every two hours, 24 hours a day, seven days a week. She said if I chose that option, the odds of him surviving past the first one or two weeks would be very low. She left me alone with mom and the pups to think it over. I did quite a bit of crying as well as quite a bit of praying. I am not a spring chicken anymore, and I didn’t know if I’d be up to the challenge. In addition to mom and her pups, I have two other fur babies and a full-time job. Within a few minutes, I realized that I had never backed down from a challenge and that this new baby deserved a shot at life. Then and there, I named him Rocky, after Rocky Balboa. I knew he was going to be a fighter. Fast forward three months later. After several weeks of very little sleep, lots of prayers and perseverance, little Rocky is thriving. He is tube-fed puréed veggies four times a day. He cannot run around on the floor or outside on the ground as he will put anything and everything in his mouth, and because of the cleft palate, it goes directly into his lungs. So I have to watch him very closely. We made a trip to Capital Veterinary Specialists in Tallahassee today for Dr. Kevin Drygas to check him out and see if he is a good candidate for surgery to repair his palate. The bottom line...he is. It is scheduled for December 15. The estimated cost is $1,600 - $2,000. So, here I am, asking for help. I have a little extra money available to me. But I’m hoping family, friends, and coworkers will help offset the remainder and help Rocky be the healthy, active dog he was created to be.

How Beth, The Fairy CatMother gave Rutherford a home During COVID, Beth started fostering cats. She nicknamed herself “The Fairy CatMother,” because she said, “my job is to take these cats in and clean them up, give them somewhere safe to hang out, and help them get dressed up for the ball to find their forever homes.” In April 2021, Beth began to foster Rutherford, the sweetest friendliest kitty in the Cativerse. The rescue estimated him to be about 2 years old. He won her heart right away as an unusually doglike cat with an adorable face that has been described as looking like he was caught eating a jar of peanut butter. He is the rare magical cat that kisses strangers to greet them, actually likes belly rubs, and politely gazes up at visitors asking if he can sit in their lap. As time passed, Beth and Rutherford developed a unique bond. Beth realized she didn’t want to let him go. There was just one problem: Rutherford had been diagnosed with a rare, fatal congenital heart defect. On average, cats with this type of diagnosis live 6–18 months. Heart Trouble in Catland Part of Rutherford's heart is growing the wrong way, causing it to be unable to work as well as normal. This leads to congestive heart failure, where fluid builds up in the chest surrounding the lungs. The condition is fatal. The question is when? It could be a month, or perhaps a few years if he’s very lucky. Getting his treatment right has been a high-wire balancing act between Beth and his University of Minnesota Cardiology team. They need to give enough medicine to reduce the fluid around his lungs so he can breathe, but not so much that it damages his kidneys. Repeated chest taps (manually removing the fluid around his lungs with a needle), heart scans, and other procedures to find out what's going on, without giving him trauma. ﻿But if you know Beth, you know that there's no one else in the world who will work harder to make sure he gets everything he needs. Hope for Rutherford His veterinarians all agree that Beth's care has extended Rutherford's life and continues to make it a good one. At some point, she will likely have to make a heart-wrenching decision about his quality of life; the most likely end for him is suffering from fluid buildup that they can’t control, or suffering from kidney damage caused by his medications. But Beth doesn't want to make that decision based on the cost of Rutherford’s care. Not before he's ready. His life is filled with love, snuggles, friends, neighbors, and cat tv looking out windows at trees full of birds and squirrels, and yard theater watching all the bunnies and critters a kitty could over dream of from the safety of his kennel. How to help Rutherford The cost up to now finding the right balance in his treatment is a lot for a Fairy CatMother to handle. This is a preexisting condition, so pet insurance isn't an option. In the year since his adoption, Rutherford's heart-related medical needs have cost nearly $7,000. And it's not over yet. More scans and tests will be needed as his vets continue to evaluate the best way to care for him, and he is likely to need more chest taps when his disease progresses. To that end, Rutherford and Beth are looking for some support from their community. They are so thankful and appreciate all support, including any amount of donation, sharing of this fundraiser with other people, and your prayers and good thoughts. Here are some approximations of costs until now, just to give you an idea. $800–$1200: Emergency room visits for dangerous declines $450: Echocardiogram/heart scans to check on his condition $400: Chest taps to remove fluid from around his lungs $200: Check-ups to make sure medications aren’t damaging his organs $130: Five kinds of medicine (monthly) $50: Appetite stimulant to counteract medication (monthly) Please help Beth give Rutherford more beautiful days! Rutherford and Beth THANK YOU, and want you to know that ANY amount of help is greatly appreciated For every $300 reached we will share a photo or video from Rutherford, right here on his GoFundMe page. ********************** WOWEEE!!! This community is giving lots of love to Rutherford fast! Rutherford reminded me he promised to post 1 photo/video per $300 donated to thank everyone. We cleaned his eyes and made him as comfortable as we could and he lay motionless on a duvet - closed his eyes and slept. This morning we took him to see vet Gema Gonzalez Garcia at Clinica Veterinaria Amik in Campanillas who with her nurse Marina, ‘cleared the decks’ for him and began what we hope will be a recovery - but it will be a long and arduous road ahead for him. Gema has taken blood for a full biochemistry profile and to check for many diseases. She did a quick ‘snap’ test to try to get ‘ahead of the game’ re Leishmania but that showed negative result but we will wait also to see what the laboratory tests show. We can list a few of Chesney’s problems. - Dehydration, his skin is dry and ‘tough’ his eyes sunken ... - Emaciation - he weighed only 23kgs and we estimate he should be at least the same size as our boy OJ who is 55kgs. - His right hind leg in the hock (ankle area) has been bitten some time ago by something quite small ... maybe even rats. It is very infected, hugely swollen and very painful - it is oozing and bleeding. His paw is constantly bleeding and oozing due to the infection from the bite but also due to embedded grass seeds and cactus spikes. - His left hind leg is swollen and his paw had huge embedded grass seeds between his toes and some large holes in the flesh between his toes there. It is very infected. - His hips have open sores due to injury and also from lying being unable to move with absolutely no fat or muscle under his dry, sagging skin - His front legs are also very sore indeed, and his paws are oozing and bleeding due to infections caused by injury, seeds etc - He has multiple areas of no hair, broken skin and infections all over his body. His shoulders are particularly bad. - He has a bilateral eye infection. - He has broken teeth - Chesney is not a young dog - it’s possible he is maybe 8 years old or older - His ears outside are sore with large scabs on them. - His nose is very dry and cracked probably due to dehydration - His hair is falling out in clumps and he had many scabs from previous injuries. - He has of course - engorged ticks and fleas - He has intestinal parasites. - His nails are very over grown, some Gema clipped, some need to wait until the next visit due to the infections. - Mentally he is broken, we think he wonders why his life is like this, what did he do, what didn’t he do ... So that’s our starter for today, we wait now for the laboratory results to come back and Chesney will see Gema again on Saturday. He had an antibiotic injection and pain killer, we have antibiotics to give him twice a day. He also had a worming tablet. We will keep bathing and treating his sores, bathing his eyes and he will continue to have small nutritious meals regularly - he has fresh water constantly available. He has had topical treatment for the ticks and fleas and hopefully in 24 hours they will at least be gone and no longer leeching from his dishevelled, abused shell of a body. He was more alert this morning and looked at his surroundings when he got out of the car. We also have to thank IKEA - their bags come in very handy to customize into dog slings and stretchers! Although only 23kgs he is a big lad and it is very painful for him to be carried in your arms so slings it is for now. Chesney is wearing a muzzle in the photos as some of the procedures to clean and investigate his wounds were very painful for him and even giving him an injection there was little muscle anywhere to put it in to - all of that makes things very painful and frightening but he carried himself very, very well in the circumstances. Our thoughts ... humans are evil beyond belief... If the lab test come back with no Leishmania or any other underlying condition they don’t even have that excuse of ‘Well he was ill!’ to use, it is total pure utter neglect and abuse over a considerable length of time. Even if he has an underlying condition the level of abuse this boy has endured is disgusting and they failed to do the slightest thing to help him, never mind seek veterinary assistance, they just left him to deteriorate, didn’t feed him and left him to endure terror and attacks from some other animals .. They knew when they dumped him yesterday what a horrendous state he was in, the pain he has been suffering is impossible to miss, the bleeding and oozing from infections clear to see, the infections in his eyes, the discomfort that must be giving him is also impossible to bypass ... These people are excuses for the human race, they are out and out abusers, they are the worst of the worst and sadly they will never face justice for what they have done to this boy ... and one also has to think and fear how many have gone before him suffering the same appalling abuse and neglect .. because we doubt he had been the first and horrifically he won’t be the last. We have to hope for positivity from the test results when they come and we have to hope with the help of antibiotics his body can battle these horrid infections attacking his body ... he isn’t for giving up we saw that today and so we will not give up either - we will battle with him and vet Gema to turn his sad, painful life around. We fully understand that everyone is experiencing difficult times right now - but if you wish to help Chesney in even a small way we and him would be very grateful. This won’t be a quick fix for this boy, his vet treatment and cares will be on going, his body will get all the practical and medical assistance that it needs - his broken heart and soul of course that’s different but we will try to help him understand what to be loved and to be valued is and we will show him that not all humans are cruel and some of us can be trusted, some of us can be relied on and some of us are ready to hold a paw and cradle a head in our arms ... we hope he will eventually feel warmth in his heart. Saipan Cares for Animals (SCA), provided a low cost Community Clinic/Rescue and Shelter for the Northern Marianas Islands (U.S territory) for over 8 years. There are no other animal care services here. These islands have a long history of dogs and cats over-populating our streets, beaches and jungles, who are homeless, diseased, injured and starving. The local Government’s solution to this terribly sad problem has been 100% euthansia. SCA’s humane, and more long term solution, is to provide spay/neuter surgery. We invite volunteer Veterinarians from around the world to visit our islands to perform the necessary surgeries. Eight months ago our constant financial struggles to stay open became very serious and consequently we had to close our physical shelter. We have been able to keep the much needed and only Community Animal Clinic open and have created a “Virtual Shelter” ; individuals and families in our community provide the shelter and SCA provides the medical care and spay/neuter surgery that we use to provide our shelter animals before adopting out. Since opening our Virtual Shelter in April, 2022, we have had no budget for this program and now, today, our low cost Community Clinic is struggling to stay open as it provides for our Virtual Shelter as well. We are asking everyone who has compassion and love for animals, and a desire to keep our beautiful tropical islands clean and safe, to please donate to support our Virtual Shelter. The homeless dogs and cats on Saipan are grateful for your help!

I called every vet in the area and ended up scheduling an appointment two hours away at SW Animal Hospital with Dr. Burgess. I cleaned Mayonnaise up, bathed her, and treated her eye every night. Luckily, the infection cleared up fast, she's putting on weight, and Dr. Burgess was able to trim back her teeth (they were too long for filing). He also gave me some sad information. Mayonnaise's teeth are likely warped from chewing on her cage bars, not biology, and she has 2 mammary tumors that need to be removed as soon as possible. She's too light for the surgery right now, but we're working on getting her to pack on some grams as quickly as possible. To be clear, we can afford the smaller expense of the vet visits, but we can't afford the surgery in the time she needs it. Schmidty the Kitty needs your help!!! Schmidty was rescued 12 years ago from a local shelter at one month old. A litter of all boys, but the only one with white paws! A month before Schmidty was adopted, my family sadly lost my Grandmother to cancer. This was a hard for me as I lost a best friend. Because of losing such an important person in my life, I wanted to honor her while naming this new kitten. The name Schmidt was my Grandmother's maiden name. Which is where the name "Schmidty" was decided. Schmidty's name has definitely fit his personality so well throughout these years. My grandmother would have adored him. Just recently, Schmidty became quickly and suddenly ill. Refusing food, fever, lethargy, strong discomfort. All happening within a couple of days. Once brought to the veterinary clinic, they immediately had him on an IV catheter, pain management, antinasea mediation. Radiographs were taken; ultrasound completed. In house bloodwork done. The diagnosis of Pancreatitis was confirmed. Still showing signs of a lot pain and not wanting to eat, he is to stay at the clinic for further treatment and examination. (Edit: please check the updates for more information on Sesame's health journey) I started this fundraiser on fb initially. Then I discovered that nearly 2⁄3 of people I sent the link to (on & off Facebook) were unable to access the page. So I switched platforms because there's no time for that kind of nonsense. I'm sitting here with Sesame, watching her try to breathe with her nose stuffed up, trying to lay in a way that doesn't further irritate her raw, pink nose... and I'm scared. I just spent 20 minutes laying with her on the floor, massaging her face. Today has been a difficult day. ... About 5 years ago I went to the local animal shelter seeking a dog for my family. My friend and I walked throughout the building, eyeing the excited pups, asking questions, and getting puppy kisses. As wonderful as each dog was, I didn't feel an instant connection with any. My friend and I were about to leave when we realized we missed a few stalls. That's when I saw her, laying there quietly at the back of her stall, silently staring up at me with her piercing golden eyes. In that moment I knew she was the one for us. A black German shepherd/Siberian husky mix with bright eyebrows and a silver belly we decided to call Sesame. At that time Sesame was about 1.5 years old. The shelter explained to my family at pickup that Sesame had run away from all 5 of her previous homes! Plus she could jump a 4ft fence without even touching it so she needed watched constantly outdoors or she'd run away at her first chance. So we did our best, keeping an ever watchful eye on this elusive escape artist, doing our best to stay proactive. But she never ran off (still true to this day and she's now 7) despite having the skills and opportunities to do so. In the beginning, Sesame was very aloof and didn't show much affection. I believe she was afraid to develop an attachment because we might return her too. Over time she has become so animated and affectionate, my sweet goofy girl seemed to feel safe enough to be herself. I think she really understands that we want her around. Recently our baby girl has become sick, stricken with sinusitis, upper respiratory infections, as well as severe bronchitis. She has a nonstop mucus drip from her nose that keeps getting into her airways (dogs lick their noses frequently). It has also turned her left nostril pink and raw. I do my best to keep her clean but it hurts her so much whenever I touch it. Some days, it feels like I'm pushing a boulder uphill during a flood. At this point she is in need of a CT scan and/or a rhinoscopy to see what is causing the problems and do what we can to fix them. I have called around Michigan and a few neighbouring states for pricing for these procedures and it remains consistent; $150-$200 consultation and $3000-$5000 for the procedures themselves. I've yet to find a program/organization to help (the recommendations I've gotten have been gr8 of course but so far it's been a hopeless game of "sorry, we can't help! Have you tried [insert other orgs]" that has me running in circles). In the meantime Sesame is sick and I'm afraid of what could happen if I act too late. She lights up my life and brightens my day as a lightning bolt of love, energy, goofiness, and just a touch of chaos. I don't know if I can convey in words how difficult it is to see her struggling with chronic illness. She's still playful but the respiratory troubles are making it difficult. As a person with asthma troubles, I have an idea of how she's feeling and oh boy does that break my heart. I sing to her every day. I cook for her. I cry a lot. I give her steam baths (she hates water like a cat in a 90s cartoon so this is *not easy*). What I'm trying to say is that I'm doing my best to care for her right now but she needs (unfortunately expensive) help from a licensed vet. We're asking for $5000 to help cover all upcoming medical expenses and adjacent costs. Any extra money raised will still be used to care for Sesame (food, medications, gasoline for transportation, future vet visits, etc) because she is a wonder-child who deserves the very best. Thank you so much for taking the time to read our story. Any amount donated is *INCREDIBLY* appreciated. And thank you to everyone sharing our story.

Hi All, About a week ago we received the heartbreaking news that our 4-year-old wolfdog, Sage, was diagnosed with a very aggressive form of lymphoma and given only months to live. We want to share a little bit about her and our journey with her in the hopes that you might join in helping us make the last few months of her life as wildly comfortable as she is sweet and sassy. It was four years and ten months ago that Sage came into my life. She was a scared wolf-dog pup I adopted from a less-than-savory situation. She had a fair amount of attitude and needed a whole lot of help getting used to this world. If you have ever had the privilege of being a guardian to a wolfdog you know it is an experience unlike raising any other dog. If you haven’t, let me tell you a little bit about what life with Sage included. Hours with a trainer, countless hours building trust with her, a lifelong commitment to socializing her to the world, an entire couch chewed through, at least five pairs of shoes destroyed, my whole bookshelf torn apart, kitchen cabinets frequently opened and contents confiscated, and a whole lot of other sassy antics. All of this has been beyond worth it because the bond formed with a wolfdog is like none other. It is to be accepted and belong to one’s pack; it is to find family. From the joyous howls when I get home, the gentle head nuzzles for pets, to the sheer awe of sharing in her wildness, Sage has taught me what it means to allow all parts of myself to belong, what it means to be accepted, and that its ok to be a little wild in this domesticated world. Fast forward to 2022, and Sage has been living her best life here in Nederland, CO with my partner Adam and I: fully emersed in nature, chasing squirrels, swimming in creeks, summiting mountains, and enjoying an array of amazing (at least from her perspective) smells. Adam and I had noticed how much more affectionate Sage had grown since living here. Then, about a week ago, Sage suddenly stopped eating (one of her favorite things); she refused to go on walks or even get up to go outside. We brought her to the animal hospital to find out she was close to death due to extreme hypercalcemia (very high calcium levels) and her kidneys were very damaged. During the first two days at the hospital Sage barely lifted her head when we visited. It took a week-long hospital stay for Sage’s calcium levels to return to normal, her to get hydrated, and the vets to figure out what was wrong and say it was safe to take her home. We were heartbroken when we learned Sage was diagnosed with T-Cell Lymphoma originating in her spleen. We couldn’t help but think “she is so young, how is this possible?” Unfortunately, this is the most aggressive form of lymphoma and the most advanced chemotherapy treatment program would give her a maximum of 6 months to live. We have started this gofundme page to help make Sage’s end of life as wildly comfortable as she is sweet and sassy. In partnership with Sage’s vet, we have decided not to pursue the most intensive chemotherapy as the weekly IV treatments would be far too stressful for Sage and would only give her a 10% chance of remission. We have decided to pursue an oral chemotherapy treatment that will make her more comfortable and, although unlikely, would still give her a chance at remission. Her initial hospital stay was $8,200, which is quite a challenge for us. After taking out a loan to cover the cost of her hospital stay, we can’t afford the treatment to make her life more comfortable at the end. The palliative care chemotherapy that we would like to pursue consists of 6 treatments that the vet has estimated would cost between $4,500 - $7,000. We humbly ask for financial help to make these last months of Sage’s life as easeful and comfortable as possible. We understand that many of you may not know Sage or us very well but perhaps you might relate to a similar experience with your own beloved pets. In addition, we have 2 other offerings that would serve to support Sage and us during this time. How You Can Help: 1. Donate directly to this gofundme page (Any donation amount is deeply appreciated and will go directly towards Sage’s medical expenses). 2. Buy a Sagebrush Sassafrass t-shirt: my partner Adam has designed a t-shirt which includes an artistic rendering of Sage and 100% of proceeds will go to Sage’s medical care. You can buy the shirt here: <URL> 3. Book a massage or personal training session: If you live in Boulder County Colorado, you can book a massage or personal training session with Adam. He will donate 50% of the proceeds to Sage’s medical care. You can book with him here: <URL> We know there are so many posts like this, so we just wanted to say that if you read all the way to the end, we deeply appreciate you.

Nox is a stray cat that has lived in Sonoran University (previously SCNM) garden for over 5 years. He is well-known to students and alumni as a very friendly cat who loves treats and people’s company. He does not fear people and will often greet them excitedly. Nox has been through a lot, as a previously indoor cat surviving in the wild. He was malnourished, depended on others’ kindness for food and water, especially during Arizona’s heat waves. Unlike feral cats, stray cats are unable to survive on their hunting skills. They are often not part of any group, susceptible to attack by other cats and large birds, and are often alone and lonely. Nox often followed people to their cars or tried to get into the school buildings, in an attempt to find his way back to an indoor life. He would cry as people he knew walked away, indicating he does not want them to leave. Nox is currently being fostered by me and went for a vet visit recently. He has no serious or communicable diseases, but has bladder inflammation and pain with passing urine, that according to his vet, is likely due to prolonged stress. Dehydration could also have contributed to it, as he did not always have access to water. The prognosis is well once he’s treated. Nox has clearly suffered some kind of trauma relating to garbage trucks, as he is fine with cars and trucks passing by, but hides and shakes uncontrollably when seeing or hearing a garbage truck. Likely, he had a traumatic experience while foraging for food in the dumpster. Garbage truck compactors have been known to accidentally kill cats and other small animals whether it is due to the weight of garbage dumped on the animals or the blade. Nox received complete vaccinations, blood work, urinary and stool sample checks, heart worm medication, prescriptions to help with the urinary inflammation, antibiotic shot, anti anxiety medication to help with adjusting to the change, and a prescription urinary diet. He has been neutered previously without an ear tip, confirming that he was once an indoor cat. Nox is very happy indoors and much calmer than he was in the garden. He belongs in a home, especially as he ages. Nox’s vet bill came out to $919 and $173 quoted for the follow up visit and second round of vaccinations. I covered his supplies, some medications, and one screening test bill of $117 and $45. A Sonoran student fully covered his second bill of $173, so I am fundraising to cover the largest bill of $919. Anything you are able to help with, no matter how small, would be great! Update: It warms my heart to see how our community came together to rescue Nox. Your kindness and care for Nox’s well-being is overwhelming. This fundraising event has met its goal and enough to cover the website’s percentage of the donations! I will keep it open for those who want to contribute to future veterinary care (microchipping and potential medication or additional tests on his follow-up).
