So many people that love Sophie recommended we start a GoFundMe, so here we are. Last week, my two-year-old rescue pup named Sophie started showing signs she wasn’t feeling herself eating less, urinating more often, and being more tired than normal. I also noticed her belly area seemed bloated on both sides, but I wasn't sure if it was something as ordinary as gas or a blockage. I took her to urgent care Tuesday night 10/25, and the doctor noticed fluid in her belly area that was abnormal. They then completed blood work and did an ultrasound. During the ultrasound, they saw a large tumor and several smaller tumors throughout her abdomen. They took a needle biopsy and called me the following day to tell me that Sophie has cancer. They told me since the cancer is metastatic cancer (it's already spread) and that surgery would not be helpful. They then emailed me a list of at-home euthanasia companies. My world crumbled, and I've been devastated, to say the least. Sophie is young and isn't ready to stop fighting, and neither am I. She's my best friend and literally the perfect dog. I contacted Animal Cancer Center here in California, and after reviewing her results, we have an appointment for her tomorrow, 11/1/22. The urgent care visit cost me $1,834, and I was quoted around $10K for surgery and another $6-10K for chemo if we go that route, of which I don't have that type of money sitting around. I wish treatment and options didn't come down to finances, but they do. I don't want anything to stop her from getting the best treatment possible; she deserves it. We appreciate your love and support

Due to the pandemic, abandonment of animals being at an all time high, climate change and breeding seasons never ending, not to mention inflation, the number of homeless animals out on the streets have doubled if not tripled. Local rescues are literally bursting at the seams and it feels like we rescuers are all drowning in this battle of overpopulation even with more people doing the work, it’s endless. So many folks in rescue that I know personally are all exhausted beyond belief but we push on through because we know if we don’t that means a lot of animals will suffer and die without human intervention. As most of you know, I’m not a non-profit organization and I don’t get financial backing to do this volunteer work. Eventually, I plan on starting my own non-profit, that’s my long term goal to be able to help the animals even more in the future and create a team of people to help me do so. For now, I need to be able to raise money to continue spaying/neutering these poor forgotten animals to be able to stop them from breeding and dying on the streets. Winter is coming so this is even more urgent to get them altered and healed up sooner than later. Thankfully, one of the veterinarians I work with gives me discounted prices for what I do with the ferals which includes spay/neuter, vaccines, flea/tick and internal parasite preventive and snap combo testing for feline aids and feline leukemia. This does not include anything extra like antibiotics or steroids if a cat needs such medications due to injuries. I have listed total costs below for people who are interested. A lot of these animals are able to be pulled off the streets and get socialized and get into good homes. Zudem hat Suncica mit einem Arbeiter das Tierheim aufgeräumt, damit nächste Woche, wenn das Wetter mitspielt, die Betonplatte für die Hundezwinger gegossen werden kann. Spannende und auchso anstrengende Zeit für unsere Suncica. Wir können ihr aus der Ferne nur mental zur Seite stehen. Und wir können helfen, dass weitere Spenden für das Projekt zusammenkommen. Helft bitte auch fleißig mit! Teilt bitte unsere Spendenaktion! Unterstützt Suncicas Aufopferung für die verlassenen Tiere in Serbien! Gemeinsam können wir es schaffen! Herzlichen Dank für eure Spenden und dafür, das ihr hinter unserer Arbeit steht! Das gibt Kraft und Mut, für unser Tierheim weiter zu kämpfen! Wir können mit dieser Summe starten aber um das Tierheim aufzubauen, brauchen wir weitere Spenden. Jetzt gilt es diesen Aufruf weiter zu teilen, damit wir die Chance bekommen unsere Zielsumme zu erreichen! Folgende Aufgaben aus der Auflistung haben wir bisher erledigt: - Alle Hunde mussten gechippt werden, 90% war bereits erledigt, 9 Hunde waren noch nicht gechippt (Kosten ca. 170€) Alle Hunde sind nun gechippt und alle Impfungen wurden aufgefrischt. BILD VON DER RECHNUNG FOLGT NOCH DIE UHREN IN SERBIEN TICKEN LANGSAMER, DESWEGEN WARTEN WIR NOCH AUF DIE TIERARZT-RECHNUNG. - Tierschutzgesetz-Seminar für Suncica (Kosten ca. 170€) Suncica hat das Seminar und die darauffolgende Prüfung erfolgreich bestanden! Wir sind sehr stolz auf sie :-) - Heizung ist notwendig (nicht vorhanden, Kosten für ein Heizkörper ca. 300€) Wir haben eine Infrarotheizung gespendet bekommen. Somit haben wir uns die geplante Ausgabe für den Heizkörper gespart :-) Nächste Schritte: - Quarantäne mit 10 Einzelzwingern, betoniert mit Wasserabflusssystem (Kosten geschätzt 5.000€). Dieses Teilprojekt wird ein sehr erfahrener Baufachmann erledigen und betreuen. Vor dem Ausbau müssen noch einige bürokratische Abläufe erledigt werden. Wir hoffen dass das gute Wetter noch anhält, damit zumindest die Bodenplatte vor dem Winter steht! Die erste Frist von 30 Tagen läuft in den nächsten Tagen ab. Suncica wird im Laufe der nächsten Woche bei der zuständigen Behörde mit den Nachweisen über die bereits erledigte Aufgaben um eine Fristverlängerung bitten. Drückt us die Daumen das sich das serbische Amt mit den Teilerfolgen aus den letzten Wochen zufrieden gibt und uns noch Zeit für die Erledigung weiterer Punkte schenkt! Alle die unsere Arbeit auf unserer Homepage und den sozialen Netzwerken verfolgen und uns kennen wissen, dass wir seit mehreren Jahren in Zentralserbien (Pozarevac) eine Rettungsstation für gerettete Straßenhunde aufbauen. Eine Umzäunung des Geländes, fließendes Wasser, Strom, Hundehütten und abgetrennte eigene Bereiche für unsere Rudel: all das sind große Meilensteine für Team Pfote gewesen, die wir mit Herzblut und Schweiß erreicht haben. Sowohl wir als auch Suncica haben einen eingetragenen Verein gegründet. So kann der Verein Team Pfote dem Verein Sunce gemeinnützig am besten unterstützen. Team Pfote: Das sind meine Familie und ich. Neben den oben genannten Projekten organisieren wir von Deutschland aus jegliche Tierrettungen, Kastrationen, ärztliche Versorgungen und Unterbringungen in Serbien. Zudem sammeln wir Futter und Sachspenden in Deutschland, die wir selbst 5-mal im Jahr mit einem Anhänger nach Serbien transportieren. Dennoch wäre unsere Arbeit von Deutschland aus nichts ohne unsere Schlüsselperson vor Ort in Serbien: Sunica Ljubic. Unsere Suncica hat ihr Leben der Tierrettung gewidmet und sorgt sich tagtäglich von morgens früh bis abends spät um unsere knapp 60 Hunde. Ihre Mission hat lange vor unserem Kennenlernen begonnen. Ihr Mann und sie haben bereits vor 25 Jahren Welpen aus den Containern serbischer Dörfer gerettet. Sie teilten sich die Aufgaben aber auch das Leid und die Trauer, die einem bei der Rettung von Straßenhunden jederzeit begegnet. Ende 2020 erlebte Suncica einen Schicksalsschlag und muss seitdem allein weitermachen, denn ihr Ehemann ist tödlich verunglückt. Seit diesem Verlust laufen unsere Aufbauarbeiten noch langsamer, denn unsere größte Priorität hat das Wohl der Tiere und Suncica kommt zeitlich kaum hinterher ganz allein für die Versorgung der 60 Hunde aufzukommen. Suncica ist die einzige Person im gesamten Umkreis von 50 Kilometern, die die Straßenhunde rettet. Alle Hunde sind durch Suncica tierärztlich versorgt, kastriert und müssen nicht hungern. Trotz dessen sind die Bedingungen auf der Rettungsstation nicht rosig. Die Tiere leben draußen, manche Hunde müssen sich ihren Schlafplatz zu zweit teilen und Suncica hat keine Zeit jedem dieser 60 Tiere genug Zuneigung zu schenken. Wer die Situation der Straßenhunde in Serbien kennt und mal in einem staatlichen Shelter war, weiß aber genau, dass im Vergleich dazu die Lebensbedingungen auf unserer Rettungsstation eine „Oase“ für die geretteten Hunde sind. Doch trotz unserer Aufopferung und 100%igen Hingabe für den Aufbau der Rettungsstation, verzögern sich die Arbeiten immer und immer wieder. Unzuverlässige Arbeiter, finanzielle Engpässe, Probleme mit Nachbarn, keine Unterstützung der Einwohner, immer wieder neue und kranke Hunde und die Untätigkeit der Behörden und neue Auflagen werfen uns immer wieder zurück. Neben all den Herausforderungen kam es jetzt auch noch zu einem Super-GAU. Letzte Woche besuchte das örtliche Veterinäramt die Rettungsstation und ordnete an, die Rettungsstation innerhalb von 30 Tagen auf einen Stand zu bringen, welches die Registrierung eines offiziellen Tierheims entspricht. Darunter fallen ganze 60 (!!) Punkte, die zu erfüllen sind und uns in dieser zeitlichen Knappheit quasi handlungsunfähig machen. Einige dieser Punkte haben wir ohnehin bereits erfüllt: das Grundstück ist umzäunt, Wasser und Stromanschluss gibt es, eine Isolierstation für Welpen wurde aufgebaut, alle Tiere sind gechipt, geimpft und kastriert. Wir waren also bereits intensiv und unseren Möglichkeiten entsprechend auf Hochtouren dabei die Rettungsstation für die Registrierung eines offiziellen Tierheims aufzubauen. Diese Forderung des Veterinäramts aber kam aus dem Nichts. Wir sind fassungslos und bangen um unsere Tiere. Sollten wir innerhalb von 30 Tagen die Anforderungen nicht erfüllen besteht die Gefahr, dass uns alle Tiere genommen und in einen staatlichen Shelter gebracht werden. Was mit unseren Tieren in den Sheltern passiert, ist unklar aber wir alle wissen, wie solche „Probleme“ in Serbien gelöst werden. WIR DÜRFEN NICHT ZULASSEN, DASS DIESE 60 TIERE STERBEN! WIR DÜRFEN NICHT ZULASSEN, DASS UNSERE UND SUNCICAS ARBEIT ENDET! Auf Anfrage, ob die 30-Tage-Frist verlängert werden kann, antwortete die Veterinärinspektorin das die Entscheidung von einer Fristverlängerung vom Aufbaufortschritt des Tierheimes abhängt. WIR MÜSSEN SCHNELLSTMÖGLICH MIT DEM AUFBAU STARTEN! Wir brauchen also unbedingt eure Unterstützung! Der Dreh- und Wendepunkt des ganzen Registrierungsprozesses ist der Aufbau einer Quarantänestation mit mindestens 10 Einzelzwingern, inklusive eines Abwassersystems und eines Sanitärbereichs. Dieser Komplex muss räumlich von der gesamten Rettungsstation abgetrennt werden. Um die Quarantänestation muss also ein Zaun aufgebaut werden. Neben all den 60 Anforderungen hat der Aufbau dieser Quarantänestation für das Veterinäramt momentan die größte Bedeutung. Was müssen wir also alles erfüllen, um ein Tierheim registrieren zu können? - Quarantäne mit 10 Einzelzwingern, betoniert mit Wasserabflusssystem (Kosten geschätzt 5.000€) - Der Eingang muss rund um die Uhr überwacht sein - unsere Lösung wird eine Kamera sein (Kosten ca. 400-500€, Angebot inklusive Installation und Internet-Router steht noch aus) - Alle Boxen (in unserem Fall umzäunte Freiläufe) müssen unter Verschluss stehen (80% bereits vorhanden) - Feuerlösch-Equipment (Kosten ca. 100-150€) - Aufenthaltsraum für TH-Mitarbeiter, Raum für die Futter-Zubereitung und Umkleide (provisorisch, aber vorhanden) - Tierschutzgesetz-Seminar für Suncica (Kosten ca. 170€) - Alle Hunde mussten gechippt werden, 90% war bereits erledigt, 9 Hunde waren noch nicht gechippt (Kosten ca. 170€) - Desinfektionsbarrieren für die Schuhe - Sanitärraum mit Dusche, Waschbecken im Quarantänebereich (Kosten ca. 1500€) - Waschraum für Hunde in der Quarantäne und im "sauberen Bereich" (Kosten ca. 1.000€) - Lagerraum für Futter (zT. vorhanden) - Teilbetonierung des gesamten Tierheimes (Kosten ca. 2000-2500€) - Überdachungen für die Tiere im Freilauf (Kosten unbekannt) - Zusätzliche 15 Hundehütten (ca. 1.500€) - Isolator für Welpen (vorhanden), Heizung ist notwendig (nicht vorhanden, Kosten für ein Heizkörper ca. 300€) - Ca. 50 Gummimatten und Paletten als Liegeplatz für Hunde (Kosten ca. 600€) Es liegt viel Arbeit vor uns und wir wären unendlich dankbar, wenn ihr uns zumindest bei einem Teil des Aufbaus und der Erfüllung dieser Punkte unterstützen könntet. Bitte helft uns, dieses Ziel zu erreichen! Ohne die Hilfe von jedem einzelnen werden wir es nicht schaffen... Unser kleiner Verein hat im Monat höchstens 350€ feste Spenden. Die geschätzte Summe, welche wir jetzt benötigen, ist für unsere Verhältnisse ein Vermögen. Die Zeit rennt uns davon! Wir müssen schnellstmöglich mit den Arbeiten starten! Jeder einzelne Tag der 30-Tage-Frist bedeutet eine Chance für das Leben unserer Schützlinge. Suncica, ihre Tiere und Team Pfote zählen auf euch! Jeder Cent und jede helfende Hand hilft! <URL>

Hi! This is Sprout! He is the most loving little meatball on legs and my boys absolute best friend. Living in a world with no Sprout is not an option for us which is why we have done everything in our power to make sure he is always very well taken care of. In February of this year we noticed he had a limp and was super uncomfortable walking or playing! Well we found out he not only tore his ACL but when they got into the surgery the doctor noticed he also tore his MCL. These surgeries are not cheap for a human or an animal by any means, you have to pay for the appointment to diagnose the problem, the surgery, the medications for after, and the check ups after. Sprout is only 4 years old so of course we got his leg all fixed up so he didn’t have to be in any sort of pain or discomfort! That surgery was no joke to heal from! Fast forward to last week when we started to notice Sprout rapidly declining. For 6 days straight he threw up a ton, he didn’t want to play, didn’t want to eat, he only wanted to sleep and be left alone, all of which are absolutely not like him at all! He loves to be with his human brothers, playing, and eating any and everything. So I picked up the phone to call the vet to make an appointment in hopes of finding a solution to making him feel better! During his appointment they did blood work, x rays, and an ultra sound and nothing was making sense. Nothing showed up crystal clear besides that there was blood flow that was being blocked but we couldn’t see anything other than a giant bulge in his intestines. The vet suggested we had to do another major surgery because he felt as though this could be serious. We brought in Sprout the next morning for his surgery and I was warned he might not make it and to give him a good hug and kiss goodbye because 1. we weren’t sure what was in there and 2. If the intestine had any blood supply left in it and 3. If any of this was worth repairing and a life worth living for him. This shattered me. We impatiently waited and waited all morning to find out that our guy made it! He had eaten two balls from a ball pit that went rock hard from being in his stomach for so long, and a pair of our sons underwear which is what the giant bulge was!! AHHH!!! He made it!! It was amazing news but with that came more HUGE bills with no warning. Again, we had to pay the appointment, the surgery, the medications, and the after care appointments to pay for. Everything has come straight out of left field and landed onto our laps overnight and it’s a lot. This pup means the world to us and to know Sprout is to love Sprout! As humbling as it is to say out loud or type it’s too much for a single income household to manage. If you feel the urge to donate we would sincerely appreciate it from the bottom of our hearts. With the holidays coming up and just life in general I just don’t want to drown my husband who works extremely hard with another giant bill that got here with no warning or preparation. I love and appreciate you so much, thank you for taking the time to read this

Two days ago, Stanley was a rambunctious, happy, curious dog, chasing rabbits in the yard and wagging his tail a mile a minute whenever we called his name. When he suddenly was whimpering and stumbling over his hind legs, we knew something was wrong. After an after hours rush to Waterloo Emergency Vet and a pedal-to-the-floor drive to OVC late last night, he has been diagnosed with IVDD - intervertebral disc disease. The padding between two of his vertebrae in his spine has slipped out, putting pressure on his spinal cord, causing immense amounts of pain and is quickly progressing to him not being able to stand on his back legs this morning. The wonderful neurologists, vet students, and vet techs at OVC have been amazing at communicating with us the severity of this disease, but also the excellent prognosis after surgery. As long as Stanley can feel “deep pain” in his hind legs, he has a 95% chance of regaining his ability to walk again after surgery. Since this came on so suddenly, we were put in a difficult financial position. The cost of the surgery and post-op care is $7,000 - $9,000. This is a huge sum which we are more than happy to pay for our beautiful baby, but we are asking for a little help from our friends. Anyone who has met Stanley knows what an incredible dog he is. He’s friendly, social, hilarious, loves playing with his basketball and ripping apart stuffed animals. He adores his baby sister, Pepper, whom he plays with and cuddles all day long. He’s the sort of dog that ruins all other dogs for you - he’s that perfect. His bark is loud, but he’s sensitive and comforting whenever you need him. I can’t imagine my life without him giving me kisses and sitting perfectly for treats like the good boy he is. For anyone who doesn’t know, Stanley is an 8 year old dachshund with the biggest heart. You’d fall in love with him if you ever met him, just like we did 3 years ago when we adopted him. Three years is not enough time with our little Standit/Stan Man/Standard/Stanny. It’s never enough time. But any extra time we get with him is worth the financial and emotional cost. When he comes home from surgery, he will be on crate rest for 4 weeks, and then will slowly start rehab to walk. It is going to be a long hard road for all of us, but any tiny donation will help take some of the burden off our minds, allowing us to focus our attention on getting our best boy back to us, healthy and walking (and loud and long). Thank you all so much in advance. Love, Sara, John, Stanley and Pepper

Hi, my name is Abby, and I am devastated that one of my dogs is in critical care at the emergency hospital. She has been in the ICU since 2am on Wednesday, November 9th. She was vomiting blood and needed urgent foreign body surgery. The foreign body was lateral, so instead of a standard removal, it folded her intestines tightly together and required emergency surgery. It was a struggle to get her stable enough to undergo surgery, as her blood pressure and blood sugar levels were dropping rapidly, and her tiny body could not regulate itself. The decision was made to put her through surgery while unstable in a last-ditch effort to save her life. Thankfully, she made it through surgery but couldn't wake up, and we found out she went septic. Since 10:45am on November 9th, she has been hooked up to multiple IV fluids, antibiotics, and medications to boost her blood pressure and glucose levels. She managed to pull through the rest of the night and could open her eyes and breathe on her own. The doctors are doing all they can to save her life, and there is a 50% survival rate at this point. I am doing all I can to continue to pay for her care, and if she continues to pull through, she will need three more days in the ICU at minimum. Currently, her medical bill is up to $12,000. I work for a small non-profit animal rescue and do not make the type of money to continue to pay for this care, but I will NOT give up on her. Please, share her story, and if anyone can help me pay for her life-saving care, I will be forever grateful.

Hi everyone! I would like to raise funds to have a Raytripper trap located in Huron to help trap lost/stray/abandoned animals. We’ve successfully trapped 3 abandoned dogs in the past 7 months...all three traps had to be borrowed which required driving to Pierre and Aberdeen. I would love to have a trap located in town so the animal can be trapped quicker. If a citizen loses their animal in town, I would love to help reunite them with their beloved pet if it cannot be caught. This will be a great asset in our community as well as surrounding communities. The Raytripper is an electronic system using a sensor and electromagnet that releases the gate on a Missy Trap when the dog steps into an invisible infrared beam. The dog does not have to step on anything or pull on anything to close the trap door. I calculated the cost of the supplies and it was a little over $500. Once the funds are raised, I will be buying the supplies and building the trap so it is ready for use. Thank you everyone! The picture is of Hazel who was trapped with a Raytripper trap...once she went past the beam, the door closed and she was contained...all she had to do was walk on in towards the yummy food!

On Saturday morning (10/22/2022), a guest at The Dog Park at Immanuel (Indianapolis, IN) pulled up to the park and saw eyes looking at her that didn’t quite belong - when she saw there was also a bowl of food, she realized that someone had dumped their dog at the park and that she was all alone. The poor girl was skin and bones and couldn’t stand or walk on her own. Luckily this guest has a heart of gold and took her to IndyVet Emergency Services to get her help and notified a board member of the park. We rushed to the vet right away to see if there was anything we could do for this poor pup - as you can see from the photos, she is extraordinarily emaciated/underweight. She also had fleas and needed to be tested for other illnesses. Indy also has refeeding syndrome, which happens when dogs are malnourished. She would have been sent to a shelter unless someone could pay for her expenses, and she would have likely been euthanized due to her condition and the shelters in Indianapolis being at capacity. This is Indy at the vet. You can't see it in this picture, but they set up a little tablet for her to watch TV! One of our fantastic board members immediately fell in love with those sweet eyes and agreed to give her a home - one where she will be loved and incredibly happy! They named her Indy Imm after the park, and she is improving daily. This campaign is to cover Indy’s vet expenses. So far, Indy’s vet bills have totaled $2500, and they are expected to reach about $3500. Any extra money raised will go to a non-profit supporting care of pets in similar situations to Indy. We are so grateful that we were able to help Indy. She is the sweetest little dog and how anyone could leave her like this is beyond comprehension. Please donate and show Indy that humans can be kind, too. You can follow Indy’s Journey on her Facebook page, Indy Imm’s Diary! Thanks for helping Indy on her journey to good health and happy life! A note from Indy’s Diary : October 22, 2022 I don't remember a lot about this day. I woke up at the place they left me in the morning and boy did it look really cool. If I just had strength, I would have had a blast. But I was just too weak. The visitors to the park found me. They said I could barely take a couple of steps before falling over. They were really concerned so they took me to the emergency vet clinic where they signed a Good Samaritan form - which meant that the clinic would make me well enough to send to a shelter. Then the visitors called the dog park people - did I mention that the park I was left at was a dog park? What good luck. It is called "The Dog Park at Immanuel," but when they made the call, things started moving fast. The people in charge of the dog park - Indy Dog Park Co. - told the vet people to take good care of me. I got food and medicine to help make me feel better. The only thing I really did not like is that they stuck needles in my doggie legs. They are using that to take blood from me and to give me fluids. One of the dog park people, Emily, came by to check on me but I was too weak to be seen. They told her I was also covered in fleas (no wonder I was so itchy) and they were concerned about flea anemia. Well I am so glad they want to help me.

As I grew up, I saw my family's constant love and care: Masae, Jason, Miyuki, Shari, and my new mommy, Gabby, gave my brother, Taiko and me even when we were crazy troublemakers. We both love to play around in the backyard loudly, sleep, eat carbs and cheese as treats, and bark at the squirrels that come by to taunt us. In later years, my mommies, Miyuki and Shari, discovered that health and wellness decline as animals age and some complications could arise. This past week on November 1st, I wasn’t feeling well, and my tummy began to swell over a short period of time. I didn’t know why but I didn’t feel like eating anything (which I love most, no matter what) and could not get up off the floor. My family got worried and took me to the emergency room quickly because they thought it was due to my stomach flipping, a severe life-threatening complication if not treated fast at the ER. It took some time, but they were able to diagnose it, and luckily while it didn’t turn out the way we expected, we did find the issue was due to internal bleeding from a tumor on my spleen. The blood needed to be drained, and my spleen needed to be removed immediately to save my life. The doctors told my family that I may have hemangiosarcoma, cancer in the blood vessels. They became more concerned after learning that this type of cancer can metastasize or move to other parts of my body. The doctors say I’ll probably have 1-3 months of life with the surgery to remove the excess blood and tumor they found. I was in the ER for 2 days after my surgery, and I'm feeling better and resting at home while my family watches me 24/7. Even through it all, I am still my happy, hungry self. I’ll have a follow-up appointment soon to see if everything is okay with me and to remove the stitches on my stomach. Due to surgery, ER visit, and possible chemotherapy, the amount that my family has to pay is a heavy one. My family does not want to give up on me and wants me to be around as long as I comfortably can. If you or anyone you know would like to donate or share this link to help my family, we would appreciate it so much! They do so much for me, and they want to have as much time with me as possible. My family will post more updates as soon as they know more about my condition. Thank you, woof <3

Many of you have asked how Into the Light Horse Rescue and Sanctuary, a 501c3 non profit was started. Since I am using my birthday to inspire my friends and my larger network to donate to my life’s passion, I would love to share our story here. It all began with Dove, a newborn foal. In 2015, on a Colorado feedlot that sold horses to slaughter, a young black and white mare with dreadlocks in her mane and tail, gave birth to this sweet filly with a little white dove marking on her side. The filly was born amongst the chaos of the feedlot, surrounded by 100 horses all awaiting their fate to be shipped to slaughter. I had learned of the newborn foal and her Mother, and knew immediately they needed to be saved. Without hesitating, I paid for their freedom and had them rushed to a quarantine facility. While Phantom and baby Dove were in quarantine, Dove developed an infection. Feedlots are no place for any horse -- especially a newborn. The disease and sickness Dove developed from being there for the first few hours of her life, compromised her ability to fight off infection. As infection attacked Dove’s eyes, she went blind before the vets had an opportunity to save her sight. Her illness continued to develop, and at exactly six weeks old, she succumbed to her sickness and passed away while her Mamma Phantom stood helpless. The loss of baby Dove left me devastated. More than ever, I felt that she and the three other horses I had saved, needed to continue on for Dove. In the weeks following Dove’s passing, I saw the urgent need to stand up for the thousands of horses that continue to be tossed away and lost to the slaughter pipeline. So that Dove's loss would not be in vain. Into the Light was born from this chain of events, and the name represents the feeling our horses experience when they are at the end of the line in the slaughter pipeline, but are brought back into the love and light of freedom when rescued. Dove continues to inspire our rescue every day, and we carry on her memory with each horse we have the honor of saving. To date, we have rescued 90 horses, and intend to continue our mission of working tirelessly to ensure our horses are loved and cared for, and that they never again experience the horrors of the slaughter pipeline. Our focus in recent years has been caring for our sanctuary horses, If you decide to donate, your valuable funds will be used to support our 10 special needs sanctuary horses. Instead of buying your daily latte, could you spare $5 to help us buy the meds our sweet rescues need on a daily basis? Thank you so much for reading this and for sharing on social media, by private messenger or text. EIN 47-4975780 Into The Light Horse Rescue & Sanctuary Inc

Hi, I am Jenna and this is Phillip! A little over a month and a half ago, I was doing my daily puppy window shopping on the internet and came across this little fella’s face and fell in love. I drove over 6 hours to go get him - at the time, I didn’t realize I was rescuing him, but come to find out, I was. He is a retired stud from a puppy mill and his previous life from what I have gathered, was not a good one. The day before I went to pick him up, the breeder took him to her vet for a health check.. The vet signed off on a “clean bill of health”, so I obviously thought that he was in good health and well taken care of. After having him for a day, I quickly found out that was not the case. I wanted to check him out so I could know if there would ever be something abnormal come around. I opened up his little mouth to find a giant oronasal fistula on one side and black/gray teeth on the other with inflamed gums. (If you don’t know ((I didn’t hah!)) an oronasal fistula is a hole connecting the mouth and nose; food, water, and saliva can travel from the mouth to the nose, which can irritate the respiratory tract that can cause pain and discomfort.) I could not believe that a vet had signed off and did not think there was anything wrong with his mouth as I had never seen a dog’s mouth look so bad. I texted the breeder and asked if her and her vet thought that his mouth was in good health, because to me it was very concerning. Her response was that she didn’t even know that he had that, but it could have been from him “fighting possum and other occasional vermin” (note, he is a 10 lb mini dachshund...) I immediately called the next day to get an appointment with my vet. He was just as shocked as I was that a vet had signed off on a clean bill of health for him. Oronasal fistulas are very painful and who knows how long he had this. We got him scheduled for a surgery to close the oronasal fistulas, get his teeth cleaned, pulled and lab work done to make sure he did not have any other issues. He had to have 6 teeth pulled, including his canine, which then created a second oronasal fistula. Both were closed, but unfortunately, a week later, they reopened. We scheduled a 2nd surgery to close the holes back up and again, the holes reopened. This past week, we just went to a dental specialist that is hopefully going to fix his entire mouth for good.. Unfortunately, he found some other possible issues in his mouth that will need fixed as well. I am a lot more in debt that I thought I was ever going to be getting this sweet boy and am hoping that I can get a little help to get Phil pain free as soon as possible- for as long as I have had him, he has not been! I have had him for 7 weeks and have gone to 7 vet appointments with 2 surgeries included- a record for me and more than likely, Phil. So!! I really really want to get him fixed ASAP so that he can finally feel better and start fully living the life he deserves pain free! Thank you so much for reading and thank you so much if you are able to donate to Phillip and help in getting him good and healthy :)

When my wife, Lisa, showed me the pictures of our friend's litter of puppies I knew we would be taking one home as soon as they were ready. 8 weeks later we brought Tango home with us. He immediately started following me everywhere. When we would play outside it would only take a few minutes for him to start begging for me to carry him. It wasn't until a week later that I began to notice a rasp in his breathing. I feared he had swallowed something and hoped it would pass before Lisa saw it. The next day he was lethargic and collapsed unconscious in Lisa's arms. After rushing Tango to the emergency vet, hours of waiting and tests, we were told he had a respiratory infection and sent home with antibiotics. Unfortunately, he did not improve. Weeks of tests and veterinary visits later, we found that our otherwise healthy, now 3-month-old Husky has a paralyzed larynx. This means he can't get air in very well, as his throat won't open up to take breaths or pant. He also gets air in his stomach from trying to exhale, leading to lots of vomit. Our worst fear is that he will aspirate some of this, and there will be nothing we can do for him. We love Tango, and while most puppies suffering from this congenital nerve condition are put down, we can't imagine life without his bright blue eyes meeting ours each morning. Frankie is a 4 year old Pembroke Welsh Corgi. On October 3rd, 2022, his parents, Ed and Geri De Guzman, received the devastating news that Frankie’s primary/initial diagnosis based on a biopsy performed on September 27th, 2022 is lymphoma. Ed and Geri noticed a lump under his left jaw that grew in size and had spread to his right side under his jaw as well. On October 5, 2022 Ed and Geri visited the internal medicine specialist at Pulse Vet for a consult on his diagnosis. That was when it was confirmed that Frankie has lymphoma, specifically multicentric lymphoma, based on the swelling to multiple lymph nodes in his body. The specialist described Frankie's cancer as at least stage 3 and up because it has spread and caused swelling to multiple lymph nodes. The specialist gave Ed and Geri the option to run more diagnostics and tests to confirm what stage Frankie's cancer is and also if it is B-Cell or T-Cell lymphoma, but they have decided not to because of the cost, and as per what the specialist verbalized to them, they know that it is confirmed lymphoma and that treatment should be started right away if they wanted to do so. Multicentric lymphoma, which involves multiple lymph nodes and may also affect the liver, spleen, and/or bone marrow, accounts for 80% of canine lymphoma cases. There are numerous chemotherapy treatment protocols for dogs with multicentric lymphoma. Most dogs with lymphoma experience cancer remission following treatment, and side effects are usually not severe. The treatment that Ed and Geri decided to proceed with is called CCNU (Lomustine, CeeNU) chemotherapy. It is a form of chemotherapy that Frankie would take orally. This oral medication is given every three weeks to help address the cancer. He will need to come in, get blood work and, once that is ok, get the medication. This will cost $700-$1000 minimum per 3 weeks for about 6 weeks. This will go along with prednisone and a liver protectant, which can cause liver issues. As of today (October 18, 2022), Frankie is doing well. Ed and Geri are happy to say that he still has his appetite and energy. Some of their family members have told them that they couldn’t even tell he was sick. However, the swelling has been worsening daily, making it harder for him to breathe. They have been monitoring him for any signs of distress. Although Ed and Geri have pet insurance with Pet Secure, this only covers a maximum of $1000/condition. They have already used $500 to have the biopsy done. Ed and Geri are looking at costs between $4200 - $6000 for treatment. This does not include any additional costs that could arise due to complications or the need for hospitalization. Ed and Geri have a challenging journey ahead, and it is not easy to ask for help. So, let's help them out, as the last thing they need to worry about is finances. Please donate if you can and help spread the word so that we can ensure that Frankie continues to live his best life.

Please read and share! We are looking to raise $2500 to cover the cost of surgery, medicine, and follow-up appointments. I adopted Fred in the summer of 2020 after he had been rescued from owners who mistreated him. He came to me not knowing how to play with toys, interact with other dogs, walk on a leash, etc. In the few years we’ve been together he’s learned how good life can be with a mom who loves him. Shortly after his adoption, we noticed that Fred was having issues with stairs, and he would chase after toys in the wrong direction. Then his eyes began to cloud over... this seemed very strange because he was only 4. After going to a specialist, we learned that he has early-onset glaucoma. Glaucoma is a condition that causes a build-up of fluid and pressure in the eye. As the disease progresses the pressure of the eye increases and causes damage to the retina and the optic nerve. This can ultimately lead to blindness, which is what happened to Fred. There is no cure for glaucoma, but there are ways to treat it and in some cases manage the condition. Over the last few years, we’ve done our best managing his pressure with medication and routine pressure checks at the vet. Sadly, the disease has progressed to a point where the veterinarian recommends surgery. The operation involves a general anesthetic, the hair around his eyes will be shaved; his eyes will be completely removed and the eyelid skin is then stitched closed over the eye socket. After the initial healing, he will have his stitches removed and the fur on his face will grow back. While this is a very emotional procedure, the vets ensure us that Fred will feel so much better after he heals from the surgery. The operation is scheduled for December 9. Any and all positive thoughts are very welcome. As are donations to this surgery. Thank you all so much for reaching out to show so much love and support to our sweet nugget. We love you.

We decided to take him to a vet to get it checked out and to find out what was the growth. After looking at it, doctor told us that it was "Inflammatory Polyp". the growth was closing in his throat, which was making it difficult for him to breath and eat. Doctor advised that we need to take him in ASAP to get it removed so that it does not end up closing in his throat completely to the point where he is not able to breath. While there we consulted the doctor about getting him a surgery to close in the cleft palate. Doctor said that it was possible since his opening was mostly in the soft tissue, but only after removing "Inflammatory Polyp" and having him gain some weight. We have an appointment scheduled to remove "Inflammatory Polyp" on Monday November 7th at 7:30am. Estimate to remove "Inflammatory Polyp" is between $1,683-$3,004 Estimate to close in the "Cleft Palate" is between $4,067-$6,000 We decided to start a GoFundMe page to save Jumbo and to help Jumbo with his surgical procedures so the little guy can have a healthy, happy, thriving life and bring joy to everyone around the world. In the early morning hours (1 am) of October 16th , while sitting around the fire with some friends, we noticed a white pickup truck pull into the paddock area of NCCAR. This is a racetrack in a remote area of Garysburg, NC. Vehicles coming in and out isn’t uncommon during an event, so we didn’t pay much attention at first. After a while, one of the truck’s doors opened and a dog hopped out. It began to trot around smelling the area like most dogs would do. After inspecting for a minute or so, it started to head back to the truck’s open door, but before it could get back in, the door closed. As the truck pulled away, the dog chased it, crying. At this point, we realized that the person/persons were abandoning this poor animal on this cold 40ish-degree night. The truck sped off into the night out the main gates as the dog trotted around wondering where they were going without her. We coaxed the dog over to see if we could help. We got her some water and decided to make a bed for her in our warm RV for the evening until the morning when we would find some help for her. Sunday morning, after a nights rest, a few of us began to care for her, getting food, more water, and some type of collar/leash. With racecars zipping around we were afraid she would be hit. We tried to see if it was a mistake and the owners were there, but unfortunately, this wasn’t the case. I contacted my wife who was at our home in Sanford, NC, and told her of the situation. She began to try to contact the local no-kill shelters, rescues, and even the Northhampton Sheriffs' office. Unfortunately, nobody could help until Monday. At this point, nobody could take the dog or wait until Monday to bring her somewhere. My wife and I decided that I would take her home that evening and we could get her some help. She is a very sweet, well-mannered dog. She had some snacks, took some walks, and a few naps while she waited for me to finish my morning and get packed up to head home. When I arrived home, we got her some toys, flea treatment, and a good meal. Our current dog and two cats seemed to like her and there were no issues between them. Once we realized that it wasn’t going to be an issue with our current animals, we wanted to have the dog checked out and potentially decide on what we were going to do. We took her to the vet on the morning of October 18th. Unfortunately, this sweet girl has heartworms, Lyme Disease, and Ehrlichia from her previous miss care. We were able to get her vaccinations up to date and scan for a microchip (no luck). Lynn and I have created this GoFundMe to raise some funds so that we can get the treatment she needs. The treatment process is about 6 months long and costs over $2,000. We will be applying this to her heartworm treatment, spaying, and some of the other miscellaneous costs associated (antibiotics, overnight stay, etc.). Our hope is to make her a permanent fixture in our family but if that doesn’t work after the 6 months for any reason, we feel this will give her the best chance of getting adopted.

My name is Jordan and my girlfriend is Paige. I am writing this on behalf of our beloved rescue-dog, Turbo. I know many of you have dogs or pets that you couldn’t bear the thought of losing, especially when it’s not their time and they still have so much life left, so I am writing to you, asking for help. Turbo did not choose the hand he was dealt and a lot of people seeing his hand would fold, but we have not, and will not. When we first got turbo, almost three years ago now, he was a sickly sight. His ribs and hip bones protruded due to a lack of feeding, his muscles were atrophied due to a lack of exercise, his hair was missing from the shoulder blades down and covered in open sore’s and scabs due to a severe skin infection, and he was covered in scars due to God only knows what. He had been severely abused and neglected at the very least. We never met the previous owners, so we had no back story except for the way he looked, which couldn’t lie, unlike the people that did that to him would have. When we first brought him home, he was good with people; skittish, but good. He would shy away from strangers at first, but once he warmed up, he was the biggest cuddle bug you’d ever meet! The only problem at the time is that he didn’t like the other animals, so we had to keep our other pets separated. We eventually hired a professional trainer, but she was fearful of him and worked indirectly, through us, only furthering the isolation. A few months into being part of the family he began showing aggression towards people. At this point, as responsible owners, we had to muzzle and leash him around strangers to protect them and him. His aggression—which is fear based, combined with believing he must protect my girlfriend and me from this world that he remembers as so cruel—has made it so he must be kept away from any human or animal except my girlfriend and me. So, Turbo now lives in a large cage, only able to venture out when no one else is around and all other animals are secured. And even then, we must worry about him somehow encountering another person or animal. We have healed his body from what people have done to him, but not his mind, thus far. Short of the unthinkable, his veterinarian has suggested a particular rehabilitation center. The rehab is going to start around $7,000 and they will keep him in their facility for at least 3 months, to retrain his brain to be the loving good boy we know him to be; but not just with us, with everyone else too. Rehabilitation comes with no absolute guarantee, but he has a lot of love in him, and a lot of life, being only five years of age. I won’t be the one to fold his cards, no matter what. I Hope the picture and story will help you decide he is worth all the help he can get. Anything to help would be greatly appreciated. It is caused by the obstruction of a spinal artery and loss of blood supply to the spinal cord, leading to paralysis. The treatment for FCE is getting an X-Ray or MRI to rule out any other diagnosis, like ANNPE. Then based off of the diagnosis, either physical therapy or surgery. As of right now Tutt is extremely dependent on me to get up, eat, or use the bathroom, all of which I have to manually help her do. Her bills so far have consisted of two emergency vet visits, pee pads, certain additives to her food to encourage her to eat, 4 different medicines, and payments to the people helping to watch her while I am at school or working. Recently I was told that since she has not shown any sort of use of her back legs that I should proceed to getting an MRI, which at minimum would cost $3000. Our names are Joanna and Andrew, and this is our beautiful hellion of a cat Ula. Ula has been a part of our family for four years, healthy as a lioness until mid-October when our usually very hungry girl wasn't eating much. After a vet visit, her blood work showed her kidney levels were dangerously high, and she needed emergency admittance to the local animal hospital, Angell. The hospital told us that both of Ula’s ureters were blocked, causing her to go into kidney failure. We decided to have an emergency SUB (subcutaneous ureteral bypass) surgery, where they installed an implant to help her kidneys function and save her life. After a nerve-wracking five days in the hospital with a whirlwind of emotions and a nearly $10,000 bill, Ula was back home. Albeit confined to a friend's massive dog crate for a while so she wouldn't jump around and break her stitches. We were told that she would require follow-up visits to flush the implant with fluids every three or four months (~$750/visit) and a new prescription diet (~$75/month), but having our girl back home playing and looking out the window at squirrels made it worth the sizable investment. It looked like Ula was on her way to a full and speedy recovery until our follow-up visit on 11/11. During this visit, we received good and bad news. The good news is that Ula's kidney levels are normal, and the SUB on her right kidney is working. The bad news is that the blockage of the left kidney they couldn't operate on at the time and hoped would clear on its own, has worsened. Because of this complication, she is increasingly at risk of kidney failure and will need a second surgery to save the left kidney as soon as possible. A surgery we were told would cost us another $7000, an amount we can not feasibly do without some help. For anyone who has experienced the joy of having a pet like Ula in their family, we hope you will be willing to help us provide our girl with the best chance possible to live the long, healthy life she deserves. Thank you for reading, and we are so appreciative of any help you're generous enough to give.

Donut is a sweet 14 month old cat who belongs to two of my best friends, Liz Baatz and Sage Silva. Donut is normally an active, little girl, but suddenly her stomach swelled. Unfortunately, the vets suspected feline infectious peritonitus (FIP). While they waited for test results to come back, they reieved diagnostic papers that read the words every pet parent dreads: 100% mortality. Yesterday, October 21, they received confirmination. Donut has FIP. But they weren't about to give up on their little girl. There's an experimental treatment for FIP, but it's still in clinical trials. The treatments will require daily injections for at least 84 days. The cost is roughly $28 per day, excluding additional medical supplies (syringes, etc) and blood tests/ultrasounds with their veterinarian. They've been able to secure two vials already, but the total cost of treatment is well over $2,000. They have pet insurance for Donut, but this experimental treatment is not yet approved nor covered. They will be administering the treatments themselves, learning to administer the doses. Because this is the only option they have. It's this or give up. Please consider making a donation to support this emergency treatment for Donut. I've included more information about FIP and Donut's story below. Best, Katelyn Fatzler On behalf of Liz Baatz & Sage Silva Donut's Story Liz and Sage adopted Donut in February 2022, just 8 months ago. She came from a foster home in Texas and traveled to find her forever home in Piscataway with Liz and Sage. When she arrived, she was diagnosed with giardia, gingivitis, and feline herpes. They quickly got pet insurance in March 2022, knowing something unexpected could happen in the future. Donut loves to nap in her cat condo in the window and play with her favorite toy, a colorful, fuzzy little spring. She's very playful and friendly, welcoming all her parents' friends with a curious chirp. Symptoms started on October 13 as her abdomen swelled. Donut has had three vet visits since the symptoms started and has had the following: A physical Fluid therapy (to drain her abdomen) Antibiotics (for her fever) Two ultrasounds Blood work Initial cytology (fluid test for FIP) PCR Test (for FIP) The total costs for these diagnostic procedures were $1,563 - above the $2,500 needed for Donut's daily treatments. We are unsure how much the insurance will cover at this time. Liz and Sage would appreciate any/all support toward Donut's treatments. The biggest concern is spending from their savings, which they are trying their best to save for their future together. Feline Infectious Peritonitus (FIP)

How it began Having started her legendary career at PetSmart, for more than two decades, Laura has helped families understand their dogs. Our endlessly loving 3-year-old cat, Wallace (aka Wally Boy, Wally Kitty), is having emergency surgery today (11/2) to remove multiple bladder stones and the urethra blockage preventing him from emptying his bladder. We have been able to manage the cost of his initial urgent care visit ($1,300), but the unexpected cost of the prolonged emergency stay ($1,700) and surgery ($6,100-$7,500) has been staggering. We appreciate your support as we try to help Wallace recover and heal. Below is a more detailed account of his struggles this week: Our Wally kitty visited our family vet's urgent care on Monday after struggling to pee. They sedated him and emptied his grapefruit-sized bladder, then sent him home for monitoring with his IV still in place. He progressively worsened throughout the night, so we rushed him back to the vet. They had to replace his IV because he had chewed on it and then determined he had a complete blockage in his urethra. They sedated him again and put in a urinary catheter to flush it out. They recommended overnight monitoring with the catheter, so we transported him to the emergency vet to stay overnight. In transport, his catheter fell out, so they informed us he would need to be sedated again to replace it. Overnight, they were not able to get the catheter back in due to swelling and obstruction, so they emptied his bladder with a syringe and requested a surgical consult. After x-raying his bladder, they found multiple urinary stones with a blockage higher in his urethra, confirming that surgery would be required to remove the bladder stones and clear his urethra (cystotomy). Additionally, they will be performing a perineal urethrostomy in order to open his urethra more and decrease the likelihood of future blockages. His recovery will take a few days in the emergency vet clinic and three weeks of medication, monitoring, and care at home.

Some of you who receive this may already know some, parts, or all of the story. For those who do not let me introduce you to Stormageddon, The Dark Lord of All aka "Stormy". Don't let his grim-sounding name scare you or dissuade you from helping out. Storm is a 2 1/2 yr old fluffy and friendly St. Bernard. Stormy is the 2nd St. Bernard in the family, so they are no strangers to the issues that may befall a giant breed dog. Stormy is a purebred Saint they purchased from a breeder who made statements to the effect that:Quoting from their web (Facebook) FAQ "· Are registered with AKC (American Kennel Club)" "· Do not have history of hip dysplasia or any other genetic health issues" "· Previous litters (from our Saint parents) do not have any history of hip dysplasia or any other genetic health issues" There were a couple of testimonials and they thought nothing of the issue and reasonably relied upon the statement. They picked out one of the pups and put down a deposit, later paying quite a bit of money for him and taking him home to meet everyone. Unfortunately, they took it on face value that those statements were true and now have found themselves with a vet bill of over $9000, excluding the costs I know they have already expensed up to this point. As a puppy, Stormy was like all puppies, very playful and excited to see people and have a good time rolling around and playing in the yard. They noticed early after his 1st birthday or so that he was not a big fan of going on walks, even just around the block. They thought nothing of it at the time and knew Saints were somewhat lazy, sometimes stubborn dogs. Towards the next birthday, they noticed he would limp a bit and not put pressure on his left leg, but it wasn't often, so they chalked it up to a minor issue. Eventually, it became more frequent, and they took him to the vet, who initially diagnosed a sprain, gave him some medication, and ordered less activity (not sure how you can get any less active, lol). The issue did not subside, so they had xrays ordered, and the complete picture of the problem was obvious. Stormy's left hip never developed, and his right hip socket was not fully formed either. They sent the xrays off to a specialist in Frederick (Skylos), who multiple vets and others highly recommended. He was examined thoroughly by Dr. Peter Lotsikas, and his staff at Sklos ( <URL> Dr. Lotsikas reviewed the xrays and noted significant muscle atrophy because Stormy carries all his weight on his front two legs. He confirmed this is a genetic issue; unfortunately, the only options were a life of pain or a hip replacement. Skylos was founded in 2015 by Dr. Lotsikas and is the leader in their field. Skylos works up a flat fee guaranteed follow-up without additional costs. The total bill for Stormy would be a total of $9590.00. They, unfortunately, do not have a pile of money stashed in the walls of their house or a rich uncle to call. They have always been generous with others, sometimes to a fault, and hope that generosity will be revisited upon them. I know it is humbling and it pains them to ask for help from others. They, however, in this case, are asking on behalf of little (well, not so little) Stormy. Let Stormy know if you have some spare change, a dollar or two, or a rich uncle we can borrow for a bit. If we raise more than needed for the procedure by some miracle, we will donate any remaining funds to local animal charities such as For Otis Sake and The Washington County Humane Society, etc. Feel free to suggest others. Thank you for reading all of this. Please feel free to forward and share this story.

Hello y’all. This is Lauren and Tony Riffle. Owners of Old Folk Farm. If you follow us on social media I’m sure you have seen where we had a catastrophic loss on our farm Monday evening. We had 3 does kid early and of 8 kids born, only 1 is still with us and it’s a miracle she is. This is not something we’ve ever done but enough people mentioned it to me that I finally caved after a night of no sleep with a tiny baby (is a goat babysitter a thing?). Down to the brass tacks: 6 weeks ago I was laid off from my job that helped support roughly half of our breeding operations. Obviously when we bred these does I was still employed happily. These kids were meant to be the foundation of our herd. I have had many interviews even one company that interviewed me five different times and I’ve had all rejections. It appears that there are not very many people out there that are hiring right now but I am still very diligently looking for work every day. Now that the little one is here we have ran through a decent amount of our stock pile of medications. All of the does are still getting medication every day which is further straining our medicine resources. The mamas will all have to still be in the breeding barn for a few weeks to be monitored due to the stressful labors that two of them had. Those of you that raise goats know that this just means more shavings, more lime -more everything. Perhaps even worse than that, one of our does, Lucy, we have decided to retire after the difficult labor that she had and the other two will not be re-bred for a full year to give their bodies plenty of time to recover. Since we have consulted with two different veterinarians and still can’t seem to figure out exactly what happened with these three does and their kids we will be sending off blood samples to most likely Texas A&M to test for a variety of things such as brucellosis, leptospirosis, chlamydia, Q fever and cache valley virus, among others. Thankfully, prior to my lay off and due to the generosity of some family members we did have a very decent stock pile of blue seal dairy goat feed but over the last 2 to 3 weeks that has started to dwindle as we had pregnant mamas that needed additional nutrition towards the end of their pregnancy. Anyone that knows me and my husband pretty well knows that it’s very difficult for us to reach out and ask for help when we need it and that we’d rather be the ones helping others than to ask for the help but we’ve come to a point now where we are the ones that are asking for the help. Our herd is at Jeopardy right now with the financial loss of the seven kids that were intended to help us weather the storm of my lay off, compounded with the extra cost of medication, veterinary services, and feed. We both understand that times are difficult for everyone right now and there are a lot of people that are being laid off or are making less than they were just a few months ago - the cost of everything has went up and we don’t expect anything from anybody. This is not us begging or pleading or telling you that you must help - we aren’t like that, but if you are able to and if you feel that you would like to, we would greatly appreciate it. If you don’t want to or can’t help in a monetary way we would appreciate words of support, encouragement, and any ideas that anybody might have. Also if anyone has a small amount of Bovi Sera that they would be willing to donate we would greatly appreciate it as finding small doses is almost impossible and the large dose is quite expensive. I want to thank all of you for being the wonderful people that you are - not only our family and friends, but our fellow breeders and people who have reached out, offered ideas, let me just talk to them on the phone and cry, watched a million different videos that I have sent them and just tried to be the best people that I’ve ever known. It has been so encouraging to see the people that support us and support what’s going on and we’re very grateful for our community that we have and and the love that you guys have shown us - we really appreciate that above all else We’re really hoping that little girl will pull through. I’ve decided that if she is still here on Sunday I will give her a name and I might do a poll and let everybody kinda pick what they think would suit her best. She’s a fighter for sure and I’d like to include everyone who’s been here with us on this journey to help pick a name for her. I don’t think that you have to raise livestock or even own animals to understand that there’s a reason why she’s still here (and it’s not because I have not slept in four days lol) it’s because she has fight, she has a will to live and that matters a lot

On the night of November 6th, Lt. Dan attempted to jump off of the couch after watching a movie with his family. He unfortunately got caught in a blanket and fell at an odd angle. He immediately showed signs of being unable to feel anything in his hind quarters and was rushed to Gulf Coast Animal Hospital. The doctors confirmed that he had severe swelling in his lower spine and retained no feeling in his back legs. We were told that in cases like this, Dan had little to no chance at a normal pain free life without immediate surgery. Even with surgery, dogs who have lost feeling in their hind quarters stand a 40-60% chance of a full recovery. After being monitored overnight, Dan was given an MRI where the doctors were able to confirm that he had herniated a disc in his lower back and that surgery would remain his best path forward. He was immediately rushed into an operation and will be kept at the hospital for the next few days. Once he returns home, Dan will need constant supervision and can take up to a month to see any results. Lt. Dan (believe me we understand the irony of that name) is an energetic and loving 4 year old dog. His favorite activities in life include frolicking on hiking trails, playing a mean game of tug of war, and unsuccessfully chasing squirrels. Please help Dan get back to his normal happy self. - Update 11/07/22 @10:30The surgery went well, they removed a lot of calcified herniated disc from his spine but the doctors are optimistic about his recovery. He’s going to remain at the hospital for the next few days to be monitored and receive physical therapy to hopefully get feeling/movement back into his legs. Thank you so much to everyone who’s helped! I’ll be sure to keep this page updated.

After being homeless for a while, I moved to Contra Costa County. Feeling good about securing an apartment, I thought I was in a good position to finally get a dog. I went to the nearest animal shelter where I first saw her: Lady. After walking around the shelter and seeing a bunch of dogs, there was no dog as excited to see me besides her. She was so excited when I approached the door that she peed and started doing the pig-like snorts everyone loves about her. I let the shelter know I was interested, and they let me do a meet and greet that day. The area where they held the “meet and greet” was full of toys and even a kiddy pool. But Lady paid no attention to any of it. She stayed by my side the entire time, giving me all the kisses and cuddles. I walked around the area, and she followed, still passing up all the other fun things around her. Based on our connection, I applied to adopt her and was approved on the same day. The shelter let me know she was found on Christmas Day and had just given birth to a litter. However, when she was found, her puppies were not with her. She had gone through a rough time recently, just like me, so our finding each other on Valentine’s Day was definitely a day of love. I took Lady home, and she settled in instantly. She refused to sleep on her new bed, full of all her new toys, so she chose to sleep with me in mine. This began our journey together. I was lucky to have Lady for almost five years, where she showed how much of a fun-loving sweetheart she truly is. She is excellent with other dogs and adults and beyond fantastic with children. I faced more complex situations during our time together, such as facing homelessness again, but she was right there with me – still giving me all her love. Thankfully, I was homeless for a short time. However, landlords were not open to pets when finding a new place. No matter how hard I fought, no one would accept pets. And I, unfortunately, had to rehome my Lady in 2019. I began interviewing people to see who would be the best fit to take her in and found a family through a friend. They were a big family that had another dog and children. The family had previously owned a dog similar to Lady and were very interested in her. We met at a local dog park where Lady could meet them and their dog to see if they would be a good fit. Lady connected with them. She got along with their dog and was gentle with the entire family. I had talked to the family before the meeting, so I already sensed they would be a good match. After the meeting, I felt reassured and agreed to rehome Lady with them. When moving Lady into their house, I saw she would have access to a vast backyard to roam and parks nearby for her walks. Additional family members at their home greeted Lady with excitement and love. So, although rehoming her was one of the hardest things I’ve had to do, seeing how accepting this family was gave me peace of mind that she would be safe. They sent me pictures and videos of Lady for the first few months, and she was happy, so I felt more at ease, even though I missed her a lot. At the beginning of the pandemic, I heard the family had given Lady to the person who referred them. Things had changed for the family, which surprised me. The family had failed to reach me. They were unable to keep Lady with them. But for some reason, they thought Lady originally belonged to the person who connected us. Luckily I still had the family’s number, so I reached out to see what had happened. They let me know the “friend” claimed to have been the original owner from the beginning, regardless of my name being on all of Lady’s paperwork, and mistakenly gave Lady away. Relations had become strained, but I reached out and tried to arrange a way to have Lady return. Despite the hearsay of the past, I put aside any fleeting emotions and focused on letting any party concerned to know that I was now in a position to home Lady and would like the opportunity to have her back. My “friend” refused. We went back and forth for a while, but there was no getting her back. I even sought advice from the animal shelter, as well as Animal Care and Control. They stated that I lost my rights to her since I gave up ownership. It was hard to give her up, and finding out I could have gotten her back was even more challenging and frustrating. But I accepted the facts. Some time passes, and the former friend reaches out to me, asking to talk about Lady. I was surprised since our last conversation about Lady was unpleasant, but I listened. They wanted to know if I could take Lady back but were unforthcoming as to any details of the situation and extremely vague about everything, including Lady’s well-being. They felt they didn’t need to explain anything to me; they just needed a yes/no answer. I needed to know what I was getting myself into. For example, whether Lady had developed any health conditions since our time apart. Things needed to be aware of to ensure she is properly cared for. But, they refused to say. Based on another unsuccessful negotiation, I declined. I didn’t feel prepared to take Lady in until I knew more about what was happening. A few months pass, and I get a call from the microchip company that Lady has been lost. Shortly after, I received another call from a vet hospital who stated someone found Lady. They told me they did a quick exam, and Lady was fine, but the woman who found her decided to keep her for the time being until they connected with me directly. The woman who found her called me directly and let me know they found Lady at night in a tennis court at a park near their house and kept her overnight until they could get in contact with me. I was in such a mix of emotions that I dropped everything I was doing, left work and met with the woman who found her. I was extremely nervous on the drive over as I wasn’t sure if Lady was genuinely okay if Lady would recognize me or even want to come with me, but the second she saw me, she let me know she did remember me. She got in the car right away. Later that day, I received a message from my former friend asking if I had her and, if so, to keep her if I wanted. My former friend was giving up on Lady, and I took the chance to save her and sort things out later. Lady got a bath and new pet supplies. I brought her home, and she settled in just like when I first got her. I spent the rest of the day focusing on her and reconnecting while ensuring she was comfortable. We were both happy to be together again. Later that week I took her to the vet for a routine exam and to get her up to date on her shots. During this visit, the vet discovered that Lady had a few bumps under her neck that needed to get biopsied, which concerned me. They took a sample and told me they’d get back to me with the results. A couple of days later, the vet let me know Lady has a Mast Cell Tumor(MCT). After being reunited for less than a week, we get hit with this news. Amazingly, we're together again, and I couldn’t be happier, but I don’t want this for Lady. She is an adorable and loving dog. Unfortunately, this was unexpected, and I don’t have the means to cover the treatment. The vet alone is quoting a lot to remove the tumor, and the treatment after is costly and doesn’t include the meds. After all this time apart, I am hoping to have more time with her, so I am asking for any donations to help with Lady’s treatment. Anything is truly appreciated. Thanks, Josephine and Lady

As a FedEx delivery driver, I meet a lot of people. And a lot of dogs! One of my elderly customers could always be seen with his trusty sidekick riding alongside him on his golf-cart (his only mode of transportation) to the mailbox at the end of his rural street. One day in the late Spring, I saw him there, on the cart, without Lucy. “Where’s your copilot?” I asked. With big tears in his eyes, he told me he’d buried her earlier that morning. He was heartbroken. He postponed getting another dog for a few months, until I showed him the picture of “Oreo” at 13 weeks old. She was one of a litter of 11 for whom another customer of mine was trying to find homes. He was sold. I picked up the sweet pup and took her to him. As my customer has very limited means, I told him I’d take care of her immunizations. I contacted a mobile vet in the county and explained the situation that I would be handling the financial part if they could just provide the care. It didn’t happen in time. On October 15, I had a delivery in the neighborhood and stopped by to see the pup and my customer. Oreo had stopped eating the day before and had begun throwing up even her water. I told him I’d check again the following day. That following day, she was terribly ill. I called my boss and asked to get a driver in to take over my route so that I could get this pup to the vet, ASAP. It was on a Sunday, so an Emergency Vet visit was the only option. We booked it to the University of Florida School of Veterinary Medicine Small Animal Hospital where this poor little lady was diagnosed with parvovirus, a potentially fatal disease that can only be treated with supportive care of intravenous fluids, nasogastric feedings, medicine for pain, nausea, and appetite stimulants. Her health and recovery are of the utmost importance. I’m doing everything in my power to provide for her care. The initial visit/assessment/treatment was $346. For the hospital admission, I agreed to a low-end estimate of $2500 and a high-end of $3500 and put down a deposit of $2700+. These costs will rise even higher if her treatment lags on for more days than expected. I’m asking for your help, especially those of you who are pet lovers. I can’t do this alone. I feel obligated to help this man save his beloved pup and I’m obligated to her as well. Please find it in your hearts to help me help Oreo survive this dreadful disease by helping me cover the costs of whatever treatment is necessary. From the bottom of my heart, I thank you!

Hello everyone. My name is Ron but I am sure most of you have seen Chester in my social media stories and feeds as I have pretty much evolved from a dog lover to a full-time cat dad. But what most of you did not know is this little fellow's insane backstory. Chester was born on October 31st, 2017, behind my restaurant in Artesia. It wasn't until New Year's Eve on December 31st, 2017, that my customer brought Chester to me. At first, we thought that he was scared, but it turned out he was paralyzed. Many of my friends and family warned that I would be in for a wild ride if I decided to take him in, but despite all the warnings, we grew close, and with the love and care I poured into him, he started to recover and learned how to walk and run once again three months later. We still do not know what caused this issue, but we suspect it might be some tick infection, combined with his genetic makeup, that caused it. Fast forward to May 15, 2019, Chester was spooked by a dog and ran off; we couldn't find the little fellah for the longest time. Chester would go missing for another 2 years before we miraculously came across him in our neighborhood. What's even crazier is that we found him on the morning of Nov. 1st of, 2021, a day after his birthday. Many people, including myself, thought that he would had no chance after being gone for so long. But despite the odds stacked against us, we were reunited. Yesterday, October 31st, 2022, on Chester's 5th birthday, I rushed him to Orangethrope Animal Aid Hospital. At first, I thought he was feeling under the weather and might have caught the flu as he was having difficulty breathing. In the lobby, while we were waiting, Chester started coughing out liquid and blood. Other waiting patients began to help and clear space for Chester as he was going into a seizure state. He stabilized 5 minutes later, thanks to everyone and the team at Orangethrope Animal Aid Hospital. We immediately began transferring to a more extensive, special care facility - Fountain Valley/West Coast VCA under the advice of our family vet at Orangethrope Animal Aid. Both facilities broke the news to me that Chester was found to have liquids in his lungs and heart, and that his heart is enlarged and he suffers a type of heart problem we called RCM (Restricted Cardiomyopathy). This means that his heart muscle has thickened, and he has problems pumping blood. The doctor informed me that he had been recovering slowly but surely after an overnight stay. However, it is recommended that he stay another night tonight to completely drain his fluid and keep him in the oxygen room for another night. They informed me that it's very likely that Chester will be on medication for the rest of his life. To top it off, they told me that cats that suffer from heart failure usually has about 6-12 months to live, but there are cases where the cats continue to live a good life after that period. I have been a pet owner my entire life and never had a significant issue with my pets like this. I have dug into my savings, and I would be lying if I said I was not exhausted by this new revelation for the past few days. I couldn't say no to the birthday boy, to the cat that's been through hell with me and back and through the worst time of my life. The least I can do is suck up my ego and seek for help. I know times are tough, so I appreciate any help. Whether it be donation, or spread the word for me. We had odds stacked against us before, and we prevailed. This is no different. We have proven this to everyone before, and I am sure we can do it again. Thanks for your time <3 - Ron

Hi. This is for my furbaby, Yuri. In the timespan of just three weeks, Yuri has spent three nights in the hospital and seven days on IV fluids on and off. She had come home needing anywhere between six through nine different medications throughout the day, and each with their own complicated set of instructions. e.g. give with food, give with no food, give two hours before or after any other medication on an empty stomach. It is so complicated that her vet makes hospital treatment sheets to record how and when I give her medications. This all began about a year and a half ago when Yuri started urinating blood a few hours after being taken out for a walk. She was treated multiple times for a UTI before a doctor found out that it wasn’t blood in her urine. It was pigment. After waiting three weeks for results from a special laboratory in Pennsylvania, we found out that Yuri is probably the first German Spitz to be diagnosed with a rare, autosomal recessive genetic disorder called PhosphoFructoKinase deficiency. This disease is one where any type of activity, stress, play, and even panting can result in the destruction of her red blood cells. This in turn would cause her urine to turn red and yellow. In the middle of October, it got so bad that her urine turned black. Since then, she has been treated for hypertension, pancreatitis, cholangiohepatitis, and jaundice. She was also presumed to have immune mediated hemolytic anemia, but once she tested positive for PFK, we have slowly started taking her off steroids in hope that she only has the PFK deficiency, though there may be multiple issues going on that complicate her case. The doctors tell us that from now on Yuri needs to live a quiet life with minimal activity. She just turned three years old and we are told it is possible her life span may be normal. But she will have ups and downs of anemia for the rest of her life. We hope you may be able to help us support Yuri’s current crisis and start planning for her future care and comfortability. Thank you! Megan

We decided to try adding a splint /cast to see if we could prevent further shifting. Now, I don’t know if you’ve ever had to nurse a 75 pound lame Doberman back to health, but it is quite taxing. Both for us and for Zeus. But we powered through and are doing our best. More unfortunate news hit us this past week when Zeus developed sores on his foot and at the site where the plate was shifting. If not, we’re looking at a fourth surgery, which would be a full hind leg amputation. We are desperately hoping that it does not get to that, as Zeus doesn’t really have enough functioning limbs to successfully get around if they amputate one leg.
