This GoFundMe is to help Kendal Hendrick, my friend and former student. Here is her family's story. The Short Version: Three years ago, Kendal’s two young sons (then aged 4 and 6) were undergoing care for life-threatening genetic conditions in a hospital in Massachusetts. They were taken from Kendal’s custody in the middle of the night by the state following a disagreement about their medical treatment. It’s a phenomenon known as “medical kidnapping” (read more about it here and here). Kendal was investigated, but evidence of child abuse or neglect was never found. Yet, three years later, the children remain in foster care on the other side of the country (Arizona), begging to come home. This terrible situation is due to a poorly designed law, ineptitude in applying the law, and the failures of a justice system biased against poor people, people with disability, and single mothers. Kendal has long since exhausted her savings, but she is still fighting for her day in court to bring her children home. This GoFundMe is to raise money for her to secure expert testimony for her initial hearing on October 29 and, in the worst-case scenario, enough money to see her children one last time before they are put up for adoption. The Long Version: Kendal is an alum of Georgetown University, where she studied Classics and Archaeology as an undergraduate, taking many of my classes and coming with me to dig in the field in Israel. After graduating, she went to law school at George Mason University to pursue Cultural Heritage Law. She had her first son while in her first year. Later, while pregnant with her second child, she unexpectedly became a single mom. Nonetheless, she still managed to juggle motherhood, a part-time internship at the Virginia Commonwealth Attorney's Office, and a full course load, graduating with a 4.0. And she did it all with her elder two-year-old son battling a life-threatening genetic disease called Common Variable Immune Deficiency, as well as a genetic lung disease, Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (similar to Cystic Fibrosis). When her second child was born, all seemed well at first. But then he developed severe failure to thrive from a partial lack of a pancreas and required pancreatic enzymes to live. Further, he started aspirating food into his lungs and needed a G-Tube and J-Tube to prevent choking. Like his brother, he was diagnosed as immune-deficient with specific antibody deficiency and presumed primary ciliary dyskinesia. He suffered dangerously low glucose levels, struggled to walk, and eventually was found to need emergency brain surgery which could only be done in Boston. (read more about her younger son’s struggles here ). Kendal set aside her career aspirations to focus on her sons’ health. The family headed to Boston. All seemed promising for a while as the doctors worked to determine the best way forward. But then, doctors started to disagree about the nature of the boys’ illnesses and the direction of further treatment. As a lawyer, Kendal started questioning the piles of papers the hospital asked her to sign. Before she knew what was happening, the unthinkable happened: the children were taken from her custody by state authorities in a textbook case of “medical kidnapping” (read more about this phenomenon here and here). The boys were removed from their specialized treatment and put into foster care. Since then, for three years, despite her limited resources, Kendal has been trying to undo this injustice, meeting every demand the system has required of her. She has submitted herself to numerous evaluations (all of which she passed). She has kept a low profile on social media. She has presented evidence from doctors and colleagues testifying to her children’s diagnosis and her fitness as a mother. On the few visits with the boys she has been allowed (and could afford), she has adhered to the state’s absurd restrictions, such as “no talking of memories” and “no reading books to the children”. Kendal has been a lawyer, teacher, and government worker, and has no criminal background or domestic abuse history. No evidence or charge of child abuse or neglect was ever put forward by the state for either child. Her children have received real diagnoses of life-threatening conditions verified by doctors at both Childrens’ Hospital of Richmond and Boston Children’s Hospital; these diagnoses were not based on a mother's description of symptoms but on biopsies, x-rays, CT scans, lab work, and genetic testing. Yet, because of a failed and flawed justice system, the boys, now aged 7 and 9, remain in foster care on the other side of the country in Arizona. They are not receiving the treatment they need for their conditions, and their health is declining. They beg to come home. Kendal is still fighting and finally, after three years, has a trial set to begin October 29, where the boys’ fate will be decided (either returned to her custody or given up for adoption). She has exhausted her savings (and then some). But Kendall needs additional funds to secure further expert testimony to persuade her case, and, in the worst-case scenario, to fund a trip to see her boys one final time before they are put up for adoption. Many of Kendal’s friends and I followed her and her sons’ journey over the years on Facebook, from the joy at their birth and growth to the stress and sadness surrounding their illness, admiring the indomitable spirit shown by both these boys. I have included a few pictures from that journey below. Even if you can’t donate, I hope you will at least read the linked articles below. If this can happen to someone as well educated and committed to her children’s well-being as Kendal, it can happen to anyone. Read more about medical kidnapping and some recent high-profile cases: If You’ve Never Heard of Medical Kidnapping, Pay Attention (Epperson Law Group) Link to Article The New Child Abuse Panic (NYTimes) Link to Article (this article has been gifted and thus free to read) When Medicine Attacks Motherhood (The Coalition Against Pediatric Pain) Link to Article After Being Kidnapped by Department of Children and Families, Justina Pelletier is Home Free (The Valley Patriot) Link to Article Escape from the Mayo Clinic: Teen accuses world-famous hospital of 'medical kidnapping' (CNN) Link to Article

My father, Brook Smith, had a nosebleed on September 6th, 2022. What started as a simple nosebleed after 16 hours escalated to respiratory failure and fighting for his life while needing mechanical ventilation, several units of blood and plasma. It has been a rollercoaster of emotions for the whole family as his health declined but showed signs of improvement in the following days, and the process would repeat and continues to be a vicious cycle. After hurricane Ian, they transferred my dad to an ICU unit at Mercy hospital in Miami because Healthpark Medical Center the hospital where he was being cared for before was under a boil water notice. He stayed in the ICU for another 12 days on the Ventilator before being transferred from Mercy to a long-term acute care facility in Coral Gables. It has been an ongoing battle for him to be transferred home based on his condition and other contributing factors, such as a bill we can not afford and no beds available in Fort Myers. Gas, hotel, and food expenses are too much for my family, so we have not been able to see him as often as he needs, and it has not allowed us to stay on top of his medical care. The whole situation has been extremely difficult for us all. My dad struggled with alcoholism; it was an ongoing battle and he showed signs of depression starting when he lost my grandparents and he would recover and relapse; he never wanted people to know he was struggling. My dad tried his best to keep things hidden from everybody, and it was clear how badly he struggled with his addiction when he was admitted to the hospital. He has cirrhosis of the liver and metabolic encephalopathy, which caused his issues to progress into something we aren't sure of the outcome. He is unable to communicate or move his body below the neck. He has also developed atrophy from long-term hospitalization, which will require long-term physical therapy if he recovers. My dad Brook was the type of person who always tried to put a smile on your face or make you laugh. He has a kind heart, always looks out for people to the best of his abilities, and puts his family before everything. He loves with his whole heart and is not afraid to show it. After every phone call and kiss goodnight, he always said he loved us and ensured we knew he was proud of us. I will forever cherish these memories of my father, the good and the bad, because I know he loved my brothers, his grandchild and the rest of my family. My dad doesn't have a voice based on the current state of his encephalopathy, which has progressed to where he can not communicate or understand what is going on and needs someone to advocate for him. My whole family will greatly appreciate any donations, thoughts and prayers. Thank you for taking the time to read this. The Smith Family

Hi there, I never expected to have to do something like this and don't know where to begin, but here is my family's story. My name is Sarah Knieff and my papa, Dennis or Dan Knieff, had unexpected brain surgery on Oct. 22, 2022. He was born with an arteriovenous malformation near the right side of his cerebellum, which means he had an abnormal connection between the arteries and veins. Now our family had no idea he had this. Unfortunately, this condition often leads to a rupture and bleeding in the brain, which is what happened last Saturday. That day was typical for our family - he went to work, and my mom, Marie, and I had a morning at home. Around 9:30 a.m., we got a call that he was being taken by ambulance to a nearby hospital in Minnesota because he was feeling sick. My mom and I rushed to the hospital, thinking perhaps he was dehydrated or just feeling under the weather. We never expected the doctor to come out and tell us my papa was very sick with a massive brain bleed. He needed immediate surgery to drain the bleeding and elevate the pressure it was causing on the brain stem. At this time, we had no idea if he would make it or not. We just prayed and hoped for the very best. My dad is a strong man, and we put faith in him and God. Around 3:30 p.m. that day, the neurosurgeon told us my dad had made it through surgery and that he was the best-case scenario for something like this. The surgeon said he was glad they could operate quickly because my dad would have been gone within a few hours otherwise. My mom and I will always be grateful for his neurosurgeon and his work best friend Allysa, who called 911 as soon as she noticed something was wrong with my dad at work. Fast forward to October 26, my dad is on his healing journey. He was only in a coma for about a day (another miracle because we were told it should have been three days at the least), and he is moving his arms/legs a lot. He can follow commands, squeeze our hands and open his eyes. His breathing tube might also come out today, but we have not been updated on that as of this morning. And that is my family's story. My dad has a long recovery road ahead with motor and speech function therapy. Every day, my mom and I are so grateful for how far he has come, and we feel so blessed by God. We couldn't have asked for a better outcome. Now, as anyone can imagine, this was extremely unexpected, and we are just starting to understand the financial burden this will have on our family. My dad is the primary worker for my parents, and we aren't even sure when/if he will be going back to work. If I had it my way, he would retire at the young age of 61, but he is a stubborn papa and might try to work more after recovery. My parents are hard workers and never ask for help - I mean, I know my mom will be a little upset when she hears I made this gofundme -but we need some support right now. That support can come from prayers, positive energy, happy thoughts and donations. Anything will help my family get through this. We are strong and happy to be blessed that our Dan is still fighting. Thank you for reading this, and please don't feel the need to donate money. Reading this and sending a happy thought to my family is enough. Thank you!

Joe and Mary Brennan have had a tough few years. Around midnight on November 7th, Joe woke up to some strange noises and discovered that the basement was engulfed in flames. They have lost everything: clothing, shoes, furniture, toys, bedding, blankets - absolutely everything. This also includes medical and care supplies for their son, Rush, who has GSD and has extreme medical needs, including expensive Dexcom supplies and special formula. Due to his GSD diagnosis, medically, Rush needs to eat every two hours, or he will experience life-threatening blood sugar levels. These are monitored with Dexcom devices, which are not covered by medical insurance as this usage is not within the normal scope or usage of said devices, making Joe and Mary pay for them out of pocket. GSD, or glycogen storage disease, is a rare metabolic disorder where the body cannot properly store or break down glycogen, a form of sugar or glucose. GSD affects the muscles, liver, and other areas of the body. This means that Rush must be fed every two hours. When he was diagnosed, Rush spent a month in the hospital after being life-flighted to children's hospital, and even now, they still have been paying off remaining medical debt from Rush's hospitalization and ongoing treatments. Joe and Mary had home insurance and will go through the process of filing a claim, but they have critical needs to replace needed medical equipment which would not be covered, or even if covered, would not be paid out in time to be replaced. Funds would be used to take care of their immediate needs for medical supplies and household items. Please give as you can to help them rebuild and take care of the unique needs of their family.

The Story: On September 29, our friend Mo launched his 1968 wood troller, Galaxy from Boat Haven in Port Townsend. Mo has lived aboard Galaxy for seven years, and had just spent the summer hauled-out in the shipyard working on some projects that included repairs in the plywood deck, rebedding hardware, bottom paint, and most importantly a new paint job on the hull. Upon launch Galaxy took on water, as wood boats are expected to do, and Mo waited until she took up and the water slowed to a trickle before heading off. About a mile from the marina, Mo noticed that Galaxy had become bow down, with water trapped behind the forward-most bulkhead. Unfortunately it was already too late. Water began flooding in through seams in the top side of the hull that were still open. The pumps were not keeping up, water was rising above the cabin floor, and Mo made the necessary decision to alert the Coast Guard, who rescued Mo, and called in a tow boat to save Galaxy. Within several hours, Mo was dropped off by the tow boat back at Boat Haven, and Galaxy, who'd become submerged above the cabin top, was turned upright and hoisted into the Travelift by the skilled Boat Haven operators during an emergency haul-out in the middle of the night. Galaxy stayed in the travelift slings overnight draining, while friends surrounded Mo for support, food, accommodations, and love. Galaxy was blocked back up in the shipyard in the morning and Mo got right to work, surveying the damage, pumping out the bilge, cleaning up, and salvaging as much as possible. A Little About Mo: Mo is one of the kindest, gentlest, most generous people I've ever met. I first met Mo at the Northwest School of Wooden Boatbuilding, where I was a student and where he works. Mo has attended both the Wooden Boat Building program and the Marine Systems program, and has become a highly knowledgeable and skilled shipwright and systems technician. Mo's patience, warmth, and willingness to always help are just some of the characteristics that his friends love him for, and what makes him a particularly important member of the community both at the school and in the larger Port Townsend area. Mo is an avid sailor and outdoors person; he enjoys exploring the Salish Sea and Puget Sound along with Mt. Rainer, the Cascades, and the Olympics. The Good: Galaxy's engine is a Detroit Diesel, and Mo reached out to Walt Trisdale, Port Townsend's renowned diesel engine expert who shared several strategies to dry out and revive the engine. Mo followed Walt's protocol and in a giant win, fired up the engine on October 4th. Luckily Mo has also been able to salvage and clean some of his essential belongings, including clothing, kitchenware, some books, and non-power tools. The Not-So-Good: All of the electronics aboard Galaxy are destroyed, including multiple battery banks, chargers, inverter, GPS, chart plotter, depth sounder, engine gauges, cameras (film and digital), and laptop. The wiring will all need to be torn out and replaced. All of Mo's power tools are also destroyed, despite an attempt to de-salt them. Nearly everything on board Galaxy that made her a home; books, bedding, and cushions have been destroyed. Aside from the expenses that come with replacing items, Mo is also facing a $20,000 tow boat bill, along with Boat Haven's emergency haulout fees, and additional unanticipated shipyard fees. The good news is that Mo has an insurance policy for Galaxy which will cover the cost of the salvage operation and at least some of the destroyed equipment. What We're Hoping For: We're launching this fundraiser at $10,000, all of which will be used to cover the replacement of Galaxy's electronics, Mo's tools, personal belongings, emergency haulout fees, shipyard fees, and ongoing living expenses as Mo continues to clean Galaxy up and restore her to her former glory, so that he can continue living aboard and caring for this sweet boat. Wood Boats and Their Caretakers: Wood boats are one of the things that Port Townsend is famous for, and are known for the unique processes required to build them and the craftsmanship that is needed to maintain them. Owners of wood boats see a beauty and a soul in them that is different from other types of hulls. Most boat owners shy away from wood, claiming it is a needy type of boat, but wood boat owners claim their wood boats give back exponentially. A few wood boats continue to be built today, but it takes a special type of person to care for and maintain these sweet relics of the past. Mo is committed to being one of the wood boat caretakers, and he wants to give Galaxy the love and attention she deserves.

For hundreds of graduate students who passed through the Department of International Health and Development at Tulane SPHTM, Penny Jessop represented the heart and soul of the department. After completing Peace Corps in Niger, Penny earned an MPH at Tulane in 1977, and she was immediately recruited to join Tulane’s staff. When the Department of International Health and Development was created in 1984, Penny took on the role of Academic Program Coordinator. She went on to coordinate the Humphrey Fellows Programs for mid-career health professionals from other countries who came to study at Tulane. Speaking fluent French and Spanish, she was a tremendous source of comfort for newly arrived international students trying to find their way in New Orleans. She was excellent at helping with logistics, but even better as an informal life counselor. When prospective students called the department, they often talked first to Penny and as a result, opted for Tulane. Later Penny became a Clinical Assistant Professor, sharing with the next generation of students her breath of experience, before retiring in 2012. When faculty, staff, or students needed assistance, Penny was there to help. Now it’s our turn to help Penny. Please join in showing Penny how much she meant to the Tulane community by contributing to this fund. Donations will be sent to Penny to help her settle in her new home. Saddleback is raising & donating money to purchase an ambulance for civilians injured in Ukraine. All money raised will go directly to the Greater Lansing Jewish Federation. The funds will be used to purchase the ambulance(s), and provide generators, sleeping bags, fire extinguishers, cooking gas, and other valuable supplies. What inspired this? Okemos resident, Ody Norkin, is the Vice President of Michigan Flyer. His grandparents were killed in Odessa, Ukraine, in 1941. He knew he wanted to do anything he could to help the people of Ukraine today. He texted Rabbi Avraham Wolff in Odessa, Ukraine: “I am tired of sitting on my hands. I know all about buses and transportation. Is there anything I can do to help the folks in Odessa?” The Rabbi replied, “Actually, we don’t need transportation help but it would be extremely helpful if you showed up with an ambulance. You could drive passengers who can’t handle buses, who must lie down. We have many infirm people here who need to be taken to a safe place.” Ody has since made the incredible journey to personally deliver an ambulance, generator, and more needed supplies to the people of Ukraine. This will be the 4th ambulance he has delivered. How did Saddleback Get Involved? We were completely unaware of this unbelievable act of generosity until Tuesday when I (Travis) was having lunch with a friend, and he had to take a phone call, and I overheard him say “We need to raise $20,000 more to send another ambulance to Ukraine”. I instantly knew that we needed to help and that Matt would be on board. Why an ambulance? Many older adults and injured civilians cannot handle the stress of a bus ride to get to areas of assistance. Ambulances can also travel after dark when other vehicles are not allowed to travel because of curfews. Ambulances also serve as a perfect hub to store useful pharmaceuticals. How can you help? Donate to our GoFundMe. What is Saddleback doing to help? We will be providing an initial donation to the GoFundMe of $500. Beyond that, we will add additional donations for every significant milestone raised. $5,000 - Saddleback will donate an additional $250 ($750 total) $10,000 - Saddleback will donate an additional $250 ($1,000 total) $20,000 - Saddleback will donate an additional $500 ($1,500 total) If we reach our goals, we expect to contribute $1,500. We will also pay to advertise this campaign out of our pocket. Saddleback and Slice by Saddleback are open to all people of all types. This campaign is not a political statement in any way. Our goal is simply to help people in any way we can. *All of the money from GoFundMe will be given directly to the Greater Lansing Jewish Welfare Federation (MIEIN: 382106869) less any fees that are charged by GoFundMe. GoFundMe charges 2.9% + $0.30 to cover credit card processing fees. We will be fully transparent with the total GoFundMe amount and show proof of the money going to the Greater Lansing Jewish Welfare Federation for use towards this effort. We are using GoFundMe so that we can incentivize and track the donations that are coming from our Saddleback community. Using GoFundMe allows us to provide incentives for hitting important fundraising milestones. We are not a non-profit organization. However, Greater Lansing Jewish Welfare Federation is a non-profit. Please consult your tax professional about any applicable tax deductions. **No raffles, sweepstakes, giveaways, or promotions are offered in exchange for any donations made. "More information about Greater Lansing Jewish Welfare Federation Inc: The Greater Lansing Jewish Welfare Federation is an affiliate organization of the Jewish Federations of North America, an umbrella organization that represents 157 Jewish Federations and 400 independent Jewish communities. The Federation movement places collectively among the top ten charities on the North American continent in charitable activities and has the goal of protecting and enhancing the well-being of Jews worldwide through the values of tikkun olam (repairing the world), tzedakah (charity and social justice) and Torah (Jewish learning)." Hello everyone. I want to start off by saying this is incredibly uncomfortable for me, but in the name of vulnerability and genuine need, I am asking for help. On 10/24/22, I was the victim of an exceptionally well-executed scam. Somebody impersonating a Sergeant from Scott County Sheriff's Department contacted me and stated I had failed to appear in court to provide expert witness testimony. This is something within the realm of possibility, given my job as a therapist and recent practice change. He told me I was charged with failure to appear and contempt of court. This person had a remarkable amount of my personal information, something that made it very believable from the get-go. They also told me there was a gag order on the case, so I could not tell anyone about it or end the phone call without being arrested. When I asked him to prove that he was truly calling from the Sheriff's department, the phone number on my screen verified it as Scott County's Sheriff's department. I also Googled this number and confirmed it myself. I then was able to confirm that the name given to me was in fact the name of a Sergeant that worked for the county. This entire phone call I was being threatened with arrest and told I needed to resolve this matter immediately. At this point I was in the middle of a panic attack and incredibly concerned for my career, so I moved forward with the transaction to "pay my bond." I was then told to go to the Hennepin County's Sheriff's Department, where a detective informed me that I had been scammed and instructed to file a police report. I have since filed fraud claims, a police report, and contacted my bank. Due to the nature of how the funds were stolen, it is almost certain that we will not be able to track who did this or recover my money. I was told this type of scam is nearly impossible to trace. I have also contacted local news stations, the MN Board of Behavioral Health & Therapy, the clinic I contract with, and I am notifying any person I know who works in the mental health field about this. It was a big life lesson for me, and it is now my goal to make sure this does not happen to anyone else. The amount stolen from me was everything I had in my savings account. This money was set aside to cover things like rent, health insurance, student loans, and all of my other bills. It was also funds for the wedding of Nate, my fiance, and I in October of 2023 that I had regularly been setting money aside for. I no longer have a safety net, and the money I do have will be depleted quickly. I recently began working as a therapist in an independent contractor role, which has come with a very different pay schedule than I was accustomed to and is not necessarily consistent. As I am still building my caseload, I was heavily relying on my savings to carry me through this transition period -- and without it, I am in trouble. I completely understand that in today’s economic environment everyone is struggling and trying to stay afloat. Asking for financial support is not something I take lightly or thought I would ever need to do. Any funds contributed will be used for paying bills, rent, living expenses and to make sure we are able to fulfill the contracts Nate and I have signed with wedding vendors. I'd also like to ask that you share this information with anyone you know who works in mental health/social work -- after researching online, this is a scam happening all over the nation, specifically targeting the innocent workers who are in these roles. I sincerely appreciate everyone's love, support, kind words, and actions. I consider myself incredibly lucky to have the folks in my life that I do. I believe in the power of community, and promise to work diligently to find avenues to pay it forward once I am stable. Thank you for taking the time to read this and for your consideration.

On Friday October 14th the X-rays showed something much more serious than the arthritic behavior we all expected. We also might need to buy things like ramps, slings, gates, stairs, carts etc.. This is a very aggressive type of cancer. They give her 3-6 months as of now, and we don’t know exactly how far on that timeline we are, but she’s been showing small signs of pain for about 2 months. Her lungs are currently clear and we need to keep it that way as long as possible. How this progresses is the blood carries the disease to the lungs. She came into my life as a wee babe, and I thought she would be going out as an old lassie, but nothing is permanent. I am so very grateful for our life together, and for the short amount of time we have left. It’s not easy to ask for help, but here we are. Thank you from the bottom of the depth of me.. This past December, our daughter Brandi and our son-in-law Matt thought they were purchasing the perfect home for their family of 6. Unfortunately, in June of this year Matt discovered a small leak behind a panel of their master bathroom tub. Hoping it would be a quick fix, a contractor was called in to assess the situation. He discovered that the water damage was very extensive and had spread into the bedroom. Brandi and Matt were asked to move everything out of their bedroom in July so the contractor could tear out carpets and demo the bathroom and the subfloor of the bedroom. In the middle of the reconstruction, while on a camping trip with the family, Brandi fell and broke her arm and has since been placed on light work duty until nearly the end of the year. This has been devastating to their income until she is released to work. With a few delays from the contractor and Brandi's reconstructive surgery, they continued to sleep in their living room for nearly two months. During the contractor's last visit, he removed a section of the wall behind the walk-in shower and stopped work immediately. He had found what he thought was mold and called Servpro to investigate further and determine if it was mold. An air quality test was performed inside their bedroom, living room, and exterior of the house and they were told results would be in within a week. Two days later, while at work Matt received a call and heard the words no homeowner and father of four ever wants to hear. He was told that the family had to vacate and leave the property immediately. The black mold spore count of the air quality test was the highest the specialist had ever seen. Brandi and Matt were devastated and feared that they purchased this home only to put themselves and their children in harm's way. Especially Gracelyn and Annabelle, whom both suffer from Cystic Fibrosis. Since the discovery of the mold, Brandi, Matt and the four kids have been displaced, bouncing from house to house to have a place to stay. Currently, with help from some friends, they are staying in a camper at their property, trying to have some normalcy and not bothering friends and family. It was recently discovered that moisture and mold had spread into their living room. They've been informed that the potential cost of the mold remediation could exceed $50,000, of which their insurance will only cover up to $10,000. With the high cost, they fear they will have no choice but to walk away from the property. Not only are we looking to assist Brandi and Matt with the cost of the mold remediation, but we are also hoping to find their family a more suitable place to live while this process continues through what we hope will be reconstruction. Thank you for all of your continued prayers and kindness as we continue to help Brandi, Matt and the kids get through this difficult time.

Dear Friends and Family, I hope this message finds you and yours safe, healthy and happy! Not sure how many of you are aware, but our dear friends, the Paxtons, were hit hard by Hurricane Ian, which devastated their hometown of North Port and surrounding areas of Florida's southwest coast. The family sustained lots of damage to their properties (they’ve had three homes on the same street in North Port for decades). They have some unbelievably high insurance deductibles and other unexpected storm-related expenses piling up on them. They are such amazing friends to so many of us and truly need us to come together and assist them in their time of need. There is no question that if the roles were reversed, they would be here helping any of us. I know I can count on you all to help me share this page with anyone you think would be willing to help. Bill Medley and I will proudly get the ball rolling with the first donations. I asked for a breakdown of all they expect to pay for out-of-pocket, and on the conservative side, it’s in the neighborhood of $30,000. Brooks and Di live on a fixed retirement budget, and I’m not sure what this close family will do without our help. Thank God we don’t have to figure that out because here we are, coming to the aid of our dear friends. I feel certain many of us will want to help, so I am trying to share this with as many of you as possible. In closing, I love you all and cherish our friendships. You guys take care of each other and hold your loved ones tight. I hope our paths cross again in the near future. Now, I’d like to turn it over to Di & Brooks’ sons, Sean and Brooks II, for an update on what they went through and are dealing with moving forward. Thank You Bucky, and all those taking the time to read this response and update on behalf of our parents and family affected by Hurricane Ian. When Bucky first reached out in the aftermath of this event with an idea of helping in this way, we were reluctant. However, with his urging, we took an honest and humble look at the reality of what we went through and are now facing on the road to recovery. The adrenaline is just now wearing off from those immediate weeks of survival, emergency repair and clean-up. Now, with some time to reflect and look forward, we realize it makes no sense to let our family pride prevent others’ willingness to help. Bucky - you’re right. It’s a lot to deal with. Suddenly and all at once. Especially now with our focus and energy shifting to the unforeseen financial impacts of this event. The challenges have compounded because all our homes sustained simultaneous wind and water damage in the hurricane. Externally and internally. As a result, we’ll be facing financial fallouts in multiples of three. High insurance deductibles, repair and replacement for uninsured losses to property and personal effects, furniture, work equipment, vehicles, and loss of income. While we face these challenges, our thoughts remain with our fellow Floridians affected by this historic natural disaster. North Port, Florida has been our adopted hometown since 1978. Three generations of our family have roots here, so it’s difficult and sad to see our neighborhood and surrounding communities hit so hard. To friends and neighbors in the tight-knit community here on Marius Road who helped us and each other immediately following the storm. Thank you, and others who came in from Tampa and Florida’s east coast to provide critical post-storm survival supplies. Extra generators, gas, food and water. All in short or zero supply locally at that time. We’d also like to thank those who reached out to check on us before, during and after the storm, and others who mailed us food care packages. It all helped us through those tough first few weeks. We’ll be sharing updates as our recovery progresses from here, but in the meantime, we extend our heartfelt appreciation to everyone for your time, your caring thoughts, prayers, and your support. Every bit of that matters and makes a difference. We’re fortunate and blessed to have so many good people in our lives. All the best from us and ours to you and yours, Diane Paxton, Brooks Paxton Sr., Sean Paxton, Brooks Paxton II, Tom Larkin

Funds will also be used to help pay their rent and hopefully fly her parents out of Ukraine, where the war continues. I am also setting up a signup genius for those who want to contribute to their basic household needs. But for them to come out of this net they are caught in, affording an immigration attorney and rent is their number one goal. For my sister, in her honor and for myself, because I have a lot of love to give the world and I didn't want to waste any more of it on people who only exploit others. I will step back into myself and spread that joy in every way possible. Thank you for taking the time to read my story, I am grateful for such a giving community, and I am daring to be hopeful for a bright future. With love, Hannah (and the cats) Cupid + Marbles ,

Through these efforts, they discovered the plight of local Jewish children suffering homelessness, abuse, neglect or living in bleak and destitute State orphanage environments. Following their harrowing escape from Odesa, they are now trying their best to maintain their humanitarian mission in Romania, a foreign environment and highly challenging operating conditions. Tikva has, in essence, taken an entire community of almost 1,000 Jewish children from Ukraine and transplanted them (after the first two horrifying weeks of the war) to Romania. Their main objective has been keeping the community together as a family. The hope is that in the absence of their physical community and facilities, they can at least replicate that feeling of home as much as possible while maintaining the psychological cohesiveness and comfort that unity provides. FoR is passionate about providing all the help we can for the Tikva orphanage to survive and thrive in Romania. My sister Pat had substantial damage from Hurricane Ian. She needs help to repair the damage to her home. Like so many retirees, Pat and Fran Mercier moved to Florida from Spencer/Webster Massachusetts to follow their retirement dream in 2011. They choose Fort Myers because many friends from their former summer residence at Indian Ranch Campground on Webster Lake Massachusetts had also moved to the area. Also, Patty’s Aunt Betty Trifone LaMountain lived close by at the time and needed some assistance from family to remain independent. Prior to retiring in 2011, Pat and Fran both worked at LUTCO Bearing in Worcester for many years. Life was good, but like many small manufacturing shops in Central Massachusetts, there was no pension or health insurance plan for retirees. Selling everything and relocating to Florida close to their many retired friends seemed like the best economical plan. Social Security would be their sole source of income, so Fran decided to continue working part time as a repair person, golf cart mechanic. Like so many Florida dream retirements, Life got harder as good friends and family passed away or moved somewhere else to be closer to family support systems. Pat and Fran stayed, made many new great friends in the area. Life was hard, but good! A few years ago, Fran developed serious back issues and underwent surgery many times. Unfortunately, none of the surgeries provide real relief and he had to quit all outside work. Being over 80 years old, Fran had physically done enough to try to give Patty and himself a good retirement. As most of you know, hurricanes are part of the way of life in Florida. You always prepare, and always hope, the big one never hits you. Southwest Florida has a good record of missing the big ones over the last 50 years. Not this time with Hurricane Ian! Hurricane Ian was originally thought to be coming ashore north of Tampa Bay, but Mother Nature had another plan. At the last moment, Ian took a right turn into the Fort Myers area. Patty and Frans Florida dream retirement home took a major hit. Their home is still standing, but their carport, shed and covered air-conditioned lanai were totally destroyed. Their home itself needs many repairs to remain habitable. Fran’s health had been deteriorating now for years, and he had just recently returned from an extended hospital stay and rehabilitation. Fran and Pat were struggling during the hurricane to try to hold their home together. Fran went into distress and needed medical help. Unfortunately, even life-threatening situations were impossible for EMTs to respond to calls for help. After days, Fran was eventually transported to the hospital a few days later, and after many more days of diagnosis and testing’s, they discovered he had an aggressive, terminal lung cancer, not just back issues. Franny is now under hospice and is living the last days of his life in a severely damaged home, they both refuse to leave. To make matters worse, economically, Fran dropped all insurance, because there was not enough money to pay the exorbitant home insurance costs for their home. I know it turned out to be a bad choice but living on Social Security alone does not offer many luxuries. FEMA was contacted by Patty, but cannot provide any permanent help to repair their devastated home. Patty very soon, cannot continue to live in their devastated home alone, without major repairs. Right now, Patty is totally focused on making Franny’s final days as comfortable as possible. To make matters worse, Patty will be facing final expenses and funeral costs very soon, on top of trying to live in a severally damaged home that needs major repairs, with Social Security payments decreasing to one check. Life seems impossible right now, and that is why we are starting this GO Fund Me Page, to try to lessen the burden of living and dying in this devastated state of conditions. For those that know Patty and Fran, they would do anything to help a friend in need! They are both immensely proud, salt of the earth people, and asking for outside help was exceedingly difficult, but there is no other option! If you know Patty and Fran, please help if you can! If you do not know them and can identify with their dire situation, your kindness and generosity is sincerely appreciated during this extremely difficult time! Any contribution is greatly appreciated! God Bless You! Thank you in advance for your consideration and help!

In order to do this, they placed a breathing tube to put her on a ventilator to help assist her breathing and provide her with oxygen. Shortly after that a CT was performed which revealed how bad her lungs were. They were not only infected but filling with blood continually. In order to keep her still to reduce the amount of bleeding they placed her in a medically induced coma, where she is incapacitated and unable to speak, move or speak. The surgery was to place an ECMO machine, which in layman’s terms is a type of life support. The machine allows a bridge to her heart that bypasses her lungs to draw her blood out where it then gets oxidized and put back in her body. Hi I'm Dave Meldrum-Green from Orlando, FL. I am raising funds to directly help out a friend of many, who suffered substantial losses due to Hurricane Ian. Very simply...after a very wet, rainy August, Ian's September torrential rains had nowhere to go. Fortunately, FEMA has been paying for her expenses for temporary housing in a hotel and a modest living stipend. But all FEMA can offer many folks (including Kathy) is simply a low-interest rate Federal loan to help them pay for the damages done to their homes. Kathy has decided not to undergo the intense stress of trying to restore her home and is unable to afford the financial burden to do so. She will be selling her home to someone who buys distressed properties, but unfortunately having to do so at a deeply discounted price. Thus, losing a sizable portion of the equity she has built up. Alla and Oleksii Kryvda and their three children Nikolai (6), Sofiia (9) and Matviei (11) have finally arrived in the US after an arduous journey fleeing the war in Ukraine. They’ve lost everything and need our help to create a safe home for their family. Before the war, the Krvyda family lived in the town of Vinnytsia, where Oleksii worked as a graphic designer and Alla worked for a bank. From the start of the war, Vinnytsia has been a Russian target. Many cruise missiles have been launched into the city, destroying the Havryshivka International Airport, the Vinnytsia TV Mast, the Ukrainian Air Force National Military Command Center, and, most tragically, the medical center, offices, stores, and civilian homes. Many citizens have lost their lives, including children, and Vinnytsia has been declared a city of war crimes. To save their children, in early March Oleksii and Alla decided that Alla and the kids would flee to Poland via train and Oleksii would stay behind in Ukraine. They believed that the war would end and they would soon be reunited. Of course, this hope was not to be realized. In Poland, Alla and the children were separated from Oleksii for two months. She found temporary housing, but rent prices continually increased due to the massive influx of Ukrainian refugees, so remaining in Poland was no longer a viable option. Meanwhile, Alla’s mother saw reports that the US was allowing Ukrainians fleeing the war to enter the US via Mexico. Alla learned via the internet that volunteers were meeting Ukrainians at the Tijuana airport and driving them to the US border. The family flew to Mexico on April 24th, ready to reach a safe harbor. However, after days of grueling travel with the children, when they arrived in Tijuana on April 25th, the border had officially just closed to Ukrainians. They missed crossing into the US by three hours. That day, the Uniting for Ukraine (U4U) refugee program was announced. Alla, Oleksii, and the children remained in Mexico for three months awaiting approval of their U4U paperwork. Speaking neither Spanish nor English, far from home and sharing a small room, they waited and hoped. On July 25th, they finally arrived at Newark Airport. Veterinarian Louise Murray and her firefighter husband, Peter, welcomed them into their home in Guilford, Connecticut, and connected them with local Ukrainian speakers who are helping the Kryvdas navigate life in the area. Their journey has been incredibly challenging physically, emotionally, and financially and the Kryvda family is still in great need of additional funding and supplies. Oleksii is a graphic designer who needs an appropriate computer to work and support his family; the cost would be approximately $4,000. The Kryvdas also need funding to rent their own apartment or house, including at least three months’ rent to start (first month, last month, deposit). Rent in Guilford for a family of 5 is approximately $4500/month, equaling $13,500 to secure a home. The children will need clothing, shoes, winter coats, boots, and school supplies, and funds are needed for basic staples such as groceries and medical costs. Estimated Costs: Computer 4,000 Housing 13,500 Car insurance, maintenance, fuel 5,000 Clothes, shoes & school supplies 2,000 Food and household supplies for three months 3,000 Utilities, medical copays, and other incidentals 3,000 We hope to raise $30,000 for the Kryvda family to secure a home and care for their children for the next few months, until they are settled in and able to support themselves. Please consider a donation. The past eight months have been traumatic and frightening for the family. They are so happy to be safe and welcomed here in the US but need help getting back on their feet. No amount is too small. Thank you so much!

Lisa and her son woke from sleep and ran between rooms looking for the source of the smoke, not knowing that the burning was inside the walls. In the kitchen, Lisa saw sparks jetting from under the dishwasher, and when she opened the under-sink cabinet the pipes were in flames. While Lisa’s insurance company fights with the neighbors’ company over who is going to pay, Lisa is stuck navigating emergency finances and hoping one day to be reimbursed, at least for part of them. Of immediate concern are first/last/deposit on a rental home (the firefighters said to expect to be displaced for no less than six months), boarding for her dogs if the rental isn’t pet-friendly, cleanup costs including (not insignificantly) whatever laundry can be salvaged, meals while she and her son are in motel lodging, and lost hours at her jobs. Among Lisa’s fans are those of us who work with her and know her as the one who wrangles the chaos inherent in bureaucracies. We want to help, and we want to open the “help pipeline” to everyone whose lives Lisa improves in her roles as colleague, volunteer, Zumba instructor, sports coach, and all-around good egg. Please join us in contributing support as she navigates this daunting road. All funds, minus GoFundMe transaction fees, will go directly to Lisa Denker.

She had kidney failure and more blood clots; she couldn't breathe on her own, she couldn't talk, and she couldn't walk... they had her in a medically induced coma for the first two and half weeks of being there. When the doctor decided to bring Brittney out of the coma, she was forced to depend on a breathing and feeding tube for an additional three weeks after the coma. The four large openings on her legs were forced to remain open as she has developed compartment syndrome, which makes her muscles swell to where she would have lost her legs if they didn't stay open. After conquering several emergency dialysis treatments and learning to breathe on her own again, she was sent to Brooks rehab. Once Brittney got to Brooks rehab, she was there for one day when they found she had a severe bacterial infection and had to be moved back to the hospital ICU for intensive treatment. She was back at the hospital another week, fighting extremely high fevers and other infectious complications. At the time of her beating that infection she was approved to have her trach taken out and has had to go through speech therapy to learn to talk again! Once the infection was gone and the trach was taken out, the hospital transferred her back to Brooks. She was there for two weeks when Brooks told her that her insurance would not cover any more care at their facility and she would need to begin at home care! Brittney still has four large wounds in her legs; she cannot walk or move her feet. She goes back and forth to treatment, hoping to get approved to have her wounds closed and eventually learn to walk again. Ya'll trust me, I know this is a lot to hear, but my friend needs some help. If you genuinely know Brittney, she will never ask anyone for anything. I had to convince her to allow us to create this on her behalf. Brittney has been out of work since August; she has two amazing young boys to care for; her mortgage, car note, and medical bills are crazy now; on top of everything else she will need in the coming days, she needs us to stand up for her now. The lawyers we have reached out to have required us to wait until she has no more procedures needed at the hospital before they will take her case, as they do not want to cause more issues for her there. Any lawsuit she may eventually be entitled to will take years to see success, if any. Anything you can donate for her, I promise she will be so touched and thankful. Hi, my name is Michele, and this story is about my son Matt and his dog Ralph. It is a story about a challenging and scary time for Matt. He recently lost everything he owned in an accident that totaled his truck, and had his bank account emptied out by thieves. It is also a story about life changes, loss and finding peace, and I appreciate you reading it. Matt is one of the sweetest and kindest men I know. He will always have your back if you are lucky enough to be his friend. Matt is loyal, brave and wickedly funny. He is also friendly, caring, and stubborn. He is generous, and if you decide to help him, I know he will "play it forward" when he can. I have seen Matt take off his coat on a cold and rainy night and give it to a stranger with no coat just because. This story starts last year when Matt's dad (my ex) died from colon cancer only two months after diagnosis. It was a shock to Matt and his sister, and they both grieved, but Matt took it very hard. Shortly after that loss, I moved out of state to be closer to Matt's sister. Family is important to Matt, and he decided to leave the city where he was born and raised, a job that wasn't a good fit, and to seek comfort in hard work, the outdoors, and volunteering, things he inherited from his dad. Matt packed up all his belongings and put everything in storage except what would fit in his truck. Over the next 12 months, he volunteered for room and board on a goat farm, a bison ranch, and several other farms and homesteads. Matt found his dog "soulmate" on the bison ranch (more about Ralph the dog later). He also fell in love with the mountains in Montana and found a community of kind and lovely people there. He's a volunteer firefighter and plans to apply to become a firefighter full-time in the spring. Ten days ago, Matt returned to Seattle, removed everything from storage (furniture, clothing, beds, kitchen items, mementos of his dad) and filled up a U-Haul van. He parked it overnight in front of the place he was staying and woke up the following day to an empty space. The U-Haul and everything in it were gone. After the shock, a police report, and a discussion with U-Haul, he started to face the reality that his belongings were gone. U-Haul insurance covers items in the truck if there is an accident but not if things are stolen. Since he hasn't had stable housing, he has no renter’s insurance. All his childhood reminders were the hardest to lose, especially his dad's mementos. Matt returned to Montana with a heavy heart, trying to keep a good attitude. Then, a mile from the cabin where he is staying, his truck hit black ice and went over an embankment. The truck rolled, and Matt ended up trapped upside down. His first thought was of his dog Ralph. I'll leave you with the idea of Matt hanging upside down to tell you a bit about Ralph. Matt was on the Bison Ranch and missing his dad. He was hiking, and a less-than-year-old puppy came running up to him with no tags, chips or collar. He had obviously been tied up somewhere, was painfully skinny, and had cuts and marks that let Matt know he had been badly treated. He followed Matt back to the Ranch and has not left Matt's side since. The ranch owner understandably did not want another dog on the ranch, so the dog was not fed, but he stayed by Matt's side anyway. He became known as Ralph, and after Matt took him to the vet and he healed, Ralph has been the best dog ever. Matt and Ralph are a lot alike. They love Montana, are loyal and can be a little wild. So, back to the upside-down truck. Matt knew he needed to get out of the truck, but Ralph took priority. Ralph was tucked in the collapsed backseat, and Matt was able to get to him and open a small back window to get Ralph out of the truck. Ralph then stayed by the truck barking until two very nice young men stopped, climbed down the ravine, broke the truck's back window, and got Matt out. They helped him back up the ravine and kept him warm until the paramedics arrived. Matt's truck is totaled. Matt and Ralph are cut, beaten up, bruised, and sore. Matt will need physical therapy, but he and Ralph are alive. I headed to Montana to offer support. The next day Matt discovered that the thieves who stole the U-Haul with all his belongings somehow got enough information out of it to empty out his savings and checking account (he is working with the credit union on that one). I think that felt like too much of an invasion, and he realized he was not getting any of his belongings back. It was a tough day. Matt needs to replace his winter clothing, bed and bedding, silverware, towels, couch, and chairs since every item he owned was stolen. If you can help Matt replace/rebuild his life, that would be great and much appreciated. If not, that’s okay. Thank you for reading this, and I hope your day is filled with good things. I also hope an easier road is in store for my sweet son. Michele

Hi everyone,My name is Susanna Lovsky and I’m a singer/songwriter from San Francisco, CA based in Los Angeles, and I’m a first generation Ukrainian-American. In the late 1980s, my parents and my older sister (who was 4 at the time) left what was known as the Soviet Union and made their way to America as political refugees. Their route before getting to America: Praha, Czech Republic, to Vienna, Austria for 30 days, to Rome for 6 months, and finally flying through NY to settle in SF. They were invited by a host family to live in San Francisco, and with zero English, $90 amongst the three of them, and many hardships, they overcame adversity and established themselves. My parents were some of many that fled the tyranny of the Soviet Union, but not everyone left. For the ones that stayed, the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991 meant regaining a nationality that had been kept from them for 70 years. Ukrainian people are strong, rich in culture, and proud, so they rebuilt. Fast forward to 30+ years later, my mom’s side of the family are among those that proudly stayed in Ukraine. Sadly now, this beautiful country and culture is under attack. And the regions my uncles live in have been continuously targeted. Down below are some descriptions about each of them and their situations-My mom’s youngest brother, Vitya, and his family live in Gorodishche (Shepetovka). This is the same village and house that my mom and her siblings grew up in. Vitya has a son, Yarik, who is 17 years old and still high school. Vitya recently got a letter that he would be drafted in the spring to serve in the army. We’re praying that the war is over before this time comes. My second uncle Andron (Andrey) and his family, live in Nikolaev (Mykolaiv) in an apartment building. During the day, Andrey risks his life delivering oxygen tanks around different war zones in Ukraine to help the wounded and sick. His wife is a nurse and tends to many sick and elderly patients, some injured by attacks. In the evenings, they hide in a bomb shelter. My uncle Sergei lived in Slavyansk (Slavyansk - Donetsk region) and was the only one that was able to get out as the war developed. A few months ago, him and his wife fled as refugees to Portugal. Men aren’t allowed to leave Ukraine at all because they have to serve somehow to protect the country, but because he had X-ray proof of a serious neck injury that wouldn’t allow him to serve in the army, he was let go. Sergei and his wife are currently living in a small apartment by a farm, where they’re fortunately able to exchange help on the farm for housing. At this time, they are not making any sort of income. If you donate, you will not only be helping all of these families survive, but also saving the lives of others who are relying on them for aid of some sort. Whether it’s Vitya being given the chance to provide food for his son and wife, Andrey putting money into more oxygen tanks and fuel for driving around Ukraine, or Sergei and his wife taking the risk and uprooting their lives to settle into a completely new, foreign country...your generosity allows these people to have a chance, a lifeline.

Thank you for your interest in this fundraising campaign and for hearing our call for help. My sister, Natalie, is in a difficult situation and near danger of losing her home in southern MN. Some of you are familiar with her circumstance and the medical condition that has put her in this position. For those who aren't familiar with her story, please read on: In September 2017, Natalie experienced a seizure unexpectedly while working at the Diamond Jo Casino, where she had been happily employed for ten years. She was nearly 40 years old and had never experienced anything like this before. That was five years ago; her life since would be changed entirely. The seizures persisted, and she continues to have them multiple times weekly. The episodes are accompanied by migraines, disorientation and often days of physical exhaustion due to the bodily exertion associated. If you're wondering what these seizures look like exactly, imagine somebody having a seizure. That thing you're imagining, that's what they look like. Immediately, the Mayo Clinic became involved as Natalie began the process of finding out what the cause was. MRI testing was done. The results were inconclusive. EEG testing was done, and the seizures were determined not to be caused by epilepsy. After many months spent meeting with specialists, it was determined that Natalie's attacks result from Cognitive Behavioral Disorder. Through this process, Natalie had to keep working, even though this put her at risk of injury from falling, as her job at the casino required her to be on her feet, dealing cards and running games. Natalie loved her job, thrived in it, and was doing everything she could to manage her condition so that she could keep working. Her employer made accommodations for her as best they could and allowed intermittent leave per FMLA requirements. But, in addition to the fact that she was unable to operate a vehicle (for obvious reasons), Natalie was regularly having seizures during her shifts and increasingly unable to work - due to both the seizures and the physical toll they were taking on her. Three years ago, Natalie applied for disability. She was denied. She appealed, tried again. Again, she was denied. In April 2021, her employer of 14 years officially terminated her employment. Without income, her mortgage had to go into forbearance while she continued to appeal for access to disability benefits. Bottom line: for five years, Natalie has been regularly having seizures that she cannot control, which make it impossible for her to work; she has been denied disability THREE times. A few weeks ago, Natalie was notified by mail that if her mortgage forbearance is not repaid by December 14, 2022, her home will be repossessed and auctioned. Ten thousand dollars. One month. To those still reading, thank you again for your interest. This is how you can help: I am asking you to think about whether you can contribute $200 to help Natalie. I know that is a big ask. If you can't do that, I'm asking you to help as much as you are able. And, if you can contribute more than $200, I'm asking you to do that. Finally, I am asking you to share this link with others who may also want to help her. We don't have much time to ensure that Natalie retains possession of her home. Even if we are successful, it doesn't end there. She is still working with her lawyers to plead her case for disability assistance. Without that security, it will still be a struggle to keep her paid up on her mortgage. But I believe we can figure that out. In the meantime, it would be a tragedy for her to finally be approved for disability benefits, only to have lost her home in the process of waiting. The social trust that our country is built on is failing my sister, in remarkable fashion. If you can, please help us to intercede that failure.

Nigeria has been hit by one of the worst flooding events in recent memory. Houses have been submerged, farmlands destroyed, roads are inaccessible, schools have been shut down, infrastructure destroyed, and people are losing their lives and means of livelihood daily. The poorest communities are the most hit by this disaster and are further impoverished. So far, according to This Day Newspaper, over 500 persons have died, 45,249 houses have been destroyed, and 70,566 hectares of farmlands have been damaged. The VOA also reports that 1.4 million people have been displaced in the worst flooding Nigeria has experienced in a decade. With these funds, the Nigerian Libertarian Project will: 1. Assist at least 2000 victims of the flood in 3 locations worst hit by the flood 2. Supply relief materials to at least 5 IDP camps across the locations worst hit by the flood 3. Support other organizations that are on the ground conducting relief efforts Some of the current needs include: mattresses and beddings, cooking stoves, drinking water (bottled and sachet), toiletries, baby products, medicines, etc We will be posting updates here as the funds are disbursed and utilized to provide relief for these communities

Since then, his recovery has, thank goodness, gone well, and we are keeping our fingers crossed it continues to do so. He is almost back to being the goofy 11-month-old pup I love so much. It seems as though, as far as we can figure out, he was bitten by a spider or ingested some other foreign substance that caused him to have a severe systemic reaction. This is hard for me to do, but I'm asking for help. The total vet bills and time lost from work to care for him 24-7 has been pretty devastating. I've never been a good, money-saving kinda guy, to my detriment. Always the cricket playing, and never the ant saving. Anything donated would be appreciated wholeheartedly and deeply. After retiring from the Army as a Sergeant Major, Mom and Dad moved to South Daytona where Dad had a second career in the Post Office. They bought their brand new home, inland, and laid down roots for the family. They've been living in their home for over 40 years. About a month ago, they went overseas to visit family. Ian wasn't even a storm yet. No doubt that Mom and Dad had the house company-ready and locked up like Ft. Knox when they left. While they were gone, Ian developed. And they got a text from their next door neighbor a week before they were coming home that the whole neighborhood flooded, including their home. No one had a key. No one could get in. By the time Mom and Dad landed, my older brother Rick had driven down to try and help. He couldn't get in. Once my parents left the airport, they wanted to see their home. I can't imagine what they felt when they opened the door and discovered the a/c had tripped out and the house had been sitting closed up with standing water. It was heartbreaking. Absolutely everything in the house was destroyed. All of their furniture, all of their kitchen appliances, their flooring, carpeting, cherished items they've had for over 50 years, destroyed by the two feet of standing water. Family photos - gone. Clothing, shoes, stereo, computer, tvs, just everything. Their vehicle which was useful to them with their current health reality, was totaled. Dad is a totally disabled Vietnam Veteran with a Purple Heart who needed the van to be able to get in and out of with independence. Mom is the survivor of open heart surgery and this was an easy vehicle for her to maneuver and drive, as well use for shopping, helping friends and/or travel needs. They were so proud of their minivan - gone. They're such proud people who don't want help from anyone. But they need help. FEMA gave them less than $5,000. They have to replace every appliance in the kitchen, the washer/dryer, flooring, wall repair, cabinetry, closets, bathroom tiling, vacuum, clothing, shoes, groceries, everything. What they have is what they traveled with two pieces of luggage each. It is my hope, prayer and wish that if anyone is able to help them, they will. No matter the amount, small or big. It will help. Please help. My Dad has lost his appetite from all the stress. My Mom is so overwhelmed by it all. Dad loves her so much and wants to fix this for her but he can't. Not alone. This is the first time in my life I've ever seen my Father, who has been the matriarch of the family, sound defeated. My family is doing what we can to help them, but this is more than any of us can handle. So, I am asking for the Village at large to come together and help them. A lot of people are worried, reaching out to ask questions etc. We really appreciate it. Knowing that so many people love and care about you means a lot. Right now she’s just trying to rest and get adjusted to life and being home, and she’s tired. We know that a lot of you have been worried, so she’s asked me to summarize everything that’s happened to share with our friends and family. Keep in mind that all of this has occurred over a 7 day span. It feels like it’s been forever and just a few seconds all at the same time. I’m also not exactly Ernest Hemmingway but I’m going to give it my best shot.. In life you will find no shortage of situations that will test you. Whether it be getting cut off in traffic, losing your job, a tough breakup, or a literal test in school. There are lots of situations we all inevitably have to go through at one point or another because... that’s just life. This is not one of those situations. In late October of this year Sarina started to experience what she thought were side effects from new medication. Headaches, mood changes, fatigue, etc. At the same time she was also suffering from a sinus infection. We never thought too much into it. After all, going to the doctor would have only resulted in being prescribed an antibiotic, some Tylenol and a pat on the ass wishing you the best luck. With 3 kids, work, & celebrating your 1 year wedding anniversary there’s much better ways to spend your time. On November 1st she started to have more severe headaches and confusion. We also noticed she was stumbling on her words and being really clumsy which is not typical for her at all. She decided to schedule an appointment with her doctor the next morning to discuss these side effects and see what she thought we should do. Her doctor told her to immediately go to the ER. After a few hours of testing we got the worst possible news. They found what appeared to be a brain tumor on her CAT scan. They sent in a Chaplin, recommended that we have our kids visit ASAP, and informed us that she would be transferred to a better-equipped hospital to handle something like this. I asked the doctor to level with me and she said that it does not look good. Because of the size and location they thought that emergency surgery was a strong possibility. This forced us into having some of the most difficult conversations we’ve ever had. What do we tell the kids? Funeral arrangements, final wishes, etc. Every conversation that a 29 year old shouldn’t never have to have. We spent about an hour with the kids before transferring to the new hospital. Holding back tears and holding them tight. Telling them mom is sick but will be better soon. Holding each other, more crying, numbness, disbelief. Once we got to the new hospital the process was pretty rapid. Test after test made it very clear that surgery was not optional. We were told that without removal, she would only have 6 months to live. The risks of surgery? Everything from death to loss of speech, motor function, comprehension, vision and memory. Despite all of the risks, surgery was scheduled for first thing Monday morning. My wife is the strongest human being that I’ve ever met. I don’t know anybody who could have handled this situation with such grace, poise and determination. She’s a fighter and was determined to do anything she had to do to survive. Not just for herself, but for the kids, for me, for our family. In fact, I don’t recall her ever being worried about herself. Just me, just our kids. Wondering if we would be okay if something happened to her. I never knew how strong she was until now. We spent the weekend visiting with our kids, family, friends and lots of amazing hospital staff. We played cards, we went shopping at the gift shop. We ate great food (thanks Brad), we drank coffee, we lived life as if there may not be a tomorrow. We took no moment for granted and we found comfort in the belief that this would not be our last opportunity to be together. *** TRIGGER WARNING: Graphic Descriptions Monday morning came and I held her hand tightly before they took her back for surgery. I went back to the waiting room and sat for the 4.5 hours it takes to perform a surgery like this. The entire time everything the surgeon told us was playing over and over in my head. I pictured what was happening to her, as it was actually happening. First, they shave a small section of hair and make a 6 inch incision into the scalp, peeling it back to reveal the skull. Then, using a surgical saw they cut a small section of skull and set it aside it giving easier access to the brain. They use navigation tools and precise instruments to locate and remove the tumor. Disconnecting all things vascular that connect the tumor to the healthy brain tissue and removing the cancerous tissue. All while keeping within the estimated margins to preserve all functions of the brain. One slip of the finger and she looses sight, take too much she looses speech, don’t take enough the cancer spreads and the tumor regrows more rapidly. Once the tumor is removed they send it out for full pathology to determine what type of cancer it is and the best methods of treatment. For now, they just put the skull back together using two titanium disks and a handful of surgical screws and then suture the scalp back together. *** After the surgery, I get pulled into a consultation room and find myself face to face with the person who just performed her brain surgery. He looks concerned and says the initial pathology shows that this is a very aggressive cancer and is very vascular. She lost a fair amount of blood, and he had to take out as much (of the tumor) as he possibly could. I was told that when she wakes up, she may not be herself. She may not remember me or be able to speak or read. She may be angry and not know who she is or where she’s at and to be prepared for anything. We talked about possible follow up treatments. The chemotherapy, radiation, physical and occupational therapy. The support groups. I didn’t care about any of that. I just cared that she was alive; even if there are complications, we still have her. She was still under heavy anesthesia when I saw her for the first time after her surgery in ICU. She was laying in a hospital bed being wheeled into the room with her eyes closed, blood all over her beautiful blonde hair and IVs, tubes, wires and monitors everywhere. She opened her eyes and looked at me blankly. I thought for a minute that she may have forgotten who I was until she slowly reached and held my hand. We didn’t say anything but by saying nothing we said everything. The doctors started to unhook her from some of the equipment and talk to her. They asked her who she was and she answered. They asked her the year, where she was and who is the president. She answered. I was so happy. Then they asked her how she was feeling... She paused and then sluggishly said “Well I just had brain surgery so obviously my head is **** killing me, but other than that I’m fine.” Yup that’s my wife. In that moment I knew that she was back and she would be back to herself in no time! The first night was hell. She was in so much pain and no pain reliever in the world was going to change that. It was hard but she got through it. The second day was much better. She was able to get up and walk to me, give me a hug and even sit down in a chair vs the hospital bed. They downgraded her from ICU back to a normal room and the next day the sent us home with a bunch of meds and follow up instructions. As grateful and happy as we are for a successful surgery we know there is still a long road ahead. We will find out Monday the full results of the pathology on the tumor and what the next steps are for recovery.

It is with a heavy and very sad heart that we announce the passing of our beautiful girl Maryah. Our sweet girl has suffered beyond what a human can go through on this earth. She has spent over a decade suffering from chronic illness and chronic pain; Doctors over the years guessing and nothing they tried worked. She has spent more days than we can even begin to count inside the hospital walls and confined to a hospital bed , fighting and never giving up. Marayah was finally given a diagnosis at age 25 of MNGIES Mitochondrial Neurogastrointestinal Encephalopathy Syndrome). This disease is incredibly rare, less than 70 reported cases in the world. It’s also eventually fatal by mid-30s as your body just begins to break itself down. Marayah finally made the move to New York to receive life-saving treatment and organ transplants. There were ongoing complications that occurred weekly and daily, as she still fought with every single ounce of her body. Her mother and father alternated flying up so she always had a loving hand by her side. Ultimately on November 8th, her body could no longer fight, and now it is time we say goodbye to our hero and lay her to rest. Maryah, will live in our souls and our hearts while remembering her fight on this earth. We hubmly ask for any donations you can give to assist her parents now with putting her body to rest, and she speads her angel wings and is pain free with Jesus. When her older brother, Manny our hero, died at age 30 in 2018, these are some of the words Maryah wrote. These words resinate deep in my bones as now we are applying this to her passing: In Maryah words: Two things are for sure in this life. (1) We don’t get to choose when we are born and (2) we don’t get to choose when we die. Now my world doesn’t seem to make any sense. It has started to turn in the other direction, knocking me off of my feet and sending my mind into a frenzy; then, all of a sudden, there’s nothing. I’m blinded by darkness, groping the air for some sense of footing and stability, but there’s just nothing.. Although, truthfully, me and God are a bit on tumultuous terms as of the present. But my brother, he never wavered. Not even for a moment did he question his relationship with God. He didn’t always have the answers for everything but when it came to his faith, there was nothing he was more sure of, nothing he was more reliant on, nothing he was more proud of. Many have said and will continue to say that Manny was truly a man of God. I don’t doubt them or the truth in that statement. However, I feel in my soul that the connection he had with God was much deeper than any of us could fathom. It’s true that the bible says that we will never understand all the ways of God and as I sit here in my unimaginable grief and pain, I know that that’s true but I think that Manny understood God more than anyone I have ever known and, I will dare to say, that I ever will know. It was otherworldly, almost angelic. So maybe the world is a bit darker now because we lost the brightest light my life will ever see. And I won’t be okay for a long long time, if ever. This wound is deep and the pain is beyond comparison. It hurts. It just hurts so much. So I’m sorry I don’t have some resolved conclusion to all of this. Some may expect some encouraging words of comfort or maybe you’re waiting for me to express my fight to be everything I can be and that I am going to live life to the full but.. I got nothing. Right now, I’m nothing for no one and just for now I’m okay with that. Thank you kindly, Megan Molyneux Manny and Hilda Hernandez
