Pues él quería hacer el deber de vender una mercancía y visitar algunos clientes, pero a la 1 pm, me sorprendió con una llamada en la que pude sentir su voz angustiada diciéndome que me preparara, pues iba llegando a casa a buscarme para salir de inmediato al hospital debido a que sentía un dolor intenso en el pecho. Esto me alarmó muchísimo porque él suele estar muy bien de salud. Gratamente, en el hospital "Seguro Social de San Cristobal, Edo. tachira" lo trataron de inmediato. Primeramente, realizándole un electrocardiograma. En ese momento, pensé que no era un malestar mayor. Me había quedado afuera y cuando entro al cubículo, el doctor me notifica que deben dejar internado a mi esposo porque acaba de sufrir un infarto importante (IAM - Infarto Agudo al Miocardio) y que necesita hacerse mucho estudios; por lo que debe quedarse hospitalizado, noticia que me dejó consternada porque no esperaba algo de esa magnitud, Lo primero que pensé fue que me encontraba sola en ese instante con él. ¿A quién iba a llamar? Me quedé bloqueada. Pasados cinco días de su ingreso al centro de salud, habiéndole realizado todos los exámenes y tratamientos pertinentes, se concluye que amerita de forma urgente UN CATETERISMO CON ANGIOPLASTIA Y STENT en la arteria coronaria; debido a que el infarto fue importante. José Gregorio siempre ha sido un hombre trabajador, independiente, responsable con suscompromisos económicos en cuanto a sus gastos familiares, de salud y en general. Cabe destacar que fue precisamente trabajando cuando sufrió dicho infarto, así que debido a esto mismo es que ahora nos vemos en la necesidad de recurrir a ustedes. solicitando ayuda por medio de esta plataforma, ya que él obviamente no se encuentra en condiciones óptimas para trabajar y generar ingresos para costear dicho procedimiento médico, que por cierto en nuestro país sólo es realizado en clínicas privadas. ¿Cuál es el costo de este tratamiento? El cateterismo tiene un costo de 1200$. La angioplastia más implante de un stent cuesta 4000$. Si requiere otro stent, son 1000$ adicional (por stent). Gastos medicos, estudios, medicina y otros posterior de control medico 1000$ Total a recaudar 7200$ ¿Quién es José Gregorio? El siempre ha sido una persona que desde muy joven se ha trazado metas para evolucionar en la vida y ser independiente. Técnico superior universitario, proveniente de una familia con valores muy sólidos de todo tipo. Esposo, hijo y padre abnegado, amoroso y responsable. Un hombre que da todo de sí para el bienestar de su familia, amigos y a quien pueda brindar ayuda; pero que en este momento es él quien la necesita. Por lo que con antelación, les expresamos nuestra gratitud y bendiciones. Agradecemos todo su apoyo en este duro momento de nuestras vidas. The main goal of this fundraiser is to help five year old Mason and his family manage ongoing healthcare for his rare, severe life-threatening infection of the head and brain. Two weeks ago Mason battled with ongoing high fevers, which would temporarily subside, but persisted for several days. He had bad headaches and no appetite. One morning he woke up with his left eye completely swollen shut and that is when his mom Teresa and her family decided to take him to Nationwide Childrens Hospital in Columbus Ohio to figure out what was going on. After an immediate CT scan of his head the doctors found a large abcess, indicative of ongoing infection, behind his left eye, which quickly spread to his right eye. To make matters worse, they also found an epidural abcess on his brain nearby. An emergency surgery took place to drain the infection behind his eyes to prevent extensive eye damage from ocurring. He made it out of surgery OK, but to make matters worse they then had to go back into another surgery next day to pull several teeth which were indicated as a possible contributor to his condition. Unfortunately, after his surgery they also found a small blood clot in his brain due to the infection. Because of this he will now have to be on blood thinners to dissolve the clot. To further treat the brain abcess and blood clot, a central IV line had to be placed near his heart to facilitate ongoing high-dose antibiotic treatments and blood thinners which he will be on for several months. As you can imagine, Mason has had a very tough time coping with all of this but is doing his best to have good spirits. Having constant teams of doctors and nurses in and out of his room, multiple surgeries, and many IVs attached to him is no situation any five year old should have to endure. To make the situation more difficult and stressful, Mason does not have health insurance. His mom and dad are very hard workers but struggle to make ends meet. Including Mason, they have three small boys five years old and younger. His healthcare over the next several months will likely require extensive attention and many trips to the hospital to monitor the brain abcess which requires one or both of his parents to take off time from work. The hospital is working with their family to get Mason on insurance, which certainly helps, but is no guarantee to cover the extensive costs of surgeries, treatments, transportation, and living expenses that will be incurred because of this condition. Mason’s parents are extremely grateful for the outreach they have already received and appreciate all the well-wishes and prayers. They are hard-workers and are very loving to their children, friends, and community. Recently, Teresa and her husband Clay both received awards from their community for their hospitality to high-school students during a school shooting. Students sought shelter at a nearby Waffle-house, where Teresa and Clay both work, and they ensured the safety and well-being of the students during this traumatic experience. This is just a small testament to the character that both Teresa and Clay exhibit throughout their lives. This fundraiser is to help alleviate some of the burden from their family as they struggle with what the next several months will bring, especially during the christmas season. Any donation at all is greatly appreciated and will be used to ensure the health and well-being of Mason. Words of encouragement and support are also welcomed and appreciated.

I went to try to and take her pulse oxygen level and touched her back and she was burning up, yet her lips were shivering and she was covered with a blanket. She is immediately admitted into the Critical Care Unit and start antibiotic treatment. Doctors assure us that she will start to turn around once she has 24 hours of antibiotics. Nurses and doctors have said that Jayda’s husband Cameron must remain at the hospital with her because he’s the only person who can keep her calm although she doesn’t recognize him. He is and will remain to be her primary care giver. Lab test are in and the good news that Jayda doesn’t have Covid-19, flu, pneumonia, RSV, or a UTI. So no answers but doctors start to think the infection is bacterial meningitis. Spinal Tab is taken for bacterial meningitis. On Wednesday, October 26, 2022 after antibiotic and antiviral treatment Jayda finally was able able to state her name and birthdate. Doctors suspect bacterial meningitis, but official diagnosis still unknown. As of today, Saturday, October 29, 2022 Jayda is still in CCU. After multiple MRI’s and a spinal tap doctors have determined that she does not have bacterial meningitis and so her diagnosis is unknown. Jayda has met with the infectious disease doctor twice. Now that meningitis has officially been ruled out she has not met the infectious disease doctor because she is out of the out office. Prior to her illness Jayda had 31 hours of time off, she has used those days and will not be paid for any more days. She does not have any supplemental insurance such as short term disability so she is not being paid. She was able to have her FLMA paperwork completed to keep her from being fired from her job. We all know that their is no money tied to FLMA. The hospital has required that Jayda’s husband stay at the hospital with her. Additionally they both have car notes and insurance to pay as well as utilities

So this is Mishu’s story: My partner and I began feeding the strays from our block, but were feral and would not allow us to pet them. One day, “new cat” (aka Mishu), appeared. She wasn’t like the other cats though. We noticed that she was living in the bush outside an abandoned house next to mine and she didn’t interact much with the other cats. She was very human friendly though, and would come up to us each time she saw us and would rub herself on our legs, and at times, would even try to follow us back inside to my house. Unfortunately, I was unable to bring her in due to my grandmother’s allergy to cats. Coincidentally, the upstairs apartment became vacant and the first thing I thought was, “its October. The cold is on its way and she needs a home”. So what did we do? We decided to give her a home! Everything was great for the first year. We had family cuddles every night, she loved her new indoor bush, made buiscuits on every soft surface she found in the house, had no concept of personal space, and made an appearance during every zoom meeting mommy had while at work. Everyone who came into contact with Mishu immediately fell in love with her. Unfortunately, on 10/27/2022 we noticed that her right eye was red. At first we thought it was just pink eye, and decided to wait to take her to the vet. But the next day, her eye became a bit worse and would either stay dilated or not dilate at all. We took her to the Vet and they decided to run blood work . They sent us home with eyedrops (Prednisolone Acetate) to put in her eye two times a day. On 11/2/2022, we received a call from the Vet who informed us that her blood work showed that she tested positive for antibodies for toxoplasmia, and stated that this may be the underlying cause and prescribed antibiotics for her (Clindamycin). We gave them to her for 5 days, but her condition only became worse; her eye had turned completely black. On 11/7/2022, she had a follow up appointment and were told that she had Anterior Lense Luxation, and it needed to be treated immediately by an eye specialist due to its emergency to try to prevent glaucoma and her loss of vision in that eye. We called all the local vets and were constantly told there are no eye specialists in Brooklyn, so we had to take her to Shwarman Animal Medical Center’s emergency room in the Upper East Side. We were told that Mishu already has Glaucoma and that loss of vision in that eye was inevitable. The doctor informed us that there were three routes we could go down. The first option would be to treat the symptoms from the Anterior Lense Luxation and glaucoma. This required giving her eye massages, giving her eye drops multiple times a day, and constantly giving her medication for the pain. Her loss of vision would be slow and painful. The second option was for her to undergo a surgery in which her lense would be removed to relieve the pressure, and later treat her glaucoma which would result in her retaining some of her vision. This surgery though, did not ensure that she would not lose her vision in her right eye in the future, and the possibility of pain lingering in her eye was very real. The third option was for her to undergo an enucleation surgery and have her eye removed. It would completely relieve her of all symptoms, and we were told she would be back to normal in about ten days post surgery. This was not an easy choice to make, but we decided that we want to relieve her from present and future pain with option #3 and will show her the world through her one good eye. With all the doctor visits, exams, medications, and now surgery, we have found ourselves in a tight situation. To make matters worse, they don’t know the underlying cause yet, which means there will most likely be more exams to come to rule out cancer or other severe diseases. Although it’s not an ideal situation, I find myself grateful that we decided to take her in, and that she has people who care for her. My heart breaks just thinking of all the cats who are out there suffering by themselves, especially in the cold. If you made it this far, thank you from the bottom of our heart. Thank you for taking the time to read her story and learning about her situation. If there’s any way that you can help, we would be eternally grateful. Whether it’s $1, a share, or recommendations, it is all very much appreciated. We are also asking for something much greater than helping Mishu. We’re asking for you to be kind to those cats that you see wandering around the streets. They are simply trying to survive in this world, which we as humans, struggle so much to do sometimes. We have posted her medical records and pictures of our soon to be pirate. We will continue to post pictures and update you on her surgery and recovery. Thank you!

Our friend Tai needs our help. Let me start by saying that Tai is infinitely generous and caring, someone who has gone through incredible difficulties her whole life and yet still shows up so fully for her friends. I met Tai through the Portland writing community in 2020. Since then, she has checked in on me, commiserated with me (dark humor is a specialty of hers), and cared for me. Tai also has been struggling with chronic disability for many years of her life. Tai has Myalgic Encephalitis (ME), known as Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (CFS). CFS is a much-stigmatized illness with very little acknowledgment from doctors. It is often seen as one of the new forms of hysteria (along with Lyme, POTS, and Post Viral Syndrome), IE, another way for the system to deny largely marginalized populations the care they need. In reality, CFS is incredibly debilitating, and Tai's case is severe. Tai is no longer able to work. She must sleep many hours of the day, cannot leave the house often, look at a screen for very long, and often needs aids to walk. As with most chronic illnesses, so much of this struggle remains invisible to doctors and insurance agents. However, Tai is a champion for advocacy for herself and others and has been very upfront about her experiences so that others may not have to go through what she has. She has been navigating a broken system for a very long time now. Tai hasn't had any income since February of 2021, when her disability insurance denied her. She has used up all of her savings and credit to stay afloat. Tai has been jumping through all of the hoops to reinstate disability but is now waiting on a judge to rule, and unfortunately, judges aren’t held to timelines, which means Tai no longer has the money to pay her rent. Tai is currently waiting on her SSDI hearing, which she started applying for in 2019. The hearing should take place in the next 4 months. Tai's doctors are on her side and agree that she needs to be on disability, but again, it is entirely possible she could be denied again, and in the meantime, she cannot afford her basic needs. If Tai could work and be independent in this way, she would. Tai has had to make her way for a long time, building her community, family, and finances with very little support. She has advanced degrees to her name, and she has worked at Google. That I even have to highlight her accomplishments demonstrates that we live in a terrifying capitalist hellscape requiring proof of disability and, thereby, worth to get basic needs met. The money donated will cover Tai’s basic needs until she hears back from the judge about her SSDI—her rent, utilities, food, and insurance so she won’t be out on the streets, go hungry or lose access to crucial medical care. Her rent is $1500, and her expenses are $450 (insurance, utilities, and prescription cat food). We are asking for 10,000, but this is not a finite amount and depends on Tai’s case results. Tai has no family support. Many of us who know Tai understand that she is a survivor of abuse, severe and pervasive trauma, a broken healthcare system--a broken everything. Honestly, Tai is one of my heroes. Also, she’s a damn good writer. I’ve been telling her if I had disposable income, I would pay her to write her book, no matter how long it takes. Tai deserves shelter, rest, medical care, and community support, as we all do. But Tai has had to fight for so long to get her basic needs met, and I would like her wonderful community to show her, in whatever way we can, that we have her back.

From John's sister Michelle: On the evening of October 28, 2022, Diane Elaine (Schwartz) Evans was received at last into the arms of Jesus. Her 75 years on this Earth were gift to all who were privileged to know her. While she battled Alzheimer's bravely for the last 14 years, that will not be her legacy. Her legacy is love. As her children our greatest gift is the love story she shares with her husband David, her beloved for 53 years. They met in 1968 when they were both young, and working at the convalescent hospital in Lodi California. They married June 22nd 1969 with little money and no prospects but they had each other and that was all they needed. Theirs is a love story for the ages. Despite the struggles and challenges that 53 years and 3 children can bring, they always remained devoted to each other, supporting one another through better and worse. Many remark on the incredible devotion that our father, Dave had for Diane as Alzheimer's slowly took her, but he would tell us that Mom gave him all her best years, how could he do any less for her now when she needed him most? Their love for each other is a beacon of hope for all who witnessed it. As their children, we hope to be so blessed as to have even a glimpse of that kind of love. Our Mother, Diane, was without a doubt our hero, best friend, and greatest cheerleader. She was devoted to us while still being her own person and taught us that you can do everything you dream. She sewed our clothes, canned every food imaginable, she was an awesome cook, PTA president, room mom, and homework checker. She read us books, played games, and the memories of our family vacations keep us laughing until our sides ache. She went back to school to become a nurse while we were young and her example of sacrifice and dedication inspire us still. She was healer both at home and to all she came in contact with. When we each married she loved our spouses in equal measure. Always supportive and always wanting our happiness. But we believe the job she loved best of all was being a Nana. Known to her 4 beautiful grandchildren as "Nana Tickle", she was larger than life and always ready with love and hugs. She made songs for her grand babies, crocheted blankets, and would do anything for them. They were her brightest jewels in a very crowded crown. The love she had for her family seemed without bounds. It began of course at first with her parents Jeanette Emhoff and John Henry Schwartz. She loved her parents with all her heart and we know that they ushered her into the gates of heaven. Her beloved brothers and their families meant the world to her and even in her last days their names brought a smile to her lips. She loved her inlaws just as much and the Evans family felt as close as if she had been with them her whole life. She was always the life of the family gatherings with her silliness, fun, and laughter. As her children we also know that our mother's greatest legacy of love lies with her Lord and Savior Jesus. Our mother loved the Lord with all her heart, with all her mind, and with all her strength. It is this love that gave her the courage to fight as long as she did. We take some comfort in the knowledge that she is now singing the Hallelujah chorus with the angels and helping to prepare our homes. For now we grieve with weight of a great love lost. Funeral services for Diane will be held Friday, November 4, 2022 at 1pm, graveside at Sunland Cemetery in Sun City, Arizona. A link to her obituary and memorial page will be available online shortly and we will update Facebook.

In 1980, Dennis and Mary Ann Roberts welcomed the birth of the first of their two sons, Shawn Roberts. The new parents were naturally thrilled and overjoyed; but unfortunately, their initial excitement was suddenly replaced with feelings of uncertainty, worry, and anxiety. The doctors had informed Dennis and Mary Ann that their first child, Shawn, had been born with congenital kidney disease. The prognosis was devastating. Shawn was given 3-6 months to live! But somehow, miraculously, Shawn survived. At three years old, Shawn was able to undergo the first of three transplant surgeries he would have. Shawn's Dad, Dennis, donated the first kidney. Surgery was successful and life at the Roberts' house was pretty much as normal as things could be. In 1999, however, Shawn needed another transplant. This time, Shawn received one of his Mom's kidneys. Again, surgery was successful. Up to this point in his life, Shawn lived pretty much as anyone his age and the Roberts family continued to be as robust as always. Although their lives included a constant stream of doctors' visits, hospital stays, various treatments, and many trips to the emergency room, that was their "normal" and they never brought this anywhere other than their home. As close friends of Dennis, we would ask him, now and then, how Shawn was doing, or how things ni general were going, and Dennis would only say that they were managing, one day at a time. Sometimes, Dennis would politely add that we all have problems to deal with and that he didn't see any sense in depressing anyone else with his. In 2010, Shawn needed, yet, another transplant. This was to be Shawn's final transplant; his Aunt Cheryl, was the donor. But, tragically, the surgery was fraught with complications from the start, and Shawn eventually lost the kidney. Life as Shawn knew it, drastically changed. Shawn's survival was now dependent on ful time dialysis. Soon thereafter, Shawn was dealt another setback when he developed Reactive Arthritis. Now, in addition to all that he had been through, Shawn had to endure crippling pain, swollen joints, and frequent high fevers. Despite al of the setbacks they had experienced, Shawn and his family continued to live life as best they could. Holidays were celebrated, frequent gatherings were held, and the Roberts family continued to be at the center of good humor and spirit. Dennis' pregame Thanksgiving breakfasts with "the boys" continued, as did card games, Friday "Knights", making fresh tomato sauce, quick excursions to the Cape, .life went on. However, in June of this year, tragedy struck once again. An abscess had developed on Shawn's colon and subsequent surgeries required a colostomy. Further complications evolved from the surgeries. One was sepsis, which nearly took Shawn's life, twice, during his 43 days in the hospital. As a result of his hospitalization, Shawn is totally immobile. His muscles have completely atrophied and he is extremely weak and fragile. Shawn is in need of 24 hour care. Kelly, Shawn's girlfriend of nearly ten years, has been there to take care of him. Somehow, she has managed to balance work and taking care of Shawn. But now, given Shawn's additional limitations, Kely has had to quit work ni order to take ful time care Shawn's Story of him. This includes tending to his wounds, providing ostomy care and dialysis, among a myriad of other responsibilities. Sure, Shawn gets PT, OT, and a visiting nurse, but all of this pales ni comparison to his needs. More and more bills are going unpaid, and Kelly's car is about to be repossessed. Shawn's insurance only provides for home health aide two hours a week. Clearly, they need help. Even as life long friends of Dennis and Mary Ann, wereally only knew little of Shawn's daily battle to live. We suspected things were bad, but we were not prepared for what we eventually learned. This past weekend, we firmly pressed Dennis to share as much as he felt comfortable with telling us. Finally, we heard Shawn's story. As friends, we were devastated by the harsh realities of the news. It was at that point, we said to Dennis that enough is enough and that there had to be a way to help. Simply put, they cannot exist like this any longer. So, here we are, setting up a GoFundMe for Shawn and his family. Shawn is at another critical juncture in his life, but this time we are here to try to make a difference. With fingers crossed and hopes abound, we are asking all of you for your prayers and support. We ask that you share our GoFundMe campaign on your social media. As we approach the holiday season and reflect upon our own lives and those of our family and loved ones, perhaps in the spirit of the season you can find ti in your heart to make a monetary donation to Shawn and his family. We are well aware that these are challenging times for almost everyone. fI you are not financially able to contribute monetarily, we fully understand, and hope that you wil offer your prayers. No matter what happens, we thank you from the bottom of our hearts for allowing us to share Shawn's story. "When we give cheerfully and accept gratefully, everyone is blessed." Maya Angelou

This will be hard to read. Skip to the last paragraph to skip the exposition. There once existed a young man. A tortured young man, both literally and figuratively. He grew up being taught that he was barely worth the meat on his bones, much less worth anything as a person. Merely a legal obligation and a burden to those at school and at home. As you might guess, this takes a toll on a person. He tried to kill himself for the first time at 8 years old and it wouldn't be the last. Life seemed like a series of loss and pain. But he survived. He persisted. He persevered, often against his own volition, feeling broken and unlovable. During all of this, he still tried his best to spread love and kindness to everybody he could. He decided since he couldn't justify living for himself, why not live for other people? So he did. This lack of self care of course takes a toll. His physical and mental health continued to decline as time went on, becoming more and more isolated and unable to connect with people. Then that fateful day occurred. That wonderful... crazy... magical day... The day that young man felt real love for the first time in his life. Of course, it was love at first sight. One look into those beautiful brown eyes, and he felt something he'd never seen before. Hope. Light. Love. Warmth. Things he believed were nothing more than abstract biochemical processes. You see, this young man often allowed old friends, new friends, and strangers the space and support to share his home with him while they became independent. A kindness he had experienced many times during his teenage homelessness. One of these houseguests wanted a dog from a shelter in Oklahoma. So they went to Oklahoma to a shelter to pick up a dog they only saw pictures of. When he met the dog, he couldn't help but feel that even though the dog seemed friendly and loving there was a coldness behind their eyes. Sure enough, this dog would end up attacking the young man as he defended two innocent strangers from being attacked. This is not a story about that dog. This is the story about a beautiful and loving black lab/German Shephard mix that the young man met at that shelter after feeling relatively concerned about the first dog. That's when we... I mean he locked eyes with that beautiful baby boy we now know and love as the eponymous Rocko Bissinger. There was a connection. A spark that immediately ignited something new inside this young man. That dog showed that young man that he could be loved. He could make mistakes and still be loved. He could lose his temper and still be loved. He could feel his feelings, and still be loved. That dog allowed that young man to grow and flourish to start his own company, take over as the organizer for a support group for autism, build healthy loving relationships, and become a complete person. That young man was me. I will do anything and everything I can to try to pay back what this dog has done for me, what this dog has helped me do for my community, what this dog has helped me do for the world. I know that's impossible, but my baby boy is very sick. The bloodwork is bad, it's possible he'll need his spleen removed, he might have stomach cancer, and a few other potential issues and they need to do an exploratory surgery just to find out if it's something more serious or if it's something treatable. I am not the kind of person who wants to keep the dog alive for my own selfish reasons, I want him to live a happy and healthy life. Right now that is still an option, I don't know how much longer we have but I won't be able to live with myself if I feel like I didn't try everything I can. I am begging you from the bottom of my heart to please help me afford the surgery he needs on Tuesday the 25th of October. Anything you can do to help is wonderful. If you can't or won't donate, even just sharing this to somebody who might would mean EVERYTHING to me. They say the deposit alone is going to be $5,700 (gofundme takes a portion, that's why the goal is higher.) and that it will likely end up being much more, probably over 10,000 once everything is said and done. If you've ever been lucky enough to meet Rocko, you understand why this is worth doing. Please help and save Rocko, the goodest of boys. You may be saving more than you realize.

I never thought I'd be here writing this, but I suppose everyone who makes a GoFundMe of this nature feels the same way, to an extent. My parents- Francine and Patrick- are on the brink of financial poverty due to the irresponsible actions of the United States Army. In December, they will be forced to sell their home of 12 years and move. My sisters and I are starting this page to help raise funds for them and hopefully improve their transition. Now for the extended version of the story: My dad, Patrick, was a decorated ENT surgeon and served on active Army duty for 13 years. He left the Army in 2006 as a Lieutenant Colonel and started his private practice career, in which he was very successful, as he was incredible at his job. In addition to being a certified Otolaryngologist, Patrick is also an entrepreneur and has been creating his startups ever since I can remember. Dad's first attempt to use a digital camera with an endoscope attachment. Dad reaching for his "Go Bag" the day after 9/11/2001 My dad's current business, ChitoRhino (or most recently CleanWash), focused on nasal saline rinses for the sinuses to initially be used in post-surgical healing. Eventually, the company found its legs and received numerous grants to expand and potential partnership opportunities, such as the Burt's Bees Natural Launchpad Grant in 2017. You may have even seen CleanWash products stocked on the shelves of certain Walmarts, CVS Pharmacies, and wellness stores in the south. (homemade ads my dad made to promote his nasal rinse product) Cute vid my dad made demonstrating how to use the product: CLICK HERE Things were going well until the COVID-19 pandemic hit the United States in 2020. My mom, Francine, is immunocompromised and has struggled with respiratory infections for the last several years. As an MD, my dad knew that if he continued to work in the medical field during this time, it would mean putting my mom's health at risk because he would be sure to catch COVID and bring it home to the family. He took a leave of absence and has since been unable to return to medicine. While my parents were figuring out their next steps financially, an incredible opportunity fell into their lap: The United States Army took notice of my dad (a veteran) and his company. They contacted him and wanted to enter into a contract to supply this nasal wash, which would become a life-changing event. To get this done, the Army requested that dad's business be put on hold so they could investigate his company, suppliers, etc. Because they were dealing with a branch of the US Government, things were slow-moving (which was to be expected). The Army needed to be thorough in its investigations to ensure everything would go smoothly when they placed the order, specific required licenses needed to be obtained, etc. Still, the contract looked promising, and the Army appeared enthusiastic about contracting with CleanWash. My dad would be living the American dream!! What a blessing this would have been for our family, and he would no longer have to worry about what to do about the family's finances before he could retire peacefully. My parents have worked hard their entire lives. They both grew up in impoverished homes before going to college and meeting each other. My dad went to medical school to become a doctor and joined the Army because, at the time, they would pay his medical debt if he would repay them with service. This deal with the US Army was going to be their way out. This process got dragged out for two excruciatingly long years. My parents' finances dwindled year by year until about six months ago when the Army suddenly decided that it wouldn't be placing the order after all. All those years of business were lost for NOTHING. My parents' savings have been completely drained, and while my mom and dad seek employment, they cannot recover enough funds to keep their house. Their debt is insurmountable, and my mom revealed to me recently that they have been living off of four credit cards for the past three or so months. The mortgage, medical bills, and general loans have caught up to them, and they need a lot of help. I don't need to tell you how infuriating it is to watch my parents go through this because of something that was supposed to be monumentally life-changing in a positive way. To watch the way the United States Army wronged one of their own veterans of 13 years. We're proud as hell of my dad and the work he's put in to make the world a better place, but right now, my parents need as much help as they can get. ALL funds raised will go towards my mom and dad so they can hopefully get some relief from this nightmare. I know this goal amount pales in comparison to their debt, but my sisters and I are not in positions where we can significantly help our parents. Thank you for reading.

He was the only man in history to win (6) NCAA College Titles in Wrestling, despite his high school not even having a wrestling team... Carlton Haselrig was a man of incredible athletic ability and a drive to excel in everything he did. Still, even with great heart & spirit to accomplish these feats, he could not beat the monster that is Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy or CTE. Unable to work and bedridden, Carlton filed a claim in 2017 for the NFL Concussion Settlement, which was later denied due to the adjusted 'race norming ' on the cognitive scoring, despite having all the symptoms and testing to affirm a CTE prognosis. While Carlton had earned a pension from the NFL from playing in the league, his benefits were stopped the day he passed. In the documentary released on 11/16/2022, his battle with CTE in his final years is heart-wrenchingly shared in, Bloodsport How the NFL failed its black players In June of 2021, the #NFL agreed to stop race-based testing, which allowed Carlton's widow, Michelle, to refile his claim. During the arduous process, the loss of the pension and denial of the first claim devasted Michelle financially. She had $5 in her account at the time of the documentary production and was being forced to possibly sell Carlton's medals and keepsakes to make ends meet. She desperately needs your help now. Through this GOFundME, the goal would be to provide Michelle and her family with a means to cover basic necessities and catch up on her house payment until she can find gainful employment or the second settlement can be processed & hopefully awarded. Without this fund or your caring support, Michelle will likely lose the family home and be unable to sustain herself long enough for a potential award to be made. I met Michelle after seeing her brave story in the Bloodsport documentary and felt compelled to act. I was connected via a mutual friend as part of my non-profit, 4CTE by CTE, which assists in locating resources & support for caregivers and warriors with suspected CTE. This fund is made with her approval and blessing, with 100% of all proceeds going directly to her for immediate emergency use. She has also graciously provided personal pictures used to share her family story. The Steelers Fans are some of the greatest and most loyal people in the world of sports and undoubtedly will rise up to help one of their own. For the NFL enthusiast and humanity at large, this social injustice of profits over athletes should be our concern too. Please consider providing what you can and share this campaign to help the widow of a great man who left everything on the field, including, sadly, his life. Thank you and God Bless. Hi, my name is Maureen, or Mo to many. I am fundraising for my partner Craig's medical expenses and our living expenses while we cannot work for an undetermined amount of time. In January 2022, Craig went to the ER after injuring his neck. The doctors cleared him of serious injury but found an abnormal growth on his thyroid. After a referral to a local ENT (Ear, Neck, Throat doctor), lots of biopsies, and CT Scans, they decided he needed a partial, if not complete, thyroidectomy. On November 2, Craig went to the ER with pain in his neck and shoulder area. The doctor prescribed Craig muscle relaxers, said he probably slept wrong, and sent him on his way. On November 7, Craig went in for his partial thyroidectomy. Before his procedure, Craig informed his surgeon that he was having level 8 pain in his neck and shoulder, and if he lifted his head past a certain point, it quickly rose to level 10. His surgeon decided to continue with the planned surgery. For the thyroid removal, the surgery team needed to place Craig's head as far back as possible to access his throat, a position he would not have been able to do had he not been under anesthesia. Once Craig came out of anesthesia, he could not feel his hands or legs from the knees down. His ENT doctor initially dismissed this as a side effect of his diabetes. When he could not grab a cup to drink, the nurse rushed to get his doctor. Craig had an emergency MRI. The XRAY from January 2022 and MRI results from November 7th both showed a bulging disc in Craig's neck between the C4 and C5 vertebrae. The bulging disc from the January 2022 XRAY was never once addressed or relayed to Craig during his many doctor visits, specialist visits or CT Scans. Instead, it was dismissed as "sleeping wrong" on multiple occasions, even the day of surgery. The surgery exacerbated an underlying issue, turning it into an emergent issue. Craig was temporarily paralyzed from Monday evening until Tuesday when he finally took a few steps with a walker. His ENT came into the room, apologized and said she thought he was talking about his lower back when he described his pain. After a meeting with a neurosurgeon, Craig was informed he needed immediate surgery on his C4 and C5 vertebrae for a fusion process. He said it was dire and needed to be addressed ASAP to avoid permanent damage. Insurance did not approve the surgery because he was admitted for an unrelated surgery (the thyroidectomy). The neurosurgeon has submitted another insurance claim and is awaiting the results. Initially, the vertebrae fusion surgery was to be performed November 8th. Then a tentative date of Monday November 14th. November 10th, the neurosurgeon called and gave a date of December 9th, pending insurance approval. If approved sooner, the surgery date will be expedited. Until the surgery is completed, Craig is incapacitated. Craig has since been released from the ICU, due to insurance not covering anymore time in the hospital. He has limited mobility and is unable to lift anything over 5lbs. He cannot go up the stairs and has been set up in the basement/guest area of our home. I cannot go to work, as I need to care for Craig and our 3 children, ages 3,5 and 9. Normally, Craig works from home and can take care of the kids as I go to work in the evenings. Craig is unable to sit at his desk, work on his computer or care for the children. I am unsure how long we will both be out of work, and this is a pretty scary time for our family Thank you for getting this far and for taking the time to read this! We are rather embarrassed that this is a route we have to take, but with no money coming in and bills still coming, we have done this as a last resort. Anything is greatly appreciated, especially warmth from those of you we love. Also, if anyone has a recommendation for possible legal rights Craig may be entitled to, that would be so helpful. Thank you all, Craig, Mo, Kai, Layla and Liam

Hi, my name is Jason. My Family and I recently had a house fire on 10/11/2022 around 12:30 a.m. We are currently in a hotel, but everyone is safe and not harmed. Late at night on Monday, October 10th, I was streaming some on twitch. The rest of my family was asleep. I started to smell something burning and thought it was cold outside, so it’s typical to smell things like this in my neighborhood as the neighbors use a fireplace. Still, I said to the twitch chat I smelled something burning, and even though I think it’s the neighbor's fireplace, it’s always better to be safe than sorry, so I’ll brb going to check around the house. I walked around the house for about 30 seconds investigating and thought I better wake up my family members so they could check around since it did seem like the smell was coming from inside the house. Upon us walking into our living room, I flicked on the light, and we saw the room had a fair bit of smoke filling it up, but we couldn’t tell from where. The smell was getting stronger by this time too. I proceeded to check more of the house. As I turned on the kitchen light, I noticed the smoke was really thick in the kitchen, and I instantly started to look over towards the stove, oven, coffee pot etc., just assuming that would be a likely place to have smoke emitting, As I got closer to those appliances, I was not seeing anything, but then I looked to the left at the basement door, and it looked like a full-blown factory smoke stack with a thick dark rolling cloud of smoke just blasting out from it. This all was happening within seconds, and I instantly spoke out loud OH GOD, THE HOUSE IS ON FIRE HELP US as I turned around going to my room, yelling down the hallway the house is on fire call 911, we gotta get out, As all of this was happening, I had already been having problems breathing coming from the kitchen with all of that smoke. As I went down my hallway to open the door to my room which was closed, I was surprised and frightened to see my room filling with a crazy amount of thick dark smoke. My tv was flickering, and the ceiling was black. Small little holes in my walls from nails, thumb tacks etc., had smoke just spewing out, sort of like a tea kettle that is boiling. My room looked like it was being cooked and about to burst into flames at any moment. A thought crossed my head for seconds. “What do I do? What do I grab? I’m about to lose everything I own” panicking and being overwhelmed, unable to breathe. I quickly decided none of this stuff matters. Everyone needs to get out now. This is life and death. I quickly grabbed my phone, two shirts and a pair of shorts that was sitting on my bed, sticking them over my face hoping to breathe better as I gasped for breath stumbling around in shock, saying out loud again, “Oh God, Please help us” I stumbled out of my room and yelled down the hallway again GET OUT NOW THE HOUSE IS LOST. By this time, I was so disoriented and oxygen-deprived that I fell over as I left my room, trying to escape the house. I felt so lightheaded that I was close to passing out, needing to get fresh air. I dropped my phone and tripped over a box, and fell about three times trying to get up and crawl to the front door just 15 feet away. I managed to get up, leaving my phone in the middle of the floor. I was finally out of the house and able to breathe. One of my family members started calling 911. As I came down the steps of my porch and tried to collect myself and my breath, I heard my other family member calling from the living room, so I quickly marched right back into the house, which was completely pitch black and filled with smoke at this point, you couldn’t see anything. It was absolutely terrifying. We were both falling down low, and I felt their arm which I grabbed probably way too hard. I had them, they were okay, but we needed to get out. I still couldn’t fully breathe. I quickly walked out and yelled to the rest of my family for help. So they put the phone down and ran into the house. I heard the 911 operator on the phone, so I grabbed it and started to speak with them, giving the home address, telling them I could see my remaining family members coming out of the house etc. Seeing everyone out of the house and safe was such a relief. Even though my house was on fire and we were about to lose everything we owned, I didn’t care. All that mattered was seeing everyone outside safe, walking around, and no one was harmed or burned etc. everyone seemed to be breathing okay, and the fire department was on the way. I stood there thanking god for helping us all escape unharmed. My family means everything to me, and losing one of them would have never left me the same. We stood around collecting ourselves, and the firefighters arrived within about 10 minutes. If I had to guess, I’m really not sure how long it was, but they got there pretty quickly. They dispatched three trucks full of firefighters from three different stations, and there were probably about 25 to 30 firefighters. They quickly got dressed in their suits, got their hoses, and started to work on putting out the fire which was blazing in the basement. While they were fighting it, there was a person speaking with us about things we needed to do, asking questions about the home, insurance, hotel, food etc. the firefighters had to bust out all of our basement windows and remove the security bars from them as well they busted out a window upstairs and had large fans positioned around pulling out smoke. They cut the power to the house, as well the water too. I think it took them about 30 minutes to put the fire out fully, spraying water around in the basement. After about 2 hours, they told us the house could not be lived in any longer. It was not safe. They said they think the fire started around the washer and dryer 220-watt electrical outlet, which is directly under my room. My room has a few holes burned through the floor that is large, you can look up and see my bed through them, my tv stand fell in a hole and was turned over, and another large hole had a bunch of various cables for my pc, xbox etc. hanging through it. They let us go into the house to get some personal belongings out and things that thieves might target etc., but they told us not to enter my room as the floor can’t be trusted. The house has extensive fire damage in the basement. A lot of the flooring will need to be replaced, the electrical and plumbing will all need to be replaced, and there is major smoke damage throughout the entire house. They informed us all our food would need to be thrown away, medicine, canned goods, etc., anything plastic. It’s wild. They even said sealed canned goods and 2 liters of soda, medicine containers and whatnot. All of that stuff gets penetrated by the smoke and is unsafe. We had so much food that was being tossed, and it was a shame. The inspector looked at the home and said he has been doing this for 25 years and doesn’t understand how the fire stopped where it did and why the entire house didn’t go up. We think God stopped it where he wanted it to stop. It’s a miracle looking at the aftermath. The fire was hot enough to melt the metal shelving we had on the inner wall, but yet didn’t consume the entire wall or spread to boxes and other things easily flammable right next to it, which it should have and spread to the rest of the house. You can see in the picture where the fire stopped and didn’t spread any further. It’s wild to me you can see our basement walls and ceiling burnt and fell, the air ducts burnt, in the room to the right, the massive PVC pipe plumbing is drooped down melted, electrical wiring etc., but to the left, the boxes and other stuff never caught. It’s a good thing, too, because further in that room, we had some high-power rifle ammunition from a gun collection that could have gone off like a bomb sending out shrapnel. The room to the right is where they think it started, and it goes far back. There were clothes hanging in there. And some were brand new. Some were old. There were Jackets, suits, all sorts of things, just all destroyed. Thankfully everyone got out of the house safe, and no one was harmed. Everything else is replaceable. We are fortunate to have insurance which should really help us recover our home in time. We are going on over two weeks living in a hotel at the moment, things are awkward, but we are doing great, all things considered. Insurance expects us not to be in our home for 6 to 8 months. Currently, they are trying to look for a rental home for us to live in temporarily. Thanks to my streaming, I can rewatch the VOD and see the time stamp of when I mentioned I smelled something burning til my stream ended, which was on its own via my electrical wires melting. It was just 4 minutes. Just that quickly, everything happened. I’ve always thought to myself in my head, if there were a fire, I would do this, or I would do that, I would be fine. Well, let me tell you, the movies don’t do the real thing justice. We were overwhelmed in such a short amount of time. I Thank God for helping us get out, and I am so happy I was awake that night because had I been asleep, everyone likely would have died. You never know when a day might be your last. Be sure to stay on good terms with the people you care about. Let them know you love them. I've felt much love, care and support from many friends during this time of need. Some friends suggested I make a Go Fund Me for donations as they wanted to help, and that seems like a good idea to share my story and seek help from anyone willing and able to spare a little to help us recover. So far, donations could be helpful for food, medicine, lost electronics, clothing, furniture etc. As I mentioned, insurance should cover many things, but in the end, I am sure it won't cover everything lost, so any help is appreciated. Thanks for taking the time to read my story. I hope you have a blessed day!

Hi, my name is Jason Ring. I became a widowed father of Andrew (18), Abigail (17) and Aaron (12) in March of 2017, after my wife Jennifer's short battle with stage 4 breast cancer took her from us. Life has been a little tumultuous the last five years as my children have had to live without their mother, and has also seen us move from the west coast to the east coast here in South Carolina. My youngest and oldest are both autistic. Aaron is high functioning, while his older brother is low functioning and intellectually disabled. Our current situation begins and ends with him. When we first moved to South Carolina, Andrew was still a pretty amiable personality. Yes, he had his moments, but by and large, he was in good spirits most of the time (as seen the THEN image of the cover photo). Today is a much different story. Andrew is increasingly moody, with very high highs and extreme lows. Many times these all happen throughout the day. As an intellectually disabled, autistic person, Andrew is supposed to be in school until he's 21 in South Carolina. Because of Andrew's extreme leaning toward aggression, we held an IEP to place him in a new setting outside of his local high school in September (he only went to two days of school this year). I have yet to have him placed in a new school two months later. Andrew's aggressive behavior has led to my two other children and myself to suffer PTSD symptoms. Every moment is walking on eggshells as Andrew is here all day, every day. Andrew requires specialized supervision that costs more money than I can afford. Because of this, I am the "specialized supervision". This has led to great financial hardship for us as we only receive social security survivor benefits monthly. I've looked into working from home, but with an aging computer not meeting minimum requirements most companies ask for, and the constant interruptions by Andrew, it's out of the question. I even tried to run a business from home this past year, but business costs, along with low brand awareness and of course Andrew, made it very difficult to run. I had to close up shop and use what little money I had in my business checking account for groceries in September. I am also in the arduous process of getting Andrew on the South Carolina Medicaid Waiver Program. Once approved he'll be qualified for many services, one of which will hopefully see me hired as his caregiver. We are still months away from this, but it will be some income that we aren't seeing now. This is where the story gets more exciting! At the beginning of 2022, I received a letter from Social Security (SSA) stating that because Andrew was turning 18, he would lose his benefit. Since he was going to be an adult child with a disability, I did have options to continue receiving social security in one form or another. This process is taking some time to get through and it hasn't been without problems that we are still seeing eight months later. Since June, we have not received any payments for Andrew, making a tough time dire. In this process, SSA's computer system did something lovely. It created overpayments for my other two children and myself through retroactive payments that went back to June. This means it credited us with payments we didn't receive while making the payments we did receive at the time, too much. I know this sounds confusing (it really is), but even though we received less money during this time period, the retroactive payments saw those payments we received as too much money, and we have been penalized! All that retroactive money (over $4000) paid for most of the "overpayments". We still owe $1700 more. To put this perspective, we only receive $2600 a month between the four of us. This is what we have to live off of. But wait, there's more! We haven't received the $2600 yet. The last four months we have only received $2304 and this month (November) we have only received $1950! You may ask, how we've managed with so little money the last couple of years? A few things: 1. Stimulus checks 2. Tax refunds based off of 2019 income 3. Two low balance credit cards 4. Help from a friend 5. Other random surprises from God (kind of like finding the checking account yesterday with $21!) and a local person who paid for all our late utilities (electric, water, sewer). The stimulus checks and tax refunds that went off of my 2019 California income were allowed because of one of the stimulus bills at the end of 2020. They were allowed for the 2020 and 2021 tax seasons only. And as you know, the stimulus checks ended around March of 2021 or so. Having zero income this year is probably going to lead to no refund at all, which make sense. In the last several months I have borrowed money from a friend to get groceries. I use the term "borrowed" loosely in that I can't pay any of that money back anymore. Even if I were to pay back $100, I just "borrow" it again later, and I am borrowing more than $100 a month because food prices are outrageous due to high inflation in the food industry. Unfortunately for my friend, she has received some very distressing financial news and her ability to help me out has been compromised. This is one of the main reasons I have decided to do this Go Fund Me. I can't see her feel my stress while trying to deal with her own financial problem. Currently, I am overdrawn in my bank account and couldn't make a payment on my maxed out, low balance credit cards. My bank and SSA are to blame for this one! Thankfully I had another bank account that I forgot about that had $21 in it yesterday. Talk about excitement! Woohoo! I was able to pick up a few things while also "borrowing" another $100 from said friend. It was yesterday that I learned the full scope of her financial problems and began creating this page. So what's this mean? It's November 11, 2020. I'm almost $200 overdrawn in my primary checking. I have a little money (about $26) in my newly found "old" checking account after spending $80 for some groceries yesterday. This means we've got $26 for the rest of the month with very little food in the house already. We are also a month behind or more on our utilities and a few other payments. Thanksgiving? Christmas? In terms of $, canceled. I have only eaten no more than once a day since August. I frequently go 1-3 days without food, so I have enough for the kids to eat. I can handle it; they cannot. We don't have money to buy much needed clothes. We don't have money to even buy stuff like paper towels and cleaning supplies. I finally bought a bottle of dish soap the other day because washing dishes in hot water only is just too gross for me to handle anymore. I only put $5 in my gas tank at a time. The back tires on my care need to be replaced, but I can't. We don't eat out. We don't go anywhere and even if we had the money to go somewhere, I can't take Andrew. I get kicked in the head, and hit while driving a few minutes from the house. Andrew is out of control. On top of all this, Andrew is costing me money by destroying things with his aggressive behaviors. Without getting into the details about what he is destroying, just know it's going to be a lot of money before everything is said and done...even if replacing or repearing these things frugally. My other two children are just as stressed about that as I am because they know how money is tight. I hate seeing this. Why did I choose to raise $3000? This amount can help us with food over the course of SEVERAL months. It's hard pinpointing a target in these fundraisers, but I am trying to be optimistic as far as getting a job taking care of Andrew through the waiver service. We could still be six months away from that, but I am hoping much sooner! South Carolina Department of Disability is still trying to find legal documents that are sufficient to prove his disability. This has been a problem because our original school district in Cloverdale, California, destroyed his psychological evaluations without telling me. SCDD need only come to my house for a visit and they'd know right away! This process has been going on for four months and will most likely continue for another four to six months! Though the target is $3000, we will have to surpass that to get us through. God has brought us this far, and I know He will continue to carry us through this. There are people around the world that are in much more dire situations than us that make it through the day, so I know we can too. To say I am tired at this point is an understatement, but I am thankful for each of my children and what we do have. Though we don't enjoy the struggle, it helps us to count on Jesus as our primary Provider just as He has promised in his Word. If you feel led, we would greatly appreciate any financial help you can lend us at this time. You won't be just helping us, but my friend as well. We also would appreciate your prayers not only for our situation with Andrew (as well as our financial difficulties), but also for our friend. I know this was a lot to read, and I thank you for hearing a little about our story. Most Sincerely, Jason, Andrew, Abigail and Aaron

Sloane update 12/21/2022 Today marks 6 weeks that we have been in the PICU at Children's Mercy in Kansas City. Sloane is such a warrior girl, she has truly shown us what strength is. She is truly a bright burst of light and love to everyone that she meets. Even after all that she has been through. I am going to recap and give our newest update just to keep things streamlined, as I know that many people are following her journey. - On Nov 7 I took Sloane to the Dr's office to get checked out because she wasn't getting better from her cold, in fact seemed worse - Upon arrival to the office she had a very low oxygen reading and was sent to the ER. In the ER she was diagnosed with RSV and Parainfluenza and pneumonia. - At that time she was placed high flow oxygen and was then flown to Springfield PICU - Once in Springfield she continued to decline and was intubated and placed on a ventilator. Things were not progressing, so they decided it was best to ship her to Children's Mercy in KC. - Upon arrival to KC she was treated and remained intubated and had a variety of testing completed. Chest imaging and cardiac imaging showed that she had an AVM in her left lung - An AVM is a blood vessel malformation that causes low oxygen blood from veins to mix with high oxygen blood in from arteries, causing lowering of the blood oxygen. Several illnesses can cause these to form, so genetic testing was sent off to look for these illnesses. - She was successfully extubated on 11/11 - She was taken for a heart catheterization on Dec 1 and at that time was found to have much more diffuse (widespread) AVM than originally thought based off imaging. At that time 3 coils were placed in the AVMs in hopes that it would "block" them. They did not get the results they were expecting. - She was weaned off Nitric last week (a gas that was helping her lungs to "accept" oxygen better"), but started to have worsening oxygen levels so they restarted her Nitric, which she remains on now. - She is totally back to herself and is full of personality and spunk, from this standpoint it has been very hard as she's tied to her room with tubes. - The genetics panel came back and she is negative for HHT, a gentic disorder that causes AVMs. She does closely mimic an HHT patient so the HHT center in St Louis is going to closely follow her. For now this means there is no concern that the other kids have what she has. This was our biggest fear because if she was HHT positive then we would have to screen the other children and worry about them developing an AVM. - Negative HHT...then WHY does she have the problem them? We don't know and maybe never will. For some reason she grew the abnormal blood vessels in her lungs, meaning it is congenital and is just a part of how her body grew and developed. - In the interim, the team has reached out to Boston Children's who has reviewed her case as well as St. Louis Children's Hospital. The team in STL has asked that we establish with them, as they have all reviewed her case (pulmonary, cardiac, ICU, lung transplant team, HHT team). -They have decided that they would like to have her transfer to them now, to continue to work with her and to move forward with more testing. They will likely do another heart cath to do some further embolization if possible. They also want us to go ahead and establish with the lung transplant team so that we have all of our ducks in a row if we get to that place. - We feeling every single emotion that you can possibly imagine right now. We feel helpless. The only thing that we can do is stand strong together and guide Sloane and our other kids as we walk on this journey. It is something that we never thought we would have to go through, just like many other parents before us. - We are waiting on all of the insurance and social work stuff to be completed and then we will transfer to STL. I will keep everyone posted on our next steps moving forward. Thank you from the bottom of our heart to all of those who have and continue to love us and our kids through this unimaginable journey.

Su’Myrah Jones was born on November 9th, 2022. This beautiful baby’s entrance into this world wasn’t easy: she suffered a traumatic brain injury from a difficult birth. Su’Myrah is only days old, yet we know that the life ahead of her and her parents will be a test of perseverance and faith. Su’Myrah had severe brain damage. She has been diagnosed with HEI-Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy. Her brain was deprived of oxygen for an undetermined amount of time, causing the death and decay of brain cells. After her initial birth, she was transported to Cincinnati Children’s Hospital, where she underwent therapeutic hypothermic treatment to slow down the decay of her brain. On November 14th, Su’Myrah and her parents received her MRI results: a vast majority of her brain has severe damage, including her brain stem. Su’Myrah may never be able to walk. To talk. To sit on her own, or even swallow food. It’s difficult for doctors to give a solid prognosis for the rest of her life as right now, her life is being measured in minutes. Her mother, Makayla and her father Del are keeping their faith in God. They are praying for a miracle. For the past 3 years, the Lipowy family has been living through that dreaded scenario that many of us have thought about and counted our blessings that it is not happening to us. A young child is battling through multiple rounds of cancer, and a family living in hospitals fighting for the best chance for their boy. In January 2021, at age 5, young James was first diagnosed with bone cancer in his leg and underwent a long journey of chemo, hospital stays, and sickness. When James was 6 years old, he underwent surgery (rotationplasty) to amputate his leg, which allowed the removal of the cancerous section. Since James was young, this procedure would offer him the best chance to have the most mobility as he continued to grow. The surgery was a success and James now has a prosthetic below the knee. James could now pursue his love of hockey and participate in the normality of being a kid. This summer, the Lipowy family's worst nightmare hit for the 2nd time. At age 7, a screening revealed that cancer had returned and had now migrated to James’s one lung. There was concern with how quickly the cancer had spread and grown because it meant that all the rounds of chemo he went through didn’t work to kill the cancer cells in his body. A rushed, minimally invasive surgery was conducted to remove the cancerous cells with the hope to have caught it in time, as it was the only option. Only 8 weeks after the removal of the two spots on the lung, 4 new spots have appeared on the same lung and are spreading quickly. Further surgery will be much more invasive and riskier, with lung removal potentially the only option. Surgery is not the best path at this time as the cancer is close to James’s throat and heart. As cancer spreads to vital organs, James’s battle is becoming life-threatening. The Lipowys are now in need of significant support. Things had seemed manageable with each setback looking to have an endpoint in sight. With this latest news, there is a realization that more drastic and severe measures will need to be taken as this battle escalates. As the Lipowy family explores all options for treatment for James, they will need help with the ability to access funds and react quickly to opportunities as they arise. If they may need to pursue options in the United States or elsewhere, the costs will be astronomical and escalate quickly. As James' cancer continues to be aggressive, time is not a luxury they can afford. Hopefully, James’s treatment plan can be resolved in Canada, but whatever occurs, James will require various supports throughout his life. Jacquie, James’s mother, has been on leave from her teaching career in Calgary as her days are filled with supporting her son through the many surgeries, dealing with chemo treatments, and encouraging the healing process. Ryan, James’s father, has been working throughout this timeframe and has been juggling his attention and focus between the two lives he is forced to live. James also has a younger sister who has greatly supported him through this time. Please support this family facing this continued UNFAIR onslaught of this disease and give them every opportunity to find treatment for James. If you cannot provide support financially, sharing this post to spread the word would be appreciated. Update Nov 4th, 2022 James is two weeks into a month-long treatment cycle, which is an attempt to reduce the size of the cancer and allow for it to be operable. During the initial week of the treatment, James was feeling weak and ill; however, the second week had him rebounding thus being more active and in good spirits. Each day brings various challenges; however, with James feeling better, we are hopeful that the treatment is working. The Make-A-Wish Foundation has been working with the Lipowy family. With great determination and teamwork, they were able to grant James his Make-A-Wish wish on November 4th, just over a week and half of their request! As travel is not an option at this time, James had indicated that he would like to have a treehouse; a special place for him and his sister to hang out. The Make-A-Wish foundation was able to find a “He-Shed” that was promptly delivered to the Lipowy’s residence. They successfully granted James’s wish. It is truly a sight a site to see. Please see some pictures below. In their ongoing search for the best outcome, the Lipowy’s have been reaching out to experts from all over and getting second opinions from US medical experts. Information gained from these consultations has led to the notion that undergoing radiation and/or chemo treatment in conjunction with the current treatment could result in a better outcome. Adding these treatments would be hard on James, but, if it can lead to a better chance of success it will be worth it. The Lipowy family would like to express their gratitude and thankfulness. They are truly amazed and humbled as the support for James continues to grow. Words cannot express how much your generosity is appreciated. To date your support has allowed them to access additional consultations, in the hope that they can provide the best possible care for James. Thanks again, and we will update further as things progress. NOTE: When you donate, the note might indicate that you are donating to Mike Provost. Please know that this is not the case, all funds raised through this GoFundMe go directly to the Lipowy family. To clarify who the organizer is: I am Ryan Lipowy's long time (20 years or so) close friend. I have put this post together with the help of other friends of the Lipowy family who are familiar with the families struggle. The Lipowy family knows we have posted a GoFundMe on their behalf.

To our friends, family, and fellow Turkey admirers, Writing this has been one of the most challenging tasks I’ve ever had to do. Please bear with me. On Friday, November 4th, our sweet boy had what appeared to be a seizure around 3 am. A panicked phone call to the wonderful staff over at Veterinary Emergency Group culminated in telling me these things sometimes happen (especially in our senior pets)- for several different reasons and is not necessarily a reason to freak out -yet. So long as he resolved out of it, and was eating, drinking, and going potty normally, we could probably wait until Monday to be seen by our normal vet to avoid a trip to the hospital. Especially since to my knowledge, this was his first seizure and he is otherwise a pretty healthy dude. Just closely watch and monitor him and bring him in immediately if he has another episode. The next day, Saturday, seemed to be a pretty good day for our boy. Happily eating, drinking, going for walks...though he was sleeping more and maybe a little “dull.” I thought we were making progress and his body just needed extra rest. Come Sunday morning; Turkey had another full seizure. He lost function in his back end, falling over, and was unable to walk or stand. We rushed him to VEG. Once at VEG, he had another large seizure followed by two shorter episodes. His pupils were two different sizes and non-reactive. We pulled blood and tested for everything under the sun, which revealed nothing- pretty much perfect bloodwork. Which normally would be good news, but not in our case. Next, we did a full series of x-rays to check his organs and look for potential growths or tumors. Unfortunately, again, x-rays revealed nothing obvious beyond the fact that before I adopted Turkey, he was shot at some point in his puppyhood and his back was covered in buckshot. I’ve attached the x-rays here- each round little white dot is a piece of buckshot. Turkey is almost beyond stoic, and it is a miracle he has never shown signs of pain or discomfort living with this. I say it is unfortunate that bloodwork and x-rays reveal nothing because this is likely the worst-case scenario. I was hoping to see maybe his liver or kidney function were off, maybe he has diabetes...something easily treatable. After going over the x-rays with the radiologist, Dr. Sotiropulos warned that because we didn't see anything in the bloodwork and no obvious growths in his abdomen, she feared this means he has a brain tumor. The only way to know one hundred percent is to do a CT scan or MRI. Dr. Sotiropulos wanted to try a medication before we pursue a CT or MRI. Turkey was prescribed Keppra. Initially, he seemed to be responding and was able to come home. I was told Keppra may help him, it may not. It takes about 36 hours to become fully effective, so we have been playing the waiting game. If he did not improve on Keppra, Dr. Sotiropulos said it is time to consider his quality of life. The Keppra really knocks him out. One of the main side effects, beyond drowsiness, is trouble walking or standing. We have transformed the main level of our house basically into one giant floor bed. I've been sleeping next to him on an air mattress as going up the stairs to the bedroom is too much for our guy, and he needs to be closely monitored. He enjoys napping by the fireplace, being fed "hot dinner", and his new grippy socks. It appeared the Keppra was working, Turkey had no other episodes until yesterday. Turkey had another seizure but resolved fairly quickly, except it took some time for his pupils to even out. We have another big and tough appointment tomorrow (Thursday) to decide our next steps. Thank you for reading thus far. As you can imagine, working this week has been nearly impossible. I am struggling: mentally, emotionally, physically and now financially. Often I say, "I owe this dog my life" because I do. On the days when I thought I just couldn't, I did because of Turkey. He is the absolute light of my life. So now, I'm asking for your help. Our hospital bills are rapidly increasing. I need help. Making a decision without having full knowledge of what the CT/MRI can provide seems impossible. He needs the CT/MRI. If you are able to contribute to his fund, we will be forever incredibly thankful. Let's get our boy healthy again. I would do anything to hear him "woo-woo" one more time, to take him swimming and to get an ice cream after, another romp in the mountains, watch him roll around in the snow. This just can't be it for us. Please send us all of your positivity, juju, and healing vibes. -Callan and Turkey
