Hi, thanks for taking the time to read this. I'm Christine, I live with my big sister/best friend Veronica, and we are genuinely in danger of getting evicted. Veronica and I both lost our jobs earlier this year, and getting new ones has been an agonizingly slow process. Our meager savings were used up by health emergencies months ago, credit cards are a double-edged sword, and our small circle of friends and family have already given us all they can. But having a roof over our heads, food on our plates, and medicine in our bodies – none of them are optional, and none of them are free. We need help. I’ve spent my whole life desperately trying to not be a burden on others. We both have. We tried and tried to hold things together on our own, but we ended up with no choice but to ask our friends and family for monetary support anyway. And they’ve given us all they can – they’re far from rich themselves – but time is still passing and jobs still aren’t calling us back and bills are still demanding to be paid. So we’re on GoFundMe now, hoping strangers have something to spare. The advice blogs said to include photos and/or videos, but we’ve never been as camera-shy as we are now, and I’m too tired and anxious to edit a video together. Any recording I tried making right now would just end up with me crying, anyway, and no one needs to hear that. I’ve always been better with words than pictures, anyway. We lost our jobs because we kept getting sick. Unsurprisingly, losing our incomes and our health insurance hasn't made us any healthier. The vicious cycle of illness preventing work, no work meaning no money to see the doctor, no money to see the doctor meaning getting sicker and more often...we’ve been trapped on that wheel for a long time. Despite being vaccinated, boostered, and masking, we’ve both caught COVID-19 multiple times, and come out worse each time. We went from having health issues but doing okay to being barely functional in less than two years. We can’t do things that used to be easy, like go to the gym or to shower without being completely exhausted from the effort. We’re still struggling to adapt to the new reality Long Covid has left us with. Veronica used to have trouble keeping still. She’d always be jumping up to go and accomplish something. Cleaning the apartment was a relaxing household chore that she enjoyed. We used to go to the gym together several times a week. I used to have to scold her for moving furniture while I was at work. Now, she has enough energy to do one “big” thing for the day, and usually she’s still exhausted the next day. “Big” things include: taking a shower, folding and putting away the laundry, making tuna fish sandwiches or frozen chicken and rice for dinner, walking to visit our friend who lives just two buildings away in our complex. Without warning, there’ll be days where all of Veronica’s energy and strength is just gone. I’ll double-check that she’s taken her medication, that she’s eaten something, that she’s had water, and everything’s accounted for but she’s just...”a lump,” is what we usually call it – too drained and drowsy to move or even talk, with no choice but to sleep it off and hope it doesn’t take all day to feel alive again. It doesn’t get as extreme, but I’m not much better. Some days, even making instant ramen will be too exhausting to consider. I tend to handle the cooking, and our meals have become whatever fits in the narrow window of “quick & very easy to make, but also really inexpensive.” Very few things exist in that window. On my bad days, even the thought of stepping outside and being seen by another human being, of answering the phone and speaking to another human being, is terrifying beyond words and can reduce me to a sobbing wreck. We’ve been rescheduling and rescheduling and rescheduling seeing the dentist, because an uninsured dentist appointment – or even an insured dentist appointment – costs money, and we just do not have any. There was dental work I needed done, but it’ll have to wait. I’m hoping that my consistent dental hygiene is good enough to stave off any issues. Every week there is agonizing over groceries and worrying there might not be money for the less-than-a-dollar-each frozen vegetables. Breakfast for me is a small bag of frozen vegetables. For Veronica it’s two pieces of toast. Lunch is instant ramen with frozen peas. Dinner is whatever we have in the cupboards that we have the strength to prepare. We haven’t bought new clothes in over a year. Our already meager wardrobes have become increasingly threadbare t-shirts, increasingly worn-out jeans, battered flip flops, a single pair each of careworn close-toed shoes, nightgowns that have been washed so many times they’ve gone translucent in places ...I hope you get the picture. And as if things weren’t hard enough already, Veronica’s hard drive died recently. Technology to retrieve the data exists, but with a price tag we won’t be able to afford any time soon. Almost all of Veronica’s school documentation, the countless examples of the work she’s done, her older resumes...all effectively gone overnight. It’s been a huge setback in her search for work. And that’s not even getting into the things that can’t be replaced – her photos, her art, her letters...it was a huge blow to suddenly lose them. Resumes and job applications and interviews are all about showing off your skills and strengths and convincing hiring panels that you’re the best person for the job. It’s next to impossible to do that when your clothes are threadbare, your body needs an hours-long nap after a single household chore, and you feel like the least-competent human on the planet. We actually have the education and the skills to get ourselves set up for the long term as work-from-home specialists, but the long-term isn’t quick to get set up, and rent still needs paying in the meantime. Some people say they work best under pressure. I am not one of those people. Fear is a roadblock, not a motivator. If I’m not being crushed by the ever-present weight of unpaid bills and their terrifying consequences, if fear isn’t slamming a wall in front of my thoughts – hunting for jobs with my best foot forward would be possible again. I’ve found myself eyeing a stuffed dinosaur I’ve had since I was three, wondering if it’s worth anything as a collectible. I haven’t looked, because I’m scared to know the answer. Because if it can be sold, I’ll feel like I have to sell an irreplaceable part of my childhood in order to pay just one of the innumerable bills I’ll face in my life. Like if I don’t sacrifice everything but the clothes on my back I don’t deserve to be helped. Anything without sentimental value that’s worth selling is long gone at this point. I burst into tears almost every day because it feels like nothing is ever enough and never will be enough. Because I’m scared and don’t know what to do. The specter of failing to be a functional human being never goes away. We scrape by one bill and the next one is less than a week away. Any odd job we pick up, any handout we’re given – just one bill and it’s been used up, leaving us back where we started. We need breathing room. If we could just have a month or two where we knew the bills could be paid, where we could get an interview-worthy shirt or two, where we aren’t frantically applying for jobs and begging them to call back right away because there’s rent coming up soon and any kind of paycheck is better than none, where my waking hours aren’t a frenzied haze of desperation and self-loathing...to say it would help would be a major understatement. It would be the difference between having an apartment and not, between having unspeakably important medication and not, between eating and not... Even now, with November’s rent looming and my checking account sitting in the double digits, with groceries yet to be bought and clothes slowly growing transparent, even now, I worry I’m being melodramatic. I worry I’m being a bother, that I’m overstepping, that anyone who sees this will hate me for posting it. I worry that no one will care, that our situation will be tossed aside and assumed to simply be a case of buying too many lattes and crying about the consequences. I worry. I’m scared. But I know that the world isn’t full of cruel people – just looking at this site and how much people have given to help each other is already a mountain of proof. I know that people are good, that people care. I know there’s countless people who, like me, donate what they can when they can, even if it’s only a dollar or ten cents or some kind words. I know that every drop of water raises the sea, and the most successful fundraisers aren’t made by a single donation. So... Help me, GoFundMe-Kenobi. You're our only hope.

I met my nephew Corey in the Spring of 2017, after looking for my biological family. He was the first one I found in my journey to discover my blood relatives. Over time, we became very close. Corey enjoyed being a family man, spending time with Shannon and Kayden, when he wasn’t working full-time in the fulfillment department at Amazon. Then came June of 2022. He started having immense back pain which started as what the doctors claimed was a pulled muscle. But Corey didn’t think that was right. So week after week, he went back and he pressed for more tests. Eventually they did a few scans, as well as an MRI and found tumors in his back. They told him his diagnosis was Stage 4 Renal Clear Cell Carcinoma. The doctors operated, took out the tumors they could find. Then during his recovery period, he went in becuase more pain started and... *BAM*... they discovered tumors EVERYWHERE. The cancer had escalated and was extremely aggressive. This was not supposed to happen. Shannon and Corey were beyond worried now. They thought he was going to just need some time to recover and then everything would go back to the way it was. What happened to the life they planned together? What about their son? The clock was ticking now, very loudly and very quickly. They weren’t ready for this to be over. The doctors told him there was nothing they could do. By the end of September, Corey was completely paralyzed from the waist down and had undergone 5 surgeries in attempt to help with the pain while he started cancer treatment. Before the time they had together was completely up, they decided it was time to get married. Shannon shopped for a dress, picked out a shirt for Corey, arranged for a cake... all by herself. This was supposed to be preparing for the happiest day of their lives and she was alone. But this was for Corey, and it would be the last fond memory they would ever have together. So they gathered friends and family at the hospital. The staff generously helped them set up for the day and helped Corey get ready. Shannon arrived in her beautiful gown, and the overwhelmingly happy couple joined their souls forever by saying, "I do." 10 days after their happy day, Corey Snetselaar passed away. Leaving Shannon with a life that she has no idea what to do with or how to keep going through her grief. He was her life partner, and anyone that knew them knew that they were meant to be. The joy they found in each other was undeniable, and just like that, her joy was ripped away from her. Their son lost his dad at the young age of 8 years old. Shannon has their beautiful children, but no idea how to function without her mate. Thankfully, through insurance, she has a therapist to help her and Kayden wade through their grief. However, with the loss of Corey’s income, she is financially taxed and has nowhere to turn. Her job as a barista can only provide so much for them right now, with everything including rent steadily rising. We are asking for your donations, no matter how much, to help this grieving family and ease their burdens just a little bit right now. You have no idea how much they will appreciate your help and how much I, as a grieving aunt, appreciate you taking the time to read this and to consider helping.

... Here we are again. I (Michael) have complicated feelings about doing this again, but Katie, the children, and my therapists all suggest I do...so here we go. Long story shortened...Katie went to the emergency department on July 17th, 2020 for what we now know as “Long Covid” symptoms that had been escalating. Upon arriving, initial testing indicated she was in kidney and liver failure. The next hundred days were a blur of dialysis, repeated intubations and prolonged heavy sedation, pulmonary hemorrhages, and a tour of four different facilities. Nearly four months later, she left the hospital...unable to walk and dependent on care, and had refuge at her family home in Vincennes. The children went with her, as school was still remote. I (Michael) remained at our Indianapolis home and spilt my weeks between working full time and driving south to be with Katie and the boys. After another four months of care from visiting OT and PT and her wonderful parents, she came home and returned to work! At this point I changed my schedule to nights so that when the kids were out of school I would be home. Things went well for more than a year. We had many good times, and everything was falling into place again. Until mid July of this year, 2022. Katie began noticing a persistent abdominal cramp, and though her 2020 nightmare left her never wanting to be hospitalized again, her pain demanded attention. July 17th 2022...exactly two years to the day of her last life changing medical event; she was admitted to Community again. Two days later, her colon ruptured. An emergency resection was performed...which failed a few days later. Several more emergency surgeries were performed, and she eventually transferred to St. Vincent, and then to Seton Specialty Hospital, which is a long term acute care facility. We are still in the early stages of recovery from this episode, but Katie’s life is significantly more affected this time, as far as needs and level of care. Thankfully, the tracheotomy that was performed to avoid damage from long-term intubation has begun to be reversed, she no longer requires supplemental oxygen, and she can communicate verbally, which was not an option for around three months! Currently, she has a small “button” that she calls her PTT (Push To Talk) button on her neck. Eventually that will no longer be present. She will require more surgery to return her GI system back to “factory settings” once her colon has completely healed and she is a little farther along in her healing. Katies short-term disability ran out in late September, and are struggling with balancing our expenses against a 60% loss of family income. We had been planning to move before the hot real estate market conditions began last winter/spring...and I believe that perhaps it has cooled off enough to begin searching again. Katie is not currently walking, hopefully upcoming intensive PT will help with that, but we need a ground floor home to rent that will allow Katie to get around easily so that she can participate in activities of daily life. Also, Katie would very much like the property to be appropriate and welcoming to a dog...we would like to adopt one soon to help with Katie’s recovery from not only this illness, but previous one as well. Some damage isn’t visible, and the multiple extended periods of deep sedation definitely left some scars. I am working full time, any time I am not there I am with with Katie+Kids. We understand that money seems like it gets less and less every week, and we truly appreciate your willingness to share a bit with us. This entire situation has been a intensely stressful and challenging experience, and the realization that even by budgeting to the dollar it was not going to work added an entirely new dimension of depression and panic. We need financial assistance to move to a home more conducive and accommodating to Katie’s recovery, and to stay current with regular bills and utilities. We have made it the past couple of months with help from our closest family, but that is an incredible burden and is not sustainable. Katie is quickly nearing another crossroad, and we want to do whatever possible to keep her from becoming a long term nursing home resident. This is all to say...please don’t be offended or think ill of us for asking for help again. If you can help, thank you, and bless you. If you cannot, that is fine. Please reach out to any of us, we love and miss you all. Anyone coming through Indianapolis, please reach out and we can maybe rendezvous and let our kids play and socialize while we catch up. If I can begin to repay your generosity by assisting you in any way, please let me know! Thank you, we love and appreciate you.

She's been hospitalized and sick numerous times in the last 6 months. There's only one antibiotic, Macrobid, that this bacterial strain is not resistant against. Hello and thank you to anybody taking the time to read this! My name is Claire. I’m 34 years old and looking for just a little bit of help. I would like to share my story of how, just over a year ago, I had the scariest experience of my life. It was just a normal day. Except I woke up a little more tired and unrested than usual. As the day progressed, I started to really not feel well and eventually noticed that I had lost my taste and smell. With a pit in my stomach, I went to the doctors and confirmed that I had Covid. Due to the fact that I have preexisting autoimmune diseases, the doctors thought it best to put me on the steroid Prednisone to help my stuffy nose and also to assist my asthma as the Covid infection progresses. Even though this was a standard prescription given, no one could have predicted what would happen to me next. Quite exhausted, I came home and immediately settled myself in bed after taking the medication that the doctor prescribed. After all, maybe sleeping would make my body heal faster. However, upon waking up, I immediately knew something wasn’t right. My left hand felt quite weird. My fingers had curled in and I couldn’t straighten them. It was like my fingers weren’t even connected to my body. My muscles would just not listen to my brain and any movement that I got was extremely painful. Trying not to freak out, I said “well maybe I just slept on it wrong”. Trying to shake it out, I decided to head towards the bathroom. Maybe I just needed a hot shower. Feeling very disconnected from my body because of Covid, I sat on the edge of my bed for a second (it’s a high bed so my legs dangle), and then I pushed myself off to put my feet on the ground. Instead of my feet planting so I could stand, I immediately fell straight to the ground. Almost like my legs were swept right out from underneath me. I anxiously tried a couple of times, but no matter how hard I tried, I couldn’t put any pressure on my legs. Now completely panicking, I sit up and lean myself against my bed. I was able to reach my phone charger enough to pull my phone to the ground and make an emergency call to the doctor who tells me to get to the hospital asap as she’s worried that I could possibly have meningitis. After just a little bit of blood work, the hospital decided to immediately admit me. Day after day, the doctors poked and prodded. But couldn’t seem to figure out exactly what was happening to my body. Over the next 4 months, still admitted in the hospital, I would have multiple MRIs, CT Scans, and Spinal Taps, along with endless amounts of blood work. The only thing that was certain was that I couldn’t walk or use my hand and I had some sort of infection that was elevating my white blood cell count. After being seen by dozens of specialists from leading hospitals, the diagnosis was Acute Inflammatory Polyneuropathy and Upper Ambulatory Disfunction. With a common response to most of my questions being “we just don’t know a lot about Covid”. The doctors decided to do 5 rounds of the highest dose of IVIG. It was a Hail Mary move, but I kept my hopes high and desperately prayed that it would work. The IVIG ultimately led to a new unfavorable symptom of aseptimatic meningitis. Which is having all the extremely painful symptoms of meningitis without the infection. For me, it felt like my brain was physically swelling through my skull and at any moment, it would explode or pop like a balloon. It was and still is a pain far worse than any migraine I have ever experienced. However, I was not going to let that stop me! I did physical therapy 3x a day and eventually got stable enough to be moved to subacute care (nursing home). Being that I was the youngest patient they had and the fact that I had been in hospital for 3.5 months at that point, I worked my hardest to get home as soon as possible. I learned how to properly use a wheelchair, walk with a cane, sit and stand, go up and down stairs, and how to use my hand for simple tasks. Another 3 weeks later, I was so happy to go home. Unfortunately my apartment lease had ended while I was in the hospital. But I was lucky enough to have friends and family move my belongings while I watched remotely. This meant that I came home to an unfamiliar apartment full of boxes. Living alone, I was terrified of what was to come. But I was ready for the challenge. It might have even been the secret medicine I didn’t know I needed! Over the next few months, I learned how to walk with little to no assistance and all the unpacking was great therapy for my hands! And a year later, I have come 200% from where I started. Even though I still have some minor side effects, my daily life and functionality is around 97% I truly am so grateful and lucky! But life doesn’t stop just because you are in the hospital. Bills still need to be paid and there’s little compassion for late excuses. I chose to not dwell on the experience I had just had. I was grateful to be alive and had a new outlook on life, so I tried my hardest to get back to work as quickly as possible. Ultimately, I was out of work for around 5 months. I did qualify for a very small amount of short term disability, but unfortunately started to cause things to fall behind. And then I received the dreaded hospital bill of a whopping $125,000!!! I was able to dispute this a little and get it to $95k. Over the past year, I have worked so hard to just stay caught up with things. I am a crafter and artist. I have tried avoid asking for help by selling as many of my hand crocheted items and art as possible to make as much extra as I can. I crochet as fast as my little hands let me with each piece taking about a week. Unfortunately, it just hasn’t been enough. Sadly, I got Covid a second time a few months ago (luckily it was not as bad as the first time) that brought me back down and out of work for 3 weeks. Because of what happened the first time, I needed to be closely monitored and was given an experimental infusion to prevent severe Covid symptoms and prolonged hospitalization. Despite my absolute best efforts, this caused me to go from just barely making it to falling severely behind and now facing eviction. So here I am, asking for help to anybody who is willing to help me. I am really just asking for enough to get me ahead of the bills. I know there are a ton of causes, and with recent natural disasters many people who need aid more than myself. Any immediate money raised will go to saving my apartment (I am a month and a half behind on rent) and getting anything past due caught back up. Should I be fortunate enough to go above my goal, the rest will go to my $95,000 hospital bill. I have come so far and learned so much over the past year. I learned that we are capable of going through and handling so much more than we could ever imagine. I also learned just how strong physically and mentally we all are. I was lucky to have an amazing support system through this experience. To all my family and friends that have been there for me every step of the way, I love you and I thank you for being so patient with me. To anyone new, I thank you for taking the time to read my story. I tried not to make it too long. And even if you say a small prayer, I am so grateful and I truly appreciate all of you! Kind Regards, Claire Mann First time getting fresh air after being bed bound for over a month!! My custom hand cast to help straighten my fingers from myopathy My first steps!! A year later <3

Hello, I’m Jewel as u probably know. What u don’t probably know is, I have been battling active addiction since 1991! My mom began supplying me with opioids and other medications at a very young age (6-8 years old). I have been a “successful addict” for many many years!! My mom passed (O.D’d) in 2001 and my dad passed (Liver Failure) in 2014. I have no siblings, or extended family to speak of for support!! I managed to survive until 2021 when I became homeless and I basically went into residential treatment so I had somewhere to sleep! I thought, I was getting sober for the right reasons... my “friends” and their families, my dogs, maybe get my significant other back... everybody BUT me!!! So, I successfully completed 120 days in residential, and it was suggested I go into sober living, however... I had other plans!! The plans DID NOT involve using at that time... However, I did get a full time + job within 5 business days of completing treatment! I was staying in Red Bluff with a 25-30 minute commute to work 5 days a week. I was attending therapy 1x per week, and outpatient treatment (1.5 hours each day) 3x per week, plus NA meetings 1-2 hours each) as many as I could go to, and my MAT treatment appointments 2x per month. I just put too much on my plate... Not one thing MADE me relapse... it was a very slow process!!! First I missed 2 therapy meetings, so they took me off the schedule! Then it was hard to work from 6-6:30am til 5pm then have outpatient classes till 7:30pm. I stopped going to meetings because in my head, “I’m not as sick as these people!! Im a successful addict, I just need to get my shit together!!!” Well slowly but surely all of my recovery tools and coping skills just fell to the wayside!!! Then, I finally got my own place... and BAM, first night there... I call an old friend and get loaded!!! I had 9 months sober!!! It was all washed down the drain!! Because I didn’t stop with one mistake!! I made two, then three, then everyday my life became a process to get and stay loaded... AGAIN!!! Truth is, I had NEVER tried to get sober before!!! I never attempted a live of recovery... so I didn’t know what a “reservation” was... I didn’t know what a “relapse” consisted of!!! After 4 months of using, I went from having pretty much everything I needed... to everything I had, GONE!!! My own place - Gone!! My job - Gone!! My dignity - Gone!! What I kept for decades was completely washed away in 4 months!!! In July 2022, I was taken to the hospital by ambulance... I left the hospital without being released... I kept using... I went home and there was a message on my phone, the hospital wanted me to come back because I was sick and they wanted to admit me!! I used again!! The next morning, I took the few dollars I had left and went to Red Bluff where I knew someone who would help me! I told her the truth!! She already knew, but she helped me anyway!! She took me to St. Elizabeth’s Hospital and I was admitted! I stayed for almost 4 days until I was “healthy” enough to leave!! I couldn’t feel my legs anymore and I was so weak I had to sit down every 1-3 minutes!! When I got out of the hospital I had called Visions of the Cross... told them what was going on and asked for help!!! The amazing people that work there said call beacon and have them call me back!! I did just that!! Within 15 minutes, I was back on the phone with her again!! She said the following Wednesday they would have a bed for me!! To stay sober and bring 7 days worth of clothes!! During the next few days, my amazing friends stepped into action!! My friends mom came with her truck and helped me move all my furniture and belongings out of the place (that was going to evict me anyway!) and my other friend allowed me to stay at her home in Red Bluff until I went into treatment the next week!! When I got into treatment I was, Horrified!!! Embarrassed!!! Ashamed!!! Guilty!!! Any word u can think of for how just UTTERLY BROKEN, I truly was!!! A woman named Mary saw me on the couch and she said welcome back babe, and hugged me!!! At that moment, everything in my life changed!!! I was going to do every single thing different this time!!! I was going into this program with an open-mind and heart, with honesty about who I am and what I have done, and a willingness to be uncomfortable, try things that sound crazy, try things that I don’t want to, try things that are suggested, try things that I’ve never done before!!! Because I want what every single lady that works in that program has!!! And they got it by listening to suggestions from the women who walked before them!!! So I ran a different program than I did before!!! I did every single packet that was given to me, whether it was required to turn in or not!! I journaled!! I prayed!! I meditated!! I talked about what was in my head!!! I didn’t hold mine or anyones secrets!!! I wouldn’t sit on my phone at night talking to guys... I wasn’t looking for any attention from anyone, but attention from and for myself!!! I thought about what I was thinking about!! I was honest with myself about my disease!!! My mom died when I was 19, at any point after that I could have said to myself - I don’t want to live like this!!! This disease is what I did to myself!!! And I want to do something different!!! My dog of 16 years passed while I was in treatment!! All I wanted to do was lay in bed and cry!! But I KNEW that was the OLD me!!! The NEW me got out of bed, and went on a houseboat, and went to a recovery festival with the program!! I wasn’t happy when I was there... But I did something different!!! Another thing I’ve done that’s different... I’ve been honest on Facebook!!! I am an addict!!! Period!! I need support and people that want to help me!!! So, that’s kinda where y’all come in!!! I have completed 90 days at residential and graduated! I was able to get my first month of sober living rent paid by CleanCause.com. It’s an amazing program, and energy drink that supports recovery!!! I also was able to get, $100 from St. Vincent de Paul for my next months rent!! Rent is $500 each month! I made my goal $950 because I am about $45 overdrawn in my bank account and my rent for November 23rd is $400 and December 23rd will be $500. My plan for the near future is to complete the FASFA before the Winter/Spring semester at Shasta College, take an aptitude test to see what I would be good at doing, talk to a counselor and make a 2-3 year plan to get either an AA or a AS... I don’t want to start school with a full load, I want to make baby steps... and I will also get a part time job to fill up a little more time in my day!!! Nothing too stressful... Just something that I can do that hopefully makes me feel useful!!! So hopefully by January 23rd I will have grants from school, income from a part time job, and a plan to continue my journey in recovery!!! Soooo, there it is... The cat is out of the bag... I am an addict!! I am recovering more every day!!! But I will always be an addict, and that’s ok!! Just like people have diabetes or cancer... you do what you can to keep it in remission!!! That is what I do everyday!!! Currently, I am enrolled in intensive outpatient treatment which runs Monday - Friday from 1:30-4:45pm!! Plus I attend meetings (when I can get rides), and do homework assignments that my counselor assigns me!!! I also go to therapy each week, and continue to attend my MAT treatment appointment!!! I do know the holidays are coming up, and funds are tight EVERYWHERE!!! So if u can’t help financially... Please keep me in your prayers!!! If you CAN help financially... Even $1 puts me in the right direction!!! THESE DONATIONS WILL BE SPENT ON SOBER LOVING RENT AND OTHER NECESSITIES FOR LIVING (toilet paper, laundry soap, trash bags, etc). IF for some reason more than requested is donated, (which I doubt will happen) I will make sure it gets donated to the VOTC (Visions of the Cross) program!!! They are PHENOMENAL human beings who just want to help people fight the disease of addiction and help get people with dual diagnoses help with mental health help and the tools to fight addiction!!! Thank you so much for reading all this!! I know I write A LOT!! AND, THANK YOU IN ADVANCE, IF YOU CAN DONATE ANYTHING, OR IF YOU JUST KEEP ME IN YOUR PRAYERS!!! BOTH WILL HELP ME!!! GOD BLESS YOU AND YOUR FAMILIES!!!

My name is Mia, and I am looking to raise funds to help my parents with their sudden move. Full back story (scroll to the bottom for a summary): Back in 2008, my little sister was born. Just before the bank took the house, my parents were scrambling to find us a new place to live. They had zero credit, little money, and two children to take care of. One day, my dad was able to find a place. The landlady of the home talked to my dad, and she recognized our last name: Hollenback. She said that my dad's great-grandmother was the first female doctor in Brevard County and took good care of her. So, she made my dad a deal. She would rent us a 3 bed, 2 bath house just on the county border for $950/month. So, we moved in immediately, just before the bank placed a large lock on our old home's front door. Keep in mind, it's 2008, so price for rent was nothing like it is today (and wages have stayed the same). Fast forward a few years, our land lady passes away. We discovered that, in her will, she wished that the rent would not be raised on my parents. So, for 12 years, they've lived in that house for $950/month. My parents have been barely getting by this whole time, as both have working-class jobs and no college education. On top of that, we always have car troubles, so a lot of money goes into repairs for the cars and appliances in the home. Now, there is a new landlord, and she's decided that she is going to sell the house. They were told to be out by December 1st. Now that the housing market is completely wild in my hometown (Cocoa, FL), the average price to rent a 2 bed 1 bath apartment is at least $1600. I have a new full-time job, so I have taken some of the financial burdens off of my parents by getting my own car insurance policy and phone plan. I am also helping them find a new phone plan and ditch cable to save some money every month. However, I am slowly losing hope in finding them a comfy place to live that is also affordable. If I'm being honest, I feel desperate. I am so afraid of my family becoming houseless, and I don't want that for my parents, who have worked so hard their whole life... and I DEFINITELY don't want my little sister (she's 14) to go through that. So, I've laid it all out and I am so appreciative if you have taken the time to read my family's story. Please, if you can, share this with your network, with your friends, family, etc. Every single penny is appreciated and will go toward moving costs and rent for the first couple of months so my parents can get on their feet after landing in a new living situation. Thank you so so much for your time. TLDR; My family is being forced out of their rent-controlled housing because the new landlord is selling the house. They've been paying $950/month; now, even smaller apartments cost $1,600+/month. My parents are both employed full-time, and my sister is in high school. They are the hardest-working people I know and don't get paid nearly as much as they should. Because they have virtually no savings and this decision is sudden, we are finding it hard to find someplace within their budget, let alone have enough money to pay the deposit + first month's rent simultaneously. That's at least 3k, not including a moving truck rental and other costs associated with moving. On top of this, we are grieving the loss of my grandfather, who we lost this past weekend suddenly. I am doing my best to take the financial burden off of my parents, but I also have virtually no savings. If you can donate even $1, we would appreciate your help during this challenging time. All my best, Mia

Thank you, Julie-Family Friend MERY's Story The Umanzor Family, after William took ill Hi everyone, I thank you in advance for taking the time to come thru the page and read a little about my family and me. William and I met in High School in 1996; we were young when we decided to make a family together for better or worse. We were 19 when we had our first son. We were both done with school but working. Many years after, we had our 2nd, 3rd then 4th child. We are now a family of 6 total; we have three boys and one girl. They are so precious to us. We have always worked so hard to provide for our kids. William worked tough jobs like probably most hard-working fathers. There were times that he would leave at 4-5 am and come back home after 9 pm due to the demand of his job. Sometime before 2015, he was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes, something new for us. He was doing everything to control it. His job sometimes demanded more time, making him skip meals and not take his blood sugar levels on time, making it hard for him to balance his health. In early 2017, We were already in our house, probably less than a year. One day, all of a sudden, my husband started having these horrible cramps on the side of his ribs. We didn't know what it was. He just screamed so loud every time he was in pain. The next day he went back to work. I was taking care of our 3rd son, who was one year old at the time, and our daughter was about two months old. So, after a couple of days, I decided to take him to ER, and they told us that he was retaining liquids in the lungs. After many hours in the hospital and exams, blood withdrawal and many other things, they sat us down and told us that he had Renal Kidney failure due to his high blood pressure. He already had diabetes, which contributed more to his illness. Whoa! The news just crashed us, making it hard to take it in. Now, what are we going to do? He was treated for the pain, the doctors prescribed medications, and they would follow up on his health. He wasn't doing well, and bills just kept coming. He couldn't work, and every little bit of money we saved went towards medications and bills. A couple of months later, missionaries from the LDS church knocked on our door. We have never denied entrance to the word of God in our home; religion doesn't matter. Coming from a Catholic background, we had prayed for health to get us where we needed to be, but He had other plans. We remember inviting other missionaries and members from church for dinner, and they always brought the word into our home. After a couple of months of my husband’s job lowering his hours at work and myself working part-time at home, we decided we couldn't keep up with the house cost. We moved to an apartment because it was hard not having enough financial stability to keep up with bills. Around 2017, a day or so before Thanksgiving, I had to take him back to the ER because he had this horrible pain again, and once they called him in and checked everything, he was admitted. We thought, "Okay, it will probably be just 2 to 3 days once they stabilize him and get a plan together." But it wasn’t. He had to stay over for a couple of weeks because he wasn't doing well; his condition was delicate, and they wanted to start dialysis. Wait a minute?? What is dialysis? What is it?? That's the first thing that came to our mind. They needed to do a biopsy of his kidneys as well. Too much going on. By December, the doctors decided for him to get surgery. He needed to get a catheter in his chest to release the liquids in his lungs. It was so hard to understand what was going on for him; they did the surgery. After three days, he was released and back home, but it didn't end there. The catheter got infected and needed to be replaced. A second one was put on, but he got a worse infection because his body was rejecting it. Two weeks after he had it put on, he went back to get the third surgery for the third catheter, which he could finally hold onto for a couple of months without any problems. It was hard not only for him but for me to see him go through all of it. It was just heartbreaking. He couldn't play with or carry the kids like he used to. Having the catheter in his chest makes it hard to carry them properly. How much can a person endure?! On some days, I dropped off the kids at my uncle’s house, and my aunt would ask me how I was doing. I just held my tears in my eyes, and she would say it will be ok, don't lose faith, just let it out, because she was helping me by taking care of the kids sometimes, as well as my friend Julie did for many days. I would hide in the closet at my apartment where the kids and William couldn't see me and cried my eyes out because I couldn't bear all the pain and carry all the weight on my own. I couldn't see the light at the end of the tunnel. Our son’s 3rd birthday and our daughter’s 1st birthday were coming up, December 3rd and 5th, and William couldn’t celebrate with us. That broke our hearts. The missionaries and our friend Julie were there with us, making that day special for them. I also remember one of my aunts and my cousin’s daughter were able to come a little late, but they made it, and we enjoyed every little moment with them, even though my husband was in our minds and prayers. A couple of weeks after my husband came home, I remember the missionaries asking us, “Is there anything we can do for you?” My husband said a little jokingly, though nervous and embarrassed; however, it was a really serious question, "Can you help us with the rent?" She said, “We can't, but we will inform our bishopric.” We were so thankful. We worked hard to get the money we needed because we didn't want to bother anyone. We had always found a way to cover our bills. We had always been independent and had our pride. We had to be humble, leave our pride aside, and let others serve us. We have had these amazing missionaries, family members and church family that have been with us for many years, in thin and thick. We can’t be any more grateful for every single person that's been there for us. Many months after, the doctor gave the green light for my husband to get a draw on his arm, so three more surgeries on his left arm were done. He was able to have his draw, and after three months, they took out the catheter within his chest so they could start dialysis using his arm. There's a lot more pain there since big needles must be inserted into his arm to do dialysis properly. Dialysis is his life from now on. Since then, my husband William has been on dialysis three days a week for 4 to 5 hours every time, making it hard to keep a job. I’ve been trying to work from home as a self-employed insurance agent and multi-services facilitator. However, it’s not enough steady income to support our family. Because of Williams's dialysis, our lives took a turn in which we now live more in hospitals and the doctor’s office than in the apartment. Since all this happened, it has been hard to keep up with rent, electric and phone bills, car insurance, or even buy clothes for our kids. It’s hard when they need something and you cannot afford it. I think this is the most painful thing above everything. Not having money to provide your kid's needs or wants, or a meal they would like, because of money issues hurts. We lost our vehicles at some point during the process, but as my family and friends said, “God does not leave you alone.” A friend and her family gave us a car as a gift, which was a blessing while it lasted. We were so over the moon that she and her husband could do that for us; no words could express our gratitude. Our family and friends may not fully know and understand the difficulty of our situation. We've been blessed by many angels here on earth. Our church and other places have given us a hand for all these years and been there to help us along the way of this ordeal; however, there is only so much those we know and organizations we work with can do to help. This trial has not been easy, and we fear getting evicted because it is difficult to find steady work to keep up with our rent and bills. Not having a roof to live under is the hardest thing. We will be dealing with this for years to come. William will need a kidney transplant in time...but that's a worry for another day. Right now, we want to stay where we're at, together under the same roof. I ask if you find in your heart to help us, even if you can only offer a prayer on our behalf, Thank You and God bless. Bismillah AlRahman AlRaheem, This is a story of how I met Kim and hope to help her out of homelessness. She needs a little support for a few months while she waits for government assistance. If Kim can get support, she might be able to start again. She's a very kind person who takes care of other homeless in the area. She also dreams of opening a homeless shelter one day. I hope you can support her during this rough time. In shaa Allah. A little bit of kindness goes a long way! I met Kim in front of a shopping center. She looked tired, pushing herself in her wheelchair across the parking lot. I looked at her, and she smiled at me with a wonderful smile. Then she complimented me. I remember she said, “You look pretty.” “Thank you,” I replied. “You too!” It felt genuine. I asked her if she needed some help getting around. She thanked me, and I pushed her a few steps when she said I could go. I refused, in a polite way, trying to complete my mini mission. I wanted to help her get to her destination. She thanked me again, and I kept pushing her along. Finally, when we reached the end of the sidewalk, she told me I could go again. I refused again, thinking the stop was some store nearby. She paused and said she had a confession to make. Kim wasn’t trying to go to a store nearby. Kim was trying to hold up a sign. She wanted to go to the highway to hold up a small green sign. I had a feeling. I did. But I kept telling myself, praying inside, that Kim wasn’t homeless. I know we’ve seen it many times before. The highway sign holders. It takes a lot of cold blood to drive past people who are just like us but have been dealt different circumstances, yet we do it all the time. I guess the biggest issue that goes through our mind is “what can I possibly do to help?” Even if I did give them the extra cash I have in the cupholder in my car, what difference does that make? And so we see them, but we don’t. We really don’t. I stopped pushing the wheelchair. I didn’t know what to do, so I just placed my hand on her head and gave her a sort of hug. Kim cried. And I felt I had reached into the realm many, many exist in. A realm we’ve blinded ourselves to. I had never truly felt a homeless person cry. It became so real I could not ignore it. I moved in front of Kim, and I told her I was sorry. I was sorry and this situation should not have been the case for her. She told me that she had been homeless after moving out from a family member's place, where the living situation became very dangerous. Kim has lupus and a combination of other health issues that require her to use a wheelchair to move around. She also needs a lot of medical care and says she is eligible for 30 hours a week of home healthcare, which she has a very hard time receiving. Due to her disabilities, Kim can’t get a blue-collar job, and without a job, it's kind of hard to get out of homelessness. I asked Kim about any organizations she had tried reaching out to; did she apply for section 8 housing? Did she look for homeless shelters that could help her out? Kim replied that there is only so much organizations can do to help. She explained that they assist with basic necessities like food, water, and new clothes. This can be really helpful; however, the effect is limited. Not only that, Kim explained that homeless shelters are often filled to capacity and can also be extremely dangerous. An NPR interview titled Why Some Homeless Choose The Streets Over Shelters explained that lots of people feel more comfortable on the streets than in many shelters because of this. As for section 8 housing, she’s on the waitlist; however, the waitlist can take up to 18 months, according to Kim, and even two years, according to eligibility.com, a website that explains eligibility requirements for government programs. This is not ideal. Along with inflation, increasing rent, and Kim’s unemployment, it's a real struggle to just get by day to day. Currently, Kim is staying in a motel, raising money on the highway to keep this temporary shelter. What's more, Kim explained to me that she isn’t the sole profiter from the money she raises. She makes it a point to donate what she can afford to other homeless people she knows. Kim explained how frustrated she feels about the stereotypes of the homeless, ideas that often dehumanize and blame normal people for financial issues they could not have anticipated. This idea that has seeped into our worldview makes people feel invisible. She made me face what I already knew; Kim used a word our hyper-individualistic American culture often refuses to admit influences our lives, “Circumstance.” It could have been any of us. According to World Population Review, there are over half a million homeless people in the U.S., Texas being number 4 on the list of the most homeless in America. With these numbers, it's difficult to imagine how we can blame all those people for being at fault for their situation. What touched my heart the most is that Kim told me she dreams of opening her own homeless shelter one day, despite all the hurdles! A shelter that keeps families together. One that shows the care Kim sees is lacking. “I have a special love for the homeless,” she said. In shaa Allah. In shaa Allah, Kim will be able to start again. In shaa Allah, Kim will achieve that dream. I believe she can with the help of God. I know that it feels like helping Kim out will not make much of a difference, but that idea is wrong. It will make a difference for her. It could also be that if Kim can get out of homelessness, get the medical treatment she needs, and start her life again, your kindness will ripple. From the woman I saw waving to other homeless individuals on the street, calling them by name, and asking each how they were as I pushed her across the parking lot to the highway, I have little doubt she would not make the most use of your donation. In the end, I did not want to take Kim to the highway to hold up her sign, and I did not want to leave her to push herself there. As a sophomore in college, I do not have the money to change her life. I made Kim a promise. I promised her that I would make her a gofundme page and look into other places that could give her a leg up. I will do my little part to help Kim, and in turn, the homeless in shaa Allah. I want to ask if you might find it in your heart to do yours. Sincerely, Aisha

Where were you Sunday afternoon? Many of us are fortunate enough to be with family, resting, or enjoying Sunday football. Most New Orleanians on October 9th were watching Taysom Hill make 4 touch downs as the Saints beat the Seahawks. Survivor “X” was working. At 1:15pm, she was sweeping a client’s front porch when a man approached. Politely declining the conversation, she turned to go back inside. It is then the man went onto the porch and aggressively pushed her inside the house. “X” was brutally attacked in the hall, and the man attempted to rape her. “X” fought. She fought hard, being punched and bitten, but she was able to prevent the rape. Screaming and pleading for her life, the man grew more angry. He wrapped his hands around her neck, squeezing hard in attempt to take her last breath. He is still at large. “X” survived, but she is left with a badly beaten body, and even worse, severe mental and psychological trauma. Dark bruises remain on her chest and throat, and she has difficulty speaking and eating. Her food is thinned. Her hands are severely swollen and she can’t hold things. She has stitches, bruises and contusions all over her body. She is scared to leave her home, or open the door. She can not work. To feel safe, family and friends stay with her. She has good days and some really bad days. Her memories come and go, and she fights every minute of every day to stay in the now, and look to the future. Our names are Katherine Sauska and Sarah Hillery, and “X” is a great friend. We have independently known her nearly fifteen years each. She has helped us in our homes, with our children, and is there for us even when we don't know we need her. Her daughter is friends with our daughters. She, and her family, have become our family, and she is a woman we trust more than almost anyone. We want to help “X” as she has helped us and so many others. “X” is a woman of faith, family, friendship and service. She is honest, kind, and the epitome of integrity. She puts the needs of others in front her own, so much so she works every day to provide for her family and the community she serves. Even on Sundays. A mother of two daughters (one still living at home), a wife, and a grandmother, “X” needs our help. While we continue to search for this violent, dangerous man, in a time with little police resources and political chaos, “X” and her family are suffering. Unable to work, her bills will go unpaid. Unable to use her hands, she can’t cook meals or care for her home and family. Medical bills from this horrific event will not be small. She needs help getting her daughter to school. More than that, she and her family need therapy to get through this traumatic event. The time it will take to recover is unknown. While the physical wounds disappear, survivors of this kind of trauma will experience weeks, months and even years of mental anguish, especially without the economic means to get therapy and to take the time needed to heal. Knowing the man is still out there only makes it worse. This go fund me is for her. The funds will be used entirely to help “X” and her family get through this event. It will be used to help alleviate the financial stress of daily bills, meals, transportation, chores, medical bills and to provide therapy for she and her family. Rape survivors often struggle with guilt and shame preventing them to share their stories. “X” dealt with her own version of these feelings, but as we rally around her, she has agreed to share her story publicly. She has even agreed to use her name, but per advise from officers we have hidden her name. Being the beautiful soul she is, she wants to do so to help other women. She wants women to know they must be safe. She wants them to know that a busy street, or a nice neighborhood, or the time of day doesn’t make you safe. We must keep guard, always. If sharing her story can help others, and we in turn can help her, perhaps we all can make the world a little bit better. Please consider helping “X”, her family, and all the lives she touches. Every little bit helps. News Article

It’s true that heroes don’t always wear capes. However, many do wear a uniform. They serve and protect our communities without regard for their safety or well-being – always running towards the crisis. Ray Astorga, a proud, dedicated father, husband, brother, and son is a decorated deputy sheriff. He serves under a Colorado law enforcement agency. Ray has placed his life and safety on the line for his community, serving since 2015. Each day, those who choose to protect and serve walk out their front door, understanding they may not return home the same way they are left. Their families know this risk as well. Sunday, October 16th, was just another day at work—until it wasn’t. Ray suffered a debilitating spinal injury while on the job. As a result, Ray was immediately unable to feel or move his left leg, with these problems persisting to this day – almost 3 weeks post-incident. His right leg has limited use and is experiencing excruciating nerve pain. The worst part is that doctors cannot say if he will ever return to being the same or even close to the same. Uncertainty drapes over this life-altering circumstance for this young family. As the incident continued to play out, Ray’s fellow deputies selflessly protected him until he was able to be safely moved away from danger. As the situation stabilized, Ray was rushed to the emergency room. His brothers and sisters in blue stood by his side, 24 hours a day, throughout his entire hospital stay. His lower spin suffered severe trauma, and several discs were ruptured/fractured, crushing his spinal nerves. The medical team operated on his spine. The effects to date have made little difference. The nerves in his back, called cauda equina, were compressed so severely, and for such a prolonged period, the function of his entire spinal canal is forever compromised. The long-term prognosis may leave him with permanent weakness and/or paralysis in his left leg and reduced usage in his right leg with ongoing nerve trauma. Ray is only 32 years old. We hold out hope Ray will make further progress. Ray is a driven young man, a true fighter with fierce determination. Ray and his family are facing a long road ahead. Ray returned home to his family from the hospital and rehab center in early November after re-learning how to walk and care for his basic needs. He will have PT and OT at home potentially for months to come. Ray is currently unable to work. His wife balances work, caring for their son and caring for Ray at home. He will require a minimum of six months to one year or more of therapy, pain medications, and the use of aids (currently a wheelchair and walker). If no improvements in functionality occur, Ray may be a candidate for additional surgeries. Only a small number of patients are eligible. If the injury shows degeneration has affected more than one disc, or he continues to have significant leg pain, he will not be a candidate for additional surgery. His ability to return to work—doing the work he loves—is a long way off, if ever. Ray, his wife, Hannah, and their five-year-old son, Kacen, recently purchased their first home. When the accident happened, they hadn’t even finished unpacking boxes. They are now faced with mounting bills--all payable dependent on both Ray and Hannah’s full-time salaries as public service workers. Workers comp. or long-term disability will help replace a portion of his salary. However, this will not be enough to cover their monthly mortgage and expenses. Ray has given so much to the community and his family. As a deputy sheriff, he has gone above and beyond to voluntarily train and receive certification to serve on specialized teams—SORT (similar to what many people know as SWAT) and as a Wildland firefighter. Ray received the Meritorious Service Medal for being a first responder to a critical incident in downtown Denver during the Black Lives Matter protests in 2020. Ray was called into action again to assist his firefighting brethren on the front lines of the destructive December 2021 Marshal Fire in Boulder County. The call came out to serve for the Marshall fire moments after the Astorgas’ sat their son down to tell him their beloved fur-baby was dying of cancer – and yet, he ran to his service call to selflessly help others and their homes when his family was also experiencing pain and loss in their own home. Ray has a very long road ahead. He and his family need financial assistance to allow him the grace to heal properly without the stresses of not being able to cover their new mortgage. Ultimately, they understand they will lose the dream home they acquired just six weeks before this violent accident. Ray is not asking for help. He is not that person. However, his family is. We ask those who can to please help this amazing young man and his beautiful family. Ray was put on this earth to do good for others. He has proven this far and wide. Our goal is to raise funds to provide the Astorga family with a portion of their expenses for the next year. Expenses that will not be covered by long-term disability insurance coverage, unexpected expenses to retrofit their new home, and uncovered medical expenses. This is difficult to request—but the need is real and significant. Ray has given so much to so many people. Please help to pay it forward so Ray can focus on healing and returning to the job he loves so much- in some capacity for the great state of Colorado law enforcement team. Ray is a fantastic husband, father, son, and community member and truly deserves your support. We thank you for your support, The Family of Ray Astorga

Recently: They didn't hesitate when my sister Amber Gagne, and her adorable pets, needed a place to stay temporarily. Amber has a back injury, is currently unable to work, and is anxiously awaiting surgery to correct her back. The surgery will tentatively be this spring, and the recovery will be 6-8 weeks. Before her back injury removed her from the workforce, Amber did what she loves, working with animals. She adores all animals and dotes on her Dog, Aleia and her cats, Doodle and Layla. All have costly medical conditions, but Amber has always done what needs to be done to ensure they have all they need. They were making it work and enjoying a full house again. Tragedy Strikes: Time is a funny thing... it seems to pass along so quickly when you're busy with life's hassles. Then, suddenly, you get the news that your world has been turned upside down, and time stands still. On September 23rd my sister and I were kicking off our birthday weekend. Then we got a call that forever changed our lives. Bernie found Laurie unresponsive in bed. He reached out to touch her and found her body cold, and his efforts to resuscitate her were futile. My mom had gone to sleep and never woke up again. We didn't understand; she was fine, Amber and Mom had talked before she went to bed, and this had to be a mistake. But it wasn't a mistake, and it slowly started to hit us that she was really gone. I can still picture the palpable anguish as Amber dropped to the floor and wailed "Mama... no Mama... Mama", blaming herself for not being there, thinking that if she had been there, somehow, Mom would still be with us. But she wouldn't, and there isn't a thing we can do to bring her back. The only thing we can do now is to keep her memory alive. We can do our best to help each other when needed and show the people we care about how much we love and appreciate them. That's how Laurie lived; she gave all she had to help everyone around her. She loved deeply and taught us what it meant to be kind and honorable. Our hardship: Our focus is split between grieving and realizing the household income has been cut in half, but the bills are still due. To speak of how modestly Mom lived, she had no life insurance, and her bank account had $3 at the time of her passing, as well as balances at local stores, which she planned on paying at the beginning of October when she got her social security. There are monthly bills, balances on credits and the costs for cremation. We can't afford any memorial services at this time but hope to in the future. I was able to pay off the credits at the local stores and pay for the cremation and a month's worth of their expenses, but I can't offer any more financial support due to my personal financial obligations. We humbly ask for your support: Amber and Bernie need your help to get through the next six months, and then Amber will be back at work, and they'll get back on their feet. Laurie's half of the monthly expenses were around $700, and she was helping Amber with her pet's expenses. They need $1,200 monthly to scrape by, pay the mortgage, utilities and other living expenses. Any amount of help you can offer will be greatly appreciated. The last thing I want is for them not to be able to pay the bills or for Bernie to lose his house, which they have lived in for 25+ years. Unfortunately, VT doesn't have a common-law marriage, so Bernie isn't entitled to survivor's benefits that usually help cover the financial burden in these situations. Each day is filled with grieving, life's everyday stresses and now the financial burden of not having enough money and no way to earn more income in the foreseeable future. Once the basics are covered, we hope to celebrate my mother's life and give her the send-off she deserves. What your donation means: Any donation, no matter how large or small, will help ease the financial burden of their household bills and provide necessary food and medications for their pets. Your donation will help cover the following monthly expenses: $170 car payment $250 mortgage $225 utilities $35 car insurance $60 credit card $200 pet medications $200 pet food There are just over $1200 monthly expenses, and every other dollar is accounted for. We will be tremendously grateful for any help that you can give. Thank you, we appreciate your support during this time of hardship. If you prefer Venmo use @Alexia-Gagne-1

I had no choice but to return to the ER, where I received another scan, more antibiotics, and found out that I had to have emergency surgery to remove the infected cyst. I was informed that the cyst was in fact still bleeding, and that the pain was because my blood had essentially gone septic. This trip back here quite literally saved my life. I have worked for Starbucks, a company with a 90% local turnover rate, for five years. I am a full time student, and a full time supervisor, which means that I run the store, do inventory, and cash management. In Raleigh, North Carolina, the livable wage is currently considered to be $18.36 per hour. Most partners are not being paid enough to live. The wage discrepancies were a major motivation for me to organize my store, which was the first to file for a union election in this state. During the time of our campaign, I faced harassment from upper management and fear of retaliation. One of our partners on the organizing committee, Sharon Gilman, was fired in a retaliatory manner after a three compartment sink fell on her and the company claimed she did so intentionally to harm other partners. I also witnessed not one but three unlawful labor practices, testified in court against my company and won our case, which was historic as the NLRB had never granted a new election to a store under the premise of a ULP ever before in the US. I was considered the lead organizer to this day, had given interviews with multiple national publications, and been on the cover of a local publication, IndyWeek. I also was invited to give a speech with the Poor People’s Campaign, a movement which was founded by MLK. It was the very first speech I had ever given, and was given to a crowd of hundreds of people downton. Clips of my speech have gone viral, and one in particular is sitting at 1.4 million views. I’ve given several speeches since then, mainly for other labor organizing groups such as Raise Up and Fight for $15. I led a strike at my work place in September, where 90% of the partners working that day either called out or walked out with us in solidarity. To say that Starbucks is aware of me or my activities would be an understatement. Today, over a month later, I was fired for that strike. No other partners were targeted for exercising their right to strike. I am disappointed that after my years spent with Starbucks that they would choose to see me as a villain and not as someone who loved their job enough to speak up about what changes could make things better. I arrived at this store in August of 2021, and had never received a write-up or complaint from the company until I started organizing. No other stores had issues with my work ethic or reliability. One previous manager even referred to me as her “secret weapon”. I dedicated hours of my free time to installing murals on our community board that multiple corporate partners recognized as a benefit to customer connections and atmosphere at any store I worked at. I was nominated as Partner of the Quarter at every store I had been at previous to this location. I know that I am a good worker. In the hours before I was fired, I was making drinks during peak on drive bar while we were understaffed after two call-outs, and my manager had no shortage of compliments about my work ethic when I was making them money during the busiest part of our day on the busiest day of the week. They know I’m good at my job. I was their most senior partner at that location. That’s not their issue. Their issue is that I am well educated on my federal rights as a worker. I am afraid for other workers across their country who are not aware of their rights and power. I will not stop helping them organize and will continue to fight for the respect and dignity that workers deserve, regardless of the illegal consequences I faced today. This Gofundme is meant to be a safety net for me while the NLRB processes the charge against Starbucks related to my separation and while I look for another job. I will update with character statements from several partners I have worked with from different stores, including my most recent store. Alyssa White

We are Steve & Jill Rudolf, please take the time to read this . . . Talia, our 4 year old Granddaughter is gravely ill, and her family needs your help!!! Talia is a VERY strong, smart, funny, energetic, beautiful little girl. Her smile brings light and positive energy into every room she enters. She has fallen critically ill, and we need your help. On August 28th, Molly & David (her parents) noticed Talia beginning to feel ill. Nothing too crazy, but a little stuffy and warm. To be safe, they gave Talia an at home Covid test. The test did come back positive. This would be Talia’s 2nd round Covid positive. Unfortunately, this time battling extremely high fevers. Talia’s temps hit as high as 105.7! Under Dr. direction, was given Tylenol and Motrin every 3-4 hours alternating. On the evening of August 31st, it seemed Talia’s temp had finally broke. Though it was low (96.9), the doctors assured it was ok and to just monitor. On Thursday, September 1st everything changed. Talia was again feverish, and beyond out of it. Most of day, she was comatose and sleeping. Molly & David took her to the doctor. Upon examination, they determined it was most likely dehydration. They advised getting fluids into her however possible. If she did not urinate by 3 pm to call them back. She did not want to drink anything, and they tried everything, water, smoothies, Pedialyte, etc. Finally, around 2:30 pm they got her into a shower, with hopes that it would stimulate her to not only drink, but to urinate as well. Getting her ready to shower, she did have to pee. While showering, Molly & David noticed Talia doing weird things. They described as gripping/clinching her hands, “she seemed to be looking through us”. They could not tell if she could see them. Though out of it, they determined she knew them, her name and she was also determined in Talia fashion, to stand in the shower on her own. Once out of the shower, Talia almost instantly fell asleep again. At around 9:30 pm, they agreed this was not okay and called the doctor again. He agreed and felt it was time to take the trip to the emergency room for some IV fluids. At the hospital, got checked in and Talia was examined. The hospital doctors and nurses agreed that it seemed like classic dehydration. They told us that it would be okay, and this is something they know how to fix. They got the IV line in and began fluids. While giving Talia fluids, they saw their baby girl regaining some of her color, as well as smiles and movement. Once the IV was complete, for a moment, it was like their little girl was back again. She opened her eyes and blew both Mom & Dad a kiss. This is when everything changed. After blowing each a kiss, Talia had a full-blown seizure. The ED immediately started working on her. While treating her, Talia seized again. At this point, Talia was intubated and sedated. Her next stop was CT scan, and then admitted to the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit. Where she has been since. Talia was tested for every known disease and sickness that exists. All came back negative. It has been determined that she is suffering from F.I.R.E.S (Febrile Infection-Related Epilepsy Syndrome) which they believe is stemming from an unknown auto-immune disease. F.I.R.E.S is a 1 in 1,000,000 thing and there is very little known about how to treat or stop it. Due to the seizures, Talia had to be put on very high dosages of sedation drugs. Thus, placing her into a medically induced coma. Unfortunately, no medication comes without risks. One often in rare cases could cause colon issues. Talia had just that happen. It started with distension in the belly which got worse. After trying to treat it twice with no success, Talia had to undergo major surgery, and have over half of her colon removed. Talia now has a temporary ileostomy bag, which hopefully once she is better, can be reversed. However, it again is going to be major surgery. At the moment of writing this, Talia has been in the hospital, in the PICU, in medically induced coma for 57 days. She is still having seizures and they are still trying to fix it. Life for this wonderful young family is changing, beyond what anyone could imagine. Molly has been living in the hospital room at bedside since day 1, fighting and advocating for Talia with all her strength. This is no easy task as their 8-year old daughter is still at home trying to still live somewhat normally. Molly is doing her best to get out at least twice a week to spend time with her. However, now it has been almost 2 full months, Talia being more susceptible to infection, and Flu, we must ALL be even more careful and conscious of who we are around. If anyone is even a little sick, although we love you, we need to keep our distance. David has been traveling back and forth between the hospital and home. He started a new job 4 days before Talia went into the hospital. This was a job to be a long-term career where he could grow and support his family. Due to insurance reasons, David just had to resign from his job in order for Talia to keep her current insurance benefits, otherwise her health plan and coverages would change and plunge them into HUGE medical debts. Molly & David are very proud and private people, but we are now asking for your help. While Talia’s current medical care is covered, it may change as we progress and hopefully leave the hospital and go to rehab. Also, their monthly bills and expenses are starting to pile up, and they have not worked since Talia and her family began this traumatic journey. The future is unknown and is forever changed for this beautiful family. Talia is amazing, courageous, and still fighting. Molly & David are too. Please continue to pray for TALIA. Any help for her and her family would be greatly appreciated. God Bless you for taking the time to read her story.
